iOS 27 adds a native Custom EQ for compatible AirPods with an H2 chip or later. Go to AirPods settings > Audio and Routing > Equalizer > Custom, then adjust lows, mids, and highs to tune bass, vocals, and treble to your taste.
Apple has officially started rolling out iOS 27 for eligible devices, and it brings a lot of useful additions. If you are using any Apple audio product, iOS 27 gets a new native custom equalizer to fine-tune the music from your AirPods and other Apple audio products (requires Apple’s H2 chip; you can see full compatibility here).
In this guide, you will learn how to use the new custom EQ for your AirPods and other Apple devices.
Table of Contents
How to Use the New AirPods Custom EQ in iOS 27
The new native equalizer is only available in the latest iOS 27. If your iPhone is eligible for the latest iOS 27, you can go to General > Software Update and update to the latest iOS 27.
Custom EQ Supported Device List:
Custom EQ for Apple iOS 27 is only available for audio devices with an H2 chip or later. Here is the official compatibility list.
- AirPods Pro 2
- AirPods Pro 3
- AirPods 4
- AirPods Max 2
Now, if your device supports it, follow the steps below.
First, Update Your iPhone to the Latest iOS 27
Step 1: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 2: Scroll down.
Step 3: Tap on General.
Step 4: Tap on Software Update.
Step 5: Tap on Update Now (if the update is available).
Please ensure that your iPhone is on the iOS 27 eligible device list.
Next, Update Your AirPods Firmware
Step 1: Connect your AirPods to your iPhone.
Step 2: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 3: Tap on your AirPods (you will see this option if your AirPods are connected to your device) and next go to Step 5.
Step 4: If you don’t see it, open Bluetooth.
Tap on the “i” icon next to your AirPods.
Step 5: Now, scroll down and tap on AirPods Beta Updates.
Step 6: Enable the option that says AirPods Beta Updates.
Ensure your iPhone is connected to the internet and your AirPods are connected to your iPhone. Your AirPods will automatically update to the latest software.
How to Use the Custom Equalizer on iOS 27
Step 1: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 2: Scroll down and tap on your AirPods.
Or else, you can go to Bluetooth and tap on the “i” icon next to your AirPods.
Step 3: Scroll down and tap on Audio and Routing.
Step 4: From here, scroll down and tap on Equalizer.
Step 5: Select the Custom option.
Step 6: Now you can adjust lows, mids, and highs based on your preference. You can move the slider to the top and bottom. The line above refers to high, and the line below refers to low.
1. Lows: Increase or decrease bass.
2. Mids: Meant for vocals, where you can increase or decrease the vocal presence, especially if the music has singer vocals.
3. Highs: Treble, which AirPods are mainly known for. You can adjust treble sound using high settings.
Step 7: If you want to reset, tap on the Reset option.
Step 8: If you don’t want custom controls, you can tap on “Recommended,” and it will use Apple’s default recommended sound signature.
Currently, the iOS 27 custom equalizer is very basic. Even though Apple has the best ecosystem, Apple only decided to give you basic controls to customize the sound output from your audio devices.
I know most people are fine with the default settings on the AirPods, but sometimes even I prefer more control over the music.
Adding custom equalizer settings natively on your iPhone eliminates the need to download third-party apps, which sometimes have compatibility issues. However, Apple’s basic equalizer still leaves room for third-party options. Apple also offers you the option to reset the changes you have made.
This is a good start. Hopefully, in iOS 28, Apple will bring more features to this custom equalizer to fine-tune the sound signature of the AirPods. Using EQ does bring a noticeable sound difference. If you don’t see this option or are facing any issues, you can comment below, and I am happy to help you.
FAQs about iOS 27 AirPods Custom EQ
1. Does AirPods Custom EQ Work on iPad and Mac?
Yes, AirPods Custom EQ is also available on iPadOS 27 and macOS 27
2. Can You Save Multiple Custom EQ Presets for AirPods?
As I said before, current EQ settings are basic. As of now, you can only have one custom EQ profile
3. Does Custom EQ Work With Spatial Audio and Adaptive Audio?
Yes, it works with spatial audio and adaptive audio, but those settings are different from custom EQ. Currently, custom EQ only allows you to adjust lows, highs, and mids.
4. Does Custom EQ Affect Calls and Videos or Only Music?
Yes, AirPods Custom EQ applies to all media playing on your iPhone, including videos, music, TV shows, and much more.
5. Why Is the Custom EQ Option Missing on Supported AirPods?
If you don’t see the custom EQ option on your iPhone, make sure that you update to iOS 27. Custom EQ options are available for AirPods that have an H2 processor. At the time of writing this article, current supported models include AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Pro 3, AirPods 4, and AirPods Max 2.

Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m (£11.4m) fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice.
The launch of the fund comes as women’s rights are increasingly under attack and donor funding is in sharp decline, particularly for work led by FGM survivors in local communities. It is thought to be the largest single philanthropic contribution to ending the practice of FGM.
The United Nations has set a goal of elimination by by 2030, but progress is not on track as funding declines and legal protections are challenged.
Funding received by the largest initiative to end the practice – a joint programme operated in 18 countries by the UN’s sexual and reproductive health agency, UNFPA, and the UN humanitarian organisation for children, Unicef – fell by 45% last year, from $29.6m to $16.3m.
The Her Horizon Fund has been seeded with $14m from the Wallace Global Fund, plus an additional $1.5m contribution from an anonymous donor, making $15.5m in total.
The aim of Her Horizon Fund, set up by the US-based Wallace Global Fund, is to pool $100m from donors to reach a “tipping point” towards ending FGM within a generation.
Ifrah Ahmed, a Somali-Irish activist and survivor of FGM who set up the Ifrah Foundation to end practice in Somalia, where it is nearly universal, said: “By giving $14m, the global fund will ensure activists can continue their work in this area.”
UN funding worth $300,000 to her organisation was cut by UNFPA last year, but Ahmed managed to raise money from elsewhere. The Ifrah Foundation has helped push for anti-FGM legislation in Somalia, she said.
Three of Somalia’s seven federal member states have enacted anti-FGM laws, while in two other states bills banning the practice have been endorsed by cabinet and are awaiting parliamentary approval, albeit with opposition by religious leaders in some areas.
“If we don’t continue to raise money, the dream where this practice will end will have died for young girls,” she added.
Advocates warn that while international recognition of FGM as a human rights violation has grown, and countries such as Burkina Faso, the Gambia and Kenya have criminalised the practice, progress remains fragile.
In recent years, survivors and frontline groups have been trying to protect gains made over several decades.
The Gambia’s supreme court, for instance, is considering a constitutional challenge to the country’s 2015 ban on female genital mutilation and cutting. The case follows a 2024 parliamentary effort to repeal the ban, which lawmakers rejected after months of debate, amid strong resistance from women’s rights groups. In Sierra Leone, the new Child Rights Act does not prohibit FGM, despite sustained campaigning from rights groups.
Susan Gibbs, the Wallace Global Fund’s senior adviser on women’s rights and FGM, said: “Female genital mutilation is a global crisis, an extreme manifestation of gender-based violence and violence against children, and a public health emergency.
“There has been decades of progress, and UN data indicates declines in prevalence in a number of countries. But there have also been anti-rights pushback and political crises. Obviously, donor funding is in decline. So it’s a mixed picture.”
She added: “We’re at this critical inflection point. Most frontline organisations have been absolutely starved for resources, and so more direct funding would allow them to sustain and scale [up] their work.”
Gibbs, who attended a Justice for Girls global gathering in Kenya earlier this month, where the fund was officially launched, said the momentum at the meeting was “incredible”.
“Lasting change must be led by the frontline – it cannot be imposed from the outside. Frontline survivors, activists, they know their communities and they know what it will take. They must have the resources and power to lead.
“I’m convinced the impact [of the fund] will be catalytic,” she said. “There’s no doubt in my mind that with adequate funding, these frontline activists have what it takes to get this done.”
FGM is the partial or total removal of female genitalia for non-medical reasons. It has been endured by more than 144 million women and girls in Africa, 80 million in Asia and 6 million in the Middle East. The practice can cause immediate health complications such as severe pain, excessive bleeding and infection, as well as long-term consequences that include complications during childbirth, chronic pain and lasting psychological trauma.
A 2025 study estimated that FGM causes approximately 44,000 deaths each year in the 15 countries examined, making it one of the leading causes of death for women and girls in those countries.

Sweden heads into final stretch before key election
The results could see either the centre left take back power or the far-right enter government for the first time
Sweden’s party leaders campaigned on Friday in the final stretch of a close election race that could see either the centre left take back power or the far-right enter government for the first time.
Outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson was hoping for a renewed mandate to “make Sweden great again”, he told Agence France-Presse on the sidelines of a campaign rally, in a nod to US President Donald Trump’s catchphrase.
While Europe is dominated by right-wing governments, opinion polls in Sweden have for months shown the opposition left-wing bloc holding a strong lead ahead of Sunday’s general election, although this has narrowed considerably in the final days of the campaign.
“The most important thing is that the right-wing wins, to continue what they have started,” pensioner Kurt Flodin, 79, said of Kristersson’s outgoing government.
He said he wanted Kristersson to continue focusing on curbing the organised crime plaguing the country.
For their part, the centre-left Social Democrats – which governed for the better part of the 20th century and remain Sweden’s biggest party – have pledged to help struggling households pay bills and bolster the welfare state.
Jenny Larsson, a theatre worker who turns 54 on election day, said these issues mattered.

Tripura, Mizoram hold first meeting over inter-state border dispute: Tripura CM
Tripura and Mizoram held their first meeting over the long-running border dispute, with officials beginning preliminary talks to find an amicable solution.
Agartala: Tripura and Mizoram held their first meeting on Thursday to discuss their prolonged inter-state border dispute and explore an amicable solution, Tripura chief minister Manik Saha said on Friday.
The dispute centres on Phuldungsei, a village located in the hills along the inter-state border, as both states claim it as part of their territory.
“I was told that Mizoram officials came and the meeting was held (at the state guest house with officials of both the states) on Thursday. I don’t have the entire details about the talks held in the meeting. I shall say after getting it,” CM Saha said.
CM Saha said that he spoke to Mizoram chief minister Laldohuma about finding a solution after sitting together.
He added that the Mizoram chief minister agreed to it and expressed his willingness to visit the capital city to hold talks. Later, it was decided to hold the preliminary discussion among officials from both the states.
The Tripura government in 2020 had ordered a probe after the names of 130 residents of a border village were included in the voters’ list of Mizoram. Phuldungsei village, located in Kanchanpur sub-division of North district of Tripura, has been accepted as part of Tripura, though its eastern side falls in Mizoram.
Mizoram’s Mamit district magistrate Lalrozama stated that a Tripura-based organisation, SONGRONGMA, planned to construct a Shiv temple at Thaidawr Ylang in the district without seeking permission from the state government.
In October, the Mizoram government imposed prohibitory orders in and around the village in Mamit district. The order was withdrawn after the Tripura government termed the move “highly objectionable”.

Saima Wazed, the World Health Organization’s (WHO) South-East Asia Region head and daughter of ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, resigned on Wednesday (September 10, 2026) following fraud investigations by the U.N. agency and Bangladeshi authorities, according to sources.
The WHO placed Ms. Wazed, who took office in early 2024 for a five-year term, on unpaid administrative leave late last year. She was first sent on leave in July 2025, in a move that followed Bangladesh’s Anti-Corruption Commission filing cases for fraud, forgery, and misuse of power against.
The WHO accused Ms. Wazed of “committing financial fraud in relation to her travel to China” and of misrepresenting her academic credentials, according to a separate letter from her lawyers to the WHO on July 3, 2026. She has denied the allegations.
The WHO also alleged she had illegally acquired a plot of land in Bangladesh, according to her resignation letter to WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.
What Saima Wazed said in her reisgnation letter
Ms. Wazed said she acquired the land before she joined the WHO and was entitled to it under a Bangladeshi law that covered the families of the country’s independence leader, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, osuted PM Hasina’s father. “I was elected to the position of Regional Director in order to serve the countries in my region, which I had sincerely done,” Ms. Wazed said in her resignation letter to Mr. Tedros sent late on Wednesday (September 10, 2026).
“Since you continue to prevent me from effectively carrying out my duties, I have lost all trust and confidence in your leadership of WHO,” she wrote. “Moreover, after nearly one year without any remuneration following your decision to place me on unpaid leave, my financial situation has become untenable. In these circumstances, I am choosing to step aside.” She declined to comment further.
Saima Wazed | Rise of the daughter
The role of WHO regional head
In the role of South-East Asia regional director, Ms. Wazed was mandated to direct international health work in 11 countries, an area with a population of over two billion people. She is a licensed school psychologist, nationally certified in the U.S.
Ms. Wazed’s appointment as Regional Director had also been under the scanner, with charges of having used her mother’s influence during the campaign, and of providing false information on her academic record during in her candidature for the post, allegedly violating Section 468 of the Bangladesh Penal Code (forgery for the purpose of cheating), and Section 471 (forging a document).
Regional directors are among the world’s most influential health policy officials, with their duties including responses to outbreaks and emergencies and adapting WHO policies to local conditions. They are elected every five years by member states, which include Bangladesh and India in the South-East Asia region.
Two sources told Reuters earlier that the U.N. agency was planning to formally remove Wazed. One of them said the WHO would announce nominations for the role on October 12, vet applications in December and hold elections on January 24. The sources declined to be named given the sensitivity of the matter.

Ex-Canada PM Jean Chretien tells US: ‘never mistake our generosity for weakness’
His pointed message was issued in Gander, the Canadian town that sheltered thousands of stranded Americans after the September 11 attacks
Standing in the town that sheltered thousands of stranded Americans after the September 11 attacks, former Canadian prime minister Jean Chretien marked the 25th anniversary on Friday with a pointed message for the US: “Never mistake our generosity for weakness.”
The 92-year-old former leader, who was prime minister at the time of the attacks, drew a standing ovation after telling his “American friends” that Canadians may be tolerant and kind but “we bow to no one”. US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra rose afterwards and hugged him.
“I say that not in anger, but as one friend to another,” Chretien said. “Friends need to be honest with each other.”
The unusually blunt remarks came during a solemn ceremony honouring the nearly 3,000 people killed in New York, at the Pentagon and aboard Flight 93, and remembering Gander’s extraordinary response to the attacks.
Gander, Newfoundland, opened its arms to nearly 6,600 airline passengers diverted there when the US government shut down airspace during September 11.
The remarks came at a striking moment in Canada-US relations. The long-time allies are embroiled in a trade war under US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly talked about making Canada the 51st US state.

Bed at 6:45am - US Open semi-finalists fight effects of late-night finishes
- Published
New York is known as the city that never sleeps - and so it has been at this year's US Open.
A number of matches have started late and finished in the early hours, backing up the city's reputation as a playground for the nocturnal.
But when some players - including men's semi-finalists Ben Shelton and Alexander Zverev - are heading to bed as Manhattan commuters are waking up for work, it raises questions about fairness.
Three of top seed Zverev's five matches over the past fortnight have finished past 1am.
"I've been to bed as late as 6:45am in the past week so I'm kind of a bit jet-lagged," Zverev said.
"I feel like I'm playing the Australian Open in New York right now."
Friday's semi-final against Karen Khachanov - not before 15:00 local time/20:00 BST - will be the first time the German has played in the day at this year's US Open.
By contrast, unseeded Khachanov has not been on court beyond midnight. He also has slightly longer to prepare after his quarter-final against Alexander Blockx finished shortly before 19:00 local time on Wednesday.
American eighth seed Shelton did not complete his last-eight victory over Carlos Alcaraz until 3:34am on Wednesday.
Shelton faces 11th seed Frances Tiafoe, who wrapped up his quarter-final about 19:00 on Tuesday after beating US compatriot Alex Michelsen in a five-set epic.
"The advantage of the opponent who has played earlier in the day will be big - they've had that full evening's rest and a good night's sleep," Matt Little, who was Andy Murray's long-time strength and conditioning coach, told BBC Sport.
"We can all relate to it - if you have one really bad night's sleep, you have the knock-on effect of that for the coming days."
Little saw the effects first hand when Murray infamously finished a match at 4am at the 2023 Australian Open, with the former world number one managing only three hours sleep before returning to Melbourne Park about 11am the following day.
Zverev did not go to bed until gone 5am following his opening three victories at Flushing Meadows and stayed up to watch Shelton beat Alcaraz on his night off.
Shelton, who meets Tiafoe in Friday's night session (19:00 local time/00:00 BST, Sat), insisted he would pull up "all right" after two days off court.
"He'll have to be napping to catch up some sleep," said Little.
"On the nutritional side, he'll be making sure he gets as many carbs and as much protein as he can in for that next match, and trying to get back to a bit of a routine.
"It's about making sure you can optimise the hydration and get as much sleep as possible without completely going into a full slumber."
Murray described the situation in Melbourne - where he beat Thanasi Kokkinakis in the second-latest finish in Grand Slam history - as a "farce".
Few disagreed, and slight tweaks have been made in an attempt to limit matches finishing at the crack of dawn.
In response to Murray's match, the Australian Open cut the number of day-session matches on the main courts from three to two to reduce the risk of night sessions being delayed.
In early 2024, the ATP and WTA created new rules which prevented tour matches - played over three sets and not five like the Slams - starting after 23:00. These rules, however, do not apply at the majors.
Last week, former world number one Venus Williams and her opponent Sofia Kenin began their first-round match at 12:13am - the latest start in US Open history.
It was one of three matches which finished post-2am in the first seven nights, with three others ending after 1am, while Shelton's victory over Alcaraz was the latest finish in US Open history.
"Something has got to give," said 18-time Grand Slam singles champion Martina Navratilova. "This is not OK and it is not normal."
Some argue these occasions are the essence of the US Open - and a raucous sporting representation of the city which never sleeps.
The volume of early-morning matches has increased at Flushing Meadows this fortnight, although Tuesday's play finishing at 3:34am on Wednesday was the product of unusual circumstances.
All three preceding quarter-finals on Arthur Ashe Stadium - Aryna Sabalenka beating Linda Noskova and Jessica Pegula overcoming Emma Navarro, with Tiafoe's win sandwiched in the middle - went the full distance.
Data shows matches are becoming longer - so what is the solution?
Starting the US Open night sessions earlier is the most common proposal.
That is met by a resistance from television executives and the practicality of New York life, with many fans unlikely to arrive at Flushing Meadows much before 7pm.
There is a more extreme suggestion - cutting back on the best-of-five sets format at the Slams.
That idea gained further traction after Andrew Abdo - Tennis Australia's recently-appointed chief executive - suggested the Australian Open could look to reduce men's matches to three sets in the future.
Abdo's comments provoked a backlash, with Tiafoe among those defending the traditional way.
"Do I love five-setters? Absolutely not," Tiafoe said.
"But it's tennis, man. I grew up watching so many incredible five-setters.
"Novak-Rafa, Federer-Rafa, epic five-setters that go on for hours and hours. That's the history of the game."

Content warning: The following article has references to suicide. Please avoid reading if you feel distressed by the subject.
The semicolon, a punctuation mark often used while writing, signifies a pause -- one that is longer than a comma but shorter than a period. It signifies a break and not the end. And sometimes, such a pause might just be what a person needs -- to ensure that the end can stay away, if not forever, at least for the time being. This is what prompted Amy Bleuel to use the punctuation mark as the symbol for the movement that she founded to raise awareness on suicide prevention and mental health.
Today, the semicolon tattoo is one of the most recognised symbols of mental health awareness in the world. But how and when did it all begin?
Project Semicolon was founded in 2013 by Bleuel, a suicide prevention and mental health advocate, to honour her father, who died by suicide ten years ago. The intention was to create a space for people to talk about mental health openly and without any shame. According to the project’s website, the semicolon became a symbol for the movement as it “is used when an author could’ve ended a sentence but chose not to… the semicolon became a symbol for anyone who could’ve ended their own life but chose to keep going.” The movement caught the attention of people worldwide and so did the semicolon tattoo.
People began tattooing the semicolon on their bodies, either as a standalone or by adding it as an element within other hybrid tattoos. These tattoos were used by survivors to honour their personal mental health battles. People have also embraced the tattoo as tributes to their loved ones who had died by suicide, while others don their tattoos as an expression of solidarity to the movement and raise awareness about mental health and suicide prevention. “For many, it’s a daily reminder to keep fighting, to keep writing, to keep living,” reads a quote on their site.
The placement of the tattoo is a matter of choice and people sport them on various parts of their body including on visible locations such as the neck, wrists, etc., while others place it in more intimate areas. The tattoos are not just meant to express but also serve as a means of personal affirmation.
The project deals with spreading awareness not just on suicide prevention but also on various other aspects of mental health including depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), borderline personality disorder (BPD), and various other struggles. “What started as one woman’s act of hope has grown into a global movement — one inked semicolon at a time,” says the project’s website.
In 2017, Selena Gomez, Alisha Boe and Tommy Dorfman got the semicolon tattooed on their wrists to commemorate the premiere of their Netflix series 13 Reasons Why. The web series deals with themes of suicide and mental health and it was reported that the stars got the tattoo as a tribute to the show’s handling of the theme as well as the death of Bleuel, a victim of trauma, child abuse and rape.
Various regional organisations, projects, campaigns, etc., inspired by the semicolon project have come up in various parts of the world. India has also not shied away from embracing the movement. Semicolon (;) The Mental Health Awareness Project – India is one such initiative.
Founded by the Medical Students Association of India (MSAI) under the International Federation of Medical Students’ Associations (IFMSA), it was designed as a campaign model that could be leveraged by other local chapters. The project aims to create awareness regarding mental health and tackle the stigma associated with the same, among high school students from classes eighth to 10th.
If you are in distress, please reach out to national helpline 104 or any of these 24x7 helplines.

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.
Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.
The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.
Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.
Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.
Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.
The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.
Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.
The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.
The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.
Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.
“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”
Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.
Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

The government may soon notify a framework for levying a merchant discount rate (MDR) on select Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions, with the fee potentially set at around 40 basis points (bps), or 0.4% of the transaction value. According to an Economic Times report, issuing banks could receive 40% of the MDR, while the remaining fee could be divided equally between third-party application providers (TPAPs), such as PhonePe and Paytm, and acquiring banks, with each receiving 30%. At an MDR of 40 bps, this would translate into around 16 bps for the issuing bank and 12 bps each for the TPAP and acquiring bank. The framework is yet to be formally notified, and the final MDR, transaction threshold, and merchant eligibility criteria could change. The notification detailing the proposed fee is expected in the coming weeks, the report said, citing sources. The NPCI is reportedly working on the modalities of the framework. Inc42 has reached out to NPCI for a comment on the proposed MDR framework. The story will be updated upon receiving a response. The development comes weeks after Parliament cleared amendments to the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, paving the way for the Centre to notify which electronic payment modes would continue to remain exempt from MDR. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman had maintained that the amendment itself does not impose an MDR and that no final MDR framework has yet been decided. Notably, the reported 40 bps MDR is significantly higher than the 0.05%-0.07% rate that had emerged in earlier discussions around a targeted UPI fee. Last month, it was reported that the government was considering an MDR of 5-7 bps on UPI transactions above ₹2,000 for businesses with annual turnover of around ₹1 Cr-₹1.5 Cr or more, and there may be differential fees for businesses across sectors. The proposal was also expected to include different fee structures for businesses across sectors. The government has indicated that any MDR introduced on UPI would be nominal and restricted to a limited set of merchant transactions above a specified threshold. The finance ministry has also clarified that consumers would not be charged for making UPI payments and that person-to-person transactions would remain free. Why UPI MDR Is Back On The Table The debate over MDR has resurfaced as UPI has grown into India’s dominant digital payments system, while banks and payment companies continue to depend heavily on government incentives to cover the cost of processing transactions. UPI transactions reached 24.51 Bn worth ₹29.82 lakh crore in August, marking a 20% annual growth. The zero-MDR regime was introduced in 2020 to accelerate the adoption of digital payments. Instead of allowing banks and payment companies to charge merchants, the government introduced an incentive scheme to compensate ecosystem participants for processing low-value UPI and RuPay transactions. However, a parliamentary finance committee said that the incentive mechanism does not adequately cover the costs incurred by banks and payment companies in maintaining the payments infrastructure. The government’s incentive outlay for UPI and RuPay transactions peaked at ₹3,631 Cr in FY24. The initial budgetary allocation subsequently fell sharply, with ₹437 Cr earmarked for FY26 before the government revised the allocation upwards. This has widened the gap between UPI’s transaction growth and its monetisation. While the payments system accounts for a significant share of payment aggregator volumes, much of this activity generates little or no direct transaction revenue for the companies processing it.

Japan has asked for the revision of a new world map adopted by the UN because it said it made the disputed Kuril islands appear to belong to Russia.
The UN general assembly voted on Friday to adopt the new map, which makes the African continent larger while also shrinking North America and Europe, drawing condemnation from the US.
Japan was among the 164 UN members that supported the resolution, but has now taken issue with it because it shows the Kurils, known in Japan as the Northern Territories, in the same colour as Russia.
Japanese government spokesperson Minoru Kihara on Thursday said the new map – known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection – “contained a depiction contradicting the Japanese government’s position”.
“We lodged a protest with the map site’s operator through our diplomatic channel to demand the correction of this depiction,” Kihara told reporters.
He declined to say when the issue was brought to government’s attention but said Japan “needs to prevent misconceptions of our territories and geographical names from spreading”.
The disputed islands were seized in 1945 by the former Soviet Union, which then expelled the Japanese population.
Relations between Japan and Russia soured significantly last month, when Russian president, Vladimir Putin, made a surprise visit to the disputed islands for the first time.
Japan swiftly summoned Moscow’s ambassador, with the prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, saying Putin’s visit “offends the sentiments of the Japanese people”, adding that it was “absolutely unacceptable”.
She said the islands were “an inherent part of Japan’s territory, both historically and under international law”.
Moscow quickly hit back, saying it “categorically” rejects such statements, “which we consider politically inappropriate, insulting and, of course, legally unfounded”.
The UN said the new map aimed to present “a more accurate representation” of continental landmasses than was portrayed by more traditional Mercator projections.

The Comptroller and Auditor General has flagged discrepancies in data used to report Gujarat’s 100% functional household tap connection coverage under the Jal Jeevan Mission, saying it could not vouch for the reliability of the data.
According to the e-Jalshakti portal and the State Annual Action Plan, Gujarat had declared 100% functional household tap connection coverage, covering 91.18 lakh rural households, by October 2022. However, the District Annual Action Plans of 27 districts showed 14.84 lakh households were waiting for functional household tap connections as on April 1, 2024.
“Due to this contradiction, Audit could not vouch for the reliability of the data,” CAG said in its report tabled in the Gujarat assembly on Friday.
“The absence of basic records, discrepancies between State Annual Plans and District Annual Plans, and mismatched figures between State Annual Action Plan and District Annual Action Plans collectively reveal issues in data reliability,” it said.
In its response, the state government said districts could only upload incremental progress on the Jal Jeevan Mission dashboard and could not modify opening or closing balances. It said the mismatch was technical and procedural and maintained that the goal of providing safe and adequate drinking water through tap connections to all rural households had been achieved.
Gujarat had 91.18 lakh rural households when the Centre launched JJM on August 15, 2019, with the goal of providing a functional household tap connection (FHTC) to every rural home by 2024, on a 50:50 cost-sharing basis between the Centre and the state.
At the mission’s launch in 2019, 65.16 lakh households or 71.46% of the total already had tap connections through earlier schemes.
The audit also found that all 18,024 villages in Gujarat had been reported as Har Ghar Jal compliant, but only 16,920 villages, or 93.87%, had achieved certification as on August 2025.
Also, the report said that reported water connections did not always translate into the prescribed water supply. In four of the six test-checked districts, 71,842, nearly 15% of the surveyed households, remained without functional household tap connections as of November 2024.
Its analysis of 493 bulk water meters installed on a pilot basis at village storage tanks in four districts found that 193 meters recorded an average daily supply below 55 litres per capita over 24 months, while 296 meters recorded zero supply for at least one full month.
The audit also found delays in major projects.
Of 11 bulk pipeline projects undertaken by Gujarat Water Infrastructure Limited, five were completed with delays of 8 to 25 months and six remained in progress. Of 111 Gujarat Water Supply and Sewerage Board works examined in six districts, only 41, or 36.94%, had been completed by December 2024.
The report also cited gaps in water quality monitoring.
Only 46 of Gujarat’s 249 talukas had a taluka-level laboratory. Also, it said 26% samples tested before the monsoon and 24% of post-monsoon samples lifted between 2019 and 2024 were found to be unfit.
Against total funds of ₹19,471.61 crore, the state utilised ₹19,128.18 crore (98.23%) during 2019-24.

Two days after being placed on a paid leave of absence, Matt Mullenweg says he has been reinstated as CEO of Automattic, according to a Slack message seen by TechCrunch.

Since the days immediately following the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, U.S. President Donald Trump, a native of New York City, has made numerous claims about what he saw that day and his involvement in the recovery efforts.
One such claim Trump has repeatedly made is his assertion that he was at Ground Zero within days of 9/11 and that he sent workers to the recovery effort at the site of the World Trade Center.
In September 2026, multiple X users debated the veracity of the claim. For example, one user (archived) wrote, "There's no proof Trump sent a large group of construction workers to Ground Zero."
Other popular (archived) posts (archived) said there was no evidence Trump, himself, went to Ground Zero and helped with recovery efforts.
Another X post (archived) alternatively claimed, "President Trump is dropping VIDEO PROOF for every Fake News outlet lying to millions that he was nowhere near Ground Zero after 9/11."
(X)
Many Snopes readers searched the site to find out if Trump's claims were true.
A couple of days after the Sept. 11 attacks, Trump told multiple news media outlets that he sent at least 100 workers to Ground Zero to help pull people and bodies out of the rubble, with 125 to 150 more on the way. However, Snopes has never been able to identify any public evidence that crews he hired helped in the immediate recovery of the 9/11 attacks. Since we cannot independently confirm with certainty whether Trump had crews on site somewhere, we are leaving this claim unrated.
Footage of interviews Trump conducted in the immediate days after 9/11 placed him within blocks of Ground Zero. Trump said in those interviews that he visited Ground Zero to encourage the workers he said he brought to assist with clearing rubble at the site. It was not possible to find evidence showing Trump helped clear the pile of debris at Ground Zero, as some posts disputed.
In a phone call with a local news media station immediately after the planes crashed into the Twin Towers, Trump said he watched the towers fall from the window of one of his buildings.
Trump's September 2026 remarks
On Sept. 8, 2026, in a post on Truth Social (archived), Trump continued to maintain that he was at Ground Zero with construction workers after 9/11, clarifying that it was "obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter":
The Failing New York Magazine wrote a story that I wasn't down at the World Trade Center after the Tragedy of September 11th, because nobody saw me there. Well, I don't think I would be the first thing on anyone's mind but, I was there, obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter, with a large group of Construction Workers.
He then added he "was there as soon as the Law allowed."
The president was referencing a New York Magazine article disputing his comments about where he was on the day of, and the days following, the attacks.
Trump also made this claim (archived) in a Fox News interview two days prior, in which he added the additional context that he was constructing a new building in New York City. This is the reason, according to Trump at a 9/11 anniversary event on Sept. 8, why he had workers who he could bring to the rubble of the World Trade Center:
I was building a big building in New York and I took the whole crew down there right after this happened and they had no hesitation. Everybody went down with me. We went down as a big group of people. It wasn't too much we could do, I'll be honest.
What Trump told the media in 2001
Trump spoke to the media multiple times a few days after 9/11. On Sept. 13, he told a German news channel, that he had more than 100 men down at the site of the World Trade Center and more than 125 on their way. According to the German-speaking reporter, the interview was conducted a few blocks from Ground Zero.
That same day, NBC News interviewed Trump at what appeared to be the same location as his interview with the German news channel. Trump said he had "hundreds of men inside working right now" and was bringing down another 125.
PBS has a recording of another Trump interview from Sept. 13, in which Trump said he had 100 workers helping to dig people and bodies out of the rubble at the World Trade Center, with another 100 to 150 workers "coming." He told PBS that those workers were "digging out" at the site.
In another interview from that day, Trump told reporters his workers had been at Ground Zero "for about a day and a half." He said they were men from his company and that a couple had gotten hurt while working at the site. He also said he was just down at Ground Zero and was there to support them.
The evidence
When Snopes first researched this claim in 2018, we spoke to Richard Alles, a retired deputy chief with the New York City Fire Department, who later served as director of 9/11 community affairs for the law firm Barasch McGarry Salzman and Penson. Alles said that in all his time he spent at Ground Zero as a New York City Fire Department battalion chief, starting 20 minutes after the buildings collapsed, he never saw a large group of workers whom Trump had hired at the site assisting with search and rescue efforts. "This is the first I'm hearing of it," Alles said via phone call. "There would have been no need for that. Between police, fire and the construction crews, we had it all covered."
Alles added that the construction crews he saw at Ground Zero helping rescue workers were from the trade unions and were not hired by Trump.
John Feal, founder of the 9/11 first responder health advocacy nonprofit the FealGood Foundation, told Snopes at the time that he responded to Ground Zero on Sept. 12, 2001, as a construction demolitions expert and that he didn't see evidence of hundreds of workers hired by Trump at the site.
The Trump Organization was building in New York City in 2001, according to the Skyscraper Center database on skyscrapers. In fact, it finished a series of residential buildings in the city at Trump Place between 1998 and 2004. He was also building the Trump World Tower residential building near the United Nations Headquarters that year.
However, it was not possible to find verifiable information about how many people, either directly employed by Trump or contracted to work on one of the Trump Organization's projects, were working on these buildings and in New York City at the time.
A New York Times fact-check from July 2019 referenced Timothy O'Brien, the author of "TrumpNation: The Art of Being the Donald," who reportedly said the Trump Organization numbered "a little bit over a dozen people" at the time of the attacks, making it impossible to send as many workers to the relief effort as Trump claimed.
Neither the White House nor the Trump Organization responded to Snopes' requests for corroborating evidence in 2018. This lack of response is consistent with past attempts by Politifact, The Washington Post, The New York Times and Politifact again to reach out to the White House and/or the Trump Organization to corroborate evidence of Trump's claims.

The Allahabad High Court on Friday stayed the recovery of ₹6.41 crore damages from the committee of a mosque demolished at the Saharanpur Collectorate complex, last week. The court has also sought responses from the Uttar Pradesh government and local administration over the demolition exercise.
Justice Rohit Ranjan Agarwal passed the stay order while hearing a petition filed by Mohammad Tanveer Ahmad who had challenged the eviction proceedings initiated against him under Section 5 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971.
According to the petitioner, he had objected to eviction proceedings and had filed a written statement to the authorities concerned that the mosque exists on the land in dispute and he is in possession of it for more than hundred years.
He claimed that despite this, the Saharanpur City Magistrate ordered his eviction on July 16, 2026, and imposed damages of ₹6.41 crore.
A subsequent appeal before the District Judge, Saharanpur, was dismissed on September 2, 2026.
The petitioner further submitted in the court that authorities moved quickly to demolish the mosque, tearing it down within three days of the eviction order. He also argued that the land’s original owners, who he identified as Yaqub Khan and Wahid Khan, had dedicated it as waqf property for use by worshippers.
Additional Advocate General Manish Goyal, who appeared on behalf of State, countered the petitioner’s claim stating that official records list the disputed property as belonging to the Collectorate. Terming it as “inconsistencies” in the petitioner’s case, he noted that while the written statement named Yaqub Khan and Wahid Khan as the original landlords, it did not specify when the land was supposedly dedicated as waqf, nor was any waqf deed produced as evidence.
State further submitted that the named landlords themselves had never approached the courts to stake a claim to the property.
State also said that a post office operates over the land in dispute and eviction proceeding was initiated because the mosque was constructed after taking rooms on rent.
Stating that the matter “requires consideration,” the HC issued notice to the state and directed it to file its counter affidavit within three weeks.
“Till the next date of listing, the realisation of damages imposed by the City Magistrate, Saharanpur vide order dated 16.7.2026 shall remain stayed,” court said.
The matter will next be taken up on October 12, 2026.

Beijing can rewrite China’s property rules, but it can’t undo the damage
A narrower supply pipeline, industry consolidation and years of balance-sheet repair are inevitable as China seeks stability, rather than a perpetual housing boom
Michael Han is assistant president and Shanghai general manager at Yuepu Technology Group.
Financial markets are notoriously prone to mistaking a fundamental institutional shift for a temporary liquidity crisis. The futurist Roy Amara is often credited with the observation that people tend to overestimate the short-term effect of a transformation while underestimating its long-term impact. China’s real-estate sector is furnishing a textbook case of an analogous dynamic.
On August 28, Chinese housing authorities and financial regulators announced a package to overhaul the commercial housing sales system. The measures include a gradual shift towards sales of completed homes, tighter supervision of presale escrow accounts, new project-based financing arrangements and extended mortgage terms. The announcement initially sparked excitement among global financial centres eager for another round of sweeping property stimulus.
Equity markets quickly delivered a far more complicated verdict. When trading resumed on Monday, shares of major property developers plummeted. China Jinmao and Greentown China dropped by more than 10 per cent; China Resources Land and other major builders also suffered losses. This whiplash – early optimism followed by a punishing sell-off – underscored a disconnect between policy intentions and investor expectations. The market initially misinterpreted Beijing’s intent, only to reprice as the reality of structural deleveraging set in.
Global investors often evaluate Beijing through a simple binary lens, expecting either aggressive credit expansion or policy neglect. The recent regulatory actions reveal a more deliberate objective. By reshaping the architecture of project sales and commercial credit, Beijing is not attempting to revive the speculative boom of past decades. It is rewriting the institutional rules for an industry that has entered a mature, lower-growth era.
For over two decades, real estate expanded through a high-leverage feedback loop. After the 1998 housing reforms that ended state welfare housing allocation, rapid urbanisation created immense demand. Municipal governments relied heavily on land sale proceeds for revenue, while state commercial banks provided abundant credit. Developers acquired land with borrowed capital, sold flats long before completion, used presale proceeds to clear debt and buy more land, and repeated the cycle.

A Chinese rescue team has reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time and found “nothing but ruins” as Nepal and China continue their arduous rescue operations in the flood-hit Himalayas.
Surveillance camera footage from the worst-hit Gyirong border crossing complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only on Friday were rescuers able to reach that area.
State media reported that the Chinese team of 21 rescuers and a search-and-rescue dog crossed mountains and valleys and used ropes to navigate forests and cliffs after roads to the complex, hemmed in by steep Himalayan slopes, were destroyed.
“There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi said. At the complex, “as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins.”
The glacier collapse which unleashed a deadly torrent through Himalayan mountain river systems has killed at least 579 people in Nepal and seven in China’s Tibet. The number of missing in Nepal has nearly doubled to 1,924, officials said on Friday. At least 558 were missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, Chinese state media said. Among the missing are at least 540 foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India.
More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.
Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign help in specialised and technical areas in which it does not have expertise, but not in search and rescue.
Earlier on Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage the rescue efforts on its own for now and declined foreign involvement.
The areas Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storing bodies for longer durations, foreign minister Shisir Khanal said late on Friday.
Asked about that stance of his government, Khanal said there was no need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.
India and China, between whom Nepal is wedged, have been requested to supply bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges had been destroyed.
Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.
Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.
China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geo-hazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be unstable and that over 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.
In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.
China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No. 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of the highest national priority.
In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.
The BBC and NY Times have reported videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.
Chinese state media has carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports have focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.
Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.
The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s Belt and Road network linking the country to South Asia, with logistics zones and parking lots built there in the past decade.

The interview Trump doesn’t want you to see
Why ABC won’t air an interview with a Democratic Senate candidate.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s FCC wants to keep a Democratic Senate candidate off the air.
What’s happening? On Wednesday, late-night host Jimmy Kimmel announced that his upcoming interview with James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, would not air on TV. Instead, he said, “due to circumstances beyond our comprehension,” it would be posted only on YouTube.
According to Kimmel, Trump’s Federal Communications Commission “has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions — guest bookings it would seem they don’t like.”
Can Trump do that? It’s unclear — but he can at least make it painful enough for companies that they decide it’s not worth the headache. Kimmel said on Wednesday that his show’s decision was made “out of consideration for our local stations…who would have to deal with this nonsense” if they aired the interview.
Late-night shows like Kimmel’s Jimmy Kimmel Live! have long been considered exempt from something called the equal-time rule, which requires broadcasters to give equal air time for candidates contending for the same office.
In January, however, the Trump administration said that late-night shows needed to comply with the rule; the next month, CBS declined to air an interview with Talarico on its late-night show, The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. (That interview was also posted to YouTube, where it’s since garnered about 9.5 million views.)
What’s the context? This is not Kimmel’s first brush with Trump or the FCC. He was briefly suspended around this time last year after threats from Trump’s FCC chair, and Trump tried again to get him fired earlier this year, with less success.
Last month, ABC and its parent company, Disney, sued the FCC over its attempt to force a review of ABC’s broadcast licenses.
What’s the big picture? This kind of attack on the media is a familiar tactic from competitive authoritarian systems like Hungary, as my colleague Zack Beauchamp explained last year. Trump’s efforts to do the same in the US have often been clumsy or unsuccessful — but in this case, it seems to be working.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

India and the European Union on Friday moved closer to finalising a landmark free trade agreement (FTA), with the European Commission seeking approval for its signature and conclusion. If authorised by the Council, this will be the largest trade agreement ever concluded by both the EU and India. The EU and India already trade over €180 billion in goods and services per year, supporting nearly 800,000 EU jobs. Once the FTA is adopted and entered into force, it will improve market access, reduce tariffs, tackle unnecessary barriers to trade, and provide predictable rules for trade and investment between the two countries. The EU and India started negotiating an FTA in 2007. The talks were suspended in 2013, relaunched in 2022, and successfully concluded in January 2026. Alongside the free trade agreement, the EU and India are also negotiating agreements on geographical indications and investment protection. The FTA is expected to come into force by later this year or in the first half of 2027. Hailing the landmark India-EU FTA moving "one step closer to the finish line”, European Ambassador-designate to India and Bhutan Jean-Eric Paquet on Friday said that the proposal is a “bold leap for two economic powerhouses”. The ambassador-designate’s comment comes shortly after the European Commission presented the agreement to the EU Council for approval, as he said the agreement has cleared the path for early approval. “Fantastic news! FTA just moved one step closer to the finish line! @EU_Commission has sent its proposal to @EUCouncil, clearing the path for early approval; while the full text is now public,” Ambassador-designate Paquet posted on X. Sharing the text of the proposed text in his post, he added that the proposal “is not just another agreement. It’s a bold leap for two economic powerhouses!” India ranks as the EU’s ninth-largest trading partner in goods, with bilateral merchandise trade reaching EUR 118 billion in 2025. Machinery, transport equipment, and chemicals account for the bulk of EU exports to India, while Indian shipments to Europe primarily consist of machinery, chemicals, textiles, metals, and refined petroleum products. Trade in services between the two economies reached EUR 67 billion in 2025, with EU service imports totalling EUR 37.8 billion and exports EUR 29.2 billion. More than 20 children killed in DR Congo school fire
- Published
At least 24 schoolchildren have died in a stampede as they tried to flee a fire that engulfed two schools in rebel-held Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, officials there have said.
Adults are also reported to have died in the fire and there are fears that the death toll could rise further in the densely populated Kadutu commune.
Survivors have been taken to nearby hospitals, and footage of the scene shows children lying on hospital floors in pain.
Some 300 houses have also been destroyed in the fire, the cause of which is unknown.
Rebel‑appointed authorities released a provisional death toll of 24 on Thursday evening, confirming previous reports, but there are fears that more people may have died.
Pictures circulating on social media show young children lying motionless on the ground.
A witness quoted by Reuters news agency said the fire had been put out by afternoon but smoke was still rising from rubble and corrugated metal.
Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu province and one of DR Congo's most crowded hillside cities, was captured by M23 rebels in February last year.
Meanwhile the government in Kinshasa released a statement on X, without specifying numbers of casualties.
"The Ministry of National Education and New Citizenship expressed deep sorrow over the deadly fire," it said.
"With several lives lost and many injured, the toll remains provisional. The minister offered condolences, affirmed solidarity with families, and ordered assessments of affected schools to ensure learning continuity."
The tragedy follows a similar fire in Kinshasa last weekend, where residents died in a stampede at a wedding banquet hall.
In response, the government has ordered strict safety measures and deployed teams nationwide to enforce standards at public gathering places.

Experts say there is no universal clock time that works for everyone. What matters more is when dinner falls in relation to the body’s biological clock and bedtime. An earlier dinner may be beneficial, but there is no fixed 7 p.m. or 8 p.m. cut-off. The gap between dinner and sleep, the quality and composition of the meal, physical activity and individual health needs all play a role.
Insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance generally decrease as the day progresses, so the body may not handle a heavy meal as well later in the day. However, dinner timing is only one part of the picture. The amount and quality of food, physical activity, sleep and health conditions such as diabetes and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) also affect how the body responds to a meal.
The gap before sleep
“There is no evidence-based ideal dinner time,” said Aafrin Shabbir, medical director, senior consultant and diabetologist, Tambaram Medical Centre and CODE Clinic. The body’s metabolic efficiency is generally better during the daytime, she said, making a smaller and lighter dinner preferable.
She also cautioned against assuming that eating at 10 p.m. is unhealthy for everyone. Someone who sleeps at 1 a.m. has a different biological rhythm from someone who sleeps at 10 p.m. “One rule doesn’t fit all,” she said.
Saravana Bharathy S. P., internal medicine, Dr Mehta’s Hospitals, recommends leaving about two to three hours between dinner and bedtime. This is particularly relevant for people with reflux or digestive discomfort, as lying down soon after a meal can worsen symptoms.
Swathi Padmanaban, consultant, paediatric & adolescent endocrinologist and diabetologist, Rainbow Children’s Hospital, Chennai, said eating dinner earlier is generally better for metabolic health when practical. She advised against making dinner the largest meal of the day, particularly when it is eaten close to bedtime.
Meal timing is linked to the body’s circadian rhythm. The liver, pancreas and gastrointestinal tract have their own biological clocks that work with the brain’s central body clock. As the biological day progresses, insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance tend to fall, meaning the same meal may cause a greater rise in blood glucose when eaten later.
Late eating
Studies have found that eating dinner at 10 p.m., compared with 6 p.m., led to higher overnight blood glucose and changes in fat metabolism, despite the meals having the same calories and nutrients.
“Late eating may have greater metabolic implications for people living with diabetes, prediabetes and obesity. A carbohydrate-rich meal late at night can cause a larger rise in blood glucose, particularly when physical activity is low,” Dr. Swathi said.
Late, heavy meals can also cause bloating, indigestion and acid reflux and may affect sleep. However, an occasional late dinner is unlikely to carry the same significance as a regular pattern of late-night eating.
Eating after a particular hour does not, by itself, cause obesity or heart disease. Overall calorie intake, food quality, physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep also play major roles. “People who regularly eat late may also snack more, sleep less or have irregular work schedules. This makes it difficult to separate the effect of dinner timing from other lifestyle factors,” Dr. Bharathy said.
Healthier dinner timing
For children and adolescents, the focus should be on regular meals, adequate nutrition, appropriate portions, physical activity and good sleep rather than restrictive eating windows.
If a late dinner is unavoidable, a moderate and balanced meal is preferable. Vegetables, protein and fibre can be included, while sugary drinks, sweets and fried or fatty foods should be limited. It is also better to avoid coming home extremely hungry and eating a large, carbohydrate-heavy meal just before bed. If possible, part of the meal can be eaten earlier and the later meal kept smaller. A short walk after dinner may also help with post-meal blood glucose control.
For people living with diabetes, meal timing should be planned around their medication, insulin requirements, blood glucose levels and HbA1c rather than a fixed cut-off.
The practical approach is to eat earlier when possible, leave about two to three hours between dinner and bedtime, keep late meals light and balanced, and maintain regular eating and sleep schedules.
