Transport expert calls for Bendigo, Geelong to join light rail resurgence
In short:
Bendigo Heritage is calling for a light rail connection to link the city's retail, arts, sport and hospital precincts.
Regional cities across Australia are looking to trams, trackless trams, and dedicated bus networks to solve congestion on roads.
What's next?
Bendigo Heritage wants a feasibility study on trams as public transport as part of a review into the city’s bus network, while Geelong is exploring its connections to the Surf Coast.
Almost 20 years ago, transport expert and Professor of Sustainability Peter Newman recommended that the City of Greater Bendigo turn its heritage trams into a public transport option.
After three trials over the following months, the city's bosses decided not to adopt it, saying people still preferred their cars.
But now, with light rail making a global resurgence, Bendigo Heritage is proposing the city use light rail to connect key destinations.
The proposal calls for a short city-centre tram route of roughly 1 kilometre linking the Bendigo Station with the retail core and continuing to the Bendigo Art Gallery and Queen Elizabeth Oval precinct.
The proposal also wants trams to run along Barnard Street and connect with the hospital precinct.
Professor Newman says it is time Bendigo returned to the idea of trams as public transport.
"The communities need to want it, as well as the developers," he said.
"That process should begin straightaway because the opportunities are going to be there.
"The politics is going to be right. These are the areas that people are saying, 'we want to be like the city centres'."
Trams ran along Mitchell and View streets until 1972, and the plan by the city's heritage body is to have battery-powered trams traverse that same path.
Bendigo Heritage chief executive James Reade said the resurgence of trams would improve connectivity for Bendigo residents and visitors.
"Their absence is still keenly felt in the character of the city,"
"We propose a short city centre tram route of roughly 1 kilometre linking the Bendigo Station with the retail core and continuing to the Bendigo Art Gallery and Queen Elizabeth Oval precinct.
"With significant anchors at either terminus, it is a modest line with a mighty job to do."
The plan would involve reallocating one traffic lane in each of Mitchell Street and View Street to make way for the tram lines and stops.
Figures from the International Association of Public Transport's report on light rail in 2019 showed that, since 2000, more than 100 cities worldwide have opened their first modern light rail line, and light rail now runs in close to 390 cities.
It was found that in Europe more than 210 tram and light rail systems carry billions of passengers a year, and it is the fastest-growing corner of the sector.
Tram revival must meet passenger need
It's not the first time the return of light rail or trams has been proposed as a public transport option in Bendigo.
In 2005, the City of Greater Bendigo scrapped its plan to extend the heritage tram network around Lake Weeroona after the community opposed it.
Three years later, Professor Newman suggested modernising parts of the heritage tram network so it could function as a daily public transport service, but after a week-long trial of trams running every 20 minutes it was not continued.
This week, Professor Newman said Bendigo Heritage's plan was needed to attract private investment and unlock the urban development required to make the tramway a success.
"The right quotient is to bring into the room the people who would be putting money into that project in terms of the urban developments around it and the local, state and federal governments that would be contributing to it," Professor Newman said.
"If you do that, then you'll get an integrated solution rather than a tramway organisation saying, 'Oh, we just like this'.
"This is a proper urban development project that will transform Bendigo if done right."
Professor Newman backed the idea of battery-powered trams and said Auckland was considering "trackless trams", and there was a proposal for similar to be added to Parramatta Road in western Sydney, while Brisbane's metro used three-carriage battery buses which mirrored a light rail system.
But Public Transport Users Association spokesperson for regional Victoria, Paul Westcott, said light rail would have to run far more frequently than the current hourly heritage tram service along Pall Mall.
"Frequency is always the key to good public transport, not necessarily the mode by which the service is delivered," he said.
"It's pretty clear that if a bus and tram deliver the same frequency on the same route, people would probably prefer a tram.
"But it's not much good putting a tram in unless you are going to provide the level of service and route coverage that is going to be attractive and useful to public transport users."
'Tram boulevards' for regional cities
The Gold Coast is one of the latest regions to add light rail to its public transport.
The 6.7-kilometre-long Stage 3 of its light rail opened early last month and cost $1.55 billion to build, more than double its initial projection of $709 million.
This week, the G21 conference in Geelong launched its campaign for $12.5 million for the planning and design of a rapid transport corridor between Geelong and the Surf Coast.
At the moment, commuters rely on a 53-minute bus ride to travel the 23 kilometres between the two destinations.
City of Greater Geelong mayor Stretch Kontelj said trackless trams, or a dedicated rapid bus lane, had already been touted as options.
"I particularly love the sound of trackless trams,"
"As they do between Adelaide and Glenelg, that's sort of my vision of how that could potentially work.
"I could see it would be hugely advantageous to people daily for commuting between the two areas, but also a great tourist attraction."
Mr Kontelj said the next stage would be about getting the costings of establishing the transport corridor.
Surf Coast Shire mayor Libby Stapleton said the Surf Coast Highway was already at capacity during peak times, and studies had shown that a business-as-usual approach that relied on cars would not work.
"We know that demand is increasing," she said.
'Cheaper and more accessible'
Ian McBurney has spent 25 years working with communities on sustainable transport and said arriving at Bendigo on the train and catching a tram to the art gallery, Queen Elizabeth Oval and hospital would be a great look for the city.
He said that while the tourism market loves trams, inner-city workers and residents needed a faster and more modern system that ran regularly and got passengers from A to B regularly.
"I'm pretty sure that running ten-minute electric buses would be far cheaper and more accessible," he said.
"Buses can take a lane of the current road, but we would need to build better bus stops. Laying tram tracks would be a complete redesign of the road."
The request for a feasibility study for a new Bendigo tram route has been sent to the Department of Transport and Planning as part of a review into Bendigo's bus network.

When Man City call you don't say no - Ndiaye
- Published
Iliman Ndiaye says "you don't say no" when Manchester City come calling, and playing in the Champions League is where he belongs.
The 26-year-old could have gone to Tottenham but made a £60m move from Everton to City on transfer deadline day and was thrown straight into the starting XI for his new side in a 1-0 Premier League victory over Coventry at the weekend.
In the final week of the transfer window, it appeared as though Ndiaye would be moving to Spurs after they agreed a deal with Everton, but they were unable to proceed with the move having failed to sell Richarlison.
"There was no stress or panicking," said Ndiaye.
"I always say whatever comes, comes. God decides your future - it is already written.
"I was just being patient and when City came through I was buzzing. It was always going to be City.
"I wanted Champions League and playing at one of the best teams in the world. I am not saying Tottenham is not, but when Manchester City comes through you don't say no.
"It has been a good week for me and topped off with a win."
Despite Everton finishing in the bottom half of the table in his two seasons at the club, Ndiaye became a fans' favourite for his skills on the flanks and scoring 17 goals.
"When I was speaking with my wife, I was telling her that if I had to leave Everton it would be somewhere where I know I would be playing Champions League," he said.
"It was difficult to leave Everton. I created a great connection with the fans and the players there, but we have to move on sometimes and it's how football is."
- Fernandez and Ndiaye show signs of promise on Man City debuts 
  - Published5 days ago
Ndiaye started his professional career in non-league with Boreham Wood before playing only seven miles away from Etihad Stadium at Hyde United seven years ago.
Ndiaye played in the Championship with Sheffield United and had a season at Marseille before joining Everton for £15m in 2024.
Ndiaye said: "I don't really look back. I just look to the future and work hard. I never stop. I just look at the next step and this is a big step to join Manchester City.
"It is one of the biggest clubs in the world. There are world-class players, world-class stadium and the fans are brilliant.
"This is where I think I belong. I have worked hard to get to this point."

The Spectacle of 1980s Hollywood
Jackie Collins wrote flashy Hollywood thrillers, but isn’t often thought of as a canonical Los Angeles writer.
This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here.
Jackie Collins, who wrote flashy, sex-filled Hollywood thrillers, isn’t often thought of as a canonical Los Angeles novelist. I didn’t regard her as one, at least—until I read Sophie Gilbert’s essay about Collins, the latest entry in The Atlantic’s series “The Writer’s Way.” Collins wrote shiny 1980s “bonkbusters,” as one critic called them; in her novels, including her breakthrough, Hollywood Wives, she turned gossip about scheming producers and backbiting socialites into gripping, soapy dramas long before reality shows made such stories commonplace. Until I learned more about these works, they felt to me like a surface treatment of the complex city best captured by Raymond Chandler, Joan Didion, Octavia Butler, and Eve Babitz. It didn’t help that they were set in Beverly Hills, which, in my nearly five years living in L.A., I knew mostly as a nexus of unaffordable baubles and posh podiatrists’ offices. But Gilbert’s exploration of the writer and the enclave made me realize that her novels fit right into the city’s long literary tradition.
First, here are four new stories from The Atlantic’s Books section:
In addition to creating steely characters who advanced the idea of middle age as a woman’s powerful prime, Collins was a “devoted” fan of Mickey Spillane, the hardest of hard-boiled-detective novelists, and the influence of noir comes through in her treatment of Beverly Hills: “Jackie genuinely loved the neighborhood for its clean white lines and endless sky,” Gilbert writes, “but she was also drawn to everything it contained beneath the surface: its roiling currents of fame, power, and degradation.” Beneath the shimmering surfaces, dark shadows always lurked.
“Sunshine or Noir?” Mike Davis asked in his nonfiction masterpiece about Los Angeles, City of Quartz. The binary of light and dark is ingrained in the L.A. canon; it animates not only Chandler’s literary potboilers, but also Babitz’s sad-girl stories, Butler’s numinous dystopias, and Didion’s alienated meditations. Collins was, like these writers, an insider with an outsider’s soul. “I don’t live the Hollywood lifestyle,” she told an interviewer (while sitting poolside at her stark-white mansion, mind you). “I move in it. I’m an observer.”
Gilbert does some observing of her own as she roams Jackie’s neighborhood—she refers to her by first name, like a friend—and she discovers that the city has changed a great deal since Collins’s time. The author captured a different Hollywood, before it was supplanted by “brand-activation opportunities and AI-drafted emails,” before celebrity became “its own art form.” L.A. in the 2020s requires a new kind of best seller, and the city still produces them. This summer in The Atlantic, Carolyn Kellogg wrote about the work of Angeleno Jordan Harper, whose latest novel, A Violent Masterpiece, concerns a TMZ-style celebrity videographer and a plotline ripped from the Epstein files. Steph Cha, Gary Phillips, and Ivy Pochoda “are also bringing today’s Los Angeles, in all its awful, beautiful chaos, to life on the page,” Kellogg notes. Their books don’t repudiate the existence or value of Collins’s 1980s spectacle: They’re proof that L.A. is constantly evolving, and also that it is perennially, insistently itself.
Jackie Collins Wrote Her Own Revolution
By Sophie Gilbert
The novelist imagined women enjoying equality in the bedroom and the boardroom. Are we any closer to living in that world?
What to Read
Guilty Pleasures, by Arielle Zibrak
The smutty hockey romance Heated Rivalry is passionately beloved, yet many of its fans admit to being embarrassed by their obsession with the TV series and novels that inspired it. (Ardent and committed lovers of other things—such as, say, hockey teams—tend not to feel the same way.) But Zibrak, an English professor at the University of Wyoming, insists that no novel, film, or show is more shameful, or less worth consuming, than any other is—and that even art dismissed as lowbrow has “much to tell us about ourselves and the world.” In this short, snappy tract, she confidently surveys the landscape of “guilty pleasures”—usually those written by, about, or for women—and unearths newfound complexity. She manages to cover the obscure 1850 best seller The Wide, Wide World as well as Judy Blume’s Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret, along with critical essays from thinkers such as Hilton Als and Saidiya Hartman; each volume mentioned is worth tracking down. So are other volumes in the series this belongs to, NYU Press’s Avidly Reads. — Sophia Stewart

A Great Novel Becomes a Bad Show
By Jeremy Gordon
For many readers, the career of the novelist Bret Easton Ellis is the standard for mainstream literary stardom. The biopic writes itself: While still a college undergraduate, Ellis strikes it big with his debut novel, 1985’s Less Than Zero, an unsentimental stenography of disaffected, privileged young adults in swanky Los Angeles. It’s soon adapted into a movie starring Robert Downey Jr. and James Spader, which itself bears little resemblance to the book. Nevertheless, Ellis’s renown skyrockets. By the time he turns 30, he’s seemingly done it all: published multiple best sellers (American Psycho, The Rules of Attraction) filled with materialistic ennui, cheap sex, and lurid death; been mythologized as part of a literary “Brat Pack” alongside writers including Jay McInerney and Tama Janowitz; rubbed elbows with celebrities of the music and film worlds; made lots of money (for a writer, at least); and become addicted to drugs.

The Centre has amended the ecommerce rules to curb dark patterns on online marketplaces and quick commerce platforms. Called Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) (Amendment) Rules, 2026, the norms will replace the existing Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020. The new regime will come into effect starting January 2027. In a statement, the consumer affairs department said that the new rules promote transparency and strengthen provisions related to consumer grievances, sponsored listings and seller disclosures. “The amended rules seek to address emerging consumer concerns in the digital marketplace while taking into account the need for ease of doing business and a balanced approach that protects consumer interests without imposing unnecessary regulatory burdens on ecommerce entities,” read an official statement. Under the new regime, all ecommerce platforms will be mandated to become convergence partners of the national consumer helpline (NCH). For context, a convergence initiative is a process to resolve customer grievances quickly and amicably. In an official statement, the government noted that the new amendments will introduce the following changes: All ecommerce platforms will be required to provide the complainant with a copy of their complaint as recorded by the grievance officer. Online marketplaces will be barred from manipulating search results, which may mislead users or adversely affect the relevance of results to the user's search query. Sponsored listings shall be identified through clear and prominent disclosures. In case of price reductions, ecommerce platforms will be required to display both the reduced price and prior price. The “prior price” will be the lowest price at which the specified good was sold 30 days before the announcement. All ecommerce platforms will be required to undertake an annual self-audit to comply with the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023. Online marketplace will also be mandated to provide key information, including best before dates, refunds, warranty, delivery and payment details, to enable informed consumer decisions. Ecommerce platforms will be barred from using consumer information without express and affirmative consent. Online marketplaces have been prohibited from collecting bundled fees for services unrelated to the ecommerce platform, except for loyalty or membership programmes. Importer details and country of origin will now have to be disclosed for imported goods. The new norms come as ecommerce and quick commerce platforms are gearing up for the upcoming festive season. While dark patterns continue throughout the year, the issue grabs headlines during the peak festive season. Earlier this year, the government informed the Parliament that more than 5.1 Lakh complaints were registered against ecommerce and quick commerce platforms on the National Consumer Helpline in 2025. A majority of these complaints were registered against Flipkart, Amazon and Meesho. Not just this, Inc42 last year reported that dark patterns ruled the roost during the 2025 festive season sale. From Flipkart’s Big Billion Days to Amazon’s Great Indian Festival sales, several buyers reported orders being cancelled after payment, refunds delayed, delivery dates pushed back, and “sale” prices that sometimes were worse than the regular listed price on the manufacturer’s site. Cognisant of this, the consumer affairs ministry has been clamping down on online marketplaces over the past few years. In 2023, the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) identified and prohibited 13 dark patterns, including confirm shaming, subscription trap, bait and switch, false urgency, basket sneaking, disguised ads, among others. Doubling down on this, the CCPA issued yet another advisory in June last year, directing all digital platforms to conduct a mandatory self-audit to detect and eliminate dark patterns. Despite this, violations continue. In June, the CCPA imposed a penalty of ₹1 Lakh on beverages brand Storia for allegedly misleading consumers through the use of “100%” claims on their products. In the same month, it also slapped a fine of ₹5 Lakh on edtech major PhysicsWallah for employing dark patterns on its platform.

ఇండోనేషియాలోని జావా, సుమత్రా దీవుల మధ్య అనాక్ క్రాకటోవా అగ్నిపర్వతం ఉంది. ఇది తరచూ బద్దలవుతూ ఉంటుంది. 5 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న భారీగా అగ్నికీలలు, లావా, బూడిద బయటకు వచ్చాయి (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ). ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, అనాక్ క్రాకటోవా అగ్నిపర్వతం నుంచి ఎగసిపడుతున్న అగ్నికీలలు, ఉప్పొంగుతున్న లావాకు సంబంధించిన వీడియో అంటూ ఒక వీడియో సోషల్ మీడియాలో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ)  వైరల్ అవుతోంది. టైమ్స్ ఆఫ్ ఇండియా, న్యూస్18 గుజరాతీ వంటి వార్తా సంస్థలు కూడా అనాక్ క్రాకటోవా అగ్నిపర్వతం ఇటీవల విస్ఫోటనం చెందడంపై ఇచ్చిన కథనాల్లో ఇదే వీడియోను ఉపయోగించాయి.
క్లెయిమ్: అనాక్ క్రాకటోవా అగ్నిపర్వతం నుంచి ఎగసిపడుతున్న అగ్నికీలలు, ఉప్పొంగుతున్న లావాకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలను చూపిస్తున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్ (నిజం): ఇండోనేషియాలోని అనాక్ క్రాకటోవా దీవిలో అగ్నిపర్వత విస్ఫోటనం జరిగినప్పటికీ, వైరల్ అవుతున్న ఈ దృశ్యాలు ఏఐ ద్వారా రూపొందించబడినవి. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టిస్తుంది.
వైరల్ వీడియో గురించి తెలుసుకోవడానికి వీడియో యొక్క కీ ఫ్రేములను ఉపయోగిస్తూ ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతికితే, ఈ వీడియోకు సంబంధించి ఎటువంటి ఆధారాలు మాకు లభించలేదు. కానీ ఈ వీడియోను జాగ్రత్తగా పరిశీలిస్తే కొన్ని అసమానతలు కనిపించాయి. ముఖ్యంగా పరుగెత్తుతున్న వ్యక్తుల కదలికలు, వారి రూపాల్లో కొన్ని అసమానతలు కనిపించాయి.
తదుపరి, మేము ఆ వీడియోను Hive Moderation టూల్లో పరీక్షించగా, ఆ వైరల్ క్లిప్ AI-జనరేటెడ్ అని నిర్ధారించబడింది.
అనాక్ క్రాకటోవా అగ్నిపర్వతం విస్ఫోటనం చెందిన అసలు వీడియోను ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ చూడవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, అనాక్ క్రాకటోవా విస్ఫోటనం అంటూ వైరల్ అవుతున్న వీడియో ఏఐ వాడి తయారు చేసింది.

A worker fired by the makers of Grand Theft Auto has said he believed employees were put on a “watch list” after signing a petition about remote working.
Dayne Oram told an employment tribunal in Glasgow examining whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 employees for trade union activity on Friday that he thought the company started keeping an eye on a group of workers after the petition was sent to leadership in 2023.
Rockstar, which disputes the claims, says Oram and his colleagues were dismissed for gross misconduct after confidential company information was shared, not because of trade union membership or activity.
The workers had been helping to make Grand Theft Auto VI, which is set for release on 19 November and will probably be among the biggest launches in gaming history. The production for the game, which has reportedly generated more than $3bn (£2.27bn) in preorders, is led from the company’s Edinburgh office Rockstar North.
Much of the case relies on what was shared in a Discord forum, used by about 300 Rockstar employees to discuss the company. Oram was involved in setting up the forum and helped moderate it, which is where Rockstar says sensitive information was shared and discussed.
Oram told the tribunal that discussions on the forum could “get a bit out of hand”. Thomas Cordrey, representing Rockstar at the tribunal, read Oram the forum rules requiring workers to remain “professional and constructive” when posting. Cordrey suggested that the rules had been “routinely broken”.
Cordrey read out a number of Discord posts where he suggested employees were making disparaging remarks about the company and management, including messages in which one was called “cowardly corporate fucks” and another was called a “cunt”.
Oram told the tribunal that he would probably “remake” some of the moderation decisions if he had the chance to do so again, but said moderators did not want to “over-police” the channel.
Oram also said he believed there was a connection between the list of names who signed the 2023 petition about remote working and the eventual firings in 2025. But Cordrey questioned whether this was really the case when 141 of 154 people who signed it were not fired.
“It was maybe the start of them keeping an eye on things,” Oram told the tribunal.
The case is expected to last about six weeks, with testimony from Rockstar Games witnesses set for October. The company remains in talks with current workers, who hope official union recognition can be secured before the release of GTA VI.
In total, 34 Rockstar workers were fired last year, including three in Canada who are not taking part in the tribunal. Of the 31 who were based in Scotland, 23 are involved in the case and are being represented by the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain.
A spokesperson for Rockstar Games said: “Rockstar Games’ position has been clear and consistent throughout.
“Individuals across the UK and Canada were dismissed for gross misconduct following the sharing of confidential company information, not because of alleged trade union membership or activity. We reject the claims and will defend them vigorously before the tribunal,” the said.
The tribunal in Glasgow continues before the judge Lucy Wiseman.

This week, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), prodded by the Supreme Court, proposed a simple but overdue idea. Packaged foods high in fat, salt, or sugar should carry a bold red warning on the front of the pack, not buried in fine print on the back. Someone picking up instant noodles, a breakfast cereal, or a “health drink” will finally be told, at a glance, that it is not as wholesome as its advertising claims. This is a welcome step. It is also, on its own, nowhere near enough.
The number of children presenting with morbid obesity and diabetes has climbed sharply within just a few years. The World Obesity Atlas 2026 bears this out — 41 million Indian children and adolescents aged 5 to 19 are now overweight or obese. This is not just because children are eating more; it is about what they are being sold. Breakfast cereals, sweetened yoghurts, and “health drinks” are marketed to parents as filling gaps in a child’s diet, emphasising “energy” and vitamins while saying little about the sugar content inside. In 2024, a leading multinational was found adding sugar to infant food sold in India and other lower income countries; sugar was left out of the same product in Europe. When a health drink, popular in Indian homes, turned out to be nothing more than flavoured sugar syrup, it took a social media storm, and not a regulator, to force the company to prescribe a 15% cut in its added sugar.
The problem is worse around schools and colleges, where studies show that the cheapest, most easily available snacks are also the least healthy. A popular “energy drink” among teenagers, priced at just ₹20, packs close to 17 grams of sugar, caffeine, and artificial colour into a single bottle. Its label says it is not meant for children, yet nothing stops a child from buying it. This is the market pricing unhealthy calories to fit within the range of a child’s pocket money.
Need for enforcement
None of this is a secret. What has been missing is enforcement. The FSSAI and the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) have long recommended what schools should not sell, but optional rules get treated as optional, and canteens stock whatever sells cheapest. A red warning label only works if it is actually enforced.
Moreover, the new rule stops at the edge of organised retail. Most of India’s sugar, salt, and trans fat is eaten unbranded, from street stalls, dhabas, and sweet shops that make up the unorganised sector, none of which is required to declare anything. A red label on a biscuit packet does nothing about the jalebi sold loose beside it. Regulation that reaches only packaged food leaves the unregulated half of the plate untouched.
Then there is the conversation India keeps avoiding — a tax on sugar. When the U.K. introduced its soft drinks industry levy, sugar consumption among both children and adults fell. Manufacturers reformulated their drinks to slip below the tax threshold rather than raise prices. A well-designed sugar tax does not just discourage people from buying a product, it pushes the industry to make the product itself less harmful.
India already taxes sugary drinks heavily; just not usefully. Since September 2025, aerated and sweetened beverages, sugar free versions included, were folded into one 40% GST slab — so a ‘normal’ cola and its zero-sugar counterpart pay the same tax, leaving manufacturers with no reason to cut sugar. The U.K.’s levy worked differently, taxing drinks in tiers by sugar content, so that companies could lower their bill by reformulating the product. India could tax products in the same way so that manufacturers have a reason to cut sugar.
The standard objection — that such a tax would hit the poor the hardest — is not wrong, but it is only half the argument. Unregulated, cheap sugar already extracts a heavy price from the poor, who bear the brunt of the diabetes, hypertension and childhood obesity epidemic that sugar heavy diets drive, with the least means to treat it. Doing nothing is not neutral; it is a slower, costlier tax, paid in ill health rather than rupees at the till. The answer is to design the tax calibrated to sugar content so that it nudges reformulation, with part of the revenue set aside to make healthy food cheaper.
The FSSAI’s proposed red label is a genuine, if belated, first step. What India needs now is the resolve to finish what it has started — mandatory food standards; limits on how unhealthy food is marketed to children; rules that reach the unorganised sector; and an honest debate on taxing sugar in a way that protects families with the least room to absorb either cost, the tax, or the disease.
Dr. Praveen George Paul is Assistant Professor, Pediatric Endocrinology and Metabolism, Department of Pediatrics, Christian Medical College, Vellore. Dr. Vandana Jain is Professor, Pediatric Endocrinology Division, Department of Pediatrics, All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS)

The Gauhati High Court had upheld the validity of ‘talaq-e-hassan’, a Muslim form of divorce where a husband pronounces the word ‘talaq’ once for three consecutive months.
While affirming its validity, the court directed petitioner Rakibul Bhuyan of Barpeta district’s Gelabil village to register his divorce under the Assam Compulsory Registration of Muslim Marriages and Divorce Act, 2024.
The petitioner said that his wife allegedly left him in 2018, two years after their marriage. After attempts at reconciliation failed, he pronounced talaq-e-hassan on March 22, April 26, and May 27, 2026.
He said that with the pronouncement of the third talaq, the marriage had broken. On June 2, he submitted an application to the sub-registrar-cum-marriage and divorce registrar in western Assam’s Barpeta under Section 12 of the 2024 Act.
His application was not accepted. The State government submitted in court that the 1935 version of the Act dealing with Muslim marriages and divorces had been repealed and the authority appointed under that law could no longer register the divorce.
The petitioner said that the marriage and divorce registrar could not have refused to register the divorce under the 2024 Act as ‘talaq-e-hassan’ was not prohibited in India.
Issuing the order on September 8, Justice Arun Dev Choudhury observed that ‘talaq-e-hassan’ remained a valid form of divorce in the country and directed the petitioner to approach the jurisdictional marriage and divorce registrar under the 2024 Act to register the divorce.
“On such approach being made, the jurisdictional Marriage & Divorce Registrar shall consider the application of the petitioner and satisfy himself with regard to the fact as to whether the divorce was effected by the petitioner, who claims to have pronounced the same and also after identifying the petitioner to be the person pronouncing the divorce, proceed to decide as to whether the divorce would mandate a registration,” the order read.
The judge further said that if registration is refused, the petitioner could appeal under Section 17 of the 2024 Act.
Disposing of the petition, the judge also observed that the wife, who was not present in court despite notices being served, remained free to challenge the ‘talaq-e-hassan’ before an appropriate forum.

The Best Robot Lawn Mowers
Featured in this article
Lawn care is a monotonous, thankless task. Who wants to mow the lawn when you could be lollygagging in a hammock with a cold drink, watching a robot do it for you? That’s right: no one. Robot lawn mowers were once the preserve of the wealthy, and yes, they can still be on the pricey side. But they’re getting cheaper and better all the time.
I’ve tested a handful of the best robot lawn mowers over the past three years, and after comparing a fresh crop this mowing season, I'm delighted to tell you that robot mowers are actually good now. I've got some recommendations, honorable mentions, and a list of robot mowers you should avoid. Read on for everything you need to know about lawn-tending bots.
Updated September 2026: I added mowers from Roborock, Segway, Eufy, and Sunseeker, added information about night mowing to the FAQ, and updated prices.
Other Robot Mowers I Tested and Liked
Roborock Rockmow X120H Lidar for $3,200: Better known for its robot vacuums, Roborock also makes robot mowers, and the X120H Lidar is its flagship model (discounted to a far more reasonable $2,000 at the time of writing). I actually tested the UK model, the identical Z120 Lidar (£2,299). This mower employs Lidar and AI vision, so it can cut without satellite connections, with no RTK antenna required. It also supports 4G and comes with a 3-year data plan. It is Four Wheel Drive (4WD) and has ingenious front wheels that pivot and turn independently to navigate tight areas smoothly, with minimal churning of your lawn. There’s a single disc underneath with six cutting blades and a reasonably wide, 9.5-inch (24 cm) cutting width. It supports a 0.8 to 2.7-inch (20 to 70 mm) cutting height, can cover up to around 21,500 square feet, and, most impressively, can handle an 80 percent (up to 39-degree) slope. A full charge gives you 110 minutes of mowing time, and it takes around 50 minutes to charge.
After some minor setup hassles (battery error), the Rockmow Z120 has impressed me. It looks to be the most capable mower I have tested yet for navigating uneven terrain. Apparently, it can automatically create maps, but it defaulted to the manual mode for me, prompting me to remote control it around the borders of my lawn. Edge mowing is the big disappointment, with the mower regularly leaving a strip on one edge of my lawn. I’m not keen on the optional PreciEdge Module (£150) that promises to reduce edges to 3 cm. I haven’t tested it, but feel it should be included in a mower this expensive. Why is it optional? Who doesn’t want their edges properly cut? It avoided most obstacles just fine, but was occasionally oversensitive, avoiding plants swaying over the border edge. The Rain Protection mode is a little too sensitive, preventing the mower from starting several hours after rain, so I had to override it. It also lacks a Spot Mode, though it is so heavy I would not want to carry it between lawn areas. I think this design, with the rotating wheels, has real potential if Roborock can improve the AI/software. Unfortunately, it's not currently available in the US right now, but hopefully be back in stock soon since it was released just this past summer.
Eufy Robot Lawn Mower E15 for $1,300: This is another wire-free mower that uses a camera system to automatically map lawns and avoid obstacles. It’s very similar to my top pick, and also has a super handy Spot Mode that lets you drop and mow on unmapped areas. But even after a big price drop from its original RRP, it’s still more expensive than the TerraMow, and it’s not as good at cutting edges. It can cover up to 0.2 acres (8,700 square feet), cut from 1 to 3 inches, and handle up to 18-degree slopes. It is also fairly quiet and has GPS tracking, but you must have Wi-Fi coverage in your backyard, or you'll need a 4G data subscription. I found the setup lengthy due to a firmware download, but the mapping and the first cut were decent. Object avoidance is very good. The E15 can only run during the day, and doesn't cope very well with inclines. I also found it frequently failed to cut the edges of the lawn and doesn't perform well if the grass is damp. The more affordable Eufy C15 (£999) is very similar, but designed for smaller lawns (up to 5,300 square feet) and only available in the UK and Europe right now.
It kept my back lawn neat without issues, but my front lawn has a dip and ill-defined border that it struggled with. That said, every time it looked as though it might get stuck, it managed to maneuver out of trouble. There’s a dial to adjust mowing height for the C15, whereas you can do it in the app with the E15. Both come with a covered charging base, which often costs extra with rivals. If you’re interested, watch out for a sale event (I’ve seen the E15 drop below $1,000, which makes it far more tempting).
Segway Navimow X430 for $2,249: My backyard is both a Wi-Fi and 5G dead zone. Before manually mowing the yard I save all my podcasts and music to offline mode, and I let my fiancee know she’ll need to deploy a carrier pigeon if she needs to get my attention. So, it was a relief to see just how quickly the navigation system of the Navimow X430 recognized the unit across the treacherous triple lot that surrounds my house. It connected within seconds of beginning the initial setup and twenty minutes later, the robot mower was on its way using the handy auto-mapping function. As it turns out, I didn't need the three beers I'd brought with me when I embarked upon this process, assuming it would be on par with the weeks-long headache it took to get the Mammotion Luba 2 connected and operational last summer.
It did an above-average job on its first pass despite the endless flurry of compost piles, stray bushes, fencing and detritus from half-finished gardening projects that litter my half-acre lawn, though I opted for manual mapping to take advantage of its aptitude at hugging the wobbly brick borders of some raised beds with relative ease. The sites claims that it can handle “tall, thick and dense grass," which I had the perfect scenario to test. After a two weeks of dealing with an endless cycle of torrential downpours and blistering heat, I was left with few open windows for a good mow before my patchy, crabby grass got too unwieldy for the Navimow’s 4-inch height maximum. I watched with disappointment as it casually drove over some stray blades that went to seed without making any impact whatsoever. Despite that, the Navimow X430 has impressed me with its ease-of-use. We'll update our impressions here with additional testing, but so far so good.—Pete Cottell
Sunseeker X7 Gen 2 Wireless Robot Lawn Mower for $2,700: If you have a large, challenging lawn, this could be a mower worth considering. It combines built-in NET-RTK, GPS, and AI vision, has floating dual disc blades for uneven terrain, and can work at night thanks to an Indirect Time of Flight camera. It is also all-wheel drive (AWD) and can handle 70 percent slopes up to 35 degrees. It can cover more than 32,000 square feet. I love the wide 14-inch cutting width, the relatively quiet operation (it never went over 60 decibels but was usually even quieter), even though I’d advise against mowing at night because of the risk to wildlife. Sadly, the automatic mapping was mediocre, and there’s no Spot Mode for a drop-and-mow. This Gen 2 mower brings a raft of improvements over the original, including night vision, faster processing, enhanced durability and traction, a built-in screen, and onboard RTK without a separate antenna. But only the original Sunseeker X7 ($2,700) is available to buy on Amazon. You currently have to go through a dealer to get the Gen 2.
Husqvarna Aspire R6V for £999: While the reliable Husqvarna 410XE Nera was my top pick for a long time, you can get more affordable mowers now, without the hassle of RTK antennas. The Husqvarna Aspire R6V is just such a mower. It uses a combination of GPS and AI vision with a camera on the front. It was easy to set up and map the lawn in the app, but you will need a good Wi-Fi signal across your yard for it to work effectively. I was a little disappointed in the sensitive obstacle avoidance, as it left large uncut strips around the edges of my lawn. I was able to reduce the verge a little with some tinkering, but it was still larger than the recommendations above. Note: This model is currently not available in the US.
Anthbot Genie 3000 for $900: This often-discounted mower was my budget pick for a while, but mowers have moved on, so you can get better performance without the satellite antenna now. It offers auto-mapping, but the remote-control option works better. The mower cut my lawn effectively, but even after repeated map updates, it left an uncut verge. The obstacle avoidance works well, and it cuts in neat lines. It had no issues returning to charge or following a schedule. The voice that says it has connected or started mowing began to annoy me, but thankfully, it can be turned off. There were some glitches with rain alerts that prevented it from mowing, even long after the rain had stopped. I also experienced some flaky connection issues with the GPS, and it occasionally got stuck. While there is support for multiple areas, the mower often struggled picking up a signal in my front yard. Ultimately, this is still a decent mower when discounted, provided you have a modest-sized, straightforward lawn.
Mova Lidax 2000 for $1,199: With a sleek design and a mixture of 360-degree lidar for 3D mapping and a camera with AI vision, this mower proved very effective. Setup was straightforward, and there’s no need for wires or an antenna, though I did have to adjust the map manually. You can set multiple areas, and its navigation is generally very good. It mowed in neat lines, successfully avoided thin posts for the badminton net and other obstacles, and completed an excellent edge pass at the end. With some of the closest edge mowing I’ve seen, I was all set to recommend this mower, but then it got stuck. A couple of times, it seemed to be stuck, then managed to free itself, but an uneven problem spot proved to be its nemesis, and it chewed up a patch of grass trying to get free. Eventually, I had to make that spot a no-go zone. This mower is still worth considering, particularly if you see it on sale; just be prepared to tweak the map. The 2000 covers up to half an acre. If you have a quarter of an acre or less, the Mova Lidax 1000 ($1,299) is much cheaper but has the same features.
Avoid These Mowers
Stiga A6V: I like that this mower only needs the charging station and has no need for an antenna. The buggy setup was my first red flag, as a firmware update failed and had to be repeated. Once up and running, I found the mower always left a big verge, even after adjustment. The AI vision camera is very slow to react to obstacles and not very good at navigating around them. It hit the ball several times in my test, and I had to hit the stop button as it got too close to my cat. It lacks useful features like automapping and spot-mow, and there are better options for the money above. The yellow finish is a bit garish for my tastes too.
EcoFlow Blade: While it was easy to set up and cut my lawn nicely without the need for any boundary wire, the EcoFlow Blade sometimes struggled with GPS navigation and ended up stuck in a flower bed. It also left an untouched strip around the edge of my lawn. The object avoidance was solid, and it can be automated in the app, though it occasionally failed to start a scheduled cut for me. EcoFlow seems to have discontinued this model, though it is still on sale in Europe. Probably best to avoid.
Yardcare E400: Curious about the budget end of the robot mower market, I agreed to try the Yardcare E400, but this mower was an unmitigated disaster from start to finish. It’s a boundary wire model, so you must run wire around the area you want mowed. Yardcare suggests it can cover up to 4,300 square feet and cut grass between 0.8 and 2.4 inches. The problem is that it gets stuck frequently and struggles to even get on and off its charging station reliably. After trying multiple fixes to no avail and going through customer support, I had to conclude that this model has a serious design flaw.
How Do Robot Lawn Mowers Work?
Perhaps counterintuitively, the setup instructions for your robot lawn mower will likely tell you to start by cutting the grass. Robot mowers mostly can’t deal with long grass. Unlike traditional mowers, these robots don’t collect grass cuttings; they mulch instead, and they are designed to cut frequently, keeping your lawn short and simply leaving the cuttings on the ground, which can also improve lawn health. Most robot mowers are designed to run two or three times a week during the growing season (from late spring to early fall).
They have rechargeable batteries onboard and can last from half an hour to several hours on a full charge. They return to the charging base and recharge automatically when their power runs low. Most mowers have simple controls, a small display, and an emergency stop button. You can generally start and stop mowing, set schedules, and create or edit mapped areas using the onboard controls or the companion mobile app, very much like a robot vacuum.
What Features Should I Look For in a Robot Mower?
There are many factors to consider in choosing a robot mower, and the best choice for you often depends on your yard.
Robot lawn mowers are generally rated to cover a specific square footage, with wider coverage requiring models with larger batteries. Alongside yard size, you should consider the shape and topography of your lawn, as most robot mowers will struggle with steep inclines. While you can often map out separate areas so your robot mower can mow front and back lawns, for example, it will generally need you to lift and carry it between those areas. If you have an uneven garden or steep slopes, look for a four-wheel-drive (4WD) or all-wheel-drive (AWD) mower and check the manufacturer's rating for inclines.
There are a few types of navigation that robot mowers employ. We’ve tested five different approaches, though some mowers combine multiple technologies for better performance.
- Satellite: Often employing something called Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) Global Positioning System (GPS), these mowers need a satellite signal to navigate and will have a receiver that must be placed in the open with a clear line of sight to the sky. Satellite navigation mowers are not suitable for areas with tall trees or buildings.
- Light Detection and Ranging (lidar): This technology sends out rapid laser pulses to 3D map the terrain (it is also used by self-driving cars). It enables mowers to cut grass under thick tree canopies or near tall buildings where GPS signals usually fail.
- Cameras: Cameras and onboard AI are used for obstacle detection and avoidance. AI vision can automatically map areas and cut the grass while avoiding obstacles it encounters, much like how most robot vacuums navigate a home to clean the floors.
- Wire boundary: These mowers require you to install a perimeter wire as a boundary around your lawn that marks out the border the mower should not cross. It's a messy job that can be tricky.
- Remote control: You mow your lawn from the comfort of your home using a remote controller or an app on your phone. Some only work via remote control, while others can also cut automatically.
Robot mowers generally come with large charging docks, and you’ll need to earmark a suitable spot for yours. They usually have extensive weatherproof cabling, but you will have to find a route to an outdoor socket.
To connect to your mower and schedule a mow, update the firmware, or remote control it where supported, you need a decent Wi-Fi signal or a Bluetooth connection. It’s best to set up your mower’s charging station within range of your Wi-Fi network. Some mowers also need a strong Wi-Fi signal to operate effectively, so you might consider adding an outdoor mesh router. If you want to connect your phone via Bluetooth, you will have to get quite close.
How Noisy Are Robot Mowers?
Most robot mowers are far quieter than their traditional counterparts. You can expect them to operate at around 55 decibels, though they may go as high as 75 decibels. We only tested battery-powered mowers, but expect gas mowers to be louder. While the operation is often quiet, I did find that several mowers made annoying beeping sounds when backing up or had a loud recorded voice during setup or upon receiving a command.
Do Robot Mowers Work in Any Weather?
Robot mowers and their charging stations usually have IP ratings and can cope with rain, but you should pack up and bring your mower indoors during the winter months. Many robot mowers have some kind of rain sensor and will pause mowing when it gets too wet. Some mowers may need to be paused manually. The wheels can churn up your lawn and get caked in mud if mowers continue to labor in the rain, especially with larger and heavier models.
How Well Do Robot Mowers Cut?
Mowers of different sizes will have varying cutting widths, denoting the width of the strip they can cut on each pass. Most also have floating cutting decks that enable you to choose the length of grass you want (typically 1 to 3 inches). Many robot mowers seem to struggle with cutting around the edges of a lawn, especially if there’s a wall or fence that prevents them from getting close enough.
It’s common to find an uncut verge around the edge of your lawn, so you might need to occasionally get the string trimmer out. Every robot mower I’ve tested has also struggled to cut the area around the charging station, so I recommend placing the unit on a deck or pavement if possible.
Can I Install a Robot Mower Myself?
Yes, most robot mowers can be installed by anyone, but you might want to set aside an afternoon to work out any snags. Finding the best spot for the receiver for a satellite mower can be tricky. The mapping process can also take a while; usually, the mower will prompt you to remote-control it around the border you want to set. After the first mow, you should review its performance and make tweaks to ensure it’s covering the entire area you want to cut.
Can Robot Mowers Mow at Night?
Some models are capable of mowing at night in the dark using headlights, Lidar, and Time of Flight sensors, alongside their usual navigation capabilities. This can be convenient and also removes the risk for pets or children playing on the lawn during the day. However, there is a risk of injuring nocturnal wildlife, like hedgehogs in the UK and Europe. Mowers are also more likely to make mistakes and get stuck in the dark. It may be better to schedule mowing for dawn or dusk.
How I Test Robot Lawn Mowers
I test each robot lawn mower for at least a month, on at least two different lawn areas, assessing the ease of setup, the mapping process, automatic scheduling (where available), navigation, obstacle avoidance, and the quality of the final cut, looking for length, uniformity, and any missed patches. Where applicable, I try extra features, tweak settings in the app, and check how the mower handles different weather conditions. I also keep an eye on battery performance and charging time to ensure it aligns with the manufacturer's claims.

Drone-powered ad for PC Health chatbot slammed as 'dystopian' by some residents
Series of health-related questions appeared in skyline at around 11 p.m. Thursday
On Thursday night, drones lit up the sky above Toronto's waterfront displaying a list of health-related questions in what turned out to be an ad campaign for a new President's Choice AI-powered chatbot.
"Can Melatonin lose its effect?" read the display. "Do I really need 8 hours of sleep?"
"What are the symptoms of insomnia?" it asked, before displaying a QR code for the service.
The display, which began around 11 p.m. and lasted 15 minutes, advertised a free chat service, that PC Health, owned and operated by Loblaw Companies Limited, says uses Canadian clinical guidelines to provide a "convenient" way to ask health questions and get real-time information.
Not all residents thought the ad was convenient, however.
Videos of the ad near Fort York surfaced on social media, garnering a wide array of reactions. On Reddit, some users expressed disgust, with one replier saying "these need to be banned immediately." Another said it obstructed their view while driving on the Gardiner Expressway.
"What dystopian hell are we in for now?" asked local urban planner Sean Galbraith on CBC Radio’s As It Happens Friday. "Do we not have enough advertising along the highways and such that we have to now pollute the night sky with more ads?"
Ad inspired by what 'Canadians find themselves asking late at night': company
Galbraith, who learned of the ad after the fact, called it "horrible" and even "ironic."
"It being dynamic and having all that movement and being so large in the sky, it was a real problem," Galbraith said. "It was maximally disruptive."
"Are you having trouble sleeping with a drone show buzzing in the night sky?" he said.
In a statement to CBC Toronto, Loblaw Companies Limited said the drone show was inspired by "many questions Canadians find themselves asking late at night."
"The drone show held in the downtown core was designed to illuminate those moments of uncertainty," the company said. "Canadians have questions about their health and wellness and they're looking for trusted answers."
The company added all required permits were obtained.
Transport Canada told CBC News it regulates drones "based on the risk to aviation safety and the safety of people on the ground."
"Higher-risk" activities may require a special flight operations certificate for a remotely piloted aircraft system (SFOC-RPAS), spokesperson Sau Sau Liu said in an emailed statement Friday.
The agency said it did issue such a certificate for the ad campaign, "however, due to privacy requirements, the department cannot provide the information contained in the SFOC-RPAS application."
It also said it reviews all complaints and reports of drone violations to determine if an investigation is required, and that reports can be made through its online drone incident reporting tool.
Companies need to consider 'boundaries': resident
West-end local Jessica Matheson heard about the drone advertisement through social media.
"It definitely has a very dystopian vibe," she told CBC Toronto.
Matheson says the product is intriguing at a time of shortage of health-care practitioners and long wait times. But the drone show itself wasn't welcome, she said.
"This came out of nowhere. It was blatant advertising," Matheson said. "This is just literally plastered where everyone can see and not everyone wants to engage in constant advertisement."
Matheson says she hopes there will be more nuanced discussions about the use of drone shows as advertising.
"There still needs to be a relationship with people and how they want to view [a company’s] product," Matheson said. "You should seriously consider the ways you are marketing to people and not overstepping boundaries."
CBC Toronto has reached out to the city, Coun. Ausma Malik (Spadina-Fort York) and police for comment.
Meanwhile, Galbraith says the drone campaign is very different from billboard ads along Toronto’s waterfront because it wasn't static and draws attention away from what one might be doing.
"It's extremely tone-deaf on their part and really speaks poorly of what they think people in downtown Toronto should have to be subjected to," he said.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

In September 2026, a rumor circulated online about a black bear that apparently took a wounded raccoon, and later a wounded fox, to a wildlife center where the bear itself had been treated.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) said:
The first time, nobody believed it. Security cameras at a wildlife center captured a black bear approaching a rear entrance carrying a wounded raccoon in its mouth. It placed the animal gently beside the door. Then disappeared into the woods.
[…]
Several weeks later, cameras recorded a bear approaching a side entrance with an injured fox. Same careful approach. Same gentle placement near the door. Same quiet exit into the trees.
Both animals were found alive and received treatment.
Workers compared the two recordings. Both bears had the same unusual white mark on their chest. Same bear. Two deliveries. Two injured animals brought to the one place that could help them.
Staff searched old photographs and records of bears previously treated at the facility. That's when everything clicked.
Years earlier, the same bear had been rescued, treated at that very wildlife center, and released back into the wild. He had been a patient there. And now he was bringing patients back.
Officials believe the bear remembered where it had once been helped and returned because it somehow understood that injured animals would be safe there.
Other Facebook (archived) posts (archived) shared the same text. The black bear story also appeared in a YouTube short (archived).
Snopes readers sent emails and searched the website wondering whether the story was true.
There's no evidence supporting the rumor that a black bear took a wounded raccoon and a fox to a wildlife center it had previously received treatment at. It was posted online by a page with a history of posting heartwarming — though fictitious — animal stories generated with artificial intelligence tools.
As such, we've rated this claim false.
We searched Google for "bear brought raccoon to wildlife center" and "bear brought fox to wildlife center," and also searched DuckDuckGo, Bing and Yahoo using the same phrases. None of the searches yielded credible evidence supporting the story's veracity.
Snopes also used Google Lens to conduct a reverse image search on multiple different images posted alongside the story purportedly taken at the unidentified wildlife center.
That search revealed the story appeared to originate from the Facebook page StoryTime, which posted (archived) prior to the other social media posts linked in this fact check.
StoryTime's history
Snopes has been fact-checking StoryTime's animal rumors for more than a year. The page frequently posts fictitious, AI-generated animal stories supported by AI-generated images that are usually purposefully grainy and/or blurry, all meant to generate clicks because of their surprising or heartwarming nature.
At one time, the intro section on StoryTime's Facebook page read, "story (noun) - an account of imaginary or real people and events told for entertainment." At present, the page's intro section reads, "Animal rescue storytelling from around the world 🌎🐾 Real moments, inspired stories, and emotional second chances ❤️."
Facebook users can subscribe to the page using real money, which gives the page incentive to continue pumping out the animal stories it's known for, regardless of their reality.
AI-generated text
StoryTime's version of the claim begins with the headline "Wildlife Center Releases Statement After Bear Saves Two Injured Animals." StoryTime, much like the other Facebook pages telling the story, doesn't name the wildlife center or the worker quoted, or describe any geographic details about where these events took place. (Even without those identifiers, the wildlife center's statement, which isn't directly quoted in the post, should have showed up in search engine results, if real.)
When we input the text of StoryTime's version of the claim and that of another version of it into Pangram, which is widely considered the most reliable AI-text detection tool available as of this writing, it concluded that 100% of both versions were written or assisted by AI.
It's important to note that even the best AI detection tools can be fallible. Snopes cautions against using them to find definitive answers on the authenticity of texts or images without additional corroborating evidence.
AI-generated images
Each of the four Facebook posts linked in this story uses a different pair of images of the black bear carrying the raccoon and fox to the wildlife center, which is already a major red flag for the tale's authenticity.
In one version, the size of the object at the bottom left of the building's wall is sized differently in the pair of images presented.
In another version, the building is different in each of the two images presented. The bottom of the pair appears to depict a door opening inward from the right even though the door's handle is on its left side.
In a third version, the building and its door are once again inconsistent from one image to the other.
In StoryTime's version, neither the building, the stone patio nor the gravel-covered grounds around the building are the same between the pair of images.
The general lack of consistency between images is a telltale sign of AI generation, as artificial intelligence tools usually generate each image from scrap and therefore sometimes struggle in keeping details consistent when trying to emulate multiple images of the same place.
StoryTime does not keep its DMs open, leaving Snopes unable to contact the page for comment. StoryTime has not replied to past attempts by Snopes to contact the page's administrators, either.

Why isn't Canada blocking the Welland Canal? Other trade war questions answered
CBC News answers your questions about export taxes, sales bans and toilet paper
Reading through the emails that readers send to CBC News, one gets the impression they don't want just "elbows up" in the Canada-U.S. trade war, but also sticks, knees, skates and whatever else might be lying around.
One of the most common questions is some variation of, "Why isn't Canada doing X?" — where X is a tactic or tariff the reader supposes will hit the U.S. where it hurts.
Here's a look at some of those suggestions and what key players or observers have had to say about them.
Why doesn't Canada put export duties on energy as the cost is borne by Americans not Canadians?
Don Drummond, former chief economist for TD Bank, told CBC News late last month that export taxes are an option. Former prime minister Jean Chrétien said this week that an export tax on oil, gas, electricity and potash might be needed.
In 2025, Canadian commodities accounted for 63 per cent of oil imported into the U.S., 81 per cent of imported electricity, 99 per cent of imported natural gas and 80 per cent of imported potash.
However, Wolfgang Alschner, the Hyman Soloway Chair in Business and Trade Law at the University of Ottawa, warned that the long-term effects of such a move could be severe for Canada, both through lost revenue and damage to the relationship with its biggest customer. The U.S. could respond much as Canada has to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs: by trying to diversify away from a partner it can no longer count on and finding new suppliers.
- Canada has leverage in this trade fight, but economists warn it comes with a cost
- AnalysisThe art of inflicting pain: How to select targets for Canada's counter-tariffs
University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe and Christopher Ragan, founding director of McGill University's Max Bell School of Public Policy, made the same point separately: targeting U.S. energy could play into the hands of the U.S. administration and unite Americans against Canada.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said in July he doesn't "see the value" in using energy exports as a bargaining chip. Carney said being a reliable supplier is important.
"Canadians are reliable. Canadians can be trusted," he said.
Why not ban sales of certain goods in Canada?
This has mostly already happened at a provincial level with alcohol, in every province except Alberta and Saskatchewan. Saskatchewan this week added a retaliatory levy on U.S. alcohol.
Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has shown no interest in that sort of approach, stressing that Canada's response will be proportionate, strategic and targeted.
- Poilievre tells U.S. TV Canadians are 'wounded' and 'confused' to be in America's crosshairs
- Trade war, Alberta referendum loom large as Carney charts cabinet's year forward
The U.S. may, of course, reply in kind to any ban, as it has with alcohol: Most imports of Canadian-made alcohol will be banned from the United States on Sept. 29.
Tombe, discussing tariffs, told CBC News late last month that Canada has to be careful when selecting products to target because they need to be items Canadians can replace relatively easily but Americans cannot.
If tariffs are applied to harder-to-replace items — "a particular type of circuit board, say, or piece of machinery," that merely complicates life and increases costs for the Canadian importer, Tombe said.
Can Canada stop U.S. ships using the Welland Canal?
The Welland Canal is on the western half of the St. Lawrence Seaway, which connects the St. Lawrence River to the Great Lakes. The canal links Lake Ontario to Lake Erie using eight locks, all in Ontario, that can be filled with water or drained to move vessels between different water levels.
But the seaway is overseen by both the U.S. and Canada.
The Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation administers the seaway on the American side as a federal agency within the U.S. Department of Transportation.
In Canada, the federal government owns the Canadian portion of the seaway, but it is managed by the non-profit St. Lawrence Seaway Management Corporation.
The U.S. also controls several important locks, including ones in New York state between Lake Ontario and Montreal and others in Michigan that connect Lake Superior and Lake Huron.
John Boscariol, a Toronto-based co-head of international trade and investment law at the Canadian law firm McCarthy Tétrault, told CHCH News in Hamilton that closing the canal would be "shooting ourselves in the foot" and would hurt Canadian businesses just as much as U.S. businesses.
Trump critic Jennifer Hillman, formerly general counsel at the Office of the United States Trade Representative under then-president Bill Clinton, told CBC News Network it would "absolutely be a total violation of international law, and I think not really a good idea because you're blocking both sides' goods.
"I would hope that's not a road anybody would go down."
What questions do you have about the latest tariffs? Send an email to ask@cbc.ca.

Filming “The Uprising” gave British actor Woody Norman, who plays 14-year-old King Richard II in the historical fiction drama, a massive headache.
It turns out the only crown they had for him to use during the shoot got damaged the first day of filming. “So it didn’t fit my head,” Norman, 17, tells me over Zoom from a hotel room in Los Angeles just a few hours before the movie’s premiere at the DGA in West Hollywood. “I would leave every day with a splitting headache because it was bent. We had put foam in it, but it didn’t work. It was steel against my head.”
“The Uprising,” written and directed by Paul Greengrass, is based on the real-life Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 England. Andrew Garfield toplines the film as a fictional farmer – known only as Ploughman – who sparks and helps lead thousands of commoners on a march to protest the king in London.
Popular on Variety
In addition to the dented crown, Norman had to endure the royal wardrobe, including “really heavy” robes. “I don’t weigh much,” he tells me later on the red carpet at the premiere. “I weigh 46 kilograms [about 101 pounds] and they weigh as much as I do, so it was really really painful.”
Even so, it’s fun to be king. “It’s a power trip,” Norman says. “All of the supporting actors would go, ‘Your highness,’ and they would bow to me when I walked by. That really got to my head because they would do it every day.”
Norman’s first day shooting with Garfield was a pivotal fight scene between Ploughman and the king. “I was very intimidated,” Norman says. “It’s Andrew Garfield, you know that’s big. He immediately went, ‘I love you, and come on, come on!’ I was like, ‘OK,, we’re both actors. We can do this.’ It completely removed that sense of awe and made us both professionals. We’re here to do a job. Let’s do it together. I’m very, very grateful for that.”
The scene involved Ploughman shoving a paper scroll into the king’s mouth. “I have an Invisalign wire in my teeth,” Norman says. “The paper was in my teeth until after we wrapped. It was cool to rub my tongue on my on my teeth and go, ‘Oh, the uprising.’”
Norman first gained attention when he was just 10 years old and starred opposite Joaquin Phoenix in the 2021 Mike Mills drama “C’mon C’mon.” “One of the great men on the planet is Joaquin,” Norman says. “I don’t know if I would still be acting if I didn’t work with him.”
He continues, “I didn’t really understand what I was. I didn’t know I was an actor. I didn’t know this was a job. I was having fun, and then he made me realize that it doesn’t have to be a job. It’s a way of living. It’s a way of creating, and you know, now after working with Joaquin, I’m fully vegan because of course I am.”
Norman laughs.
“There was a interaction we had where I was eating meat and he was like, ‘Why don’t you just stop eating meat?’” he remembers. “And then I said, ‘Why don’t you stop smoking?’ He’s still smoking, so he hasn’t kept up his bit.”
Up next? Variety’s Leo Barraclough exclusively reported that Norman will star in the British urban horror thriller “Skag & Bone” along with Malachi Kirby, Tuppence Middleton, Conrad Khan, Kola Bokinni.
“The Uprising” is in theaters now.

President Donald Trump’s posts on social media and comments to the mainstream media are, to put it mildly, often difficult to interpret. If that were to be stated straightforwardly they can be bizarre, completely contrary to what is expected of the holder of the world’s most powerful office. But even by his own standards he excelled himself when on September 7, in a post on Truth Social, he placed the US flag over a large part of the Caribbean, Mexico, Canada, Greenland and Iceland. In the Caribbean the post covered British, French and Dutch territories too.
Reactions to the post varied. The government of Iceland was enraged. It summoned the US ambassador to protest against what it considered as an affront to its sovereignty. Its Prime Minister Kristrum Frostadottir said “There is nothing funny or normal about making fun, especially today, when sovereignty cannot be taken for granted”. Clearly, being in Europe but not part of the European Union–indeed, recently the people of Iceland decided against joining the EU—Frostadottir’s reference was to the Ukraine war.
The Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said that the people of Greenland had repeatedly made it clear that they do not want to be part of the US. Greenland is an autonomous part of Denmark. Its autonomy is increasing but the Danish connection is there; hence, Frederiksen had the right to comment on Trump’s post.
Mexico’s President, Claudia Shaunbaum, was also not amused by Trump’s post. She forthrightly said “Mexico will never be a protectorate or a colony”. The Mexicans are sometimes treated disrespectfully by the American administrations but in contemporary times never has any US president spoken so derisively about them. 
The Canadians do not seem to have reacted. This post has been part of a series of provocations which began with Trump asserting that Canada would be better off if it became a constituent state of the US. The two countries are in the midst of great tensions on trade. Both are taking action through imposing increasing tariffs against the other. Also, Trump has renamed Lake Ontario as Lake America. Canadian Prime Minister, Mike Carney, is dealing with Trump’s statements and actions through increasing the country’s contacts with other states to reduce its dependence on the US. He has also maintained dignity in his responses to Trump.
The Caribbean states and the Dutch, British and the French seem to be brushing off Trump’s comment. Perhaps that is not a bad way of dealing with it because it is puerile but is unlikely that the people of various states which are sensitive on issues of sovereignty consider it so. This is because sovereignty is always connected with a people’s pride and self-esteem. Trump should understand this but does not. 
Trump’s latest tweet raises the issue of how countries should react to Trump’s provocative comments. The respected US daily The New York Times in its report on the matter stated that Iceland’s Foreign Minister Katrin Gunnarsdottir told reporters “...Trump administration officials had repeatedly offered her advice about their boss: “We should perhaps not take the current U.S. president literally, but we should take him seriously,” she said she was told”.
During Trump’s first term he tweeted erratically in the early hours of the morning. US officials spent the day attempting to clarify US policies and positions amidst the confusion and even turmoil which the tweets caused. From that to saying that Trump’s words and posts should be taken seriously but not literally is making confusion worse. For, if they are not taken literally then how he be taken seriously? 
The fact is that while leaders may not be dour and drab and like ordinary people laugh and crack jokes on domestic and foreign policy matters they do not have the luxury of creating confusion or wounding the honour of other peoples. Certainly, this has to be avoided, especially by the leaders of great powers, because their words can wreak havoc nationally and internationally in the security, financial and diplomatic sectors, among others. 
That is why in the pre social media age leaders seldom spoke off the cuff. When they spoke each word was carefully chosen because they represented the distilled decisions of their countries. These decisions were not easily or often changed. In the realm of foreign relations the official positions of states were left to be stated, in the normal course, by official spokespersons of the Foreign Ministries. The top professional diplomats of the Foreign Ministries also briefed the media on important issues. On very major issues the Foreign Ministers spoke and sometimes on issues of vital importance Heads of Governments articulated their views. 
Now this structure remains but alongside social media is also used by political leaders and Foreign Ministries. Thus, in India the Spokesperson of the Foreign Ministries uses social media platforms but not the professional diplomats. However, the External Affairs Minister and the Prime Minister have social media handles and invariably post comments on their meetings with other world leaders. More often than not these are of an innocuous nature and consist of ‘good words’. It seems that political leaders all across the world feel the need to be on social media, if for nothing else, than to be in touch with their followers. Certainly, Modi has millions of them.
While all political leaders tread warily on global issues and do not give offence in their choice of words on social media platforms Trump is a case apart. He will not change and the world will have to deal with his ways. Different leaders are seeking to do so in different ways.
