The U.S.-Canada trade war is creating a headache for auto-parts makers
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
The U.S. and Canadian auto industries have been tightly woven together for decades. But the latest tariff flareup between the two countries may complicate that.
Think of that sticker on the windows of new cars breaking down how much of the vehicle's content comes from the U.S. and Canada. From a manufacturing point of view, content from both places has long been considered deeply intertwined.
But the U.S. and Canada failed to reach a new trade deal this summer, and the trade war between them has escalated quickly. In August, the U.S. enacted new tariffs on aluminum and steel, and President Trump has also threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel effective on Jan. 1. On Tuesday, Canada enacted retaliatory tariffs on a variety of U.S. goods — including on American steel and aluminum.
All of this puts the auto manufacturing industry in a jam.
For major U.S. carmakers, analysts say, the tariffs introduce uncertainty as companies determine whether to adjust their supply chains in the long run, or to absorb new costs in the short term. But for the smaller businesses that supply those big companies with thousands of parts — think bolts, or the steel rods for steering wheels — the tariffs could spell bigger, more expensive trouble.
" It's really, really damaging to the industry and to the financials of the industry. It makes planning for things very difficult," says Dan Hearsch, global co-leader of automotive and industrial at the consulting firm AlixPartners.
For these companies, he says, the new tariffs follow years of chaos — the aftermath of Covid supply chain shortages, the start-and-stop ramp up to making more electric vehicles, the need to grapple with pre-existing tariffs.
"It's one more thing, on top of the one more thing, that was on top of the one more thing, that was on top of the one more thing," Hearsch says.
The U.S. and Canada's auto relationship
The U.S. and Canada started weaving their auto supply chains together in 1965, when they signed a pact with a goal of consolidating their auto industries and expanding their combined market. The pact removed duties on auto products or equipment crossing the border when they are made of at least 50% of U.S. or Canadian content.
Their trade relationship deepened with the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement, which included Mexico and removed many duties between the three countries, as long as they contained a certain proportion of North American parts. The 2020 United States Mexico Canada Agreement, which revised that deal, included a requirement that auto content be 75% North American to be able to pass borders without any tariff.
For the auto industry, the free flow of many goods meant that components could be assembled in plants in each country, and ultimately combined in another. The auto supply chain grew into a single ecosystem.
"I've often described it like an omelet" with ingredients from all three countries, says Jim Jarrell, president and CEO of Linamar Corporation, a Canadian manufacturing company that handles both auto and agricultural products.
"Think about a casting that starts in Mexico and that gets sent into the U.S. to get processed. That part then jumps over to Canada to get further processed," says Jarrell, referring to a molded piece of metal. "Then we ship it back into the U.S. sub-assembly, to get it finished and assembled," Jarrell says.
"And that story is, quite frankly, not unusual," he continues. "That is actually how the industry works."
Linamar Corporation has a roughly equal number of plants in the U.S. and in Canada, but they also have plants in Mexico and in Asia, Jarrell says. And each of them make slightly different things, Jarrell says, making it potentially difficult to alter those supply chains in response to new tariffs — or the threat of additional tariffs in January.
To alter where or how parts are made would mean re-evaluating entire supply chains, Jarrell says. "So it's a lot of cost and time."
Aisin Corporation, one of the world's largest transmission makers and suppliers, is based in Japan, but does about 20% of its business in North America, and often moves materials back and forth as their supply chain warrants it. " We've always looked at North America as totally North America, not Canada-specific or U.S.- specific," says Chuck Sanders, the executive vice president for the company's North American division. " When there's rapid changes or new tariffs that are introduced suddenly," he continues, "that kind of creates chaos on the business."
Shifting production means moving jobs around. That's a problem both the company and its workers would like to avoid. "We want to continue the business so they have a long-term future with us," Sanders says.
The effect on the auto-part supply chain
Cars are made with tons — literal tons — of steel and aluminum, and with thousands of parts. How many? It depends on when you stop counting.
For instance, take a steering wheel. There's a metal rod, often padded in leather or vinyl. Then there are sensors, an airbag, an instrument cluster with "lots of dials and things that move," Hearsch from AlixPartners says. In that steering wheel system, he says, "There's probably 50 to 100 different parts coming from all over the world."
Manufacturers occupy different tiers within the automotive supply chain. "Tier one is a supplier that delivers a part or a system to the automaker," Hearsch says. Think of a headlamp, for example. " A tier two is a company who makes something that goes to a tier one" — the smaller pieces that make up a headlamp, he says. And then a tier three company feeds parts to tier two.
Any of these components might be made from raw metals like steel and aluminum, which could have been subject to tariffs when they were first imported to North America. Now, those components could be subject to additional tariffs as they repeatedly move across the border.
For now, many auto suppliers are taking a watch-and-wait stance. Bosch and Magna, two of the biggest suppliers to North American companies, emailed NPR statements saying that they are monitoring the situation and its potential effects, particularly on customers.
The Motor & Equipment Manufacturers Association trade group also wrote in an emailed statement that it's "concerned by the continued escalation of trade actions between the United States and Canada."
"The vehicle supplier industry has built deeply interconnected North American supply chains over decades, and policies that increase costs or create barriers ultimately weaken the competitiveness of the entire region as we face challenging global competition," the statement continued.
That global competition comes from the makers of Chinese electric vehicles, which are becoming increasingly popular, says economist Sue Helper, who studies the auto industry at Case Western Reserve University.
Like Hearsch, she says the uncertainties of the post-Covid supply chain and the transition to EVs, as well as potential disruptions from AI, make it hard for automakers to decide when to make changes to their supply chains, so they "don't make the wrong investment and don't jump too soon or too late," she says. "So it's a really difficult time. It's always a tough business, but it's particularly tough right now."
"The challenge is that the automotive industry does not move at the speed of politics," says Sean Tucker, an editor at Cox Automotive, an automotive services and technology provider. It takes time for automakers to reconfigure their supply chains — or decide whether they should, since tariff policy could change under a future presidential administration.
If Canada and the U.S. do manage to disentangle their supply chains, Jarrell of Linamar says, it could cost years — and a lot of money for auto-parts makers. "The more uncertainty there is, obviously the harder it becomes to invest and grow in a confident way," he says.

Pink had fallen silent in the face of backlash from many quarters following her reposting a call for Macklemore to be dropped from the Ed Sheeran tour in the wake of his nightly pro-Palestinian songs and statements. Now she has spoken up about the controversy and her part in it in a big way, with a 1,300-word social media post that has her exploring why she repeated the sentiments asking Sheeran to drop Macklemore, why his statements alarmed her as a Jewish woman, and how it has felt “lonely” facing an onslaught of criticism this week.
The singer noted that she may have been a typical “cheap and fast” social media user when she first reposted the anti-Macklemore meme, rather than speaking up in her own words, which she is now belatedly doing. “A repost isn’t a statement, and a meme isn’t a spine,” she argued, saying that she would “rather be disagreed with for what I actually said than hated for what anybody else wrote, so let me say it.”
Popular on Variety
Pink noted how her feelings about Macklemore have evolved, from support for him when “I was in the room at the Grammys in 2014 when Macklemore rapped ‘Same Love’ and 33 couples, gay and straight, got married to it, and I cheered, no questions asked.” Then, she pointed out an antisemitic costume the rapper wore a short time later, for which he subsequently issued a mea culpa. “Macklemore put on a hooked nose, a black beard and a bowl cut, performed in it, and called it a ‘random costume.’ Every Jew I know knew exactly what it was. The same love, it turned out, had a guest list, and we weren’t on it. But he apologized, and I let it go, because that’s what we do. We let it go.” Nonetheless, she suggested, his wearing of the costume informed how his statements might be received in years to come.
The singer said that “last weekend he stood in front of a stadium full of music-loving families, with violent images from a war on the screens, dedicated a song to the movement of his choice, and then took the mic to tell all of the Jews in the stadium that it wasn’t about them.” She added: “You don’t get to decide that for us.”
Her current position, as she explained it in her post: “Of course I don’t speak for Israel, or for any government. I never have. What I said in October 2023 is still exactly what I believe: Hamas is a terrorist organization. Palestinians deserve a future that honors their humanity and their aspirations. Protecting innocent life comes first, everywhere, and nobody should ever celebrate the death of a child. Anybody’s child. I’ve spent a decade as a UNICEF ambassador for kids who didn’t choose the country or the war they were born into, and I have grieved every one of them, on both sides of that fence. I didn’t do it from behind a screen; I went to those children and held them. I’m not going to litigate a complex war in an Instagram caption, and I’m not going to recite anybody’s slogan to earn back a follower.”
The singer declared that her response earlier this week was prompted not by Macklemore saying “Free Palestine,” but by his statements on stage — in response to the backlash he was facing from some quarters — that his statements were aimed at Israel, not all Jews.
“That’s what prompted my repost. Not ‘Free Palestine,’ and not anyone’s right to say it. I have never asked for another artist to be silenced and I’m not asking now. I don’t need anyone fired, and I don’t need a refund. What I need is to be able to say, as a Jewish mom, ‘that scared me, and it scared people I love,”’without being told our fear is just propaganda, and without being told I’m somehow cool with genocide because I noticed?”
	Pink pointed to some of the causes she has supported over the years that have drawn fire, mostly from the right wing. “I have stood up for other people’s people my whole career, and I know exactly what it costs. And now I’m standing up for my own people, and I thought I knew going in how lonely that would be. And it’s lonelier than that. But I’m doing it anyway.”
She added, “Something has changed in this country, and I can read it in my own comments. ‘From the river to the sea.’ ‘Zionist,’ spat like it’s a slur, by people who couldn’t tell you the details of what I believe, because I hadn’t told them yet. I wasn’t asked. I was told. I don’t think most of them hate Jews. I think somebody handed them a story where the Jew who won’t apologize for existing must be the villain, and they’ve been putting words in my mouth ever since.”
On her Instagram post, Pink divided her lengthy statement into two parts, the first half of it coming in the post itself and the second in the comments. But the second half is no longer visible. An hour or so after posting, as pro and con responses accumulated from fans and detractors, she opted to switch off commenting for that post. Unfortunately for her ability to explain herself, cutting off comments meant she also eliminated her own comment that contained the crux of her explanation. But you can read it all below, including the part she inadvertently deleted.
Before Pink or her social administrator cut off comments on her post, the responses were sharply divided, with mostly hostile or disappointed comments appearing at the top of the replies, followed by many supportive ones echoing her “Shana tova” sign-off further down. Among the negative replies, before all were blocked: “A repost is a statement. Just saying. (esp w 11M followers).” “Said all this to say nothing at all. This was truly not on my bingo card. Doubling down is insane as well.” “I grew up respecting your rebellion against things that were wrong in the world. But now you seem to have switched to supporting those very same people that cause the pain to children and women. I hope that is how you want to be remembered.”
And a sampling of the positive replies: “This was beautiful. And not trite. And not prepared by AI or a publicist. This was an authentic monologue and I appreciate so much how strong you are. And I’m proud to have you in my same tribe.” “I wish all other Jewish celebrities were as brave as you. We love you.”
In his most recent comments addressing the controversy, Macklemore said, “To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality…. So I say free Palestine, I say free Lebanon, I say free Cuba, I say free Congo, free Sudan, I say free all people in America living in fear of this terrorist organization, ICE. None of us will be free until we are all free.”
Pink’s statement, in full:
	I’ve been quiet in my own words for a week, which you know isn’t like me. So here they are.
Last Sunday I reposted somebody else’s post about Macklemore’s set at Ed Sheeran’s show. It said things in words I didn’t write, and I wouldn’t have chosen all of them. Then the comments came, and I did what I do when I’m hurt, which is post snarky memes and act like I’m fine. That’s on me. A repost isn’t a statement, and a meme isn’t a spine. Social media makes all of us cheap and fast, and we all know it. But I’d rather be disagreed with for what I actually said than hated for what anybody else wrote, so let me say it.
I was born a Jew. I didn’t pick it, and I’ve never hidden it. And this week a whole lot of people decided what I believe without asking me, without checking a single thing I’ve ever said or done, because a repost and the word “Jew” were apparently enough to fill in the rest. But let me fill it in… myself.
Of course I don’t speak for Israel, or for any government. I never have. What I said in October 2023 is still exactly what I believe: Hamas is a terrorist organization. Palestinians deserve a future that honors their humanity and their aspirations. Protecting innocent life comes first, everywhere, and nobody should ever celebrate the death of a child. Anybody’s child. I’ve spent a decade as a UNICEF ambassador for kids who didn’t choose the country or the war they were born into, and I have grieved every one of them, on both sides of that fence. I didn’t do it from behind a screen; I went to those children and held them. I’m not going to litigate a complex war in an Instagram caption, and I’m not going to recite anybody’s slogan to earn back a follower.
Here’s what I was reacting to. I was in the room at the Grammys in 2014 when Macklemore rapped “Same Love” and thirty-three couples, gay and straight, got married to it, and I cheered, no questions asked. Four months later Macklemore put on a hooked nose, a black beard and a bowl cut, performed in it, and called it a “random costume.” Every Jew I know knew exactly what it was. The same love, it turned out, had a guest list, and we weren’t on it. But he apologized, and I let it go, because that’s what we do. We let it go. Then last weekend he stood in front of a stadium full of music-loving families, with violent images from a war on the screens, dedicated a song to the movement of his choice, and then took the mic to tell all of the Jews in the stadium that it wasn’t about them.
You don’t get to decide that for us.
That’s what prompted my repost. Not “Free Palestine,” and not anyone’s right to say it. I have never asked for another artist to be silenced and I’m not asking now. I don’t need anyone fired, and I don’t need a refund. What I need is to be able to say, as a Jewish mom, “that scared me, and it scared people I love,” without being told our fear is just propaganda, and without being told I’m somehow cool with genocide because I noticed?
And please don’t talk to me like I’ve never stood up for my beliefs when it was unpopular. In the middle of the Gulf War in 2006 I put out a song called “Dear Mr. President” and sang it every night on tour while my country was in a war I didn’t support, and I took the hate for it, and I sang it anyway because my sharp criticism was of a government, not this flawed country I love and who my dad fought for. I stood with gay kids before it was fashionable and with trans kids now, when it isn’t, and with their families, and I handed out the books that got banned, and you know I got called every name there is, and I’d do all of it again tomorrow. I have stood up for other people’s people my whole career, and I know exactly what it costs.
	And now I’m standing up for my own people, and I thought I knew going in how lonely that would be. And it’s lonelier than that. But I’m doing it anyway.
Something has changed in this country, and I can read it in my own comments. “From the river to the sea.” “Zionist,” spat like it’s a slur, by people who couldn’t tell you the details of what I believe, because I hadn’t told them yet. I wasn’t asked. I was told. I don’t think most of them hate Jews. I think somebody handed them a story where the Jew who won’t apologize for existing must be the villain, and they’ve been putting words in my mouth ever since.
But I’ve been portrayed as the villain before. I can take it. I just won’t take it quietly, and I’m not going to teach my kids to.
So, to the ones who are furious with me: you don’t have to agree with me. You never did. That’s been our unspoken agreement for twenty-five years, and it still stands, and so do I. You don’t have to agree with one thing Israel’s government does to not want the Jewish family two rows down from you to be scared or targeted at a concert. That’s the only thing I’m asking anybody for. To the ones who are frightened this week, Jewish or Muslim or Palestinian or Israeli or just tired of all of it: I see you. And if anybody wants to really know what I think, just ask me. I’m right here. I’ve never been hard to find. And I’ll keep speaking out, in my own words.
It’s Friday. For working people who have more to worry about than pop stars and pile-ons, it’s the end of a hard week. It’s also the 25th anniversary of September 11th, and my prayers are with the innocent souls we lost that morning. And at sundown, for Jews, it’s Rosh Hashanah, our New Year.
Now I’m going to go make dinner for my kids, light the candles, dip some apples in honey, pour a glass of wine and be full of gratitude. That’s my tradition. It also happens to be a Jewish one.
Shana tova.

Walmart truly updated its privacy policy on Aug. 20, 2026, adding one new descriptor for how the company handles voice interactions occurring on Walmart.com and in the company's mobile app. Also, the retail giant has truly replaced traditional price tags with digital shelf labels in thousands of its stores. However …
… Walmart added mentions of biometrics, geolocation, household income and other descriptors years earlier. The privacy policy specifies Walmart "may collect or receive" personal information based on various products and services used, as well as that not all categories of personal information will be collected or received about every customer.
No evidence credibly confirms Walmart engages in misuse of customer data involving the practice of using in-store digital shelf labels for surveillance pricing, a term defined as the act of raising or lowering prices on a per-customer basis based on previously gathered personal data.
In late August and early September 2026, social media users alleged Walmart had recently updated its corporate privacy policy with concerning information, likening the purported changes to a dystopian future.
According to users' posts, the retail giant added numerous bullet points to its privacy policy about the types of sensitive personal data the company collects, for example biometrics, geolocation and household income. Users claimed Walmart added the language to engage in surveillance pricing — raising and lowering prices on a per-customer, digital-footprint basis — through the use of new in-store 
Essentially, users claimed that prices on a store shelf would change, with the potential for price gouging, depending on the data previously collected from the customer walking near specific products.
For example, on Aug. 31, 
The user displayed Walmart's privacy policy page, detailing data collection and reception practices involving customers' IP addresses, household income, voice prints, facial imagery, palm prints, fingerprints and more. The user also mentioned descriptors about inferences related to shopping patterns and behaviors, automated license plate readers and in-store cameras.
Other users shared the rumor on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), TikTok (archived) and X (archived). Snopes readers also emailed us seeking information about the claim.
In sum, this rumor is a mixture of truth, falsehood and unproven speculation.
While Walmart did update its privacy policy in August 2026, the mentions of biometrics, geolocation, household income and other descriptors were added years earlier. No evidence credibly confirms Walmart engages in misuse of customer data for surveillance pricing.
Walmart spokesperson Kelly Hellbusch pointed us to the company's full privacy policy, which contains some information users failed to include in their posts and videos.
Privacy policies for other big-box retailers feature some of the same data collection descriptors as Walmart, including Costco, The Home Depot, Ikea, Lowe's and Target.
Digging into the misleading rumor
Walmart truly updated its privacy policy on Aug. 20, 2026. The update added only one new descriptor laying out how the company handles voice interactions occurring on Walmart.com and in the company's mobile app, including receiving only text transcriptions, not using voice data for biometric analysis and capturing a voice only when a customer interacts with a voice feature, such as a search.
Earlier in 2026, the retail giant truly announced the installation of new digital price tags on shelves in thousands of its stores, eliminating the need for workers to manually update many printed labels.
However, a check of website archives found that mentions of biometrics, geolocation, household income and other data have been part of Walmart's privacy policy for years. For example, 
Walmart's privacy policy specifies the retailer "may collect or receive" — meaning not only collect — personal information based on various products and services used, as well as that not all categories of personal information will be collected or received about every customer.
As some users' posts mentioned, the company also added details about the usage of automated license plate readers — in 2024. The policy cited efforts to "ensure security, prevent theft and fraud, and to help maintain the safety of individuals and properties."
Regarding biometrics, Harvard Business School has reported most consumer devices, such as smartphones, securely store fingerprints and face-scan data on the device itself. "The fingerprint or face scan is converted into a mathematical template, which is kept in a protected part of the hardware. Apps simply get a 'yes/no' from the system: 'Did the biometric match?' They never see your actual fingerprint or face image."
In August 2026, Courthouse News Service reported the details of a lawsuit against Walmart about the alleged collection and storing of "a voice print or biometric identifier" from people calling the company's customer service phone line.
For further reading, we previously reported the facts about whether Target uses a Bluetooth device on its baskets that tracks in-store shoppers.

The genetics of one's personality, or gene variants that predict it, could be more relevant to human experience and associated with health, education, career paths, among other major life outcomes, new research suggests.
An international team of researchers forming the Revived Genomics of Personality Consortium combined results from 46 distinct cohorts around the world to study the genetic basis of personality.
Findings published in the journal Nature show that more than 1,200 gene variants are associated with the Big Five personality traits -- openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism -- and that the personality genetics are linked to dozens of life outcomes, including health behaviours.
The DNA of two randomly selected people is approximately 99.9% identical -- differences in the remaining 0.1 per cent of the genome can influence individual traits, including appearance, disease risk, and the body's response to medications, the researchers said.
The small amount of genetic variation may also be linked to several personality traits, they found.
The authors wrote, "(Genetic) analyses indicate that personality traits have widespread, potentially causal associations with consequential behaviours and life outcomes." "There is no single 'personality gene'," lead author Ted Schwaba, faculty at Michigan State University's Department of Psychology, said.
"Personality traits are associated with many genetic variants, but even the largest effects of individual genetic variants are still very small. However, even though any individual genetic variant makes very little difference in personality, the effects of many variants together can be more sizeable," Schwaba said.
For example, the same variants linked to extraversion in a young adult in the Netherlands also predicted extraversion in an older adult retiree in the U.S., the study found.
The researchers used methods that compared relatives to one another and "confirmed" that the genetic links weren't actually the byproduct of a shared upbringing.
However, despite the genetic associations, environment was still found to play a major role in personality.
For example, the study found that common genetic variants linked to openness to experience predicted that a person would move to more cosmopolitan neighbourhoods. In turn, living in those neighbourhoods may reinforce and further shape that same trait.
The researchers noted that the genetics of personality are relevant to many parts of the human experience.
The genetic variants that predict personality can also partially predict mental and physical health, longevity, education, career paths and outcomes and even how people are perceived by close others, they said.
Genetic variants linked to conscientiousness were associated with being more active during the day, while variants linked to openness to experience and extraversion were linked to being more of a night owl.
"Personality seems to be relevant nearly everywhere you look. We hope this study will encourage many other scientists to incorporate personality traits into their fields of study," Schwaba said.
"For example, genetic variants associated with neuroticism predict more time spent in the hospital, which is relevant to physicians and health researchers, and variants associated with openness to experience are linked to income and switching jobs, which is relevant to vocational researchers," Schwaba said.

Emergency responders have rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate operations as authorities continued to search for thousands of people missing 10 days after massive floods hit Nepal.
The Nepali military said on Saturday a joint team comprising personnel from its army and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre (740ft) tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Pictures showed him being evacuated by helicopter after being carried out of the tunnel.
Rescue efforts have focused on a dozen hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing, 500 of whom are thought to be trapped in huge tunnels. International rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the US have been searching through debris and damaged structures at the projects to try to find survivors.
Two Nepali workers were rescued from another tunnel in a hydro-station on the Trishuli River on Friday.
Experts have said the possibility of finding missing people alive in the tunnels is diminishing.
The Nepali woman, 64, was rescued from a damaged house in the devastated town of Nuwakot. Photos published by the Nepali army showed rescuers discovering the woman submerged in mud before she was pulled to safety and airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment. 
 Members of Nepal’s police force cheered as she was pulled from the home, the lower half of which was buried in thick sludge.
Emergency responders have been working to find survivors from the devastating floods in Nepal, which were triggered by a glacial and rock collapse on 26 August. Their work has been complicated by the massive infrastructural damage caused by the floods, with more than 40 bridges having collapsed and rivers swelling unpredictably.
At least 1,375 people have been killed in the floods, with more than 5,000 missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

The latest Avatar: Seven Havens trailer gives us a deeper dive into the characters and story
It's also pretty easy on the eyes.
We are less than a month away from the premiere of a brand new show in the Avatar-verse, which is happening 12 full years after The Legend of Korra ended its run. Avatar: Seven Havens starts streaming via Paramount+ on October 9 and we finally have a real beefy trailer to get us pumped.
We got some footage back in July, but that was more of a teaser. This is nearly three minutes of the show, complete with character voices and plenty of hints as to where the story is going. The animation also looks very nice, which is typical for the franchise.
The story looks steeped in post-apocalyptic flavor. Something bad happened after the events of The Legend of Korra and the world is in shambles, forcing survivors to retreat to the titular seven havens. As a matter of fact, Korra is being blamed for these events (which is on brand) so public sentiment has shifted negatively toward the entire concept of Avatars.
Enter Avatar Pavi, a young girl who will likely have to go on the run once people figure out her identity. She has a twin sister, which could be setting up some wild spirit world shenanigans. Just like the other shows, she has a friend group that (hopefully) has her back.
For the uninitiated, this franchise started with Avatar: The Last Airbender more than 20 years ago. Each of the following shows introduces a new Avatar, after the previous one has died. It's a Dalai Lama type of thing, but with element-based superpowers.
The Legend of Korra was set a full 70 years after the first one. The showrunners of Seven Havens, including franchise co-creator Michael Dante DiMartino, recently confirmed to Polygon that it takes place a full 200 years after Korra. That likely means we won't be getting older versions of supporting Korra characters, like the bad-ass grandma Toph and old-man Zuko in that series. How did Korra live that long? We'll find out, though it's not unheard of in the lore.
The first three episodes drop on October 9, with the show following a weekly release schedule after that. It's already been renewed, so two 13-episode seasons are coming our way.
This has been a busy year for the franchise. We just got a movie that followed the adult version of Avatar Aang. It was pretty awesome, even if it did leak in its entirety online months before it came out. The second season of the live-action Netflix show also dropped earlier this year, with a third and final one on the way.

iPhone 18 Pro vs Pixel 11 Pro: How Apple and Google's flagships stack up
More AI, better cameras and few reasons to switch ecosystems.
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro are the latest examples of a familiar story: Apple and Google refining, rather than reinventing, mature flagship smartphones. Both are expensive, powerful phones with top-notch screens, three rear cameras and (like it or not) an ever-growing list of AI features. They both come in two sizes and have similar price tags.
There are still plenty of subtle differences. But neither phone likely gives you a compelling reason to switch ecosystems. If you're happy with how your iPhone plays nicely with your MacBook, iPad, Apple Watch and AirPods, there's no reason to jump ship to Android. Ditto for the Pixel if you're invested in Google's devices and services.
While the ecosystem question is easy, there's still plenty to learn from the details. Let's line them up and see where they differ.
Design and dimensions
Design-wise, both phones (mostly) stay the course. The Pixel keeps its signature full-width camera bar, but adds edge-to-edge glass for a more seamless look. Its aluminum frame matches the phone's color, whether you go with Canyon, Fog, Olive or Obsidian.
The Pixel also has an easy-to-overlook improvement: the new camera bar keeps the phone more stable and balanced on a table. It's not exactly a marquee feature, but "doesn't wobble annoyingly on a flat surface" may be more useful than half the things that get stage time at launch events.
Then there's the iPhone 18 Pro, with its familiar aluminum unibody. It has a Ceramic Shield back, which can help with durability. The phone comes in black, silver and two new additions: Glacier (an icy blue) and Burgundy.
The smaller phones in each line weigh nearly the same. The Pixel 11 Pro weighs 7.2 ounces, slightly lighter than the iPhone 18 Pro's 7.44 ounces. The discrepancy grows a bit with the larger models: at 8 ounces, the Pixel 11 Pro XL is nearly nine percent lighter than the 8.78-ounce iPhone 18 Pro Max.
Elsewhere, the size differences are subtle enough not to worry about. The standard Pixel is slightly taller and narrower than the iPhone, while the Pixel 11 Pro XL is a tad shorter and narrower than the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Google lists both Pixels as 0.04 inches thinner, though that might be more about rounding than anything else.
Displays
Both phones have OLED displays with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz, so that shouldn't be your deciding factor. The Pixel 11 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro both have 6.3-inch screens, while the larger models differ only slightly: 6.8 inches for the Pixel 11 Pro XL and 6.9 inches for the iPhone 18 Pro Max. (That's roughly 4.5 percent more screen area, for those keeping score.)
Google claims a peak brightness of 3,600 nits, compared with the iPhone's 3,000 nits outdoors. But the companies use different measurement techniques, so that isn't quite an apples-to-apples comparison. Regardless, both phones are bright enough that this shouldn't sway your decision.
Google added a new anti-scratch coating this year, which it says more than doubles scratch resistance. Apple brought back last year's Ceramic Shield 2, which works towards the same goal. It also has an anti-reflective coating, something Google doesn't advertise for the Pixel.
Apple also made the Dynamic Island smaller and a bit more useful, now showing up to three Live Activities at once. The Pixel 11 Pro's punch-out camera is smaller still, but it's worth remembering that the tech Apple includes for Face ID takes up more space than just a camera lens. And the iPhone's screen can dim to as little as 1 nit.
Resolutions are in the same ballpark, with the Pixel phones having a slightly higher pixel density: 495 ppi for the Pixel 11 Pro and 486 ppi for the Pixel 11 Pro XL, compared with 460 ppi for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. As with brightness, both are sharp enough that this won't push you in one direction or the other.
Cameras
Both companies offer the same camera system in each size, so fortunately, you don't have to buy a bigger phone just to get a better camera. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL pair a 50MP main camera with 48MP ultra-wide and 5x telephoto lenses. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have three 48MP rear cameras, including a 4x telephoto that can also produce an 8x "optical-quality" shot.
Google's photography approach increasingly relies on AI to make more decisions for you, whether that's how it handles lighting conditions or how much detail it recovers or generates. The Pixel's Instant Night Sight can capture low-light photos much faster than before, a handy feature for night shooters. Its 5x Portrait Mode uses the telephoto lens to shoot portraits from farther away. Pro Zoom extends digital zoom to 120x. However, its results can sometimes be a bit too uncanny: think birds with suspiciously well-groomed feathers.
Apple's angle is more about user control. This year's Pro-series iPhones add a variable-aperture main camera. (You can actually see the blades move!) The feature could lead to better low-light photos and more control over depth of field. It can choose the aperture for you, so you don't have to know the ins and outs of advanced photography. But pro users can still control the aperture manually. Apple also added new manual controls for shutter speed and white balance, plus a histogram.
There's an ironic role reversal here. Android has historically been the platform for people who like to customize and tinker with advanced settings, while Apple has been more comfortable crafting a specific experience. But with cameras, Google increasingly uses AI to make decisions for you, while Apple's approach hands the user more control. It's a topsy-turvy world.
Elsewhere, Apple's new Reference Image feature seems designed to stay ahead of growing AI fakery. In Reference mode, the camera captures signed sensor data that Private Cloud Compute develops into an unalterable reference image. It's essentially a digital negative showing what the sensor originally saw. You can still edit the photo, of course, but the signed reference remains as something to compare against.
The iPhone appears to have a clear edge with video. The Pixel 11 Pro can shoot 8K through Video Boost, with tools like Night Sight Video and Pro Stable Video. But the iPhone courts professional videographers, with 4K Dolby Vision up to 120 fps, ProRes RAW, Apple Log 2, external recording and genlock. Most buyers won't need any of that. But those who do will appreciate the advanced options.
AI: Gemini and New Siri
Google's phones have been all-in on AI for several generations now, so the Pixel 11 Pro is arguably more mature in this area. It runs Gemini Nano on-device and adds features like Rambler, which cleans up dictated text as you speak. Magic Capture can shoot a short scene and pick out the still photos it thinks are worth saving, while Circle to Search now works directly from the camera.
On the whole, the Pixel seems more inclined to proactively suggest AI actions across the phone. Some of these tools might be genuinely useful; others feel more like product teams seeing how much AI they can stuff into every corner.
Apple is taking a narrower approach, focusing more on making Siri useful when you need it. It can draw on personal context from messages, email, photos and whatever is on your screen to answer questions or take actions. It can also perform tasks across apps, and a new Siri mode in the Camera app can identify or otherwise act on what you see.
Apple developed some of the underlying models in collaboration with Google, so you may be getting at least a taste of Gemini no matter which phone you use. But Siri isn't simply running the same Gemini models you'll find on a Pixel.
In iOS 27, Apple is also adding generative photo tools, Safari website monitoring and better camera-based visual search. But keep in mind that Siri AI is launching in beta, won't initially be available in the EU and some server-based features have daily usage limits. Most iCloud+ plans offer higher usage allowances for heavy users.
Performance and battery
Both phones have new chips with different strengths. Google says Tensor G6 brings faster app launches, web browsing and on-device AI. With the iPhone's A20 Pro chip, Apple is claiming a breakthrough in sustained performance, thanks in part to a larger vapor chamber. That could help with gaming, video editing or other demanding workloads. In practice, though, both will be plenty fast for everyday use.
Battery comparisons are harder to gauge right now because the companies use different tests. (Plus, the new iPhones aren't yet available for first-hand testing.) Google rates both Pixel 11 Pro models for more than 30 hours of use, while Apple claims up to 24 hours for the iPhone 18 Pro and 30 hours for the Pro Max. The larger phones are the safer bets if battery life is a priority.
Apple makes a more aggressive fast-charging claim, with the new models going from 0 to 50 percent in about 15 minutes. Google says the Pixel 11 Pro XL can reach 75 percent in about 30 minutes. Naturally, you'll need the right power adapter to hit those speeds.
Which should you buy?
Pricing is close across the board, but Google has an advantage with the smaller phones. The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099, while the iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199. The larger models have the same $1,299 price at the entry level. All four start with 256GB of storage. Apple offers models with up to 2TB, while the Pixel line caps out at 1TB.
For most people, this decision is less complicated than the spec sheets might suggest. Again, if you already use an iPhone and other Apple devices, the iPhone 18 Pro is the obvious choice. If you already occupy Google's world, the Pixel 11 Pro makes more sense.
Beyond that, the Pixel has a few practical advantages. It's a tad lighter, especially in the XL size, and Google's camera and AI tools tend to insert themselves more into your workflow, which some people might appreciate. The iPhone, on the other hand, prioritizes professional-grade camera tools and video, along with sustained performance and a more restrained approach to AI.
There's no absolute winner here. Both are top-notch 2026 flagships aimed at slightly different audiences, and neither offers a compelling reason to switch platforms. The better question is which fits your devices, apps and habits.

Trump says no after Saudi crown prince pushes for US strikes on Houthis: report
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called President Donald Trump twice on Thursday and urged him to launch strikes against the Houthis
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman made two phone calls to President Donald Trump on Thursday, pressing him to execute military strikes targeting Houthi forces, according to an Axios report citing two American officials.
Trump turned down the request, with U.S. officials stating the administration currently has no intention of taking direct military action against the Houthis.
Neither the White House nor the Saudi embassy in Washington immediately responded to requests for comment outside standard business hours, and the details could not be independently verified.
According to the report, Washington is increasingly concerned about the rapidly intensifying conflict in Yemen and is bolstering support for Saudi Arabia while seeking to avoid direct military involvement.
Admiral Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, traveled to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for urgent coordination talks.
American military and civilian officials have informed their Saudi counterparts in recent weeks that Trump's mandate is to keep U.S. forces focused on Iran and safeguarding the Strait of Hormuz, rather than opening another military front.
The diplomatic push follows reports earlier in July that Saudi Arabia is attempting to build an international coalition to shield Red Sea shipping lanes from Houthi strikes amid rising regional instability.
Tensions escalated in early July after Houthi forces claimed to have confronted Saudi "warplanes" that were trying to block an Iranian civilian flight from landing at Sanaa International Airport.

Why we should expect another Solheim Cup thriller
- Published
Recent history suggests this week's Solheim Cup will be another epic clash to follow hot on the heels of Great Britain and Ireland's dramatic victory over the United States in the Walker Cup.
The extraordinary climax at Lahinch last Sunday, where GB&I won with the last putt of the match, evoked memories of the past three Solheim Cups staged in Europe.
Three years ago in Spain the contest ended in a dramatic 14-14 tie to allow a delirious European team to hold on to the trophy, having initially wrestled it from American hands with a single-point victory at Gleneagles in 2019.
Then it was Suzann Pettersen's gut wrenching and ultimately successful putt on the final green at the Scottish course that decided the outcome.
And the previous Solheim Cup held on continental soil was a 2015 single point away win that capped an astonishing comeback by the United States in Germany.
So the past three matches in Europe have had no more than a point in them and the home team and the US are tied on aggregate at 42 points apiece.
"I think it just shows how important each game is," said British number one Lottie Woad, who makes her debut for Europe this week.
"Even if you're a couple down early, you can get it back and even just getting a half point could be vital. So I think you've just got to have that mentality that any half point or point helps."
Woad's compatriot and potential partner Charley Hull believes it can be tougher playing at home. "We get big crowds in both places, but obviously, it's a little more pressure over here when it's a home Solheim Cup," she said.
"You've just got to deal with it, just stay focused, and be in the zone."
Europe's quartet of debutants
Woad is among four rookies in the European team joining fellow Englishwoman Mimi Rhodes, France's Nastasia Nadaud and the big hitting Spaniard Julia Lopez Ramirez.
"I can't wait for them to tee it up," said European captain Anna Nordqvist. "It's always easy to try to describe to the rookies what it's like playing in the Solheim, but it's something that you need to experience.
"And you have to get your own feel for it. But I can't wait for them to feel what it's like stepping up on that first tee."
Players prepare for the intimidation of packed crowds in a huge grandstand around three sides of the opening tee, but of more significance will be the play as matches reach their climax down the closing stretch of holes.
And that will be amplified further if it is again close in the closing singles matches on Sunday. "Obviously it's elevated," said 2025 US Open winner Maja Stark.
"But you're still just playing golf and you're trying to do your best and you're trying to beat one person. There's not much more you can do.
"You can't rely on team-mates on Sunday afternoon. You have got to go back and remember what's important for me now."
The three-day contest starts on Friday with four foursomes - alternate shot - matches, with four fourball matches to follow. That format is replicated on Saturday before the 12 singles matches on Sunday.
Form means little at Solheim
American captain Angela Stanford is bullish about her line-up's ability to handle the unique pressure of the Solheim Cup. "I think they're very mentally tough," she said.
"They don't let things bother them. They let things kind of roll off their back if something doesn't go the way they planned and they seem really focused."
Ironically none of the 24 players are bringing stellar individual form into this match, not even Nelly Korda, the world number one who claimed her fourth title of the year by winning the US Women's Open in June.
Korda has had only two top-10s since that major triumph at the start of the summer and finished in a lowly share of 50th place at the recent FM Championship.
Since Korda's US Open victory there have been no LPGA wins for any of the Solheim players.
For Europe only Celine Boutier and Woad have claimed titles this season and American Lauren Coughlin is the sole other tour winner in 2026 on show.
But that backdrop will be forgotten when it comes to head-to-head matchplay. As the Walker Cup showed it goes to a rarified level when put into the team environment.
"You can lose or win any match regardless of rankings or how you're playing at the moment," said Linn Grant, Stark's Swedish compatriot who has missed the cut in five of her past six events.
"When everyone shows up on Friday, you're just going to bring your best game.
"It's so different playing matchplay in this setting. It's kind of like just everyone's best game just shows up normally which makes it a lot more fun to play as well."
Bernardus' key holes
Solheim Cup
11-13 September
Bernardus Golf Club, Netherlands
They are competing on a testing course at Bernardus Golf near Hertogenbosch in the Netherlands, which hosted the Dutch Open on the DP World Tour from 2021-23. It has a Surrey heathland feel, that can play like a seaside links in certain areas.
But that fast running aspect has been compromised by the storms that lashed the layout on Wednesday. "I think it's a great course for matchplay," said Stark.
"There are a lot of bunkers that you don't really want to be in. You can have a lot of really long irons into par-four holes as well."
The par threes are also likely to generate plenty of drama, especially the 15th where matches will reach a crucial stage. "It is my favourite hole both visually and strategically," says Bernardus club professional Roel Verdonschot.
"It is built for drama. Players must decide whether to take the risk and attack the pin for a short birdie opportunity or play towards the middle of the green and accept a longer putt.
"The tee is sheltered, so the wind can be difficult to feel, even though it is still influencing the shot."
And any match that goes the distance will involve an exceptionally tough 389-yard par-four closing hole. There is water from the left of the tee, while bunkers await players attempting to play safely towards the right.
And the green is tiny with a deep run-off to the left and water to the right. "The 18th is the most difficult playing hole at Bernardus," said Verdonschot.
"You face a tee shot that you cannot afford to miss left, but you do not want to miss right either. If a close match reaches the 18th, there is a very good chance of drama."
Which is completely in keeping with Solheim Cup matches, especially those staged in Europe.

The shot seen around the world: How an amateur photographer captured the ultimate sacrifice of FDNY heroes on 9/11
The lone fire truck racing across the Brooklyn Bridge toward the burning towers has become a defining image of the courage of so many first responders on September 11. The man who took the picture tells Bruce Golding what remains seared in his memory
Aaron McLamb was cleaning a bookbinding machine in a Brooklyn factory when he happened to glance out a window and see history unfolding on the morning of September 11, 2001.
Then a 20-year-old volunteer at the headquarters of the Jehovah's Witnesses, McLamb recalled that he momentarily turned away from his work and noticed a “very large fire” in the north tower of the World Trade Center, across the East River in lower Manhattan.
“I knew that this was gonna be something really big,” McLamb, now 45, told The Independent. He immediately got his 35 mm Canon Rebel 2000 camera and climbed to the top floor of the 10-story building, snapping photos until he ran out of film.
One of his pictures — of a lone fire truck racing across the Brooklyn Bridge toward the burning twin towers — is among the most remembered from that terrible day, symbolizing the bravery and sacrifice of the city’s first responders.
All six crew members on the Ladder 118 fire truck were killed when the south tower collapsed at 9:59 a.m. while they evacuated people from the adjacent Marriott Hotel.
A total of 2,753 people were killed in New York City after two hijacked passenger planes hit the towers, along with 184 people at the Pentagon and 40 victims on United Airlines Flight 93, which crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, when the passengers and crew fought back against the terrorists. Nearly 10,000 more people have died from illnesses, many related to toxic air from at Ground Zero, in the years that followed.
Ladder 118, based at the Middagh Street firehouse in Brooklyn Heights, was crewed by Lt. Joseph Agnello, Vernon Cherry, Scott Davidson, Leon Smith, Peter Vega and Lt. Robert Regan. Two others from the firehouse — Capt. Martin Egan and Lt. Robert Wallace -- also died that day but weren’t on the Ladder 118 truck.
They are among the 343 fire department personnel killed on 9/11, along with 37 Port Authority police officers, 23 city police officers and eight paramedics and EMTs.
On the morning of September 11, McLamb, an amateur photographer with a longtime interest in firefighting, said he was “intentionally shooting fire trucks” as he took pictures of the emergency response.
“I always wanted to be a firefighter, but I just never got an opportunity to go into that field,” said McLamb, who left New York City in late 2005 and now lives in Leland, North Carolina.
He recalled spotting Ladder 118 leaving its firehouse, and noted that the tiller-style truck, operated by drivers in both the front and rear, has “always been my favorite.”
McLamb said he watched the truck as it traveled “right underneath us on Prospect Street and circled our building, and then got up on the Brooklyn Bridge.”
“So, I was just waiting for them to get in position for that photo,” he added.
After the Ladder 118 firefighters arrived at the World Trade Center, they were helping others escape from the Marriott when the collapse of the 110-story south tower — more than a quarter-mile tall — buried them under thousands of tons of rubble.
The collapse created a “huge dust cloud,” McLamb said, and he and other workers watching from the 10th floor “were asked to go close all the windows in the whole building.”
“So that — that put a stop to taking any more pictures,” he said. “My final pictures, I think, were the dust cloud from the first tower falling.”
After all the windows were closed, McLamb said, everyone was sent home.
“I'll never forget that part — walking home — because I lived further south than most in Brooklyn Heights...and the dust cloud and the debris cloud was actually in that area,” he said. “It had already subsided, but the damage was done.”
McLamb recalled walking through “at least an inch or two of dust on the ground” and “watching my feet kick up all this dust.”
“It was everywhere. There were papers everywhere, like office papers, 8 1/2 by 11,” he said. “Some of them were burned, some of them were not, some of them were just fine.”
In retrospect, McLamb said, he wished he'd “picked up some and, you know, see if I could get them to any of the names of the people that were on the, on the papers, or maybe their families or something.”
At the time, McLamb lived in a Brooklyn Heights apartment building with other Jehovah's Witnesses from around the country who got free room and board in exchange for their volunteer work. Like millions of others around the world, he spent the rest of his day watching live TV coverage of the horrifying events.
During the next week, he had his film developed and the photos printed. Word spread through the neighborhood that not one of the Ladder 118 truck crew had “come home,” he said.
McLamb decided to bring his negatives and some prints to the firehouse, which he'd always intentionally walked past on his way to work so he could wave and say “Good morning” to any firefighters outside.
When he showed up at the firehouse, McLamb said, the firefighters were initially “kinda incredulous” until he explained how he’d “watched the truck leave the station” before taking the photo.
“Once they figured out that I knew what I was talking about, then they got out a magnifying glass, and they started realizing really quick that, yeah, I really did capture 118,” he said.
In a separate interview, retired Ladder 118 firefighter John Sorrentino told The Independent that although the numbers on the truck aren't visible, it's one of only a handful of tiller-style models in the city. In addition, Sorrentino said, crew members had mounted an exterior box on the truck's right side.
Sorrentino, who was off-duty on September 11 but raced to the scene to help out, said he remains haunted by the sound of alarms worn by the hundreds of firefighters who were buried under the rubble.
“We knew what that sound was — and there was nothing we could do about it,” he said, adding that the feeling of helplessness was “the one thing that — that really sticks in my mind about 9/11.”
Less than a month later, McLamb’s photo appeared on the front page of New York's Daily News under the headline, “The last run of Ladder 118.”
After 25 years, McLamb said he’s grateful he could document the doomed crew’s heroism.
“Part of my identity as a Witness is I try to help people as best I can,” he said. “So, I knew that I had an opportunity to help those families and the coworkers of the firefighters that didn't come home because I had this picture.”

Following the 25th-anniversary commemoration of the Sept. 11 attacks, news media outlets reported U.S. President Donald Trump planned to fly to Ireland for the weekend to take in the Irish Open at Trump International Golf Club in Doonbeg.
Snopes received a reader's email asking, "Is it true that in Ireland in flight path for Shannon airport is a F*** Trump message in someone's yard?" The reader attached an image of the alleged sign — apparently captured from a high-angle position, similar to that of a drone — showing a grassy field, with the "U" in the first word marked with an asterisk.
A reverse image search found users sharing the same image on Bluesky, Facebook, Threads and TikTok (archived), some also claiming the sign appeared along the flight path into Shannon Airport in County Clare.
(@electra75 via Threads)
Snopes could not independently verify the sign's authenticity as of this writing, but did note a report about the image from CorkBeo, a publication primarily covering matters involving Ireland's County Cork. We reached out to the White House to request comment about the subject matter and will update this article if we receive further information.
The CorkBeo article cited as its source a video that Irish personality Ray Foley posted on Sept. 9, interviewing a woman who said she asked her husband to help prepare the sign for Trump's trip.
Foley's post says the woman, not identified by name, sent a message and the image to him, saying she prepared a "warm welcome" on the flight path into Shannon Airport "for the guest this weekend" — referencing Trump. "We've already had a few black helicopter flybys," the message apparently read.
Speaking about her husband, whom she identified as Paul, the woman reportedly said the following:
I've been troubling him for a long time to do this because we knew he [Trump] was gonna be comin' and I just said, "Come on, come on, keep needlin', and keep putting the idea in his head," so, I think he just gave up and said, "Come on, we'll do it."
We contacted a Foley representative with Today FM's owner, Bauer Media Audio Ireland, to ask for contact information pertaining to the people who created the supposed sign and will add more details if we receive a response.
BBC reported Air Force One, with Trump onboard, would fly into Dublin Airport on Sept. 12, and into Shannon Airport later the same day. CorkBeo's article featured news of a second protest sign that appeared in Dublin, reading "No Kings," as well as mentioning Gaza, Iran and ICE. Reuters published a photo confirming the Dublin sign's authenticity.

The story so far: Last week, the Supreme Court ruled that adoptive mothers could avail themselves of 12 weeks of paid maternity leave regardless of the age of their children at the time of adoption. Striking down Section 60(4) of the Social Security Code, 2020 (previously Section 5(4) of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961), which limited this benefit only to mothers who adopted children under the age of three months, the Court said that an adoptive mother had the same rights and obligations towards the child as a biological mother.
What is the law on maternity leave in India?
Statutory maternity benefits for working women in India began to be granted in colonial times. The Bombay Maternity Benefit Act, 1929, covered women factory workers. It was followed by similar laws in other parts of the country in the run-up to Independence. In 1961, Parliament passed the Maternity Benefit Act to provide paid maternity leave of 12 weeks to working women across the country.
In 2017, the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act not only extended the period of paid maternity leave for biological mothers to 26 weeks, but also inserted a provision extending maternity leave for the first time to adoptive mothers or surrogate mothers. Section 5(4) of the Act stated that surrogate or adoptive mothers legally adopting a child below three months would be entitled to maternity leave for a period of 12 weeks from the date the child is handed over to the mother.
Why was this law considered inadequate?
Also Read: What legal protections exist for women returning from maternity leave?
This provision was challenged in 2021 by Hamsaanandini Nanduri, a lawyer who adopted siblings in 2017. Ms. Nanduri told The Hindu that her Bengaluru-based law firm gave her only six weeks of paid maternity leave. “I could not leave my young children at home to turn up in office after just six weeks, so I took some additional months of unpaid leave. But it made me angry that there was no policy about it,” she said.
Terming the 12 weeks of maternity leave granted in 2017 to adoptive or surrogate mothers as “mere lip service”, the petitioner contended that when compared to the 26 weeks of maternity leave granted to biological mothers, the provision violated the fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution.
The three-month limit was unjust to both children and parents, depriving older adoptees from receiving the maternal care they need for their development and integration into their adoptive families, her lawyer argued.
The petitioner also pointed out in Court that adoption procedures take much longer than three months in India.
Also, as Ms. Nanduri told The Hindu: “I found on filing an RTI (Right to Information) application with CARA (Central Adoption Resource Authority) that less than 5% of children adopted at that time were under the age of three months.”
What did the Court say about motherhood?
The Court made it clear that motherhood cannot be seen through the “narrow lens of biology” alone. It referred to adoption as part of the “right to reproductive autonomy”. It noted that “the period of leave plays a crucial role in fostering [an] emotional bond between the mother and the child”. The Court added that stress hormone levels in children raised in orphanages are often higher than those in children brought up in a familial environment, which pointed to a greater need for paid maternal leave for older adoptees.
How will the judgment help adoptees and their parents?
Madhumitha Venkataraman started interviewing for jobs as a senior HR executive while waiting for an adoption referral, stipulating in every interview that she would need paid time off to support her child. Several multinational organisations balked at the idea of granting leave for more than a few weeks. But Ms. Venkataraman was finally recruited by a global media company that promised her one year of paid maternity leave. “My son came home at the age of three and a half months in 2023, so I was not eligible for maternity leave under the old law. But because this company was so accommodating, I did not have to choose between my career and my parenting,” she said. “There are emotional needs, and not just for the child. The time at home with my son gave me space to grow into motherhood,” she said. It is this time and space that other adoptive mothers say they will be entitled to as well, from now.
Noopur Goyal’s daughter was 15 months old when she came home in 2021. “I worked as a paediatric cardiologist at a top hospital in Delhi. I knew there was no provision for maternity leave, so I had to give up my job,” said Dr. Goyal, a single parent who works as a freelance consultant in Noida. “I had brought her into a new world, so I had to be present for her. An adopted child has been uprooted twice. I needed the time at home with her to build attachment and give her a sense of security.” Dr. Goyal said she was financially stable to be able to do this, but she is “glad now that there is a law mandating 12 weeks of paid maternity leave for all adoptive mothers.”
What did the Court say about paternity leave?
The Court also called on the Union government to examine the need for a formal law recognising paternity leave for all fathers, adoptive or biological. Noting that India’s legal framework does not adequately account for the role of fathers in childcare, it underlined the importance of shared parenting. As of now, only male government servants are entitled to 15 days’ paternity leave for the birth of a child or adoption. Leaves in the private sector are generally determined by company policies.

New reports claim that some fans have tracked down the real-life Florida nudist resort featured in the GTA 6 nudist town leak, and unfortunately, haven’t stopped there.
GTA 6 Fans Are Flooding the Real-Life Nudist Resort with Fake Reviews
While unconfirmed, fans have discovered that the nudist town located in Port Gellhorn (as seen in the leaks) on the GTA 6 map, Leonida, might be a recreation of the Cypress Cove Nudist Resort in Kissimmee, Florida, and it’s quite a nice place.
However, multiple users are leaving fake five-star reviews on the resort’s Google page, mentioning the GTA 6 leaks. If you filter the reviews from “Most Helpful” to “Most Recent”, you’ll notice flocks of users referencing Jason‘s massacre at the nudist town, as seen in the leaks.
A user named For Neb has given the resort a five-star rating with a GTA 6 reference, saying, “Will be trying to book a reservation on Nov. 19th. I will be playing GTA 6 for 3 days straight while nude in my RV.”
Another user named Evan Burger commented, “Jason Duval?”, and the name was enough to escalate the situation. The owner of Cypress Cove Nudist Resort has spoken out, confirming that some users are demanding money to remove their reviews. Here’s what he had to say:
These reviews appear to be part of a coordinated series of fabricated posts using GTA VI references and attaching them to our actual business. They were then followed by a request that we PAY MONEY to have the reviews changed or removed. We will not pay. We will not negotiate.”

In the days after the assassination of conservative activist and Turning Point cofounder Charlie Kirk, the online reaction was a mess. Graphic videos of the shooting were everywhere within minutes of his death, far-right figures called for violence and vengeance, and right-wing lawmakers and influencers called for the cancellation—and worse—of anyone celebrating. Then, the conspiracy theories began.
It’s been one year since Kirk’s death, and conspiracy theories about the shooting have persisted, supercharged by social media algorithms and right-wing influencers like Candace Owens, who has used her huge following to push baseless allegations about the incident.
Experts believe these conspiracy theories will continue for a long time to come. “There’s no reason to believe conspiracy theories about Kirk’s murder will lose steam anytime soon,” Jared Holt, senior researcher at Open Measures, tells WIRED. “If anything, I expect them to escalate further as the criminal trial against Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing Kirk, plays out over the next year or so. The trial is bound to draw major media attention and offer conspiracy theorists a source of new material to work from.”
In the immediate aftermath of Kirk’s death, some conspiracy theorists claimed the assassination was a false flag operation designed to deflect attention away from President Donald Trump’s connections to Jeffrey Epstein. Others claimed the entire thing was staged. There was the AI-powered gun theory, the claim that the shooter was a Kirk supporter, and even claims that Kirk was still alive.
But ultimately, the baseless claim that persisted is that someone close to Kirk, or operating on behalf of Israel, was responsible for his death, that Robinson was simply a patsy and what really killed Kirk was an exploding microphone. This is the narrative that has been central to Owens’ months-long conspiracy theory campaign. Her Kirk content has racked up hundreds of millions of views.
Owens’ success is fueled in a large part by the way that social media platforms today encourage their users to post content. “X and YouTube are rife with speculation about Kirk’s death, where it is both still possible to recruit new audiences and monetize them,” Joan Donovan, assistant professor of journalism and emerging media studies at Boston University, tells WIRED.
The end result is that Kirk’s death has become yet another rabbit hole, or a way for viewers to distract themselves from reality. “Candace and other conspiratorial influencers make things seem much more mysterious and exciting,” Renée DiResta, an associate research professor at Georgetown University who tracks disinformation, tells WIRED. “For many, her explanations are preferable to the reality of an act of violence by a solo individual.”
There have already been real world repercussions: Researchers at the Network Contagion Research Institute recently found that “Candace Owens caused a measurable, statistically significant surge in death threats and calls for violence against [Charlie Kirk’s wife] Erika Kirk.” In May, a man was arrested for allegedly threatening to kill Erica Kirk ahead of her appearance at a Turning Point USA event in San Antonio, though the man has yet to be charged. Owens did not respond to a request for comment.
Erica Kirk and Turning Point have repeatedly called for Owens and others to stop spreading baseless rumours about the assassination. While those calls have not been heeded, Turning Point believes the impact the conspiracy theories are having is fading.
“The conspiracy theories have much less reach and potency now than they did six months ago, and I think I’ll say the same six months from now,” Andrew Kolvet, a Turning Point spokesperson, tells WIRED. “They won’t stop because many of these personalities were completely unknown and broke before Charlie was killed and this is their money maker, but their influence and credibility has collapsed and will continue to do so.”
But some experts disagree, arguing that conspiratorial thinking has been an aspect of American life for decades.
“Historically, this is quite normal,” Joseph Uscinski, professor of political science at the University of Miami and author of American Conspiracy Theories, tells WIRED. “Majorities of Americans have believed for decades that JFK was killed by a conspiracy rather than by a lone gunman. In fact almost 80 percent of Americans believed in the 1970s there was a conspiracy behind the assassination.”
