73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

Scholar Rock on Friday received Food and Drug Administration approval for the first-ever therapy that targets the loss of muscle in spinal muscle atrophy, raising hopes that patients with the rare neurological disorder might have a better chance of moving and walking independently.
The FDA approved the drug, Isembyld, for use in adults and children 2 years and older who are currently receiving SMA therapies that target SMN2, a key gene for neurons that control movement. A late-stage clinical trial found that, when combined with an SMN2-targeting drug, Isembyld caused young patients’ motor skills to improve after a year, while those in a placebo group declined, a difference that was statistically significant.
“Today’s FDA approval of Isembyld marks a defining moment for the SMA community,” said David Hallal, CEO of Scholar Rock, in a press release. “After decades of failed industry-wide efforts to unlock the potential of myostatin inhibition, Scholar Rock has delivered a therapeutic breakthrough.”

Newly released Top Secret docs show warnings about Osama bin Laden threats to US in years before 9/11
CIA declassifies presidential briefings that trace al-Qaeda threats to hijack plans and target US cities before 9/11
Donald Trump’s administration has released more than 100 pages of declassified briefings provided to U.S. presidents in the years before the terror attacks on September 11, 2001, marking what the CIA is calling its largest-ever disclosure of intelligence about Osama bin Laden and events leading up to the attacks over the last 25 years.
Friday’s release of 71 presidential briefs includes a document from 1998 during Bill Clinton’s administration discussing a potential operation led by Bin Laden to hijack a commercial airliner, and that two accomplices may have successfully evaded security checks in a trial run.
The heavily redacted documents also discuss “potential U.S. targets” and reports from "questionable sources” that Bin Laden was preparing for an attack on U.S. soil.
Other documents appear to trace how CIA analysts came to understand al-Qaeda’s operations and intentions under bin Laden, stressing his desire to bring “war to America,” despite what analysts characterized as limited or incomplete intelligence, as they delivered warnings to White House officials about the terror network.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe said he declassified the documents “in an act of exceptional transparency” to “honor the memory of those we lost on that tragic Tuesday.”
“Generations of CIA officers have since dedicated their careers to securing justice for our fallen Americans and ensuring al-Qa'ida would never again harm our country,” he said in a statement. “In the years that followed, numerous CIA officers made the ultimate sacrifice in the Global War on Terror. We honor their memory and service through our commitment to disrupt, dismantle, and defeat those who wish to cause us harm.”
The documents — with heavy redactions to protect the names of informants — do not appear to produce any major new revelations about the attacks but paint a fuller picture of what intelligence officials were sharing with Presidents Clinton and George W. Bush in the years leading up to 9/11, with memos from February 1998 through September 12, 2001 showing incomplete strands of intelligence presented by analysts in their typically detached style.
Those findings largely reinforce what was previously reported by the National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States and its 2004 report that examined threats from al-Qaeda.
A memo written on September 10, 1998 reported that Bin Laden’s “preferred option is to strike the U.S. on its own soil in Washington” and “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a U.S. city.”
Another document from August 6, 2001 to then-President Bush notes that Bin Laden is “determined to strike” the U.S., potentially relying on al-Qaeda members living in the country. The FBI discovered activity “consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York.”
A document from August 28, 2001, days before the attacks, determined that Bin Laden’s operations are “expert and flexible” though vulnerable to “short-term delay and disruption.”
The document also notes that al-Qaeda stresses “careful planning, tight security practices and flexibility” throughout its operations — “sound operational practices” that allow it to pose a threat to the U.S. “even in a heightened security environment.”
But analysts also appeared to struggle with pulling together a cohesive narrative based on their limited intelligence on al-Qaeda’s operations.
A memo from August 3, 1999, suggested that al-Qaeda may have been leading “a deliberate effort to mislead us” by pitching so many different targets identified by analysts.
“The diverse targets mentioned in the reporting, combined with a high incidence of Bin Ladin-related walk-ins, suggest a deliberate effort to mislead us,” analysts wrote.
The release of the documents comes as mourning Americans across the country honor the nearly 3,000 people killed in the attacks, which have profoundly reshaped the U.S. and triggered a series of world-shaping events.

The family of a British father who was found dead in the Caribbean in January is urging authorities in Grenada to work with UK police to uncover the truth about his death.
Andrew Frederick’s body was found in the property he was staying at in Grenada on 4 January. An autopsy, performed in the same week by a privately hired pathologist, concluded that the 47-year-old’s death was a homicide.
In June, Grenada’s director of public prosecution, Howard Pinnock, said at a press conference that Frederick’s and another pending case would be sent to the coroner to determine the cause of death “because there is no basis in terms of both investigations that any homicide has occurred”.
After a sustained campaign by the family, British authorities became involved and Frederick’s body was repatriated to the UK last month, where a second autopsy was carried out.
The UK coroner has noted that Frederick’s organs are missing and the death is currently “unascertained”.
At the start of an inquest at West London coroner’s court last week, senior coroner Lydia Brown said the Metropolitan police are now investigating Frederick’s death.
The family, who attended the court hearing by video link, said the coroner’s “decision to suspend Andrew’s inquest to allow the Metropolitan police to conduct a criminal investigation marks a significant turning point”.
In statement to the Guardian, they urged Grenada and the UK to work together to find out what happened to Frederick.
“We are encouraged and grateful that the Metropolitan police investigation is now under way. Justice for Andrew depends on everyone with the power to act, on both sides of the Atlantic, doing what is right,” the statement said.
It added: “Andrew was a deeply loved member of a close-knit family; a son, brother, father and grandson. He leaves behind his cherished daughter, who should be growing up with him beside her, not learning to live without him.
“Our family remain determined to uncover the truth about what happened to Andrew and to see justice follow. We hope this ruling is the step that finally enables a complete, properly coordinated investigation and that everyone who can assist will now do so.”
Earlier this year, the family had called for an urgent review of the policies governing UK assistance to the loved ones of Britons killed abroad, after they were forced to launch their own public appeals for information, and commission an independent forensic pathologist and a private investigation.
“Eight months have passed since Andrew was taken from us. In that time, we have learned what no family should ever have to learn, and fought battles no family should ever face alone,” their statement said.
It added: “We have relentlessly sought answers and support while carrying the weight of Andrew’s loss and the horror of what was done to him. We still do not have a complete account of what happened, and important questions remain unanswered.
“We hope the Grenadian authorities with knowledge of the case will now share that information and work collaboratively with the Metropolitan police, allowing the investigation to proceed without further delay. We are also seeking urgent answers as to why Andrew’s organs were absent when his body was returned to the UK for further examination.”
In Grenada, the Office of the Commissioner told the Guardian that “the matter will be progressing to the coroner’s court for the parish of Saint George”.
A Met spokesperson said: “The Met is investigating the death of 47-year-old Andrew Donald Frederick, who died in Grenada on 4 January.
“Mr Frederick’s family are being supported by specialist officers.
“No arrests have been made at this stage and inquiries are ongoing.”
Officers have contacted the Royal Grenada Police Force (RGPF) to offer assistance and discuss how the investigation can be progressed.
Inquest proceedings have been suspended pending the outcome of police investigations.

In a boost for the pharmaceutical industry, a European Union Advocate General recommended annulling part of a directive that requires drug and cosmetics manufacturers to finance at least 80% of the costs of wastewater treatment.
The directive, which revised an earlier version and went into effect early last year, was designed to protect human health and the environment from harmful discharges of urban wastewater and ensure cleaner rivers, lakes, groundwater, and coasts across Europe. The effort was projected to save about $7.5 billion annually by 2040.
A key portion of the initiative is a “quaternary treatment stage” that involves removing micropollutants — which are mostly created by pharmaceuticals and cosmetics — from wastewater. Member states must ensure that companies contribute to programs to deal with the waste they generate by December 2028.

Snapping shots in daylight with the main camera resulted in lovely photos I’d be happy to share. There’s plenty of detail, decent sharpness, pleasing dynamic range, and vibrant but not over-the-top colors. Main camera
Video quality is good with the main camera (4K at 60 fps or 8K at 30 fps), and it has solid stabilization to reduce shakiness, including horizontal lock to keep a fixed orientation even if you rotate the phone (though you must turn it on before you start recording). In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

Fresh photos offer clearest view yet of China’s ‘WZ-X’ spy drone
Analysts say the stealthy aircraft appears to be designed for reconnaissance deep inside contested airspace
New photographs circulated on Chinese internet forums earlier this month that appear to show the massive drone in the air, offering much clearer views of its wing shape than earlier images. The original source of the photos and exactly where they were taken have not been independently verified.
Andreas Rupprecht, a specialist on Chinese military aviation, said the photographs showed the clearest view yet of the aircraft’s serrated trailing edge – a sawtooth-like shape along the rear of the wing characteristic of stealth design. He added that the aircraft appeared to have been flown in daylight, suggesting such flights might have reached a degree of normality.
Rupprecht said he was “100 per cent certain” the photographs showed what military aviation watchers have dubbed the “WZ-X”, citing its dimensions, proportions and other visible details. Beijing has not publicly confirmed the aircraft’s designation, purpose or specifications.
Rupprecht said the aircraft was designed as an intercontinental high-altitude, long-endurance (Hale) intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) drone – a platform intended to operate deep inside defended airspace and function as an advanced communications relay node.

Pakistan’s Razaullah made a stunning impact on his Test debut as he scored a quickfire fifty against England in the third match in Edgbaston on Friday.
The 21-year-old smoked eight sixes in the second innings to prevent an innings defeat for Pakistan. Earlier in the first innings, Razaullah had taken four wickets with his right-arm pace.
The young all-rounder put on a century stand for the ninth wicket with Mohammad Abbas to keep Pakistan alive in the Test.
Only one player has hit more maximums on his Test debut – New Zealand’s Tim Southee, who carted nine sixes against England in 2008.
Interestingly, Razaullah’s heroics happened with Southee as a witness – the retired Kiwi pacer is at the Edgbaston as a consultant with the English side.

- The claim that Donald Trump was rescued by firefighters in or around the United States Steel Building (also known as One Liberty Plaza) after 9/11 in Manhattan is unproven.
- According to some versions of the claim, Trump said firefighters pulled him from the rubble at Ground Zero. That was a misrepresentation of his actual words.
- The rumor stems from a speech Trump made on Sept. 8, 2026, while commemorating the 25th anniversary of 9/11. In it, he said the United States Steel Building was "creaking" a lot and "we thought it was going to fall down" when two firefighters "grabbed [him] under the arms" and got him out of there.
- Video interviews of Trump place him a few blocks from the World Trade Center in lower Manhattan in the days following the attack. However, there is no concrete evidence that Trump was inside or around One Liberty Plaza and no firefighters have come forward to corroborate his account. We also know that the building itself was not in danger of collapse in the days after 9/11, despite rumors at the time.
- We reached out to the White House, which did not respond to questions about Trump's whereabouts and actions in the wake of 9/11. A spokesperson called the speculation from the media a "disgrace."
In 2026, the U.S. marked the 25th anniversary of the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. As U.S. President Donald Trump commemorated the occasion in a speech on Sept. 8, he claimed that he was rescued by firefighters in New York City just after the attack.
Snopes readers asked us to confirm if Trump was indeed rescued by firefighters from the possible collapse of the United States Steel Building, a historic name for the building now 
Other readers claimed Trump said firefighters pulled "him from the rubble at 9/11."
Posts sharing versions of the rumor appeared on platforms including Facebook and X.
Some posts incorrectly claimed Trump said the firefighters pulled him from the rubble at Ground Zero. That was a misrepresentation or misunderstanding of what Trump actually said.
On Sept. 8, 2026, Trump recounted his purported rescue by two firefighters during a speech (emphasis ours):
I was building a big building in New York, and I took the whole crew down there right after this happened.
And they were -- they had no hesitation. Everybody went down with me; we went down as a big group of people. Wasn't too much we could do, I'll be honest. It was raw; nobody had seen anything like it ever. We had other buildings -- the United States Steel Building was creaking, really creaking, and we thought it was going to fall down. The truth is, it creaked a lot; it creaked, it still creaks, but it never came down. And I'll never forget two firemen -- we thought it was coming down on top of us and two firemen, big, strong guys -- and I'm not the smallest guy in the world. They grabbed me under the arms, said got to get out of here, and they literally lifted me up. This is not easy to do, I'm big.
They lifted me up and they started running with me. I said fellas, I can run myself. But they were amazing, but they thought it was coming down; it didn't come down, US steel.
Trump made several claims in this part of the speech: first, he said he "took the whole crew down" to Ground Zero to help after the attack. Second, he claimed that the "United States Steel Building was creaking" and in danger of collapsing on him. Third, he claimed he was saved by two firefighters.
We investigated Trump's claim that he went to Ground Zero with a group of workers immediately after the 9/11 attacks in a 
We have no evidence to support Trump's claim that he was rescued by two firefighters at One Liberty Plaza, though television interviews place him in the vicinity in the aftermath of 9/11. As such, we leave this claim unrated until more information becomes available.
We reached out to the White House to ask about Trump's location after the attack, the identity of the firefighters and more. The White House did not answer our questions and sent us the following statement from spokesperson Davis Ingle over email:
President Trump spent the morning yesterday paying tribute to the heroic first responders who laid down their lives in service to others in the September 11th attacks and honoring their incredible families. The President was relaying his experience of a city reeling immediately after and in the days and weeks after the horrific attacks - and the fact that the failing legacy media is using this to try to attack him is a disgrace and yet another reason why Americans' trust in the media is at an all-time low.
Below, we address the claims Trump made about being at One Liberty Plaza and his alleged rescue by firefighters.
Was Trump at One Liberty Plaza?
There is video evidence that Trump was near Ground Zero in the days after the attack, but we found no proof that he was actually inside the nearby One Liberty Plaza. Trump's remarks are not clear about where he was standing when the building was supposedly creaking.
The White House did not respond to our request for photo or video evidence of Trump's proximity to One Liberty Plaza specifically.
Trump's claim that the building was in danger of collapse was incorrect. Right after the attack, many reportedly expressed concerns that the building would collapse, but officials at the Department of Buildings debunked the claims. According to an October 2001 New York Times report, the building remained structurally sound even on Sept. 12:
''There are no structural concerns with this building,'' said Ilyse Fink, the director of communications for the city's Department of Buildings, reinforcing a message she has delivered almost daily since Sept. 12. ''It is not and was not in danger of collapse. The building is structurally sound.''
Did firefighters save Trump from a potential building collapse?
Given that we do not know exactly where Trump was around One Liberty Plaza, and that we know the building was never in danger of collapse, it is not clear which building and which firefighters Trump was referring to in his Sept. 8 speech.
The White House also did not respond to our question about the identity of the firefighters. Without any firefighters corroborating Trump's account, this claim remains unproven.
In sum, while we know Trump was in the vicinity of Ground Zero in the days after the attack, we do not have evidence that he was in One Liberty Plaza, nor that he was rescued by firefighters. We also know that the building was not in danger of collapse. Trump did not mention other buildings in his remarks.
Snopes has fact-checked many of Trump's claims in the aftermath of 9/11.

Retired New York City police officer John Aris sat in my office recently waiting for the results of his latest CT scan.
Seven years earlier, I had removed part of his right lung because of cancer. Since then, every follow-up appointment has carried the same anxiety. Before I had even closed the examination room door behind me, I offered the words he had hoped to hear: “No cancer.”
He let out a long breath and settled back into his chair. As always, we lingered and talked about life, politics, and family.
Then I asked him what he thought about something different.
On Friday, during the 25th anniversary ceremony at the World Trade Center, organizers will add a new moment of silence. It will honor those who died not on Sept. 11, 2001, but in the years that followed from illnesses linked to their exposure at ground zero.
His smile faded. He stared ahead for a moment before speaking. His voice cracked as he began talking about the people he had lost. Not the people killed when the towers fell, but those who died years later.
He remembered his friends. Construction workers, firefighters, and police officers, who stood shoulder to shoulder with him for months amid choking dust, burning debris, and twisted steel. He remembered the smell that lingered as they worked.
Many of his friends went home. At least at first. Then, years later, the funerals began.
One friend developed esophageal cancer. Another died from leukemia. Another succumbed to a respiratory illness. The phone calls never seemed to stop. Every year brought another diagnosis, another funeral.
Beside him sat his wife of 44 years, Kathleen. She had lived through every one of those losses with him.
Each obituary reopened a wound that had never completely healed. I realized we had spent most of the visit talking not about his cancer — which could have been related to his exposure at ground zero, though we can’t say for sure — but about everyone else’s.
Later that afternoon I saw another patient, retired firefighter William Corrar, whom I had operated on for esophageal cancer. Like many responders, he spent months working at ground zero after the attacks. For years he dismissed worsening reflux as simply getting older before learning it was cancer.
Sept. 11 is personal for me, too.
On the morning of the attacks, I was already a thoracic surgeon at Memorial Sloan Kettering in New York. I was in the hospital operating on a patient suffering from cancer caused by asbestos exposure when I heard what had happened. All of our remaining cases were canceled, so I got on my bike and rode downtown to see if I could help.
There was surprisingly little for a surgeon to do. The people who could escape the towers largely walked away. So many who could not were simply gone. I had ridden downtown expecting to help take care of the injured. Instead, like so many New Yorkers that day, I was left trying to comprehend what had just happened.
My connection to the World Trade Center went back much further. I’m a native New Yorker and skateboarded through the plaza between the Twin Towers as a kid. Later I worked in the South Tower making deliveries for UPS as I was going to college. The towers had been part of the landscape of my life.
I could not have imagined that they would eventually become part of my life as a surgeon as well.
In the years after the attacks, the patients began appearing. First responders, construction workers, and others who had spent months breathing the dust and smoke came to us with diseases that surgeons treat. What had begun as a catastrophe I had witnessed was becoming something I encountered in my operating room.
These scenarios have become a familiar part of my practice. I have spent much of my career caring for people exposed to the toxic aftermath. I continue to treat patients with lung and esophageal cancer, mesothelioma, and other illnesses associated with their exposure to the disaster site.
But there is an important distinction between association and certainty.
I cannot look at an individual’s lung or esophageal cancer and prove that it was caused by something he inhaled at ground zero. Cancer can take years to develop, and an individual patient may have several potential risk factors.
That does not mean there is no connection. Medicine rarely establishes environmental risk by identifying a single exposure that caused a single person’s cancer. We study populations. We ask whether disease occurs more often among exposed people, whether the timing makes biological sense, and whether substances involved are capable of causing disease.
The cloud that engulfed Lower Manhattan contained pulverized concrete, glass fibers, asbestos, heavy metals, and combustion products. Thousands rushed toward danger without knowing exactly what they were breathing.
Others never chose to be there. Residents, office workers, and students were exposed simply because they happened to live, work or study nearby.
They believed the air was safe. Then came asthma, chronic sinus disease, and persistent cough.
Today more than 140,000 responders and survivors are enrolled in the federally administered World Trade Center Health Program. Tens of thousands have developed cancers, respiratory diseases, digestive disorders, and mental health conditions linked to their exposure. More than 8,000 enrolled members have died, and that number continues to grow.
Disease rarely captures the nation’s attention the way catastrophe does. It unfolds one diagnosis at a time, one funeral at a time. But for thousands of families, the attack did not end when the fires were extinguished. It simply changed form.
When the crowd falls silent this September, John will not only remember those who have died. He will think of friends still living with illnesses, like himself, and the uncertainty they carry into each new year.
Because for them, Sept. 11 was not just one day. It has been 25 years.
And it is still not over.
Raja Flores is the chair of the Department of Thoracic Surgery at Mount Sinai School of Medicine, where he treats patients with mesothelioma, lung, and esophageal cancer.

NEW DELHI: Noting that the Brics grouping now represents 50% of the global population, 40% of GDP, and 25% of trade, PM Narendra Modi said Friday that their collective economic might has grown at nearly double the global pace since the bloc was formed in 2006, and called upon member countries to reduce barriers to trade and increase opportunities for businesses.In his address at the Brics Business Forum, PM also underlined the need to keep trade flowing. "Global trade can move forward only when sea lanes are secure, supply routes are open, and seafarers are safe. And, therefore, Bharat is a firm supporter of freedom of navigation and the safety of seafarers," Modi said, his remark coming against the backdrop of disruption of traffic through Strait of Hormuz and the growing threat through Bab al-Mandab Strait, another crucial artery for India.His pitch for deeper engagement significantly contrasted the themes of 2 other key members: Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.Putin, like PM, also invoked the growing economic heft of Brics members. However, he and Pezeshkian, with their countries reeling from sanctions, were resentful of the West's continuing sway."The world is changing... Over the past 5 years, as it has been said today - I think it was our Indonesian colleague who said it, the Brics countries accounted for over 40% of global GDP, while the contribution of Group of Seven, the so-called leading economies, although I don't understand why they are called 'leading', was just 29%," Putin said.
PM Modi's 'Intra-Brics trade' call seen as aimed at US and ChinaAt a time when trade barriers are increasing, India is building economic bridges, PM Narendra Modi said, adding, “Our approach in Brics is also the same: to reduce barriers and increase opportunities for businesses.”He has been averse to Brics being turned into an anti-West bloc and has resisted the push from China, Russia and Iran for de-dollarisation. Also, his call for greater intra-Brics commerce can be seen as aimed at both US President Trump’s strong arm tariff tactics as well as a reminder of New Delhi’s contention to China that it needed to let in more Indian goods and should not weaponise supplies of equipment and raw materials needed by Indian manufacturers.“In these years, the combined GDP of Brics countries has grown by about 4.5 times while the global GDP has grown by around 2.5 times. Brics’s economic strength has grown at nearly double the pace of the world,” Modi said, pointing to the bloc comprising emerging markets and developing economies.He called upon the Brics Business Council to identify the top 10 trade barriers to be removed, while charting the growth trajectory of the Indian economy in the last 12 years since his govt took office with its focus on innovation and resilience.“Can we support 100 Brics startups every year to scale in other Brics markets? Can we develop 1,000 new partnerships among our businesses? On all these benchmarks, we have to review our progress every year. Let us turn the ambition of Brics into action and its collective strength into global solutions. Let Brics move forward and take the world forward as well.”Lauding Brics nations for becoming key centres for global innovation and solutions — from grassroots to frontier tech — he said the bloc’s growing scale, speed, and optimism are clearly visible.With the theme of India’s Brics presidency being “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Co-operation and Sustainability”, he said India has made this foundation of its economic and trade policy.India has made supply chains from energy to technology more diversified and reliable, he said, adding that it is offering confidence in growth and stability even amid global uncertainties.
“We are rapidly expanding roads, railways, ports, and airports. Along with this, we are building new capabilities in strategic sectors such as ship-building, semiconductor, quantum, critical minerals, and bio-tech,” he said.Turning to his govt’s call to the global business for “Make in India, Innovate with India, Scale for the World”, he said the country has more than two lakh start-ups, and over 120 unicorns, which are transforming education and healthcare through AI, crossing new frontiers in defence and space, and working on green hydrogen and batteries as well.

Anthropic said it stopped multiple attempts by scientists this year to use its technology for research that could help develop biological weapons, as experts increasingly fear the threat that AI poses to public safety.
The startup gave five examples of times actors “circumvented controls” and made other efforts to “obfuscate” the purpose of their research to dodge safeguards. The cases involved some users in nations that it prohibits from accessing its models, which include Russia, China, and Iran.
“We hope that by sharing these examples, we spark a conversation within the AI industry and with governments about emerging biological risks and how best to counter them,” Anthropic said in a report about efforts to use its models for malicious activity.
The case studies of possible biological misuse that the company provided included a researcher from an “unsupported region” who “spent weeks planning” experiments involving avian influenza with Claude, Anthropic’s AI model. The company said its safety filters restricted the work to its weakest models.
It emphasized it could not be sure that the scientists in its examples intended to cause harm. The same information needed to create biological weapons could also be used to develop a vaccine.
Anthropic said it had banned the accounts mentioned in the report, but it did not disclose the names of the research institutions or the nations where the incidents took place.

Prescriptions for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs among children under 12 in the U.S. have risen more than 300-fold since 2019 as doctors seek new, effective treatments for younger patients with obesity, according to a study published on Friday.
The study, which included more than 3.5 million children aged between eight and 11 years with obesity but not diabetes, found that prescriptions for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs rose from 0.03% in 2019 to 9.3% as of June.
Although the drugs are not approved for use in children under 12 years, clinical guidelines allow the medications to be used for obesity in children as young as eight years old in certain cases.
94% of the children prescribed GLP-1s had severe obesity, and about 65% had at least one related condition, such as high cholesterol, high blood pressure, and sleep apnea.
Overall, 20,282 children received GLP-1 drugs during the study period - most often, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy. Doctors also prescribed Novo's Saxenda and Eli Lilly's Zepbound.
While the absolute numbers of children under 12 receiving GLP-1 treatment is still low, the study shows that GLP-1 use is accelerating rapidly, said lead investigator and obesity medicine specialist Dr. Babak Orandi of NYU Langone Health.
Orandi added that long-term safety monitoring is needed to ensure the drugs remain safe and effective.
Children living in higher-income communities were 55% more likely to be prescribed the medicines, suggesting emerging disparities in access, according to the study published in the journal Pediatrics.
"Physicians and health policymakers alike have a responsibility to ensure ... these valuable and sometimes costly treatments become available to more than those who have access to health insurance and can afford to visit pediatric clinics," said Allan Massie, co-author of the study and associate professor of surgery at NYU Grossman School of Medicine.
Researchers used Epic Cosmos, a national electronic health records database encompassing more than 300 million U.S. patients. Epic had no role in the study.

A native Gemini app is finally available for Windows PCs
There's a keyboard shortcut to open it up, just like the Mac version.
Google has finally released a native Gemini app for Windows 10 and 11. This provides a streamlined way to use the AI tools on Windows PCs and follows a Mac release earlier this year.
Once downloaded, users can pull up the Gemini app via a keyboard shortcut, just like how it works on Mac computers. The company says this is great when people "need a quick fact-check on a document or a few catchy title ideas for a presentation." I would recommend fact-checking that fact-check because, you know, it's generative AI.
The @GeminiApp is now available for Windows
Just press Alt + Space to bring instant Gemini assistance right to your desktop alongside your favorite apps and tools. pic.twitter.com/g3wbdvzxii
— Google (@Google) September 10, 2026
The app integrates with other Google AI products, so tasks can be sent to the agentic assistant Gemini Spark. It even works with stuff like Gmail and Google Drive. It can also generate images and videos via Nano Banana and Gemini Omni, if that's your bag.
Google promises the app is "lightweight and quiet," so it won't slow down Windows PCs. It's available for download right now and the company says more native desktop capabilities are coming down the pike in the future.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

Agents being tested by OpenAI attacked software service RubyGems, uploading hundreds of malicious packages according to researchers.
OpenAI confirmed the incident and said it would investigate as part of its "broader review of agent activity during training and evaluation".
The attack came two months before OpenAI agents hacked into open-source platform Hugging Face in July.
AI agents being tested by OpenAI attacked software service RubyGems two months before they hacked open-source platform Hugging Face, researchers say.
It is the latest revelation of cyber attacks that have spooked the public and spurred calls for tighter regulation.
Many incidents involving agents hacking or attempting to access external systems have heightened concerns over the increasing capacity of AI models and developers' ability to contain them.
AI agents uploaded hundreds of malicious packages to RubyGems on May 11, according to a group of researchers who posted their findings online on Friday, local time, saying they believed "these were authored by internal OpenAI agents".
OpenAI confirmed the incident.
"Based on our review, our agents used the RubyGems platform to access the internet to carry out benign tasks and retrieve public information. We'll continue to investigate as part of our broader review of agent activity during training and evaluation," a spokesperson said in a statement.
The RubyGems attack would mark at least the third major instance of OpenAI agents attacking another company's infrastructure.
A swarm of OpenAI agents previously hijacked a German-language wiki site and turned it into an improvised messaging platform for cheating on tests.
In May AI agents tried to steal RubyGems user credentials by exploiting a previously unknown vulnerability in the site's servers, though it is unclear whether the attempt succeeded, the researchers said.
The agents also exploited RubyDoc.info, a site that generates code documentation, to run their own code on its servers, the researchers added.
This week Anthropic disclosed a fourth instance of an AI model hacking external systems during testing.

Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland, a remote state in north-eastern India bordering Myanmar, have expressed joy and relief that human remains belonging to their ancestors that had been on display in a British museum for nearly a century are finally being returned.
On Monday, the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford announced that 39 pieces of human remains – including parts of skulls, a finger and a piece of skin with hair – belonging to the Naga tribes, will be returned to Nagaland after six years of negotiation between the community and the museum.
For the Nagas, the repatriation is not just about “bones and ancestral remains … It is about memory returning to where it belongs,” the community said in a statement.
“We are at peace,” said A Peihwang Wangsa, an Indigenous Konyak man involved in the repatriation negotiations. “Our forefathers are coming back.”
Wangsa, whose ancestors’ remains are among those being returned, added that the homecoming would be a moment of “mourning and celebration”.
NT Thamlong Phom, a Naga community leader from the Phom sub-tribe, said: “I feel joy, I feel blessed.
“Ever since the announcement was made, my entire community has felt happy,” he said. “Our ancestors’ spirit will have a final resting place.”
Thejao Vihienuo, who is also part of the repatriation discussions and went to Oxford in 2025, said he had been “angry and unhappy” to see the remains of his ancestors, which he said had been “taken in a most dubious manner”.
“It was displayed as if it was a trophy, but they silently spoke of the atrocities the British committed on our people,” he said.
The return caused “mixed feelings”, he said, but added: “We owe it to our ancestors to bring their remains back and put them to peaceful rest. And also to our younger generation to decolonise their minds and show that our children are not inferior to any white man.”
The Nagas are a transnational Indigenous group of tribes living in India’s north-east and parts of Myanmar, once associated with headhunting but now predominantly Christian.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, home to one of the world’s largest ethnological collections, has more than 6,500 Naga objects, 898 of which were on display. Most of the collection was “coercively” acquired by the colonial administrators James Philip Mills and John Henry Hutton.
The human remains were displayed at the museum for 80 years. In 2020, they were put into storage during a revamp aimed at addressing the institution’s colonial past and how exhibiting human remains “reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking” of other cultures.
The museum said in a statement: “Thirty-nine Naga ancestors will soon begin their journey home from Oxford to Nagaland.”
In November, a Naga delegation will visit Oxford for a handover ceremony and the remains are expected to arrive in Nagaland before the end of the year. They will be laid to rest in a traditional community ceremony in the state capital, Kohima.
The repatriation negotiations were led by representatives from all of the Naga tribes.
“It has been a journey of redemption,” said Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist. “This shows that we are no longer victims of colonial violence. We embrace our roles as people who find redemption and healing by giving dignity and honour to a very violent past.”
The negotiations started in 2020, when Kikon wrote to the museum after reading “an article in the Guardian that they were doing an ethical review” of the collection. “They replied within 24 hours,” said Kikon.
That was just the beginning of a lengthy process that soon expanded into a wider community-led campaign.
The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a community peace group, assembled a team known as Recover, Restore and Decolonise, bringing together Naga volunteers from across the region to work on the repatriation effort.
“They travelled to villages and organised meetings to inform people about the remains,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a Naga anthropologist who worked closely with Kikon to lead the initiative, which he described as “open and transparent”.
“It was an intergenerational journey that brought together students, civil society, tribal leaders and the church,” said Longkumer, who teaches at Edinburgh University.
A Naga delegation, including tribal leaders, visited Oxford in 2025 to officially register a claim to the remains.
“I had never known our ancestral human remains had been taken away like that,” said Wangsa. “I felt angry when I saw them.”
Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum and a professor of museum studies and ethics at Oxford University, said the museum was completing paperwork to enable the return of the remains.
“We will then start working towards the ceremonial aspects so we can have everything ready,” she said. “In our experience, handover ceremonies can be very emotional.”

Leeds want boss Farke to stay 'long-term'
- Published
Leeds United managing director Robbie Evans says the club and boss Daniel Farke are "on the same page" as they look to agree a new contract.
Farke, who guided Leeds to a 14th-placed finish in the Premier League and an FA Cup semi-final last season after winning promotion in 2024-25, is in the final year of his current deal.
The Whites have taken five points from three league games this campaign and Evans said the German had done "a fantastic job".
"As far as the contract discussions themselves, Daniel and his team and I have had really good chats for the past three months and they're all on the same page," he said.
"Unlike signing him back in 2023 or doing a deadline day deal kind of thing the time pressure is far reduced and so we have a time to get it right as far as what he wants and what we want.
"I don't feel it's taking a long time. It just means we're getting it right and also we have time to get it right and so as long as we're still operating together as a group, and we're doing great on that front, I'm not worried."
He added: "The the short answer is that he's done great, we want him to be here long-term and we're working on it."
'A good window and a good deadline'
Leeds brought in England goalkeeper James Trafford from Manchester City in a deal worth up to £45m in the summer, as well as defenders Tarik Muharemovic and Nico Elvedi and Fulham winger Harry Wilson.
They also added Nice defender Melvin Bard and Eintracht Frankfurt forward Jean-Matteo Bahoya on deadline day.
"I think last year the phrase was we had a good window and a bad deadline. I would say this summer was a good window and a good deadline," Evans said.
"The key for us was we had a couple of top objectives to accomplish and those all got done early in terms of a left-footed centre-half, right winger and goalkeeper. Having signed our top targets in all three of those positions we were able to go and pursue roles around the pitch that gets better and stronger and have time to do so.
"So we're quite satisfied with the window."
Netherlands international Pascal Struijk was sold to Brighton in a deal worth a reported £20m on 30 June.
The last day of June is when clubs needed to be compliant with profit and sustainability rules (PSR) to avoid charges and possible points deductions. This is now being replaced by squad-cost ratio (SCR) moving forward.
Evans said he was "thankful" the club only needed to sell one player in order to come into line with the regulations.
"I was pretty confident coming into the year we'd have to sell some guys in June. Frankly it was the FA Cup run and the minimal work in January that kept it being just one player," he said.
"Pascal's appeal to other teams was clear before the year was over and then he was debating going or not and he was helpful in deciding pretty quickly so we could decide to sell him before 30 June.
"We were prepared for that possibility all season and so we did tonnes of work on a left centre-half last year. Having that news early was helpful, but we had, like always, various contingencies for Pascal."

Buddhist monk arrested in suspected $3m embezzlement scandal
- Published
Thai police have arrested a Buddhist monk on suspicion of embezzling 100 million baht ($3m; £2.2m) from his monastery, along with a suspected female accomplice he was filmed having sex with.
Phra Wachirayan Wi, a former abbot at the prominent 14th-Century Wat Phutthaisawan in the ancient capital of Ayutthaya, allegedly pocketed donations meant for the temple on more than 20 occasions over two years.
In Thailand, Buddhist monks take a vow of celibacy and also renounce material possessions. He was defrocked after his arrest. He has yet to comment publicly.
The latest arrests come just over a year after another sex-and-blackmail case involving senior monks rocked Thailand's monastic community.
The 66-year-old was known for creating a highly-coveted coin amulet. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul reportedly owns some of his creations.
Thailand's Buddhist institution has long been plagued with reports of monks breaking their vow of celibacy, trafficking drugs and committing financial crimes.
In July last year, police opened a hotline for people to report "misbehaving monks" after at least nine monks were found to have had sex with a woman. She then blackmailed them with photos and videos of the acts for nearly $12 million.
Police on Friday said they identified two streams of money linked to donation receipts Phra Wachirayan had issued in the temple's name – one was meant for temple renovations, while the other was payment for amulets and other sacred objects.
"But the money from both streams did not enter the temple's account. Not a single baht," lead police investigator Pattanasak Bupphasuwan told a news conference, according to reports.
Police found cash and gold bars worth more than 100 million baht while raiding Phra Wachirayan's residence on Thursday, with counting going on until late into the night, Thai news outlet The Nation reported.
While examining CCTV footage in the residence, police found a clip of him having sex with a woman on his dining table.
Authorities identified her as 47-year-old Punyavee Rungrueang, who has been arrested on charges of abetting a state official in illegal activities. She has yet to comment publicly.
Many monks in Thailand receive stipends from the government and are therefore considered state officials.
Police seized 35 gold amulets, along with about 1.5kg of gold bars and jewellery, worth an estimated 6.04 million baht, from Punyavee's home.
Police believe Punyavee helped Phra Wachirayan manage his embezzled proceeds, noting that tens of millions of baht circulated through her bank accounts each year, The Bangkok Post reported.
Investigators say they started looking into the case in mid July, after receiving an anonymous tip alleging Phra Wachirayan of misconduct and misuse of temple funds.
Two or three other people could be involved in the case, they say.

London tourist tax on accommodation will be capped at 5pc, mayor says
A new tax on overnight stays in London will be capped at 5 per cent of the cost of accommodation, the BBC has reported.
Under the legislation, local authorities will be able to charge a flat fee or a percentage of the cost of an overnight stay for domestic and international guests in London accommodations.
London Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan told BBC London that he welcomed plans by the government and promised it would not be above 5 per cent per night.
The exact amount has not yet been determined.
"I fully support the government's decision, after years of lobbying, to give us the same powers that other cities, from New York to Los Angeles, from Chicago to Paris … have, which is the ability to raise a levy on those who come to our great city," he said.
"We've got to invest in making sure that [our] city continues to be attractive."
There are concerns the costs could put visitors off heading to London, an extremely popular destination for Australians heading abroad.
How will the tax work?
Between November of last year and February of 2026, the UK government consulted on the design of a new power for English councils to introduce overnight visitor levies or a "tourist tax".
The legal framework to do so will be introduced in the Overnight Visitor Levy bill, which has not yet been tabled in parliament.
A visitor levy set by English mayors would apply to hotels, guesthouses, bed and breakfasts, hostels, campsites, self-catering properties, and short-term lets, and university and religious accommodation when let commercially.
The levy would be set as a percentage of the price of the accommodation.
Mayors would be able to set local exemptions.
They would also be able to choose to set a visitor levy in some of their local authority areas but not others.
Members of the combined authority would be able to reject a levy by a two-thirds majority.
It will bring England in line with Scotland and Wales, which have already introduced powers for local authorities to raise a visitor levy.
Why is it being implemented?
The bill proposes that English mayors can spend revenue from the levy for "broader initiatives which have a positive impact on the region's economic health."
"Mayors will be empowered to deliver more long-term, locally led investment in transport, regeneration and cultural assets that can unlock growth and make places more attractive for residents, businesses and visitors," the bill said.
"The government will not compel any mayor to introduce this levy, nor will central government reduce funding for mayors if they decide to do so."
The levy could raise up to £240 million ($450 million) annually, according to Central London Forward, which represents 12 London local authorities and is based on a 3 per cent levy on the cost of a room.
Where else has it been applied?
Similar schemes have been implemented around the world.
In Europe, a city tax is the norm for many popular locations, including Venice, Rome, Amsterdam, Barcelona and Berlin and is used to fund local infrastructure and manage over-tourism.
In Paris, travellers pay from $2 to $15 per night depending on how the hotel is rated.
In New York, several taxes are applied to an overnight stay, which total about 14 per cent per night.
Japan also charges an overnight stay tax for foreign visitors per night.
How has Australia responded?
According to the most recent data from Visit Britain, 1.2 million Australians travelled to the UK in 2024.
During the travellers' visits, their total expenditure was a record £1.7 billion, with an average spend of £1,358 ($2,561) per visit.
Australians have criticised the proposed changes amid the growing expenses of overseas travel.
Australian Travel Industry Association chief executive Dean Long previously told the ABC the decision to tax travellers would add to an already expensive long-haul destination at the top of many Aussies' bucket lists.
"We're entering a new era where governments are increasingly targeting travellers with taxes," he said.
"It's a never-ending battle that ultimately means less money spent in the economy and less revenue for the small businesses employing the people who deliver the experiences."

Weeks after suspending production of select cars in India, Vietnamese EV maker VinFast is now reportedly eyeing the development of two new electric vehicles for the Indian market. As per a report by Reuters, VinFast is currently in initial discussions with suppliers in India for the two new models, internally codenamed VF X and VF Y. Inc42 has reached out to VinFast for comments on the development. The story will be updated based on their response. The two models mark a shift in VinFast's India strategy, with the company looking to develop vehicles specifically for the Indian market instead of adapting its global models. The VF X is expected to be positioned as an affordable compact EV with a targeted price below $12,000, the report added. As per a report by Autocar India, the EV maker has also filed design patents in India for the facelifted versions of its VF6 and VF9 electric SUVs. The EV cars are some of its most sought after cars internationally. For the Indian market, the models could potentially get revised lighting elements, new alloy wheels, among other upgrades. VinFast appears to be changing its India strategy after reassessing the economics of localising its global models. The development comes days after reports suggested that the company is halting its production in India. However, a VinFast representative told Inc42 that it will continue CKD assembly of these models at its Thoothukudi plan. To note, VinFast has committed to invest $2 Bn in India as it seeks to establish the country as a global manufacturing hub. The company had commissioned its Thoothukudi facility, with the first phase involving an investment of up to $500 Mn. The Thoothukudi facility currently has an initial annual capacity of 50,000 vehicles, which is planned to be scaled to 150,000 units. It currently focuses on assembling the VF 6 and VF 7. The strategic reset comes as VinFast has started gaining traction in the Indian EV market. The company retailed 2,198 electric passenger vehicles in August, its highest monthly sales since entering India, as per industry data. Its sales rose 44% from 1,531 units in July, giving it a 7% share of the electric passenger vehicle market. “Recently, we have been actively engaging with local suppliers and have organised consecutive supplier conferences in both Vietnam and India, with the participation of more than 300 Indian suppliers, to explore deeper cooperation opportunities and promote localisation,” the representative added. The recent strategic shift comes at a time when the company is doubling down on the Indian EV market commercially. Earlier in June, the company also forayed India’s electric ride-hailing market with the launch of its Green SM Limo service in Delhi NCR. Green SM, owned by VinFast parent Vingroup, operates an all-electric fleet comprising VinFast's Limo Green, a seven-seater electric vehicle. The EV maker was also planning to enter India’s electric two-wheeler (E2W) market this year, following the launch of its VF6 and VF7 electric SUVs in the country in 2025.

Actor Dipika Kakar’s noticeably slimmer appearance has sparked fresh discussion among fans after her husband, actor Shoaib Ibrahim, featured her in one of his recent YouTube vlogs.
The couple was seen working out together at the gym, where Shoaib spoke about the visible changes in Dipika’s appearance. While he did not specify how much weight she had lost, he said the change had been significant.
“She has reduced a lot of weight, like in the olden days. She has lost a lot of weight with the treatments, diet, etc,” Shoaib said in the vlog.
Dipika, who was exercising alongside her husband, also reflected on the transformation. “It has been a long time….4-5 years later, I have reduced,” she said.
The conversation comes against the backdrop of Dipika’s widely documented health journey. The actor was diagnosed with stage 2 liver cancer in 2025 and underwent surgery before continuing treatment. More recently, she began immunotherapy as part of her ongoing medical care.
Over the past several months, Dipika and Shoaib have also spoken publicly about gradual changes to her routine, including dietary modifications and walking. Earlier reports noted that she had been making lifestyle changes under medical guidance, while the couple also cautioned against blindly copying another person’s diet or fitness routine.
Her latest appearance, however, has also highlighted an important distinction that can often be lost amid social media conversations about celebrity transformations: visible weight loss does not necessarily reveal the full picture of a person’s health.
As reported by The Indian Express, consultant dietitian and fitness expert Garima Goyal said the circumstances surrounding weight loss were crucial when assessing whether it was beneficial.
“Weight loss is not always intentional, and being thinner does not automatically mean someone is healthier. Planned weight loss achieved through an appropriate diet, exercise and lifestyle changes is very different from weight loss that occurs during illness or as a result of medical treatment,” Goyal said.
She further noted that prolonged illness and treatment could sometimes lead to a loss of muscle mass and reduced nutritional reserves, making adequate nourishment and strength equally important considerations.
The distinction is particularly relevant for people undergoing serious medical treatment. Weight can change because of deliberate lifestyle modifications, but it can also fluctuate due to illness, treatment-related side effects, changes in appetite and other medical factors. During cancer treatment, nutrition may need to be carefully tailored rather than approached through conventional weight-loss goals.
“Social media often celebrates a smaller body immediately, but the weighing scale alone cannot tell us whether weight loss is healthy, intentional, or beneficial,” Goyal said, adding that energy levels, muscle strength, nutritional status, recovery and a person’s overall medical condition also matter.
For someone undergoing treatment, she emphasised, the priority may not necessarily be further weight loss. Depending on the individual's condition and treatment plan, maintaining calorie intake, protein, muscle mass, strength and quality of life could be more important.
Dipika’s visible transformation may have caught the attention of viewers, but the wider conversation serves as a reminder that appearance alone cannot define recovery. A smaller number on the weighing scale may be noticeable. Health, however, is rarely that simple.
