Schools in Northern Ireland must give girls the choice to wear trousers as part of their uniforms as well as for PE and games, according to revised guidelines.
From next year schools would no longer be able to prohibit female pupils from wearing trousers, Paul Givan, the country’s education minister, said on Friday. “Today, I am taking that decision, that will be formally communicated, schools will be hearing from me,” he told the BBC.
A law passed last year that was aimed at reducing the cost of uniforms gave girls the legal right to challenge schools that banned them from wearing trousers.
However, campaigners said the change did not go far enough and put pressure on Givan, a Democratic Unionist party member of the Northern Ireland assembly (MLA) who said his own daughters wore skirts to school, to revise the guidelines.
Givan said he had to strike a balance between schools’ autonomy and the level of prescription in departmental guidelines. “I have listened carefully over recent months to young people and the message is clear: girls want the choice to wear trousers as part of their school uniform.”
The revised guidelines would not go into immediate effect to give schools time to update their policies, said Givan.
Other parties welcomed the change but accused the education minister of dragging his feet.
“I’m glad that it appears the minister has seen fit to U-turn on his decision not to ensure that all girls have the right to wear trousers as part of their school uniform,” said Nick Mathison, an Alliance MLA and chair of the Stormont assembly education committee.
“I want to thank all of the young campaigners who have been bravely raising their voices about this, and whose dedication will lead to seeing this wrong righted. The fact that in 2026 young girls and women had to campaign for this at all will not be forgotten.”
Substantial sums of public money were spent on drafting legislation to fix the minister’s error of judgment, Mathison added.
A girl’s right to wear trousers should not have been controversial, said Cathy Mason, a Sinn Féin MLA. “It should not have required further legislation from the education committee to force movement on something so basic.”
Cara Hunter, a Social Democratic and Labour party MLA, said young people who challenged the existing rules and refused to let the issue disappear deserved credit for the change. “The department must now deliver. This cannot be a right that exists on paper but becomes an argument at the school gate,” she said.

For most of history, menstrual blood has been dismissed as biological waste. But emerging research is now recasting this material as a goldmine for non-invasive diagnostics and regenerative medicine. Its potential applications are surprisingly broad, ranging from innovative cervical cancer screenings to advanced cartilage repair.
Much like saliva or blood plasma, menstrual fluid is rich with biological information. It is packed with immune cells, endometrial tissue, proteins, and genetic fragments.
Scientists are now digging into these biomarkers hoping to find ways to detect diseases early, and thus drop the use of invasive clinical procedures.
Stem cells
Researchers have recently reported that they had used menstrual blood to spot cancer early. Normally, medical workers have screened for cervical cancer using clinical check-ups that many people skip due to discomfort, cost, limited access to healthcare, and in fact plain embarrassment. As a result, screening rates remain low even in economically developed regions.
In 2025, a large population-based study in The BMJ by researchers from China offered a workaround. The team found that menstrual blood collected directly from sanitary pads could be tested for human papillomavirus DNA and precancerous lesions just as accurately as cervical swab samples collected by a clinician. Of course, the method excludes those who do not menstruate, but the fact that it offered a non-invasive, inexpensive, and suitable test that could begin from home is notable.
Menstrual blood is also gaining research focus thanks to stem cells derived from it. The groundwork for this was laid back in 2007 when a team from the U.S. and Canada successfully isolated menstrual stem cells from menstrual blood. These cells came from the endometrium, the uterine lining that breaks down and rebuilds itself on a monthly cycle without scarring — something other human tissue cannot do. The researchers believed the stem cells had something to do with that ability. In the lab, the menstrual-blood-derived stem cells readily divided and proved to be tough and versatile.
Researchers are already using them to grow uterine organoids — small functional models of the uterus located outside the body and used to study conditions like endometriosis. The stem cells could reveal traces of exposure to chemical compounds like phthalates and parabens, which was previously not possible to discern without an invasive examination.
Indeed, while bone marrow stem cells are still the gold standard for many therapies, extracting them is a gruelling process. It is painful, requires anaesthesia, and bears significant surgical risks. Menstrual-blood-derived stem cells however can be collected non-invasively, and sans the ethical baggage that often complicates stem-cell sourcing.
Future of regenerative medicine
As the science of these cells has matured, so have their applications. For instance, in 2025, a team in China studied the role they could play on Niemann-Pick disease type C1. This is a rare and devastating inherited condition that is caused by cholesterol and lipids build-up inside cells, leading to rapid neurological decline, loss of motor function, and dementia. The study found that menstrual-blood-derived stem cells could significantly lower neuroinflammation and cell death in experimental models of the disease. The work is still in its early stages, but for a condition whose therapeutic options are currently limited to drugs easing the clinical symptoms, a potential new advance is welcome.
A 2023 study by Iranian researchers showed that when these cells were delivered alongside their conditioned medium — the nutrient-rich fluid they had been cultured with — they helped accelerate heart recovery in rat models after a heart attack.
In hepatology, menstrual-blood-derived stem cells have been found to suppress the specific liver cells responsible for scarring and fibrosis. Because they naturally migrate towards areas of inflammation and cancer, researchers are also exploring engineering these cells to deliver therapeutic genes directly to a tumour site, sparing the rest of the body from the toxic side effects of chemotherapy.
Many experts increasingly believe extracellular vesicles (EVs) are the future of regenerative medicine. They are easier to standardise than whole stem cells — which are complete, living biological units that can divide and adapt within the body, but vary significantly from one batch to another. They also carry risks of becoming unintended tissue types. Because EVs are not whole cells, but rather clumps of proteins, lipids, RNA, and signalling molecules enclosed by membranes secreted from the parent cell, they can’t divide or differentiate into other tissues. This makes them safer, more stable alternatives and less likely to trigger immune rejection, can be engineered to evade immune detection, and can be frozen and stored just like conventional biological drugs.
Menstrual-blood-derived stem cells can be made to release these EVs when cultured in specific conditions in the lab, such as hypoxia (low oxygen) or by adding inflammatory cytokines.
Ordinary challenges
In a notable study published in Scientific Reports in February, a team from Lithuania isolated EVs from healthy donors and introduced them to human cartilage cells taken from patients who had undergone joint surgery. Within hours, the cartilage cells had absorbed the EVs and produced a new extracellular matrix, the scaffolding of healthy joints. When the team simulated joint inflammation, the vesicles reduced the release of markers associated with cartilage degradation.
Since osteoarthritis disproportionately affects women, the researchers also tracked hormone receptors. Specifically, when they examined how EVs affected receptors in the joint tissue, they found that the EVs had increased the expression of the progesterone receptor in cartilage cells, potentially restoring a hormonal signalling pathway that tends to deteriorate in women following menopause.
While most current treatments for osteoarthritis mask the pain, these findings suggest a way to actually slow or reverse the damage. Even though the research is nascent, if the findings hold up in future trials, any benefits will matter considering the number of people living with this condition, estimated to be 595 million worldwide in 2020.
Some significant hurdles remain as well. Scientists do not yet know how long these cells will survive once they are introduced into the body. There is no long-term human safety data— partly because there are no reliable markers to track the cells once they are inside a patient. Producing consistent, high-quality batches also remains a challenge, since no standardised benchmarks exist to verify the cells before use. The cells must themselves behave differently depending on the donor, varying with age, hormonal status, contraceptive history, and the conditions in which the cells were grown in the lab.
Then again, these are ordinary challenges of early-stage biomedical research rather than reasons to dismiss what has already been found.
Manjeera Gowravaram has a PhD in RNA biochemistry and works as a freelance science writer.

- There is no evidence that the FCC issued a direct threat to Jimmy Kimmel or threatened his network to specifically prevent him from airing an interview with James Talarico, a Texas Democrat running for a U.S. Senate seat.
- Kimmel said in September 2026 that ABC would not air his interview with Talarico on television because the FCC had threatened him, ABC and its affiliates over "simple traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don't like." That could reference any or all of a large number of disputes between the Trump administration and ABC.
- ABC and Disney are suing the FCC for various alleged retaliatory measures, including the FCC's decision to require early renewal of ABC's broadcast license after Kimmel made a joke about first lady Melania Trump.
- Under President Donald Trump, the FCC has also issued guidance stating that late-night talk shows are not exempt from the equal-time rule, which essentially means broadcast stations must provide equal opportunities to political candidates, regardless of partisan affiliation. ABC may have pulled the interview for fear of running afoul of this rule.
- The White House denied that FCC Chairman Brendan Carr had threatened Kimmel and said Kimmel was "play-acting" to create a "false narrative" about the Trump administration's policies. A "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" spokesperson did not immediately return a request for more information.
Jimmy Kimmel announced on Sept. 9, 2026, that his show "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" would not air his interview with U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico on television, citing the Federal Communications Commission's threats against the talk-show host's network, ABC, under U.S. President Donald Trump's administration.
Social media users circulated Kimmel's accusations; some claimed Trump or the FCC tried to "block" the interview from airing. In response, readers searched our website to determine whether the FCC actually threatened Kimmel or blocked him from airing the interview with Talarico, a Democratic Texas state representative.
Here's what Kimmel said about the situation (see 9:33 in the video below):
I interviewed Donald Trump when he was running for president in 2015. And at that time, when he was the one sitting next to me, he seemed to have no problem with the idea of talk-show hosts interviewing candidates. In fact, he was very eager to come back for another interview, which he did just before he became the nominee in 2016.
But for some reason, and I can't seem to figure out what that reason is, something has changed.
Now that he is president, his FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations based on simple traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don't like.
And so out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television. It will be posted on YouTube instead.
A closer look at Kimmel's words indicates he didn't actually say whether the alleged threat issued by the FCC specifically related to his Sept. 10 interview with Talarico. Kimmel said the FCC threatened him and ABC based on "simple traditional editorial decisions" and "guest bookings." That could be a reference to past disputes between ABC and the Trump administration or changing guidelines from the FCC.
The White House said Brendan Carr, chairman of the FCC, has not threatened Kimmel "regarding interviewing James Talarico, or any other candidate."
"Jimmy Kimmel is play-acting—as he often does—to create a false narrative about this administration's policies," Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, said in an email. "Any media outlet blindly amplifying Kimmel's egocentric delusion should insist on proof. Of which they will find none."
A spokesperson for "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" didn't immediately respond to a request for that proof, nor to a request to clarify whether Kimmel and ABC had received a specific threat — or whether the network made a proactive decision based on past experiences and Trump administration policy.
We left this claim unrated pending answers to those questions.
Here's more on why ABC might have pulled Talarico's interview from network television, aside from a possible direct threat:
ABC's disputes with Trump administration
Kimmel's accusation that the Trump administration has threatened him and his network could reference any or all of the many disputes he and his network have with the Trump administration.
In fact, Trump has repeatedly called for Kimmel's firing and for the FCC to strip ABC of its licenses in response to various broadcasts he hasn't liked.
In September 2025, ABC temporarily pulled Kimmel off air after comments he made about the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. The decision came after Carr suggested he might take action against Disney, ABC's parent company, if it didn't pull Kimmel's show.
The president also called on ABC to fire Kimmel in April 2026 after the talk-show host made a joke about first lady Melania Trump. Shortly after, the FCC ordered ABC to seek early broadcast license renewals, an unprecedented move that can signal "significant concerns with the value" of the station's operations, Carr said.
ABC and Disney sued the FCC in August 2026 for allegedly violating its free-speech rights, arguing (Page 3) that the Trump administration has "waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts."
FCC policy changes
It's also possible ABC may have pulled Talarico's interview from network television because of FCC guidance on giving equal time to political candidates on broadcast television under the Trump administration.
Some forms of broadcast media are exempt from this rule, including "bona fide," or legitimate, newscasts and news interviews. But in January 2026, the FCC issued guidance stating that late-night talk shows don't have a blanket exemption from the equal-time rule.
The FCC's guidance said that, in 2006, the agency determined the interview portion of "The Tonight Show with Jay Leno" qualified for as a "bona fide news interview" and thus would be exempt from the equal-time rule. Networks have relied on this ruling to mean that all late-night talk shows are exempt.
"This is not the case," the FCC said on Page 4 of the notice. "The FCC has not been presented with any evidence that the interview portion of any late night or daytime television talk show program on air presently would qualify for the bona fide news exemption."
The FCC's guidance has had real effects. In February 2026, for example, talk-show host Stephen Colbert claimed CBS blocked an interview with Talarico on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" from airing on broadcast television because the network's lawyers said in "no uncertain terms" that the interview could violate the FCC's guidance.
(CBS reportedly disputed Colbert's account and said its lawyers provided only "legal guidance," not a direct prohibition.)
The bottom line
There's no evidence the FCC directly threatened Kimmel, and a closer read of Kimmel's comments indicated that Kimmel never accused the FCC of specifically blocking his interview with Talarico from airing on television.
However, that doesn't mean the FCC hasn't threatened Kimmel and ABC in other ways. The FCC and ABC are embroiled in several disputes, and ABC has alleged that the FCC is engaging in retaliatory measures because the Trump administration doesn't like the network's content.

Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war
- Published
The Houthis' lightning advance across the southern reaches of the Tihamah – Yemen's arid coastal plain – appears to have taken most observers by surprise.
Until recently, the anti-Houthi coalition known as the National Resistance held significant territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast. In a matter of days, much of this has fallen to the Houthis.
According to some estimates, the Iranian-backed rebels have captured as much as 130km (81 miles) of the country's strategically important coastline.
It's the group's most impressive military coup for several years, proving that despite a civil war that has lasted 12 years, devastating Saudi air raids and attacks by American, Israeli and British forces, the Houthis remain a force to be reckoned with.
With their opponents stunned and demoralised, it's unlikely the Houthis will be dislodged any time soon.
- Houthis claim major advance in Yemen and tighten grip on Red Sea shipping lane 
  - Published1 minute ago
- Oil hits $100 a barrel for first time since July after US and Houthi strikes 
  - Published2 days ago
"Now that they are there, they're going to be entrenched," Hisham al-Omeisi, senior analyst at the Brussels-based European Institute of Peace, told the BBC. "And it's going to be a lot more costly to push them out."
Of course, the Houthis are not alone. They enjoy the backing of Iran, support that has become even more important for Tehran in the wake of the setbacks and defeats experienced by other parts of its so-called "Axis of Resistance" – Lebanese Hezbollah, Hamas in Gaza and the Assad regime in Syria.
"So they redirected their support to the Houthis," al-Omeisi said. "And of course they need that support."
Even though most analysts agree that it's a mistake simply to describe the Houthis as Iranian puppets, events of the past few days raise an uncomfortable new reality.
Seven months after the US and Israel launched their huge, combined assault on Iran, the regime in Tehran now exerts authority over not just one, but two of the world's most important maritime passages: the Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the Bab al-Mandab, gateway to the Red Sea (and the Suez Canal).
"Now Iran, directly and through proxies, controls two of the most strategic choke points in the Middle East and the world," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, "controlling more than 35% of the fuel and oil trade globally."
"This is as much leverage as a nuclear bomb," he says.
If the Houthis have also taken control of several key islands in the Red Sea, including Perim - which sits in the middle of the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandab - then the group's ability to interfere with international shipping will be greatly enhanced.
As the group's actions in the wake of Israel's war on Gaza proved, shipping in the Red Sea is highly vulnerable to Houthi missiles, drones and small attack boats.
"They were able to control what was going in and out of the Bab al-Mandab and up towards Suez without having these territorial gains," Yemen expert Iona Craig told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.
"But of course now they're controlling the area immediately overlooking the Bab al-Mandab, and this gives them far more leverage."
Shipping companies are likely to be sceptical about the sincerity of a statement released on Friday afternoon, in which the Houthi military said that maritime navigation was "safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels, which have already been subject to a blockade".
In their earlier attacks, the Houthis said they were only targeting vessels linked to Israel, but in fact hit ships with no such connection, including a Norwegian-flagged tanker.
Craig said the Houthis may nevertheless refrain from indiscriminate attacks, fearing a repeat of Operation Rough Rider - six weeks of major US air and naval strikes in the spring of 2025.
"They've already felt the wrath of the US," she said.
But would the US want to get involved anyway?
President Donald Trump's war with Iran is already unpopular. With oil prices creeping back up, it's doubtful that a new front would do much to enhance his approval ratings or his Republican party's chances in November's midterm US elections.
According to the Axios website, appeals for US intervention from the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman have so far gone unanswered.
Axios writes that the US "is increasingly concerned about the escalating conflict in Yemen and is working to intensify its support for the kingdom while simultaneously seeking to avoid direct military involvement".
But it's not just the potential threat to the Bab al-Mandab that's causing fear in Saudi Arabia.
Satellite images of an apparent Houthi missile-and-drone attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline – a vital alternative route for oil exports following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year – point to an effort by Iran's Yemeni allies to add to the economic pressures generated by the US-Israeli war with Iran.
Even if Iran did not directly order the attack, it clearly stands to benefit.
Baraa Shaiban, a researcher and analyst at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, says the origins of the latest upsurge in fighting – the worst since a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 - can be traced back to July, when a Houthi delegation returned from the state funeral of Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
"Immediately after, the escalation started," he says, "and it looked very clearly that [Iran was] determined to now have a bigger foothold on the Red Sea".
With Yemen teetering on the edge of a return to all-out war, Saudi Arabia anxious about preserving its economic lifeline to the Red Sea and Donald Trump apparently reluctant to get involved, America's conflict with Iran just took on a new and potentially dangerous dimension.
For the people of Yemen, displaced, bombed, starved and impoverished by a dozen years of civil war, recent developments can only make their lives worse.

US diesel prices soar past $6 a gallon, deepening strain for hauling everyday goods
Diesel prices in the U.S. hit yet another record on Friday, soaring past $6 a gallon on average as Washington's war with Iran disrupts the world's flow of fuel.
The national average of $6.05 is up from $5.85 last week and $3.70 this time last year, according to motor club AAA.
Higher diesel prices mean more expensive transportation for a long list of everyday goods. That's because diesel is used for many freight and delivery networks. And some businesses have already passed along steeper costs to consumers in the form of added fees on online orders and packages in the mail.
Shoppers may feel more and more sticker shock, particularly in the grocery aisle. Perishable foods, like meat and produce, face one of the most immediate strains of expensive diesel because they need to be hauled in and restocked frequently — or may be harvested using farm equipment powered by the fuel.
It can take time for those costs to trickle down. But the surge in diesel prices doesn't appear to be going away anytime soon.
Prices at the pump for diesel and regular gasoline — which hit $4.29 on average in the U.S. Friday — closely follow that of crude oil. And oil has renewed its rise recently. This week, both Brent, the international standard, and U.S. crude surpassed $100 a barrel for the first time in months as fighting between the U.S. and Iran escalated again.
Political ramifications may pile up in the meantime. President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly tried to downplay the effects of the Iran war, said that oil prices likely won't come down until after November's midterm elections.
What's driving the latest jump for diesel
American diesel prices are now significantly higher than they were before the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran in late February, when the national average sat at about $3.76 per gallon per AAA. Prices quickly climbed as the cost of crude oil — the main ingredient in refined fuel like diesel, as well as gasoline — soared amid supply chain disruptions across the Middle East, notably with most tanker traffic bottlenecked in the key Strait of Hormuz.
Despite prices cooling some during hopes for peace earlier in the summer, oil has now renewed its climb as fighting once more escalates. Brent crude, the international standard, was trading at more than $105 a barrel Friday, up from roughly $70 before the war.
When adjusted for inflation, however, prices have been higher in the past. Ahead of the 2008 financial crisis, for example, diesel hit about $4.74 a gallon, equivalent to $7.20 in 2026, according to the government's latest data. And 2022's then-record of nearly $5.82 — reached just months after Russia invaded Ukraine — would be about $6.56 this year when accounting for inflation.
That doesn't take the pain away from today's steep prices, which are already bringing ripple effects for the economy and wider costs of living. Drivers are feeling the pain with gasoline, too.
Friday's average $4.29 for a gallon of regular unleaded is up from $2.98 before the Iran war, although still below the 2022 peak of nearly $5.02 a gallon nationwide.
Diesel has been more expensive than gasoline in the U.S. for decades, and its price has risen at a faster pace before. Some reasons include less flexibility in demand and diesel's position in global commerce overall. Individual households may find ways to drive less when gas prices are high, for example, but there's fewer immediate substitutes for networks that rely on diesel to haul goods worldwide.
All eyes on food
Diesel is integral to every part of the food supply chain. It powers farm equipment and fishing boats, as well as the trains and trucks headed to grocery stores.
Fuel accounts for roughly 15% to 30% of the total cost of food, according to the Independent Grocers Alliance, a grouping of 7,500 global supermarkets. So higher diesel costs often result in more expensive groceries, although it can take a while for energy shocks to wind their way through the supply chain.
Items that need to stay refrigerated while they're transported are often the first to see prices rise, according to David Ortega, a professor of food economics and policy at Michigan State University. In July, for example, overall U.S. grocery prices were up 2.7% compared to a year prior, but seafood prices were up 7% and fresh fruit prices were up 4.9%.
Ortega cautioned other factors can be at play, too. Lettuce also faced higher transportation costs in July, but a drop in demand due to the cyclospora outbreak caused prices to fall.
Still, consumers could feel more of a squeeze the longer diesel prices remain high.
"Early on, much of the cost increase gets absorbed along the supply chain through existing freight contracts and retailer margins," Ortega explained last week. "But as contracts reprice and fuel surcharges take hold, more of that cost makes its way to the grocery store."
Fuel shocks range far and wide
Back in April, e-commerce giant Amazon rolled out a temporary 3.5% fuel and logistics surcharge on some third-party sellers. United Parcel Service, FedEx and the United States Postal Service also moved to add fees on some of the packages they ship earlier in the war, citing rising costs for fuel overall.
Experts warn that price hikes could mount the longer diesel remains expensive. A range of other products are also transported by diesel-powered networks, including clothing, cosmetics and furniture.
The ramifications extend beyond consumer goods. Some public transit buses and trains also run on diesel. And diesel generators are often used for backup or emergency power, if not central electricity sources in some remote parts of the world.
Experts warn the consequences could continue to deepen, particularly in African and Asian countries, which rely more on Middle East imports and have already been hit the hardest by energy shocks.
According to the latest data from Global Petrol Prices, diesel prices in Nigeria have surged over 90% since late February — followed by nearly 87% in Indonesia and 80% in Lebanon.
Price tags vary widely between countries, due to factors ranging from fuel taxes to local economic conditions. As of Monday, diesel prices in Nigeria were about $4.95 per gallon (1,730 naira per liter) on average. Meanwhile, the highest sticker price reported by Global Petrol Prices was in Hong Kong, where diesel costs have jumped almost 26% during the war and averaged at $17.78 a gallon (nearly 37 Hong Kong dollars per liter) Monday.
A long road of constrained supply — and perhaps higher and higher prices — could be ahead.
S&P Global Energy said Thursday it now doesn't project crude oil production in the Middle East to return to prewar levels by the end of 2027.
"The market is not returning to calm, it is adjusting to the new normal," said Jim Burkhard, VP and global head of crude oil research at S&P Global Energy, noting security and logistical challenges continue to limit oil flows.

Trump’s Dream World in Dallas
At a midterm convention, Trump tries to defy the odds one last time.
President Trump began his midterm-convention address last night by casting his spell on the crowd in Dallas. “This place is packed,” he announced from the stage, pointing to the back of the American Airlines Center, where everyone could see hundreds of empty seats. Those who looked up saw thousands more, whole sections without any people at all. But the crowd cheered anyway. A deal had been struck. Reality would be ignored.
After more than a decade in politics, Trump is facing his last great electoral test—his popularity is waning, his party is down in the polls, Republicans could lose control in the U.S. House and maybe the Senate. He demanded greater complicity minutes later, seeming to invent a person in the back of the room. “He’s leaving for the bathroom. He’ll be back in two minutes,” he said, pointing. “They’ll take a picture of his seat while he’s gone. And they’ll say Trump did not fill up the arena.”
Laughter joined with the cheers for their political wizard. It was working. Trump could say that he had passed “the largest tax cut in the history of our country,” even if that was not the case. He could claim to have won the presidency three times, when he’s actually done so twice. He could describe the recent past as “the most successful two years financially and every other way in the history of the presidency,” despite six in 10 voters saying he had made the economy worse. He could promise to pay every adult U.S. citizen $5,000 if Republicans held both legislative houses, as if that sum did not amount to about 80 percent of the federal discretionary budget. He might even be able to convince the country to embrace the big fantasy, a chance to defy history and seal victory for Republicans in November.
“I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” he said. “I’m on the ballot. I’m on the ballot. Just one more time.”
The night was all about Trump. He was the alpha and omega, the focus and the solution. Attendees wore pictures of the president on lanyards around their necks, the ticket for entry to the arena. VIP boxes were stocked with Trump was right about everything hats. Oversize photos of the president lined the hallways. Five hours before he arrived, he received his first standing ovation. A video montage played on the big screen, images of the president narrated by a reading of Rudyard Kipling’s “If”—“If you can talk with crowds and keep your virtue.” When each speaker dropped Trump’s name, it was cause for riotous celebration.
Until now, national political conventions have been held only during presidential-election years, when delegates from each state gather to select their nominee. In the 1970s, the gatherings shifted from smoke-filled rooms for party business to televised infomercials for the candidates. Trump this year created a simulation of a simulation. The balloon nets had no nominee to drop for. The state delegations, sitting under signs on the floor, had no procedural purpose. (The smart party leaders, one strategist told us, were selling their “delegate” tickets to donors.) The convention-in-name-only was for, by, and about one man—who, importantly, cannot be a candidate for president again, according to the U.S. Constitution.
“The only way to keep dangerous, radical, weird out of the Senate is a united Republican Party standing with our president, Donald J. Trump,” Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina, the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, bellowed from the stage. “Stand for the president, Donald J. Trump. This is a battle for the heart of our nation. I said the heart of our nation.”
No president has tried something like this before. None has had so much money to spend on themselves at this point in a presidency. None has chosen to make the midterms a referendum on themselves while polling so badly. But this is Trump, and Trump has come back from worse. For a decade, the GOP’s electoral success has risen and fallen on his energies. The strategist in chief has bet that turning out Trump voters, the ones who typically stay home when he is not on the ballot, is the only path forward. This is why the first ads he bought for the cycle were not about any candidates who are running this year, but about himself. This was why his latest show was a celebration of the unlimited possibility of his incantations.
“Vote Republican, and we will leave the world in our dust for generations to come,” he told the crowd. “There’ll be nothing like it.”
Outside Trump’s curated fantasy world, not everything has gone according to plan. Trump’s political strategist, James Blair, announced after the off-year elections in 2025 that the president would be “very, very focused on prices and cost of living.” White House aides told us in the new year that the pivot would come after Trump scratched his itch for another confrontation with Iran. By May, as that conflict dragged on, Trump advisers told us quietly that if it had not receded, along with gas prices, by Labor Day, there would be trouble. Two weeks ago, multiple Trump advisers told us they expected the kinetic part of the Iran war to mostly cease in September, clearing the way for lower gas prices.
None of that has happened. Missiles are still flying in the Strait of Hormuz. Since the 2025 elections, gas prices have risen 39 percent, from $3.08 to $4.28; 30-year mortgage rates have increased 8 percent; electricity prices have gone up more than 4 percent. Charlie Cook, a political analyst and the dean emeritus of legislative-election handicapping, says that Republicans should brace themselves for a tough result. “The worst-case scenario for the GOP and best for Democrats today would have sounded ludicrous eight months ago,” he wrote recently. “The most plausible today resembles Republicans’ nightmare scenario at the beginning of the year.”
Those Republican nightmares, both new and old, are unlikely to be worse than the 40-seat gain made by Democrats in the House of Representatives during Trump’s first term, in 2018, thanks to increased polarization and mid-decennial redistricting. But few Republicans still pretend off-camera that they will be able to maintain control of the House. Narrow Democratic control of the Senate, once outlandish, could be within reach. On the sidelines of the convention in Dallas, strategists muttered about recent polling in House races that shows jump balls where Trump won by double digits in 2024.
The outstanding question is whether Democratic candidates can emerge from the dim shadow of President Biden. “While there is a lot of focus on the Republicans’ problems, Democrats have a real problem—they have a real party-image problem,” the Trump pollster Tony Fabrizio told us.
Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic strategist, depicts his party in PowerPoint presentations as a backpacker hiking up a steep mountain with gusts of wind at his back. The incline represents Trump’s financial advantages, and the challenge of winning seats in gerrymandered districts and Republican states such as Ohio, Iowa, Texas, and Alaska. The wind is voter sentiment and the enthusiasm advantage inside the Democratic Party. “Democrats have won the message fight. Republicans have lost the governance fight,” he told us. “The question is whether they can use structural advantages to overcome it.”
On the whole, Democrats are delighted by Trump’s strategy—to put front and center a man whose unpopularity fires up their voters and further alienates the newly skeptical. “If the Democrats have a great year, it will be because they got their base out to vote in large numbers,” Rich Thau, the moderator of the Swing Voter Project, told us. “It won’t be because they magically converted these swing voters into Democratic senatorial and gubernatorial voters.”
But they may not be accounting for Trump’s magic. Two years ago, he bounced back from two impeachments and an attack by his supporters on the U.S. Capitol to win the presidency. Now the odds are against him again. By multiple measures, the president who appeared on the Dallas stage last night had lost a step. When he first won the White House, in 2016, he denounced the folly of distant wars of choice, promised to remedy the reigning economic turmoil of globalization, and boasted of his independence as someone who eschewed campaign donations. A decade later, he is managing a reescalating war in Iran that he started. He has positioned himself as a champion of data centers, the latest lightning rod for populist resentment. And he controls a massive $850 million slush fund he acquired in office through seemingly transactional demands of companies, lobbyists, and wealthy individuals seeking government favor.
His economic approval rating this summer, according to Quinnipiac University, stood at 34 percent, down from 53 percent on the eve of the last midterm elections on his watch, in 2018. The 2024 presidential election hinged on the rising cost of living, and after Republicans won the trifecta—the White House and both chambers of Congress—the expectation was that Trump and his party would fix what many still view as Biden’s economy. “I want to emphasize that this wasn’t to just slightly improve things,” David Winston, a Republican strategist who works with congressional leadership, told us. “They viewed a substantive outcome as what they were looking for.” It has not come to pass.
Trump has not lost his talent for showmanship. No longer tied to a single hit program in a single slot on NBC, he has spent much of the year creating television spectacles from the Oval Office—a Formula One race, a UFC fight, a Fourth of July party, a World Cup championship celebration where he lingered in the frame. This string of network debuts gave him the confidence to schedule his convention against the first two games of the NFL season. Only Trump would choose to go up against the Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots.
For those who watched, the first night in Dallas had production quality that has escaped many recent Republican conventions. All the tropes and tricks were hit—the testimonials of a Pennsylvania steelworker and a Florida grandma about policy wins, the glitter reels of alleged Democratic bad behavior, the plea for campaign donations for Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee from Texas. Multiple speakers gave mock “land acknowledgements” praising the national heritage of European colonizers. The comedian Adam Carolla did a bit about Trump’s hair: “You ever see underwater footage of a kelp bed?” There were “everyday Americans,” “American workers,” and Border Patrol agents who gathered onstage, many in work gear. “President Trump refuses to surrender,” Senator Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania said, after a friendly video introduction from his Democratic colleague John Fetterman. “This November there can be no surrender.”
There was even a moment to lay out the core contrast that Trump’s advisers hope will frame the election, the sort of message that any other Republican president in his position would be entirely focused on delivering at this point. In a short video, his team spliced together clips from fringe voices on the left—the “woke,” the America-bashing, the revolutionary—before defining the decision on the ballot. “This is no longer simply Republican versus Democrat, or conservative versus liberal,” said the voice-over. “Today the choice is unmistakable: extreme versus mainstream.”
But the centerpiece remained Trump. Speaker after speaker described him in near-messianic terms. “As it turns out, Washington wasn’t incapable of working for the American people; all we needed was a new president,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. T. W. Shannon, a candidate for lieutenant governor in Oklahoma, placed the entire GOP in the president’s shadow. “We’re also the party of the greatest president in American history, President Donald J. Trump,” he declared.
But no comments mattered more than Trump’s. He talked for nearly two hours, a rolicking, weaving address that only occasionally stuck to the teleprompter. It ended where he began. “Please pretend that I’m running, and get out and vote on November 3 or sooner,” he said. “Because, in actuality, I really am running.” In actuality, he is not. Or maybe he is, in a way. His crowd remained in their seats to the end. The room, at times, felt packed to the rafters.

When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of all
- Published
As he picked his way past the frozen slope towards two bodies, Mingma Gyalje Sherpa knew his friends were gone.
Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Nirmal Purja and Kili Pemba Sherpa were two of the strongest climbers Mingma G had ever known.
But this July, an avalanche swept through Pakistan's Broad Peak while the two were on their way up, engulfing everything in its path.
The drone images seemed clear: no-one had survived.
And yet, as Mingma G came closer to the fluorescent down suits, sharp against the snow, he couldn't shake the idea they were waiting for him.
"I told them: 'It's ok. You don't have to be here in the cold anymore.'"
Speaking to the BBC in Islamabad, he recalls the terrible moment he reached for their bodies.
Holding one of them, he promised: "I'm here to take you guys home."
Mingma G and Nirmal Purja met in Pakistan in 2021, where they were part of the first team to summit the world's second-highest mountain, K2, during winter.
Mingma G knew of Nirmal - or Nims, as he was known - from his Netflix documentary 14 Peaks, in which he successfully climbed the world's 14 highest mountains in just over six months.
The pair, both avid climbers from Nepal, had taken different paths.
Mingma G came from the Sherpa community and built his reputation as a mountain guide over 20 years. Nims was a former Gurkha and British Special Forces soldier who quickly became one of the world's best-known mountaineers.
Many saw Nims as an incredible climber who helped Nepalese climbers gain international recognition in a field dominated by foreigners. But he also had his critics: they said he focused too much on records, and on marketing his expeditions to a growing social media following.
In 2024 the New York Times published sexual misconduct allegations from two women, which Purja strongly denied through his lawyer at the time, who said they were "false and defamatory". Purja again denied the allegations in a lengthy interview soon after.
Before Mingma G met Nims, he wasn't sure about him: "In the beginning, I had the feeling he was very arrogant."
But that changed when their paths crossed five years ago, as competitors on their way to K2, who then decided to climb the mountain together and share the record. Mingma G says he found Nims to be "very kind-hearted, one of the most beautiful human beings I've met".
Over the years the two would meet on various mountains around the world: Nims "would always be on Everest".
This summer they met again, walking into the Karakoram range, before they would split up for different climbs. Nims headed for Broad Peak and Mingma G for K2, around 8km (five miles) apart.
Nims asked Mingma G to wait another day so they could meet once more before embarking on these separate missions, but that meeting never happened.
"That was the last thing he told me. I still regret it."
On 30 July, "we had perfect weather, sunshine, no winds," Mingma G says.
By then, he was leading a team up K2. Nims's team of climbers had joined others to form a larger group of 10 that was making its way up Broad Peak.
At 08:30, Mingma G spoke to Kili Pemba Sherpa - better known as Kilu - a childhood friend and expert climber in Nims's group. Snow conditions looked good, Kilu had said, and the two agreed to speak again when they both reached the next camp on their respective mountains.
The BBC spoke to two trekkers who spotted the climbers scaling Broad Peak. "We were cheering them on," one says. He took a photo of them on the slope, small silhouettes against the snow.
The group continued ascending. But less than an hour later, there was a "thundercrack", the other trekker says: "a huge avalanche, starting from the top going down both sides of Broad Peak".
"We were hoping and praying that the climbers were above the avalanche," the first trekker continues. But they couldn't see the silhouettes on the slope.
The trekkers' guide notified base camp about what they had witnessed.
The cause of the avalanche is still being investigated, but the Alpine Club of Pakistan told the BBC that while it had snowed heavily earlier that week, their initial research suggested that it was caused by the collapse of an ice slab, irrespective of snowfall.
By the time Mingma G reached the next camp on K2, his team had not heard from the Broad Peak climbers. They didn't panic because climbers often turn off the radio to save battery life.
But something was bothering him.
One of the Broad Peak climbers, Wang Zhong, was a close friend and a client. He would normally message Mingma G through his Garmin satellite tracker to let him know he'd arrived safely at the next camp. But there was no message from him.
Thousands of metres below, Pakistani mountain guide Waqar Ali says he was also trying to contact the group, but to no avail. He thought they may have been sleeping, in preparation for a final push towards the summit that night.
But by 15:00, no-one at base camp had had any contact with the group on Broad Peak.
Mingma G was 7,300m up on K2, where communication was difficult. His team started calling officials, families, contacts in Kathmandu and anyone who might have been in touch with the climbers.
He says it was probably 20:00 when they first heard that the altitude readings from the Broad Peak climbers' trackers had dramatically fallen: one of them had dropped by around 1,600m.
It was too late to climb and too dark to send up a drone, so he decided to wait for sunrise. "I had hope," Mingma G says. Especially for Kilu and Nims, who were "experienced and physically… strong".
Early next morning, a drone was sent up and soon after, the operator radioed them. The drone had spotted bodies down the mountain. It looked like there were no survivors.
"I was totally blank," Mingma G recalls in a low voice.
He wasn't quite ready to accept he had lost so many dear friends at once.
"Maybe still I had a feeling they might all be alive [and] wanted somebody to help them get down. That was just something I had in my heart and mind."
Later that day, Mingma G called off his K2 expedition.
Down at the base of Broad Peak, Waqar wept as he arrived with another climber to start the difficult job of bringing the bodies back.
They retrieved the bodies of Nadhira Al Harthy, the first Omani woman to climb Everest, and Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepalese climber who had summited 12 of the world's 14 highest peaks.
But there were still bodies on the mountain and Mingma G was determined to bring his friends home.
When he called Nims's wife and brother-in-law to tell them the tragic news, he says they struggled to believe it. Kilu's wife "couldn't say much, but told me: 'don't leave your brother on the mountain'".
Organising the next steps of the recovery mission was complicated.
The climbers who'd been heading up K2 with Mingma G were unsettled, he says, and facing pressure from their families to go home.
Then there were the logistics. From the drone images, Mingma G thought the bodies could be recovered using a helicopter and a long-line rope, but says he was told this wouldn't be possible. "In Nepal it would have taken like two minutes," he says.
The Pakistani army which would have provided the helicopters didn't respond to the BBC's questions. The Alpine Club of Pakistan says a request made on 1 August was approved, but poor weather meant it could not be carried out for days.
There was only one other option for Mingma G - a recovery operation on foot.
On 1 August, Mingma G says, his team of rescuers set off in search of four bodies they believed they'd seen in the drone shots - those of Nims, Kilu, Zhong and a fellow climber called Nima Sherpa. Gyaljen Sherpa would also be discovered nearby.
With the slope so unstable, there was a risk of falling rocks and further avalanches. A larger team could potentially lead to more casualties, but a smaller team would struggle to bring the bodies down.
The moment the rescue team reached the bodies and began sending them down on ropes, another avalanche hit, he says.
The torrent of snow sent one of the bodies down to the bottom. Three others, including Nims, ended up in a more dangerous position - in the centre of a slope with large pillars of glacial ice precariously balanced to the left and right. If either were to collapse while the rescue team were trying to reach the bodies, the tower of ice could sweep them away.
The team needed a new plan. As the days progressed, some of its members started leaving. Their numbers went from nine to six, then four.
Given how precarious the slope was, the group decided Mingma G would hang back and monitor by drone, instructing the three climbers. The arduous operation took five to six hours, but they finally managed to bring the bodies back down the slope.
The moment Mingma G first saw his friends on the mountain still haunts him.
Nims and Kilu had covered their faces with their jackets - Mingma G believes they had seen the deadly avalanche coming and prepared. The two were attached to the same rope, their legs wrapped in it. Mingma G thinks they may have hit each other on the way down - which he fears killed them rather than the fall.
"They didn't fall that much, almost 500m. But unfortunately they hit each other a lot, I think. If they were not on the rope, maybe there was a possibility that Nims and Kilu might have survived."
The team brought the bodies back down the mountain. They were flown by helicopter to the nearby city of Skardu, then on to the capital Islamabad and finally, home to their families.
Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi's body was found a few days later, as was the body of American climber Mallory Geis. The body of Nepalese climber Nawang Thindu Sherpa remains on the mountain.
Nims's family say they are deeply grateful to the "extraordinary team led by our brother, Mingma G, who worked in incredibly challenging conditions to bring Nimsdai home".
This recovery operation has stayed with Mingma G. It doesn't compare to any other mission he has done.
As he looks back with deep sorrow, he feels the end of his career could be coming.
Memories of Kilu and Nims - the three of them singing together as they marched up to the summit of a freezing but sunny K2 a few years ago - will always be with him.
But, he says, "I'm not sure if it helps, if the memory helps me to keep climbing or it makes me stop."

Usually, when the San Francisco 49ers and the Los Angeles Rams play, it’s a relatively short commute. But this evening, the teams will kick off the NFL’s first-ever regular-season game in Australia.
The two teams have taken diametrically opposite approaches to preventing the 8,000-mile journey from disorienting their stars. The 49ers boarded their 16-hour flight to Melbourne nine days ago and have spent the intervening time training, watching Aussie rules football, and winning the majority of local support. The Rams landed yesterday, just 24 hours before the game. They’re betting on being in Australia so briefly that players’ brains and bodies won’t notice the difference. That makes the game the most high-profile test of jet-lag-evasion techniques in American sports history.
Anyone who has hurled across several time zones in one go knows how wide-awake and helplessly sleepy you can feel at inappropriate hours upon landing—a major inconvenience for professional football players, whose career depends on how they perform during one very specific period. Circadian rhythms can also affect performance in less obvious ways. Compounds that encourage inflammation, for instance, spike at night, when the body is doing less and can direct more energy toward fighting infection. A new time zone throws that optimal function off tilt and can cause stomach issues, cognitive impairment, headaches, and mood changes.
Teams at a circadian disadvantage tend to play worse. One study that analyzed every NFL game from 1970 to 2011 with a kickoff after 8 p.m. ET found that West Coast teams did better than oddsmakers expected in two out of every three games, regardless of whether they were home or away. Head coaches are also more likely to make the risky call to attempt an offensive play on a fourth down during evening games when they travel west compared with any other direction.
Because the consequences of jet lag are well established, the real question is how to avoid them. In 2021, 26 sleep researchers and clinicians articulated their best answer in the journal Sports Medicine. Among other recommendations, they noted that fully recovering from jet lag takes one day for each time zone crossed. The 49ers seem to have followed that model by leaving more than a week ahead of the game. (Melbourne is 17 hours ahead of California, but for body-clock purposes, that’s the same as being seven hours behind.) Kyle Shanahan, the 49ers’ head coach, told reporters last month that he would have loved to have just shown up in Australia the day before but that the experts he’d spoken with had all recommended arriving earlier. “I was a little bit on the fence,” he said. “Science wasn’t.”
The Rams, by contrast, are attempting to not switch their body clock at all. They have spent the past few weeks practicing in the late afternoon, which aligns with Friday’s mid-morning kickoff in Melbourne. Their head coach, Sean McVay, said at a Sunday press conference that the team will “have kind of a rhythm” when they land. “We’ve tested it out with some guys, and we feel like it’s been positive,” he added. The strategy is not without precedent: In 1994, Allen Johnson, an American hurdler, decided to live as if he were on East Coast time when competing in European tournaments. His coaching team strongly disagreed, but he won four world championships and Olympic gold. Last year, the Rams arrived in London the day before a game against a strong Jacksonville Jaguars team and won.
Jamie Zeitzer, a circadian physiologist and a co-director of Stanford’s Center for Sleep and Circadian Sciences, described the Rams’ strategy to me as “high risk, high reward.” If the Rams really feel as though they’re playing in the afternoon, they might have a slight advantage over opponents who feel as though they’re playing in the morning. During the late afternoon, circadian rhythms prompt optimal muscle strength and coordination, and core body temperature peaks, increasing alertness with it. Plus, a week might not be long enough for the 49ers to stop suffering the effects of their travel. Some people just take longer to recover, and a long-haul flight, jet lag, hotel life, and unfamiliar foods can lead to days of poor sleep, Zeitzer said. The 49ers have spent their September experiencing time as a pliable, erratic force. Shanahan told reporters that he was “a little confused” in a recent press conference, during which he also struggled to identify the day of the week. (It was Monday.)
Still, Zeitzer thinks the Rams have chosen the worse jet-lag strategy. If the players are to get any rest at all, their 24-hour stretch in Melbourne before game time needs to be carefully managed. From his experience consulting with professional teams, adults are hard to control. Meeta Singh, a doctor who has served as a sleep consultant for multiple NFL teams, thinks that players simply won’t be able to sleep. Singh is one of the co-authors of the Sports Medicine recommendations, which suggest that athletes maintain a “reduced exercise schedule” and do hand-eye-coordination drills in the 72 hours after a long-haul flight. The Rams won’t even be in Australia for 72 hours.
Sleep became a major metric for all sorts of professional sports teams after the NBA distributed more than 2,000 Oura rings to its players during the depths of the coronavirus pandemic. “Once you can show a coach numbers, sleep stops being a soft topic and becomes something they can manage, like training load or nutrition,” Singh told me. Many NFL teams now have a sleep specialist and a performance-science team working on circumventing jet lag. To prep players for time shifts before they depart, 14 NFL teams, including the 49ers, have installed in their training facilities lighting systems designed to mold circadian rhythms. The system, called BrainLit, mimics daylight according to a “recipe” that each team specifies, Kyle Harris, the CEO of the company, told me. On the 49ers’ flight to Melbourne—on the world’s largest and most expensive passenger airliner, with lie-flat seats that extend to seven feet—each player received his own sleep guidelines. Tom Clark, a sports scientist who advises NFL teams with international games, told me that many teams establish each player’s chronotype, or natural preference to sleep and wake at certain hours, and use that information to prescribe optimal sleep habits.
Roger Goodell, the commissioner of the NFL, eventually wants 16 international games to take place each season. By the time Super Bowl LXI rolls around this February, teams will have played in Rio de Janeiro, London, Paris, Madrid, Munich, and Mexico City. For future seasons, the league is considering adding games in the United Arab Emirates and Japan; Goodell insists that an NFL team will be based outside the U.S. in his lifetime.
Perhaps such a punishing schedule will settle debates once and for all about how to handle jet lag. Whatever the marginal impact of sleep strategy, though (and some games are decided on the margins), usually “the better team will win even if they’re playing on the moon,” Clark said. And the Rams are this year’s Super Bowl favorites.

Congress shifts Rahul Gandhi's Indore event to leased ground after stadium denial
Congress has secured a leased ground in Indore for Rahul Gandhi's 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' after being denied the stadium. The venue row has triggered a fresh Congress-BJP clash over permissions and political intent.
The Congress has leased an alternative venue in Indore for Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's upcoming 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' programme after it was denied permission to use the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium. An official of the Indore Development Authority said the party paid Rs 10.08 lakh for a temporary lease of 12,000 square metres of land in front of the Regional Park from September 17 to 19.
Congress leaders accused the BJP of delaying permissions because it was nervous about Gandhi's visit, while the BJP dismissed the charge and accused the opposition party of propaganda. The programme, which the Congress says has drawn registrations from around 1.5 lakh students, is now scheduled for September 19.
An Indore Development Authority letter to Indore City Congress Committee president Chintu Chouksey said permission for the event would be issued after the funds were deposited and subject to prescribed conditions. The letter also said the organisers would be responsible for security arrangements at the venue and for obtaining no-objection certificates from the relevant departments.
Talking to PTI, Chouksey said, "We have deposited the agreed amount into the IDA's bank account." He alleged that the BJP government was nervous about Gandhi's upcoming event in Indore and, in that panic, had been harassing the Congress over the venue.
"We initially wanted to hold the event at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium on September 12, but after not receiving permission, we had to change the date to September 19. We were made to run around for 10 days for the land located in front of the Regional Park," Chouksey said.
The Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium, where the Congress had first sought permission for the event, falls under the municipal corporation. Indore Mayor Pushyamitra Bhargava said that under an old order of the Madhya Pradesh High Court, the stadium can only be used for sports or state-level government events.
BJP state co-media in-charge Alok Dubey said the Congress was indulging in propaganda politics and that the public knows the truth about the party. Taking a jibe at the Congress, he said the name of Gandhi's event should be changed from "Chhatron Ki Goonj" to "Jhooth Ki Goonj." The Congress has named the new venue "Bharat Jodo Maidan".
'Chhatron Ki Goonj' is a student dialogue campaign launched by Gandhi to target the BJP on issues such as question paper leaks, expensive education, irregularities in government recruitment and unemployment. Four editions of the programme have so far been held in Kota, Dehradun, Prayagraj and Pune, with the previous one in Pune on August 22 held for female students. With the Indore venue now secured, the Congress has shifted the event from the stadium to the leased ground in front of the Regional Park.

A few weeks before her Asian Games debut in mixed martial arts, Suchika Tariyal is back to basics. On a synthetic mat above a restaurant in Mumbai’s Andheri suburb, she splits her sessions between sparring and rules briefings from a referee who will officiate at the Aichi-Nagoya Games.
It’s an unusual position for someone who has spent nearly three decades fighting. Tariyal has been a national-level judoka, reached a bronze medal bout at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games, represented India in Kurash at the Asian Games, won a world title in fighting Jiu-Jitsu and had a brief run as a professional MMA fighter. Yet the rules of amateur MMA remain new to her.
“I was already fighting professionally but I saw a post on Instagram about trials for the Asian Games in Mumbai. I signed up without knowing the rules,” she tells Sportstar. She won those trials, beating three opponents, then travelled to China for the Asian Championships, where she reached the semifinals and secured a bronze before a defeat rooted less in ability than in unfamiliarity with the scoring system.
“I got her to the ground but was thinking like professional MMA, where you score for damage even from the bottom. Amateur rules are different,” she says.
At 36, Tariyal is relearning a sport at an age when most careers are ending. She laughs at the thought of saying it aloud, but there is no regret in it. “I’m still competing. I’m still having fun. The most fun I’m having is in this,” she says.
For Tariyal, though, this is only the latest chapter in a career that has repeatedly required her to start again.
Where it started
While she can’t imagine life without fighting, Suchika admits her entry into combat sports came by chance. It was a response to childhood trauma. The youngest of four daughters growing up in New Delhi, she recalls being sent to a neighbouring salon to get her hair cut when she was 10 years old.
“I hadn’t learned anything about good touch or bad touch but I knew what was happening was wrong. I ran back home with my hair only half cut,” she recalls.
The anger that followed, she says, turned into fights at school and a hostility towards boys, until her mother enrolled her in judo as an outlet.
“I’d start hating boys. I’d pick up fights with everyone in school. Finally my mother decided it was best to let me actually train in a martial art so she took me to a judo class,” she recalls.
It quickly became more than that. Tariyal discovered she had a genuine talent for the sport, winning her first national medal in 2011 and progressing through the age groups.
Progress off the mat was harder to come by, and harassment shadowed much of her career. At the Uttarakhand Police, she says she asked for time off to train and was instead met with inappropriate suggestions from seniors about how she could secure a promotion.
“It was just harassment. I was under so much mental trauma after that incident that I just left that job and returned to Delhi. It was always like this, where I wasn’t ever encouraged to improve as much as I wanted,” she says.
She later took another government job, but the setbacks continued. In 2018, after qualifying for the Asian Games through trials, her weight category was dropped from the squad 10 days before departure.
“My weight category (57kg) was dropped from the team 10 days before we were to leave but the weight category of others who had a worse record in international judo was kept. I always wondered whether things would’ve been different with a supporter in the system,” she says.
Her husband, Kapil Hooda, describes her as unwilling to defer to anyone for the sake of convenience.
“She has this sense of pride in herself that she’ll never do ji huzuri (be subservient). She’s also stubborn. If she has a goal in her mind, she’s going to keep chasing it. Not everyone likes that but that’s who she is,” he says.
She did eventually represent India at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in judo’s 57kg category, but the experience too left a bitter taste. The squad had initially been sent to an international camp before being recalled amid infighting within the federation following a change in its leadership.
“There was never any concern about what was in the interest of the athletes,” she says.
Tariyal reached the bronze medal bout at Birmingham against two-time Olympian Christianne Legentil, eventually losing by a solitary point. It proved to be her last appearance for India in judo.
“In India it isn’t just about how good you are. So many other things decide whether you get to show your talent,” she says of the federation politics and the ministry visits that followed.
Chasing a podium, one sport at a time
Disillusioned but unwilling to stop, Tariyal moved to Kurash for the 2023 Asian Games. Like judo, it is a jacket-based grappling sport, and she earned her place on the Indian team through trials. But she lost in the first round and injured her knee.
Still, she wasn’t done.
“I was still looking at what other sport I could do,” she says.
She switched to fighting Jiu-Jitsu, a hybrid discipline that combines judo-based grappling with open-hand strikes and submission holds. She won the national championships before earning a chance to compete at the World Championships in Greece, where she won a world title.
Success brought its own frustration. Sponsors, she found, were reluctant to back an athlete past 30.
“Everyone wants to support young athletes. They saw that I was over 30 and they didn’t want to have anything to do with me,” she says.
Largely self-funded through her career, she has appeared on reality shows including Roadies and India’s Ultimate Warrior to raise her profile and cover costs.
“One of the challenges if you aren’t taking part in a mainstream sport is that it’s hard to get sponsors interested in you. But you still need to make money to go and train and compete. I needed to raise my profile and make money. Sport by itself doesn’t pay my bills,” she says.
Her husband knows this well too.
“At one of her first national judo competitions, Suchika had injured her hand and barely had enough money to travel. She didn’t have 50 rupees. She went on a train without a ticket. Her mindset has always been bas pahunch jaun (just let me get there),” Hooda says.
That same need to earn pulled her towards MMA, via an offer to fight for BRAVE Combat Federation after her Jiu-Jitsu world title. Lacking a striking background, she was persuaded to take the leap by UFC fighter Puja Tomar, whom she considers a sister.
“I wasn’t sure at first because I don’t have a striking background but I spoke to Puja Tomar, who I consider a sister and she told me I should go for it,” she says.
Tariyal took the leap and built a 2-1 professional record. The experience also revealed how much she enjoys the sport.
“A lot of people are excited about fighting until the first time they get hit in the face but that only gets me hyped up more! From childhood, dhakke khaye hain. (I’ve always been pushed around). I was never scared of punches. If I get punched once, I won’t stop until I hit you twice,” she says.
Then came another opportunity to compete at the Asian Games.
Standing on the podium at a multi-event Games had always been the dream.
“I’ve not had the best experiences in going through federations but it’s always been my dream to stand on the podium at a multi-event Games. I still can’t let that go,” she says.
Qualification required top-eight finishes at Asian level, sending her to two separate Asian Championships, in China and Tashkent. She won bronze both times, while still adjusting to the format.
Amateur MMA differs sharply from the professional game. Fights happen on a mat rather than in a cage. Elbow strikes to the head are banned, as are submissions such as heel hooks and knee bars. Grounded fighters get only 20 seconds to advance position before being stood back up. The bouts are shorter and, unlike professional MMA, weigh-ins happen on fight day itself, leaving less scope for drastic weight cuts.
Learning once again
That 20-second limit cuts against her judo instincts, honed around throwing an opponent and then working patiently towards dominance. Now she has to learn to work faster.
“At the end of the day it’s fighting. I know I can fight,” she says.
For the past month, Tariyal has been training in Mumbai, figuring out the nuances of this format. It is another reminder that she is still willing to learn all over again.
Not everyone understands the choice to keep going.
“A lot of people wonder why I’m 36 and still fighting. They think after a certain age you should just go home and be with your family! But my husband supports me. He tells me I can stop when I want,” she says.
But the age question has also become part of what she wants to prove.
“I myself want to prove there isn’t an age limit to pursuing your dreams. I still beat all the new kids to get to this position. So why should I quit now?” she says.
Tariyal enters the Aichi-Nagoya Games as a medal contender on the strength of her recent results at the Asian Championships. But the medal isn’t the whole point.
“A lot of people get one chance in one sport to stand on the podium for the country. I’m getting one more. There’s something inside me that’s continuing to push me. Sometimes I wonder if I win a medal here would I still be as hungry as I am now? And I think that’s not true. I think I’ll still be fighting in some way or the other. I don’t think I can stop,” she says.

Maharashtra's food safety crackdown has gathered remarkable scale under Food and Drug Administration Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe, with 875 people arrested and food stock worth around ₹67.20 crore seized during a three-month enforcement drive across the state.
Between June and August 2026, the Maharashtra FDA carried out 12,083 inspections, according to the figures from the crackdown. The operation also led to 655 FIRs, the suspension of 603 food licences and the issuance of 5,269 improvement notices.
The numbers offer a measure of the scale of an enforcement campaign that has increasingly put restaurants, food manufacturers, roadside eateries and quick-commerce facilities under scrutiny.
Mundhe's FDA has adopted an aggressive approach towards food safety violations, with inspections extending beyond small establishments to prominent restaurants, institutional kitchens and warehouses operated by major food-delivery and quick-commerce businesses.
Recent inspections have exposed a range of serious shortcomings, including cockroach and rodent infestations, rotten food, poor sanitation, improper storage and food-handling practices that could increase the risk of contamination. In one crackdown on quick-commerce facilities, the Maharashtra FDA suspended permits for warehouses linked to major platforms after inspections flagged serious hygiene concerns.
The wider drive has also focused heavily on suspected adulteration and unsafe food products. Fake paneer, analogue or synthetic dairy alternatives, adulterated milk and concerns surrounding food oils have emerged as key areas of enforcement.
The FDA had earlier taken action against the use of analogue paneer, including suspending the licence of establishments found using the product after the regulator imposed restrictions on its manufacture, storage, distribution and sale in the state.
Food safety concerns have not been confined to one category of establishments. The regulator's inspections have covered hotels, restaurants, canteens, dairies, snack manufacturers and dark stores, reflecting the breadth of Maharashtra's rapidly expanding food economy.
In recent days, inspections in Mumbai and Thane have continued to uncover unhygienic conditions. A raid on food manufacturing units in Thane found dirty and sticky floors, pest infestations and unsafe storage practices, leading to the seizure of food material worth more than ₹20 lakh.
The crackdown has also reached well-known establishments. The FDA recently suspended the licences of food outlets linked to Mumbai's ISKCON-run Govinda's and other establishments after inspections flagged alleged hygiene and food safety lapses.
For Mundhe, the campaign appears to rest on the principle that the size or profile of an establishment should not determine the level of scrutiny. Earlier enforcement actions have covered everything from roadside food businesses to major commercial kitchens and prominent restaurants.
The scale of the current drive is also consistent with Mundhe's stated emphasis on stricter compliance. In August, he said food businesses that did not comply with the law could not be allowed to continue operating, while acknowledging the challenge of enforcing food-safety standards across Maharashtra's vast and diverse food sector. The three-month numbers now underline how extensive that enforcement push has become.
With more than 12,000 inspections and hundreds of licences suspended, the Maharashtra FDA's campaign has moved beyond isolated raids. It has become a statewide test of how food businesses - from neighbourhood eateries to large commercial operators - respond to a regulator that has made hygiene, labelling, storage and food safety a central enforcement priority.
