Three years after India-Canada ties were blown apart by allegations that Indian officials were involved in the killing of a Khalistani activist in Canada, and New Delhi and Ottawa downsized missions and sent back High Commissioners, both sides celebrated restoring embassies back to full strength this week. In a wide-ranging conversation at The Hindu MIND event moderated by Suhasini Haidar, Canadian High Commissioner to India Christopher Cooter said the two countries have now gone well beyond a reset in ties. He also confirmed that they are discussing a bilateral visit by Prime Minister Narendra Modi to Canada this December, when the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) will be announced. Mr. Cooter, however, sidestepped questions about whether Canada owes India an apology for the public allegations that spurred the rift. Edited excerpts:
Suhasini Haidar: You took charge of India-Canada ties at a time when relations hit rock bottom. Would you call yourself the reset ambassador?
It’s taken us some time to get here. It’s been over a year since Prime Minister Modi was invited to the G7 summit at Kananaskis in Alberta. But we have built momentum. I happened to arrive at the time that we started this reset, and now we have gone well beyond a reset. We are in a kind of dangerous time globally. We have two very hot wars going on (the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the West Asia conflict). We’ve got trade disruptions going on. We’ve got climate change. We’ve got AI, the challenge and opportunity. And it happens to be that this period in which we are re-establishing our relationship is the one that works the best for us. In all of the 80 years or so that we have had diplomatic relations, I don’t think we have ever had an environment which draws us together in that same way.
Suhasini Haidar: Do you see a big announcement round the corner? Prime Minister Narendra Modi is heading to North America in December for the G20 summit in the U.S. Do you expect his first bilateral visit in more than a decade this year?
Yes, a continuing string of events over the last year will culminate this year, we expect, in the visit of Prime Minister Modi to Canada. The two Prime Ministers, when Prime Minister [Mark] Carney came here in March, set out this kind of road map in a joint statement. I think it has 50 or more deliverables and we are trying to fulfil those commitments. There are commercial deals in the offing. There’s a broader range of areas where we are doing things together, for example, in defence. So, it’ll become a bit more tangible to the average person. In October, we have the largest trade mission coming to Mumbai and Bengaluru.
Suhasini Haidar: Have Canada-India trade relations been spurred by the Donald Trump administration’s actions? And will the push remain once Canada and the U.S. sort out their problems and go back to normal?
A lot of people ask that question. The Canada-U.S. trade deal is a negotiation and there’s no question we will get there at some point. Mr. Trump is a hard bargainer. Well, so are we. That’s why the Prime Minister pulled out of talks that were going to produce a deal that wasn’t good enough for us. The pressures that we are getting from the U.S., yes, have accelerated certain things in Canada, but already Canada was shifting. The polling, the recent byelections we had, all demonstrate that across the country, from one end to the other, Canadians actually support the direction that we are taking. We can see that we had too many eggs in one basket. We don’t want that degree of dependence. We want to diversify. And I think it will be good for India and the relationship with India because at the top, at the political level, the two Prime Ministers have a good chemistry. They have met four times over the last year. There’s a lot of political eye-to-eye view at this point. I think even if there were changes in government, that would survive this.
Sharad Raghavan: Can you estimate what level of progress we are at on the trade deal? What are the sticking points?
Canada is the ninth biggest economy in the world. India is the fourth biggest, and we should have a lot more trade. While the trade itself is rather modest, we generate a lot of employment and investment. Canadian pension funds and other big institutional investors have invested about $80 billion (U.S. dollars) in India. That makes us, along with Singapore and the UAE, the largest investors in your country, which is kind of funny – little, tiny countries in this big country, and we are the biggest investors. There are some tax issues, but generally speaking, they (Canadian investors) are very bullish on India. On the CEPA, the free trade agreement, we are now going to have the fourth round of discussions here in Delhi in a few days’ time. Previously, we discussed for 12 years, and we got no trade agreement. This time, we started in March 2026. We’ve probably done more in these six months than we did in those 12 years. That looks like pretty good math. Our hope is that we get there by the time of a Modi visit to Canada, which would mean achieving this in about nine months [since March]. That’s like a child – we hope this is a really nice baby.
Varghese K. George: In which sectors could India and Canada enhance their bilateral cooperation in trade and meet the $1-trillion investment goal?
Canada has huge amounts of natural resources and technology that would be very apt in the Indian setting. Take nuclear, for example. We have been cooperating on nuclear since the 1950s. So, most of your reactors are based on Canadian CANDU (Canada Deuterium Uranium) models. Eighteen of India’s 24 reactors are actually CANDU-based. We are looking at different types of technologies, different kinds of reactors, smaller ones, medium-sized ones, and then the whole cycle, right up to the decommissioning of other plants. I mean, we have got the things that you actually need, like energy. Canada is the fourth largest producer of oil, fifth largest in LPG, fifth largest in LNG. We have 20% of the world’s tungsten. We are No. 1 in potash, No. 2 or 3 in titanium. We are the only G7 country that can produce batteries for EVs (electric vehicles).
Saptaparno Ghosh: Why has the hydrocarbon trade between the two countries not really picked up?
On fossil fuels, what Canada lacks, which the U.S. has, is enough west coast ports. India has got some Canadian oil through the Gulf ports of the U.S. as well, but we have just completed the TMX (Trans Mountain Expansion Project) pipeline in 2024, and it can produce about 9,00,000 to 1,000,000 barrels a day now, and that’s coming out in Vancouver. Vancouver is a little bit shallow for some of the largest ships, so we’ve got to look at getting deep water ports. We have just announced another pipeline project that will go to deep water, and that will allow us to really have economies of scale, which we don’t have yet on the west coast of Canada for India.
Suhasini Haidar: The more you describe this almost utopian state of the relationship, we have to see the contrast to exactly three years ago, when then Prime Minister Justin Trudeau came to India for the G20 summit and had a tense meeting with PM Modi over the investigation into the killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar. How are security talks progressing now, given that the officials involved are the same – the Canadian officials who accused the Indian security apparatus of carrying out a killing in Canada, and the Indian officials who accused Canada of harbouring terrorists?
I don’t want to say the issue [over the Nijjar killing] is gone. I want to say that we have made progress, but relationships require investment. They require maintenance. We have had a security dialogue established. To tell you the truth, I was at the first meeting of that security dialogue, and it was like everybody took a deep breath. Where are we going to go with this? Are we going to continue what we had before, or are we going to go forward? Prime Minister Carney inviting Prime Minister Modi to Canada was a big leap. That took some political courage, but it was an important step forward and I think that risk was worth it because it set the stage for this discussion. It’s going to continue in a way that benefits both countries, not only for the overall bilateral relationship. I think there are some issues that actually go beyond the two countries. Scam centres, for example, in south-east Asia; fentanyl, which is a plague in Canada. We want to prevent precursors coming into North America. Things like that. I’m sure there are other areas. So, you know, as we calm down, establish trust, realise who we are, make that connection at the official level, this whole process is moving forward. But it requires maintenance. And we never know, something will happen, somebody will say something. But now we have got the channels of communication to manage it. We are putting in place mechanisms to deal with future difficulties. It’s not simply being naive and saying, well, let’s just ignore what happened. [We are saying] let’s take into account what happened and let’s build from that to make sure it doesn’t happen again.
Suhasini Haidar: Why is the trial taking so long? It has been three years since Mr. Trudeau stood in Parliament and accused Indian officials of involvement, surely some evidence should have been produced by now?
I can’t comment on that. It’s a court process. Every case is different. What I can say is other things have happened in Canada, which have improved the atmosphere. Declaring the [Lawrence] Bishnoi gang a terrorist organisation, for example. We have a financial crimes task force that is looking at some of these issues. We have taken firmer action on extortion cases that have been affecting the Indian community in Canada.
Suhasini Haidar: The High Commissioner of India, your counterpart at the time, was declared a PNG (persona non grata) along with other diplomats. If they were indeed guilty of something, we should have heard some evidence by now. If not, does Canada owe India an apology?
Well, again, it’s a judicial process, so we’ll see what comes out at the other end. And that could take, I don’t know how long. I have no idea when the date for the trial, actually, if it’s even been set. So, there’s nothing more I can say about that.
Vijaita Singh: As part of Operation Hardball, which was announced in July, has India provided any specific information on how Lawrence Bishnoi was running this gang from jail because his lawyer has said he is in solitary confinement and does not have access to any communication devices?
I can’t answer that question. I don’t know what Lawrence Bishnoi is able to do. The joint operation was a good example of cooperation. It wasn’t just India-Canada but also the Europeans and the Americans working together on a common problem. And I think the outcomes are, again, part of this, at least between India and Canada, part of this overall improvement in the way we work together to solve problems and to make both our countries more safe for our citizens. We also declared the Bishnoi gang a terrorist organisation. That’s a pretty strong step. I think there’s tangible results happening for the communities in Canada, so it is going in the right direction.
Vijaita Singh: Have you sought Lawrence Bishnoi’s extradition and has India sought the extradition of his Canada-based aide Satinderjeet Singh alias Goldy Brar?
Not to my knowledge.
Suhasini Haidar: Another sore point in India is over students, where Canada is cutting down on visas, raising guarantees required, and making education and housing more expensive. Does Canada want less Indian students now?
Look, we remain the host to more Indian students than any other country in the world – more than the U.S. – at about 4,27,000 students. We think they are a great bridge between the two countries. What we had found for a period was that there were just too many students, not just Indian students, students from all kinds of countries, and we couldn’t accommodate them. Housing was a problem in certain smaller communities. Some of the colleges, frankly, took too many students and too much of their income; too much of their revenue was coming from foreign students. They were overdoing it. And there were fraud cases. So, the rules were clamped down. They were tightened. But the signal seems to have gone out that somehow Canada’s closed to any students. And that’s not at all the case. We welcome all good students. It’s true that the financial requirements have gone up, but they go up with inflation. I can tell you, having spoken to the university presidents, including of our very top universities; they all say the same thing – we would love to have more great Indian students. Now, Prime Minister Modi has said he would like universities to come in and open bricks-and-mortar campuses, and they’re looking at that too, but already there are joint degrees and joint programmes that are up and running.
A.M. Jigeesh: Are there specific Canadian universities that are going to open in India?
We have had a lot of universities come through here. They have met government [officials], but they are also speaking to institutions, the IITs, and some of the new up-and-coming private universities. Yes, they are looking at campuses in India. McGill [University] made an announcement when Prime Minister Carney was in India, and 13 new MoUs between different universities, Canadian universities, and Indian universities were also announced.
Suhasini Haidar: How does Canada really see India’s hosting of the BRICS summit? Given the Western consensus against Russia, what are your hopes from President Vladimir Putin’s visit here?
We do recognise that the Global South is a more and more important factor in global geopolitics. India is hosting BRICS, it hosted the G20, which we are part of. We have had India at our G7 summit. India’s practically a member of the G7, frankly. It is true we have some differences with some of the people that will be coming to your summit. But Prime Minister Carney has been very clear that we will not refuse to talk to people. That doesn’t mean we have to agree with them, but we will have a broader approach to discussions with people because we have to do that. We look forward to seeing what the outcomes of the BRICS summit are.
Suhasini Haidar: Do you see a role for India as a mediator in the Russia-Ukraine conflict?
I think anything that brings peace would be welcome. It’s been five years. So, if India can help achieve that, absolutely. And on any other conflicts that are out there as well. India has a credibility and a weight; it is the world’s largest nation by population. And if you can use your gravitas, your influence to bring about outcomes that we all want, then we would say more power to you.

The White House claims the Donald Trump-owned Truth Social is the “most powerful and popular social media platform in the world.” The statement, provided to The New York Times by White House spokesperson Davis Ingle, is at odds with the user counts from some of the biggest social media platforms on the web.
The White House says Truth Social is the ‘most powerful and popular social media platform in the world’
YouTube and Facebook are the world’s most popular platforms with billions of active users, while Truth Social traffic has declined.
Data gathered by Search Engine Land shows YouTube is the most popular platform in the world, with 2.65 billion monthly active users. Facebook comes in second with 2.39 billion active users around the globe, followed by TikTok with 2.21 billion and Instagram with 1.99 billion. Truth Social doesn’t make Search Engine Land’s top 10 list, which shows Elon Musk’s X and Meta’s Threads at the bottom with 450 million and 223 million users, respectively. Even those platforms trail Pinterest, which is listed with 579 million global users.
Truth Social’s traffic appears to be declining. As reported by the NYT, data from Similarweb suggests that the number of monthly visitors to Truth Social dipped 36 percent in July compared to the same time last year. From January to July 2025, an average of 28 million people visited Truth Social each month, while this number fell to 25 million during the first seven months of 2026, according to the NYT. Last month, Truth Social launched its $100,000 / month subscription to gain early access to posts from Trump and other prominent users, raising concerns about corruption.
The NYT report details Trump’s posting patterns on Truth Social, which often include AI-generated images, such as one showing his head on Hulk Hogan’s body and another hitting a cut-out of Iran with a hammer brandishing the American flag. Ingle cites President Trump’s “authentic voice” as the reason for the platform’s so-called popularity, adding it’s where “he communicates directly with the American people and the world without the biased media taking him out of context.”

The Best Windows Laptops
Featured in this article
The fight between MacBooks and Windows laptops has never been tighter. There are now more competent alternatives to every MacBook in the lineup. Whether you're choosing Windows because you don't use Apple, you need it for certain software, or just because you like the variety of hardware options, there are tons of great Windows laptops to choose from right now.
I've already tested dozens of Windows laptops this year, and have been reviewing laptops for over a decade. These are my recommendations you can buy right now, including many that were recently refreshed.

Other Windows Laptops to Consider
Dell 14 Plus: This laptop sold for hundreds less throughout 2025. And yet, even at around $1,000, I still find it a really solid deal. I do think the XPS 13 is better in a number of ways, especially the display quality and sleek design. However, the extra ports on the Dell 14 Plus are handy, and some may appreciate the slightly larger screen. It also has an upper hand with twice the storage as the Dell XPS 13 and Surface Laptop 7th Edition.
Surface Laptop 7th Edition: I waited a long time for a Windows machine like this Surface Laptop, which came out in 2024—something that could truly compete with the MacBook Air, and it does. The Snapdragon X2 Elite version of the Surface Laptop is available and should provide extra performance. It’s much more expensive at $1,600, which feels overpriced. It occasionally drops to under $1,400, however, which is closer to what the original model sells for. One caveat: You might come across the Surface Laptop 13, which came out in 2025 and is cheaper. I haven't tested that one, but it lacks some of the features I like in the 7th Edition, such as the 3:2 screen.
Lenovo LOQ 15: For many months, the LOQ 15 (8/10, WIRED Recommended) was one of the only gaming laptops under $1,000 that came with an RTX 5060 graphics card. The price has since risen significantly. Yet, it's still a laptop I recommend, as others have also increased in price. And unlike other cheaper gaming laptops, the LOQ 15 has a higher-quality display that's both bright and colorful.
Alienware 15 Gaming Laptop: Speaking of cheaper gaming laptops, the Alienware 15 falls into many of those same traps. It's thick and chunky, yes, but it also has a lower-quality display than you might expect for the price. But it delivers decent performance, has a nice design, and offers the option of an RTX 5050 graphics card. However, the price has gone up by nearly $600.
Surface Pro 12: Unfortunately, if you're looking for a Windows tablet or 2-in-1, your options are slim. There's a newer Surface Pro 13.8 with one of the Snapdragon X2 chips, which are quite expensive. And the detachable keyboard cover (that you should absolutely buy) doesn't come bundled. That's why, at this point, the smaller (and now cheaper) Surface Pro 12 is what most people should buy.
Asus Zenbook S 16: Windows laptops haven't always been known for being lookers. The Asus Zenbook S 16 undoes that stereotype. This thing is absolutely gorgeous, and not in a way that tries to mimic the MacBook. It has its own aesthetic with its white "ceraluminum" material, and I love it. It's also remarkably thin, has an expansive touchpad, and a sharp OLED display—the complete package. The only problem is that the Zenbook S 16 is quite expensive, and prices haven't dropped as much as I hoped. For a smaller model, check out the Zenbook S 14, which is very similar, except it uses an Intel chip instead.
What to Look For in a Windows Laptop
You'll want to read our extensive guide on How to Choose the Right Laptop, but for the basics, decide what category of laptop you need. Most people should buy a 13-inch or 14-inch laptop, and spending around $750 to $1,000 is a good place to start. At this price, you should expect good battery life, a decent screen, solid performance for basic tasks, and a comfortable keyboard and touchpad. You should also expect at least 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. Anything more than that gets into premium territory where you're paying for higher specs, more performance, or extra features. If you want a discrete GPU for gaming or creative workflows, you'll need to spend more.
A laptop like the Dell 14 Plus is a great example of what you can get in this price range. You can even find laptops with OLED panels and up to one terabyte of storage, depending on how good the discounts are. I would consider anything under $750 a cheap laptop, and it will come with significant compromises, especially in panel and touchpad quality. Fortunately, laptops that use the Qualcomm Snapdragon X chip get great battery life, even when they fall under $750, such as the HP OmniBook 5 14.
Here's a list of important specs to consider:
CPU: Thanks to the huge variety of good chip options, it's never been trickier to buy a laptop. For thin-and-light laptops, I would recommend one of the following chips:
- Qualcomm Snapdragon X, Snapdragon X Plus, or Snapdragon X Elite
- Qualcomm Snapdragon X2, Snapdragon X2 Plus, or Snapdragon X2 Elite
- Intel Core Ultra 225 V or Core Ultra 7 258V
- Intel Core 5 320, Core Ultra 7 365, or Core Ultra X7 358H
There are many variations of these chips, so you'll undoubtedly run across other strings of numbers, especially on the Intel front. But the above is a good place to start. There’s lots more to say in the world of gaming laptops or content creation devices, so make sure to read our full guide to How to Buy a Gaming Laptop.
GPU: As of now, Intel's Panther Lake X7 or X9 chips have the most powerful integrated graphics. You'll find them in laptops like the Dell XPS 14, which can replicate discrete GPU-level performance like the RTX 4050. Unlike many laptops with discrete GPUs, though, Panther Lake X chips offer great battery life, making them better Windows alternatives to the MacBook Pro.
For discrete options, you'll want one of the latest Nvidia RTX 50-series GPUs, such as the RTX 5060. The biggest leap in performance is between the RTX 5070 and the RTX 5070 Ti, which increases VRAM to 12 GB.
RAM (or memory): Stick with at least 16 GB if you can. Since the Copilot+ designation was introduced in 2024, it has become the new standard. You'll even find laptops as cheap as $600 that have 16 GB of memory. Gamers and content creators should upgrade to 32 GB if possible, though the ongoing memory shortage makes this more expensive. There's been a new surge in 8 GB options, such as the Dell XPS 13, but these should be reserved for only light usage.
Storage: Similar to memory, many laptops have moved to 512 GB as the new standard, and you'll find lots of affordable laptops with that as the base configuration. Upgrading to 1 or 2 terabytes, where possible, will make your life that much easier, especially since many laptops don't offer expandable storage.
Display: Laptops are usually categorized by screen size, with 13-inch, 14-inch, and 16-inch being the most common. Consider size, resolution, refresh rate, and panel type.
Portability: Aside from display size, chassis thickness and weight are the main factors, determining how portable a laptop is to travel with. Other dimensions are important too, but more often than not, that is determined by the screen size.
Ports: Many laptops are limited to USB-C and a headphone jack these days, with some exceptions that include USB-A or HDMI. Make sure your laptop has what you need, or you'll need a USB Hub or laptop docking station to add ports or increase external display support.
Windows 11 vs. Windows 10: What Are the Differences?
If you haven't heard, if you're still on Windows 10, you're no longer getting security updates—at least not without paying extra. If you're wondering what to expect in a new laptop that runs Windows 11, here's a breakdown of the major changes:
Interface: The Start Menu is now centered in the Taskbar and looks a bit different. Visually, it's quite different, but it still functions the same, offering you quick access to applications and documents. Beyond the Start Menu, just about every app will have a different visual flair, with rounded corners and a streamlined aesthetic. While you can still do what you could in Windows 10, things like Settings, Notifications, and System Tray will feel different. You'll also find a new Widgets tray you can activate on the left side of the Taskbar. Unfortunately, you can no longer move the Taskbar to a different side of the screen.
Hardware requirements: This is where most of the frustration around Windows 11 stems from. No one likes being forced to buy new hardware, and while requirements like having at least 4 GB of RAM or 64 GB of storage seem straightforward, the need for a security chip called TPM 2.0 has forced a lot of Windows 10 users to upgrade otherwise good motherboards and CPUs just to move to an operating system they didn't want to begin with.
Performance features: There are tons of new features that help Windows 11 play nicer with accessories and third-party software. One of my favorite examples is HDR support. Windows 11 finally fixes the HDR problem that made using a proper HDR monitor so troublesome, especially in games using Auto HDR. Speaking of games, Windows 11 has features like Game Mode, DirectStorage, and optimizations for windowed games, all of which make for a faster, smoother PC gaming experience.
Is Now a Good Time to Buy?
Laptop prices have been increasing all year, thanks to the memory shortage. In many cases, that means the same laptops cost hundreds of dollars more on any given day. For example, the Dell 14 Plus currently sells for around $1,000, which isn't a terrible price for the configuration. But it was consistently selling for between $650 and $750 for most of 2025. That said, I don't think prices will drop anytime soon. The future of memory pricing is unknown, but many analysts and manufacturers say it will at least last through next year and possibly into 2028.
So yes, there are tons of good options to choose from right now at reasonable prices. All the newest models with the latest chips from Intel, Qualcomm, and AMD are finally out in the wild, along with plenty of good options from 2025. You can always wait for a big sales event like Black Friday, but the savings on specific laptops may not be as big as you might assume. The only significant new hardware we're waiting to see later this year are the new Nvidia RTX Spark laptops. A lot is still unknown about these devices, but they are slated for a fall 2026 release window.

On the 25th anniversary of the Sept 11 attacks, al-Qaida's official media wing, As-Sahab, has released a propaganda video featuring the first-ever footage of Hamza bin Laden, the son and designated heir of Osama bin Laden. The video's release has drawn scrutiny from intelligence analysts, primarily because Hamza was reported to have been killed in a US counterterrorism operation along the Afghan-Pakistan border around 2019.
The 50-minute-long video titled "A Quarter Century of the 11 September Raids" also features unseen images of slain AQ chief Ayman Al Zawahiri. The outfit has not acknowledged his death to date or issued its customary funeral eulogy. The video aims to propagate the ideological doctrine associated with the current outfit chief, Saif al-Adl, with the Bin Laden name aimed at recruitment.
Intriguingly, the video opens not with international operations, but with historical footage from the Sept 2014 al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent attack on the Karachi naval dockyard. Intelligence sources noted that prioritising this regional operation underscores the influence of Pakistani terrorists within both al-Qaida's central leadership and its propaganda apparatus.
Visually, the footage, they said, was meticulously staged to evoke a sense of ideological nostalgia. Hamza appears multiple times in the footage, seated against a stark, cracked mud wall, clad in a traditional white turban with an assault rifle propped beside him. "The deliberate choice of staging serves a clear dual purpose: establishing Hamza's authority as his father's successor while invoking the classic visual identity of early global jihadism," said a source.

Chief Minister Rekha Gupta on Friday held separate meetings with officials of the Delhi Commission for Women (DCW) and the Delhi Commission for Protection of Child Rights (DCPCR), directing the two panels to strengthen complaint redressal, safety measures and outreach.
Complaints redressal
At her meeting with the DCW, Ms. Gupta directed the women’s commission to strengthen its online complaint system and step up its activities at the grassroots level on issues concerning women and girls.
She also directed the DCW to ensure that adolescent girls have access to information and facilities related to human papillomavirus vaccine.
The CM called for making the online system for handling complaints from women simpler and more effective. She said willing non-governmental organisations, civil society organisations and residents’ welfare associations should be brought on board to expand the campaign’s reach. At her meeting with the DCPCR officials, Ms. Gupta emphasised the need to raise awareness among children about the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, and cybercrimes.
Police verification
She stressed the need for mandatory police verification of school employees, including bus drivers, attendants and sanitation workers, to ensure there is no scope for negligence in matters concerning children’s safety.

The one problem Trump can’t afford
Voters say they’re worried about affordability. But Trump still seems to think high costs are a Democratic psyop.
Republicans promised their midterm convention would feature lots of President Donald Trump. Night one of “Trumpapalooza” delivered — and then some.
For almost two hours Wednesday night, Trump exhorted his base to turn out for November’s down-ballot elections. The meandering, made-for-TV speech hit all his Trumpiest subjects, from immigration and crime to transgender athletes, the White House ballroom, and taxes. But equally notable were the issues he brushed past.
The purpose of this convention, after all, was to energize Republican voters whose enthusiasm has flagged. The GOP could lose the House and/or Senate in November, despite its aggressive (and increasingly undemocratic) efforts to retain them.
But Trump skirted several of the topics that voters care about most, like the cost of housing, food, and consumer goods. (More on the politics of affordability below.)
He never said the words “inflation,” “rent,” or “housing,” for instance. He mentioned grocery costs once in passing, when he falsely claimed they were “rapidly” going down. And his 90-second discussion of “affordability” blamed green-energy policies and Democrats for rising prices: “It’s fake. They are so fake,” he said.
Still, Trump does seem to recognize voters’ economic angst. He promised, fantastically and impossibly, to cut everyone $5,000 checks if Republicans hold Congress on Election Day.
Trumpapalooza continues tonight with a keynote by Vice President JD Vance. Personally, I’ll be watching to see if he addresses affordability — or any other important, less-Trumpy topics.
Go a little deeper
During his first presidential campaign, Trump famously said that he could “stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody” without losing supporters. Now, as his party fights to retain control of Congress, he’s again testing what he can get away with — this time, by repeatedly dismissing Americans’ growing concerns about the cost of food, housing and gasoline.
In May, Trump said he wasn’t thinking about Americans’ finances as he negotiated with Iran. Weeks later, as consumer prices rose at their fastest rate in years, he told reporters, “I love the inflation.”
More recently, Trump and his allies have called affordability a “made-up” word and insisted prices are falling, though most consumer goods cost more now than at the start of his second term. Trump’s rhetoric suggests he “doesn’t really care about the fate of his party,” the historian Julian Zelizer told Vox’s Astead Herndon last month — pointing to the high cost of gas, in particular, which has proved the undoing of several prior presidents.
Instead, White House officials and other people close to Trump say that his approach to affordability reflects a more personal concern: how history will remember him and his administration.
“When the president goes down in the history books, it’s not going to be for eggs being a dollar a carton,” Shelby Talcott, Semafor’s White House correspondent, told Vox in June. She was paraphrasing months of her conversations with White House officials, who said Trump prioritized legacy-defining achievements, like denying Iran a nuclear weapon or rehabilitating Venezuela.
But there’s an obvious and self-defeating tension here: If the Iran war raises household prices enough to cost Republicans control of Congress, then Trump may lose the opportunity to advance the rest of his agenda. Even Trump may find there are some limits to what he can do without the risk of political consequences.
One link for later
➨ Lie to your friends. Playfully! For fun! There’s been a boom in so-called social deduction games — like Mafia, Werewolf, and Blood on the Clocktower — which involve deceiving other players. Consider it a lighthearted way to work through the angst of a frequently distrustful and antisocial era.

Trump's Truth Social post strongly implied the president considers the moon to be under U.S. ownership, but it's unclear whether the post amounted to an official declaration. The U.S. previously ratified a United Nations treaty that says countries can't "claim" celestial bodies like the moon. It's unclear whether Trump's post constitutes a breach of that treaty.
In early September 2026, social media users shared (archived) an alleged Truth Social post by U.S. President Donald Trump that appeared to declare the moon a U.S. territory.
Some social media users discussed whether this meant the U.S. actually owned the moon. For example, on Sept. 7, one Facebook page wrote:
For a few hours, the internet has been asking the same strange question: can a country actually own the Moon?
President Donald Trump posted an image on Truth Social on September 6 with the words "THE MOON IS OURS" beside an American flag. The post is real, but the claim that he has formally made the Moon U.S. territory goes further than what actually happened. There was no accompanying executive order or legal declaration transferring the Moon to the United States.
Similar posts discussing whether Trump had or could declare U.S. ownership of the moon circulated on Instagram (archived), Threads (archived), X (archived) and Bluesky (archived).
Trump did appear to claim U.S. ownership of the moon through a Truth Social post. The president posted (archived) "The Moon is Ours" on Truth Social followed by a U.S. flag on Sept. 6.
However, it was unclear whether the post amounted to the U.S. officially claiming ownership of the moon and, if so, whether other nations would respect it.
Snopes previously reported that according to the United Nations Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies, no country, including the U.S., can own the moon.
The treaty's Article II said that celestial bodies, including the moon, are not subject to "national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means." This essentially means that nations signing the treaty agree not to claim celestial bodies as their own.
The U.S. was a founding signatory of the treaty and has ratified it, meaning it could face political or economic consequences such as sanctions or embargoes for breaking it. It was unclear whether Trump's Truth Social post amounted to a breach of treaty.
We contacted the White House Press Office to ask whether Trump would withdraw the U.S. from The Outer Space Treaty in order to move forward with laying formal claim to the moon.
A spokesperson for the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs, which helps countries draft and revise international space laws, said via email on Sept. 10, 2026, that the office could not "determine whether a particular statement or action by a State Party constitutes a breach of its treaty obligations."
The spokesperson wrote:
A statement does not alter the legal status of the Moon under the Treaty. Whether a particular statement by a State amounts to a 'claim of sovereignty' within the meaning of Article II would depend on its legal character, the circumstances in which it was made and the intent behind the statement.
It was unclear at the time of this writing what would come of Trump's apparent declaration. Declarations that a nation owns a territory are contingent on other nations respecting such an announcement. Given the fact that China, Russia, India and Japan (the other four nations that have reached the moon aside from the U.S.) also signed The Outer Space Treaty that said the moon was not subject to "national appropriation," it appeared unlikely that they would recognize a U.S. claim.
The Sept. 8 post that suggested Trump viewed the moon as a U.S. territory was consistent with his administration's messaging about space.
Trump worked towards establishing a U.S. presence on the moon during his second administration. In a Jan. 25, 2025, executive order titled "Ensuring American Space Superiority," Trump wrote that his administration aimed to establish "elements of a permanent lunar outpost by 2030." The executive order also said the administration would work to deploy nuclear reactors "on the Moon and in orbit, including a lunar surface reactor" that would be ready for launch by 2030.
During his first administration, Trump signed an executive order titled "Encouraging International Support for the Recovery and Use of Space Resources" that said the U.S. did not view space as a "global commons," meaning areas that lie outside of national jurisdiction. Essentially, the order suggested Trump's first administration thought that space could be governed by individual nations like the U.S.
For further reading, Snopes has investigated a series of other rumors about the moon and space.

Deaths in India due to second hand smoke increased nearly 50% in 2023, compared to 1990, even as death rates improved by about 30%, according to a global analysis published in The Lancet Public Health journal.
The estimates also suggest that while the population exposed to second hand smoke increased from 375 million in 1990 to 444 million in 2026 -- up by 18.4% -- age-standardised prevalence dropped from 43.2 per cent in 1990 to 30.6 per cent in 2023 in India.
Age-standardised prevalence is a statistical adjustment made to data to allow a fair comparison of prevalence across age groups.
An international team of researchers forming the 'Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 Second-hand smoke Collaborators' estimated prevalence of exposure to passive smoking and the disease burden it contributes to across 204 countries and territories.
"In 2023, an estimated 2.71 billion people worldwide were exposed to SHS (second hand smoke), including 767 million children aged 0-14 years," the authors wrote.
Globally, exposure prevalence was 33.9 per cent in 2023. China, India, and Indonesia accounted for nearly half of the world's exposed population, with 664 million, 444 million, and 142 million people exposed, respectively, in 2023, they found.
However, "age-standardised prevalence was highest in southeast Asia, east Asia, and Oceania (48.4 per cent), with female individuals in some countries experiencing nearly 1.8 times the exposure prevalence of male individuals," the team said.
In India, absolute deaths in 1990 due to passive smoking were 2,17,700, while those in 2023 were 3,25,600 -- death rates or deaths per hundred thousand population, however, fell from 46.1 in 1990 to 30 in 2023, down by 35%, the findings show.
"The numbers mean that despite a fall in the adjusted rates, the absolute number of people exposed to passive smoking is still increasing. This can have long-lasting effects across multiple organ systems, not just the respiratory system," Neetu Jain, pulmonologist and senior consultant at Pushpawati Singhania Hospital and Research Institute, New Delhi, told PTI.
"Second-hand smoke exposure is associated with an increased risk of several diseases, including cardiovascular and respiratory conditions. The effects of passive smoking can also be particularly concerning in people with conditions such as coronary artery disease," she said.
Children were found to account for more than 12% of the world's health burden from second hand smoke, with lower respiratory infections causing the greatest burden, according to the study.
"Passive smoking is avoidable if smokers take steps to prevent exposing others to tobacco smoke. Smoking outside the home and away from enclosed spaces can reduce exposure to second-hand smoke, particularly among family members and children. Children are especially vulnerable because their lungs are still developing, and exposure to tobacco smoke can adversely affect their respiratory health," Dr Jain said.
"The effects tend to be greatest among those who are least aware of what passive smoking is and the health risks associated with it," the pulmonologist said.
"However, we should encourage smokers to quit and focus on bringing down smoking across the country through effective tobacco-control measures, including higher tobacco prices and taxes," she said.

Zelenskyy describes Canada-U.S. tensions as 'strange,' draws comparison to Ukraine and Russia
Says Ottawa and Washington need to work out their differences
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday described the unfolding tension between Canada and the United States as a "strange" sight to behold, drawing a comparison to his own country's fight with neighbouring Russia.
In a wide-ranging, exclusive interview with CBC News, Zelenskyy described American threats to annex Canada as "dangerous" and said both countries have a duty to resolve their differences.
"Strange," the president told CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, speaking to the tension in North America.
"It's very dangerous [when] there are some problems between neighbours and we [Ukraine and Russia] are the example."
Russia and Ukraine are, like Canada and the U.S., neighbours with a lengthy border and history, though their current tensions are vastly different: Moscow's four-and-a-half year invasion of Ukraine is a deadly war, while the issues in Ottawa and Washington are largely economic.
"I think that the United States and Canada, will have to have … very constructive dialogue. They have to have it. It's dangerous. [There's] no choice," he said.
Zelenskyy's remarks come at the end of a visit to Canada, which was focused on Ukrainian air defences and winter preparation as the war with Russia enters its fourth year.
He spoke about Ukraine's new strategic partnership with Canada, efforts to revive peace talks with Moscow and his view on any potential face-to-face meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
100-year partnership with Canada
Canada and Ukraine signed a long-term strategic and political partnership on Thursday that lays the foundation for the construction of millions of drones to defend both countries. The declaration established a 100-year partnership that stretches across defence and security, trade and investment, as well as energy and critical minerals.
On Friday, Zelenskyy said the length of the deal with Canada, one of Ukraine's most vocal supporters in the war, was chosen as a symbolic gesture.
"It's about roots," he said. "It says that we will be together for a long period of time. Our children and our grandchildren, we will work together. We will share the experience of security [and] a lot of different things."
Zelenskyy's visit to Canada came not only as the relationship between Canada and the U.S. hit another low, but as the Trump administration renews its push to end Russia's war in Ukraine.
After U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner discussed potential proposals to end the war during visits to Moscow and Kyiv, Trump said the Russian leader wanted to make a deal.
- Canada, Ukraine forge 100-year pact built on drones and defence
- Ukraine has been trying to bring the war to Russia. More Russians are beginning to feel it
But on Friday, Zelenskyy expressed doubts the Kremlin is interested in ending the war. He said he believes Russia maintains its goal of occupying Ukraine, but said he would sit face-to-face with Putin if trilateral negotiations came to fruition — though he said he doesn't expect any movement until after Russian parliamentary elections on Sept. 20.
"It's not my wish … Better to sit with my family," he said of a possible meeting with the Russian president. He described Putin as an "enemy," but said sitting down with an enemy "can bring us closer" to peace.
Diplomatic efforts to end the war have been stalled for months, while both countries have escalated attacks on the other. Moscow has continued its bombardment of Ukrainian cities, while Kyiv has intensified its strikes inside Russia in an effort to reduce its economic ability to continue with the war.
"To be honest, there is no win-win in this war. It can't be so because [there's been] so many human losses. It stopped being win-win at the first day of this war between us," Zelenskyy said.
"The most important victory for everybody, it's not for Ukraine and Russia ... For the world, it's peace. To stop this war. And this is a victory for a human lives."

As Poilievre tours U.S., Conservative MP bemoans lack of 'alternative to the Liberals'
Poilievre and Jamil Jivani have disagreed over Canada-U.S. tensions in the past
Conservative MP Jamil Jivani posted a video on social media bemoaning a lack of "an alternative to the Liberals" on Thursday, the same day that his party's leader, Pierre Poilievre, launched a U.S. tour to argue for tariff-free trade.
"You have people who should be offering an alternative to the Liberals, instead going out there to appease people in positions of power," Jivani said in a video posted on X.
The MP went on to say it's his job and the job of the Conservative Party to offer an alternative in Ottawa.
"The reality is there's a great alternative to be putting out there: a vision for Canada where we have a better relationship with the United States, where we avert economic crises, where we build pipelines and infrastructure and we strengthen our economy," he said.
Jivani also argued that the Liberal government is using ongoing tensions with the U.S. to avoid public scrutiny, accused the media of smearing voices critical of Liberal policies as "traitors" and blasted the government for seeking further partnership with China.
Jivani didn't mention Poilievre specifically, but the timing of the post prompted former Conservative cabinet minister Jason Kenney to blast the outspoken MP.
In his own post on X, Kenney praised Poilievre for "effectively standing up for Canada and for free trade."
He also pointed out that others in the Conservative caucus are amplifying the leader's message and criticized Jivani for not doing the same.
"Instead, he tries to step on Pierre's tour-de-force trip by posting a self-indulgent video casting himself as a martyr, without a kind word to say about his leader's efforts, or a critical word to say about Trump's daily attacks on Canada," Kenney wrote.
Canadians 'confused' by U.S. tactics: Poilievre
Poilievre kicked off his two-day U.S. tour on Thursday, saying in an interview with CNBC that Canadians are "wounded" and "confused" over how Canada and its economy became a key target for the Trump administration.
In a separate interview with BNN Bloomberg on Friday, Poilievre said Canada is standing up for its sovereignty while arguing that building a stronger relationship can buffer both countries against strategic rivals like China.
"By trading more with Canada, we can bring down your cost of living, we can make sure you're supplied for — God forbid — a future conflict, and we can ensure the industrial base of our continent is restored," Poilievre said.
CBC News has reached out to Poilievre's and Jivani's offices for comment.
Poilievre, who has now made multiple trips south of the border, has refused to criticize Prime Minister Mark Carney in the U.S.
But he has been vocal on the file, calling on the government to recall Parliament, release the details of the rejected trade deal and present a cost-analysis of Canada's counter-tariffs.
The Conservative leader has faced questions about Jivani's comments regarding the U.S. in the past.
Jivani-Vance friendship
A noted college friend of U.S. Vice-President JD Vance, Jivani has twice travelled to Washington, D.C. to meet with U.S. trade officials.
In an interview with right-wing U.S. media outlet Breitbart News during his first trip in February, Jivani said Canada is "shooting ourselves in the foot if we continue this anti-America hissy-fit."
The comment forced Poilievre to publicly disagree with his MP's characterization of the current tense relationship between the two countries.
"Canadians are legitimately upset by the unjustifiable tariffs and comments that the president has made," Poilievre told reporters at the time, adding that Jivani "speaks for himself [while] I speak for the party."
Days before the latest tariff negotiations fell apart, Vance praised Jivani during a speech at a fundraising event for having "good relationship" with the Trump administration and for being "a pretty effective advocate" for Canada.
In the same speech, Vance called Poilievre a "non-entity" in the trade talks.
When asked about Vance's comments on Jivani, Poilievre said Conservative MPs, and all Canadians, should use the contacts they have to argue for free trade with the U.S.
The day trade talks broke down last month, Jivani accused Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford of putting "their political self-interests ahead of Canadian workers."
The MP later told the National Post that responding to the U.S.'s latest levies on Canadian goods with dollar-for-dollar tariffs would be an "overreaction" — even though dollar-for-dollar counter tariffs were a part of the Conservatives' 2025 platform.
That comment seemed to ruffle at least one other Conservative's feathers. Ontario MP Kyle Seeback reposted the article on X while commenting that Jivani "speaks for no one but himself."
Seeback later deleted the post.

BRICS Summit: The 18th BRICS Summit kicks off in New Delhi. The summit comes at a time of mounting pressure on the global economy, with the US-Iran war, the Russia-Ukraine conflict and deepening geopolitical tensions adding to uncertainty. Under these circumstances, BRICS cooperation can help countries in the Global South move beyond simply managing supply-chain disruptions and build more resilient, self-reliant economies, an opinion article in a Chinese publication has said. Quick answers to key questions BRICS facilitates cooperation among countries in the Global South, promoting diversified trade, reducing regulatory barriers, and enhancing supply-chain security, which collectively strengthen their economic resilience. BRICS serves as a platform to enhance supply-chain security for its member countries, enabling them to develop independent pathways to long-term growth and manage economic vulnerabilities. This theme emphasizes the need for BRICS countries to collaborate on sustainable development, innovation, and trade practices that can withstand global economic challenges, particularly amid rising geopolitical tensions. Increasing local currency usage in intra-BRICS trade is crucial for reducing exposure to exchange-rate volatility and enhancing economic stability, as demonstrated by its already high prevalence in China-Russia trade. BRICS countries can enhance transport connectivity by developing cross-border infrastructure, such as maritime links and transport corridors, which facilitate smoother customs processes and cargo movements. Published in China Daily, the article argues that growing geopolitical tensions and protectionism are exposing developing economies to repeated economic shocks. Against this backdrop, it presents the expanding BRICS grouping as a platform that can strengthen not only supply-chain security but also what it calls “development-chain resilience”. The world economy has entered an era of repeated disruptions, the article argues. “Geopolitical tensions are deepening, protectionism is on the rise, and global industries and supply chains are becoming increasingly vulnerable to shocks. For many countries in the Global South, the problem is not just how to keep goods moving but also how to move up the economic ladder when technology barriers remain high, financial risks are mounting and traditional sources of growth are losing momentum,” the opinion article by Lan Qingxin and Pan Juncheng reads. Lan Qingxin is the director of the BRICS Research Center at the University of International Business and Economics; and Pan Juncheng is a PhD student at the School of International Trade and Economics, University of International Business and Economics. The Global South is a term used in international relations and economics to describe developing, less-developed, or emerging economies, primarily located in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and Oceania This is where BRICS cooperation can make a difference, reads the article. "As a major platform for the Global South, the expanding BRICS grouping is not only enhancing supply chain security but also laying the foundation for what might be called "development-chain resilience". This refers to the capacity of developing economies not just to withstand disruption but also to build stronger, more independent pathways to long-term growth," it said. Chinese President Xi Jinping is landing in New Delhi to take part in BRICS Summit 2026 in New Delhi today. This will be Xi's first visit to India in nearly seven years. Xi will hold bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the evening. Apart from Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and President of Egypt Abdel Fattah el-Sisi are among the global leaders being hosted by PM Modi at the summit. Xi last visited India in 2019 for an informal summit with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Mamallapuram near Chennai. The most recent meeting between the two leaders was on August 31, 2025, on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Tianjin, China. The first step toward achieving development-chain resilience is to make trade more diversified and reliable, it argues adding that BRICS brings together major agricultural producers, manufacturing economies, energy and resource exporters and large consumer markets. “Their growing complementarity gives countries in the Global South more options for sourcing, exporting and finding partners.” By harmonizing trade rules and reducing regulatory barriers, BRICS cooperation can help more businesses in the Global South gain access to regional and international markets, it reads. BRICS countries have held three meetings of transport ministers focused on cross-border connectivity, the article says pointing to new air and maritime links and the development of the International North-South Transport Corridor as examples of expanding connectivity. It cites the Xiamen-Durban route as an example of how information sharing, regulatory recognition and law-enforcement cooperation can streamline customs clearance for participating companies. The Xiamen-Durban Secure and Smart Trade Line is a pioneering maritime shipping and customs pilot route linking Xiamen, China, with Durban, South Africa. Launched in August 2025, this initiative is a milestone cooperation project between Chinese and South African customs within the BRICS framework. Both China and South Africa are BRICS members. In areas of energy, food and minerals underpin resilience, BRICS cooperation is described as central to global supply-chain security. The article argues that increasing the use of local currencies in intra-BRICS trade can reduce exposure to exchange-rate volatility. It says local-currency settlement accounts for more than 65 per cent of trade within BRICS and has reached 99 per cent in China-Russia trade. The New Development Bank (formerly known as BRICS Development Bank) is presented as another pillar of economic resilience. The opinion piece says the bank had approved 141 projects worth $44 billion as of June 2026. Xi's India visit is expected to be a high-profile diplomatic engagement with implications for the ongoing efforts to stabilise bilateral ties between the two Asian powers as well as for BRICS cooperation amid a volatile global situation, particularly the West Asia conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war, news agency PTI said. Before the 2019 visit, Xi had visited Goa in 2016 to attend the BRICS summit. Xi made his first visit to India in September 2014, when he held extensive talks with Modi. The 2014 visit came during the first terms of both leaders. Xi's visit is significant, as it comes amid efforts by India and China to normalise relations after a prolonged freeze following the 2020 Eastern Ladakh standoff. Ahead of Xi's visit, National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi held extensive talks in Beijing last month on the boundary issue, maintaining peace along the border and steps to improve bilateral relations. During the 25th round of Special Representatives' talks held in Beijing on 25 August, the two sides reached an eight-point consensus and agreed to advance discussions on an "Early and Substantial Harvest" of boundary delimitation and border management. Against the backdrop of these substantive discussions on the boundary and wider bilateral issues, a Modi-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS summit is expected to be closely watched for indications of the future course of India-China relations. With an eye on expanding its financial services offerings, Amazon Pay is now reportedly doubling down on insurance in India. Speaking with Reuters, Amazon Pay India CEO Vikas Bansal said that the company is expanding its insurance offerings to include travel insurance and other products. As per Bansal, the expansion plans are reportedly part of Amazon Pay’s strategy to evolve from a mere payments processor to a broader financial service platform comprising credit, insurance and savings and investment products. “Obviously travel...there could be others in the future as well," Bansal reportedly added when asked if the company plans to launch other insurance products in the future. This comes barely a day after Amazon Pay partnered with HDFC ERGO to foray into the health insurance space. “Health is our next frontier,” Bansal reportedly said, adding that health insurance is an important area for expansion as a relatively small proportion of Indians have personal health insurance. It is pertinent to note that Amazon first entered the insurance distribution business in 2020, when it partnered with ACKO General Insurance to offer car and two-wheeler insurance. The ecommerce giant’s fintech arm operates as a registered corporate agent, allowing it to distribute insurance products from licenced insurers. Since then, Amazon Pay has onboarded HDFC ERGO and ICICI Lombard to offer vehicle insurance. Amazon's insurance push is part of a broader effort to build out its financial services stack in India. As of now, the fintech platform allows users to transfer money, pay bills, buy insurance, travel tickets, invest in mutual funds and purchase digital gold. But it is diversifying. Earlier this year, Amazon Pay partnered with multiple non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) and small finance banks to roll out pan-India fixed deposit (FD) service. At the recently concluded Global Fintech Fest 2026, Amazon Pay also partnered with Kotak Mahindra Bank to launch a co-branded credit card for small businesses registered on Amazon Business, the company’s dedicated B2B marketplace. On the financial front, Amazon Pay India reported an operating revenue of ₹2,097 Cr in FY25, down 8.3% from ₹2,287 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, net losses declined a mere 5% to ₹866 Cr from ₹911 Cr in FY24.

Ukraine's fortress cities under fire as Russia bids to seize rest of Donbas
- Published
It is so dangerous now in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk that police say it is time for civilians to get out. These neighbouring cities are the biggest still under full Ukrainian control in the eastern Donbas region.
In the worst affected areas, forced evacuations of families with children have already begun, says Pavlo Dyachenko of Donetsk police.
"This is the only way to save your life," he says, because security has deteriorated so much.
"If you take Slovyansk, it used to be hit by glide bombs roughly once a week, but now it's almost every day."
Slovyansk, Kramatorsk and Kostyantynivka, to the south, form part of what is known as Ukraine's "fortress belt" – a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the east.
However, Kostyantynivka only has a limited presence of Ukrainian troops left, reports say, while Russia claims to be in full control of it.
The full capture of Donbas, made up of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, is a key objective for Russia. Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The Russian army already controls almost all of Luhansk region, and is now in control of almost 80% of Donetsk region too, where all three fortress cities lie.
For the past few months, the territory near Kramatorsk and Slovyansk has been the main focus of Russian ground assaults. Capturing them would potentially make it much easier for Russia to advance to the west.
The two cities are now facing intense strikes from drones and bombs.
Many civilians have already left, and key streets there are now covered with anti-drone nets, says Viktor Makurin, a volunteer from London.
"There are often [remote-controlled] FPV drones in the air, you can hear them through the window. Driving around the city is lethally dangerous. There are drones lying in ambush on the roads, too," he told the BBC.
"You can always hear explosions in the background, plus there are mobile groups firing at drones."
Over the summer, the number of civilians wounded by Russian attacks on the two cities increased from 70 in June to 212 in August, say Ukrainian police.
Sixteen people died in June, 20 in July and 15 in August.
Residential housing comes under attack as well as infrastructure, says Dyachenko, causing "very significant destruction".
The number of glide bombs launched by Russia jumped from 40 in June to 109 in July and 92 in August, according to data published by Ukrainian police and studied by the BBC.
One morning two weeks ago, on 25 August, nine glide bombs targeted Kramatorsk. Seven hit civilian apartment blocks, wounding 24 people including a two-month-old baby, Ukrainian police say.
Two days later, it was hit again, this time with seven glide bombs, and five bombs targeted Slovyansk.
Fitted with winglets so they can glide to their target rather than fall, glide bombs are considered one of the most effective and lethal weapons in Russia's arsenal.
Usually, they weigh 250 or 500 kg, but there have been cases of Russia deploying bombs that weigh 1,500 kg.
"The devastation they cause is simply incredible," says Dyachenko.
"Glide bombs are the big fear," another British volunteer, John Auckland Abbey, posted on social media.
"They are silent killers, and when you've been abruptly woken by one exploding, you know at least another one will follow. The question you ask yourself as you lie very still in the dark is: will the next one be closer?"
Kramatorsk is currently home to the headquarters of the Donetsk regional administration. The capital city used to be Donetsk, until it was captured in 2014 by Russian-backed separatists.
What happens to the areas of Donbas still under Ukrainian control was reportedly a key issue when US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last weekend after their talks with Putin.
In the past, Witkoff has appeared to back Russian claims to the region, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is refusing to pull troops out of it.
He says Putin has given his generals until the end of the year to complete their occupation of Donbas.
"Putin's primary objective on the front line remains the same: Kostyantynivka-Slovyansk," Zelensky told journalists last month.
Faced with mounting military pressure, the Ukrainian leader has created two new taskforces headed by experienced generals, Andriy Biletsky and Denys Prokopenko, to defend the portion of Donbas still in Ukrainian hands.
"There isn't just a battle for Donbas there," one unnamed Ukrainian general has said.
"What is probably the main battle of this year and the next is now unfolding."

The air traffic control outage that caused thousands of flights to be grounded across the UK earlier in the week was caused by a military aircraft entering “spurious” flight data into the system, according to a report.
Hundreds of thousands of passengers were affected after more than 2,000 flights were cancelled on Tuesday when the system used by the National Air Traffic Services (Nats) shut down for four hours.
According to the Financial Times, four people briefed on the incident claimed that the shutdown was caused by a flight plan submitted by a UK military aircraft, which caused a meltdown in air traffic control systems used by Nats which remained unfixed for several hours.
The paper also reported that Nats operations officer Kathryn Leahy called the operations managers of numerous airports and airlines, and “tensions boiled over” after Leahy informed them their flight processing system did not have a dedicated backup due to Nats being in the midst of a “complete overhaul of its systems” and because the amount of data it keeps meant duplicating it would cost “vast amounts”.
The crisis has put pressure on Martin Rolfe, the chief executive of Nats, who was summoned to a meeting by transport secretary Heidi Alexander on Wednesday.
Alexander, who said she did “not believe the issue was unavoidable”, was understood to have given Rolfe a week to report on the causes of the shutdown, while also commissioning an independent review by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) into the incident.
The outage is the most serious to affect British commercial airspace since August 2023, when a technical problem led to almost 1,600 flights being delayed. Nats came under fire after that episode, with the CAA setting out 34 recommendations to improve its systems to avoid similar incidents, all of which were said to have been fully implemented.
Rolfe ruled out a cyber-attack, which was initially suspected, saying he “believes we’ve never seen an incident happen more than once, so this will be something different that we’ve never seen in 50 years of operation”.
Numerous airlines have already called for Rolfe to resign or be fired over the outage. Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, accused Rolfe of “telling lies to save his own skin” and said his position was “untenable”.
O’Leary added: “We don’t need more investigations, we don’t need more reports and we don’t need another parliamentary committee hearing where Martin Rolfe will promise change, will promise resilience and will promise an effective backup system.”
The delays led to someaircraft full of passengers being stuck waiting for information for more than four hours, while flights due to arrive in the UK were diverted to different airports, with some forced to land in Germany.
Despite the far-reaching effect of the outage, it was understood that passengers affected were unlikely to be able to claim compensation, as delays were due to “extraordinary circumstances”.
The Ministry of Defence has said there was no wrongdoing on the part of the military.
A spokesperson from the MoD said: “We do not believe there’s any indication of an error on the part of the military. This is subject to the live Nats investigation, so it’d be inappropriate for us to comment further while that’s ongoing.”

As the leaks hinted, Gorr, the God Butcher, has finally joined the Marvel Rivals hero roster and is bringing his unholy crusade to the game. He can teleport, summon Black Berserkers, and wield a shape-shifting sword. Gorr is quite a difficult Duelist to master in Marvel Rivals. Luckily, I have been playing as Gorr since he arrived in competitive lobbies. So, discover how to play Gorr, the God Butcher, in Marvel Rivals, along with the best tips and tricks to master the new character.
Marvel Rivals Gorr Kit and Abilities
- Role: Duelist
- Difficulty: 4 stars
- Health: 350 HP
Contrary to everyone’s predictions, Gorr the God Butcher is a melee-focused Duelist in Marvel Rivals Season 10. His massive physique might give off the look of a Vanguard; however, he is a dive-and-brawler hybrid Duelist in the game.
Gorr has a wide variety of attacking and elusive options at his disposal. For starters, he wields a shape-shifting sword that can be turned into a scythe at times. Then, he summons mini creatures called the Black Berserkers, who attack the enemies in various ways under his command. He can even switch places with these minions, like how Loki teleports using his clones.
Although Gorr’s kit may seem simple on the surface, there is more to it than what meets the eye. There is a reason why he is a Duelist with a 4-star difficulty. If you are wondering what all you can do with Gorr’s Necrosword, here are all of his abilities in the game:
| Ability Name | Input Button and Ability Type | Description | 
|---|---|---|
| All-Black | Left Click (Primary Attack) | Unleash up to a 4-strike rapid combo with All-Black, the Necrosword. | 
| Twilight of the Gods | Q (Ultimate) | Transform All-Black into the Annihilablade. Instantly spawn a Black Berserker beside all enemies in range. While active, slashes deal devastating damage. Berserkers in range will not expire and remain in a Frenzied State. | 
| Living Abyss | L Shift | Surge forward as an Invincible symbiote mass, leaving a Black Berserker behind and driving all active Berserkers into a Frenzied State. Upon landing, manifest a Necroverse that continuously damages trapped enemies, converting them into Bonus Health. | 
| Black Berserker | E | Lob a symbiote mass that spawns a Black Berserker on landing and immediately shoots the nearest enemy. If summoned beside an enemy via Necro-Power, it unleashes a two-strike melee attack instead. | 
| Shadow Harvest | F | Warp to a selected Black Berserker, sacrificing it for Bonus Health equal to half its Health and triggering a symbiote explosion. Briefly unlocks Shadow Scythe: fire a piercing shockwave forward. All-Black then becomes a scythe for a set duration or 4 slashes. | 
| Necro-Power | Right Click | Charge and launch a symbiote mass forward. Hitting an enemy slows and teleports nearby Black Berserkers to them, or spawns a new one. Arriving Berserkers unleash a two-strike melee attack to launch nearby enemies up before reverting to ranged mode. | 
| Symbiote Swarm | Passive | Black Berserker damage grants Gorr Bonus Health. Defeating an enemy instantly spawns a Black Berserker at their location. |

The weapon stays in scythe form for a short duration. Enhanced Effect: When teaming up with Hela, the scythe’s attack range is expanded. Each hit scatters symbiote fragments, granting Bonus Health to Gorr and nearby allies. |

Upon reaching max distance, it retracts, Launching caught enemies toward Gorr. Enhanced Effect: When teaming up with Venom, Black Berserkers receive a slight Damage Boost and apply a Slow effect to enemies they strike. | 
How to Play Gorr the God Butcher in Marvel Rivals: Best Strategy Guide
Now that you have a grasp of Gorr’s kit in Marvel Rivals, it’s time to put that knowledge to use. Unfortunately, Gorr’s kit isn’t as straightforward as the previous hero, The Hood in Marvel Rivals. There are many elements at play, and the best way to play the God Butcher is to combine his abilities in different sequences.
After experimenting with the new dive Duelist for hours, here is the best way to begin reaping as Gorr in Marvel Rivals:
Offensive Strategy: Slide Into the Backline
Gorr’s playstyle is similar to Magik, not Black Cat in Marvel Rivals. The swordplay and teleporting ability make them two peas in a pod. However, Gorr’s teleportation works differently. Summoning the Black Berserkers is the most important ability in Gorr’s kit. Here is how to play offensively as Gorr in Marvel Rivals:
- First, pick your target in the backline and send one of your Black Berserkers near him/her.
- Then, use your Living Abyss to glide across the battlefield and reach the target.
- Doing so will automatically enable the Necroverse, and tick damage applies to enemies within range. All this damage will be converted into bonus health (up to 175 HP) for Gorr.
- You can then press E and summon another minion.
- Now use Necro-Power to order all the summoned Black Berserkers to gang up against the opponent.
- Then join the assault. Try to attack as much as you can with your primary attack.
- The Ragnarök team-up with Hela is the best pick. Using it immediately unlocks the Scythe transformation
- Scythe deals much more damage and has a longer range than your regular Necrosword, so try to fight with the Scythe most of the time.
- Use this strategy repeatedly whenever you plan to engage in a fight.
Defensive Strategy: Escape With the Help of Minions
Since Gorr has an unusual hitbox size for a Duelist, he can be easily targeted and eliminated if you don’t pay close attention. Thankfully, Gorr is a highly mobile character like most of the Duelist characters in Marvel Rivals. So, you can escape from any situation if you play your cards right. You always need an escape route before you initiate an attack, and here are the many ways you can survive as Gorr:
- First, do not use Living Abyss to escape. This ability was designed to kick off fights, not to escape from one.
- So whenever you use Living Abyss to get near an enemy, do it from a safe location, as a Black Berserker is automatically dropped at the exact place where you start using this ability.
- In case of an emergency, you can just turn back and use Shadow Harvest to teleport back to the safe location. Now you can understand why developers intended Living Abyss for attack.
- The first step in mastering Gorr is to learn how to manage these Black Berserkers.
- Retreating from a battle is as important as engaging in a fight. And the best way to retreat is by using your Black Berserkers. Remember that!
- So, similar to Magik, your approach to a battle should be jumping in with Living Abyss and then escaping with the Shadow Harvest ability.
Best Strategy: Don’t Be Afraid of Dying
Now that you have learned how to initiate attacks and escape out of a battle as Gorr, here are some of the best tips and tricks that everyone needs to know:
- Always unleash Gorr’s ultimate ability in Marvel Rivals when your team is attacking with you. Although the Annihilablade is great, I won’t recommend using the ult when you are cornered.
- Learn some essential combos like: E (Black Berserker) -> L Shift (Living Abyss) -> RMB (Necro-Power) -> LMB (All-Black) -> F (Shadow Harvest) and E (Black Berserker) -> RMB (Necro-Power) -> LSHIFT (Living Abyss) -> LMB (All-Black) -> C (Ragnarök).
- It’s totally fine to die when you are diving at first, as Gorr lacks regular double jumps and wall climbing like other duelists.
- However, learn different ways to use your minions, and you can secure at least a kill or two whenever you dive.
- Always use Necro-Power when you have more than two minions on the battlefield, so that they can deal serious damage and launch the enemy in the air.
- Don’t rely only on the Shadow Harvest ability to turn your sword into a Scythe. Use the team-up Ragnarok to perform a sweep attack and instantly get a Scythe
Best Counters for Gorr in Marvel Rivals
Gorr indeed seems like a terrifying Duelist who cannot be beaten. However, Gorr does become vulnerable in front of certain Marvel Rivals characters.
So, here are the best heroes who are perfect counters to Gorr in Marvel Rivals:
- Hela: Gorr has a massive hitbox like a tank, and it is his main weakness. So, you can pick Hela and quickly eliminate him with rapid shots.
- Iron Man: Well, if you cannot go against Gorr on the ground, then pick an aerial hero like Iron Man. Gorr struggles against heroes in the air, so you can easily finish him off as Iron Man.
- Namor: Namor can hold his fort easily against a dive character like Gorr with his turrets.
- Peni Parker: Peni is always a great pick against dive characters in Marvel Rivals. As Peni, you can set your mines and guard your backline against Gorr without any hassle.
- Luna Snow: If you are a Strategist main, then going with a character like Luna Snow allows you to pin down Gorr. It is easy to freeze him while he dives, thanks to his big hitbox. Then you can defeat him either solo or with the help of your squad.
Best Team Comp to Play as Gorr in Marvel Rivals
Finding the right team comp for a newly launched Marvel Rivals hero is difficult. That is why we have tried out different lineups.
Here are the best team comps we recommend when you are playing as Gorr in Marvel Rivals Season 10:
- Main Comp: Magneto, Emma Frost, Gorr, Wanda, Gambit, and Cloak and Dagger
- Dive Comp: Venom, The Hood, Gorr, Spider-Man, Invisible Woman, and Jubilee
- Team Asgard Comp: Thor, Magneto, Gorr, Hela, Loki, and Luna Snow
