Pacesetter Russell says Madrid 'has less margin than Monaco'
- Published
George Russell says Formula 1's new circuit in Madrid "has less margin than Monaco" as the sport races there for the first time at the Spanish Grand Prix.
The Mercedes driver set the pace in first practice at the Madring - a street-circuit style track built around an exhibition centre near the Spanish capital's airport.
Russell was 0.286 seconds faster than team-mate Kimi Antonelli in second place.
"In Monaco, the walls are closer, but because you're going far slower, if you make a mistake, you're not into the wall as quickly, and you can recover it sometimes, a small lock-up," he said.
Russell was speaking a couple of hours before a practice session that ran incident-free.
A few drivers brushed the wall, including Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso, but no-one damaged their car.
Russell said: "There's a lot of really fast corners, but the barrier is kind of like coming back onto the track. So, if you are to go wide and hit the wall, you're not hitting it kind of at the same angle as the car is going. The wall is sort of coming in at you."
Russell singled out Turns Five, Seven and 17, where Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc went off into the run-off area during practice.
"Another element of the challenge here, which probably won't cause major crashes, but I think there'll be a lot of lock-ups," said Russell.
"You've got three corners where you're turning and braking, and if you lock up, the wall is right in front of you, which is very reminiscent of the corner in Baku - Turn 15."
There is also a section of high-speed swerves, Russell said, which is similar to the fast Jeddah street track in Saudi Arabia.
Ferrari set the pace on the medium tyres in the first part of Friday's opening session but they could not match the pace of the Mercedes on the soft compound.
Leclerc was third fastest - 0.459secs off Russell and just ahead of Hamilton - with Red Bull's Max Verstappen fifth and McLaren's Lando Norris' sixth.
Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad, Mclaren's Oscar Piastri, Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Red Bull's Liam Lawson completed the top 10.

Team GB return 'hard to put into words' - Kinsella
- Published
Olympic gymnast Alice Kinsella says "it's hard to put into words" how she feels about returning to international competition as her groundbreaking comeback to the sport continues this weekend.
The two-time European champion became the first British artistic gymnast to resume elite competition after giving birth, when she finished fourth in the beam at the British Championships in March.
Now the 25-year-old is preparing for her first competition back in Team GB colours at a senior team international against France, Switzerland, Germany and Italy at Fenton Manor in Stoke on 12-13 September.
"It's kind of crazy - it's such a surreal feeling but I am very excited," Kinsella told BBC Radio Stoke.
"It's only been a year, postpartum. Training-wise, it's been tough, but it's been good. I'm excited to finally get out there. I'm ready, I'm doing everything I can to get back where I was.
"It's been a rollercoaster but a good one."
Kinsella's pioneering journey back to the sport is so rare it became the subject of a university research paper into elite gymnasts resuming their careers after giving birth.
Her son Parker, who was born in September 2025, is already a source of inspiration and he will be watching his mum compete at the weekend as Kinsella competes in all four pieces of apparatus - balance beam, bars, vault and floor - for the first time.
"It's really special because I've wanted to try to get back into a team and this is a really good start because it's a little four-way," Kinsella, who trains with Park Wrekin Gymnastics Club in Shropshire, said.
"It's not too big of a competition which is really good. I'm definitely nervous, but it's hard to put into words - it's been so long.
"I did the British [Championships] in March but only did beam and that's all I was training really but now I'm trying to do all four so it's more on the body.
"It's not like you've done one piece and you can stop thinking about everything, you've got to move on to the next and think about that. So it's been tough."
- Pioneering gymnast targets rare return to elite competition after baby 
  - Published22 January
- 'For my boy' - Kinsella makes GB gymnastics history 
  - Published23 March
- Gymnastics now more a mental challenge - Kinsella 
  - Published25 September 2023
Putting Team GB leotard back on 'feels very weird'
After revealing she only took "three or four weeks off" after giving birth, Kinsella returned to training at the start of the year with the longer-term intention of being at the World Championships in China in 2027 and the Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028.
But, after finding herself ahead of schedule so far this year, she wanted to take the chance to step it up.
"My main goal was to try to get back next year but I'm actually a lot further forward than I thought I would be," added Kinsella, who won bronze in the team event at the Tokyo Olympics in 2020.
"So that's why I'm doing this competition because I just want to get out there, compete, because I don't like doing nothing."
What makes Kinsella's return so unique are the obvious challenges - and changes to the body - pregnancy and childbirth brings.
There are many examples of women returning to the top of their sports after becoming mothers but gymnastics, where vital pelvic floor and core strength are both weakened during pregnancy, is different.
Kinsella said her gymnastics background has played a big part in her being able to return to physical exercise so quickly but said she "didn't feel too bad" when she got back in the gym.
"I always had that goal to get back into the gym and I think when I've got a goal set I will do everything I can to achieve it," she said.
"Getting back into a leotard with how my body's changed just feels very weird but I guess that shows what my body has gone through and I try to think about it in a positive way."
'I'm just proud to be back out there'
Her body is not the only thing that has changed with Kinsella adding that parenthood has helped her become better at taking the pressure off herself as an athlete.
"Having a baby changes your life - I'm very patient, whereas before Parker I was not patient at all," she said.
"When I made one tiny mistake I would get so annoyed, but now if I just make like a little mistake I'm totally fine about it.
"You have to be patient with kids, they're crazy. So I've definitely changed in that aspect but style-wise and gymnastics-wise like I don't think that's changed.
"Things are harder to get back and to do but I think the more I train it'll probably feel a lot easier."
Kinsella said when she started her comeback "no one really had any idea what I was going to able to do" and wants to keep levels of expectation for her international return as realistic as possible.
For her, this weekend in Stoke is there primarily "just to enjoy it" and to "get the experience of all four pieces [of apparatus] again".
"My body's changed, I can't do the same amount of training I used to do but I'm definitely getting back to that," Kinsella said.
"We're definitely on the right track to be where I was before I had Parker. My goal was to start competing next year properly on all four.
"It's going to be really fun. Whatever happens, happens, good, bad. I'm just proud I'm able to be back out there a year postpartum."

In a sit-down at TIFF with his leading Obsession star Inde Navarrette, moderated by the fest’s Midnight Madness programmer Peter Kuplowsky, the duo reminisced how their lives have changed over the last year following the pic’s world premiere at TIFF where it was snatched up by Focus Features for $15M. The first change they noticed was an upgrade in their flight and hotel this year versus last when they arrived as a pure indie (Obsession was financed by Capstone for $750K).
However, had Obsession opened to $20M, Barker shared there was a plan for him and his reps to get tattoos.
Watch on Deadline
“It didn’t (do that). It made $17M. So we’re like ‘Ok, I guess we’re not getting the tattoos…still really cool’,” he said, “And then the next weekend it made $27M. It was like ‘Holy shit!’ That’s unheard of for it to go up!.”
Interesting backstory, Barker had Obsession tested and the audience was quite unhappy with Bear (Michael Johnston) and his handling of off-the-rails g.f. Nikki (Navarrette), who he put a love-binding toxic spell on.
“People were saying that they were frustrated with Bear and they didn’t understand why he doesn’t just try to do more to fix it (the spell.”
“They were like ‘Why isn’t he going back to the crystal shop? Why isn’t he doing more research and trying to fix it?’ We got an overwhelming amount of people wanting us to do that,” said the filmmaker.
“Then I was like ‘Oh, wait, that’s not what I want to do. I don’t want to try and fix it. It’s way more interesting that there’s a passivity in his character. He’s what I would call a passive antagonist,” explained Barker.
“So, it became clear to me that the way to fix the movie was not to make Bear try and fix it sooner, but to actually make it even more clear to the audience that he wants to make it work. That’s the thing that he becomes active on trying to make this work,” said Barker.
Barker thus had reshoots, which he praised his financier for; those additional resources proved to the filmmaker that his backers had complete faith in his vision.
In regards to his how his career changed: Barker no longer gets ‘Nos’ when he heads into pitch meetings. Before Obsession, he would constantly come up with new ideas which were shot down. Now, the response he gets is, “‘Curry, what is it you want to do?'” shared the director.
“It’s a little more challenging, he added, “I can pitch anything.”
In terms of Navarrette’s streak, she recently appeared at D23 where it was announced she’s playing Rogue in the Marvel Studio’s revival of X-Men.
“Everything has changed for me, I’m now in rooms I could never even imagine,” said Navarrette about her life post TIFF 2025, “I’m pitching my own projects and am hopefully can produce and direct my own stuff.”

Like Benzema & as good as Haaland - Alonso on Joao Pedro
- Published
Xabi Alonso says Chelsea striker Joao Pedro is similar in style to his former Real Madrid team-mate Karim Benzema - and at a comparable level to Manchester City's Erling Haaland.
The Brazil international, 24, has scored twice and provided two assists in his first three games of the season - and was named the Premier League's Player of the Month on Friday.
It was the first time Joao Pedro has won the award as he finished ahead of team-mate Cole Palmer, who was Chelsea's previous recipient in September 2024.
When asked whether the forward could be compared to the prolific Haaland, who won last season's Premier League Golden Boot with 27 goals, Blues boss Alonso said: "I would say yes.
"If you count how many top strikers we have in the Premier League, I'm sure that Joao [Pedro] is there, Haaland for sure is there. So I would rate him that way."
Joao Pedro signed a new contract at Stamford Bridge last month to stay until 2034, and was handed Chelsea's number nine shirt at the start of the season.
He became the club's first striker since Diego Costa to score 20 goals in a single season during his debut campaign and has struck 25 times and had 11 assists in 57 matches since joining last summer.
In his last 57 matches for City, Norway's Haaland has 42 goals and supplied nine assists.
'He is still young, but many, many outstanding qualities'
Unlike Haaland, who is a specialist goalscorer, Joao Pedro has played as a midfielder, number 10 and winger during his career and possesses a more rounded skillset.
Alonso, who made 195 appearances alongside former Ballon d'Or winner Benzema at Real Madrid, said there were also similarities between the Frenchman and Joao Pedro.
"In many things he reminds me of Benzema, because he is good in the box, he is good out of the box, he is good coming to his left side, he is good with the head, he is very complete, he is intelligent," added the Spaniard.
"So yes, he is still young, still things to develop, but many, many absolutely outstanding qualities that he has."
Benzema, now 38 and a free agent, has scored 523 goals in 994 appearances for France, Lyon, Real Madrid and Saudi Arabian sides Al-Ittihad and Al-Hilal.
Meanwhile, Joao Pedro was a surprise omission from Brazil's squad for the World Cup this summer, but has since been recalled for September's international fixtures against New Zealand and India.
Asked whether the omission by Brazil manager Carlo Ancelotti, who coached Alonso at Real Madrid, had provided added motivation this season, the Chelsea boss said: "He had enough motivation.
"He already had enough within him, so I didn't need to go there. It was painful for him, but that is in the past. We are now focused on what he is doing well and what he can do better.
"He has been outstanding. Not just in football terms, but in his personality, his maturity and his desire. He has a very clear goal this season, which is to have a great campaign and score a lot of goals."

BRICS leaders meet in India as wars and US tensions test the bloc
Leaders of the BRICS nations are meeting in New Delhi for a summit focused on trade, investment and global conflicts
Leaders of the BRICS nations were meeting in New Delhi on Saturday for a summit focused on trade, investment and global conflicts, as the bloc seeks a bigger role in shaping the global agenda for emerging and developing countries.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is hosting Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and counterparts from the other eight BRICS members. The summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising U.S.-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground among countries with competing geopolitical interests.
Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed around the summit venue and other parts of New Delhi, with traffic restrictions and diversions in place.
BRICS was founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, with South Africa joining in 2010. It has since expanded to 11 members, representing about half the world’s population and a significant share of global economic output. The group has increasingly called for greater representation for developing countries in global institutions.
The leaders are expected to discuss economic cooperation, energy, food security, technology, supply chains and reforms to global institutions. Reducing reliance on the U.S. dollar will also be a priority, with members promoting greater use of their own currencies in trade and payments as well as pushing for alternatives to Western-dominated financial institutions.
For India, the summit highlights its effort to maintain strategic ties with Russia and Iran while deepening relations with the U.S. and Europe. New Delhi has sought to balance its longstanding partnerships with Moscow and Tehran with efforts to expand economic, defense and technology ties with Washington and other Western nations.
India has maintained close ties with both Moscow and Tehran despite the war in Ukraine and tensions between Iran and the U.S., while calling for dialogue and diplomacy to resolve conflicts. Modi met Putin and Pezeshkian separately in New Delhi on Friday ahead of the summit.
The summit comes as Iran, a member of the expanded BRICS group, is directly involved in the war in the Middle East, putting the bloc’s unity under pressure as its members navigate differing positions on the conflict and relations with the U.S.
A key test for India will be whether it can secure a joint statement from leaders at the summit. Those divisions were evident in May, when BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement over the Iran war, forcing India to issue a chair’s summary instead.

The Chander Kunj Army Towers Apartment Owners Association (CATAOA) has demanded the immediate appointment of a dedicated project officer and the setting up of a project office to closely monitor and follow up on the impending demolition of the twin towers of the Chander Kunj Army apartments at Silver Sand Island in Vyttila.
The Association also demanded that the District Collector’s committee, formed at the instance of the Kerala High Court to oversee the demolition and reconstruction of the apartments, and the sub-committee chaired by the Fort Kochi Revenue Divisional Officer (RDO) be convened at the earliest to chart the future course of action without further delay. This follows the latest High Court order dismissing the petition of P.K. Unique Project Limited, a Tamil Nadu-based company, which had challenged the decision of the Collector’s committee to award the demolition contract to Mumbai-based Edifice Engineering.
“Bureaucrats like the District Collector and the RDO have their hands full and cannot be expected to always oversee the demolition and related work. Hence, it is imperative that a dedicated project officer with the requisite experience and a project office be set up for the work to progress smoothly,” said Saji Thomas, president of CATAOA. The Association maintained that there was no need to delay the demolition on account of the case since the court had not stayed the committee’s decision to finalise the tender in favour of Edifice Engineering.
In June, the district administration had issued an ultimatum to the Army Welfare Housing Organisation (AWHO) to sign a contract for the demolition of the towers or face legal action. “But they have not yet complied with the direction nor deposited the estimated ₹9.60 crore in the Collector’s escrow account in advance. The District Collector’s committee will be convened at the earliest to decide the future course of action,” said committee sources.
The sub-committee was formed to convene weekly reviews, realising that the Collector was too busy to do so. However, its meetings were disrupted by various factors, including local body and Assembly elections, with the last meeting held in June. That same month, Edifice Engineering and South Africa’s Jet Demolition conducted a two-day pre-demolition inspection of the towers and the larger property. The two firms had earlier overseen the demolition of the Maradu apartment complexes.
The agencies had stated that the towers could be razed sequentially in a matter of seconds without damage to the Kochi Metro passing by in the neighbourhood, though preparations for demolition and debris clearance would collectively take six months. No further action was taken after the award of the work was challenged in court.
Meanwhile, CATAOA is set to approach the Supreme Court against the denial of rent to 24 apartment owners by AWHO on the technical ground that they had failed to submit affidavits claiming eligibility to the Collector’s committee before August 12 last year, as directed. According to a High Court verdict, rent was fixed at ₹30,000 per month for apartments in the ‘B’ tower and ₹35,000 for those in the ‘C’ tower.
On February 3, 2025, a Single Bench of the Kerala High Court had ordered the demolition and reconstruction of the towers, citing serious structural problems. In August, the court disposed of a writ appeal filed by the Association and a few owners against this verdict. The Collector’s committee had set November 9, 2025, as the tentative date for the demolition of the twin towers and October 31, 2029, for handing over the newly built apartments. Even the original deadline for the evacuation of 208 owners on July 31 had to be revised, as owners declined to move out before payment of advance rent.

Death toll from Philippines ferry fire climbs to 35, with dozens still missing
- Published
The Philippine Coast Guard says it has recovered 30 bodies from the wreckage of a ferry that caught fire this week, bringing the total death toll to 35.
More than 130 people were on board the MV June Aster when the blaze erupted on Wednesday as it neared its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, after departing from Manila.
Forty-three people were rescued, with many receiving treatment in hospital, and searches continue for more than 50 people who remain unaccounted for.
The country's coast guard says more bodies remain on the boat, which they were unable to board until Friday due to toxic fumes and lingering heat.
In a press conference, coast guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said most bodies had been retrieved from the sleeping area of the boat, which had been making a 22-hour journey.
"Agencies are currently undertaking the proper recovery and identification of the remains in accordance with established procedures," Cayabyab said.
"We recognise the grief of the families affected by this tragic incident."
Earlier, the coast guard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that the fire started in the cargo hold. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.
A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat told the BBC he had heard frantic cries onboard when the fire erupted, and was trampled by panicked people as he tried to escape.
The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.
The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported.
The vessel was carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members.
Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry.
"Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday.

KUMAMOTO – Kumamoto Prefecture will launch a travel discount campaign on Tuesday to stimulate tourism demand following a powerful earthquake that struck the prefecture in July, Kumamoto Gov. Takashi Kimura said Friday.
The discounts will apply to overnight stays in Kumamoto between Oct. 1 and Dec. 25.
“We want many people to visit Kumamoto,” Kimura said at a news conference, adding, “That will strongly support the recovery and reconstruction of the affected areas.”
The program will provide discounts of up to 60% on eligible travel packages.
For packages that include transportation fees, the maximum discount is ¥20,000 ($130) for one-night stays and ¥30,000 for stays of two nights or more.
For accommodation-only products, the maximum discount is ¥20,000, regardless of the length of stay. Tours that include both Kumamoto and other prefectures in the Kyushu region are eligible for discounts of up to ¥35,000.
About 190,000 people had canceled accommodation bookings in Kumamoto as of Aug. 21 due to the earthquake, resulting in losses of about ¥2.7 billion, according to the prefectural government.
Kimura expressed hope that the discount campaign will help generate 300,000 overnight stays.

Americans mark 25 years since 9/11 attacks amid enduring grief, reflection
Nearly 3,000 people were killed on the day that has shaped US society for decades, influencing its foreign policy and domestic politics
Twenty-five years after the deadliest attack on US soil, Americans paused on Friday to commemorate the nearly 3,000 people killed when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Centre, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania – and to wrestle with the consequences of September 11 that reverberate to this day.
In New York, family members of the victims, many carrying pictures of their loved ones, joined Vice-President J.D. Vance and four former US presidents at ground zero in Lower Manhattan.
The ceremony began, as always, at 8.46am with a moment of silence to remember the shocking instant when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Centre’s North Tower.
Shortly after, victims’ family members began reading aloud the names of all 2,977 people who died on September 11, as well as the six people killed in the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, a sombre recitation that lasts for hours.

Other moments of silence followed, marking when the other three planes crashed and the two towers collapsed. For the first time, a seventh moment of silence was set to honour the thousands who have died since 2001 from illnesses tied to the toxic dust that poisoned the air for months afterwards.

The story so far: A rabies vaccine, that could be critical in preventing a fatal infection, has failed a mandatory potency test, after vials bearing the batch number of a genuine Abhayrab consignment were seized from an unlicensed premises in Delhi. The Central Drugs Laboratory (CDL), Kasauli, has declared the samples in question as “Not of Standard Quality” and “misbranded”, setting off an investigation into whether counterfeit vaccine was being manufactured or distributed.
Rabies is almost invariably fatal once clinical symptoms appear, while timely and quality-assured post-exposure vaccination can prevent complications and death. The immediate concern for investigators, therefore, is not only how the questioned vials came to bear the details of a genuine vaccine batch, but whether any person bitten by a potentially rabid animal received a product that lacked the required potency.
The samples, bearing batch number KE25012, were seized on April 22, 2026, during a joint enforcement operation by the Delhi Police Crime Branch and officials of the Delhi Drugs Control Department at an unlicensed residential premises in Mukherjee Nagar, Delhi. Four persons have been arrested in connection with the case, according to the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).
The laboratory found that the questioned vials failed the prescribed potency test and differed from genuine reference samples in several respects. These included packaging, labelling, artwork, QR-code verification, cap colour and licence details.
Genuine batch or counterfeit? Where is the investigation going?
Indian Immunologicals Ltd. (IIL), which manufactures Abhayrab through its Human Biologicals Institute (HBI), has denied manufacturing the seized vials.
In a statement issued on September 4, the company said the genuine KE25012 batch comprised 83,370 vials, underwent the required testing and was released on November 7, 2025, through its authorised distribution network.
More significantly, IIL said the CDL identified 17 differences between the questioned vials and the genuine retention samples of the same batch submitted by HBI for batch release.
The company has submitted its manufacturing, quality-control, reconciliation and distribution records to CDSCO and has asked authorities to trace the source of the questioned vials and take action against those responsible. The CDL finding establishes that the seized samples were NSQ and misbranded. It does not establish that the genuine KE25012 batch manufactured by IIL was defective. IIL’s position is that its legitimate batch passed the prescribed testing and that the batch number may have been reproduced on unauthorised material.
What are authorities investigating?
Investigators now have to establish who manufactured the questioned vials, where they were stored, how they entered circulation and whether they reached patients through any part of the legitimate or informal medicine supply chain.
A particularly important question is whether anyone was administered the suspect vaccine. If so, authorities may have to determine the nature of the exposure, the treatment received and whether additional medical intervention is required.
The Drugs Controller General of India has asked State and Union Territory drug controllers to maintain strict vigilance over the movement, distribution and availability of Abhayrab bearing batch number KE25012 and to take appropriate regulatory action.
CDSCO has also stated that no part of the concerned genuine batch was exported to another country.
International counterfeit rabies products
The case follows a suspected counterfeit Abhayrab episode involving batch KA24014 in 2025. IIL had reported suspected counterfeit vials to authorities, following which health warnings were issued in some countries over the possibility that travellers to India could have received counterfeit rabies vaccine.
That episode highlighted the international dimension of counterfeit rabies products. Travellers exposed to rabies may begin treatment in one country and complete their vaccination schedule elsewhere. A falsified vaccine can therefore create a public-health concern beyond the country in which it was obtained.
In the present case, however, CDSCO has said no part of the genuine KE25012 batch was exported. The investigation will have to establish whether the questioned vials were entirely domestic and, crucially, whether they entered patient use.
Why rabies vaccine matters?
Rabies is a viral disease that affects the central nervous system and is transmitted mainly through the saliva of infected animals, usually through bites or scratches. Dogs account for up to 99% of human rabies transmission globally. Once clinical symptoms appear, the disease is virtually 100% fatal.
Yet rabies is preventable. Prompt post-exposure prophylaxis involves thorough wound washing, vaccination and, for appropriate severe exposures, rabies immunoglobulin or other recommended biologicals. Quality-assured PEP can prevent the virus from progressing to the nervous system.
This makes the quality of a rabies vaccine particularly consequential. For a person exposed to a potentially rabid animal, the vaccine is not routine preventive medicine; it is a time-sensitive intervention intended to prevent a disease that, once symptomatic, offers virtually no chance of survival.
India’s rabies burden
India continues to bear a substantial share of the global rabies burden. A recent ICMR-National Institute of Epidemiology estimate cited by WHO puts annual human rabies deaths in India at 5,726, alongside an estimated 9.1 million animal bites each year.
Globally, WHO estimates about 59,000 people die of rabies each year, with more than 95% of deaths occurring in Asia and Africa.
The suspected circulation of a misbranded rabies vaccine therefore raises a question that goes beyond counterfeit packaging or regulatory compliance: whether a person who believes they have received life-saving protection has actually received a vaccine capable of providing it.
What happens next?
The Union Health Ministry maintained that the immediate task is to establish the origin and distribution of the questioned KE25012 vials and determine whether any patient received them. Authorities will also have to establish the scale of any unauthorised manufacturing or distribution network.
For IIL, the laboratory comparison, together with its manufacturing and distribution records, will help determine whether the episode concerns a manufacturing-quality failure or the unauthorised use of its product identity and batch details.
For patients and healthcare providers, the case reinforces the importance of obtaining rabies vaccines through licensed hospitals, clinics and pharmacies and reporting suspicious products to drug-control authorities.
With rabies, the margin for error is exceptionally small. A genuine, potent vaccine administered promptly can prevent a fatal disease; a counterfeit product can create the dangerous illusion that protection has been provided.

A rumor that U.S. President Donald Trump claimed in a speech he had saved victims of the 1912 sinking of the RMS Titanic is spreading online.
According to social media posts sharing the claim, Trump said he "saved more people than anybody," told the ship's captain to "turn left," and that "nobody knows icebergs better than [him]." This is despite the fact, of course, that Trump was born in 1946, meaning he was not alive in 1912 when the ship famously sank.
Some users seemed to interpret the claim about the Titanic as true, and readers contacted us to investigate its legitimacy.
We found that Trump made no such assertion, and the rumor is false.
To investigate the rumor's legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo. If Trump truly had mentioned assisting rescuers on the Titanic in a speech, journalists with reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or Reuters, would have widely reported on it, and those search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence.
That was not the case. We did not find any credible reporting suggesting that Trump had mentioned the Titanic during a recent speech.
Snopes traced the claim as far back as an X post made on the afternoon of Sept. 8, but could not definitively confirm that post as the rumor's origin. However, it neatly aligned with a speech Trump gave earlier that day at a tribute event for the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, in which he repeated a long-standing claim that he participated in relief efforts. A transcript of that speech included no mention of the Titanic.
Given the timing of those remarks, we concluded that Trump's words about 9/11 in that speech served as inspiration for the fictitious rumor, which we suspect was intended as satirical. However, the earliest account we found that shared the claim did not indicate that in its post. Snopes contacted the X user to confirm our suspicions, but had not heard back by publication.

The Thrill of Wanting AI to Destroy the World
An Anthropic researcher quit his job because he believes AI will destroy humanity. His story is going viral because so many others want to believe too.
The sky streaked orange and red as my mother drove us home to Albuquerque through the Tijeras Pass, which separates the Sandia Mountains to the north from the Manzanos to the south. “Look out for mushroom clouds,” my father said to her. “If you see them, turn around.”
He did this every time we returned to town from the rugged canyon to the east, but the sunsets always egged him on. According to legend, a part of the Manzanos, whose foothills descend into Kirtland Air Force Base and then Sandia National Laboratories, had been hollowed out to hold live nuclear warheads. My father insisted that, in the event of a nuclear attack, Albuquerque was slated to receive two bombs from the sky, one each for these secret government sites. He delivered this information as if it were a law of physics or the known terms of an international treaty. I was a child, so I took it as such, staring bug-eyed at the red sky that might evaporate me.
Nearly two decades later, I looked up at the clear blue one above Los Angeles from behind the wheel of my own car, worried about different missiles. I had gone into my dot-com job early, and I was the only one there when the planes hit the Twin Towers. The internet, barely functional on a good day, broke completely; to listen to the news, I had to turn on a transistor radio that someone had left in their cubicle. We sent everyone home early that morning. I recalled an article published a handful of years earlier, just before the stark-white, cliffside Getty Center opened in Brentwood. The writer had theorized that the Getty might finally give Los Angeles a monument worthy of destruction in an alien attack. (Roland Emmerich’s Independence Day, released the previous year, had settled for the Library Tower, a bland downtown high-rise.)
Nuclear war was a massive threat, and a real one. During the Cold War, every morning the sun rose under the shadow of destruction. Good and evil were clear, or seemed so. That clarity offered a perverse comfort. By September 11, 2001, the Cold War had been over for more than a decade, and society longed for a coherent enemy to oppose—one that might offer a similar clarity. The indisputable fact of the attacks—thousands of people dead, symbols of American culture destroyed—gave birth to a similar, if less true and more perverted, version of imminent apocalypse. As before, anyone on the street might be the enemy. But now, also, every airliner and any envelope might be a weapon.
I was already pondering these worn fantasies this week, as the 25th anniversary of 9/11 was looming, when Jacob Coxon wrote a social-media post about quitting his job at Anthropic because AI technology would, in his estimation, “kill us all by the end of the decade.” The sentiment takes up unfinished business; ruination has been building up in contemporary culture. There was a time—one longer than you probably remember—when the once-novel coronavirus also felt like The End. During the same pandemic, the 75th anniversary of the Cold War’s apocalyptic beginning—a controlled explosion at Trinity, 100 miles south of Kirtland—took place. Back in 1945, the physicist Edward Teller worried that the bomb might ignite the atmosphere and destroy all life on Earth.
This fantasy—of the end of the world, and of being present for it—is among the most powerful emblems of the 20th century. The atomic bomb inaugurated it, and nuclear armaments remain the reference technology for apocalyptic threat and reverie. We believe in the fantasy, and pine for it, because nothing feels better than the belief that you might witness the conclusion of humankind.
The threat of annihilation from nuclear weapons is simple and easy to explain. For one part, a single warhead can level an entire city. For another, the mere launch of a single missile all but assures the release of all of them. Likewise, the AI superintelligence of the Terminator films is both straightforward and obviously threatening. Skeleton-like metal robots want only to destroy humanity. Real AI is not so straightforward. I used it on the morning of Coxon’s post to help me nail down the quantity of various sugars I would use in a gelato recipe. By the afternoon, it had undergone a costume change, into the angel of death.
The nature of AI’s extinction threat is unclear and second-order. In an interview with Wired, Coxon struggled to say exactly how AI might bring about the end of civilization. “The classic example is, like, synthesizing a new virus or taking down critical infrastructure by doing some sort of hacking spree,” Coxon said, before admitting that the “latter might be less likely to kill literally everyone.” Quickly, critiques began to arrive. Belief in the unfettered power of AI seemed to rely on prior faith in AI’s unfettered power. A former Stanford doctoral student in AI safety said that he had dropped out of the program because his colleagues couldn’t prove that existential risk matters. And then, elsewhere, evidence of purity: Coxon, Axios reported, had given up his valuable Anthropic equity by quitting (although he retained stock in his prior employer, OpenAI).
Coxon is less a whistleblower than a poster; he posted a fairly common sentiment that just happened to catch wind. It’s the anniversary of 9/11. OpenAI just claimed to have solved an intractable problem in mathematics. That company and Anthropic, where Coxon worked, are racing to multitrillion-dollar IPOs. An ongoing cultural battle about the moral and aesthetic vice of AI recently turned in on itself, when the journalist Kelsey Piper accused writers who mistrust Pangram, an AI-detection tool, of essentially trying to hide their own clandestine uses of AI. As I write this, Coxon’s post has been seen more than 150 million times, a number equal to roughly 2 percent of the global population.
The situation might feel unsettling, validating, preposterous, or even stupid, depending on your perspective. AI companies and proponents have an incentive to make the technology seem powerful, even threatening, because power gives rise to profit. AI detractors have reason to take the AI-extinction threat seriously as evidence that those in charge are irresponsible and reprobate. During the Cold War, cloak-and-dagger paranoia was spread by spies, agents of statecraft, confidants, whistleblowers, and journalists—either as truth to power or as crackpot conspiracy theories. But today, in the internet age, conspiracy theories are everyone’s primary method of exchange.
Coxon’s post fell into the conspiratorial pit. Is he even real? Anthropic seems to have indirectly confirmed his employment, but Coxon doesn’t appear to have a LinkedIn page, a curiosity in the tech industry. Wikipedia editors proposed deleting a page about him on the grounds that “the guy exists, but that’s about it. He has not done a single notable thing otherwise.” The New York Times journalist Mike Isaac scratched his chin at the fact that Coxon had gone to The Wall Street Journal and Fox News first. On X, Parker Thayer posted a lengthy conjecture that the whole affair amounts to a “sophisticated and well-funded PR operation to get support for Democrats to regulate AI into oblivion.”
Information’s tendency to spread harmfully, like disease—the original meaning of media “virality,” as Douglas Rushkoff defined it in the years between the end of the Cold War and the start of the War on Terror—facilitates further spread. Whether the threat Coxon has in mind is likely or even lucid is not important. Instead, the threat’s enticement has proved so lurid that people feel compelled to embrace it.
That is different from saying that there is no threat. For example, the author Annie Jacobsen noted that the “superhuman system that can hack anything” that Coxon described could, in theory, hack the labs that store dangerous biological agents. If “what’s inside gets released,” Jacobsen wrote, “it’s goodbye humans.”
This example is both disturbing and at least thinkable. Its possibility relies not on superhuman intelligence, really, but on something far more ordinary: Everything whatsoever now runs on internet-connected computer software. And AI is a kind of software that can make and control other software, especially over a network. It feels silly and embarrassing to conclude, correctly, that people have constructed such a fragile, slapdash infrastructure of computer-controlled systems that either a dumb or a smart rogue agent could blow it all up. Yet even Jacobsen’s scenario poses questions that a high-level, post-size tizzy does not answer, including precisely what sequence of synchronized events among computers, people, architecture, equipment, and other entities would result in “goodbye humans.”
Thinking of AI as a dangerous superintelligence capable of eradicating civilization is much more fulfilling than pondering the threat of a cluster of haphazard computer programs. We will probably never reclaim, if that is the right word for it, the lucidity of threat we felt at the Cold War’s climax. We do seem to long for that clarity, and the yearning for it has inspired us to patch back together some of its structure. The most satisfying dream of humankind is to be alive to witness its end. “I caused it” and “I prevented it” and “I tried to warn you” amount to equally appealing versions of that fantasy. Even “I posted about it” feels pretty good.

Police in Thailand have arrested a senior Buddhist monk on suspicion of embezzling $2.8m intended for his monastery, alongside a suspected female accomplice he was filmed having sex with.
The case is the latest scandal to hit the clergy in the Buddhist-majority country, after a sex and extortion case involving senior monks last year prompted public outrage and calls for greater scrutiny of temple finances.
Phra Wachirayan Wi, the 66-year-old abbot of the 14th-century temple Wat Phutthaisawan in the ancient capital of Ayutthaya, was arrested on Thursday on charges including embezzlement and money laundering, according to the lead police investigator Pattanasak Bupphasuwan.
A 47-year-old woman accused of helping convert and conceal the money was also arrested.
Leaked CCTV footage of the pair having sex on a table in the monk’s residence was widely broadcast on Thai media.
In Thailand, Buddhist monks take a vow of celibacy and also renounce material possessions.
Police began investigating Phra Wachirayan in mid-July after receiving an anonymous tip alleging him of misconduct and misuse of temple funds.
Pattanasak, a commander of the police crime suppression division, said investigators identified two streams of money linked to donation receipts issued in the temple’s name.
About 89m baht ($2.7m or £2m) was donated for temple renovations, with another 2.8m baht in payments for Buddhist amulets and other sacred objects, he said.
“But the money from both streams did not enter the temple’s account – not a single baht,” Pattanasak told a news conference on Friday.
He said authorities had seized assets worth about 215m baht, including 16kg (35lb) of gold bars and jewellery and 28 land title deeds.
Police are investigating which are personal property and which belong to the temple.
“We will expand the investigation to identify other people involved and restore public confidence in Buddhism,” said Nattasak Chaowanasai, the commissioner of Thailand’s Central Investigation Bureau.
Wat Phutthaisawan is a prominent royal monastery with a large following that includes government officials, businesspeople, police and military personnel.
The former abbot, also known as Luang Pho Atichot, was well known for making amulets, with the Thai prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, reported to be among those who wore his creations.
The abbot was defrocked shortly after his arrest.
Last year, police arrested a woman accused of blackmailing at least 11 monks she had sex with, extorting nearly $12m of monastery funds from them, in a case that shook Thailand.

Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
- Published
A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.
When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; £205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to thousands of prospectors arrived in Cheporor.
And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.
It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.
Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.
People do sometimes pan for gold in these parts - but rarely find anything significant.
Lomachar's says his discovery came about purely by chance. While he was searching for a missing goat he encountered a group of women panning along a riverbed.
"I joined them, and that's how [the village] realised there was gold in this area," he says.
Farmer and herder Patrick Lokolia, from neighbouring Napawoi village, joined the gold rush hoping to earn some extra money to support his family.
"I have children in school, and paying school fees has been a big problem for me," he tells the BBC wearing an old Chelsea football top and standing amid the mining activity.
Eighteen-year-old Abigael Chelengat says she had never mined before coming to Cheporor from a nearby district, but arrived hoping to find enough gold to pay her school fees and help keep her younger siblings in school.
Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.
Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.
Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.
Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.
Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries.
"Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.
Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.
But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.
Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.
Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.
While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential.
"I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.
Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).
West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.
Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend.
He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.
However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says.
"We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.
So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged.
"We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.
For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.
More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.
Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs.
"I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.
But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services.
"This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."
For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."
Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.
Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.
The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.
Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.
Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.
Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.
Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.
Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.
For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.
He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold.
"We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.
He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty.
"If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

Lenovo's Googlebook 15 seems decidedly premium based on a new leak
The laptop will reportedly have a high-resolution, high-refresh rate display and an Intel Core Ultra 5 chip.
Google's official launch for its new Googlebook platform is still scheduled for later this year, but details on at least one of the new Android-based laptops that will be available at launch have come into focus. MacObserver reports that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 will feature more than its fair share of high-end components, including the latest Intel Core Ultra chips, and a high-resolution, high-refresh rate touchscreen display.
Lenovo is reportedly working on multiple new devices for Google: a tablet with a detachable trackpad and keyboard and a more traditional laptop. The Lenovo Googlebook 15 appears to be the latter. MacObserver writes that it'll feature a 15.3-inch 120Hz OLED display, with 2,880 x 1,800 resolution and the ability to reach 500 nits of peak brightness. The laptop is also reportedly powered by an Intel Core Ultra 5 chip and can come with either 16GB or 32GB of LPDDR5x RAM and either 256GB or 512GB of storage.
All together, that's a step up even from Google's Chromebook Plus initiative, which required partners to include at least 8GB RAM, 128GB of storage and either an Intel Core or AMD Ryzen 700 series processor to unlock exclusive AI features. As promised, Googlebooks definitely seem more premium than their Chromebook predecessors.
Some of that extra processing power is likely necessary for the laptop's Gemini Intelligence features. Google detailed several when it announced the Googlebook initiative, but the most interesting was Magic Cursor, which turns a laptop's mouse cursor into a contextual prompting tool for Gemini. Googlebooks also feature exclusive hardware features like a multicolored strip of LEDs called a "glowbar," which is also on the Lenovo Googlebook 15, according to MacObserver.
What these possible specs communicate about the price range of this first wave of Googlebooks isn't definite, but it certainly seems like they'll be more expensive than most Chromebooks. We should know more soon: ChromeUnboxed reported in August that Google is hosting a media event on September 15 to preview the first wave of Googlebooks.

Mamdani shares pleasantries with Rudy Giuliani as families gather at WTC memorial for 9/11 anniversary
Vice President JD Vance, former presidents and mourners gather at Ground Zero for 25th anniversary memorial
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani shook hands with former Mayor Rudy Giuliani as families, mourners and politicians gathered at the site of the September 11 attacks, 25 years after the devastation.
Mamdani, who was 9 years old and in his fourth grade classroom on the Upper West Side when the World Trade Center was hit, has faced an avalanche of anti-Muslim rhetoric and pleas from right-wing critics, including Giuliani, to avoid this week’s 9/11 ceremonies.
They could be seen briefly chatting and shaking hands before they each parted ways at the solemn ceremony in lower Manhattan.
The city’s first Muslim mayor has steered this week’s commemorative events to ensure focus remains on the families, victims, first responders and the city’s recovery, and his office released thousands of never-before-seen documents that appeared to reveal that Giuliani’s administration and subsequent mayors knew the dangers of the toxic aftermath despite assuring the public of lower Manhattan’s safety.
Giuliani, once seen as “America’s mayor” in the wake of the attacks, has spent the last several years in courtrooms across the country battling criminal indictments, bankruptcy and a defamation lawsuits surrounding the 2020 presidential election as he became consumed by baseless conspiracy theories.
The 82-year-old former mayor joined pleas from right-wing figures calling on Mamdani to avoid Friday’s memorial. Giuliani has said his presence “offends” him and claimed Mamdani is “disturbing the people who are the most important people at that celebration.”
“He stands in direct support of the movement that killed their children,” Giuliani said. “You’d have to be a fool to resist that.”
Twenty-five years ago, a commercial airliner hijacked by al-Qaeda terrorists struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center in lower Manhattan, the first of four attacks on September 11, 2001 that killed nearly 3,000 people and set in motion a series of profoundly world-changing events.
Mourning Americans are gathering across the country and at the site of the attacks for a familiar annual ritual: reading the names of the people who were killed at the World Trade Center, at the Pentagon, and in a field in Pennsylvania.
A ceremony at the site of the Twin Towers began with a tolling bell and a moment of silence at 8:46 a.m., the moment the first plane, American Airlines Flight 11, hit the 96th floor of the skyscraper.
More moments of silence will follow to recognize the moment a second plane struck the building when the towers collapsed, when the Pentagon was hit, and when United Airlines Flight 93 crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back against the plane’s hijackers.
All living former presidents will attend the Manhattan ceremony, along with Vice President JD Vance.
President Donald Trump, however, will not attend, purportedly because he is not allowed to deliver remarks. The president will attend a ceremony at the Pentagon.
But for the first time, the ceremony at the National September 11 Memorial and Museum will hold a seventh moment of silence to honor people who died from illnesses related to the attacks.
This week, more than 170,000 pages of newly released records, never before shown to the public, revealed that New York City officials knew of potential dangers from exposure to Ground Zero toxins despite repeated assurances to the public that the air was safe to breathe.
Over the two decades that followed, thousands of first responders and other New Yorkers developed lung disease, neurological illnesses and cancers linked to expansive recovery efforts and their lives in the shadow of the attack, as clouds of chemicals, cement dust, asbestos and other toxic debris lingered in the air and in buildings.
According to the World Trade Center Health Program, more than 9,000 people have died from 9/11-related illnesses, including 600 firefighters — exceeding the nearly 3,000 people killed in the attacks themselves and the more than 300 firefighters who died in the rescue efforts.
In Shanksville, mourners will read the names of the passengers and crew members of Flight 93, on which passengers fought back against four hijackers and forced the plane away from Washington, D.C., averting what was expected to be another devastating attack on the nation’s capital.

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”

A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why?
- Published
The images are hard to ignore.
Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation.
One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra.
They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state.
At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner.
Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation.
His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products.
"These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC.
The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant.
Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity.
But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him.
An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it.
"I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC.
Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives.
In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions.
"When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language.
But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet.
The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is.
Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five, external were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.
And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive.
By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000.
Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said.
"Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible".
Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public.
The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram.
However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic.
Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed".
Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons.
"While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association.
Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first.
His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach.
In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered, external Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law.
The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard".
The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses?
Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations.
For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone.
"Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC.
He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety.
"We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption."
The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work.
Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes.
Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools.
But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post.
"The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal.
The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds.
For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets.
Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban.
"We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

Wolves sign former Sunderland winger Traore
- Published
Wolves have signed former Sunderland and Aston Villa winger Bertrand Traore on a one-year deal.
The Burkina Faso international left Sunderland in the spring after 12 appearances in his one season with the Black Cats following his move from Dutch side Ajax.
Traore joined Chelsea as an 18-year-old and made his Premier League and Champions League debuts there before loan spells with Vitesse Arnhem and then Ajax, whom he helped to the Europa League final.
The 31-year-old spent three seasons with Lyon before securing a £17m move to Villa where he scored 10 times in 62 appearances during four seasons.
After four seasons at Villa Park, Traore joined La Liga side Villareal before returning to Ajax for a second stint.
"It's a position we wanted and he's a good player to improve the team, one more option," head coach Cesar Peixoto told the club website., external
"He has the right characteristics I want in this position - good one-versus-one, strong, left-footed to score or assist and fast to attack the space.
"He needs time to get fit because he's been working alone, and he needs time to know our idea of the game, but he is another option to help us fight to get to the Premier League.
"Like we saw on Sunday [Wolves' 2-2 draw at Birmingham], the Championship is very tough, so we need two players in each position to manage the games."

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows a girl in Ladakh being abducted from her home by Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) workers on the instructions of Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Vinay Kumar. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a Congress supporter in Ladakh being abducted by RSS workers.
Fact: The video shows a Jaranan performance. Also known as Kuda Lumping, Jaran Kepang, or Jathilan, Jaranan is a traditional Javanese dance. The video does not show a Congress-supporting girl in Ladakh being abducted by RSS workers. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but did not find any police reports, credible news reports, or records about Vinay Kumar or RSS workers abducting a Congress supporter in Ladakh.
We then conducted a reverse image search of key frames from the viral video, which led us to the same video (archived) uploaded on the Instagram handle tubagusjakaa on 29 August 2026. The post featured similar visuals, and its caption read, “Mendem Jaranan”. The post also included hashtags such as #jaranan, #mendemjaranan, #kerasukan, #mbekes, #kudalumping, and #jatilan.
Jaranan, also known as Kuda Lumping, Jaran Kepang, or Jathilan, is a traditional Javanese dance from Indonesia in which performers dance while using flat, horse-shaped props made from woven bamboo, often accompanied by traditional gamelan music. The performance traditionally depicts horsemen or warriors and, in some forms, includes spiritual or trance elements in which dancers are believed to enter an altered state and perform unusual acts. It is performed both as cultural entertainment and as part of traditional or community events, and is regarded as an important part of Javanese cultural heritage (here, here).
The account that uploaded the video has also shared similar videos featuring people performing the same art form.
To sum up, a Jaranan performance video from Indonesia is falsely shared as a Congress supporter in Ladakh being abducted by RSS workers.

Since May 2025, the Delhi government has been setting up Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs), which serve as primary healthcare centres, across the Capital. In phases, they replaced the Aam Aadmi Party government’s Mohalla Clinics, which are no longer operational. While many staff members were absorbed into the AAMs, some say they have not received their final salary dues and have been told that the budget for the payments is “under consideration”.
There were 553 Mohalla Clinics. So far, the Delhi government has set up 415 AAMs and aims to establish 1,100 in all. The centres were envisaged to provide additional services such as maternal and child healthcare, routine immunisation, free screening for non-communicable diseases and nearly 80 types of free diagnostic tests.
However, some former mohalla clinic staff who were not absorbed into the AAMs are still awaiting their dues. Dr. Amit Gupta, who worked at a mohalla clinic near Mandawali metro station, said he is owed ₹78,000. He said interviews for AAM posts were open to all staff and some were selected. He is currently practising at his own clinic.
‘Budget under consideration’
In an email to an east district health official, Dr. Gupta wrote, “It is very unfortunate that our salaries for January and February are still pending”.
He received a response from an official on August 27, seen by The Hindu, stating that the file had been transferred to the respective cell and that “the approval of budget is under consideration”.
Another senior Health Department official said, “Many of them have been retained by AAMs and have received their salaries till date. If there has been any negligence, we will look into the matter”.
Two staff members retained at AAMs told The Hindu that they had been receiving their salaries. Those who spoke of pending dues were among the staff not retained.
Pending dues
Mohalla Clinics employed four staff members each: a doctor, a pharmacist, a multi-task worker and a lab technician. AAMs have a similar staffing structure, though the number of personnel varies with the size of the centre.
A former multi-task worker at a mohalla clinic in the east district said, “I am trying to get a job in the AAM but the vacancy has not risen yet. We have been told by supervisors that the funds have not been released for our last salaries. I have been without a job since March, when the Mohalla Clinic shut.”
Another doctor said that, besides salaries, which were linked to the number of patients seen, staff had not received other dues, including cleaning and costs incurred in transporting medicines for the final month. “Authorities have said that they are doubtful that it will come through but we are still waiting.” The doctor said she was ineligible to apply to the AAMs because the age limit was 55.
Last year, Mohalla Clinic staff protested outside the Secretariat, demanding that they be retained at AAMs. Selection tests have since been conducted and several former staff members have been appointed. Some have approached the Delhi High Court over the matter, which is to be heard on September 8.
