Following the devasting flash floods in Nepal on August 26, which claimed over 1,200 lives and caused massive destruction, a video has gone viral on social media, purporting to show the Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) phenomenon. It displays footage from a search helicopter, ostensibly showing the breach of a glacial lake in China. Users on social media have widely shared the clip, claiming that this was the immediate trigger to the Nepal floods.
X user Bhavesh Mane (@iambmane) posted the clip on August 27, with the hashtag #NepalFloods. At the time of this article being written, the post garnered 2 million views, and was reshared close to 2,000 times. (Archive)
A Glacial Lake Outburst Flood #GLOF can happen when a glacier-dammed lake suddenly breaches. 🌊🧊
Pressure and fractures create a pathway for the trapped water to escape, sending a massive surge of water and debris downhill at terrifying speed#GlacialFlood #NepalFloods #Nepal pic.twitter.com/0zrw0SIEqO
— Bhavesh Mane (@iambmane) August 26, 2026
Also Read: Nepal floods: Unrelated videos of past disasters, AI visuals falsely viral
A journalist with Dainik Bhaskar, Ashish Rai (@journorai) also posted the clip on X, which received 2 million views and close to 4,000 reshares. (Archive)
Several other X users, like former MLA Rajpal Singh Sekhawat (@Rajpal_BJP), Dr. Kiran J Patel (@kiranpatel1977), Pradhyumn Sharma (@pradhyu78651514), AH Siddiqui (@anwar0262) and (@greatandhranews) posted the clip with the same claim. (Archives: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
Fact Check
To check whether the claims surrounding this viral clip are authentic, we broke it down into keyframes, then ran reverse image searches on the keyframes. This led us to an Instagram reel, uploaded by an user with the handle (@helipilotleigh), on August 22. It contains the exact same footage as the viral clip.
View this post on Instagram
In the caption, the user, whose name is Leigh Coates, explains what a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood, or GLOF is, and mentions that the video shows one happening over the Columbia Glacier in Alaska.
The description on her YouTube channel states that she is a helicopter pilot based in the United States, who specialises in ferry flights and advanced training for mountain flying, as well as airport landings.
We noticed that she had uploaded similar videos of glacial outbursts on her Instagram profile, and her YouTube channel.
In conclusion, the video that went viral recently in the context of the Nepal flash flood, showing a glacial outburst — purportedly in China — is actually from the Columbia Glacier in Alaska. It was uploaded by a helicopter pilot named Leigh Coates on her Instagram handle, a few days before the flash flood in Nepal. Thus, the claim that the phenomenon shown in this video was a direct trigger for the August 26 Nepal floods is false and misleading.

Trump set for Ireland visit amid backdrop of protests and meeting with long-standing critic
Trump will touch down on Saturday morning after what has been described as one of the biggest security operations ever implemented by the Irish police service
US President Donald Trump is scheduled to touch down in Ireland on Saturday morning, arriving amid what has been described as one of the largest security operations ever implemented by the Irish police service (An Garda Síochána).
A number of demonstrations protesting against Mr Trump’s visit have been planned.
During the trip, Mr Trump will take part in engagements in Dublin, the Irish capital, as well as at his golf resort in Doonbeg, Co Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open.
Irish premier Micheál Martin said he looks forward to welcoming Mr Trump to Ireland and "discussing the many issues of mutual interest and reaffirming the strong economic, cultural and people-to-people ties between Ireland and the United States".
Martin added: “His visit comes during a remarkable sporting summer for Ireland, and the United States and this weekend’s Irish Open at Trump International Doonbeg will be a fitting conclusion to an outstanding season of sport, and I hope we will see an Irish winner lifting the trophy on Sunday.”
He is also expected to meet President Catherine Connolly, a long-standing critic of the US president, at her official residence Áras an Uachtaráin in Dublin’s Phoenix Park, before a nearby engagement with Mr Martin, the Taoiseach at the Farmleigh Estate.
Speaking on Friday, Mr Trump’s son, Eric, said the US president is prepared to welcome anyone with open arms during the trip, while remaining equally ready to go head-to-head.
Asked how he thought the meeting with Ms Connolly will go, Eric Trump said: "Honestly, I leave it to them.
"I have seen so much political nonsense over the last 12 years where one day two people hate each other and the next day the two people are hugging.
"What I’ll say is my father is willing to open his arms to anyone, and he is also willing to go head to head with anyone. You’ve seen that in the Oval Office and around the world.”
The US president will also attend a series of events at Deerfield, the residence of the US Ambassador to Ireland.
Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said peaceful protest would be facilitated as much as possible, but there will be “no tolerance” for public disorder or attempts to impact “critical movements” of the US president.
“We have robust policing plans in place and will arrest and prosecute those committing offences”, he said, adding that water cannon will be “on standby” but said he hoped they would not be needed.
Ireland’s deputy premier Simon Harris will welcome Mr Trump as he arrives off Air Force One at Dublin Airport early on Saturday morning.
Speaking ahead of the moment, the Tánaiste said the visit offers an “opportunity to mark and reflect on the deep and enduring links between Ireland and the United States”.
“I am looking forward to getting a chance to meet again with President Trump following a brief engagement on the margins of the UN General Assembly in New York last year,” he said.
“Ireland and the US have deep and enduring political, economic, cultural and historical links that transcend the administrations on both sides of the Atlantic.
“There are clear benefits from high-level visits such as this as they offer an opportunity to engage on the deep economic relationship between our two countries which creates prosperity, jobs and opportunity for large numbers of people here and in the US.”
Mr Harris said Mr Trump’s visit will be an opportunity for the Irish Government to engage substantively as the US remains Ireland’s largest trading and investment partner.
“More than 900 US companies directly employ 245,000 people in Ireland, while more than 200,000 people are directly employed by almost 800 Irish companies in the US,” he said.
“Our economic partnership delivers for both countries. US firms present in Ireland have contributed to an economic ecosystem that has driven improvements in productivity and encouraged Irish companies to scale and grow in the US and internationally.”
The visit will cause significant disruption and road closures around Dublin Airport and across the capital city as well as in Co Clare and Shannon Airport which will also be used by Mr Trump.

What Russia Is Really Up To in Europe
Moscow doesn’t want a conventional war, but it is busy fighting a hybrid one.
On Russian state television, the Kremlin’s propagandists have for years threatened to bomb European capitals, even while the country’s diplomats insist that no such war is imminent. Lately, the denials have gotten hard to sustain, as European intelligence agencies have ascribed hundreds of clandestine sabotage operations—cyberattacks in Italy, arson in the United Kingdom, undersea-cable ruptures in the Baltic, severed pig heads left outside French mosques—to Russia.
U.S. intelligence assessments conclude that a conventional Russian attack on a NATO country is likely to happen sometime from this fall to 2029. But another possibility is that Moscow will remain content with sabotage and intimidation. This hybrid campaign is all the war Russia wants or needs—and stoking fear that Moscow just might directly strike Ukraine’s European allies is part of it.
If this is what Russian President Vladimir Putin is really up to in Europe, then he was telling the truth when he assured Trump this week that Russia has “no aggressive intentions against European statehood.” Moscow has not massed troops on any NATO member’s border. Rather, it has been sending a carefully calibrated message meant to persuade Europe to stop supporting Ukraine.
For Moscow, this has been a summer of setbacks in Ukraine. Russia stalled on the battlefield and sustained damage from thousands of Ukrainian long-range drones that plunged the country into fuel shortages. And so it escalated elsewhere in Europe: Fires broke out at ammunition plants in Italy, Bulgaria, and Estonia last month, and explosive-laden drones were discovered near a German power plant and at an airport in Leipzig, apparently intended to destroy Ukrainian cargo planes.
From the Kremlin’s point of view, Europe has been deepening its involvement in Ukraine. At the beginning of the full-scale war, Europe donated weapons to Ukraine from its own stocks. Within two years, European governments were paying Ukrainian factories to manufacture arms. Last year, Fire Point, a Ukrainian missile-and-drone manufacturer, announced that it would establish a solid-fuel production plant in Denmark, making it the first such arms company to expand production abroad. Today, Europe provides the bulk of financial assistance to Kyiv. It has also become Ukraine’s secure production base—Ukrainian weapons are manufactured in Germany, Britain, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, France, Romania, and Spain.
Because Kyiv is attacking Russia’s rear, it’s logical to worry that Moscow will attack Ukraine’s. Russian security services are almost certainly capable of carrying out a lethal attack on European soil. And Western war games have entertained many possibilities along those lines. Among them are a limited Russian incursion into a small Baltic town that has a Russian-speaking population; a full-scale invasion of the Baltic states, launched simultaneously from Belarus and Kaliningrad, Russia’s European exclave, to cut them off from the rest of Europe; the rapid creation of an impenetrable drone “kill zone” on European soil; and a strategic blockade of the Baltic Sea. Some of these scenarios are plausible; others would require hundreds of thousands of Russian troops to crisscross Europe.
Russia has not visibly prepared for any such scenario, however. Instead, it continues to wage its hybrid war—which European security services continue to thwart. Such are the headlines: Drones carrying explosives are discovered in Leipzig, improvised explosive devices are found near a German power plant, and flying objects are spotted near airports.
Moscow may not much care that these operations get foiled. In a way, the effect is similar to that of Russia’s harassment of journalists and embassy workers stationed in Moscow: Things in their apartment get rearranged, signs of eavesdropping are deliberately made obvious, or a window is left open in the middle of winter. Such interference conveys a sinister message: We’re watching you. We have access to you. You are not in control. But it’s still different from blowing up the apartment.
Putin has generally chosen to fully engage the Russian military only in conflicts that he feels (rightly or, in the case of Ukraine, wrongly) assured of winning. This does not describe any hypothetical attack on the Baltic states, which have heavily fortified borders, conduct regular military exercises, and spend 5 percent of their GDP on defense.
That’s not to mention the thousands of British, German, and Canadian troops stationed near the Baltics as part of NATO’s Enhanced Forward Presence. Moscow may be willing to wager that the United States won’t intervene should Russia attack Estonia. But Russia would then find itself at war with numerous European states armed with submarines, aircraft carriers, fifth-generation fighter jets, long-range cruise missiles, and even nuclear weapons—all while it was still fighting in Ukraine.
Russia’s hybrid war has not succeeded in its likely purpose: stopping weapons, money, and intelligence from flowing into Ukraine from Europe. Kyiv has more arms, funds, and—judging by its strikes on Russian soil—intelligence than ever before. Neither has the Russian campaign taken out a European satellite that supplies Ukraine with intelligence, say, or destroyed a shipment of Patriot missiles.
But Putin persists in this campaign for a reason. Through inexpensive means, expendable operatives, and a steady stream of chilling leaks, the Kremlin has millions of Westerners braced for it to wage a full-scale war against Europe. Regardless of whether that war is likely, Putin will be demanding concessions in exchange for bringing it to an end.

B.C. judge tosses drug case, says U.S. agents broke law and violated Canadian sovereignty
Extradition proceedings against alleged trafficker stayed due to DEA's 'shocking' conduct, decision reads
U.S. federal agents pressured a Canadian into a money-laundering conspiracy while concealing their efforts from the RCMP, amounting to "shocking and flagrant" illegal behaviour and a violation of Canadian sovereignty, a B.C. judge has found.
In her scathing decision, B.C. Supreme Court Justice Catherine Murray ordered a stay of proceedings against the Canadian, due to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA)'s "egregious" conduct.
The man had been facing extradition to the U.S. on drug trafficking charges stemming from a plot dating back to 2015.
Murray's decision, dated April 1, was posted on the court's website this week. The case was first reported by the Vancouver Sun.
Specifics, including the alleged drug trafficker's identity, his hometown and even the narcotic he is accused of smuggling from the U.S. into Canada are redacted in the public version of the ruling.
The "experienced" DEA special agent at the centre of the case is referred to only as "Jane Doe."
According to the judge's decision, the American agent showed up at the man's door with two Canadian detectives who were also operating outside of their jurisdiction. The man, identified in the court documents as "named person," said he was later summoned to meet with U.S. investigators three times.
He ultimately signed an agreement to help in their probe focused on another unnamed target.
As part of that investigation, the DEA directed the Canadian to set up a deal to move an unspecified amount of cash for the target. Agents sent the man abroad to take part in the scheme and by the time he returned home, "he felt that his life was in jeopardy," the judge's decision says.
Murray said the plan amounted to a money-laundering conspiracy and that "the DEA was leading him into criminal conduct" without Canadian oversight or authorization.

- VideoInside the ‘most sophisticated’ drug lab in Canadian history
"The DEA was aware of the protocols but chose to operate in Canada behind the back of the RCMP," the judge wrote. She said the DEA provided the Mounties with misleading information about the investigation — and it only did so months after pressuring the Canadian to co-operate.
"The DEA committed a deliberate, calculated and ongoing infringement of [named person]'s constitutional rights which was unlawful and conducted in violation of Canadian sovereignty," Murray wrote.
Foreign investigators cannot act as police in Canada. They're required to follow a series of guidelines while operating here, including having Canadian law enforcement supervise their operations.
'Public would be outraged' by DEA's conduct, judge says
Despite any deal the man may have had with the DEA, U.S. prosecutors still sought his extradition to stand trial. At the man's request, the B.C. judge ordered those proceedings to be halted.
"The public would be outraged by the conduct of the DEA in this case," Murray wrote.
"While there is a high public interest in seeing trafficking and exporting charges prosecuted, the behaviour of the DEA in this case is so shocking and flagrant that the justice system must distance itself from it. To allow the proceedings to continue would be to condone it."
Murray underlined it's not the first time a Canadian's case has been tossed due to the DEA's conduct. She pointed to a similar decision from a B.C. judge in 2002, after U.S. agents continued undercover work in Canada even though the RCMP had refused to approve the operations.
DEA agents have since contributed to high-profile investigations involving Canadian targets, including the FBI-led Operation Giant Slalom — centred around alleged cocaine kingpin Ryan Wedding — and the Ontario Provincial Police's recent Project Bay, which seized illegal street drugs with a street value of $139 million.
The DEA did not immediately respond to emailed questions from CBC News on Friday. The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa declined to comment on the B.C. decision.
In a social media post, former CSIS analyst Jessica Davis described the case as "outrageous" and "a bad sign for the future of law enforcement co-operation between Canada and the U.S."
The DEA's website lists offices at the U.S. Embassy and the consulate in Vancouver. The agency says its role in Canada "is to co-ordinate international drug-trafficking investigations between the United States and Canadian law enforcement."
"Both DEA offices in Canada work with Canadians on a full complement of cases while ensuring that our activities are in keeping with Canadian laws and existing agreements," the website says.

Enchantments are one of the most important systems in Minecraft Dungeons 2 that can help you create a powerful build. This sequel to Minecraft Dungeons expands the equipment system, so more items can now be enchanted to gain more customization in combat. So, if you’re looking for all the Minecraft Dungeons 2 enchantments that can provide you with unique buffs, keep reading this guide below.
List of All Enchantments in Minecraft Dungeons 2
The following Minecraft Dungeons 2 enchantments cover a broad range of playstyles. Some focus on raw damage, while others reward dodging, improve healing, manipulate souls, and more. So, take a look at the table below for a quick overview of all the enchantments in the action RPG.
| Enchantment | Max Level | Effect | Applicable to | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Ancient Alchemy | 3 | Grants souls when using a health potion | Armor | 
| Artifact Amplifier | 3 | Improves artifact performance after activation | Armor | 
| Dynamo | 3 | Boosts the next attack after rolling | Weapon | 
| Ender Mines | 3 | Deploys explosive end crystals | Weapon | 
| Fire Aspect | 3 | Adds a fiery wave to certain attacks | Melee Weapon | 
| Frost Crescent | 3 | Adds a freezing wave | Melee Weapon | 
| Healing Smite | 3 | Can create regeneration wells after kills | Weapon | 
| Lightning Surge | 3 | Adds a lightning-based attack wave | Melee Weapon | 
| Piercing | 3 | Lets projectiles pass through enemies | Ranged Weapon | 
| Poison Fog | 3 | Adds a poisonous wave | Melee Weapon | 
| Shadowcloak | 3 | Can grant Shadowcloaking after kills | Weapon | 
| Somersault | 3 | Grants additional consecutive rolls | Armor | 
| Thundering | 3 | Gives attacks a chance to spread lightning damage | Weapon | 
Ancient Alchemy
Ancient Alchemy is an armor enchantment that can turn your health potion into a source of souls. It can also allow the potion to be used while the hero is at full health. So, it can come in handy when you’re relying heavily on soul-powered mechanics. There are three tiers for this enchantment, described as follows:
- Tier 1: Using the health potion grants 30 souls
- Tier 2: Using the health potion grants 45 souls
- Tier 3: Using the health potion grants 60 souls
Artifact Amplifier
The Artifact Amplifier enchantment in Minecraft Dungeons 2 reduces the Artifact cooldowns and improves the Artifact damage for a limited period of time. This is an incentive who like to chain their abilities rather than sit on them indefinitely. So, here is how the effects are categorized based on the enchantment tiers:
- Tier 1: Reduced Artifact Cooldown and improved damage for 6 seconds
- Tier 2: Reduced Artifact Cooldown and improved damage for 7.5 seconds
- Tier 3: Reduced Artifact Cooldown and improved damage for 9 seconds
Dynamo
Dynamo turns dodge roll into a damage setup. With this enchantment equipped on your armor, your next melee or ranged attack receives bonus damage. So, the mechanic generally used to avoid attacks becomes a part of your offensive rotation. Now, check the damage multipliers that you can receive with each enchantment tier:
- Tier 1: +20% Damage buff to next melee or ranged attack
- Tier 2: +30% Damage buff to next melee or ranged attack
- Tier 3: +40% Damage buff to next melee or ranged attack
Ender Mines
The Ender Mines enchantment brings one of the most recognizable elements in the game: the exploding End Crystals in Minecraft. This enchantment can allow your weapon attacks to deploy a few mines that explode when enemies are nearby after a brief time period.
So, it adds a great crowd control ability to your build when repositioning yourself becomes a constant need due to the enemies in The Sift in Minecraft Dungeons 2. That said, here are the specific tiers in which this enchantment is divided:
- Tier 1: Deploys 2 mines
- Tier 2: Deploys 3 mines
- Tier 3: Deploys 4 mines
Fire Aspect
The Fire Aspect enchantment in Minecraft Dungeons 2 adds a fiery wave to final hits and jump attacks. Note that you can only add it to your melee weapon, but it adds an interesting AoE component to it by setting mobs on fire for a while. So, here are the specific tiers that state how much damage each of them can deal.
- Tier 1: Fiery wave deals 35% of weapon damage, setting mobs on fire for some time
- Tier 2: Fiery wave deals 45% of weapon damage, setting mobs on fire for some time
- Tier 3: Fiery wave deals 50% of weapon damage, setting mobs on fire for some time
Frost Crescent
The Frost Crescent enchantment works on a contradictory idea to Fire Aspect. It adds a freezing wave to your melee attacks that can freeze enemies and also slow them down for a brief time period. This can grant you breathing room and an open window to launch your next attacks. Here are the bonuses you get from this enchantment:
- Tier 1: Freeze wave deals 10% of weapon damage, freezing enemies and slowing their attacks and movements
- Tier 2: Freeze wave deals 15% of weapon damage, freezing enemies and slowing their attacks and movements
- Tier 3: Freeze wave deals 20% of weapon damage, freezing enemies and slowing their attacks and movements
Healing Smite
Healing Smite is one of the most interesting enchantments in Minecraft Dungeons 2 revealed so far. It can grant a chance to create a Regenerating Well upon defeating an enemy. Your allies can stay inside the well’s range to heal themselves. So, here’s how the chance-based mechanic works for each enchantment tier.
- Tier 1: 20% chance to generate a Regenerating Well after defeating an enemy
- Tier 2: 35% chance to generate a Regenerating Well after defeating an enemy
- Tier 3: 50% chance to generate a Regenerating Well after defeating an enemy
Lightning Surge
Lightning Surge puts you in a risk-reward situation. The reason is that melee weapons with this enchantment have a chance to zap enemies while also making them faster at the same time. Well, you might not want to activate this ability while being surrounded by Chicken Jockey enemies in Minecraft Dungeons 2.
- Tier 1: Deals 60% of weapon damage to enemies, zapping them for a short time and making them faster
Piercing
Next up, we have a Minecraft Dungeons 2 enchantment specifically for ranged weapons. With this equipped on your bow or crossbow, the projectiles or arrows fired will keep travelling through enemies, instead of stopping at the first target. Below is how the three tiers affect the enemies through which the projectiles can pierce:
- Tier 1: Projectiles can pierce 1 enemy
- Tier 2: Projectiles can pierce 3 enemies
- Tier 3: Projectiles can pierce 5 enemies
Poison Fog
Poison Fog is an interesting crowd control enchantment that adds a poisonous wave to all your final hits and jump attacks using a melee weapon in Minecraft Dungeons 2. Since the effect stays with the mobs for a short while, this enchantment offers both an instant damage boost and damage-over-time. Here are the three tiers of this enchantment:
- Tier 1: Poisonous wave deals 10% of weapon damage and poisons mobs for a while
- Tier 2: Poisonous wave deals 20% of weapon damage and poisons mobs for a while
- Tier 3: Poisonous wave deals 30% of weapon damage and poisons mobs for a while
Shadowcloak
This Minecraft Dungeons 2 enchantment grants players a chance to enter the Shadowcloaking state after defeating an enemy. Here are the three tiers for the Shadowcloak enchantment:
- Tier 1: 15% chance to enter Shadowcloaking after defeating enemies
- Tier 2: 20% chance to enter Shadowcloaking after defeating enemies
- Tier 3: 35% chance to enter Shadowcloaking after defeating enemies
Somersault
Now, we have a mobility enchantment, as Somersault grants players additional rolls to be performed consecutively. Since repositioning yourself and movement hugely affect your survival in this action RPG, you might consider this utility buff to your armor.
- Tier 1: Provides 1 extra roll
- Tier 2: Provides 2 extra rolls
- Tier 3: Provides 3 extra rolls
Thundering
Thundering gives your weapon attacks a chance to spread lightning damage. So, if you’re looking for a consistent extra damage boost, unlike Lightning Surge, which can throw you in a pickle, Thundering is the one you should go for. Here are the damage stats for each tier:
- Tier 1: 25% chance for 15% weapon damage to spread as lightning damage
- Tier 2: 33% chance for 30% weapon damage to spread as lightning damage
- Tier 3: 50% chance for 50% weapon damage to spread as lightning damage
And that is all you need to learn about all the enchantments in Minecraft Dungeons 2. So, which enchantments are you going to combine to make your build get the perfect abilities? Tell us in the comments below.
How many Minecraft Dungeons 2 enchantments are there?
There are currently 13 enchantments in Minecraft Dungeons 2 known so far, each granting a unique ability to make your progression a bit smoother.
How to get enchantments in Minecraft Dungeons 2?
You can discover the Enchant Books while exploring the world. Then use the same enchanted books at an Enchantsmith to get the required buffs.

Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
- Published
A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran.
Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates.
It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade.
"Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity."
That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north.
Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea. This is focused on a dispute with Saudi Arabia but heightens insecurity for international shipping.
"I guess the pirates believe that with those two external events in Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, they believe that the international forces will be dedicated to those crises instead of looking for pirates," says Vice-Admiral Ignacio Villanueva Serrano, operation commander for the European Union's naval force that protects shipping off Somalia's coast.
Among the latest vessels hijacked by the pirates was a Cameroon-flagged ship, the MV Lutuf, which was attacked off the coast of Somalia's semi-autonomous Puntland region on 17 August. A few days later pirates boarded an oil products tanker, the Eritrean-flagged MT Sibu 1, in waters near Yemen, on the other side of the Gulf.
The capture of the Lutuf has triggered unexpected consequences.
Thirteen men allegedly belonging to a network that supplies the pirates on the ship have been killed in two drone strikes since 18 August. No one has said they are behind the attacks, but local officials blamed them on Turkey, saying the vessel was carrying Turkish weapons.
The Lutuf is now among six vessels being held for demands of millions of dollars in ransom, four of which are anchored near the fishing town of Bander Beyla known as a hotbed for piracy, the BBC has learned.
That is nowhere near the peak levels of hijackings 15 years ago that cost the global economy billions of dollars. In 2011 Somali pirates carried out more than 200 attacks and held hundreds of crew members hostage.
A co-ordinated international naval response together with private security on commercial ships successfully drove down the scourge and contained a flare-up in 2023 and 2024.
But experts stress that while the pirate networks were suppressed, they remained intact, given the failure to address the poor economic and security conditions in Somalia that feed them.
Currently the resurgence is fuelled locally by anger over foreign trawlers which overfish in Somali waters, damaging the fishing industry that sustains communities in Puntland.
And there are more targets available now with a potentially bigger payload.
The regional maritime insecurity has driven some ships closer to the Somali coast as they divert south to avoid the conflict further north. Given the high price of oil, hijacking a tanker is more lucrative.
"You have that combined effect of less naval patrolling but more commercial shipping in these waters," according to the analyst Mahmood, "and that signals an opportunity.
"And once you've had a successful attack, I think that spurs other units to do copycat type incidents as well."
He and other researchers suspect there may be collaboration between the Somali pirates and Yemenis after several vessels were seized near Yemen's coast.
But Mahmood says these would more likely be criminal elements than Iran's Houthi allies, especially as one of the ships seized last week, the MT Sibu 1, allegedly belonged to an Iranian "shadow fleet" used to transport petroleum products trying to dodge US sanctions.
"I don't see something specifically Iran-directed," he says.
Turkey, however, reportedly has a stake in the latest hijackings.
Puntland security sources and a Somali government official have told the BBC that the Lutuf was carrying weapons bound for a Turkish military training facility in the Somali capital, Mogadishu. Ankara has an agreement with Somalia to strengthen its maritime security, as part of a wider defence and economic partnership.
The security sources say six international warships are now in the seas close to the Lutuf - two from Turkey and one each from Spain, Denmark, the US and India, something the BBC has not been able to independently verify.
"There is military equipment on the [hijacked] ship meant for Turkey's operations in Somalia," the Somali government official said, speaking on condition of anonymity, adding that the cargo included satellite equipment for a space station that Ankara is building north of the capital.
He alleged that Turkey had carried out the second drone strike that killed nine armed men on Sunday.
"The men who were killed were criminals and I don't have sympathy for them," he said, "but taking it to that level is escalating the situation even more."
Turkey's defence ministry has stated that its forces are providing "necessary support" to Somali authorities regarding the incident involving a hijacked vessel in Somali territorial waters, within the framework of their security agreement. But it stopped short of addressing the accusations that Turkey had carried out deadly drone strikes.
Publicly the government in Mogadishu has said only that it is aware of the operations against pirate groups and will take measures to address them.
Puntland authorities have been more outspoken.
Speaking to the BBC's Somali Service, Deputy Minister of Security Abdirahman Yusuf said his administration had evidence that Turkey was responsible for the attacks, citing information about Turkish activity around the vessel and along the Puntland coast.
The BBC has not independently verified his allegations.
The security ministry also issued a statement expressing opposition to "bombings by international warships targeting civilians" that "undermined co-operation… in combatting piracy", and demanded an immediate explanation for why they were carried out.
Puntland is wary of Turkey's close military relationship with the Somali government, and the incidents risk further complicating a long-standing political dispute between the semi-autonomous region and Mogadishu that hinders a co-ordinated effort to fight piracy, analysts say.
There is not yet a full-blown resurgence. But without an end to the US-Iran war, or increased international efforts at deterrence, Somali piracy stands to continue raising the threat level in a crucial maritime space that is already dangerously squeezed.

The debate about whether or not to post your kids' faces on social media isn't new. I have friends whose kids are in college now who I remember struggled with the decision about whether to post baby photos to Instagram.
But very recently, that conversation has taken a significant turn because of concerns about AI — and even prompted Meta to take action.
Two viral things have happened on Instagram in the last week or so, with pretty different origins but ultimately the same result: parents saying that they shouldn't post images of their children online anymore.
The first was a viral Instagram from Kalie Robins, a mom in Utah. Robins was shocked and creeped out when she noticed Meta AI suggestions on a video she had posted of herself and her kid.
The Meta AI chatbot suggested questions like "who's the child passenger?" Following more of the Meta AI questions, Robins found that it pulled photos of her that she believed had been deleted, and information about her kids from her mother's Facebook page.
While yes, Meta AI was pulling information that already exists online, it was also suggesting questions about the identity of children — potentially suggesting that to strangers (it's unclear if only Kalie saw this set of Meta AI questions or if a stranger would have been suggested different ones).
Meta told me that these AI suggestions were a mistake that had since been fixed.
"When someone clicks on a prompt and uses this feature, the response it generates is based on information the user already has access to," said Meta spokesperson Andy Stone. "But we missed the mark because the feature never should have prompted the individual with questions like that and we've fixed that issue."
Meta AI suggested questions about her kids
I spoke with Robins, and she expressed that she wasn't unaware of how Meta AI was able to pull up the information. To her, it was a stark reminder of just how much of our data is on social media, even if we don't realize it.
"I thought I was so careful because I never did the back-to-school photos with the school and teacher name. I never posted in front of any landmarks or in front of our house with street signs. I never did any of that," she told me. "I thought I was being so careful and ultimately that didn't matter. It didn't even get that info from me. It got it from other people, so it didn't matter how careful I was being in this case."
The online reaction to Robins' video was twofold: first, that Meta AI did something creepy and off-putting (which even Meta agrees with), and that this is a good reminder for parents to be wary of what information is out there about their kids and any photos they post.
Professional photographers are shying away from sharing kid photos
At the same time, another viral trend on Instagram is making people rethink how kids' images are posted online.
A bunch of professional family photographers, nearly all women or mothers themselves, have been posting notices announcing a new policy that they won't share kids' faces on social media or their professional websites anymore.
The concern here is over AI-generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM), and the risk that photos posted to social media could be used to either create deepfakes of specific children, or that their faces could end up in data training for AI models that end up creating this kind of content.
This is a legitimate concern, and there have been criminal cases involving AI-generated CSAM, some gaining national media attention.
A recent legal ruling about AI CSAM
A judge's recent ruling in a criminal case about AI-generated CSAM has gone viral in some Instagram parenting circles. The details of the legal ruling are complex (there's some great detail here in the Washington Post story about it), but the short version is that the judge wrote that there's a legal precedent that possession (not production or distribution) of AI-generated child pornography is protected as free speech.
The implications of the ruling — and what it means for innocent photos of kids — is what is now going viral on Instagram.
Hannah Haggard, a family and wedding photographer based in Kentucky, posted to her Instagram that she was changing her policies, and will not post any kids' faces — even with parents' permission.
"I'd been toying with the idea already," Haggard told me. "I never post without consent, but I still was already considering it. Then once the ruling happened, it was confirmation that that's what needed to happen."
A lot of the online reaction I've seen seems outraged at the ruling, which at a glance seems to be good news for child predators. But Mariefaye Bechrakis, a lawyer specializing in human rights and child rights who has written about AI-generated CSAM legal issues for the American Bar Association, says that it's more nuanced.
"What is important to note is that the judges are flashing a green light for a future appeal," Bechrakis told me about her opinion of the judge's ruling. "They basically gave a future roadmap and a real opportunity to future prosecutors. They noted that modern AI models don't create images out of thin air, but that they must be trained on large datasets."
Katey Sutton, a family photographer in Missouri, also posted about her policy of not showing kids' faces on the internet.
"I don't believe AI is truly 'synthetic'," she told me. "It's known that AI scrapes the internet and uses information it's given/finds to inform, recommend, create, etc…"
Take a scroll through Facebook or Instagram, and you'll see that clearly not all parents have ceased posting kid pics. But for some people, these recent AI scares are making them think carefully about the risks before posting. And that's probably a good thing.

'If you started running, they shot you' - inside Nigeria's growing kidnapping crisis
- Published
"If you ran into a room, they set the room on fire," says Fatima, describing a recent attack on her village in Zamfara, north-western Nigeria. "If you came out and started running, they shot you."
The gunmen, who struck at 02:00, split into groups to surround residents: one at the village entrance, one in the centre and one at the back.
"They opened fire without a care in the world, shooting indiscriminately," the 55-year-old quietly tells the BBC World Service.
It was one of many attacks that have caused havoc in the mainly Muslim community where residents live in fear of being kidnapped for ransom.
Fatima explains how the raids unfold: "You could have 100 motorcycles, and each one could be carrying three people."
About 70 people, including children, were killed from the village of Bia Buki in June, according to Fatima.
She describes how the attackers also targeted villagers as they fled and children were injured falling into ditches. Among the dead were her husband and six of his seven siblings.
Fatima is one of an estimated 800,000 Nigerians who the UN says have been displaced in the country's north-west. One of the main reasons people have left their homes is violence.
Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by gangs, locally referred to as bandits, who often move around on motorcycles and attack quickly then ride away, escaping before security forces arrive.
Thousands of people have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fight, and the BBC spoke to one who said his armed group had killed many bandits.
But the gangs keep attacking in what appears to be a deteriorating pattern of violence and abductions that is spreading southwards.
Fatima says when the bandits attacked her home, she ran into the nearby forest with other villagers to hide: "The forest became our sanctuary. We ran with our kids, if you couldn't find your child you'd take your neighbour's child."
She says people slept in the forest before moving on to the state capital, Gusau, "where we found a little bit of peace".
Fatima now lives in an informal camp in Gusau with her seven children, who are aged between nine and 30.
Dozens of women sit in groups on the dusty ground of the makeshift compound, many wearing brightly coloured hijabs. More than 1,000 people are here, she believes.
Conditions are tough with "no proper place to even lay your head". Food is scarce and assistance arrives irregularly.
Fatima describes two occasions where "good Samaritans" brought rice or potatoes. Children are sent out to gather firewood to sell so families can buy food, but 22 have been kidnapped by bandits, she says.
Gesturing towards a nearby building, Fatima says that there "you will find 100 or more women… maybe just two or three have had breakfast.
"When we had peace, we had our own wealth, but now the tables have turned and we have become beggars."
Her eyes fill with tears and she cries for a few minutes, wiping her face with her hands.
Despite being 16 miles (25km) from her village, the threat Fatima fled has not disappeared.
When she first arrived at the camp, the sound of gunshots kept her awake at night. Things have since quietened, she says, crediting patrols by the army and government-backed vigilantes, but the atmosphere is still tense.
The bandits are mostly people from the Fulani ethnic group, who traditionally make their living by raising animals. Some of them have swapped cattle trading for kidnapping and extortion, which is seen as a faster, easier way to make money.
They attack towns and villages or ambush travellers, abducting people for ransom, stealing whatever they want - and sometimes killing those who resist. They also force communities to pay protection money, only allowing farmers into their fields if they hand over large sums of cash.
Attacks are now more frequent than ever. In the bandit heartlands of north-west Nigeria, the number of incidents recorded by the international conflict monitoring group Acled rose 78% in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025.
One security consultancy estimates that kidnappers across Nigeria collected nearly $5.8m (£4.3m) in ransoms over the past year as the number of abductions surged. SBM Intelligence estimates that 7,825 people were kidnapped between July 2025 and June 2026, a 66% increase on the previous year.
The increase in bandit activity appears to be a key driver in this trend.
Malik Samuel at Good Governance Africa, a research and advocacy non-profit group, says that "there is no region in northern Nigeria currently that does not experience one form of mass abduction or the other".
Nigeria's battle with bandits is just one part of a more complex security situation facing the country.
As well as the bandit gangs in the north-west, there is an Islamist insurgency in the north-east, separatist unrest in the south-east and clashes in central regions, where the main grievance is over access to land and water for grazing and farming and where ethnic and religious elements have also fuelled some of the unrest.
Most analysts agree that armed groups have waged campaigns of violence that affect all communities, regardless of background or belief.
- The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria 
  - Published28 November 2025
Schools are a common target. When the Islamist Boko Haram militant group infamously kidnapped more than 200 schoolgirls from the north-eastern village of Chibok in 2014, it made global headlines.
At the time the group forced its captives into sexual slavery, domestic servitude or used them as suicide bombers.
But a range of groups across Nigeria now use kidnapping to raise funds, focusing on soft targets such as schools, churches, mosques and remote villages.
This was mainly confined to the Boko Haram strongholds of the north-east or the bandit zones of the north-west - areas that are largely Muslim.
Then, in May this year, gunmen on motorcycles attacked three schools in Oyo state, south-west Nigeria, one of the few regions that was previously considered relatively safe. Thirty-nine children, the youngest just two years old, were abducted along with seven teachers. One teacher was killed during the raid, another's murder was filmed and shared online.
After 56 days, the remaining 44 hostages were released. The government said it refused to pay a ransom and that the children were released after an operation by security forces. Three men were sentenced to life in prison for the attacks and confessed to being members of an affiliate of Boko Haram.
The abduction spread fear throughout the south-western town of Oriire, with parents in the community pulling their children out of school.
"There is fear because many residents have run away and are yet to return," says the traditional ruler of the area, Oba Tajudeen Abioye, whose niece was among the kidnapped children.
"And for those of us who are left here, we are relying on the security officials, the soldiers" who were sent to protect the community, he says.
Nigeria already has one of the highest numbers of out-of-school children in the world: the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) estimates the number is about 19 million.
The multiple, overlapping security issues mean Nigeria's military and police are overstretched and as a result struggle to tackle the violence.
A 2025 UN report said that police stations were often underfunded and not fully operational, citing independent sources that accused officers of lacking skills in hostage negotiation and forensic investigation.
President Bola Tinubu's administration has allocated the largest defence and security budget in the country's history, raising it by 10% in December 2025 compared to one year before. He has recently approved the recruitment of 28,000 new soldiers.
In the meantime communities are still suffering and in Zamfara thousands of residents have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fill the gaps in security.
But there are concerns about their involvement. In 2020 Zamfara banned a large vigilante group over concerns that extrajudicial killings were driving more violence, according to AFP.
The authorities say the new vigilantes are better trained, but Samuel, from Good Governance Africa, calls them a "time bomb waiting to happen".
"If citizens arm themselves how do you control them at the end of the crisis, how are you able to disarm them?" he asks.
One of the vigilantes meets us outside his group's headquarters, a single-storey concrete building, and agrees to speak on the condition of anonymity during our visit in July.
He perches on his motorcycle, an AK-47 slung over his shoulder, a scarf across his face as a makeshift balaclava, gold and silver skull rings on his fingers.
"We are some of the people the governor hired to protect the community," he says, explaining that they are sometimes told where the bandits are and "with the help of God we fight them and defeat them".
"Let the bandits understand that when they attack a place and kill, they can also be killed," he adds.
He estimates he has fought bandits at least 20 times and says the calls for his group's help keep coming.
"It's hard to go a week without these reports," he says. "There are regions that became safer… but there are other regions where the same cannot be said."
He calls on the state governor, whom he supports, to hire and arm more people to take on the bandits. "These people won't be afraid of you unless you have proper weapons to fight them," he says.
Fatima also calls for more action: "These kidnappers are in every nook and cranny.
"I am not saying the government has failed but even if it is trying, it needs to do more. There are problems and we think with more effort and more security agents, villages will be peaceful."
She wants to return home, but is doubtful that will happen as she has heard her village has now been turned into a camp for the gunmen that attacked it.
The local bandit leader has become the de facto authority, and that families look to him to solve domestic disputes, she says.
Another nearby village "is completely empty, not even a chicken lives there… empty villages like that are countless", Fatima says.
"Even if you go back to our area, it's just difficulty you will face. There's nothing there, no food… you farm and when you go to harvest, they stop you or kidnap you."

It wasn’t that long ago that ClickFix attacks were exotic. Now the technique has become mainstream as attackers reap its simplicity and effectiveness in infecting users of PCs and Macs alike. All that’s required is a compromised website—a painless enough task—a fake CAPTCHA overlay, and the inclusion of a single terminal command. So many visitors get suckered into pasting and running the command that just about every malware pusher has adopted the technique. Even Kremlin-backed hacking groups are joining in.
“Reddit is becoming post after post after post of people getting their computer infected via ClickFix,” independent researcher Kevin Beaumont observed Thursday. “Legit websites everywhere [are] getting hacked to serve the fake captcha prompts.”
How many of us make things worse
More seasoned Internet users—a fair number who read this site—are quick to dismiss the attack. They typically blame the people who fall for the scams and marvel at their gullibility and lack of attention. The reality is that for more casual users, using computers and the Internet has become so difficult—think impossible-to-close interstitials, CAPTCHAs with an endless series of pictures to analyze, and constantly changing interfaces that bury the features they’re looking for—that they have grown desensitized to instructions that seem ridiculous and burdensome.
ClickFix attackers are capitalizing on this fatigue. Typically, attacks begin with a simple CAPTCHA image, often masquerading as one from Cloudflare. After engaging with the box, the user sees a line of text, often obscured in a way to mask any malicious commands. Then the user is instructed to copy the text and paste it into the Windows Run, PowerShell, or macOS terminal and click Enter.
The instructions come from websites people have used for years. The directions seem no more suspicious than things they’ve been required to do for a decade. Why would someone without a firm grasp of computer security have any reason to hesitate?

Comedian Pete Davidson of Saturday Night Live (SNL) fame has turned 33, the same age his father, firefighter Scott Davidson, was when he died during the 9/11 attacks. Speaking to the New York Post, Davidson said he once thought of his father as an “old guy” because he was 33 when he died. However, becoming a father himself has changed the way he views the tragedy.
“I thought, ‘Oh, he was an old guy. He’s 33,’” Davidson said. “But now I’m there, and I have a kid, and that would be like my kid not having her dad.”
To mark 25 years since the September 11 attacks, Davidson is taking part in a comedy benefit at Madison Square Garden with Jon Stewart.
Quick answers to key questions
Pete Davidson's 33rd birthday is significant because it marks the same age his father, firefighter Scott Davidson, was when he died during the 9/11 attacks.
Becoming a father has changed Pete Davidson's perspective on 9/11, making him realize the tragedy's impact on his life and on his daughter, emphasizing the loss of his father.
Pete Davidson is participating in a comedy benefit at Madison Square Garden, along with Jon Stewart, to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.
Pete Davidson chose the name 'Scottie' for his daughter to honor his late father, whose name was Scott, indicating a desire to keep the name alive.
Pete Davidson hopes to 'reclaim' 9/11 through the comedy event, aiming to celebrate and bring fun to the day rather than dwell on its sadness through documentaries.
Davidson said this year feels particularly difficult but also meaningful as he will spend the day with his daughter, Scottie, who was born last December and was named after his late father.
“So, this year is extra tough, but also extra beautiful because I get to spend the day with Scottie,” he said. “It’ll be very healing and special.”
Davidson said Hewitt also wanted their daughter to carry his father’s name.
“It was really cool that Elsie also wanted to name her Scottie,” he told the Post. “My dad’s name was Scott, but his nickname was Scotty. When she arrived, we both looked at her and were like, ‘She looks like a Scottie.’ It’s nice to keep that name alive.”
The Saturday Night Live alum said he also wants to use the comedy event to “reclaim” 9/11 and have “fun”, rather than spend the day watching documentaries about the tragedy.
“And not be in the middle of 12 documentaries that are so sad and rehash it,” he added.
Davidson previously recalled on Theo Von’s podcast that his father’s crew was the first fire truck to cross the bridge towards the World Trade Center.
“So they were the first truck over there and pretty much the whole house died, which is sad, but at least he died with his pals.”
Davidson remembered his father as “f---ing hilarious” and said he has only a few memories of him because he was seven when the attacks happened.
“My memories are few and far between because I was 7, but I just remember laughing a lot, him being pretty jacked and smoking a lot of cigarettes, and driving a Subaru Impreza. That’s all I remember.”
He also recalled that his father always had a big smile on his face. Davidson said his father’s old friends continue to light up when they share stories about him.

The Pune administration on Friday revoked its 10-day liquor ban for the Ganesh festival after the Bombay High Court pulled up the authorities, questioning why Pune was singled out while Mumbai and other parts of Maharashtra faced no such restrictions, according to PTI. A bench comprising Chief Justice MC Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna said the administration should withdraw the prohibition or be prepared for judicial intervention. The court observed that imposing what it described as an arbitrary restriction only in Pune amounted to unfairly singling out the district and its residents. "What is the rationale behind choosing only Pune? We deprecate such practice. This is a stigma on Pune residents. What are you trying to portray that only people in Pune behave badly after drinking? One district you are choosing across the state," the court stated. The court was hearing petitions filed by hotel and wine shop owners challenging an order issued by the Pune collector banning alcohol sales for 10 days during the Ganesh festival, beginning September 14. The bench directed the lawyer representing the Pune collector to return later in the day with a decision on whether the order would be withdrawn. In the absence of a withdrawal, the court said it would issue an appropriate order. It also observed that while maintaining law and order and preventing public nuisance was the authorities’ responsibility, they could not impose a blanket 10-day ban that effectively prevented licensed establishments from conducting their business. Maharashtra Congress leader Sachin Sawant on Friday said the 10-day liquor ban imposed in Pune during the Ganpati festival is a consequence of the gradual rise of "majoritarian politics" over the past 12 years. Sawant alleged that the BJP, which has been in power at the Centre since 2014, has used government machinery and exerted pressure at the grassroots through organisations and workers linked to the Sangh Parivar to foster an atmosphere of majoritarianism. "Doing anything to gain power is dangerous not only for democracy but also for the social unity of the country. A government, while taking a decision, should not consider only the sentiments of the majority community. It must ensure such a decision does not adversely affect the freedom, way of life or rights of other citizens, particularly minorities," he said. Sawant stated that the issue was not limited to political responsibility and also involved a constitutional obligation. He pointed to a recent incident at a school in Mira Bhayandar, where students were reportedly asked not to bring lunch containing onion, garlic or root vegetables during the Jain community's 'Paryushan' festival. He cited the incident as another indication of what he described as such a mindset. "Everyone's religious beliefs should be respected, but those beliefs should not be imposed on others," he said. Apple would kindly like to stay far away from Meta's ongoing reputational challenges with AI glasses.
Apple CEO John Ternus was recently asked about how the company thinks about privacy in the age of AI wearables in light of backlash around AI glasses like Meta's. After all, Apple is rumored to be cooking up some AI glasses of its own in its labs.
"I know you can't talk about unannounced products, but what do you think about the backlash around what people are calling, you know, 'pervert glasses,'" Tom's Guide editor in chief Mark Spoonauer asked.
Before Ternus could answer, Greg Joswiak, Apple's senior vice president of worldwide marketing who also being interviewed, quipped: "That's quite a marketing slogan." The remark drew laughter from Ternus.
Meta is actively fighting back at that perception with a marketing blitz that emphasizes the AI glasses' light that alerts people when the recording feature is activated. It's also taken steps to thwart users who tamper with that light and pledged to remove "harassing" videos recorded by the AI glasses from Instagram (Business Insider has found those moderation efforts are off to a bumpy start.) Meta declined to comment on the Apple executives' remarks.
Beyond some laughter at a rival's expense, the pair of Apple execs instead looked to explain how the company hopes to address privacy concerns when it releases two new AI-enabled listening features alongside the next generation of Apple Watches.
"We wanted to do this in a way that people feel comfortable using it, and people around the user feel comfortable about its existence," Ternus said.
While its first foldable phone, iPhone Duo, stole the show, Apple also announced that Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 will come with optional "audio intelligence" features that, depending on a user's preference, can mean Siri is always listening to your conversations throughout the day. Apple says the features don't start working until the on-device AI detects speech and that no audio is recorded or stored.
One feature, "Siri Recap," can listen to meetings or even your whole day and generate what the company calls "high-level" notes on what happened. Another feature, Live Rewind, shows a text snippet of the last 15 seconds of what was just said around you on the Apple Watch's screen.
Ternus and Joswiak emphasized that neither feature includes speaker attribution. There's also no audio recording that the user could store for later playback. Apple also says it doesn't have access to the raw audio files. Joswiak also said this means Apple can't be compelled to turn over an audio file.
"It's just those higher-level notes to remind you of that without getting into all the stuff that really is privacy concerning which a lot of other products are doing," Joswiak said.
While they did not mention it, the Live Rewind feature also includes audio and visual cues on the Apple Watch's screen — similar to the recording light on Meta's AI glasses — to alert those around the watch wearer that the last 15 seconds of conversation is being processed. Apple says "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap" will be available in beta later this year.
Both Apple execs also said that current apps have long allowed users to record themselves and those around them. While they didn't mention anything in particular, AI-enabled apps and devices like Granola and Plaud are also designed for such use cases.
But the Apple execs' response to the question highlights that Apple is seeking to differentiate its approach to information-gathering on AI devices. Whether or not people ultimately feel comfortable about Apple Watches listening in on their conversations is another question altogether.

NASA has released a document that provides some initial details about the proposed United States Space Academy, and it’s clear that the space agency wants to move quickly in establishing the institution.
According to the document’s timeline, NASA seeks a groundbreaking for a permanent campus no later than next year, the first class to be enrolled and begin studies in temporary facilities in 2028, and a transition to a permanent campus in 2031.
What will that campus look like?
NASA is seeking a permanent site with at least 300 acres for the Space Academy, which aims to “prepare a new generation of leaders to explore, build, operate, secure, and defend the space domain.” Proximity to NASA facilities or university campuses could be a plus. The campus will initially support 1,200 undergraduates, with the potential to expand to up to 4,000 students.
Let the bidding begin
The document is called a “Request for Information,” and it essentially kicks off the bidding process among US states to house the Space Academy. This is expected to be a hot competition, with states such as Texas, Florida, and Alabama expected to put forth attractive bids to the federal government.
All 50 states are invited to submit a single response, specifying their contributions such as land, infrastructure, funding, and more. Respondents are also asked to provide a “rough-order-of-magnitude” estimate of the cost to establish and operate the Space Academy at their proposed locations. Submissions are due back to NASA by October 26.
The 14-page document sets up a competition that may look something like a major corporate relocation, with states pitching packages of free land, university partnerships, state funding, and more to lure the federal government to choose their state.

In Goods & Services Tax (GST) regime, Input Tax Credit stands as one of the most significant reforms aimed at eliminating the cascading effect of taxes. Introduced in July 2017, Input Tax Credit (ITC) is one of the foundational pillars of India’s Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime. It enables registered businesses to offset the GST paid on their purchases (inputs, input services, and capital goods) against the GST liability on their outward supplies (sales). This mechanism ensures that tax is levied only on the value added at each stage of the supply chain, eliminating the cascading effect of taxes (tax on taxes) that existed under the earlier indirect tax system VAT & Service Tax.
In simple terms, when a registered taxpayer pays GST on inward supplies used for business purposes, that tax amount can be claimed as credit in the electronic credit ledger. The net GST payable becomes Output Tax minus eligible ITC. This seamless flow of credit across the supply chain is central to GST’s design as a multi-stage, destination based value-added tax on each stage of the supply chain, with input tax credit (ITC) available to offset prior-stage taxes, ensuring only the final consumer bears the burden & cascading is avoided.
Section 16(1) of the CGST Act, 2017 provides that every registered person is entitled to take credit of input tax charged on any supply of goods or services (or both) used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of business. The credit is credited to the electronic credit ledger. Composition scheme dealers under Section 10 are not eligible for ITC. The supply must have a clear business nexus, personal or non-business use does not qualify for ITC claim.
Mandatory Conditions under Section 16(2):
Section 16(2) lays down cumulative conditions. All of them must be satisfied & failure on even one disallows the credit for that invoice. Businesses must know that there are six conditions for claiming the Input Tax Credit (ITC) and no registered person shall be entitled to the credit of any input tax in respect of any supply of goods or services or both to him/her unless:- 
(a)    He is in possession of a tax invoice or a debit note issued by a supplier registered under GST Act 2017 or such other tax paying documents (Rule 36 to Rule 45);
(b)    The details of the invoice or debit note has been furnished by the registered supplier in the statement of outward supplies and such details have been communicated to the recipient of such invoice or debit note;
(c)    He has physically received the goods or services or both;
(d)    The details of input tax credit (ITC) in respect of the said supply communicated to such registered person under section 38 has not been restricted;
(e)    Subject to the provisions of section 41 , the tax charged in respect of such supply has been actually paid to the Government, either in cash or through utilization of input tax credit admissible in respect of the said supply; and
(f)    He has furnished the valid return under section 39.
Possession of a valid tax document [Section 16(2)(a)], the recipient must hold a tax invoice, debit note, or other prescribed document (such as a bill of entry for imports or a self-invoice under reverse charge) issued by a registered supplier. The document must contain the prescribed particulars under the invoice rules, including GSTIN of supplier and recipient, description, value, tax amount, and place of supply where relevant invoice details furnished and communicated to recipient [Section 16(2)(aa)],effective from 1,January 2022, the supplier must have reported the invoice or debit note in their GSTR-1 (or IFF), and the details must appear in the recipient’s GSTR-2B. This matching requirement is critical & ITC is generally restricted to the amount reflected in GSTR-2B.
Receipt of goods or services [Section 16(2)(b)], the Goods or services must have been received. For goods delivered in lots or installments, credit is available only upon receipt of the last lot. “Bill-to-ship-to” model transactions are covered through a deeming provision, delivery to a third party on the direction of the registered person is treated as receipt of the supply by that registered person for purpose of claiming ITC. As per section 16(2)(ba), the details of input tax credit (ITC) in respect of the said supply communicated to such registered person under section 38 has not been restricted.
The tax charged in respect of such supply must has been actually paid to the Government by the supplier, either in cash or through utilization of admissible ITC [Section 16(2)(c)] in respect of the said supply. Recent judicial pronouncements have upheld the strict application of this condition. Even honest buyers can face denial of credit, if the supplier defaults, though mechanisms exist to re-avail credit once the supplier pays. The supplier must have filed the valid return under section 39 to facilitate the recipient for seamless flow of ITC. [Section 16(2)(d). Additional provisions also apply, if the recipient fails to pay the supplier the value of supply plus tax within 180 days from the invoice date (except reverse charge supplies), the claimed ITC must be reversed with interest. Credit can be reclaimed upon subsequent payment. There is also a time limit under Section 16(4), ITC cannot be claimed after the 30th day of November following the end of the financial year to which the invoice pertains, or the date of filing the relevant annual return, whichever is earlier.
Restrictions and Blocked Credits:
Even when the above conditions are met, section 17 imposes restrictions. ITC is not available (or is restricted) on certain goods and services listed in Section 17(5), such as motor vehicles (with exceptions for specific uses), food and beverages in many cases, membership of clubs, works contract services for construction of immovable property (except plant and machinery), goods or services used for personal consumption, and goods lost, stolen, destroyed, or given as gifts/free samples. When inputs or capital goods are used partly for taxable supplies and partly for exempt or non-business purposes, then the proportionate reversal is required under Rules 42 and 43.
Practical Compliance:
Businesses must regularly reconcile purchase registers with GSTR-2B/2A before claiming ITC in GSTR-3B. Supplier compliance has become a shared responsibility. Maintaining proper documentation, tracking the 180-day payment window, and ensuring timely returns are essential. Newer systems such as the Invoice Management System (IMS) further tighten the linkage between supplier reporting and recipient credit. 
In summary, ITC under GST is a powerful tool that reduces the cost of doing business and promotes seamless credit flow of ITC. However, it is strictly conditional & registered taxpayers must satisfy every requirement of Section 16 and remain vigilant about blocked credits and reversals. Understanding and complying with these conditions is indispensable for accurate GST compliance and optimizing tax costs. The key compliance rules are non-negotiable & businesses must meet these conditions or lose the credit.
Author, designated as All India Master Trainer in GST, works as State Taxes officer in Srinagar.

The Latest: Trump will commemorate 25 years since 9/11 attacks at the Pentagon
President Donald Trump is set to observe Friday’s 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks by attending a ceremony at the Pentagon
President Donald Trump is set to observe Friday’s 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks by attending a ceremony at the Pentagon. It’s the second year in a row for Trump to mark the day at the Pentagon.
The president is originally from New York and last attended the ground zero ceremony there in 2024.
Friday’s milestone anniversary will bring memorial rituals — wreath-laying, flag-flying, moments of silence, vigils and readings of victims’ names — and volunteer projects in tribute to a day that about half of U.S. adults remember as the most historic event of their lifetime, according to a new poll.
Here's the latest:
Security is tight at the ceremony in New York
Police officers stationed around the perimeter of the event are checking tickets and credentials to ensure only invited guests, such as victim relatives, survivors and first responders, and others connected to the event are allowed through. That’s before a full security screening at the entrance to the site, which is surrounded by the type of steel fencing now familiar at high-profile events.
Along with that, the streets are filled with the apparatus of police and emergency response — NYPD vehicles lining the western perimeter, heavily armed and armored counterterrorism officers patrolling the nearby subway stations, and flashing police lights abound.
As the memorial goes on, so does life around ground zero
New Yorkers going about their days mixed with 9/11 family members, firefighters and other first responders on the streets and sidewalks of lower Manhattan.
People jogged by in brightly colored running attire. Others hoisted American flags. People clasped iced coffees and bagged pastries. A woman outside a church sold buttons commemorating the occasion. A man thanked the two police officers guarding the perimeter for their service.
US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick wipes away tears at the 9/11 memorial
He was the CEO of the investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald when the attack on the World Trade Center killed 658 of its 960 employees.
He survived because he was taking his son to school when the attack happened. His brother, Gary Lutnick, was among those who died.
At the memorial Friday, Lutnick wiped away a tear, but also smiled as he looked fondly at the names of Cantor Fitzgerald employees inscribed on the parapets that ring the footprints of the fallen towers.
Former presidents attend 9/11 ceremony in New York
Four former presidents are in Manhattan for the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks at the city’s ceremony at ground zero.
Former presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, George W. Bush and Joe Biden could been seen mingling with attendees at the National Sept. 11 Memorial in Lower Manhattan on Friday morning.
Vice President JD Vance is also attending the ceremony in New York, while President Donald Trump will attend an observance at the Pentagon.
American flag unfurled at the Pentagon
In a downpour at daybreak, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and top military officials stood outside and watched as the giant American flag was unfurled on the building struck by a hijacked plane a quarter century ago.
US marks 25 years since the Sept. 11 attacks
Americans are commemorating the 25th anniversary of 9/11, remembering the shock, the dead and the sweeping consequences of the al-Qaida attacks on symbols of U.S. might and prosperity.
Friday’s milestone anniversary will bring memorial rituals — wreath-laying, flag-flying, moments of silence, vigils and readings of victims’ names — and volunteer projects in tribute to a day that about half of U.S. adults remember as the most historic event of their lifetime, according to a new poll.
For others it’s an occasion for private reflection — or, in many schools, education — about the attack that unfolded in a single morning but left nearly 3,000 dead and a decades-long trail of aftermath, from personal grief to far-flung wars.
Planned remembrances extend far beyond the attack sites, from beams of light projecting from New Hampshire’s Mount Washington to a stair climb at Mississippi State University’s football stadium to a ceremony at Honolulu’s 9/11 memorial.
