For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

In Summary
- New Apple CEO, John Ternus, announced a range of products at the Surprise and Shine event.
- While most of the focus was on the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, there was much more to the event than just devices and a CEO debut.
- We bring you eight takeaways that were buried in the buzz around the new devices, which might have escaped your attention.
It might not have surprised too many people – the leaks messed that up – but Apple did a fair bit of shining at its recent Surprise and Shine event. The event, which also marked John Ternus’ debut as Apple CEO at a launch, went on expected lines, with Apple revealing new AirPods, Apple Watches, new iPhone Pros and, of course, the iPhone Duo, which has grabbed the most attention. There was, however, much more to the event than just the launches. Here are our eight biggest takeaways from the day on which the world saw Apple’s new foldable and the CEO on stage:
Table of Contents
New Era? Presentation-wise, Apple is still Cook-ing (Pun intended)
Yes, it was John Ternus who held the reins at Surprise and Shine. But in terms of presentation style, the template that was followed was still from the menu of the preceding chef, Tim Cook. We had multiple speakers, elaborate backdrops, and a similar race through a number of products, leaving the most time for the star of the show (it was the Air last time around, the Duo this time). Yes, in terms of presentation style, Apple remains well ahead of the competition, although we miss the wit and humor of the past; this launch was more from the Cook manual than the Ternus one.
No surprises (Sigh)…
It’s been a while since Apple surprised the Dickens out of us at a launch, but in recent years, the brand’s product announcements have often been leaked out well in advance. And that was pretty much true this time around. From the iPhone Duo to the shades of Burgundy to the fact that there would be no suffix-less iPhone at the event, the leak community got a lot of things right, which, as we have said in the past, takes some of the mystique and surprise out of the event. Mind you, Apple did pull one rabbit out of its hat.
…except for the AirPods 5
There were no suffix-less iPhones at Surprise and Shine, but there sure were suffix-less AirPods. And while most of the noise was about Apple’s first foldable, the AirPods 5 might have emerged as the silent, value-for-money heroes of the show. While most people had been expecting new AirPods Pro with perhaps a camera built into them, Apple brought in a new version of the classic AirPods, complete with better ANC and battery life, even while retaining the “open” fit and, surprise, surprise, the same price tag as its predecessors. Not too many noticed…until the price of the Duo was announced, and suddenly a device with no price increase became the belle of the tech ball.
Hooray, we will now have TWO iPhone launches every year
Surprise and Shine marked the beginning of a new iPhone era, in which Apple will release its iPhones in two tranches over a twelve-month period. While Apple has released iPhones at two different times of the year in the past, the second launch has generally been a relatively low-profile and soft one (of the SE and ‘e’ mainly). That is set to change now. Even if Apple does a soft launch for the iPhone 18, the iPhone Air 2 and the iPhone 18e, rather than a full-fledged event, the fact is that close to half of the iPhone portfolio will be launched in the second half of the year, and the remainder in the first half of the next year. The iPhone schedules just got tweaked.
Apple is getting REALLY serious about AI (no, really, this time)
Two years ago, Apple launched the iPhone 16 series, saying it had been designed from the ground up for Apple’s avatar of AI, Apple Intelligence. However, AI is one area where the Cupertino brand has been found trailing the competition. So it was not surprising that the brand was clearly out to write a new chapter at Surprise and Shine. Every device it announced – iPhones, Apple Watches, AirPods – had a strong element of AI, which different presenters stressed would work wonderfully well, even while preserving the users’ security. Well, we have heard that a few times in the past, but never in such a comprehensive manner. Is Apple finally going to crack the AI puzzle? Based on what we saw, it would be no Surprise if it went on to Shine in that department in the coming months.
Whoop, Whoop, the Apple Watch is now a full-fledged fitness and health device, and is targeting Whoop
It started out trying to be a computer on your wrist, complete with apps, notifications and alerts, but the Apple Watch has of late graduated (or been demoted, depending on your perspective) to being mainly a health and fitness tracking device. And Surprise and Shine saw this trend continuing, with most of the talk about the Apple Watch 4 Ultra and Apple Watch Series 12 revolving around better sensors and measurement. The highlighting of features like Readiness Scores and Health Age seems to indicate that the Cupertino brand now has the screenless Whoop, which popularised these features, in its sights.
The narrative is unmatched, but is now very hardware-driven!
Processors, camera apertures, health sensors, ANC, battery life…these formed the major part of the narrative around Surprise and Shine, showing how Apple’s has shifted from storytelling to specs at its launches in recent times. This might be fine for some, but we do miss the time when an announcer would walk us through nuances of design and amazing (or they called amazing, and often, unbelievable) features on devices.
Yes, Apple remains the lord, master, and commander of product launches, but we prefer tales to tech, and a live presenter on stage to edited videos, no matter how sleekly edited. The fact that the Duo section stood out from the others because of its stress on design and UI only reinforces our belief that Apple might perhaps reconsider going back to its storytelling roots, and leave the specs on the spec sheet, rather than on the speech notes. Everyone else talks specs anyway.
Cosmic orange is out of the Apple cosmos… and Black is back!
This was so typically Apple. After making orange the color of the last twelve months, courtesy of the Cosmic Orange variant of the iPhone 17 Pro series, and making a number of brands come out with orange phones and other devices (JBL even had a pair of headphones in orange), the Cupertino giant pushed the shade out of its color palette. It also brought back the one color that everyone had missed in the Pro series – Black. Henry “Any Color As Long As It Is Black” Ford and AC/DC would approve of the return of the color, and so do we. We are not shedding any tears for orange, although we suspect those orange Pros are going to have great antique value some day.
And one more thing…
Craig Federighi’s hair looks as awesome as ever!

Jackie Collins Wrote Her Own Revolution
Once, when I was 15 years old and as awkward and skinny-legged as a baby giraffe, I was idling in a department store in central London when I saw the novelist Jackie Collins standing at the register.
Can you imagine the aura emanating from her, like Hermès-scented magnetic waves? She was wearing animal print and a tailored jacket and had the kind of steely composure I’ve never managed to pull off in adulthood without straining something. Faced with one of my true idols, all I could do was gawk.
I learned about sex when I was 8, but it wasn’t until several years later, when my best friend yanked me upstairs to show me a particularly juicy paragraph from her mother’s neon-pink copy of Hollywood Kids, that I learned about pleasure. Jackie—with apologies, I will call her Jackie throughout, because “Collins” feels just too formal for a woman who impressed upon me the existence of the clitoris—once told The New York Times that she published her first novel “in 1968, when no one was writing about sex but Philip Roth.” Which wasn’t strictly true, but at a moment when second-wave feminism and sexual liberation were uneasy bedfellows, Jackie simply wrote her own revolution. The World Is Full of Married Men, her debut, was a caustic social satire in which a wronged wife emerges triumphant; The Stud, out the following year, was a flashy potboiler about a trophy wife and nightclub owner with a rapacious sexual appetite who treats men like toys and exalts in her social and financial clout.
Jackie wrote 32 books in total, sold more than half a billion copies, and gained an indelible reputation as an airport novelist, the kind of writer whose books are equally devoured and disdained. But oh, what they did for me! In retrospect, I gained a slightly deluded understanding of what adulthood actually entailed. Jackie was a devoted Mickey Spillane fan, and her books tend to be stuffed with gangsters, serial killers, pornographers, and even freelance journalists who get paid in advance. But as an anatomist of Hollywood gender dynamics, no writer was sharper or more aspirational. Jackie’s heroines, as she wrote in an introduction to The World Is Full of Divorced Women (1975), “demand equality—sexual and otherwise.” She wrote about creative, ferocious women striving for power and getting it. Lucky Santangelo, a recurring character and a kind of alter ego, starts out as the neglected daughter of a crime boss and works her way up to become the head of a movie studio in 1990’s Lady Boss.
Her characters carry on being fascinating and sexually active well past the age when other writers would have them tucked in bed with a crocheted blanket and a crossword puzzle. “In Jackie’s world, women’s real lives begin after forty,” the writer Helen Ellis observed of Hollywood Wives, the book that Jackie published at the age of 45, and that established her as a celebrity in her own right.
Even if you hate women (many people do), hate explicit sex scenes, hate the kind of pulpy storytelling that has you still reading in a cold bath at midnight, you cannot help but admit that Jackie captured the entertainment industry like no one else. She seemed equally drawn to the business of movie production—the seedy dealmaking and kickbacks—as well as the rampant abuses of power embedded in the Hollywood system, both of which she exposed without hesitation. Writing in the heady 1980s, when movies were becoming brasher, dumber, and unrepentantly commercial, she scrutinized a creative industry at a notable low point, less in thrall to art than to profit.
Although her novels made her a star, Jackie never considered herself fully part of Hollywood. Like a Reagan-era Margaret Mead, she took an anthropological approach. “I don’t live the Hollywood lifestyle,” she told Vanity Fair in 1995. “I move in it. I’m an observer.” At parties, she would stalk the room listening for interesting tidbits, taking copious mental notes that she’d jot down later. Describing an A-list event in Hollywood Wives, Jackie drops in fragments of what one character calls “Hollywood conversation,” dialogue that evokes a world where money and desire meld: “ ‘He pays me, I think it turns him on,’ said the redhead in the mink-trimmed cape.” So accurate was her portrayal that when Hollywood Wives was published, Jackie noted, “The ladies of Hollywood had their drivers and housekeepers lining up at the bookstores to get an early copy,” both furious that their gilded sanctum had been breached and desperate to pinpoint which character was based on which real person.
Hollywood, as a geographical term at least, is misleading: Jackie’s characters mostly work and play in Beverly Hills, a city of 30,000 or so extremely wealthy residents enclosed by Los Angeles. Formerly a lima-bean farm, then a failed oil field, Beverly Hills was developed into lots for housing around the same time that the movie industry headed west, in the early 20th century. When the silent-film stars Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks moved into a spectacular former hunting lodge on Summit Drive in 1920—the press immediately named it “Pickfair”—they helped establish Beverly Hills as a nexus of celebrity glamour and industry cachet. Jackie genuinely loved the neighborhood for its clean white lines and endless sky, but she was also drawn to everything it contained beneath the surface: its roiling currents of fame, power, and degradation.
Early this summer, I traveled from London, where Jackie was born, to the enclave where she made her name. As a child of the ’80s, I was nostalgic for the maximalist era of shoulder pads, Giorgio perfume, and animal print. (Jackie loved big cats for their beauty and power, was convinced she’d been a panther in a previous life, and decorated her house and herself in leopard spots.) But as a cultural critic, I also wanted to revisit the era of moviemaking that Jackie had described in her novels. The ’80s saw a wave of corporate consolidation; venerable studios were gobbled up by behemoths from other industries. (Columbia Pictures was briefly a division of Coca-Cola.) This led to sillier, more crowd-pleasing movies. Even so, Hollywood was at the apex of its power, the global influence of filmmaking more potent than ever. Today, the center of cultural power and attention is shifting away from Los Angeles. Traditional storytelling has lost ground to what the consulting firm McKinsey calls “user-generated content”—TikTok and YouTube videos in which people talk enthusiastically about peptides and skinny-maxxing and the cruel feminization of the male life force.
As a teenager, I had learned from Jackie’s books to expect that adulthood for women would be a series of hard-won triumphs that lead toward power. (She also suggested that midlife would involve a lot of stalking around restaurants while wearing crepe Halston jumpsuits and enough gold jewelry to sink a yacht, but I have long since made peace with neutral basics.) I am 43, roughly the age when Jackie’s heroines enter their prime, and when she herself did. I am very tired, having spent the past 14 months working, raising two 5-year-olds, promoting a book, and falling into existential mires of despair over the degenerating state of world affairs. A small, quiet part of my brain wondered whether tracing Jackie’s literary footsteps might reinvigorate my sense of what’s possible. Or at least demonstrate that her dreams for women—that they can have creative fulfillment, families, and happiness, as she did—might be somewhat more realistic now than they were 40 years ago.
Hollywood Wives was published in 1983, a good two decades before reality television turned exposing the lives of the wealthy, married, and highly maintained into a Bravo gold mine. We’re accustomed to such excess now, but back then, Jackie’s gossipy revelations—$50 panties, discreet plastic surgeons in Palm Springs, society grandes dames who used to be French call girls—seemed otherworldly.
The primary antiheroine in the book is the delightfully unlikable Elaine Conti (imagine a hornier, more desperate Becky Sharp), the 39-year-old wife of a movie star, Ross, whose last film bombed at the box office. There’s also a former gigolo on the brink of movie stardom, a buxom man-eater who wants to be taken seriously as an actress, and a serial killer who calls himself the “Keeper of the Order.” But for me at least, the book stands out for its portrayal of early-’80s Beverly Hills as a high-society Thunderdome, where everyone is scratching and clawing for status. In addition to the titular wives, who are drawn with both humanity and mild disdain, Jackie offers up a number of female characters operating in what she describes as the “Big Boys’ Club” of the movie industry: Sadie LaSalle, one of the most powerful and fearsome agents in town, and Montana Gray, a writer trying to save her screenplay from the clutches of a ruthless producer.
This is a world where power-lunching demands tactical precision. Elaine’s mission throughout the book is to restore Ross’s A-list status, with buzzy parties the couple can’t afford and a standing Friday lunch reservation at Ma Maison, where “anybody who was anybody and in town invariably showed up.” Ma Maison closed in 1985, and so the first place I went to test out the current state of power-dining was the Polo Lounge, a clubby salon situated toward the back of the spectacularly retro Beverly Hills Hotel. In Hollywood Husbands, Jackie’s 1986 follow-up, the handsome and promiscuous talk-show host Jack Python regularly meets his best friends for breakfast there, where they occupy Table One, “a cosy leather booth directly facing the entrance.” Table placement, Jackie emphasizes, is everything—“The back of this restaurant is Siberia,” one model tells another late in the book. “Land of the underachievers. Don’t even glance in that direction.”
I was not placed at Table One. I was seated just outside what seemed to be the main dining room, next to an elderly couple and a 12-year-old wearing a World Cup hoodie having pancakes by himself. Through the doorway, I could see men in button-downs and golf shirts conversing chummily; I started to feel slightly psychotic glimmers of envy and shame at being shut out from whatever they were brokering. The server’s eyes expressed gentle but unmistakable pity. A handsome Englishman was seated at a nearby table but immediately sensed defeat and asked to be moved to the terrace, where the sun shines regardless of a diner’s Variety profile, stock portfolio, or follower count.
Failure is galvanizing, I tried to remember from Jackie’s books, as long as you don’t let it break you. For much of her early life, Jackie wasn’t known for her writing or her feline fixation. (A plaque engraved with a panther marks her place in the celebrity crypt at Westwood Village Memorial Park Cemetery, where she was interred after her death, in 2015; the image is accompanied by the words SHE GAVE A GREAT DEAL OF PEOPLE A GREAT DEAL OF PLEASURE.) She came of age as the taller, ungainly younger sister of Joan, an almond-eyed, preternaturally composed actress who made her Hollywood debut starring alongside Bette Davis in 1955’s The Virgin Queen. Joan and Jackie had grown up together in a basement apartment in dingy postwar London, the daughters of a dance teacher and a talent agent whose parties, Jackie once said, were where she first became aware of how men talk about women when they think no one’s listening. “I get an awful inferiority complex when I’m with Joan,” the teenage Jackie wrote in her diary. In a photo of the pair together from 1955, Joan stands front and center, insouciant in a fur coat, while Jackie looks at the camera semi-apologetically from behind her.
Jackie was, however, entrepreneurial; by the age of 13, inspired by Harold Robbins and Henry Miller, she had a sideline writing sex scenes longhand and charging her classmates to read them. When Joan’s career took her to Hollywood, Jackie followed, moving with her sister to an apartment in the Chateau Marmont hotel, and having a brief fling—at 15—with the 29-year-old Marlon Brando. (He was “only my height, and kind of fat,” she noted in her journal, and also recorded that he called her “sincere, sweet, and luscious.”) But Jackie couldn’t get a work permit and so reluctantly returned to England, where she appeared in a handful of schlocky B movies before marrying the businessman Wallace Austin at 22. Four years later, Austin’s drug addiction had led the couple to divorce, and he died of an overdose shortly after.
It was Jackie’s second husband, the producer and nightclub owner Oscar Lerman, who encouraged her to pursue writing, and to draw inspiration from the vivid social scenes the couple mixed in. (At one of her husband’s clubs, she told The Hollywood Reporter, Lerman had to put a guard outside the men’s room because teenage girls kept following movie stars in to offer them sexual favors.) At 31, she published The World Is Full of Married Men, which was an immediate best seller in the United Kingdom and promptly banned in Australia for its inventive array of four-letter words; the next year, the romance novelist Barbara Cartland lambasted her new novel, The Stud, as “awful, terrible, it’s evil really.”
Jackie and Lerman relocated to Los Angeles in 1980, and if you walk down the Beverly Hills Hotel’s unabashedly red-carpeted stairs and under a gloriously cinematic green-and-white striped awning, then stroll to the bottom of the hill, and wander for about 10 minutes beneath towering palm trees, you will arrive at the house that Jackie’s “awful, terrible” books built. Only a modest-seeming driveway was visible from the street. The place is now available for rent (for the trivial sum of $175,000 a month), and when I say that I begged the real-estate agent to let me view it, please know that I really and truly groveled. I spent months emailing a man who assured me that he was entreating the owners (real-estate developers who’d bought it after her death, gutted it, remodeled all the interiors) on my behalf—but to no avail. So instead I examined the signs affixed to palm trees warning me that I was on camera, to ensure the security of the neighborhood’s current residents, who—unlike the movie stars and moguls of Jackie’s day—are apparently financiers, minor Middle Eastern royals, and crypto magnates. (The current owner of the Pickfair mansion, I later learned, is the technology corporation Unicom Global, which uses it for conferences and events.)
But based on the listing, archival photographs, and the author photo on Jackie’s many hardcovers, I can tell you that it’s a 22,000-square-foot museum of a mansion, a defiant middle finger to the critics who belittled her for writing “bonkbusters,” and a visual testament to her success. The interiors are now predominantly beige, but in Jackie’s day, the pillows were all animal print. She designed the house around a huge rectangular swimming pool after seeing David Hockney’s A Bigger Splash in London. On her book jackets, she stands, radiant and shoulder-padded, next to the cool blue water and her imposing white box of a home. But she also took great pride in being a hands-on mother, cooking at home for her three daughters, doing school drop-offs in her silver Mustang, and keeping her children away from the sleazy Hollywood scenes she chronicled.
Right as Jackie’s writing started appearing on the best-seller list, Joan’s acting career was floundering—in 1977, she appeared in the dismal sci-fi horror Empire of the Ants, playing a land developer set on by giant irradiated insects. It was Jackie who revived her sister’s reputation, after Joan was cast as the lead in the movie adaptation of The Stud. (A hit in Britain, the movie paved the way for Joan to get her most indelible American role, as Alexis Colby in Dynasty.) The charged sense of competition between the pair continued apace; in a 1988 Vanity Fair profile of both sisters, Dominick Dunne noted that a publicist had instructed him to dedicate equal copy to each woman, while also citing the rumors that Silver Anderson, the prickly 47-year-old TV star in Hollywood Husbands, was based on Joan.
Mindful of the security cameras, I walked quickly past Jackie’s house to a restaurant in downtown Beverly Hills called Bacari, where I took out my notebook and tried my hand at Jackie-style anthropology. At the table next to me, a talent agent was trying to lure another agent away from a major conglomerate, where she was unhappy. “They keep trying to buy us off with ice-cream socials,” she said to him plaintively. “Everyone is on a diet!” The conversation turned to her stable of clients, who all seemed to be social-media stars. She spoke proudly about one woman she represented who, under her mentorship, went from having 700,000 followers to more than 1 million. “That’s the kind of nurturing I bring to my job,” she said. The man asked her if she might be able to double her client list in the first three months; to help her in the effort, he could offer her a “digital assistant—no person.” He paid the bill. “Let’s get those wheels turning,” he said, ushering her out, and I wondered what Jackie would make of this version of Hollywood, with its brand-activation opportunities and AI-drafted emails, where celebrity is its own art form and product is paramount.
In Jackie’s Hollywood novels, Rodeo Drive—my next stop—is where the women of Beverly Hills go to arm themselves for the soft warfare of self-presentation. When every outfit, every hairdo, is minutely studied for signs of decline, keeping up appearances is essential. In Hollywood Husbands, Poppy Solomon, the secretary turned fourth wife of a studio head, gets ready for parties in much the same way General Patton commanded the Third Army: with ostentatious and pleasurable aggression. (“She wore a turquoise frilled, strapless dress, and many real diamonds. Her new tits protruded nicely.”)
The day I was there, the picture-perfect palms gently fluttering down Rodeo bore signs for an upcoming car show, which seemed unnecessary given that every day brings a parade of tricked-out vehicles: I watched a procession of Porsches, G-Wagons, two separate Maybachs with hydraulic suspension systems that had them bouncing up and down like sugared-up toddlers. No one was actually shopping, despite the lavish window displays. Instead, everyone was posing for pictures, wearing outfits they’d put together for this exact purpose and drafting husbands and friends to play photographer. A slender blond woman clutching a tan Birkin pouted while reclining against a lamppost outside Stefano Ricci. Someone whispered that she was a Russian influencer with a superstar-athlete partner, which seemed perfectly plausible, but outside the subset of her followers, how would the rest of us know?
I was accompanied by a photographer, Dina, who approached the influencer to take her picture, but the woman scuttled away like a cartoon mouse. Something odd was happening, we quickly realized: Everyone was out posing in public, but no one wanted to cede control of how they might be perceived. When Dina tried to take photos of the Beverly Hills Hotel from a public sidewalk, a voice instantly came over a loudspeaker warning her to stop.
In a weak attempt to consider some of the box-office excess of 1980s Hollywood (Footloose, Top Gun, Beverly Hills Cop), I booked us a Paramount Pictures studio tour, but when I asked a publicist about Dina bringing her camera, I was told approval would be required, a studio representative would accompany us, and anything said on the tour could not be quoted. (All that’s worth saying about what followed is that while being driven around the lot where Citizen Kane, Breakfast at Tiffany’s, and Chinatown were shot, the most enthralling thing we saw was the plasticky interior set from the CBS reboot of Matlock.)
Jackie would find Hollywood’s new power dynamics perplexing: Many of her female characters are writers and reporters on the movie-celebrity beat, who see their job as pushing past the sanitized narratives that publicists try to present. But as media jobs have dwindled, influencers have stepped in to fill a void. Why would you trust a possibly unfriendly reporter with access to an actor or a director or a TV set when you can invite a photogenic social-media star to a premiere and be assured that they’ll rave about whatever they see to their hundreds of thousands of followers? In Hollywood Husbands, Silver, the soap star possibly based on Joan, is interviewed by an English journalist, “a middle-aged woman with brittle looks and dyed yellow hair” who sucks up to her subjects as energetically in person as she tears them apart in print. “So what?” Silver thinks. “Someone had once said As long as they spell your name right.” The internet has long since retooled this bargain.
And what are celebrities now, anyway? During my four days in Beverly Hills, which Jackie portrays as a superstar playground—Clint Eastwood, Jack Lemmon, Richard Gere, and Tom Selleck all feature in one lunch scene at Ma Maison—I saw not a single recognizably famous person. A dozen or so women looked similar enough to Kim Kardashian to stop me short; they were clearly modeled after her, but the image fell apart on second glance. One night I went to dinner at Funke, a purported newish hot spot for stars (Gwyneth Paltrow is a fan) where the chef used to have his own show on the disastrous short-form streaming platform Quibi. No sightings.
My L.A.-based friends advised heading east, to Los Feliz and Silver Lake, or west, to Venice and Santa Monica. Beverly Hills today is a bastion of the über-wealthy—Jeff Bezos owns the estate built by Jack Warner of Warner Bros.—and a drop-by for people who come to pose for Instagram. Like SoHo in New York and Notting Hill in London, the place feels like a simulacrum of a film set, where everyone is perpetually performing for unseen audiences and nothing feels quite real.
In her books, Jackie is unsentimental about creative work. Her characters tend to hustle for money and power, not self-indulgent awards or critical acclaim. When good movies get made, it’s largely by accident, because someone took their eye off the ball. But one character in Hollywood Wives seems to genuinely care about the integrity of the work she makes: Montana Gray, the tall, raven-haired, strikingly offbeat writer who—coincidentally—has a biography that seems a lot like Jackie’s own. By 15, Montana is a worldly soul who’s traveled the globe, learned French and Italian, and had two affairs. After spending a few years in bohemian circles, she meets the much older film director Neil Gray in Paris and falls in love with him. She helps him get sober and working again; he encourages her to write. At the start of the novel, her gritty screenplay, Street People, is the talk of Hollywood, with actors and agents fighting for copies.
And, because Montana is the wife of a major director, no one can accept that she actually wrote it. “Good-looking women had roles in life and they were supposed to stick to them,” Jackie writes. “They could be movie stars, models, housewives, hookers, but God forbid they should skirt onto what was strictly regarded as Big Boys’ Territory. Writing a major movie for a major director was Big Boys’ Territory. And in their own petty little way everyone wanted to let her know that.” When Neil pushes to cast the craggy movie star George Lancaster in a leading role in the film, Montana acquiesces reluctantly—he can’t act—only for George to assume that she’s a secretary the very first time they meet. “I’m Montana Gray,” she tells him. “I wrote Street People.” “You did?” he replies. “My, my, things sure are changing around here. I could still use that coffee, little lady.”
You might wonder whether things are actually different for women in Hollywood today. The statistics are still dismal: 8.1 percent of the 100 highest-grossing movies in 2025 were directed by women, a seven-year low, and the percentage of movies with any major female characters at all fell from 39 percent the previous year to 36 percent. But TV is faring better: More than a third of all streaming shows now have at least one female creator. One of those women is Lisa Joy, formerly a writer and co-creator of HBO’s adaptation of Westworld, a futuristic sci-fi show with a notably feminist question at its core: What might men do to women if those women didn’t seem fully human and the men thought they could get away with it? In 2019, Joy and her husband, the screenwriter and producer Jonathan Nolan, signed a reported $150 million deal to create shows for Amazon, including the acclaimed video-game adaptation Fallout and an upcoming TV version of Rebecca Yarros’s blockbuster romantasy series, Fourth Wing.
Jackie would have liked the all-caps plaque on Joy’s desk—I’M CEO, BITCH—that greeted me in the Hollywood offices of her production company, a glass-walled room facing the Capitol Records building. Like Montana, Joy is impossibly glamorous and all too familiar with having people presume that her accomplishments are secretly a man’s. So much of Westworld, she told me, came from her experiences being the lone woman in what felt like male playgrounds. But, like Jackie, she’s convinced that writing a different world gets us one step closer to manifesting it.
Post-MeToo, Joy said, she’s noticed some really positive changes, such as a junior writer she knows speaking out against a serial harasser whom no one had ever dared confront before, and who was subsequently fired. But reminders abound of all the ways in which things have stayed the same. “There are so many yacht trips I’ve heard about for male directors and writers,” she said. “I don’t know why they all get yachts, but there doesn’t ever seem to be a woman invited. But fuck the yachts, you know? They make you seasick. They’re no fun. Let’s make the reality we want.” I left Joy’s office feeling energized by her work, by her enthusiasm, by her determination. And then, as I was crossing Hollywood Boulevard, the universe gave me a palpable reality check: a 50-foot billboard advertising Louis C.K.’s upcoming comedy special for Netflix.
On my last morning in L.A., I went downstairs to get breakfast in my hotel, and ended up sitting near two men who were discussing potential merchandising deals for one of their clients. “Makeup is really splintered; it’s a challenging category for sure,” one said. “But fragrance is booming. What about hair?” The client has a personal connection to hair, the other said excitedly. (Who among us? I thought.) The first man proceeded to expound on how hair brands are working quickly to address the issues—thinning, shedding—that can come from GLP‑1 use. The other circled back to his client, whom he talked about with such reverence that I leaned closer, convinced she was a huge household name. “Her pull on her community is so strong,” he said. “What feeds her passion is serving her community and improving people’s lives. She’s built for this.” Only by the end of the conversation, and after much furtive Googling on my part, did it become clear whom they were talking about: a Goth-makeup influencer on TikTok who has more than 6 million followers.
You could argue that the content-creator model has democratized entertainment and broken down conventional gatekeeping, enabling anyone with a ring light, a front-facing camera, and a compelling personality to find their following. I don’t disagree. But it’s also restored youth and overconfidence as the preeminent characteristics for women on camera. Whereas what I’ve always loved about Jackie’s books is how they enshrine success and power as being hard-won and worth the hustle—and the wait. Midlife is when things get interesting for her characters, because they know the stakes they’re playing for, and they’ve accrued enough wisdom and battle scars to rival and even occasionally best the Big Boys.
But the waning public interest in traditional storytelling (because you’re reading this, I’ll diplomatically ignore the even gloomier fate of the written word) has other consequences too. If you’re someone who doesn’t just love movies and TV shows but has felt genuinely changed by some of them, it’s hard not to mourn what we lose when our mass culture has all the bells and whistles of entertainment—hair, makeup, stars, product placement—but none of the curiosity about human predicaments underpinning it. Jackie’s work was berated during her lifetime by critics (“It starts off as nothing and ends as nothing” — Clive James) and high-school English teachers like mine (“trash”), but it graphically exposed a Hollywood full of sexual harassment and gender inequity. Not least, it imagined alternative paths for women to pursue.
Now her books are mostly out of fashion; when I stopped by the Barnes & Noble inside the Grove, where Jackie liked to shop before going to the movies, the store had not a single copy of any of her novels. I was feeling despondent when I went for a last outing, to Mariposa: one of Jackie’s favorite restaurants, where she met for lunch each week with her closest friends, an elegant dining room tucked into the basement of the Neiman Marcus Beverly Hills. I had learned in emailing beforehand that Jackie was still a much-loved figure there. I was met by the store’s manager of brand experience, Mary Kate Steinmiller, who looks exactly like the actress Malin Akerman and used to be a fashion editor at Teen Vogue. She took me downstairs to Jackie’s favorite blue booth.
For days, I’d been traipsing through Beverly Hills trying to find a little spiritual proximity to Jackie, and here it was, on the lower floor, by the beauty counters. Groups of women wearing Christian Dior tennis whites and Pucci wrap dresses chatted ebulliently over cocktails (it was 12:15 p.m.). Every table featured floral arrangements nicer than the ones at my wedding. Over in a corner, an older couple wearing acid-green designer outfits sat absorbed in each other. A table of women told me that Mariposa was their country club. They had known and liked Jackie, but quickly pushed back against the lingering stereotype of the Hollywood Wife. One was a high-powered divorce attorney. Another was a sports photographer. The restaurant was gorgeous (and don’t sleep on the lobster salad), but it was also clear what it meant to these women: community, affirmation, a clubby dining room of their own. Watching them, I felt as though what Jackie’s novels had promised might actually be true: If you can muster enough ambition and persistence to keep pushing through, the payoff could well be worth the wait.
Travel Notes
Spago
Ma Maison, immortalized in Hollywood Wives, is long gone, but in 1982 its star chef, a telegenic Austrian named Wolfgang Puck, left to open Spago on the Sunset Strip, redefining L.A. dining in the process. The original location closed decades ago, but Spago Beverly Hills lives on, with its twinkly lit courtyard, casual-luxe menu (Jackie loved the smoked-salmon pizza and wrote it into multiple books), and luxe-luxe prices. If you never get to go to the Academy Awards’ Governors Ball, which Puck has catered for more than three decades, this is at least a chance to eat stardust by association.
Bob’s Coffee and Doughnuts
Doughnuts and Hollywood physiques go together like deep-dish and Ozempic. Don’t let that keep you away from Bob’s, a 56-year-old stand inside the historic Los Angeles Farmers Market, where writers have come to eat and procrastinate since the 1930s. According to legend, Robert Altman used to have breakfast here, scribbling away under the slatted awnings. And the doughnuts really are great—pillowy and sugar-sprinkled. Fun fact: A branded Farmers Market tote bag costs $2, compared with $50 for one at the nearby Erewhon.
Hollywood Books
Is this tiny spot on Melrose a bookstore in the conventional sense? Not really, at least not if you’re looking for a popular novel or Belle Burden’s monster-hit memoir, Strangers. At Hollywood Books, the shelves are stacked with secondhand art volumes and reissued classics. Despite—because of?—its unfussed approach to business, the store has become extremely chic among the literary girlies of Los Angeles; at one point it hosted an event for the supermodel Kaia Gerber’s book club, Library Science. I left with a copy of Picture, Lillian Ross’s 1952 analysis of the clash between art and corporate interests in moviemaking, just to remember that things were ever thus.
Wrapstar
I can’t endorse the wraps or salads here, because I had only a sparkling water. But for eavesdropping like Jackie, you can’t beat the location—across the street from William Morris Endeavor’s boxy Beverly Hills headquarters, and next door to Cipriani. Sit, snoop, rubberneck. (Yes, wraps are passé, but power agents sometimes need sad-desk lunches that you can eat with one hand while scrolling through social media, just like the rest of us.)
Bar Funke
Funke regrettably did not provide any celebrity sightings, but it did furnish a gorgeous twist on a margarita, made with Sicilian-blood-orange bitters and prickly pear. The rooftop, after you enter through a jasmine-strewn trellis, looks out over the palms and offices of Beverly Hills, but from my spot at the bar, all I wanted to stare at were the pink quartzite counters and Chef Evan Funke’s elaborate collection of Amaro aperitifs. Jackie’s literary alter ego, the glamorous and hot-blooded Italian businesswoman Lucky Santangelo, would have appreciated both.
Mariposa
Here’s to the ladies who lunch, and to playing one in this delightful department-store-basement restaurant, with its velvety blue booths and popovers accompanied by strawberry butter. The waitstaff are lovely, the diners’ outfits are extraordinary, and the food—lobster salad, crab cakes, tuna tartare—is opulent and calorie-conscious, and so good you’ll be wondering why the guests aren’t eating more of it. If I ever die and get to (at least) purgatory, I hope it’s a little like Mariposa.

Unlike posts featuring memes from the film KGF or the web series Mirzapur, the Punjab BJP’s post did not use fictional characters to make a point. Instead, it used AI to create a scene depicting a physical attack on a state’s elected Chief Minister, creating a fabricated image of violence directed at a real, identifiable individual. Following widespread criticism, the Punjab BJP deleted the post.
The Origins Of ‘Dimagi Naxal’
The term ‘Dimagi Naxal’ recently entered India’s political vocabulary and is now becoming a weapon wielded by BJP and its affliates to attack dissenters and opposition on social media.
The term originated during Modi’s Independence Day speech at Red Fort, wherein he declared that while the country had eliminated the armed Naxals hiding in the forests, ‘Dimagi Naxals’ remained active within society. He claimed that individuals with a Maoist mindset had entrenched themselves in the corridors of power and influenced policies while serving as advisors on government committees, he emphasised the need to identify and isolate them.
The Prime Minister did not directly mention any specific individual or organisation. However, critics believe that, much like terms such as ‘Urban Naxal,’ ‘Tukde-Tukde Gang,’ and ‘Andolanjeevi’, the term ‘Dimagi Naxal’ is another such label to attack dissenters.

The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability in Somalia.
Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August: one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey.
Over a seven-year period from 2005 there were more than 1,000 attacks on vessels in the waters off Somalia, which has Africa’s longest coastline. Thousands of crew members were taken hostage, netting $400m (£296m) in ransom payments for the piracy network’s financiers, the low-level “foot-soldier” pirates and the communities who provided them with goods and services. The attacks only petered out after a multinational anti-piracy force was deployed.
The hijacking of the Lutuf was the most high-profile of the recent incidents. Turkey has been expanding its influence in Somalia after an agreement signed in 2024 to build up its navy, and the Lutuf’s release two weeks after its capture involved a joint Turkish-Somali operation that resulted in the destruction of four pirate vessels.
However, local officials including Mohamed Mubarak, the head of the Puntland security coordination office, have said that a $2.5m (£1.85m) ransom was also paid, prompting warnings that such payments risked encouraging similar incidents.
In a comment for the Center for Maritime Security in July, Matthew Reisener, the thinktank’s national security adviser, warned that naval campaigns by Iran in the strait of Hormuz and Iran’s Houthi proxies in the Red Sea – launched in response to the US-Israel war on Iran – are allowing regional piracy “to once again thrive”.
He wrote: “Not only have the global navies that once combatted piracy off the Horn of Africa diverted their resources to counter the threats against ships in these critical waterways, but these conflicts have also drawn maritime traffic closer to Somalia’s coastline, creating openings for opportunistic pirates to target commercial ships.”
According to Reisener, about 70% of maritime traffic that passed through the Red Sea prior to the Houthis’ targeting of ships there is now being rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.
A report by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in May reached a similar conclusion: “The recent deterioration of maritime security followed a prolonged period of relative calm in the waters off the Somali coast, which resulted in the redeployment of international anti-piracy fleets and the relaxation of commercial risk-management practices. These factors – alongside the distraction posed by Houthi attacks in the Red Sea – have converged to create an opening that Somali pirates have been quick to exploit.”
Analysts also note that rising oil prices driven by the war have made oil cargoes a more valuable target.
Among the least developed countries in the world, Somalia has endured conflict and clan battles with no strong central government since the autocratic ruler Mohamed Siad Barre fell in 1991. Insufficient patrol vessels and an inability to regularly pay salaries to those involved in coastal patrols are among the reasons why Somalia has long-struggled to secure its coastline.
Piracy has historically thrived during periods of increasing instability and political, factional and regional competition. Observers say the recent rise in incidents has been exacerbated by a domestic and international focus on arms smuggling to Yemen by networks acting on behalf of Iran. Analysts suggest some of these networks have become increasingly associated with Somalia’s Islamist al-Shabaab group as it once again expands its territorial control in central and southern Somalia and seeks to build ties with the Houthis in Yemen.
Local officials interviewed by the Guardian described how in the recent spate of incidents, pirate groups have been using vessels they had already seized to attack and capture other vessels.
According to the officials, the Lutuf was approached as it sailed three nautical miles from Somali shores near the fishing town of Maraya by a previously hijacked cement carrier, the MV Sward, which had been repurposed as a pirate mothership. Eight gunmen from the Sward then boarded the Lutuf and were able to overpower the ship’s armed guards.
Officials say the recent attacks have also been marked by increased technological sophistication on the part of pirate groups, including the use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service to facilitate the tracking of potential targets and for high-speed communications between pirates.
That reflects what Lloyd’s List has described as an increasingly “more capable and adaptive Somali piracy threat” that is already exposing vulnerabilities in carriers’ existing anti-piracy security measures.
In the weeks since the Lutuf ransom was paid, residents of Galkayo, a commercial hub in the north-central Mudug region, said money had started circulating through the local economy to a much greater degree than before. Consumption of the stimulant khat has reportedly increased, and greater numbers of expensive sports utility vehicles have been seen on the roads.
During the previous piracy boom, increased flows of money through the economies of coastal communities and places like Galkayo had profound societal impacts, including an expansion of alcohol and drug use and prostitution.
Perhaps foreshadowing the regime of tougher measures that may be required to counter the growing piracy threat, the Lutuf was only released after a series of drone attacks on the pirate groups involved in the seizure, both at sea and on land. The dead included nine armed men who were killed by a missile fired from a Turkish drone as they prepared boats to join the gunmen onboard the Lutuf.
The question now is whether the growing threat can be countered.
Writing in The Conversation in May, the UK-based academics Anja Shortland and Federico Varese, who studied Somalia’s piracy problem in 2014, were uncertain whether there was an international appetite or the capacity for the same sort of anti-piracy force deployed more than a decade ago.
“What happens next will depend on how the current hijacks proceed. Pirates rely on ransoms for reinvestment and to attract young men into their no-win-no-fee contracts. Fast and generous payments … may free the captive ships. But they will lead to escalating risks for everyone else.
“No state or alliance also currently has the will or capacity to run a naval mission on the scale seen in 2011 and 2012, when navies worldwide spent more than US$1bn annually on counter-piracy operations off Somalia.
“Although piracy manifests as a sea-based problem, it can only be solved on land.”

Israel says it has destroyed major underground Hezbollah base
- Published
Israel's military says it has destroyed a large underground complex operated by Hezbollah in southern Lebanon.
It said it used more than 1,000 tonnes of explosives to destroy two tunnels spanning more than 2km (1.2 miles) beneath the Ali Taher Ridge.
The blast triggered seismic activity equivalent to a magnitude 4.1 earthquake, according to the US Geological Survey.
There was no immediate public response from Hezbollah or the Lebanese government.
Israeli forces took control of the ridge last week after months of fighting with the Iran-backed group there. The Israeli military occupies a large swathe of southern Lebanon captured after the conflict with Hezbollah resumed in March.
Images released by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) showed a fireball lighting up the sky.
"The sky lit up and about 15 seconds later we heard the terrifying sound," Ahamed, a resident in Nabatieh, about 6km west of the ridge, told the BBC.
"The house shook all together as if it was literally an earthquake."
He said people were screaming and children were crying, and that cars filled the roads as people left the area for Beirut.
Tremors were even felt in the coastal city of Saida 40km north.
The IDF said the underground infrastructure included a command centre used by Hezbollah's Badr unit and contained dozens of rockets, missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as anti-tank weapons, mines and explosives.
"This was strategic infrastructure that was constructed over two decades, funded and planned by the Iranian terror regime," the IDF said in a statement on Telegram.
"All of the terrorists who were inside the infrastructure were eliminated or fled."
The IDF said the destruction of the complex completed a mission to destroy eight tunnels and establish a "security zone" in the area.
The latest action comes amid renewed fighting in southern Lebanon, where Israeli forces have expanded operations against Hezbollah positions and continue to hold what Israel describes as a security zone near the border.
Lebanese media reported fresh Israeli strikes elsewhere in the south on Thursday, including Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Mansouri in the Tyre district.
The Lebanese army has increased deployments in areas outside Israeli control, including the southern city of Nabatieh, in efforts to strengthen stability and reassure residents, local television station MTV reported.
Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader.
Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. Its forces continue to occupy roughly 5% of Lebanese territory.
Fighting decreased following a ceasefire deal between Iran and the US in June, alongside a separate agreement between Lebanon and Israel.
Under the Lebanon-Israel framework, Hezbollah is expected to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area.
Hezbollah was not directly involved in the agreement and has rejected direct negotiations.
Despite a reduction in fighting, Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon have continued.
At least 4,362 people have been killed in Lebanon during the conflict, including 395 women and 259 children, according to the health ministry, whose figures do not differentiate between combatants and civilians.
Israeli authorities say 40 Israeli soldiers and four civilians have been killed.

The killer robots behind Ukraine’s warfare ‘revolution’ hunting the frontline
Ukraine wants to replace around one third of its frontline troops with unmanned ground vehicles by the end of the year
In a tiny Ukrainian workshop near the frontline ‘Chimera’ is preparing his robot army for battle.
Lined up in a row, the four-wheeled unmanned vehicles known as "Hyenas" will crawl toward Russian lines full of explosives. Hunting, looking to attack an enemy dugout or halt an advance.
"Imagine what 20 kilograms (44 pounds) of explosives is like: it's very powerful," Chimera, 44, who asked to be identified by his call sign, said. "Very powerful."
Workshops like this one, run by Ukraine's Third Army Corps, have sprouted up across the 1,200-km (745-mile) front as Kyiv's outmanned army seeks to gain the technological edge against Russia's unrelenting infantry assaults in the fifth year of war.
Unmanned ground vehicles are a critical new component of Ukraine's strategy to fight smarter by preserving the lives of its troops on a drone-saturated battlefield, where virtually any movement can prove deadly.
Most Ukrainian brigades and regiments feature unmanned systems units which are expanding to include UGVs as part of their forces.
Reuters visited Chimera's unit, NC13, a leader in employing UGVs to support battlefield assaults, to understand how the integration of these new weapons is shaping the future of land-based warfare.
In the workshop, a garage space is crammed with experimental drones, some with tracks and others wheeled. One is mounted with a hose for dousing fires; another is equipped with a rack to hold portable rocket launchers.
Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, who commands the Third Army Corps, described the gradual replacement of infantrymen with UGVs as the next "revolution" in warfare.
Considered one of Ukraine's premier forces, the corps wants to replace around one third of its frontline troops by the end of the year.
"The West slept through the (drone) revolution in many ways," he said, adding the infantry now performs just 10% of the tasks it did before the constant aerial threat appeared.
"If the West really wants to not just keep up with the times, but to get slightly ahead, it needs to think about the next revolution," said Biletskyi.
In frontline areas such as eastern Ukraine's "fortress belt" in Donetsk, ground drones can often be seen trundling to and from besieged cities with rations or ammunition, or spiriting away injured troops.
They have performed more than 50,000 logistics and evacuation missions this year, Kyiv's defence ministry said in June.
Inside a grey command centre in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, the ground drone operators of NC13, formed last year, are manifesting Biletskyi's vision in real time, controllers in hand.
Parked in front of screens beaming a black-and-white feed from the battlefield, they sprayed a tree line with a machinegun mounted to a UGV.
Glowing screens and the din of digital chatter over Discord, the messaging platform team members use to communicate, lend the space the air of a gaming club.
Deputy commander "Bar" said his unit runs operations virtually every day.
In one, they loaded three bombs onto a trailer that was pulled onto a bridge used for enemy logistics, then blown up. In another, a machine-gun-mounted UGV suppressed an enemy assault while kamikaze drones rained on them from above.
"To me, it's a wonderful recipe," said the 23-year-old former bartender, referring to land and aerial drones working together. At least two prisoners have surrendered to NC13 UGVs, he added.
UGVs have their limits: they struggle with physical obstacles and cannot clear a building or a trench in the way an infantry team can. Nor are they produced widely enough to send in swarms the way aerial drones are, Bar said.
But they have already begun removing humans from a wide range of dangerous tasks.
"They don't need food, they don't need water, they don't need logs delivered to build shelters," he said. "Basically, we don't need to feel for them. It's a hunk of iron sent to do the job we used to send soldiers to do."
Though not a miracle weapon, ground drones are one more step toward the automation of warfare — which also includes AI analysis of battlefield data — that will free up humans to focus on planning and decision making, said Biletskyi.
They could shape new frontline tactics, with commanders more open to daring operations that would have otherwise led to heavy losses.
"War is a creative activity; it's an art," he said. "Otherwise, a commander is not called a commander — but a butcher."
Ukraine's former top general Oleksandr Syrskyi had faced criticism for what some service members described as a Soviet style of leadership that included a high tolerance for losses.
His younger successor, Mykhailo Drapatyi, is seen as a reformer expected to promote a more troop-friendly approach, partly through embracing new technology.
Biletskyi himself was promoted last month to help oversee the defence of Ukraine's Donetsk region, handing him a considerable new operational command.
Like most of NC13, deputy commander Bar is a former infantryman familiar with the brutality of ground fighting, having participated in major battles earlier in the war.
If UGVs had been widely used back then, he said, "a great number of my friends would still be alive".

When Seher Hashmi speaks about mental health, her words do not stem from textbook theories or clinical observations. They carry the raw truth of a survivor. Having battled severe clinical depression and Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), and having survived multiple suicide attempts and self-harm, Seher knows the darkest corners of anguish. Today, she is converting her trauma into a movement, traversing thousands of kilometres across India on her Royal Enfield motorcycle to shatter the silence surrounding mental illness.
Her ongoing nationwide campaign, titled ‘Beyond the Horizon – A Ride for Resilience,’ has reached Keralam after completing its north Indian leg. Together with a group of fellow riders, Seher is engaging with youth to transform societal attitudes towards mental health.
Seher’s life began under difficult circumstances. Abandoned by her biological parents at just nine months simply for being their third girl child, she was adopted by renowned social activist Shabnam Hashmi and scientist-writer Gauhar Raza. She is the niece of Safdar Hashmi, the iconic street-theatre activist who was murdered in 1989. Growing up alongside deeply committed parents whose demanding public lives sometimes left little room to process her childhood anxieties, Seher’s struggles gradually worsened into severe mental health challenges.
Path to recovery
Her path to recovery was forged through personal determination, medical intervention, and the empathy of her loved ones. Emerging from that dark space, Seher rebuilt her life as a motivational speaker, fashion stylist, and mental health advocate.
For Seher, every kilometre ridden is a step towards dismantling social stigma. By sharing her own story of survival, she offers young people across the country something far more powerful than advice—proof that resilience is possible, and that no struggle has to be faced alone.
Second journey
This motorcycle odyssey marks her second major awareness journey. Her first expedition took place in 2025, covering over 3,000 kilometres from Delhi to Kashmir and back, reaching thousands of students across 20 cities. Her current campaign—the south Indian leg—was flagged off on August 20, 2026, at the Constitution Club of India in New Delhi by veteran actor Sharmila Tagore. Spanning 55 days, 11 States, and over 7,000 km, the initiative aims at covering 100 venues across schools, colleges, and rural community spaces.
Entering Keralam on September 9, 2026 through Kasaragod, the team will cover nine districts—Kasaragod, Kannur, Kozhikode, Malappuram, Thrissur, Ernakulam, Alappuzha, Kollam, and Thiruvananthapuram—before heading to Kanyakumari on September 18. In Keralam, the campaign is supported by the Yuva Samithi of the Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP). Parishad volunteers are accompanying the team on motorbikes throughout the State, organising mental health awareness sessions and interactive discussions in educational institutions.

At the conclusion of the men’s javelin throw competition at the Indian Athletics final series late on Thursday night in New Delhi, the top of the podium had a couple of expected names.
In first place was Rohit Yadav, who last month became the second best all-time India thrower. Also there was Yash Vir Singh, who recently clinched bronze at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games. Between the two Asian Games-bound throwers, in second place, with a slightly bewildered look on his face – as if he could hardly believe where he was standing - was Tamil Nadu’s Manoj Kumar.
“I just feel so happy that I’m seeing Rohit Yadav sir and Yashvir Singh sir. This was the first time I was even competing with them. Now I am standing along with them,” he tells Sportstar.
To finish second, the 21-year-old had thrown 80.73m in his first attempt of the evening, a personal best. It was also his first throw over 80m: the barrier that marks genuine world-level contenders, much as the 8m mark does in the men’s long jump and the 17m mark does in the men’s triple jump. Manoj is the latest of 20 Indians to have thrown this far, a list headed of course by Olympic gold medallist Neeraj Chopra.
While a steady trickle of Indian throwers have been crossing this barrier in recent years (12 for the first time in the last four years alone), Manoj’s mark was still significant. He’s the first javelin thrower of this caliber from Tamil Nadu, a state far better known for running and jumps than power events like the throws.
That had been something Manoj had often been reminded of when he pursued his passion.
“So many people said I wouldn’t ever achieve anything in the javelin throw. They would laugh at me. There’s no tradition of throwing in Tamil Nadu. They told me I’m wasting my time. Now I can tell them that I made the right choice,” he says
ALSO READ | Tanya, Nirbhay shatter hammer throw National Records as Asian Games-bound athletes give one last test
Not his first choice
Growing up in the village of Kattur Papakuruchi, just outside Tiruchirapalli, Manoj didn’t start off as a javelin thrower either. A student of St. Anthony’s higher secondary school, he took part in athletics with an early interest in pole vault.
“I used to take part in everything – sprinting, jumping. I actually had a lot of speed. But what I really liked was the pole vault. There was a very good pole vaulter in my school and at first I wanted to be like him. I even have a 3m jump at the school level,” he says.
Manoj also played a lot of cricket and although he didn’t know it just yet, both pole vault and cricket would eventually help him in his eventual choice of sport. That was javelin.
“When I was in college, I had a friend, Madheswaran, who was a really good javelin thrower. He wasn’t a national-level thrower but he had thrown 70m in Tamil Nadu. At that time I didn’t really think about whether I had a future in this event. I just thought the javelin throw was interesting. I had already trained as a pole vaulter and cricket so I had some basic strength, speed and a lot of flexibility and that really helped me out,” he says.
Although he started the javelin around the same time Neeraj Chopra created history with his Olympic gold, Manoj says he looked elsewhere for his primary motivation.
“At the time I started the javelin throw, I used to watch a lot of videos. I have a lot of respect for Neeraj Chopra but at that time I actually used to see videos of (World record holder) Jan Zelezny. I felt Neeraj has a lot of power which I didn’t have but I had a lot of speed which was similar to Zelezny,” he remembers.
ALSO READ | After long road to recovery, Avinash Sable confident of defending Asian Games gold
For all his enthusiasm, Manoj still had a major obstacle to clear. For all it’s success in track and field, Tamil Nadu has never had any tradition of top-quality throwing. That meant there were no coaches as well. Initially, Manoj trained under a sprinting coach who also had an interest in the javelin throw.
That meant that, initially at least, his progress was slow. Until 2024, he only had a personal best of 56m at a state-level meet. But that same year, he started training with Santhosh Kumar, a coach who had only just retired from the Indian Army and was training at the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu (SDAT) center in Ariyalur, a town some 75km from Trichy.
Manoj credits Santhosh with his development as an athlete.
“I had interest but I had no way of building on it. I actually believe that my real training happened under Santhosh sir in 2024. Santhosh sir, saw something in me. I hadn’t even thrown 60m when I started training with him and he told me that I could throw much further. He toughened my training and my mindset. He built my speed and technique. He also taught me what to eat and how to respect my sport,” he says.
Near-death experience
Manoj crossed the 60m mark for the first time at the Junior Indian championships in 2024, which despite his modest 11th place finish, he considers amongst the more significant tournaments of his career. It marked a steady improvement in his performance. 2026 though has been his biggest year yet.
He made a throw of 75.18m at the Indian Athletics Series in Pune in June and then improved to 77.82 m at the Indian Athletics Series in Meerut earlier this month.
But his progress hasn’t been all smooth. In 2025 he suffered a severe bout of appendicitis that ruled him out for half the year as he recovered.
“The doctors told me that if I had been brought in just three hours later, I would have suffered sepsis and likely died,” he says.
There has also been the issue that plagues most young Indian athletes – the lack of finances. The son of a farmer, Manoj says he’s always had to keep an eye on his bank account even as he trains and competes. Even the javelin he used in New Delhi was a borrowed one from Madras Christian College in Chennai where he’s currently pursuing his post graduation in public relations.
“Everything costs money and when you are just starting your career you don’t have any,” he says. “I’m lucky because although they don’t understand sports, my parents have always been very supportive. But I don’t have any sponsors and all of this costs money,” he says. Even as he prepared to compete in New Delhi, Manoj says he was calculating his expenses. “Train tickets to Delhi cost 6000 rupees. It’s another 4000 rupees for two days at a hotel and the entrance fee for the competition is 1200 rupees,” he says.
ALSO READ | Asian Games 2026: Annu Rani, Shahnavaz and Nithya dropped from athletics contingent
As such the 50,000 rupees prize money he won in New Delhi will go a long way. “I’ve taken part in five competitions this year and spent close to 50,000 rupees. So with this money, I can take part in another five competitions,” he says.
Manoj is optimistic that things will get easier for him. A couple of months ago, he was inducted to the Indian Army and has started training at the Army Sports Institute in Pune. With just two years of formal training so far, Manoj believes he has a high ceiling for improvement. Standing 5 foot 10 and weighing 76kg, he’s not the biggest thrower but feels he can gain more strength while maintaining his speed.
And while he’s managed to prove more than a few people wrong with his performance in New Delhi on Thursday, he’s looking to do more.
“This is my first major medal in India but I want to be regularly throwing at this level. Right now, I’m just one of many athletes who has thrown 80m. But I have bigger dreams. I want to be able to compete for India at the biggest competitions. I’m happy that I’ve crossed 80m but I’m not satisfied. I know I can throw much more than this,” he says.
