Moss developer Polyarc has closed
The studio produced some early hits for the PSVR and Oculus Quest.
Polyarc, the developer behind virtual reality games Moss and Moss: Book II, has closed, according to a new post on the studio's LinkedIn page. Based on a reverse recruiting sheet shared alongside the announcement, at least 29 members of the studio's staff are now looking for work.
"After nearly 12 years riding the joyous rollercoaster of emotions that is making video games, our time together has come to an end," Polyarc says. "As we wind down active development, we are saying our farewells to each other. Working together over all of these years has been an honor. Bringing surprise and delight to those who played our games has been a privilege. Thank you to everyone at Polyarc, our work is now finished."
The Seattle-based studio's Moss series was an early VR favorite, thanks in part to the way it fused traditional action-adventure gameplay with a camera system that let you peer around diorama-like levels while controlling Quill, the series' mouse protagonist. Polyarc's output also became a reliable catalog filler for various VR platforms — Moss launched on the PlayStation VR, and was also ported to the Oculus Quest as a launch title. Moss: Book II was similarly released on PSVR, Quest, SteamVR and Pico, and the studio even released one of the few VR games for the Apple Vision Pro, a multiplayer strategy title called Glassbreakers.
In May 2026, Polyarc tried to reach a non-VR audience with Moss: The Forgotten Relic, which collected the Moss series into a single game and reimagined the gameplay so you didn't need a VR headset to play. It's unclear how well the game has sold, but it evidently wasn't enough to keep the studio afloat. The bigger issue might be changes to the VR ecosystem that made it harder to get new projects off the ground. Meta began its big pivot away from the metaverse towards AI products at the start of this year. Not only did the company close several of its own VR studios, but its retreat from the space likely made getting new VR games funded even harder.
Even though the studio is closed, all of Polyarc's games remain available to purchase. If you have a VR headset collecting dust somewhere and haven't tried them, they're absolutely worth playing.

Hong Kong's Tiananmen activists sentenced to up to seven years in prison
- Published
Three Hong Kong activists who organised annual vigils commemorating Beijing's 1989 crackdown on Tiananmen Square protests have been handed prison sentences of up to seven years.
Two of the defendants - Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41 - were convicted last month of inciting others to subvert state power, under the city's controversial national security law.
A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, had pleaded guilty in January.
For years, Hong Kong was one of the only places in Chinese territory where people could hold gatherings to mark the Tiananmen Square crackdown - a topic that is highly sensitive and heavily censored in mainland China.
These gatherings were banned by Hong Kong's authorities in 2020, citing Covid-19 policies, but never resumed. That same year, the national security law, which makes illegal a wider range of dissenting acts, officially came into force.
Authorities say the law is necessary to maintain stability, but critics argue it has eroded Hong Kong's autonomy and created a climate of fear.
Lee, Chow and Ho were charged in 2021. They faced up to 10 years in prison after their conviction.
On Friday, the court sentenced Lee to seven years in prison, while Chow was handed seven years and three months. Ho, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to five years in prison.
According to a court summary in August, Lee and Chow had "incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power", according to a summary on Friday.
Chow told the court in May the law itself was on trial.
Speaking to the BBC before her arrest in 2022, Chow said she was "prepared to be arrested" and "willing to pay the price for fighting for democracy".
The defendants were leaders of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance, a group founded in May 1989 to support students holding pro-democracy rallies.
Weeks later, the Chinese Communist Party sent troops and tanks to crush pro-democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square. Estimates of the death toll range from a few hundred to many thousands.
Over the next three decades, the Hong Kong Alliance called on authorities to accept responsibility for the crackdown, free dissidents and introduce democratic reform.
The group also held yearly vigils commemorating the Tiananmen Square crackdown. Organisers said some of the gatherings attracted more than 100,000 people, though police had lower estimates of the turnout.
On Friday, the court also handed a HK$1.5m fine ($191,000; £142,000) to the Hong Kong Alliance.
"This sentencing is a triple tragedy: for the activists being unjustly punished; the survivors and victims of the Tiananmen crackdown itself; and the generations of Hongkongers denied the space to discuss one of the most consequential events in modern Chinese history," said Amnesty International's Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks.

'People were trampling me': Philippine ferry fire survivor recalls narrow escape
- Published
Passengers on board a ferry to the Philippines' Palawan province were jolted into chaos on Wednesday night, when a fire broke out on the vessel.
Frantic cries pierced the night sky as hot air filled the boat, recalls Roland Lerma, one of more than 100 passengers aboard the MV June Aster.
Five people have died and 86 people are missing after the fire, which, in a country where shipping accidents are not uncommon, could become one of the deadliest maritime disasters the Philippines has seen.
Families are anxiously awaiting news about their loved ones on board, while survivors like Lerma are coming to terms with their harrowing escape.
Speaking to the BBC from a hospital in Coron, Lerma recalled that as the fire spread and he scrambled to get off the burning boat, he slipped and fell.
"When I was on the floor, people were trampling me," said the 30-year-old.
He started crawling until he could find his footing again, before leaping off the vessel into the sea.
He said he saw children who had also jumped in the water, though he could not make out their faces in the dark.
"When I hit the water, I ditched all my possessions - the clothes I was wearing, phones, bags - so that I could float," he said.
Lerma said he floated on his back for about two hours before rescuers arrived and pulled him and other survivors out of the water.
"It was cold. If the rescue had been delayed, I would have definitely died last night," he said.
Lerma, who works in construction, is from Leyte province. He had travelled to the capital Manila with five of his neighbours, where they boarded the ferry to bring them to work at Coron, a popular tourist spot in Palawan province.
According to the Philippine Coast Guard, the MV June Aster departed Manila's Port of Baseco on Tuesday night at 20:13 local time (12:13 GMT) and was scheduled to arrive at the Coron port at 18:00 on Wednesday.
But the ferry caught fire just 1.2 nautical miles (2.2km) off the coast of Coron's Marcilla village.
The fire was first reported at 18:45 local time on Wednesday night by a staff member of Atienza Shipping Lines, which owns the boat, the Coast Guard said.
The company said in a statement on Thursday that it was co-operating fully with authorities and expressed "profound sadness" about the fire.
Authorities say a survivor had told them the flames had started in the cargo hold after a loud explosion.
The ship had been carrying several motorcycles, an electric car, a forklift, a pick-up van and other goods, the Philippine Coast Guard said.
As the journey was expected to take more than 20 hours, passengers had slept on bunk beds onboard overnight.
Lerma said that two Chileans - a couple who looked like they were in their late 20s or early 30s - had slept in the beds next to his.
Authorities have since confirmed that two Chilean nationals were among the 43 people rescued.
Lerma and two of his neighbours are now in a hospital in Coron. Another person in their group has been taken to a bigger hospital in the neighbouring island of Culion, while two others remain missing, Lerma says.
"I have a couple of bruises and my chest is still hurting," Lerma said. "Last night, I had a hard time breathing. But I am okay now."
Search and rescue operations are ongoing, though authorities say the fire on the MV June Aster has still not been put out and there was visible smoke from the ferry.
A spokesperson for the Philippine Coast Guard said in a local television interview many of the survivors "are still in shock".
Meanwhile, families of the ferry's missing passengers are enduring an agonising wait.
Anelyn Magbanua told the BBC that her husband Marlon was on the ferry. He was returning to Coron after visiting Manila to see two of their children who are studying at the capital.
"He spent a couple of days there. He even sent me their pictures," she said.
She last heard from him while the ferry was passing through a village about two hours from the port in Coron.
Magbanua and her two-year-old son had gone to bed early on Wednesday night expecting Marlon to be home soon.
But she was woken up later that night by a relative who informed her that her husband's ferry had caught fire.
On Thursday she rushed to the hospital when she heard there was a chance her husband might be one of the rescued survivors there.
But officials have since told her that Marlon remains unaccounted for.
"My two-year-old son and I are outside the hospital as we speak. We have nothing but ourselves," she told the BBC over the phone.
"I can't describe what I am feeling right now. I have been crying and praying since last night."

Yoto just announced two new audio devices for kids
They both include a giant green button to access a child's favorite content.
Yoto just announced two new audio devices for kids. There's the fourth-generation Yoto Player and an updated version of the Yoto Mini.
The new Yoto Player is still a speaker with a pixel display, but the company has added some bells and whistles. Firstly, there's a big green dial that kids can twist to play their "most loved audio." This can access up to 20 pieces of content, including podcasts, stories and songs.
This is done directly from the device, so there will be no need for a kid to borrow a parent's phone. Additionally, the functionality doesn't require Yoto Cards, which are basically little NFC keys that get inserted into the player to access unique content.
The company has also upgraded the software so routines are easier to create and access. This means that parents can set up a routine just one time and the device will automatically do stuff like adjust the graphics to reflect the time of day.
Yoto promises that the hardware has been redesigned so it's "easy for little hands." The storage has been increased up to 64GB, downloads should be much faster and the nightlight panel has been upgraded.
All of this is very good news, considering an older version of the Yoto Player already made our list of the best audio gadgets for kids. However, there is a spot of bad news. The price is shooting up to $150, from $110. It's available to pre-order right now, with shipments going out on October 15.
The Yoto Mini is also getting a nice little hardware refresh. This is the company's cheaper and much smaller audio player. The upcoming Mini looks to be designed for the kind of adventures kids typically get into. It's "rugged, water and dust-resistant." The company promises it can "handle playground grass, sofa launches and rainy-day chaos without missing a beat."
The upgrade also includes the same green button that allows access to content without Yoto Cards. The device has enough storage for "1,000 hours of audio" and it integrates with both wired and Bluetooth headphones.
Sadly, there's another price increase here. The Yoto Mini is going up to $110, from $80. It's available for pre-order right now, with shipments going out on September 30.
The company is also introducing several accessories for its devices. There are scratch-proof cases for both the Mini and Player that are available in four colors. It's also working on a wireless dock and a case for Yoto Cards. We don't have pricing or availability information on this stuff just yet.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani paid a moving tribute to those who lost their lives and were affected by the 9/11 terrorist attacks. Taking to social media, he shared a video message and called the attacks a 'horrific act of terror'. "September 11th was a horrific act of terror. A day of immeasurable loss. 2,753 parents and children, husbands and wives, friends and colleagues. 2,753 universes gone in an instant," Mamdani, 34, said while he sat at a desk outdoors, with the Manhattan skyline in the background. In the video, the New York City Mayor said, “And in the years since, thousands more have died from illness caused by the toxic air they breathed, in the months they spent working on the pile.” Quick answers to key questions Mayor Zohran Mamdani referred to the September 11 attacks as a 'horrific act of terror' and expressed the immeasurable loss experienced on that day. He shared a tribute video emphasizing the lives that were lost and the ongoing effects of the attacks. Mayor Mamdani highlighted the bravery of New Yorkers who donated blood, opened their homes to others, and assisted colleagues during the crisis, stating that these acts showcased the spirit of community in the face of darkness. The 25th anniversary was marked by a ceremony at Ground Zero where survivors, mourners, and politicians gathered. Family members read the names of the 2,983 victims, and moments of silence were observed at specific times related to the attacks. The petition, which garnered thousands of signatures, aimed to ban Mayor Mamdani from attending due to concerns over his public record and associations with individuals who allegedly minimized the significance of the 9/11 attacks. Mamdani referenced the tragic loss of 2,753 individuals, emphasizing the profound impact on families, including parents, children, and friends, as well as the subsequent deaths caused by illnesses related to the toxic air at Ground Zero. Mamdani called 9/11 the "darkest day" in the history of New York, adding, "We also remember what so many New Yorkers did in that darkness." "We remember the thousands upon thousands of New Yorkers who lined up for hours to donate blood. We remember the people who opened their homes to those who could not get home," he continued. "We remember the workers who carried their colleagues down hundreds of stairs, then turned around and went back up to find someone else who needed help." "25 years later, we have a sacred obligation to those who were stolen from us. To care for one another how they cared for strangers," the politician also said. "To live lives worthy of the sacrifices they made and to build a city worthy of their courage. A city where we run toward one another. That is how we remember," he concluded. On this day, mourners, survivors and fellow citizen gathered around the twin waterfall pools that mark the footprints of the two towers in Lower Manhattan on the somber day. They were joined by several politicians, including Vice President JD Vance, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and former mayors Rudy Giuliani and Michael Bloomberg on the remembrance day. Former US presidents were also in attendance, including Joe Biden, Barack Obama, George W Bush and Bill Clinton. Continuing the tradition, family members read out the names of the 2,983 people who were killed on the tragic day as well as the Feb. 26, 1993, World Trade Center bombing. Beginning at 8:46 am, six moments of silence were observed at the times when each of the towers was struck, when each fell, when the Pentagon was attacked and when United Airlines Flight 93 crashed in Pennsylvania. Mamdani attended the event despite the viral petition. According to multiple US media outlets, a petition with thousands of signatures, surfaced, aiming to ban him from attending the ceremony. One of the organizers of the petition, Giovanni Galante had told the New York Post earlier, "Our objection is based on his public record — his failure to meaningfully acknowledge the horror of that day, and his employment of, support for, or association with individuals who have minimized 9/11, defended terrorists, or even suggested America 'deserved' the attacks." In 2006, Donald Trump was firing people on The Apprentice and Dr. Phil was daytime television's reigning tough-love therapist.
Twenty years later, the former is president of the United States, the latter, his informal UFO ambassador—recently trusted with unreleased government files on unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) to gauge how the public might handle what's inside.
"Here's what comes in stages. First they acknowledge it, then they confirm it's real, then they tell you where it's from," Dr. Phil said in an August 7 Instagram video discussing UAP disclosure. "And somewhere down that road, maybe, is the big one—the government of the United States standing at a podium and saying out loud, we are not alone."
For most of 2026, a rumor has consumed the world of UFOlogy: President Trump is sitting on a finished speech confirming humanity isn't alone. Whether the “disclosure speech” actually exists is a topic of rabid discussion on X, the r/UFO subreddit, and dozens of extraterrestrial-curious podcasts, but the reasons so many people believe in it are very real. Humans are arguably experiencing the most consequential era for the UFO scene since the ’40s and ’50s, when a mysterious crash outside Roswell, New Mexico, and unexplained radar blips over Washington, DC, birthed decades of legends of little green men and flying-saucers.
There's no doubt that the government has been engaging with the topic. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently confirmed that Stephen Miller, one of the most powerful figures in the White House, has been handed the UAP portfolio.
Tim Gallaudet, a retired Navy rear admiral who helped run the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration during Trump's first term, testified before Congress about UAP in 2024, and now sits on a UAP Science Advisory Council reporting to the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. He called the increased government interest “a total change in executive-branch transparency from the last 80 years."
But he’s unsure if that would ever culminate in a speech from a sitting president, because they would “have to acknowledge that we're not in control, that we're not the highest level of intelligence on the planet, and that's going to be a very hard thing for any government to admit."
A White House spokesperson tells WIRED via email that “No such speech is planned—rather, the administration continues to release files as they become available, and the public to make up their own minds about the information uncovered.”
For believers, the modern UAP disclosure began in 2017, when a New York Times article revealed a secret Pentagon program quietly investigating UAPs. The Pentagon went on to confirm in 2020 that leaked videos of Navy pilots tracking seemingly impossible objects were real. A 2021 intelligence report conceded the phenomena existed and remained unexplained, and in 2022 the government established an official investigation office. Then, from 2022 to 2025, Congress held yearly public hearings where pilots, military officers, and intelligence veterans (including Gallaudet) testified under oath.
What’s also novel is that UAP disclosure has bipartisan support. Both the House task force on declassifying federal secrets and the House UAP Caucus are made up of legislators from across the aisle.
This year, the drumbeat of government interest turned into a drumroll about a potential Trump speech. In January, filmmaker Mark Christopher Lee claimed a disclosure speech was imminent, pegged to the 79th anniversary of the alleged Roswell crash on July 8. Few took him seriously.
But in February, the president's daughter-in-law, Lara Trump, gave the idea new legs, saying on the Pod Force One podcast she'd heard Trump had a speech ready touching on "some sort of extraterrestrial life." Around the same time, Barack Obama mused in a podcast interview with Brian Tyler Cohen that aliens are “real” before conceding “I haven’t seen them.” Trump then accused his predecessor of disclosing classified information, and announced that he was directing agencies to release their files on "alien and extraterrestrial life."
What followed was bizarre even by this administration's standards. In May, Trump posted an AI-generated image of himself escorting a handcuffed gray alien, and a mysterious loading page appeared on the domain aliens.gov, leading to rampant speculation within the UFO community that the big reveal was coming. But when the White House finally launched aliens.gov late in the month, it ended up being a Star Wars–style website that functioned as an ICE tip line—with aliens being a reference to undocumented people.
The machinery of disclosure kept grinding forward. Since May, the government has released five batches of declassified videos and documents onto the Department of War's website. Detractors say the files lack context and the videos prove little.
Even after the Roswell date passed, rumors about a disclosure speech intensified. In late July, Liberation Times—an independent news website with a record of breaking UAP stories—reported that a speech confirming some UFOs are of non-human origin had been prepared for Trump.
The site’s founder, Christopher Sharp, tells WIRED the story began with a call from a source he deeply trusts.
"They basically said, ‘Look, I'm quite shaken, because it looks like Trump may make some kind of announcement on UAP disclosure’." Another source described the speech itself, he says, alleging it basically reads, “we're not alone, we have captured some of these or retrieved some of these things, they're of non-human origin, and that there is a reverse engineering effort."
Sharp was also told Trump wouldn't deliver it unless unspecified conditions were met.
"If you're the president, you have to be sure that there's firm evidence," he says. "The worst thing you can do is come out with this speech and then whatever you put out could be debunked straight away ... You'll go down in history as a laughingstock."
In August, the rumor hit a fever pitch. Robert Bigelow, the billionaire aerospace mogul who has bankrolled UFO research for decades and once owned Utah's infamous Skinwalker Ranch (a 500-acre plot of land renowned for alleged alien and paranormal activity and later the namesake of a popular History Channel series), told veteran Las Vegas journalist George Knapp that he'd met Trump in the Oval Office months earlier and personally handed him a speech containing a single sentence: "A non-human, intelligent presence has been on Earth for a very long time, using spacecraft and with performances completely beyond our capabilities and our human physics.”
Bigelow said he advised the president to deliver the line casually, on his way to boarding Air Force One—no evidence, no press conference, just confirmation. Trump hasn't said it. Yet.
If the cycle of presidents and UFO disclosure feels familiar, that's because it is. For nearly 80 years, someone has always supposedly been on the verge of revealing the truth, but no president has ever delivered.
"Politicians overpromise," says Greg Eghigian, a professor of history and bioethics at Penn State and author of After the Flying Saucers Came. "The reality is that even presidents are not privy to a lot of classified information that lies within the bowels of the military and intelligence community bureaucracy."
Still, for the believers, the stakes justify the hope.
“Often in the mainstream, when this topic gets brought up, there's a giggle factor. I can tell you who is not giggling about this: senior members of the administration, senior intelligence officials, senior members of the military, senior members of Congress,” says Jordan Flowers, executive director of the Disclosure Foundation, a nonprofit that advocates for UAP transparency. “When the door closes, no one ever says, ‘Oh, this is all made up, isn't it?’ No. The door closes and they say, ‘We know there's something happening here, we know this is serious, what do we do about it?’"
But that discourse still hasn’t been confirmed, at least in a meaningful way to the general public.
"A speech from the President of the United States confirming the existence of things in our airspace that we do not understand would unequivocally contribute to the public taking this issue seriously," says Flowers.
Eghigian, however, isn't so sure a Trump pronouncement would settle anything, particularly from "this president, who has a long history of not telling the truth."
If the past is any indicator, this could be another nothingburger.
“Unless something radically different happens, which I know a lot of people are counting on, what we could probably expect is that this will eventually die down,” he says, citing an 80-year history of “intense moments where societies are really focused on the subject, and then all of a sudden interest wanes, and then all of a sudden it appears again."
Right now, interest is arguably at anall-timee high. Few politicians enjoy a public spectacle as much as Trump, and what spectacle could be bigger than news that transcends our planet, and potentially our galaxy. Maybe the rumor just becomes another footnote on presidents and UFO lore. Or maybe it becomes the most important proclamation in human history, delivered by a reality TV star, with a talk show shrink by his side.

PM Modi, Pezeshkian & Putin at Brics Summit 2026 (left); PM Modi, Xi and Putin at SCO summit in 2025 (right)
What could be a fresh diplomatic headache for Donald Trump? A picture of Prime Minister Narendra Modi holding hands with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, with Russian President Vladimir Putin standing alongside them at the Brics Summit, has brought together three countries whose ties with Washington range from strategic competition to open confrontation.The image also echoes a remark Trump made last year after PM Modi, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping were pictured together at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit. “Looks like we’ve lost India and Russia to deepest, darkest, China. May they have a long and prosperous future together!” Trump had said.This time, Iran, one of Washington’s most adversarial rivals, has joined the picture, adding another layer to the geopolitical message from a grouping that Trump has repeatedly viewed with suspicion. The US president has not yet commented on the Brics summit.
Trump pressure on Brics
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly warned Brics against challenging the dominance of the US dollar, putting the grouping’s push for greater use of local currencies at the centre of tensions with Washington. In November 2024, Trump threatened 100% tariffs on Brics countries if they backed another currency to replace the dollar.“We require a commitment from these Countries that they will neither create a new Brics Currency, nor back any other currency to replace the mighty US Dollar or, they will face 100% Tariffs, and should expect to say goodbye to selling into the wonderful US economy,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
Trump has also dismissed the prospect of Brics replacing the dollar in global trade, saying there was “no chance” of that happening and warning that countries attempting to do so should “wave goodbye to America”.The issue remains central to Brics’ economic agenda, although the grouping has increasingly focused on making trade and payments in national currencies easier rather than creating a common currency. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, speaking at the Brics Business Forum, called for greater use of national currencies among members, along with mechanisms to manage currency risks and facilitate reciprocal settlements.“One of the most important steps is to expand the use of national currencies in trade among the members. This step must be accompanied by the establishment of the necessary instruments for managing currency risks and reciprocal settlements,” Pezeshkian said.He also argued that the existing financial system was vulnerable because of its concentration around a limited number of currencies and called for the New Development Bank to play a bigger role in financing infrastructure and energy projects through local currencies and other mechanisms.Putin, meanwhile, did not directly mention replacing the dollar at this year’s forum. Instead, he described a broader shift in the global economic order, with emerging economies becoming increasingly important.“Right now, the world is undergoing structural, deep, profound shifts. It is explained by the fact that the so-called old leaders which used to be the vanguard of economic growth in the second half of the 20th century, are being replaced by new engines of growth. When I say old, this is just a formality - all of us understand what we are talking about,” he said.For Washington, the concern is not simply whether Brics creates a new currency, but whether a larger share of global trade and financial transactions gradually moves away from the dollar.
India walks a tight rope
For India, the Brics summit comes at a sensitive point in its economic relationship with the US. The India-US trade deal is “more or less” finalised, with the two sides working on a framework for preferential market access before signing it at an appropriate time. A few issues remain under discussion.The talks come as Trump continues to step up pressure on India over its purchase of Russian oil. In 2025, he had warned of further tariff action and later imposed 50% tariffs on Indian goods, adding to the economic stakes for New Delhi as it seeks to deepen trade with the US.
India is meanwhile pursuing multiple trade agreements to widen market access. It has signed nine trade agreements over the past five years covering economies with a combined GDP of $60 trillion, while talks with Chile are at an advanced stage and New Zealand has been targeted for an early rollout.The balancing act is also reflected in India’s broader trade priorities. Its total exports reached $863 billion in 2025-26, including $421 billion in services, with the government seeking to diversify services exports beyond IT and professional services and expand areas such as fintech and digital services.The conflict involving Iran and the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz have added another layer to the equation. The waterway is a crucial route for global oil shipments, making stability in the Gulf directly relevant to India’s energy security, trade and the safety of Indian seafarers.

A probe has been ordered by Bhopal Police Commissioner Sanjay Kumar, a day after at least four MBBS intern doctors suffered injuries due to water cannons that were used against them during their protest in the campus of government-run Gandhi Medical College (GMC) to demand a hike in their stipend.
On Monday (September 7, 2026), hundreds of interns of the GMC, Bhopal, protested at their campus over their longstanding demand that their stipend be increased from the current ₹14,437 to ₹30,000. However, as they planned a march to the Chief Minister’s residence, the police used water cannons on the protestors, visuals of which appeared on the internet.
The protestors also alleged that as they continued their march later in the day, the police also resorted to baton charge on them near the campus. The march was stopped less than 2 kilometres from the CM house, prompting them to launch a sit-in at the site.
The sit-in in Bhopal’s Kamla Park area continued through the night and on Tuesday (September 8) even as they boycotted the OPD and routine operation theatre (OT) services, while emergency services remained operational. Services were also interrupted at Gwalior’s Gajra Raja Medical College in support of the protest.
Four interns injured in the police action
Speaking to The Hindu, Siddhartha Kumar Rai, undergraduate student wing president of the Junior Doctors’ Association (JDA), Madhya Pradesh, said that at least four interns got seriously injured in the police action, including one person suffering a broken arm and another an eye injury.
“It was a completely peaceful protest inside the campus but still the interns who perform 36-hour-long duties and contribute the most in handling the heavy patient load at government hospitals were treated like goons by the police. They even targeted the girl interns who were standing on the side,” he said.
Meanwhile, various other doctors’ bodies in the State have also come out in support of the interns’ protest while condemning the police action.
Mr. Rai said that if a written assurance was not given by Tuesday night, the JDA and various other bodies will boycott medical services across the State from Wednesday (September 9).
Dr. Kavita N. Singh, Dean and CEO, GMC, Bhopal, also slammed the use of force in a letter to Commissioner Kumar while seeking an inquiry into the matter and action against responsible officers.
“Water cannon was used and lathicharge was done on the intern students at the emergency gate in which two students were injured.
Taking such action against intern students on the hospital campus without prior notice is completely inappropriate,” she wrote.
In an order, Mr. Kumar said that the matter was brought to attention by Deputy Chief Minister and Health Minister Rajendra Shukla and that Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP), Zone 2, Vikas Sahwal has been appointed to conduct an “impartial investigation of the whole incident”.
“It has been brought to the notice by Shri Rajendra Shukla, Deputy Chief Minister, that during the protest of intern doctors in Bhopal on September 7, 2026, the police sprayed water using water cannon near the gate of Hamidia Hospital, due to which some doctors were injured,” the order read.
Mr. Rai also claimed that Madhya Pradesh ranked 28th in the country in the amount of stipend given to MBBS interns, after the Uttar Pradesh increasing the amount from ₹12,000 to ₹25,000 in August.
“But in terms of MBBS fee at government colleges, we are at the third position with about ₹1.15 lakh. How is this fair,” he asked.
Meanwhile, Mr. Shukla also held a meeting with senior officials and the management of the GMC to discuss the issue and interns’ demand and said that a resolution will be reached soon.
“I am aware of the issue raised by intern doctors in Bhopal regarding an increase in stipends. The expectations and problems of young doctors in the state are being taken seriously. I am in constant touch with representatives of the intern doctors on this matter,” he wrote on X.
“Our effort is to engage in positive discussions with all parties and arrive at an appropriate and practical solution to this issue. Young doctors play a vital role in strengthening the health services of the state, and the government is sensitive to their rightful expectations. Following discussions and necessary deliberations, appropriate and necessary decisions will be taken in this regard,” he added.

It's Congress vs Congress again, this time over Brics Summit that is being held in Delhi.
NEW DELHI: Shashi Tharoor not being in sync with his Congress colleagues is no longer news. Especially, if the issue in question pertains to the global stage. So, when senior Congress leader Chidambaram questioned the benefits of Brics for India, Tharoor had an answer. As expected, the answer triggered another round of Tharoor vs Congress debate that overshadowed the BJP broadside against Chidambaram.On Wednesday, Chidambaram questioned the tangible benefits India has gained from recent Brics summits, and said he had not seen any significant outcomes from the last two or three meetings.“I don't know how many presidents and how many prime ministers are coming. I don't think the last two or three Brics summits have resulted in tangible benefits or tangible results,” Chidambaram stated. “In fact, we are part of Brics, we are part of SCO, we are part of G20, and we are part of QUAD. What benefits are we getting out of that? I can't see. In the last two or three summits, I didn't see any benefits. Earlier, the Brics summits resulted in some tangible benefits,” he added.Chidambaram’s remarks opened the floodgates for counter-attacks from the ruling party. The BJP leaders launched a broadside against Chidambaram and the Congress. What followed was a barrage of attacks ranging from "Dimagi Naxal", "Naraz Fufas in pain", "FOMO", "indigestion", "bitten by bug" to questions on what Congress had gained in diplomacy since Independence"Is diplomacy to be seen as a transaction like the Congress Party is projecting? What have I done for you? What will you do for me? Kind of an approach.
What is the so-called tangible result?" BJP leader Nalin Kohli wondered.Kohli then questioned the Congress party's own diplomatic record from Independence until 2014. "If we talk of tangible results, we can question what the Congress Party's entire approach from 1947 right up to 2014 was on diplomacy, including Sharm El Sheikh and projecting Pakistan as literally a victim of terror when it is the perpetrator of terror," he stated.
Tharoor joins debate
Tharoor then joined the debate and said India holding Brics was a matter of prestige. "Having a dozen heads of state and government, not only members of Brics but also some observers coming at presidential and prime ministerial level, is a matter of great prestige for us. It shows a certain diplomatic convening power, which has value in and of itself on the global stage," Tharoor said.The Congress MP maintained that the Brics Summit is providing an important platform for the Global South."This grouping, the 11 Brics countries, represents a majority of the world's population and 41 per cent of global GDP. It's not a small matter; it's something that has to be taken very seriously by the rest of the world. Secondly, of course, having a dozen heads of state and government, not only members of BRICS but also some observers coming at the presidential and prime ministerial level, this is a matter of great prestige for us," the Congress MP from Thiruvananthapuram said.Latching onto Tharoor’s remarks, Nalin Kohli said: “One has noted Dr Shashi Tharoor's statement, and anyone who understands diplomacy would see great value in the BRICS summit.”BJP leader Pradeep Bhandari also used Tharoor’s remarks to take digs at the Congress and allege that some party leaders were opposing Brics on the instructions of Rahul Gandhi.“Congress exposes Congress! Congress MP Shashi Tharoor says-" BRICS happening in India is a matter of huge prestige for Bharat." Congress MP exposes "Naraz Fufa" of Congress who were opposing BRICS on instructions of Rahul Gandhi!” Pradeep Bhandari said in a post on X.Tharoor has had frosty ties with the Congress over his “independent views” on a range of issues. In the last two years, Tharoor has often made the Congress duck for cover as the BJP has cited his views to school the grand-old-party. The Thiruvananthapuram MP has made several remarks over a wide range of issues - from lessons in nationalism to global diplomacy to the Emergency to Covid-19 vaccine distribution abroad - that have brought more cheers to the BJP than his own party, the Congress.
Tharoor vs Congress
It all started with Tharoor's surprise "out-of-turn" praise for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s US trip after Donald Trump took oath as president for a second term.Tharoor then acknowledged key achievements from PM Modi’s visit, particularly on trade negotiations and defence cooperation. He welcomed the trade deal discussions and expressed optimism over India’s diplomatic engagements.The Congress immediately issued a clarification, which said that individual opinions do not reflect the party’s official stance. But Tharoor defended his remarks and said: “When someone in the government does the right thing, it should be recognised, irrespective of who's in power. For 16 years, I have been in politics. My attitude has been that when somebody in the government, whether it’s our government or some other party’s government, does the right thing or does something well, one should acknowledge and praise it, and when they do something badly, one should criticise it. If I were to praise all the time, no one would take me seriously. If I were to criticise all the time, no one would take me seriously either… There’s got to be some give and take in democracy.”After the Pulwama terror attack and Centre's Operation Sindoor, Tharoor made several remarks that were at variance with the official stand taken by the Congress.Tharoor was picked up to lead a multi-party parliamentary delegation to represent India globally following Operation Sindoor. Later, writing for The Hindu, Tharoor praised Modi’s "energy, dynamism, and willingness to engage" as a major asset for India on the global stage. He described Modi’s multi-alignment strategy as a key pillar in projecting India's voice globally.At one stage, Tharoor said Modi’s foreign policy was remarkable as the Prime Minister was maintaining excellent relations with Russia while simultaneously pursuing strategic relations with the USA. Modi has raised Bharat as a powerful and independent force and has put forward a policy of “multi-alignment”.In May last year, during the inauguration of the Vizhinjam International Seaport in Thiruvananthapuram, Prime Minister Modi acknowledged the presence of Tharoor on stage and remarked that it would give "sleepless nights" to many in the opposition INDIA bloc.
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi held a meeting with Tharoor in January this year ahead of assembly elections in Kerala and tried to sort out the differences and project a unified picture.Tharoor has all along defended his remarks and has claimed that his stand on several international issues was "pro-India, and not pro-BJP," stressing that national interest transcends party lines.Clearly, for Shashi Tharoor, his remarks on Brics are par for the course. It is the Congress that has to decide - how to handle the independent views of its MP from Thiruvananthapuram.

In Summary
- The Redmi Turbo 5 sees the Redmi brand return to a higher price point. It had earlier released the K series in this segment.
- The Redmi Turbo 5 follows Redmi’s classic formula of offering very good specs at surprisingly affordable prices. Its highlights are a powerful chip and a large Silicon Carbon battery.
- Priced at Rs 41,999, the Redmi Turbo 5 is one of the best options for those looking for something close to a budget flagship in an era of rapidly rising prices.
Redmi is mainly known for its budget-friendly devices, mostly in the mid- and lower-mid segment. It has occasionally released slightly more expensive devices, most notably in its K series, but has then gone back to the comfort of the Redmis and Redmi Notes. Now, as phone prices get on an upward-heading escalator, Redmi is getting back into the higher price zone with the Redmi Turbo 5. It comes with a starting price of Rs. 41,999, and while that may seem a bit on the premium side for a Redmi smartphone, it brings an equally premium spec sheet to the table. But can it help Redmi stretch beyond Note-land? Let’s find out!
Table of Contents
Redmi Turbo 5 design and appearance: Classy, yet not-so-loud appearance
The Redmi Turbo 5 does not come with a radically new design – it looks very similar to its cousin, the Poco X8 Pro. And that is a good thing. The phone has all the design elements that make up a trendy smartphone in today’s day and age – a tall, display dominated front which is surrounded by razor thin bezels, a flat back with two circular camera rings jutting out just a little parked on the top left side, and has those flat sides that have become an essential part of a modern day smartphone’s anatomy.
While not out of the box, the Turbo 5 still has a few distinct design touches that catch attention, the kind that are not obvious or scream for attention, but do not get lost completely either. The right side of the back comes with a thick vertical strip filled with very dainty checkered patterns, and the cameras seem like two independent lenses stacked together, but there is a subtle capsule outline encasing them. The two camera lenses also have LED rings inside them, which is a nice conversation starter.
We received the Turbo White variant of the smartphone, which has a red Redmi logo near the base of the back. The cameras and the power/lock button also come with a very distinct red accent. These subtle touches make the design of the Redmi Turbo 5 give it a personality of sorts, making it stand out in the crowd. The back comes with a matte finish, which keeps smudges and scratches at bay and keeps the phone relatively clean. The metallic frame (a pleasant surprise at this price) is home to a handful of features as well. The top carries an infrared port while the base holds a SIM card tray, a USB Type-C port, and a speaker grille. The left side is bare while the right one bears the volume rocker and the power lock button.
Although relatively light for the size of the battery it carries (more about that later), the phone is not exactly light. It weighs 204 grams, and you can feel the weight in hand and even when the phone is in your pocket. At 157.5 mm, the Redmi Turbo 5 falls somewhere between large (160 mm and above) and compact phones (153 mm and below). It is 75.2 mm wide and, at 8.18 mm, is impressively slim, again considering the size of its battery. It is quite a sturdy phone with Gorilla Glass 7i protection on its front and back, and with IP68 and IP69K ratings for dust and water resistance, which means it can easily survive a fall in the water.
At first glance, the Redmi Turbo 5 might seem routine, but give it more attention, and little details start to pop up, and you start appreciating it for its classy, yet not-so-loud appearance.
Redmi Turbo 5 Specs: Ticks a surprising number of boxes
At a time when brands are cutting spec corners, the Redmi Turbo 5 ticks a surprising number of boxes. The phone is powered by a MediaTek Dimensity 8500 Ultra processor, which is considered to be in the budget flagship zone, and is paired with 8 GB and 12 GB RAM options and 256 GB of storage. What’s more, the 12 GB RAM variant comes with LPDDR5X RAM, and the storage on both variants is UFS 4.1. On paper, this is a very powerful setup for the price, which can not only run your everyday smartphone tasks but even handle high-end gaming.
The phone comes with a 6.59-inch AMOLED full HD+ (2756 x 1268) display with 120 Hz refresh rate and a peak brightness of 3500 nits, which can actually cover as much as 25 per cent of the display, instead of being isolated to a tiny section. Photography is handled by a dual camera setup on the back comprising a 50 megapixel Sony IMX882 main sensor with OIS, and an 8 megapixel ultrawide sensor, while a 20 megapixel sensor on the front handles selfies.
The Turbo 5 also packs in some very impressive battery numbers – it brings a sizable 7540 mAh Silicon Carbon battery (a rarity at this price, actually at any price) with support for 100W charging and 27W reverse charging. Also on board are stereo speakers, an in-display fingerprint scanner, and an IR blaster. Like all Redmi devices, the Turbo 5 also runs on Android 16 topped with Xiaomi’s HyperOS 3. Xiaomi promises four years of software and six years of security updates.
In sheer spec terms, this is one of the best specced devices out there in its segment. Some might find the display a little small, but the power of that processor and the RAM and storage options will attract gamers on a budget.
Redmi Turbo 5 Performance: A smooth, powerful operator
The Redmi Turbo 5’s speedy processor+ RAM+ storage set up, reflects in its performance as well. The phone sails smoothly through everyday duties. It moves from app to app smoothly, handles multi-tasking without a hiccup, keeps going through intense social media scrolls, and binge sessions on OTT. The phone can also handle high-end games like Call of Duty and BGMI at 120 fps for long-ish sessions. Although it does get warm while going through power-hungry tasks, the temperature comes down quickly enough.
The AMOLED display with a 120 Hz refresh rate does not disappoint. It delivers a very rich contrast with vibrant colors and is bright enough not to dull down against a very harsh sun either. The 120 Hz refresh rate kept scrolling through social media breezy. The in-display fingerprint scanner works smoothly as well. This, combined with the loud and clear stereo speakers, makes the phone a multimedia master. We did not face any call drops or connectivity issues with the phone either.
Redmi Turbo 5 Cameras: One sensor show (censor the others)
Cameras are not the forte of the Redmi Turbo 5. There are three sensors on the phone, but all the photography weight rests on the 50-megapixel main sensor’s shoulders. This performs well in daylight conditions, capturing a good amount of detail and producing sharp images, so much so that the photos look decent even after a little zoom-in. The colors seem slightly more vibrant than reality but never to a point of looking unnatural. The details do take a very marginal hit in low light, but the presence of OIS helps, and Night mode on the device also improves results a fair bit. A number of other modes are built right into the native camera app, which offer a lot of scope for creative photography.
The 8-megapixel ultrawide sensor is capable of capturing a wider area, but it does not really do an impressive job. The colors remain nice and vibrant, but the details take a nose dive, resulting in images that look noisier, especially when compared to the main sensor. Matters only get worse as the light dims down. The sensor is usable and will allow you to take some quick snaps for social media in good light conditions, but do not pin your photography hopes on it. The 20-megapixel sensor on the front delivers social media-ready snaps but has the tendency to smooth out skin texture even with no ‘beauty mode’ on. The colors also lean towards being a little oversaturated, but you can get good casual snaps, and video calls are handled well.
The main camera supports 4K video at 60 fps, but the other two cameras are limited to 1080p at 60 fps. The video performance of the main camera sensor is good in daylight and even in low-light conditions, but the others miss the mark a bit. Overall, the 50-megapixel camera is the star of the Redmi Turbo 5’s camera show, while the other two are just supporting staff.
Redmi Turbo 5 software and UI: Very nice HyperOS, but loaded with third-party apps
The Redmi Turbo 5 runs on HyperOS 3. Now, HyperOS has been one of the most intuitive, simple, and functional Android skins since its MIUI days, and while that still largely remains true, the phone comes loaded with a plethora of third-party apps. This really makes the experience feel very cluttered and might even seem overwhelming to those new to the UI. Most of these third-party apps can be uninstalled, thankfully.
That said, features like Xiaomi Interconnectivity that not only allow you to connect your smartphone with other HyperOS products but with other gadgets as well, letting you create a hybrid ecosystem, give HyperOS its productivity edge. Top this with add-ons like Hyper Island (similar to Dynamic Island on the iPhone), and AI features like AI Translate, writing assist, call transcription, and a range of customizations, and HyperOS comes across as a very functionality-forward UI. The LED rings around the camera sensors that light up when you get notifications or calls were actually very handy, even while being a nice party trick as well.
Redmi Turbo 5 Battery: Lasts for days, gets charged in a jiffy
The phone’s massive 7540 mAh battery can see you through even the heaviest work days. Emails, messaging, gaming, photography- we did all of that and more with the smartphone, and it still had some juice left even after a day. If you are someone who does not push their device as much, the phone would easily see off more than two days on a single charge. It comes with 100W fast charging support with a 100W brick in the box, which means you get a fully charged phone in slightly over an hour, while the phone goes from 0-50 percent in about 30 minutes. This makes the Redmi Turbo 5 a device that will not only last for day(s) but will also get charged in a jiffy. The reverse charging feature is quite handy too and charges our TWS at a very decent speed.
Redmi Turbo 5 Price: Typically Redmi!
The Redmi Turbo 5 is available in two RAM variants – 8 GB and 12 GB, while the storage remains 256 GB for both options. Although the phone was initially launched at Rs 37,999, this price has since been revised, given rising costs of inputs. The 8 GB/ 256 GB version of the phone is now priced at Rs. 41,999, while the 12 GB/ 256 GB version is priced at Rs. 46,999.
It might have a much higher starting price than the Redmi Note series, but the Redmi Turbo 5 brings a solid spec sheet to the table at a price tag that is typically Redmi. While there are other devices in its price range, at the time of writing, none quite match its price-to-spec equation.
Perhaps the one that comes closest is its own cousin, the Poco X8 Pro, which comes with a similar processor and a similarly sized display at Rs 39,999, but has a smaller battery. Devices like the OnePlus Nord 6 come with a comparable Qualcomm Snapdragon 8s Gen 4 chip, but are more expensive at Rs 46,999, while the recently launched Vivo S2 brings a sleeker design and bigger display to the table at Rs 39,999 but loses out in terms of processor muscle.
Redmi Turbo 5 Review Verdict: A phone that does everything well
It might come with a higher price tag, but the Redmi Turbo 5 is a typical Redmi smartphone in more than one aspect. It delivers a very consistent performance across multiple segments, making it one of the most reliable and powerful options at its price point (typical Redmi!). Its gaming and general performance are both quite smooth; the main camera delivers good snaps, its battery is perhaps its biggest USP, and the display combined with the stereo speakers make it an entertainment master. The price tag is a little higher than some might expect, but the Redmi Turbo 5 is a device for those who are looking for a very good everyday phone that does almost everything well.
- Smart design, sturdy build
- Gorgeous display
- Very good speakers
- Long battery that charges swiftly too
- Good gaming and multimedia performance
- Smooth overall performance
- Ultrawide camera is average
- Bloatware in UI

Leader of Opposition in Bihar Legislative Assembly Tejashwi Yadav on Friday (September 11, 2026) wrote to Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary and demanded life-size statues of the late former Union Minister Sharad Yadav, the late Raghuvansh Prasad Singh, and the late Ram Vilas Paswan in the state, and also to declare their anniversaries as state functions.
His move is seen as an addition to Rashtriya Janata Dal’s (RJD) broader plan of asserting itself as a party which stands for the “A to Z” castes and communities. It also signals that the RJD is going beyond its traditional MY (Muslim-Yadav) vote bank, offering an inclusive coalition aimed at taking ahead both backwards and forward castes together.
Sharad Yadav belonged to the OBC (Other Backwards Classes), whereas Mr. Paswan was from Scheduled Caste (SC) and Mr. Singh was a Rajput, an upper-caste leader. All three leaders had earlier served in the Central government as Union Ministers.
“The late Raghuvansh Prasad, the late Sharad Yadav, and the late Ram Vilas were not only distinguished figures of the state but also stalwart socialist leaders. Through their social commitment and active political lives, these leaders rendered remarkable service to Bihar. They were illustrious sons of the nation, and we, the people of Bihar, will forever remain indebted to them for their personalities and their contributions,”Mr. Yadav wrote.
In the letter, the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) National Working President Mr. Yadav also reminded that a few days before his passing, the late Raghuvansh Babu had expressed a desire—via a letter addressed to the then Chief Minister of Bihar Nitish Kumar—to have certain demands fulfilled.
“Even after six years, no positive action has been taken regarding those demands. I am confident that you will take the necessary steps to fulfil his pending requests. Honouring and fulfilling the late Raghuvansh Babu’s final wishes would be a true tribute to him,”Mr. Yadav said.
In his final days, Mr. Singh had sent three separate letters to Mr. Kumar with the demands of bringing an amendment for MGNREGA, which is now known as VB G RAM G (Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin), holding the Republic Day flag hoisting in Vaishali and bringing back bhiksha patra (alms bowl) of Lord Buddha from Afghanistan.
Describing Sharad Yadav, the RJD leader said that he was active for a long period in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, representing Bihar, and was a towering socialist leader.
“Throughout his life, he championed the politics of ‘social justice,’ making unprecedented contributions to the upliftment of the downtrodden and backward classes and improving the standard of living for the common man. Similarly, the late Ram Vilas Paswan was a proponent of egalitarian development and socialism. He dedicated his entire life to the social upliftment, struggle, security, and development of the oppressed, downtrodden, and marginalised sections of society,”Mr. Yadav wrote.

ESDS Software Solution extended its post-listing surge into a sixth consecutive trading session today, with its shares touching the upper circuit once again and climbing to more than four times their IPO price. The rally underscores strong investor appetite for the enterprise cloud and AI infrastructure play. Shares of the enterprise cloud and AI company jumped 10% to touch an intraday high of ₹1,740.40 on the NSE. However, the stock subsequently pared some of its gains and was trading 9.7% higher at ₹1,735 as of 14:00 IST. At its intraday high, ESDS was trading 305.7% above its IPO issue price of ₹429 per share. On the BSE, ESDS shares remained locked at the 10% upper circuit of ₹1,716.35. At this price, the stock was up 300.1% from the issue price, while the company’s market capitalisation stood at ₹20,117.5 Cr (about $xx Bn). ESDS made its stock market debut on September 4, listing at ₹757 on the NSE, a premium of 76.5% over its issue price. On the BSE, the shares listed at ₹746.30, nearly 74% above the issue price. The stock subsequently hit its 20% upper circuit at ₹908.40 on the NSE and ₹895.55 on the BSE on the listing day. It has continued to hit its upper circuit in every trading session since then. After being locked at the 20% upper circuit for three consecutive sessions, the stock’s circuit filter was reduced to 10%. The rally has also drawn regulatory scrutiny. The BSE sought a clarification from ESDS earlier this week over the sharp movement in its share price. The company said it was unaware of any undisclosed information that could explain the surge. “The company is not aware of any specific reason for the significant movement in the price of its security,” ESDS said, adding that the movement in its share price and trading volumes was consistent with the activity typically observed in a newly listed security. ESDS’ ₹720 Cr IPO, comprising entirely a fresh issue of shares, was subscribed 135.88X during its three-day bidding period. Ahead of the IPO, ESDS raised ₹216 Cr from anchor investors by allotting 50.3 Lakh shares to 19 entities at ₹429 apiece. The anchor investors included Motilal Oswal Mutual Fund, Bandhan Mutual Fund, Quant Mutual Fund, ITI Mutual Fund, and JM Flexicap Fund, among others. Founded in 2005, Nashik-based ESDS provides cloud computing, data centre, managed services, and AI-led digital solutions to government and enterprise customers. The company plans to deploy ₹576 Cr from the net IPO proceeds towards purchasing and installing cloud computing equipment and other infrastructure at its data centres in Airoli, Bengaluru, Mohali, and Nashik. A portion of the proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes. On the financial front, ESDS’ consolidated net profit more than doubled to ₹120.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹55.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue increased 30.7% to ₹472.2 Cr from ₹361.3 Cr in FY25.

The trip from Yokohama to Tohoku and back began at 4:40 a.m. at a local bus stop — where we lined up with a surprisingly large crowd and some early-rising mosquitoes — and ended aboard a reserved-seat green car that pulled into Yokohama Station, having freed us from battling for space on the last leg of our long train journey.
In between, my 11-year-old son and I were on a five-day trip that took us to the cities of Sendai and Ishinomaki in Japan’s northeast region. The catch: We could ride only local trains, a constraint of Japan Railway’s Seishun 18 ticket, which can be used during set periods every spring, summer and winter.
The ticket, which debuted in 1982, holds legendary status among rail-travel fans (while seishun means “youth,” there is no age limit). But a host of rule changes deployed in 2024 took the wind out of its pantographs. I planned this journey to put the revamped version to the test, convinced I could make it worthwhile despite the objectively worse conditions.

President Donald Trump on Wednesday said that he would pay $5,000 to every adult US citizen if Republicans retained control of the US House and Senate in the midterm elections, seemingly in an effort to incentivize votes for his party.
“Here is my promise: If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate,” Trump said, “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.”
“That alone should win the midterms,” he added.
The outlandish remarks came midway through Trump’s at times freewheeling speech at the Republican midterm convention the GOP is holding in Texas, as part of an effort to drive turnout among Trump’s base this November, and were quickly shot down as unaffordable.
It’s unclear whether the “Trump Dividend,” as he’s calling it, was a serious proposal or an attempt to galvanize the president’s base to turn out on election day, after he also previously promised payouts like a $5,000 “DOGE dividend” or a $2,000-per-person tariff check—neither of which has happened. Any attempt to make real on the offer would need congressional approval.
Vice president JD Vance appeared to walk back Trump’s offer in an interview following the speech, saying it wouldn’t go to wealthy Americans, but also suggested it could be paid for by US tariff revenues. “A one-time payment of this size would wipe out about a decade’s tariff revenue at current tariff levels,” wrote Erica York, senior economist at the Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy, on X.
Responding to a Fox News question that “critics will say the president is bribing voters and he’s bankrupting the country,” Vance said: “Tariffs have generated a lot of revenues. The president is saying, if you keep us in power, then you will share in some of the benefit of this incredible wealth that we are creating.”
The rough total cost of paying out $5,000 to about 240 million adults in the US would amount to $1.2 trillion, a price tag that exceeds the roughly $284 billion in gross customs revenue collected between January 2025 and June 2026, according to the University of Pennsylvania.
The shortfall would be even greater after accounting for tariff refunds the Trump administration is compelled to pay after the US Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump had unlawfully imposed tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977.
Following orders from the Court of International Trade, the administration has started to refund some of the $160 billion collected from tariffs, plus interest, which is accruing at an estimated rate of about $650 million per month.
After accounting for refunds, the administration’s net revenue from tariffs will come out to roughly $118 billion, meaning Trump would need to have Congress approve an additional $1.08 trillion, on top of the president’s proposed $1.86 trillion discretionary budget request for fiscal year 2027.
The principal concern for the Republican National Committee has been that the midterm elections will be decided in large part by voter turnout, which could be depressed for Republicans because Trump will not be on the ballot.

Mumbai has seen a surge in H1N1 (swine flu) cases over the last three months, as the number of cases have jumped to 441 this year from 62 during same period last year. This marks a 612% rise, while for malaria the cases have seen a 20% rise.
According to Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC)’s monsoon data for June, July, and August, 441 cases of H1N1, and 4,485 malaria cases were recorded between June and August as compared to 3,733 last year.
To curb the surge of swine flu, BMC has been screening suspected H1N1 patients, and prescribing Oseltamivir. Further, surveys are being conducted in the affected regions, where the H1N1 positive cases have been located.
The BMC said suspected H1N1 patients are being screened and treated with oseltamivir wherever required. Close contacts of infected patients are being monitored for 10 days, while door-to-door surveys are being conducted in affected areas. BMC also clarified that they have prepared ventilators, PPE kits, reserved beds and medicines to manage patients for hospitalisation.’
Mumbai’s E-ward, K-West ward, G-South ward, F-South ward, and H-West ward have so far recorded the highest cases of malaria. To combat the vector-borne disease, BMC has increased the field-level monitoring in most affected areas. They have surveyed 52,197 potential breeding sites for malaria control. Anopheles mosquito breeding sites were detected at 8,055 locations, along with 12,55,469 potential mosquito breeding sites for dengue control, and Aedes mosquito breeding at 27,352 areas.
Decline in monsoon related illnesses.
Mumbai saw a decline in dengue cases,leptospirosis cases, COVID-19 cases, Chikungunya, and Gastroenteritis. According to BMC data, COVID-19 cases dropped drastically by 77% this year, as 151 cases were recorded compared to last year’s 668. For dengue the fall has been by 20% — 1,563 patients recorded this year in June, July, and August. For chikungunya, cases have dropped from 370 to 46, a decrease of 87%.
Leptospirosis cases declined by 37% — from 406 to 255, while gastroenteritis cases dropped from 2,197 to 1,954, this year.

Trump Loses the Other Strait
The Houthi advance is bad news for the U.S., and even worse news for Saudi Arabia.
As recently as last week, the Iran war appeared to be turning slightly in America’s favor. The Houthis—the Yemen-based militia that is Iran’s most formidable remaining ally in the Middle East—were under pressure from their local rivals, and the Saudi air force was pounding them with air strikes. The president of Yemen’s internationally recognized government issued a triumphant statement declaring that the Houthis’ miscalculations “will open the door to their complete collapse.” With their Houthi partners wounded, Iran’s leaders would have one more reason to back down and agree to Donald Trump’s terms.
Yesterday morning, those delusions drifted away like smoke as Houthi forces broke through their enemies’ defenses and seized the towns and islands around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the most important maritime choke points in the world.
That loss leaves Trump, who had been hoping to win back control of the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, with a bitter surprise. His enemies now control both of the two important straits in the Middle East, through which a combined total of about a third of the world’s oil shipments pass every day.
It also underscores a stubborn fact: For all the setbacks suffered by Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” over the past year or two, its forces retain an ideological fervor and an esprit de corps that is sorely lacking on the other side. The Gulf states’ failure to work together against the Houthis has been catastrophic, and it echoes Trump’s own failure to devise a plausible or coordinated strategy against Iran.
Although the Houthis already had the ability to threaten shipping in the Red Sea, the capture of the Bab el-Mandeb “means you can literally sit on the coast and fire at passing ships,” April Longley Alley, a Yemen expert at the Washington Institute on Near East Policy and the former political adviser to the United Nations special envoy for Yemen, told me. “It makes it easier and cheaper, and it solidifies, from a military and political point of view, that they have a stranglehold on the strait.”
The United States might not be able to do much about this, even if the Pentagon launches a new round of air strikes on the Houthis. (The Saudi leader, Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman, called Trump twice yesterday urging him to strike the Houthis, Axios reported.) Bombs and missiles would achieve little without a ground force to take advantage of them, and America’s Yemeni allies are now battered and divided. The Trump administration waged a seven-week war against the group last year, and although it succeeded in killing some Houthi commanders, it did not dislodge the group or alter its ability to wage war, as Trump had promised.
The Houthi advance is even worse news for Saudi Arabia. For many years, the Saudis have been struggling to tamp down the Houthi threat on its border. Now the Houthis have inherited a great deal of Saudi and Emirati supplies left behind by the official Yemeni government’s retreating forces. A video circulated yesterday of Mohammad Ali al-Houthi, one of the group’s top commanders and a cousin of its supreme leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, riding though Mokha in an Emirati armored vehicle.
The mess that Saudi Arabia faces in Yemen is partly of its own making. The Houthis were born three decades ago in reaction to Saudi meddling in Yemen’s religious and political sphere. In December, tensions between the Saudi and Emirati leadership led Riyadh to demand that the Emiratis—their nominal allies—withdraw from Yemen, leaving the Saudis in charge of a patchwork of militias with divided loyalties. The various Yemeni factions continued to squabble among themselves even as their Houthi enemies were at the gates.
“There was no coordination between commanders, between the intelligence and the drones, between the coast guard and the army—nothing,” Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at the think tank Chatham House, told me.
The Houthis have clearly benefited from the Gulf’s disunity. “Last time the Houthis made a breakthrough at Marib in 2022, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia were able to jointly support a devastatingly effective Yemeni-government counterattack,” Michael Knights, the head of research at the consultancy Horizon Engage, told me.
The Houthis, meanwhile, were disciplined and focused. “They sacrificed hundreds if not thousands of fighters,” a member of Yemen’s officially recognized government, who asked not to be identified for fear of repercussions, told me. “Our bullshit activists were putting out fake news about victories, while the Houthis were working in silence.”
With the momentum on their side, the Houthis could now go on to seize more terrain in other parts of Yemen, including Marib province, where much of Yemen’s oil is located. They could also extend their power bloodlessly, by cutting deals with tribal and regional leaders in the south and east. All of this would further consolidate their power and strengthen their Iranian patrons.
The Houthi victories have already put into doubt the value of the Mecca Alliance, the mutual-defense pact formed in August by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey. Islamabad and Ankara have shown no inclination to help the Saudis, despite a rash of recent Houthi strikes on targets in southern Saudi Arabia.
Iran’s vaunted Axis of Resistance is not a bulletproof covenant either. The Houthis were absent earlier this year when the United States and Israel started bombing Iran.
But unlike their enemies, the Houthis and the Iranians have a deep ideological bond, one that their soldiers willingly die for. And the Houthis do not need to win every battle. As long as they can sink an occasional oil tanker, they will hold a whip hand over their Saudi neighbors, and over the rest of the world too.

- The claim that attendees of the 2026 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas, caused an outage of popular gay dating app Grindr circulated online in September 2026.
- The rumor stems from incident reports shared on social media, taken from a third-party service called Downdetector during the time of the event. However, the incidents were not isolated to Dallas, and Grindr itself did not report any major outages connected to the event.
- A spokesperson for Grindr told Snopes, "Grindr has not experienced recent outages. Third party sources that often make these claims rely on unreliable data such as self-reporting, while Grindr reports outages directly on its status page." The status page showed no outages in August or September 2026.

With high-stakes midterms looming in November 2026, the Republican National Convention took place in Dallas, Texas, on Sept. 9 and 10, 2026. Rumors spread that the convention's attendees were causing an outage of the popular gay dating app Grindr.
People on social media sites shared a purported screenshot that showed a map depicting hotspots of Grindr outages across the country, with the brightest spot focused on Dallas.
The popularity of the rumor led many Snopes readers to reach out via email and social media, asking if the claim was true.
We weren't able to independently verify claims of Grindr outages in Dallas, so we've left this claim unrated. The screenshots appeared to be taken from Downdetector, a third-party service that tracks outages of popular services, and did not show signs of fabrication or misleading editing.
According to Downdetector, users did report incidents at the time and location in question, but the incidents reported on Sept. 9 and 10 were not limited to Dallas or even Texas. There was also no way to confirm that the reports reflected real issues with the app, as Downdetector does not require users to submit any proof.
Grindr itself did not report any outages during that time.
A spokesperson for Grindr told Snopes via email: "Grindr has not experienced recent outages. Third party sources that often make these claims rely on unreliable data such as self-reporting, while Grindr reports outages directly on its status page."
The company's status page showed no outages or incidents in August or September 2026.
Downdetector tracks data for the prior 24 hours and does not archive its history.
Snopes first checked Downdetector's page for Grindr on Sept. 10, 2026. It showed a spike of reported outages on Sept. 9 around 8:49 p.m., with the highest number of reports clocked at 460.
Grindr outage report on Sept. 10, 2026. (Downdetector)
When we checked Downdetector on Sept. 11, the past 24 hours showed a peak of only 73 reports around 3:18 p.m. on Sept. 10.
Grindr outage report on Sept. 11, 2026. (Downdetector)
The incident heat map provided by Downdetector, which we first checked on Sept. 10, showed the highest concentration of outages in Dallas and Austin, Texas, but also indicated reports were being submitted in other major cities like New York, Boston and Chicago.
Grindr outage map on Sept. 10, 2026. (Downdetector)
A look at the same map one day later showed lower concentrations of reports of problems in the same cities.
(Grindr outage map on Sept. 11, 2026. (Downdetector))
The page explains that Downdetector "calculates a baseline volume of typical problem reports for each service monitored" based on an average over six months, and "only reports an incident when the number of problem reports is significantly higher than the baseline."
Further, Downdetector allows users reporting the issues to comment on the page. During the period of Snopes' review for this claim, multiple comments on Grindr's Downdetector page referenced the RNC with comments like, "Convention in Dallas, as always." There was no indication those comments came from people genuinely experiencing connection issues in Dallas.
So while it appeared that some users may have had trouble with the service on Sept. 9 and 10, 2026, including in and around the area where the RNC was being held, there was not enough evidence to conclude without a doubt that the reported errors were entirely authentic or that they were indeed caused specifically by attendees at the RNC.
We reached out to Ookla, the parent company of Downdetector, for further comment and will update this article if we hear back.
For further reading, we've investigated similar claims about Grindr, such as rumors of alleged Grindr outages near Charlie Kirk's memorial in September 2025.

Japan’s Digital Agency said Friday that about 246,000 sets of personal information, including the names and addresses of government employees, may have been leaked due to unauthorized access to a network system operated by the agency.
So far, no secondary damage, such as the misuse of the possibly leaked personal information, has been confirmed.
The information also included email addresses and phone numbers, but not My Number personal identification numbers or bank account information.
On June 25, the agency detected suspicious access to a large number of files on the server from an account of system maintenance and operation staff. It then began investigating the incident and found on July 9 that there had been unauthorized access from an external third party.
The agency said in a statement that it is deeply sorry for causing problems and anxiety to those concerned.

UK's Charity Commission issues regulatory advice to Board of Deputies following ICJP complaint
The UK’s Charity Commission has reminded a British charity funding the Board of Deputies of British Jews that risks arise when a charity ‘is, or perceived to be, closely associated with a company’, following a protest against a London real estate event that promoted properties in illegal Israeli settlements.
The regulatory guidance and advice to the trustees of the Board of Deputies Charitable Foundation, which also executes the activities of the Board of Deputies of British Jews (BDBJ), comes in response to a complaint filed by the International Centre of Justice for Palestinians (ICJP).
In a statement, ICJP said that the Board of Deputies of British Jews had claimed that a protest demonstration held outside Edgware United Synagogue, which hosted the Great Israeli Real Estate Event, was organised on “bogus grounds”.
The ICJP said that the Board made the accusations as it had relied on assurances from the event organisers that properties in the illegal settlements would not be marketed.
It characterised the protest as an attempt to “harass and intimidate members of the Jewish community”.
