But the organisers later apologised for including several properties in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem in their brochure.
“ICJP’s complaint raised concerns about the failure to correct or withdraw the Board’s statements after evidence emerged substantiating the protesters’ concerns,” the statement said.
“It argued that the statements risked misrepresenting a protest against activities connected to Israel’s illegal settlement enterprise as an attack upon a synagogue or the Jewish community.”
In its response, the charity regulator noted that the statements appeared to have been issued by The Board of Deputies of British Jews Limited, rather than the charitable foundation itself.
“Nevertheless, the Commission considered it appropriate to issue advice and guidance to the charity’s trustees under section 15(2) of the Charities Act 2011,” ICJP said.
“The Commission confirmed that it has reminded the charity’s trustees of the risks that arise where a charity ‘is, or is perceived to be, closely associated with a company, particularly in relation to public statements and communications.’”
The Commission will retain the information ICJP provided and may take it into account in any future regulatory engagement with the charity, ICJP said.
Shaima Dallali, ICJP’s legal researcher, said: “Palestinians are being driven from their land while that same land is marketed to buyers abroad, including in the UK. These are not ordinary property exhibitions. They are part of the economic infrastructure that sustains Israel’s unlawful occupation and settlement enterprise. Those who protested were challenging precisely the activity that the UK government is now moving to prohibit.”
“The Board of Deputies must correct the public record,” Dallali said.
Charity Commission Criticism
In a statement to MEE on 13 August, the Charity Commission criticised trustees of the Edgware United Synagogue in London for hosting the event.
The commission said it had decided to review a recent decision to close a compliance case involving the charity.
It told MEE that "should any further concerns about the charity arise, we will consider escalating our regulatory engagement".
It said: "We share concerns about the potential impact, including on public trust and confidence, of registered charities being seen to actively assist in the development or expansion of illegal settlements in Palestine.
"We are also clear that charity premises must not be misused.
"Our initial compliance case found that despite their own misgivings about the event, and an organisation-wide decision to not permit it in their premises, the charity’s trustees allowed it to go ahead in one of its synagogues and did not put in place sufficient checks and controls to make sure the terms of that booking were kept."
Properties in illegal settlements advertised
Four days before the event, Middle East Eye investigation uncovered previously unreported details of the event’s connection to illegal Israeli settlements.
Emanuel Vatari, CEO of one of the sponsors of the event, the Emanuel Group, posted a list of companies participating on his Facebook page.
The list included Harey Zahav, an Israeli real estate development company whose website advertises property in Negohot, an illegal Israeli settlement in the southern Hebron Hills in the occupied West Bank.
Also on the list was The Meshulam Levinstein Group, a collection of engineering, construction and real estate companies.
It has built residential and commercial projects in illegal settlements in both the occupied West Bank and Jerusalem.
One was a housing project and a commercial centre it built in the settlement neighbourhood of Homat Shmuel in occupied East Jerusalem.
Another participant is the Tivuch Shelly real estate agency, which advertises properties in Ma'ale Adunim - a West Bank settlement.
MEE had sent evidence of the event's connections to companies involved in illegal settlements to the Foreign Office.
A Foreign Office spokesperson responded: "Israeli settlements are illegal under international law and are a fundamental threat to long-term peace and security for both Israelis and Palestinians.
"On 9 June, we updated our Business Risk Guidance to make it clear and unambiguous: if you are a British citizen or business, you should not conduct any economic and financial activities in illegal Israeli settlements.”

Former Uttarakhand Chief Minister and Congress leader Harish Rawat has tendered his resignation from the Uttarakhand Pradesh Congress Committee and a permanent invitee member of the Congress Working Committee at the national level on Saturday (September 12, 2026) after the Enforcement Directorate (ED) recovered cash, jewellery and other valuables from the possession of his PA, Chandan Singh Jeena.
Taking it to X after the ED raid, Mr. Rawat said, “I have taken a major decision: I am not (in) any government position, so what resignation would I tender from that! Yes, I am a member of the executive of the Uttarakhand Pradesh Congress Committee and a permanent invitee member of the Congress Working Committee at the national level, and with utmost humility, I wish to step down from both these positions, because no weakness should come into the party’s struggle on my account.”
The ED on Friday (September 11) said it conducted searches linked to the 2016 VPDO exam case, seizing ₹32 lakh, gold, and luxury watches from Harish Rawat’s PA. It seized an “unaccounted” sum of ₹32 lakh, 13 gold coins and seven gold chains weighing about 200.5 gm, and 12 luxury wristwatches of expensive brands from Chandan Singh Jeena’s premises.
Mr. Rawat acknowledged that Jeena had served as his OSD and had handled important responsibilities during the various positions he held, both in the party and in government. Describing Jeena as a “very decent, humble and hard-working person”, Mr. Rawat said, “If he tampered with OMR sheets during the recruitment of Gram Sevaks, and if there is evidence to prove that he committed any such wrongdoing, I am ashamed of such an alleged audacious act. However, I do not believe this allegation at all.”
The former Chief Minister said the stakes in the Uttarakhand elections were very high. “Whenever anyone used to ask me when the elections would be held, I would jokingly say that the elections would take place when the CBI knocked on my door. If it has not come yet, it means the elections will be held in March-April next year,” he said.
“However, this time, instead of knocking on my door, an attempt has been made to knock on the door of one of my associates and create a narrative,” Mr. Rawat alleged.
He said the Congress party and its workers were united in their fight against corruption. “Rahul Gandhi is also raising his voice against corruption in the education system at the national level through the ‘Students Ki Goonj’ programme,” he said.

US secretary of state Marco Rubio gave new clarity on the approach toward combating drug trafficking in Latin American waters, saying the Trump administration was focused on working with allied countries and aligning with their laws but insisting the military will “still blow up ships if need be.”
The public acknowledgment of a shift in US strategy comes a year after Washington began a campaign of unilateral deadly strikes against those it calls “narco-terrorists” operating boats in international waters.
Late Wednesday, US Southern Command announced the latest such strike in the Caribbean Sea, saying it killed three people. That brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the US military to at least 230 in 69 strikes.
Still, the Trump administration is focused on building agreements for joint operations with allied countries in the region, including Colombia and Ecuador, that comply with their laws in their waters.
“I think its an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters,” Rubio told reporters on a trip to the Ecuadorian capital, Quito.
“The important point is that these routes are being disrupted. These routes are being ended,” he added.
He said the decision is “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depends on the threat and location of the boat.
Recent US interdictions in Latin American waters are unlike the Trump administration’s initial strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats that began in September 2025. People onboard floating refueling stations said to be supporting drug trafficking have been removed and transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. Then the US military blows up the vessels.
The shift comes after a series of strikes on boats over the year on people the Trump administration accused of being “narco-terrorists” without providing evidence.
Rubio’s comments came during a three-nation tour of South America aimed at boosting security cooperation with conservative leaders who have cozied up to Donald Trump.

The US government launched at least three previously unreported investigations into trading on the prediction market Polymarket, according to documents obtained by WIRED through a Freedom of Information Act request.
Voting records from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that regulates prediction markets, shed new light on how the government approaches these investigations. In early May, CFTC chairman Michael Selig approved an order allowing the agency’s enforcement division to launch a private investigation into potential insider trading on Polymarket event contracts related to pardons issued by former president Joseph Biden. The order granted permission to take testimony, obtain subpoenas, administer oaths, and require the production of documents in the course of the investigation.
The documents obtained by WIRED did not specify which trades were under suspicion, but the order came several weeks after an NPR report on a suspicious Polymarket trader who netted over $300,000 on pardon-related markets in the final days of the Biden administration. The trader correctly wagered that the former president would issue preemptive pardons to a number of prominent MAGA critics, including former US representatives Liz Cheney and Adam Kinzinger, and US senator Adam Schiff.
At the end of May, Selig approved another investigation order. This time, the topic was “Iran event contracts” on Polymarket. As with the Biden pardon documents, the investigation order did not provide details, but it came two weeks after 60 Minutes aired a report on a network of suspicious Polymarket accounts that made $2.4 million on Iran-related trades, with a 98 percent win rate.
“If these investigations are being prompted solely by press reports of potential violations of the Commodities Exchange Act, that’s a significant sign of weakness in this regulatory scheme,” says Joseph Konizeski, a former chief trial attorney in the CFTC’s division of enforcement. The agency has come under fire in the second Trump era for its perceived friendliness to the prediction market industry.
In July, Selig greenlit a third investigation, this time focused on suspected insider trading on Google-themed Polymarket event contracts. In an email exchange included in the documents obtained by WIRED, Paul Hayeck, the acting director of the CFTC’s department of enforcement, noted that the investigation would focus on “additional individuals who may have engaged in insider trading related to Google’s 2025 Year in Search Ranking.” Hayeck wrote that the Southern District of New York is conducting a “parallel investigation.” He specified that the CFTC's investigation would be separate from the ongoing case against Michele Spagnuolo, a Google engineer accused of insider trading.
SDNY declined to comment. Google declined to comment. It pointed WIRED to a statement it released in June noting that Spagnuolo was no longer with the company. The CFTC did not respond to requests for comment and questions about the status of the investigations.
“While we do not comment on specific investigations, we regularly refer matters to law enforcement and support ongoing investigations as part of our commitment to protecting the integrity of our markets,” Olivia Chalos, deputy chief legal officer at Polymarket, told WIRED in an email.
The CFTC is also reportedly investigating Polymarket itself. The company, which had its flagship platform banned from the United States in 2022, was permitted to launch a US-regulated version with a narrower set of markets in late 2025. It recently underwent a fundraising round led by Donald Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm, 1789 Capital, which valued the company at $21 billion.
The CFTC has also launched investigations into potential insider trading on Kalshi, Polymarket’s archrival, in the past. According to The New York Times, Kalshi has referred at least 32 cases to the agency. The CFTC fined former US representative George Santos $35,000 for his behavior related to a Kalshi contract about whether he would attend Trump’s 2026 State of the Union address.
Kalshi issued its first-ever lifetime ban to Santos for violating its rules on market manipulation for the same behavior, and also fined him just over $71,000. Santos was not criminally charged.
So far, two arrests have been made stemming from Polymarket insider trading investigations. In April, federal authorities arrested a US special forces officer who prosecutors say used classified information to make more than $400,000 in profits on event contracts related to the capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. And in May, Spagnuolo, who allegedly made over $1.2 million on insider trades, was arrested while traveling to New York. In both cases, the CFTC filed civil charges, and the Department of Justice filed criminal fraud charges. Both men are fighting back by arguing that Polymarket trades are a form of betting and not subject to commodities law.
It’s unclear if the Department of Justice has launched parallel investigations into the Iran War or Biden pardon contracts. The DOJ did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A former CFTC staffer tells WIRED that parallel criminal investigations are likely, “given the significance of the matters.”

Nearly 15 years after first stealing audiences’ funny bones as Fat Amy, Rebel Wilson has provided a new generation with a musical comedy that will have fans laughing and singing along just the same.
In Girl Group, co-written and directed by Wilson, the Australian multihyphenate stars as popstar Tassie Young, who found fame with her four best friends when they were discovered at a talent show in 1996.
But with Tassie’s party girl ways forcing her out of the group in 2006, she finds out her former bandmates are having a reunion tour in the present and don’t want her back.
After a DUI arrest, Tassie is forced to teach music to a group of teen girls at East Hollywood Community Center, where she discovers their talent and helps them prepare for an audition with a major label.
Watch on Deadline
Wilson hits all the right comedic notes as both star and director, complemented by hilarious performances from an ensemble that includes Jennifer Coolidge as her manager, Randall Park as the community center’s director and Derry Girls alum Jamie-Lee O’Donnell as a rival coach with her own girl group.
The movie is also stacked with cameos from the likes of the Spice Girls’ Mel C, Pussycat Dolls’ Nicole Scherzinger, Sally Hawkins, Chris Colfer and more.
With fun choreographed covers of Spice Girls, Destiny’s Child, Billie Eilish, Chappell Roan and others, the ensemble of newcomers puts their talent on full display, in addition to keeping up with their seasoned co-stars’ comedic chops.
Girl Group is an addictively enjoyable film blends heart and humor, and Wilson has returned to her roots with a fun, character-driven musical comedy that is sure to appeal to anyone who couldn’t stop singing “Cups (When I’m Gone)” for the majority of 2011.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
Good morning. Chelsea Cirruzzo here. Today we remember 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks. While I was too young to have many recollections of the attack, I did grow up in New York and vividly remember the impact it had on the people around me. So, I always take the time each year to reflect.
Today, we’ve published a First Opinion essay by a thoracic surgeon in New York City who treats first responders still facing extraordinary health challenges after being exposed to the toxic aftermath of ground zero. I hope you spend time with it, too.
Trump’s $500 Obamacare promise
President Trump has promised to send $500 refund checks to nearly 1 million Americans on Affordable Care Act plans, who also happen to live mostly in swing states, with checks arriving ahead of the midterms.
The checks will only go out to people who don’t receive federal subsidies for their insurance plans — after Republicans declined to extend enhanced ACA premiums that expired at the end of last year.
The White House said the money will help “Americans most exposed to the higher costs imposed by the Biden administration’s gross mismanagement of Obamacare.”
People are eligible for the $500 if they live in one of the 30 states that use the federal government’s ACA marketplace, such as Ohio and Florida. It’s unclear whether only people with current coverage qualify, or whether people who had plans in the past may also get checks.
My colleagues Bob Herman and Tara Bannow have more on the unclear legality of the move.
Can AI catch a heart attack? The FDA thinks so
A number of artificial intelligence algorithms have promised to help identify and treat heart conditions early, but how about when a patient is actively having a heart attack? Last week, the Food and Drug Administration issued a rare de novo classification to an algorithm from Powerful Medical that aims to help triage patients to the right care when they’re having chest pain. The vast majority of AI devices go to market through the FDA’s 510(k) clearance pathway; fewer than 10 each year receive de novo classification, which typically requires more clinical evidence.
Here’s how the new algorithm, Queen of Hearts, works: It can detect patterns indicating a patient is experiencing the most severe kind of heart attack, when a coronary artery, which supplies blood to the heart, is completely blocked off. In doing so, it can help doctors make sure a patient gets treatment as soon as possible to open up the blockage and restore oxygen to the heart.
My colleague Katie Palmer has more on what it means for patients and doctors if we can more quickly detect these ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction patterns with an EKG.
A valuable childhood cancer treatment with long-term implications
A platinum-based treatment for children with certain cancers can be a lifeline, but it can also cause healthy cells to mutate, potentially increasing the risk of new cancers later in life, my colleague Annalisa Merelli reports.
That’s according to a new study published Thursday in Science, seeking a clearer understanding of the long-term impact of platinum agents in children treated for hepatoblastoma, a rare cancer of the liver that is most commonly diagnosed in childhood.
The study looked at children who had received platinum therapy followed by surgery to remove the tumor. Researchers sampled both healthy and cancerous liver tissue and blood from the patients and compared the results to samples from children given different treatments.
What they found were hundreds of mutations in the samples exposed to platinum, usually found in adult livers. In other words, platinum aged the liver cells of treated children, making them look more like adult liver cells.
Read on for what this means for long-term monitoring and treatment.
Sorry to burst your (bouncy castle) bubble
What kid doesn’t love getting to carom around in a bouncy castle? But the inflated structures could be the source of skin infections, an investigation into a large outbreak of community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus — more commonly known as MRSA — in eastern Ireland reveals.
About four dozen children who attended a community party in August 2025 later developed skin and soft tissue lesions and abscesses caused by the bacterium, Irish public health officials reported Thursday in the online journal Eurosurveillance.
The event, attended by about 120 adults and children, featured three bouncy castles. Many of the kids reportedly spent considerable time — hours, even — playing in them. About a quarter of the cases had symptoms beyond skin lesions, such as fever, nausea, or vomiting. Four of the infected kids were admitted to the hospital, though all recovered. One of the infected children hadn’t attended the party but had close contact with a child who had.
The MRSA outbreak is the largest on record in Ireland. — Helen Branswell
Boycott launched against Diabetes Association includes journal
In the latest escalation of members protesting how the American Diabetes Association has handled the removal of members from its June meeting, four editors of the ADA’s flagship journal will no longer review manuscript submissions. Their move is part of a boycott announced Thursday against the professional organization.
Steven Kahn, the editor-in-chief of Diabetes Care, is one of the five members who were ousted from the conference center in New Orleans for handing out copies of an editorial published in the journal about federal cuts to research funding. The other editors are Cheryl Anderson of UC San Diego, John Buse of the University of North Carolina, and Elizabeth Selvin of Johns Hopkins. At issue are the expulsions, the immediate response by ADA leadership, and the summer-long review of what happened.
“We are aware of the efforts taking place,” an ADA spokesperson said. “We remain focused on serving the millions of people counting on us to deliver on our mission.”
Kahn told STAT their actions are effectively “a strike against a major corporation.”
“Except we’re seeing this now as a boycott by members of a nonprofit organization, where the leadership of the organization is operating like a corporate board, rather than leadership of a membership organization, and the membership has said, ‘We’ve had enough,’” he said. — Elizabeth Cooney

The Alternative für Deutschland is facing scrutiny over the suitability of some of its prospective new MPs – including a former Stasi officer and a former pornography actor – just days after its historic win in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Presented by the AfD’s lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, for a photocall in the state capital of Magdeburg on Thursday, some of the members-elect were revealed to have a range of questionable backgrounds, including criminal records, Stasi pasts and connections to far-right networks.
German media has revealed that among the 39 parliamentarians who will represent constituencies across Saxony-Anhalt in the state parliament, is a man alleged to have participated in pornography films and falsified academic qualifications; a former officer for the East German secret police, the Stasi; and several members under criminal investigation for their involvement in neo-Nazi organisations.
Two MPs are facing investigations into allegations they sought to continue the activities of the banned rightwing extremist organisation Artgemeinschaft, a neopagan group that has embraced nationalist and antisemitic ideas. The younger of the two is also alleged to have violated the law in relation to weapons, according to the public prosecutor’s office. Both reject the allegations.
The erstwhile pornography actor was convicted for stealing bedding in bulk from a hotel. A court confirmed he had been a pornography actor after he contested a local newspaper’s claims. He was expelled from a university after being found to have falsified his school leaving certificate, Die Zeit reported. The MP says he was readmitted after a legal challenge.
An ex-Stasi officer, aged 78, who won a direct mandate in his constituency, has admitted to having worked for the ministry for state security in the communist GDR, focused on East German citizens who wanted to permanently emigrate.
His role as an MP-elect has been criticised by campaign groups on behalf of victims of the former East German dictatorship.
Also, an investigation by the broadcaster ZDF revealed that some AfD ministers-elect who were also members of the previous parliamentary group, had ties to rightwing extremist groups. This included some having been members of the subsequently outlawed Homeland-Loyal German Youth group, HDJ. At one stage one of them had led the organisation, while an adviser to the AfD’s parliamentary group wrote a biography described as an “homage to national socialism”.
Among the prospective MPs are a number with pro-Kremlin links, as well as some who visited members of the Maga movement in Washington.
Asked to respond to the questionable biographies, in particular of the two MPs under criminal investigation, Siegmund, a former fragrance salesman who was unanimously re-elected as the AfD’s parliamentary group leader on Thursday, referred to the men in jest as “the bad guys” and said “we will await the results of the investigations and then discuss them”.
Siegmund himself triggered fierce criticism during the presentation of his new parliamentary group after linking the production of arms in Germany to the party’s planned deportation offensive.
In response to a journalist’s question about the planned opening of an Israeli arms company in the state, Siegmund said: “We do not categorically condemn the production of arms, because we will of course need equivalent resources for the future remigration and deportation offensive. This is also in the interest of internal security, our own instability and national defence.”
The statement was seized on by the party’s opponents. Katja Pähle, the chair of the Social Democrats (SPD) parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt, said Siegmund had issued a “political threat” by suggesting the use of “violence as a political tool”.
“This reveals the ugly face of a political system whose language and ideas are once again reminiscent of totalitarian models,” she said.
Whether the AfD, which secured 44% of the seats, forms a state government, which would make it the first far-right party to gain power in Germany since the second world war, will depend on whether it can find other like-minded MPs who might defect, or a single party willing to support the AfD. So far, the mainstream parties have refused to enter a coalition with the AfD, which has just under half of the 83 seats in the state, three short of an absolute majority.
Protests against the AfD are planned in more than 20 cities across Germany this weekend in response to the party’s win last Sunday, and ahead of two crucial state elections on 20 September, in Berlin and in Mecklenburg Vorpommen, where the AfD are predicted to do well.

Bengaluru-based restaurant company Popo Global, which operates gourmet food brands including The Pizza Bakery, Paris Panini and Smash Guys, has raised ₹532 Cr (around $56 Mn) from Artal Asia. Popo Global did not disclose its valuation and the size of Artal Asia’s stake. Founded in 2017 by brothers Nikhil Gupta and Abhijit “AB” Gupta, Popo Global began with gourmet sourdough pizza brand The Pizza Bakery. It later expanded its portfolio with Paris Panini, which offers French-inspired paninis, sandwiches, wraps, and crepes, and smash burger brand Smash Guys. The company claims to operate 41 outlets across Bengaluru. With the latest investment, Popo Global plans to expand beyond Bengaluru and scale its portfolio of food brands across India. Popo Global said its operating model combines the convenience of quick-service restaurants, the customer experience associated with fine dining, and the scalability of delivery kitchens. The company said its model focuses on core products, dine-in and delivery channels, standardised processes, and restaurant real estate selection. It also claimed to have recorded strong same-store sales growth, repeat rates, and unit economics, but did not disclose the underlying figures. Popo Global added that it had largely bootstrapped its expansion in Bengaluru before the latest transaction. “Bringing Artal Asia into Popo lets us think considerably bigger while keeping the spirit that got us here - never cutting any corners on quality. They have partnered with some of the world's most successful food businesses, and they understand that the product has to stay at the centre of it,” said the cofounders. Artal Asia is an affiliate of global investment firm Artal Group. Its India portfolio includes Capital Foods (later acquired by Tata Consumer Products), Burger Singh, and Jumbotail. The investment comes amid continued investor interest in Indian restaurant and food brands looking to expand their offline presence and enter new markets. Foodtech startup Dil Foods recently raised ₹72 Cr to expand its footprint and launch more cuisine offerings. Similarly, Gen Z-focussed cafe chain Alienkind raised $3.2 Mn in June to enter new markets and support its next phase of growth. Meanwhile, Bengaluru-based bubble tea and QSR brand Boba Bhai raised ₹40 Cr to expand its offline presence earlier this year.

The fire that gutted a passenger ferry in the Philippines, killing at least 35 people, spread so fast that one man did not have time to get a life jacket as others stepped on him in panic.
Fifty-four people are still missing since the fire tore through the ferry Wednesday night (September 9, 2026) near southwestern Palawan province. There were 43 survivors. Images provided by the coast guard showed the charred interior of the ship and what appeared to be human remains, ashes and burnt metal, including a car.
“The fire quickly spread. That’s when I dropped to the ground and my back was burnt,” Arnulfo Nokki Villanueva recounted in a video broadcast by News5. He said that he jumped from a window. “I wanted to get a life jacket but failed to get one because people were stepping on me. People were in panic.”
Rescuers on Thursday (September 10, 2026) struggled to get inside the vessel because of the heat and smoke, slowing efforts to search for passengers who may have been trapped. On Friday (September 11, 2026), the death toll rose to 35 as more bodies were recovered.
The ferry sailed from capital Manila and was around 7.4 kilometres off the village of Turda near its destination of Coron in Palawan province when the fire was reported. The cause of the fire has not been determined.
“It’s painful to think that your child was asking for help while she was burning alive,” Lira Daco said as she waited at a rescue centre in Turda for word about her missing 20-year-old daughter, Cyriel.
“I don’t know how we can find out which one is my child,” she said of the remains found inside the ship. “It’s OK if she just drowned and we can recover her body and give her a proper burial. But now we can’t recognise or hug her.” According to the manifest, 134 people were onboard, 117 of them passengers and 17 crew. The 53-metre vessel had a capacity to carry 306 passengers and 27 crew. Two passengers listed in the manifest reported to authorities that they failed to board, the coast guard said.
Two of the survivors were tourists from Chile, according to Rachel Conserman, a staffer of the ship’s owner Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc. They are recovering from injuries in a hospital in Coron, she said, adding that no other foreigners were known to have been on the ship.
Coron is a popular tourist destination known for clear blue waters, limestone cliffs and rock formations.
Ferries are frequently used for transport in the Philippine archipelago. Sea accidents are not uncommon due to storms, badly maintained vessels, overcrowding and spotty enforcement of safety regulations, especially in remote provinces.
In 1987, the ferry Dona Paz sank after colliding with a fuel tanker in the central Philippines, killing more than 4,300 people in the world’s deadliest peacetime maritime disaster.

EaseMyTrip cofounder and chairman Nishant Pitti has pledged 34.51 Cr shares of the online travel aggregator, worth ₹211.9 Cr, to Motilal Oswal Financial Services for “personal use”. The pledge, created on August 24, covers 8.66% of EaseMyTrip’s total share capital, according to an exchange filing. The shares were valued at ₹6.14 apiece at the time of the transaction. The filing pegged both the value of the pledged shares and the amount involved at ₹211.9 Cr, implying a security cover ratio of 1:1. The 34.51 Cr shares covered by the latest pledge represent about 76.1% of Pitti’s 45.37 Cr share holding in EaseMyTrip. Before the transaction, 10.36 Cr of Pitti’s shares were already encumbered. Following the creation of the pledge, his total encumbered holding stood at 44.87 Cr shares, representing 11.26% of EaseMyTrip’s total share capital. The pledged shares represent 98.89% of Pitti’s individual holding, leaving him with 50 Lakh unencumbered shares. The pledged shares account for 25.83% of the combined shareholding of EaseMyTrip’s promoter group, which includes Nishant Pitti, Rikant Pittie, and Prashant Pitti. Total Pledge Unchanged However, Pitti’s overall pledged holding remains unchanged from April, when he had pledged a total of 44.87 Cr EaseMyTrip shares. While the latest filing classifies the transaction as the creation of a pledge, the unchanged post-transaction holding suggests that existing encumbrances were restructured. The filing did not elaborate on the reason for the change. Pitti had pledged 6.86 Cr shares worth about ₹55 Cr to Motilal Oswal Financial Services in March this year. This followed a string of pledge creations and releases over the preceding year. In June 2025, Pitti pledged 9 Cr shares worth ₹94.5 Cr to Motilal Oswal Financial Services, also for personal use. At the time, his total pledged holding stood at 17.01 Cr shares. Pitti’s pledges have come alongside a reduction in his stake in EaseMyTrip. He sold nearly 5 Cr shares worth ₹78.3 Cr in December 2024 after offloading 24.65 Cr shares for about ₹920 Cr in September that year. His stake in the company subsequently declined to 12.8% at the end of FY25 from 28.13% a year earlier. Pitti stepped down as EaseMyTrip’s CEO in January 2025 and was succeeded by his brother and cofounder Rikant Pittie. At the time, Nishant Pitti said the share sale was due to “personal reasons” and assured shareholders that he would not sell any more shares. Another cofounder, Prashant Pitti, resigned as the company’s MD in August 2025. EaseMyTrip Under Pressure The pledge disclosure comes at a time when EaseMyTrip’s earnings remain under pressure. The OTA slipped into the red in Q1 FY27, reporting a consolidated net loss of ₹11.7 Cr as against a net profit of ₹44 Lakh in Q1 FY26. This came despite operating revenue rising 18.4% YoY to ₹134.7 Cr. The weak quarter followed a challenging FY26. EaseMyTrip reported a ₹47.5 Cr loss in FY26 as against a profit of ₹108.6 Cr in FY25. Revenue from operations declined 8.8% YoY to ₹535.7 Cr. EaseMyTrip's board in May approved a proposal to raise up to ₹500 Cr through a rights issue. The company had earlier said the capital would be used to strengthen its technology and platform, expand into segments such as hotels and holidays, and pursue strategic acquisitions. Shares of EaseMyTrip were trading at ₹5.83 at 15:10, 0.5% higher from the opening price on BSE.

The New Mexico Supreme Court held a ChatGPT-using lawyer in direct contempt of court for submitting a brief with “false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses,” including fake police testimony and other mistakes. The state’s top court referred the lawyer to a disciplinary board for further proceedings and concluded that he “demonstrated a lack of remorse and a lack of concern for his client.”
Attorney Stephen Aarons “admitted to the Court that he did not verify the factual claims and legal authority in his AI-generated brief before signing it and filing it with the Court, and that he did not inform his client of this failure or that the brief in chief contained multiple factual and legal misrepresentations,” the state Supreme Court said in an order on Wednesday.
Aarons has been a criminal defense lawyer in New Mexico for over 40 years and was hired by a defendant’s family members to appeal a murder conviction. Aaron’s now-former client, Oscar Renee Sandoval, was sentenced to life in prison in February 2025 after being convicted of killing Shiereen Al-Jibury, who was his partner and the mother of his children.
A little over a year ago, in August 2025, Aarons submitted the brief containing fake testimony and other errors. Weeks later, the state of New Mexico filed a motion to strike portions of that brief.
“Respondent admitted to the Court that the brief in chief contained false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses—Officer Michelle Amarillo, Officer Sanchez, Manal Al-Jibury, and Teresa Marquez,” the court order on Wednesday said.
Lawyer fed trial transcript into ChatGPT
Aarons further admitted submitting “false testimony from Danny Stanton that he received threats,” “false testimony from Linda Stanton about the threats her husband received,” and “false testimony from Mariah Chavez and Teresa Marquez (fabricated witness) regarding the shooter’s clothing and appearance,” according to the order, which said Aarons also “misrepresented legal authority” in citations to previous cases.
Many lawyers have been caught citing fake cases in briefs or inaccurately describing real cases. While Aarons didn’t cite fake cases, he inaccurately described real ones and cited fake testimony.
Aarons told the state Supreme Court at a hearing on August 21 that he fed a computer-generated transcript of the murder trial and other documents related to the case into ChatGPT, which outputted the fake quotes.
“It’s of little comfort to know that my stupidity is what brings us together this afternoon,” Aarons told the court. Aarons admitted his brief quoted “several witnesses who were never called at trial,” another “witness who was called but the brief got the name wrong,” and that his brief inaccurately described precedents.
Aarons indicated that he used a version of ChatGPT powered by the OpenAI o3 model, which was released earlier in 2025. “I assumed that it generated a bulletproof summary of proceedings,” he said at the hearing, explaining that he thought it would be accurate because of how widespread AI use is in the legal and medical fields.
Aarons was barred from appearing before the New Mexico Supreme Court pending the outcome of any disciplinary board investigation and proceedings. He was fined $5,000, to be paid to the State Bar of New Mexico Client Protection Fund, but more penalties could come out of the disciplinary proceedings ordered by the court.
The state Supreme Court ordered the public defender office to appoint a new lawyer for the defendant, struck all previous briefs from the record, and said the case will proceed in the court’s 2026-27 term.
Justice: “You buried your head in the sand”
Justices lambasted Aarons during last month’s hearing. They expressed surprise that Aarons didn’t know AI tools could generate false information and pointed out that attorneys must verify the accuracy of information no matter where it comes from. Whether a lawyer gets help from an AI tool, a law student, or a fellow attorney, the lawyer signing the brief must attest to its accuracy, they said.
Justice C. Shannon Bacon was particularly withering in her criticism of Aarons. She told Aarons that there are “at least eight or nine provisions in the code of conduct that you violated.” Bacon said she was “really struggling with” Aarons’ claim to be unaware of AI hallucinations, noting that her 13-year-old nephew and 75-year-old stepmother are both aware of the problem.
“So counsel, do you watch the news? Do you listen to the radio? Do you read anything about what’s going on in the world? Because the problem with lawyers relying on AI hallucinations is an above-the-fold story every single day,” she said. “So either you buried your head in the sand—and that’s a choice to do that, an intentional choice to be uninformed—or you took a gamble, and neither of those are consistent with the code of conduct.”
Aarons responded that he submitted the brief a year ago and “a lot has come out in the last year.” However, the problem of lawyers using AI in briefs that cite made-up cases has been in the news regularly for well over three years.
Aarons added that the cases he cited in his brief were not fake, although his brief described them inaccurately. Bacon responded that there’s no “material distinction” between inaccurately describing a real case and citing a fake one, as the rules about candor to the court apply “with equal force” either way.
“I didn’t know that AI could hallucinate facts”
Aarons provided a statement when contacted by Ars today. He said:
In March 2025 I agreed to handle an appeal and used ChatGPT to summarize the trial proceedings. I wrote the brief but the table of contents and the summary contained numerous errors. At the time, I didn’t know that AI could hallucinate facts not only in my brief but in pleadings submitted by other attorneys. I am glad the court threw out my defective pleading and ordered the public defender to write a new brief on behalf of my former client. As for myself, I am remorseful but hopeful that the disciplinary board takes into account it was an honest mistake. It is a lesson learned for all professionals who rely upon this powerful but sometimes unstable technology.
Aarons told the court that he began by using Rev.com, a service that provides AI transcripts of audio files, and then put that transcript and other materials into ChatGPT.
“I believe I did confirm” that the trial transcript was accurate, he said when asked if he confirmed its accuracy before inputting it into ChatGPT. “The problem wasn’t in the transcript. It was when I loaded it and all the other information” into ChatGPT, he said. In addition to the transcript, Aarons said he put “the record proper, the statement of issues, and some of the discovery” into ChatGPT.
Aarons said he hoped the court would take steps to prevent other lawyers from making the same mistake he did, such as by issuing a standing order requiring that briefs contain a certificate of compliance regarding the use of AI. Justices treated Aaron’s suggestion as a distraction from the main problem, his failure to verify the accuracy of the brief.
“Assume with me that you had relied on the work of a first-year lawyer that was working for you and that they had just made stuff up… and you signed it. You’d be in the same exact soup you are right now,” Bacon said. “So the idea that, the suggestion in your briefing that because the court didn’t tell you at the time that you did this, ‘be careful,’ it somehow relieves you of obligation, falls on absolute deaf ears because the rules of professional conduct already tell you what your obligation is.”
“Your client is the one suffering”
“The other thing that’s completely missing from your response is anything about what this has done to your client,” Bacon went on to say. “That’s who I’m worried about. You have presented briefing to the court that we cannot rely on, and your client is the one suffering because of this far more than you will ever suffer.”
Chief Justice Julie Vargas similarly told Aarons, “I’m really interested with the approach you’re taking in this hearing. You seem to be telling us all the policy that we’ve been thinking about for years about what to do with AI, but you’re not talking about how to address the situation that’s in front of us, which has significant impacts on a criminal defendant who is in custody, who’s going to stay in custody until we resolve this matter. And I really don’t care about the policy concerns right now. I care about what we’re going to do with your client and what we should do in this circumstance based on the behavior that you showed us.”
Justice Michael Vigil said there’s nothing wrong with using AI to help write a legal argument as long as the lawyer verifies its accuracy. “It doesn’t matter what the tool is. It doesn’t matter how advanced the AI-generated program is or what improvements they make, whatever,” he said. “It doesn’t matter whether you use a C-student lawyer or a A-student lawyer [if] you didn’t check their work before you filed the brief. That’s the issue. And I wish, or I’m hoping you would focus on that, take responsibility for it.”
Aarons replied, “I hope I don’t present myself as not accepting responsibility. I mean, my only hope is that the mistakes that I made that somehow can prevent someone else down the line from repeating my mistake because the AI capacity is amazing.”
Lawyer didn’t tell client and family about ChatGPT use
Bacon criticized Aarons for not disclosing the problem to his client. “I have not. He’s a Spanish speaker and I wanted to see what happened today,” Aarons told Bacon when she asked if he told Sandoval about the problem.
Aarons said he was hired by Sandoval’s brother and cousin, and that he told them there was a problem with a brief. “They’re aware that there was a problem with the first brief that I filed and that the court’s looking at that. That’s pretty much it,” he said.
Bacon replied, “You didn’t say, ‘I relied on ChatGPT and it submitted lies to the court and the court is mad at me and now there’s a hearing.’ I’m guessing you didn’t tell your client’s family members that.”
“I didn’t talk about ChatGPT,” Aarons said. “I just said there was a problem with the brief that I filed.” Bacon told Aarons that his client needed to know the extent of the problem so he can make an informed decision “about whether you’re the right person to represent him.”
Bacon asked Aarons whether he was working on the case on a public defender contract or as private counsel. Aarons answered that he was hired as private counsel but hadn’t been paid yet.
“I’m not sure that’s going to happen,” Bacon replied.

'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'
- Published
A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field.
David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in electrical and mechanical engineering at the University of Bristol.
He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our integrity" in front of neighbours.
"I didn't see a way out," he said.
'The poor called us poor'
Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his first book, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom.
"It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said.
"I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water.
"[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food...
"She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water.
"She was trying to protect our integrity."

Etor's first break came whilst doing a kind of national service in Nigeria, when he realised lots of locals were being hospitalised with food poisoning, because they were trying to preserve things by drying them in fields.
To solve the problem, he designed and built a kind of "solar oven".
"It worked incredibly well," he said, which led to an award from the state government and a job.
He then completed an undergraduate degree at Newcastle University and a PhD at the University of Durham, before securing his current job in Bristol.
Sir Steve Webb, the former MP and Pensions Minister, who got to know Etor through the church in Bristol, called his achievements "remarkable".
"David's message is very much that people shouldn't be defined by their upbringing or their background," he said. "They shouldn't be written off."
"I was pinching myself on my way here this morning," Etor added.
"Nothing good was supposed to come out of me."

Gaza doc NAZA earns 24.5-minute standing ovation at Venice premiere
Documentary has testimony from anonymous Israeli military interviews alleging targeting of civilians in Gaza
Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham’s NAZA, a documentary on Israel’s alleged use of AI-assisted military systems to target and kill Palestinian civilians in Gaza, received what's being called a record-breaking 24.5-minute ovation at its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival on Thursday.
Video posted to social media captured the Israeli filmmakers looking solemn — with Abraham appearing to wipe away tears — as the room erupted for the film, which is based on the anonymized testimony of 24 Israeli military insiders.
According to Deadline, it marks the longest-ever standing ovation in Venice, surpassing the near 24-minute rapturous reception for The Voice of Hind Rajab at last year’s festival, and beating the 22-minute ovation for Guillermo del Toro’s dark fantasy piece, Pan’s Labyrinth, when it premiered at Cannes in 2006.
The Voice of Hind Rajab director Kaouther Ben Hania, who is serving as a juror this year, and its producer Nadim Cheikhrouha were also in attendance for the ovation.
Also in the room were some audience members who unfurled Palestinian and Lebanese flags as the lights came up, according to video posted to social media.
Shot clandestinely under the cover of night from the rooftops in Tel Aviv over a three-year span, NAZA delivers interviews with Israeli military subjects whose identities are obscured. The interviews describe the surveillance systems and AI intelligence the film alleges are being used to identify Hamas targets to bomb their homes, regardless of whether civilian families, including women and children, were inside.
The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said in a statement that it "categorically rejects" the allegations, and criticized the use of anonymous testimonies which it said "cannot be verified." Regarding the allegations of AI use, it said decisions to strike are made by humans only, and "the IDF strikes military targets and makes unprecedented efforts to minimize harm to civilians."
The film, titled after an acronym the Israeli military used as a shorthand for civilian casualties, is a companion piece to Abraham and Szor’s No Other Land, which won the Academy Award for best documentary in 2025.
NAZA is also executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, who faced intense backlash following his March 2024 Oscar acceptance speech for The Zone of Interest. In the speech, he spoke out against the Israel-Hamas war and stated he and his co-producers stood as men “who refute their Jewishness and the Holocaust being hijacked by an occupation which has led to conflict for so many innocent people.”
When Hamas-led militants attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, some 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 73,422 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in Israel’s ensuing offensive, according to Gaza’s Health ministry. While the ministry does not differentiate between civilians and militants, it says women and children make up half of all casualties.
And civilians are still being killed inside Gaza, Abraham told The Associated Press on Friday.
“What we are showing is something that is very much ongoing,” said Abraham.
“I think our film is showing that this is not some mistake. It’s not an accident. It’s something very, very systemic … and this should have been apparent to everyone, I think, from the start. But we are showing it from the inside, with insider testimony.”

ExclusiveSenior official asked to resign over defective lifts at Queen Mary Hospital
Chief project manager at the Architectural Services Department left her post last month, sources say
A senior Hong Kong government official who oversaw faulty lift installation work that stalled the launch of a new block at Queen Mary Hospital was asked to resign and left her post last month to take responsibility for the defects and delays on other projects, the South China Morning Post has learned.
But experts criticised the authorities’ handling of civil service management missteps, which bypassed the established disciplinary mechanism, saying it lacked transparency.
Multiple sources said that Tuesday Li Pak-yee, a chief project manager at the Architectural Services Department (ASD) who oversaw the multibillion-dollar redevelopment of the hospital in Pok Fu Lam, left her directorate pay-level post in August.
“[Li] was advised by the Architectural Services Department to resign,” a government insider said. “Such a departure is extremely rare within the civil service framework.”
Another government source said the department regarded Li, who served as the main official liaising with contractors and overseeing the hospital project’s execution, as possibly having made “management missteps” over the delay, and that it tried to resolve the matter internally rather than initiate formal disciplinary proceedings.

GoFundMe accused of deceptively adding ‘tips’ to donations that go to company and not helping others
A recently filed lawsuit against the fundraising site takes issue with the automatic tip added at checkout that is allegedly difficult to opt out of
GoFundMe has been accused of deceptively adding “tips” to donations that go to the company and not helping others.
The fundraising site has skyrocketed in popularity since it launched in 2010, helping strangers connect with grieving families struggling to pay for funeral costs or those who can’t afford to pay for medical bills after a tragic accident. Donors can send money to those in need through GoFundMe with a click of a button.
But when people go to donate to a charitable cause of their choice on the site, they are also hit with an automatic tip to the company that they can opt out of, a practice that a recently filed lawsuit claims is tricking donors into paying more.
“Once automatically added, GoFundMe makes the ‘tips’ difficult to remove, forcing consumers to hunt around for a way to remove them,” according to a lawsuit filed in a federal court in Illinois last month by Sandra Donovan of Illinois and Ebony Baker of Georgia, who have both made donations on GoFundMe.
The Independent, which obtained the lawsuit from ClassAction.org, has reached out to GoFundMe for comment.
The lawsuit also challenges how GoFundMe explains the tipping option on its site.
When donors go to pay on the site, the company has a blurb that reads, “GoFundMe has a 0% platform fee for organizers and relies primarily on the generosity of donors like you to operate our service.”
But the lawsuit argues that this description is “false,” adding, “In reality, completely unbeknownst to those who donate through its website, GoFundMe funds its services by charging charitable organizations hefty transaction fees on each donation they receive.”
GoFundMe says on its site that while it's free to create a fundraiser, the company charges “one small transaction fee per donation.”
The fee varies slightly depending on who creates the fundraiser. Individuals and businesses are charged 2.9 percent of the donation plus $0.30, while certified nonprofits are charged 2.2 percent of the donation plus $0.30.
“Donors act quickly, often emotionally, and with the reasonable expectation that their money will go where they intend—toward helping others, not toward undisclosed or preselected middleman fees like the ‘tips’ charged by GoFundMe,” the lawsuit claims.
Donovan and Baker “paid money they did not knowingly authorize, conferring an improper financial benefit on GoFundMe” because of the company’s business practices, the lawsuit argues.
Donovan and Baker's lawyers are asking the court to certify the case as a class action and are demanding a jury trial to stop GoFundMe's “deceptive conduct and return its ill-gotten gains,” according to the lawsuit.
A GoFundMe spokesperson told The Independent that the company “exists to help people help each other, and we have carefully designed our business model to deliver as much support as possible to those who need it – the beneficiaries of fundraisers.
“Donors have the choice to leave GoFundMe an optional tip, which helps us provide fundraising technology, customer support, and Trust & Safety protections to our community. Tips are completely voluntary and can easily be adjusted to any amount, including zero.”
The spokesperson said the claims in the lawsuit have “no merit.”
“The majority of donors adjust the suggested tip amount, and many choose to leave no tip at all. Before completing a donation, donors are shown a clear breakdown of their donation, optional tip, and total,” the spokesperson said. “Whether a donor chooses to leave a tip has no impact on the amount the fundraiser beneficiary or nonprofit receives.”
This article was updated on September 11, 2026, to include a statement from GoFundMe.

Houthi forces in Yemen are making a concerted drive to take over the country’s Red Sea coast fully, claiming control of the key port of Mocha in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years, bringing the Iran-aligned group closer to full control of a key shipping route.
Seizure of the coast and some of the islands in the sea would be a strategic disaster for Saudi Arabia and the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two choke points for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandab at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Observers have said a reduction in hostilities – the most intense since the UN-sponsored ceasefire of April 2022 put an end to major military exchanges – now seems unlikely in what is seen as an attempt by the Houthis to open a second front in the Iran-US war, alongside the battle for control of Hormuz.
Baraa Shiban, the Royal United Services Institute’s (Rusi) Yemen specialist, a London-based security thinktank, said the situation in the country was spiralling out of control, adding that the UN-recognised Yemeni government was opening new fronts against the Houthis in the hope of putting more pressure on their forces than they could withstand. But in the past 48 hours the Houthis had major advances south, down Yemen’s west coast, taking them closer to the high ground overlooking the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait.
The fighting has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia, which on Thursday launched as many as 40 airstrikes on Houthi targets, will activate the Mecca defence agreement and ask its co-signatories, Pakistan and Turkey, to send forces. The pact is designed to be defensive in nature and believed unlikely to apply to Saudi military activities in Yemen.
By taking control of more of the Red Sea coast south of the port of Hodeidah, the Houthis’ aim is to use a new lever to put pressure on Saudi Arabia and the US to agree a deal that lifts the US blockade on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf. Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged he did not expect the war with Iran to end before the US midterm elections at the start of November.
The latest phase in the escalation began when Houthis attacked energy installations and southern cities in Saudi Arabia using drones and ballistic missiles. In response, the kingdom’s military forces launched at least 15 strikes between 3 and 7 September.
The conflict data monitor Acled estimated there were 276 fatalities over the five-day period alone. The fighting has continued, with the Houthis claiming control of Mocha in Taiz province, as well as the inland city of Hays and the Khalid ibn al-Walid camp, the largest military base in the region. One Houthi-linked estimate suggested its forces had gained control of more than 2,320 sq miles (6,000 sq km) of land.
The commander of the Yemeni government forces, Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, admitted he had organised a strategic retreat south of Mocha in order to regroup in a secure location. “The armed forces in the western coast paid a heavy price – martyrs and wounded – over the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack planned by Iran, and supported by it,” he said. Analysts claimed that the effectiveness of Yemen’s government forces was weakened by internal divisions, as well as external pressure from Saudi Arabia.
The latter, meanwhile, continues to take advantage of its air superiority to attack Houthi positions, though government sources acknowledged Houthi ground advances along the coast and their missile strikes on the strategic Red Sea islands of Zuqar and Hanish.
The clashes have raged across Yemen, including Ad Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwah, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, and Taiz. In the initial days of the renewed conflict the Houthis were forced back in some areas as battles on multiple fronts overstretched their resources and fighter numbers.
The Houthis will be hoping political divisions inside the Yemeni government, reflected in a lack of an integrated military, will slowly give them the upper hand. The United Arab Emirates, previously a powerful player in southern Yemen where it backed the separatist forces of the Southern Transitional Council, withdrew its financial and military support at the turn of the year. The southern forces have refused to fight outside their own region.
“A reduction in hostilities anytime soon seems unlikely, as both sides continue to escalate with the goal of inflicting enough damage to the other side to force a compromise,” said Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst for Acled. “In terms of military capability, both sides are more equal compared to the immediate period prior to the 2022 ceasefire when the Houthis had the upper hand.”
He added: “Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in Hodeidah and Taiz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-Yemen government have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab al-Mandab.”
The head of the Houthis’ national delegating negotiating team, Muhammad Abdul Salam, insisted non-Saudi commercial shipping would not be attacked.
The fighting has contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80.
The escalation to this week’s all-out violence has been a slow process. It began after a senior delegation of the Houthi group, which has long been in a complex alliance with Iran, flew to Tehran for the funeral of the Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in July, returning in an Iranian plane that the Saudis refused to land in rebel-controlled Sana’a.
The Saudis instead bombed the runway, leading the Houthis to announce a Red Sea naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in what the Yemeni group described as a blockade for a blockade. The 20 July announcement of the blockade was followed by a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on 25 July and on a tanker off Yanbu on 24 August.
Saudi Arabia has become reliant on the Red Sea route for trade after Iran throttled shipping through the strait of Hormuz as a result of US-Israeli attacks.

Russian attack on Pavlohrad took place in broad daylight 'when there were many people on the streets'

Russian forces had hit two other shopping malls in the cities of Zaporizhzhia and Sumy earlier in the week.
This comes as Nato allies foiled a plot where Russian subs trained to unleash a secret weapon designed to disable critical undersea cables without leaving any fingerprints, it has been revealed.
A joint operation involving Britain, Norway and the United States tracked and confronted the Russian vessels at sea, officials told Reuters after a clandestine Russian operation was carried out by Moscow's GUGI undersea warfare directorate.

Putin and Xi to hold talks at APEC summit in November

There is no planned separate meeting between the two men at the BRICS+ summit this weekend, the aide, Yuri Ushakov, was also cited as saying by Russian state media.
Two people killed and four injured in attacks on businesses
Russian forces have struck a petrol station in the capital Kyiv and an international agribusiness facility in Dnipro as Moscow intensifies attacks on logistics and economic targets.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said attacks on businesses and civilian infrastructure were rapidly growing and urged the government to "react and act in advance".
The strike on the Ukrnafta petrol station appeared to be the first jet-powered drone attack on such a facility in Kyiv. It follows around 300 attacks on petrol stations in or near Ukraine's frontline regions in recent months.
Four people were injured, said Mayor Vitali Klitschko.

In Dnipro, two people were killed in the attack on the Bunge sunflower oil facility, one of Ukraine's five largest food plants with a processing capacity of 1,600 tons of oilseed per day.
It was the second attack on a US-owned business in several weeks, said Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
"This is no coincidence, but part of Moscow's systematic terror campaign against American businesses and economic interests," he wrote.
Five people were wounded, a local official said.

Zelensky said Ukrainian and US negotiators were in constant contact and he hoped for progress in talks on energy and grain at the end of September after his meeting with US President Donald Trump.
Russia will hold parliamentary elections on 20 September, and Zelensky expects to meet Trump in the second half of this month.

Russian attacks on Ukraine's southeastern city of Dnipro hit a business owned by global agribusiness and food company Bunge , Mayor Borys Filatov said on Thursday.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Christos Garkinos, founder of Covet by Christos. It has been edited for length and clarity.
I learned from a very young age what success meant: it was money in the till after the lunch rush.
My Greek immigrant parents owned a diner in Detroit. Each day, 150 people would flood in for lunch, and my family would fall apart. My mom would be screaming, throwing things at my dad; as a kid, I wondered every day if we would make it through. But two hours later, with the money in the till, we'd all be having fun.
My dad was diagnosed with lung cancer when I was in my 20s. The business failed, and so did his health. I was making good money working for major global companies like Disney and Virgin, but I never felt financially secure. That's partially because I sent a good portion of my check home to support my parents.
I took a loan to pay for my dad's hospice medications
My dad died when I was in my mid-20s. While he was in hospice, I was trying to find money to pay for his medication. My parents didn't have any money, so I took out a small personal loan of about $2,000 to make my dad more comfortable in his last days.
That's when money became a big fear of mine. I was terrified of ending up like my dad.
At the same time, when I made good money, I felt I didn't deserve it. I wasn't comfortable with money, so I would find ways to spend it.
I was doing one thing right, however: I had a 401(k) retirement account, something my parents never had. That gave me peace of mind that I would die penniless, like my dad.
I got my dream job, but I sabotaged myself
I was living in LA, working in fashion, which had been my dream since I'd first heard the "click clack" of high heels as a boy. I had a lot going for me, and eventually landed a reality show that I leveraged into a spot on the Home Shopping Network.
I had been absolutely obsessed with the network since I was 14. When I went to Florida and saw a set with my name on it, I freaked out. A part of me thought, "What can I do to mess this up?" I was still self-sabotaging.
Then, my best friend died of cancer. I had already been running with a fast crowd, but when I walked out of her funeral, I walked out of my life. I left my husband, my business, and myself. I was in a tailspin for three years.
I spent my retirement savings and went about $500,000 into debt
Even in those days, my life looked beautiful from the outside. I was living in a gorgeous house I was renting at the top of Mulholland Drive. And yet, my whole life was put on my American Express card, because I always needed another 30-day buffer.
One day, in that fancy house, I called my mom for Easter — a major holiday for us Greeks. As I talked to her, I was rummaging through the trash, looking for drugs.
I thought, "What am I doing?" That moment started my sobriety. I had to face the fact that I'd racked up about $500,000 in debt — personal loans, credit cards, money borrowed from friends — and spent the 401(k) that had been my safety net for so long.
I've paid off my debt and rebuilt my savings
I got sober and knew I needed to address the debt. I turned to what I'd always been good at: selling things. In 2020, I started consigning on Instagram Live. I was making good money again, so for every $1 I put in the bank, I would pay off $2 in debt. I started with the friends who lent me money, then paid off the credit cards and loans. By September 2021, all my debt was paid off.
Now, I've rebuilt a lot of my financial security. I have a 401(k) again, and I could retire today if I wanted to. I don't have to think twice about spending a couple thousand on something I want.
And yet, there's still part of me that doesn't feel secure. When I worry, I remind myself of the changes I've made. I'm sober. I have a business manager. I know my habits around money. Yet I'm still working hard to build this business and sell it eventually. For me, that will mean next-level financial stability.

CA governor signs 'landmark' laws on youth use of social media and AI chatbots
They’re aimed at protecting minors, but the rules are not universally supported.
California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed multiple measures aimed at protecting the state's youth. These new laws include restrictions for potentially addictive social media features and limitations on how young users can interact with AI chatbots.
The state is enacting restrictions on how teens can interact with chatbots from AI companies, including time limits. Chatbot makers will be required to implement mental health resources, safety protocols in case a minor discusses self harm and notifications for parents if a child turns off safety settings. California will now require "independent child safety audits and annual risk assessments" by AI companies. AI companies could face legal liability under these rules if they fail to meet the new rules. Today's developments follow measures Newsom signed yesterday that created broader frameworks for auditing AI companies for compliance with California law.
One of the more divisive measures Newsom passed centers on teen use of social media. The state now prohibits social media companies from letting users under age 16 access potentially "addictive features." The bill's definition of "addictive" includes wide-ranging capabilities from autoplaying videos to notifications to personalized algorithm-driven content feeds.
Critics such as the Electronic Frontier Foundation called this measure a functional ban on social media for teens. "Denying minors access to digital forums – or stripping out basic tools needed to navigate them – is not going to help make young people safer or healthier in the AI age," EFF Associate Director of State Affairs Rindala Alajaji said. The organization added that enforcing this policy would also force all social media users to disclose more personal information to prove their age, creating additional privacy risks. This is one of the arguments many parties have long taken against other age verification laws.
Newsom signed additional measures with similar goals of protecting youth from potentially risky tech applications. Those include an expanded definition of child sexual exploitation to include generative AI-made or digitally altered images. Another bill offers new protections against targeted advertising and regulates AI systems' use of data about K-12 students.

Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels captured a strategic island at the southern entrance to the Red Sea, two officials said on Friday (September 11, 2026), opening a new front in the Iran war and further threatening Saudi oil exports through one of the world’s key shipping lanes.
The Houthis’ biggest territorial gains in years, along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, could boost Iran’s strategy of driving up world oil and gas prices to pressure the United States.

Smoke seen above the Saudi East-west oil pipeline
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia said on Friday (September 11, 2026), that it had shut down a major cross-country oil pipeline after it was attacked the day before. A statement from the Saudi Ministry of Energy did not specify who carried out the attacks and called the shutdown “a precautionary measure.”
Built in the 1980s, the East-West pipeline has played an important role in Saudi Arabia’s ability to export oil following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war. By early June, Saudi Arabia had more than doubled oil exports from the Red Sea port at the pipeline’s end to more than 5 million barrels per day, according to the International Energy Agency.
Aramco has used the East-West pipeline to ramp up crude flows from Saudi Arabia’s eastern coast to the Red Sea to its west after U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on Iran began six months ago, prompting Tehran to effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi crude supply fell 2.3 million barrels per day on the month in August to 6 million barrels per day, the lowest level in more than three decades, the International Energy Agency said on Friday (September 11), partly due to the targeting of ships transiting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait by groups linked to Yemen’s Houthis.
Global oil prices were on track to end the week above $100 a barrel for the first time since mid-May, though they were slightly lower on Friday (September 11) after the Financial Times reported that Foreign Ministers in West Asia were trying to work out a temporary deal to manage shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Yemeni government forces plot counter-offensive
Yemeni government forces, meanwhile, indicated they would try to retake areas captured by the Houthi militants in their lightning offensive this week along the Red Sea coastline.
They announced they would deploy weapons and aircraft to eliminate any movement of the “terrorist” Houthi militias in strategic areas, including the road leading to the coastal city of Mocha, which the militant group captured on Thursday (September 10) along with the Red Sea islands of Hanish.
Military spokesman Colonel Majed al-Nazili called on civilians to avoid using the route between the city of Taiz and Mocha and steer clear of equipment belonging to the Houthis, mountain fighters who withstood years of devastating Saudi air strikes during Yemen’s civil war.
Fighting between the Houthis and the Yemeni government forces has intensified in recent days, with the Iran-aligned group shifting its focus to control over Yemen’s long coastline instead of just the north and the country’s most populous areas.
Reuters reported on Thursday (September 10) that the dramatic Houthi advance down Yemen’s Red Sea coast this week came with direct guidance from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards seeking to open a new front in Tehran’s war with the U.S., according to Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources.
Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a close U.S. ally, and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said.
While Iran describes the Houthis as an ally, it publicly denies giving them military direction, saying they are “not a proxy”.
Trump rejects Saudi calls to bomb Houthis, Axios reports
Saudi Arabia has been bombing Houthi targets in Yemen but not the strategic areas the group has seized this week.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called U.S. President Donald Trump twice on Thursday (September 10) and urged him to launch strikes against the Houthis, Axios reported, citing two U.S. officials.
Trump rejected the request, and U.S. officials said the administration does not intend to take direct military action against the Houthis at this time, the report said.
According to Axios, the U.S. is increasingly concerned about the rapidly escalating conflict in Yemen and is stepping up support for Saudi Arabia while seeking to avoid direct military involvement.
Gulf Foreign Ministers plan to meet their Iranian counterpart in a push by Oman and Iran to secure buy-in for a temporary deal to manage shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the Financial Times reported on Friday (September 11).
The gathering is scheduled to be held on Monday (Septembre 14) in the Omani coastal city of Salalah, the report said, citing two people briefed on the matter.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
