After admitting earlier this year that its AI models had hacked other companies’ systems on a handful of occasions, Anthropic released a new report on Wednesday detailing the attacks. It reveals a string of incidents displaying what Anthropic deems its models’ single-minded “recklessness” — and will likely fuel already raging concerns about cybersecurity and AI.
Anthropic spent this week in hot water over cybersecurity
A researcher’s resignation letter went viral, just before the company released details about four models going rogue.
Anthropic spent this week in hot water over cybersecurity
A researcher’s resignation letter went viral, just before the company released details about four models going rogue.
In Anthropic’s report, it detailed four cases this year in which its own AI models hacked an external company or exploited vulnerabilities. In one, an “internal, general-purpose research model” broke into third-party systems, using access tokens and passwords and downloading files. In another, a Claude model attacked a company with a live web application reachable on the public internet and handled user data. A third model accessed a “machine belonging to a third party that it was able to access” — apparently believing it was part of its evaluation exercise, per Anthropic — then used a password it found inside a file to gain admin access to the third party’s internal systems, going on to harvest credentials, modify system settings, and read someone’s personal information. The saga only ended when the model “exhausted its token budget,” per Anthropic.
The most concerning incident involved Claude Mythos 5, Anthropic’s frontier cybersecurity-focused model, which the company said turned out to be the model most likely to perform a “severely harmful” action in testing. The company said Mythos 5 went to “extensive lengths” to upload a “malicious package” to a public repository used by a lot of engineers, and it seemed to try to obfuscate its real goals in its “chain of thought” (a mental scratchpad that AI researchers use to evaluate an AI model’s alignment). In many cases, Anthropic said it appeared that Claude models undertook harmful actions under the assumption they were in a simulation, but researchers also couldn’t confirm that the models truly “believed” that or were just acting like they did.
Anthropic’s incidents, though still concerning, were less coordinated and pervasive than the OpenAI incident that kicked off an industry-wide cybersecurity crisis this summer. That said, there are significant similarities. Anthropic said the most prevalent issues it discovered included a “willingness to take harmful actions in the narrow pursuit of a task,” similar to the “reward-hacking” that preceded the Hugging Face attack. Much like OpenAI, it said its prerelease tests and evaluations failed to catch severe risks.
Anthropic said it had signed an agreement with METR, one of the AI industry’s most prominent third-party AI evaluators, starting with an eight-week research agreement. The agreement grants METR access to transcripts “beyond the window in which the incidents occurred” (likely a subtle dig at OpenAI, which was criticized for limiting access in a deal with METR following the Hugging Face attack). It also said that METR would be able to chat directly with Anthropic employees, “who will be permitted to share confidential information.”
Anthropic’s report came on the heels of the resignation of Jacob Coxon, who had worked on AI pre-training at Anthropic since May and before that spent years working at OpenAI. On Tuesday, he resigned and posted a public letter to X about his reasoning. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he wrote, adding that neither OpenAI nor Anthropic is “acting responsibly” and rather “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Coxon added, “Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing.”
Coxon is far from the first AI researcher to raise these types of alarms, nor even the first Anthropic researcher to do so — in February, Anthropic’s Mrinank Sharma resigned and wrote on X, warning that “the world is in peril.”
But Coxon’s post took on additional weight thanks to its timing around the OpenAI and Anthropic hacking revelations. Though the AI industry has seen more than its fair share of hype, the recent cyberattacks by AI agents — enabled by the labs that created them — are real and concerning. Many other researchers at leading AI labs echoed his concerns and issued calls for AI industry employees to sign a public letter from July, which calls for a slowdown in AI development.
”I don’t know how you look at the steady drumbeat of news and events — and that drumbeat is models hacking themselves out of containment, hacking into other companies ,the fact that the companies increasingly can’t control their models … and think this is just hype,” said Michael Kleinman, head of U.S. Policy for the Future of Life Institute.
He added, “The vast majority of Americans, regardless of party — Republican, Independent, Democrat — are looking at the development of AI, the speed with which it’s going, the fact that the companies have no guardrails over what they do, and are saying, ‘Whoa, we do not want this.’”

A rare thunderstorm system that would normally move rapidly instead remained nearly stationary for hours over Chiba Prefecture last month, contributing to the record rainfall that killed at least 13 people, researchers said Thursday.
A preliminary analysis by the Meteorological Research Institute — part of the Japan Meteorological Agency — said a squall-line-type precipitation system (a linear rainband) was responsible for the Aug. 13 downpours.
Squall-line-type systems are characterized by highly developed thunderclouds capable of producing intense rain, hail, lightning and strong winds, and typically move quickly. In Chiba, however, the storm remained near the Boso Peninsula, with its northern portion lingering there for more than six hours.
“I was honestly surprised,” Toru Adachi, a senior researcher at the institute’s typhoon and severe weather research department, said at a news conference Thursday.
“It was shocking that a phenomenon occurred for which we have not yet accumulated sufficient knowledge, and that it led to a disaster like this. We need to properly understand what happened.”
Researchers said the storm’s movement was likely suppressed by opposing air flows. A layer of cold air generated and strengthened by rainfall pushed the storm system eastward, while warm easterly winds from the Pacific acted as a headwind — pushing against it from opposite directions.
Those forces largely balanced each other, causing the rain-producing system to stall rather than move away as squall lines normally do. The central and southern portions of the storm moved only about 20 to 30 kilometers between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m., while its northern section stayed almost stationary for over six hours.
The institute said the system developed in two stages. Daytime rainfall first created a pool of cold air over inland parts of the Kanto region. Near the Boso Peninsula, warm air flowing in from the Pacific met the cold air, forming a localized boundary known as a shear line. The warmer air was forced upward along that boundary, allowing cumulonimbus clouds to develop.
From around 5:30 p.m., rainfall from those clouds strengthened the cold-air layer and pushed the boundary outward into a bow shape, creating what meteorologists call a gust front. At the same time, a strong current known as a rear-inflow jet developed on the western side of the system, helping intensify the front and fuel further thunderstorm growth.
The clouds repeatedly regenerated above the gust front and reached heights of more than 15 km. That was almost twice the roughly 8-km height of thunderclouds observed during the 2015 Kanto-Tohoku torrential rains, according to the institute.
A linear rainband developed at around 6 p.m. on Aug. 13, and a special heavy rain warning was issued roughly 90 minutes later. The city of Chiba recorded 367 millimeters of rain over 24 hours — the highest level ever observed there.
Researchers also detected a counterclockwise vortex about 2 to 5 km in diameter inside thunderclouds in the northern part of the system, where some of the heaviest rainfall occurred.
The vortex, found at an altitude of roughly 1 to 3 km, may have locally strengthened upward air currents and accelerated the formation of precipitation particles, contributing to the extreme rainfall, the institute said.
The institute said the findings remain preliminary and that researchers plan further analysis to determine more precisely how the opposing air masses allowed the storm to remain in place for so long. The research could eventually help improve monitoring and forecasting of similar extreme rainfall events, the institute said.

SRINAGAR: A day after chief minister Omar Abdullah hit out at Congress for its criticism over full rendition of Vande Mataram and wondered if the party wanted Kashmiris to be arrested, J&K Congress president Tariq Hamid Karra sharpened the attack on ally NC, describing Omar’s comment as “detached from reality and highly unfortunate”.“The public has nothing to do with this debate. It is the govt that is expected to stand upright,” Karra said Friday in a statement. “Did a single person in Kerala go to jail when its govt chose to sing only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram at the Independence Day parade?” he asked.
Karra also questioned if Omar was “capable of standing up for secular and inclusive values like the CMs of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Telangana had done by limiting Vande Mataram singing to first two stanzas at state events?”Earlier in the day, J&K deputy CM Surinder Choudhary had also dismissed Congress’s criticism, saying “Vande Mataram is our national song and we are proud of it”.On Thursday, Omar had said singing of the national song was a statutory and constitutional obligation, while responding to Congress’s objection to full rendition of Vande Mataram at the inaugural ceremony of the International Film Festival of Jammu & Kashmir. “All six stanzas of the national song must be played across the country at the govt events,” he said.Pointing out that legal action could be taken against those who failed to stand during the entire national song, Omar questioned whether Congress wanted more Kashmiris to be jailed.

Tamil Nadu Minister for Health and Family Welfare K.G. Arunraj on Tuesday (September 8, 2026) announced in the Legislative Assembly that the State government would implement a Statewide mission to reduce the amount of salt in the daily diet of the public.
Dr. Arunraj said non-communicable diseases such as hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, stroke, and kidney disorders were among the most important public health challenges in Tamil Nadu. Nearly 50% of medically certified deaths in Tamil Nadu are caused by cardiovascular diseases. Approximately 1.8 crore people in Tamil Nadu are living with hypertension.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that a person should consume less than five grams of salt a day. However, scientific studies indicate that the people of Tamil Nadu consume an average of 7 to 8 grams of salt per day. Studies have also found that approximately 88% of the salt consumed as part of the South Indian diet comes from salt added during cooking at home. Global scientific studies have established that even a reduction of just one gram of salt per day can significantly lower blood pressure, he said.
Further, an international study involving approximately 21,000 people who used a low-sodium salt substitute, in which a portion of the sodium was replaced with potassium, demonstrated a 14% reduction in strokes and a 12% reduction in overall mortality. Based on this scientific evidence, the State government has decided to formulate and implement an integrated strategy to reduce high salt consumption in Tamil Nadu, Dr. Arunraj said.
Statewide survey
Announcing the key initiatives under the mission, Dr. Arunraj said for the first time, a Statewide survey based on urine samples would be undertaken to scientifically determine the current level of salt consumption among the people of Tamil Nadu.
Standards would be implemented to gradually reduce the amount of salt used in kitchens under the direct control of the government, including those serving the Nutritious Meal Programme, the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme, government hospitals and hostels, he said.
The feasibility of making available to the public a low-sodium salt substitute, in which a portion of sodium is replaced with potassium and which does not produce a noticeable difference in taste, would be studied as a pilot project in selected areas, he said.
Through the ‘Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam’ initiative and Health and Wellness Centres, people with hypertension would receive systematic counselling on reducing salt intake. A Statewide awareness campaign will be undertaken to educate people about salt content in food and simple ways to gradually reduce the excessive use of salt in everyday home cooking, he added.

After a plethora of new product launches and innovation showcases on day one, the second day of the Global Fintech Festival (GFF) 2026 centred more around partnerships with AI at the heart of a lot of developments to come out of the event. Traditional banks and NBFCs joined hands with new-age tech AI firms and fintech startups to upgrade their tech as well as launch new features and capabilities. Beyond partnerships, fintech companies continued to showcase their new products today. Here are some of the top headlines from the day that caught our attention… Sarvam And Mahindra Finance Scale Voice AI Partnership Leading NBFC Mahindra Finance expanded its partnership with AI unicorn Sarvam with a focus on voice AI. Sarvam's platform will now be integrated into Mahindra Finance’s sales, collections, and frontline employee engagement operations across rural and semi-urban markets. Mahindra’s dedicated AI division has developed voice agents powered by Sarvam models operating across 12 Indian languages. The system automates pre-due reminders, debt collection lifecycle workflows, and cross-selling for vehicle, SME, and housing loans. All interactions feed into custom AI pipelines integrated directly within the NBFC’s customer relationship management (CRM) and loan servicing platforms. The NBFC major termed the outcome of the partnership as “one of the largest voice AI deployments in Indian financial services”. It claimed the agents have executed over 1 Cr customer calls to date. Yes Bank and Open Launch AI Platform to Reduce Recurring Payment Failures Yes Bank and fintech unicorn Open have teamed up to launch i-Mandate, an agentic AI layer designed to prevent recurring payment failures before transactions occur. i-Mandate combines predictive analytics and autonomous execution, shifting recurring collections from a passive setup to a dynamic model. The use cases for the platform include loan repayments, mutual fund SIPs, and enterprise subscriptions. It leverages historical account patterns and payment signals through a feature called Smart Protect to identify upcoming debit risks, and engages borrowers to execute authorised corrective actions like rescheduling the payment date, switching bank accounts, or using an alternate payment method. The platform deploys an AI agent across voice and WhatsApp in 22 languages, and is integrated with Open’s AI lending layer Arc. It aims to provide organisations with real-time visibility into expected collection volumes and cash-flow positions before debits are presented. Navi Partners With IndusInd Bank To Upgrade Payment Infrastructure Sachin Bansal-led Navi partnered with IndusInd Bank to enhance the latter’s tech stack by powering its UPI payments. The partnership introduces a new UPI payment switch designed to route and process transactions across the ecosystem. The deployment aims to diversify Navi UPI’s core infrastructure, while boosting system resilience and transaction capacity to support increasing payment volumes. “Our partnership with IndusInd Bank adds another important layer to our UPI capabilities that we hope strengthens the foundation for a more reliable and seamless UPI experience for our customers,” said Rajiv Naresh, Navi’s MD and CEO. Gnani AI Launches Sovereign Agentic AI Platform Artha for BFSI Sector Bengaluru-based Gnani AI announced the extension of its sovereign AI platform, Gnani Artha, to banking, financial services, and insurance (BFSI) enterprises to help them build and deploy AI-powered workflows. The platform offers over 200 pre-built workflows designed to automate complex operational tasks, including payment reconciliation, document-driven underwriting, loan processing, and risk management. Powered by Gnani’s proprietary Evon language models and Plexus agentic AI layer, Artha enables multi-agent execution across enterprise systems while maintaining data sovereignty through private cloud or on-premise deployment options. For example, Artha-powered loan application workflows can ingest multiple documents like bank statements, GST filings, identity documents, and Account Aggregator data, cross-validate the information, find inconsistencies, and then take a call on whether to approve, decline or refer the application basis predefined thresholds. MobiKwik Expands Scope Of FX Retail Offering The listed fintech company has expanded its FX Retail offering from one to six currencies, adding AED, CAD, GBP, EUR and CHF to its existing USD service. The offering now allows users to book foreign currency, top up forex cards and remit funds overseas via the MobiKwik app. It offers live bank-linked pricing and same-day fulfilment, subject to regulatory requirements. The service is powered by NPCI Bharat BillPay Ltd (NBBL), in collaboration with the Clearing Corporation of India (CCIL), and is available through the Bharat Connect ecosystem. Overall, NBBL processed forex transactions worth ₹11.19 Cr in the first four months of FY27. The service is currently available to resident individuals, with transaction limits of up to $3,000 equivalent for currency notes and $10,000 for forex card and remittance services. Xflow and HSBC Launch India Collections for Global Businesses Cross-border payments startup Xflow partnered with HSBC to enable international companies to accept online and recurring payments from Indian buyers without establishing a local legal entity. The infrastructure leverages India’s domestic payment rails to convert cross-border transactions into local checkouts. Through the platform, overseas merchants can collect payments from Indian buyers through UPI, net banking, and cards. Traditional cross-border transactions suffer from high drop-off rates, as international card payments in India suffer from over 30% failure rates and bank wire transfers often face settlement delays. By routing transactions through local rails, Xflow and HSBC are projecting payment success rates above 95%. The product targets foreign SaaS, AI, ecommerce, consumer-tech, online travel, and edtech platforms tapping into the Indian market. Notably, the merchant can settle transactions in major foreign currencies to nearly all global destinations. CCAvenue, DCB Bank Tie Up For Digital Fee Collection AvenuesAI's (erstwhile known as Infibeam) digital payment solutions platform CCAvenue expanded its partnership with DCB Bank to offer digital fee-collection solutions to educational institutions. Under the tie-up, DCB Bank’s education-sector customers will get access to CCAvenue’s AI Forms, which allows schools and other institutions to create customised payment forms and links for collecting fees. The solution enables institutions to share payment links with students or parents through email, SMS or WhatsApp, who can then pay through multiple digital payment options. The partnership will cover schools, colleges, universities, coaching institutes and other educational organisations. DCB Bank customers will also have access to CCAvenue’s broader payment suite, including its payment gateway, link-based payments and UPI stack, with integration options for websites and ERP systems.

Whatever happened to the Taliban threat: 'We will flog the women'?
We have previously reported on the Taliban's position that public flogging (as well as stoning) are appropriate corporal punishment if they believe a citizen has violated certain precepts –- enabling girls to be educated despite the ban on secondary education for females, for example, or engaging in an adulterous relationship. Have Taliban authorities been employing these methods?
We're revisiting some of our past global health and development stories to see "Whatever happened to ..."
In March 2024, NPR reported on a statement issued by the Taliban's usually elusive supreme leader Hibatullah Akhundzada announcing a return to a type of punishment in its justice system. "We will flog the women ... we will stone them to death in public [for crimes]," he said in an audio message.
True to his words, the Taliban have gradually increased public and violent punishments. A report by the Afghanistan Human Rights and Democracy Organization (AHRDO), an nongovernmental organization that investigates human rights violations, cites 2,745 individuals who had been subjected to corporal punishment between February and April. The numbers were drawn from the Taliban's own public records.
The U.N. has documented similar figures, in a report in March 2026. Citing at least 1,110 flogging cases last year, the U.N. states: "in 2025 alone, more men and women were subjected to public flogging than in all previous years combined."
These counts are based on cases published by the Taliban's Supreme Court on their website and social media channels and in over 500 press releases. Advocates believe that there may be cases that are not documented in court records — instances when Taliban authorities confront and flog the accused on the spot, such as women violating the Taliban's strict dress code.
MA is an activist in Afghanistan who shared a video with NPR that shows the public flogging of a woman, reportedly in Kandahar province. She asked to be identified only by her initials, fearing repercussions from the Taliban for calling attention to flogging.
MA also pointed to several similar videos on social media. The Taliban bans filming in public areas where flogging as well as stoning takes place, but MA says that individuals who oppose the practice have been discretely filming these events, then posting the video.
NPR was not able to independently verify the content of the videos. A request for comment from the Taliban was not answered.
"A very important element of how they see justice"
Why has the Taliban embraced flogging?
"The floggings are an important aspect of administration of justice in the Taliban's eyes," says Shaharzad Akbar, executive director of the Afghan human rights group Rawadari. "It's a very important element of how they see justice, the rule of law and how they use it to control and repress the population," says Akhar, who is based in Europe.
Samira Hamidi, South Asia regional campaigner at Amnesty International, says she agrees. "The increased use of public floggings and other corporal punishments serves not only as a form of punishment but also as a tool of intimidation and social control."
Beyond the brutality of these punishments, legal experts say they violate the country's commitment to international law.
"Afghanistan is a party to several human rights instruments, and even after the Taliban took over, it has remained a member of these international human rights treaties, which therefore carry obligations on the government to protect these rights for all individuals in Afghanistan," explains Haydee Dijkstal, a U.K.-based lawyer specializing in international human rights who provided legal analysis for the AHRDO report. These treaties include the Convention against Torture, the Convention on Civil and Political Rights, and the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination.
"These obligations prohibit treatment that amounts to cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or torture," she says.
"When something is called a punishment but itself constitutes a human rights violation, it cannot be considered a lawful punishment or justice," she says.
Who gets flogged? Women and marginalized groups
The AHRDO report noted that women and marginalized groups such as Afghanistan's LGBT community remain most disproportionately impacted by the rise in such punishments.
One reason, the report notes, is that the Taliban officials are flogging individuals based on discriminatory and illegal charges. The crimes of the accused, such as women appearing in public without a mahram (a male guardian), same-sex relations, extramarital relations or women "running away" from homes, are protected fundamental human rights under international law.
"Women face a heightened risk because they are subject to a range of discriminatory restrictions that regulate their movement, dress, behaviour, and participation in public life," Hamidi says.
Since taking over, the Taliban have issued dozens of decrees that prohibit women from higher education, most forms of employment and political and even public participation.
"In this context, corporal punishment becomes another mechanism for enforcing gender-based discrimination and maintaining the Taliban's systematic repression of women and girls," she adds.
The Taliban commitment to these punishments is part of its dismantling of the Afghan legal system since taking power.
"The rise of corporal punishment aligns with that lack of an independent and impartial judiciary in Afghanistan and is a way of imposing fear and control over the population," Dijkstal says.
"The cases lacked due process and violated the right to a fair trial," she says, adding that in cases documented by AHRDO, not one person was allowed proper legal representation or allowed to present a defense or even speak in court. "It was a gross violation of what is considered under international law to be a minimum standard to be considered a fair trial."
At the same time, women have been shut out of the justice system, says Akbar. Since taking power in 2021, the Taliban has dismissed approximately 270 women judges as well as roughly 1,500 women registered as lawyers with the Afghanistan Independent Bar Association. Today, there are no women judges, prosecutors or officially registered female lawyers in the country.
"So for women, when they are accused of something, there's no way that they can pursue a defense. It's much harder to negotiate a way out of that punishment, because they simply can't," she says.
In one case documented by AHRDO, identified as PF003, the victim was detained from the public bazaar for wearing a long coat instead of the burqa. "They were settling the bill with the shopkeeper when several Taliban members entered the shop and questioned the shopkeeper about why he had allowed an "unveiled" woman into his premises," the report noted. The woman was arrested and beaten, causing a bleeding head wound, and then sentenced to 15 lashes.
"This is not a system meant to serve the population," Akbar says. "It's not meant to keep anyone safe. It's certainly not meant to keep women and children safe. In fact, it exposes women and children to more violence and abuse and trauma," she added.
In several case studies documented by AHRDO, women who approached the Taliban courts to complain about domestic abuse, violence and even rape were arrested and charged with moral crimes and sentenced to public lashing.
In one case, documented as PF006, the report noted that the victim, who had an intellectual disability, was detained by the Taliban in her garden and taken to a security checkpoint where she was raped. These details were provided when AHRDO interviewed a family member.
When the family tried to register a complaint against the Taliban member, the authorities instead imprisoned the victim and sentenced her on a charge of "having a relationship outside of marriage."
She was convicted and sentenced to twenty lashes and two months' imprisonment, during which she suffered life-threatening injuries, as her family shared with AHRDO.
Flogging in public has many consequences
The public nature of these punishments is also a reason for concern among activists. Several victims interviewed for the AHRDO report talked of the social ostracization that followed the sentencing.
"In cases of women being whipped or jailed, there's additional damage to her reputation which, in a place like Afghanistan, impacts her ability to reintegrate into her family and community," Akbar points out, noting that many women victims have struggled to find medical help for injuries suffered during the floggings.
"They are completely isolated and stigmatized as well, in addition to having experienced that trauma," she says.
Akbar worried about the impact of these public punishments on another group: the spectators. "I wonder about the people who are invited to watch these; what does it say about someone who would line up to see another human being beaten up?" she says.
Hamidi raises similar concerns. "It normalizes violence, fosters fear and self-censorship, and weakens trust in justice systems and public institutions," she says.
The psychological impact on the population, not just the survivors but also the community, "the people watching," is worrisome.
"The Taliban will not last forever," Akbar says, "but what if we can't break out of this chain of trauma, anger and resentment they are inculcating within the communities.

Patience, not revenge: Chandrababu Naidu takes aim at YS Jagan Mohan Reddy
At a public meeting in Konaseema, Andhra Pradesh's CM N Chandrababu Naidu said he could have arrested YS Jagan Mohan Reddy but chose restraint. He used the speech to accuse the previous YSRCP government of vendetta, stalled development and disruptive politics.
Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu on Wednesday said he could have taken “revenge” against former chief minister YS Jagan Mohan Reddy within minutes, but chose patience and restraint in the larger interests of the state.
Addressing a public meeting at Panduvaripeta in P Gannavaram constituency of Konaseema district during the Mee Bhoomi–Mee Hakku programme, Naidu recalled his arrest in Nandyal three years ago and accused the previous YSRCP government of political vendetta.
‘I CAN ARREST JAGAN WITHIN A MINUTE’
Recalling his arrest on September 9 three years ago, Naidu said he was taken into custody around midnight while he was in Nandyal to inspect irrigation projects.
“I can arrest Mr Jagan Mohan Reddy within a minute. But it will not benefit the people in any way. I do not wish to create any disturbance in the State,” Naidu said.
“But I do not believe in that kind of politics. I believe in patience and restraint. My objective is to ensure justice for the Telugu people and develop the state,” he added.
Naidu said he had spent 48 years in politics and had always followed value-based politics, with the welfare of the poor and development of Telugu people as his priorities.
He alleged that several cases were filed against him during the previous regime, but claimed that the allegations could not ultimately be established.
‘I WILL REMEMBER SUPPORT I RECEIVED FOR LIFE’
Naidu also recalled the public support he received following his arrest and said people across Telugu-speaking communities had stood by him.
He said technology professionals in Hyderabad and Telugu communities abroad had expressed solidarity with him while he was in jail.
Naidu also praised Deputy Chief Minister Pawan Kalyan, saying he continued to support him despite being stopped from expressing solidarity.
He alleged that several leaders, including Atchannaidu, were also arrested or harassed during the previous YSRCP government.
NAIDU TARGETS YSRCP OVER ‘ANARCHY AND CONSPIRACIES’
Taking aim at the YSRCP, Naidu alleged that the party's politics amounted to “anarchy while in power and conspiracies after losing power”.
He referred to various political controversies involving the Jagan family and made allegations concerning the murder of former minister YS Vivekananda Reddy and the subsequent political developments.
Naidu's remarks on these issues were political allegations made during the public meeting.
‘AP SUFFERED MORE DAMAGE BETWEEN 2019 AND 2024’
Naidu alleged that Andhra Pradesh suffered greater damage between 2019 and 2024 than it had because of bifurcation.
He accused the previous government of delaying key development projects, including Polavaram, and alleged that political decisions affected the progress of the project.
Naidu also referred to the Veligonda project and said the arrival of water had brought him immense satisfaction.
He accused the previous government of irregularities in the APPSC Group-I examination process and also alleged that poor-quality liquor supplied during the previous regime caused health problems.
‘COME TO ASSEMBLY AND DEBATE PUBLIC ISSUES’
Naidu also criticised YSRCP legislators for not regularly attending the Assembly and challenged them to raise their concerns on the floor of the House.
“If they have concerns about public issues, they should come to the Assembly and debate them,” he said.
He alleged that the opposition was attempting to obstruct development projects through litigation and accused the YSRCP of encouraging violent politics and abusive social media campaigns targeting political leaders and their families.
“Whatever conspiracies they may make, we will not be intimidated. We will fight strongly,” Naidu said.
The Chief Minister said his coalition government was focused on reviewing its performance, addressing shortcomings and ensuring that welfare and development programmes reached people effectively.

Oracle’s proposed investment in 2 gigawatts of renewable energy projects for New Mexico comes as local opposition could delay development of the Project Jupiter data center that Oracle is building for OpenAI.
The two tech companies are developing the $165 billion Project Jupiter data center in Santa Teresa, New Mexico, as part of the broader Stargate AI infrastructure project announced by President Donald Trump in 2025. But Project Jupiter faces local protests and court battles over concerns about its environmental impacts—and the latest Oracle announcement on September 8 seeking proposals for renewable energy projects does not change the fact that the data center will be powered by fuel cells that consume natural gas.
“Like all matching programs, this would be synthetic in the sense that 2 GW of renewables wouldn’t directly power the data center,” wrote Michael Thomas, CEO of the Cleanview data platform that tracks renewable energy and data center projects, in a LinkedIn post.
Oracle and OpenAI had originally planned to build 2.2 gigawatts of natural gas generation that could have resulted in 14 million tons of CO2 emissions per year, Thomas pointed out. That would have effectively “wiped out 20 years of carbon emissions reductions in the state of New Mexico,” he wrote in his post.
State residents and environmental groups have rallied in opposition to Project Jupiter with protests and lawsuits. New Mexico’s Land Office twice blocked requests to run a natural gas pipeline to the data center in New Mexico’s Doña Ana County.
Such opposition likely prompted the tech companies’ Project Jupiter plan to pivot from gas turbines to fuel-cell technology, which produces electricity through an electrochemical process without combustion.

After 52 patients from Andhra Pradesh were rushed to Bhadrachalam Area Hospital in Telangana’s Bhadradri Kothagudem district during an overnight medical emergency, the Polavaram district administration offered to support the Telangana hospital with medicines and drugs, recognising that nearly 40% of its patient load comes from Andhra Pradesh.
The 52 patients, including 47 children and five adults, were brought to the hospital from Gollaguppa village in Polavaram district, Andhra Pradesh, after reportedly falling ill post taking chloroquine tablets distributed during a health camp. One child was brought dead, while 12 patients tested positive for malaria.
A large number of children and adults arrived at the facility within a short period, but the hospital did not turn away patients from across the border. Despite having limited staff initially available, Bhadradri Kothagudem District Coordinator of Hospital Services (DCHS) G. Ravi Babu and Area Hospital Superintendent Rajasekhar Reddy and the hospital team immediately mobilised additional doctors and support staff who worked through the night, initiating treatment and closely monitoring the children and adults.
Polavaram District Collector K. Dinesh Kumar appreciated the Bhadrachalam Area Hospital team for extending immediate, compassionate and professional care to patients from Andhra Pradesh.
But the response from Andhra Pradesh went beyond appreciation. The Polavaram district administration assured that medicines required by Bhadrachalam Area Hospital would be extended to the facility. Nearly 40% of its patient load comes from Andhra Pradesh, making the Bhadrachalam facility an important healthcare centre for people living in neighbouring areas of the State.
Dr. G. Ravi Babu said the incident demonstrated the strength and responsiveness of a well-coordinated public healthcare system. “For a healthcare professional, a patient’s identity is never defined by State boundaries,” he said.

Universal Music Group is collaborating with ElevenLabs on a new AI-powered creation platform
The unnamed software will be built around licensed music from UMG artists who want to participate.
Universal Music Group and ElevenLabs have announced a new multi-year licensing agreement and "wider strategic collaboration" that will see them launch a new AI-powered licensed music platform.
The deal with UMG is the first that ElevenLabs has cut with a major label, and the new platform will be distinct from its ElevenMusic AI music generation software. The two companies also intend to collaborate on new AI audio products that can be used by artists, UMG wrote in a press release.
The AI creation software, which seemingly doesn't yet have a name, is still in development, and no release date is mentioned. It will primarily be aimed at music fans who want to make remixes and mashups of music from participating and "fairly compensated" artists that are signed to the label. ElevenLabs' tools will also be able to create "new track interpretations and personalized vocal experiences."
The music industry has had a complicated relationship with the emergence of AI. Just a few months ago a coalition of major labels that included UMG issued a collective appeal for AI slop tracks to be banned from charts worldwide, while various legal battles between labels and AI companies like Suno and Udio over accusations of copyright infringement have been well documented in the last few years.

And just this week, Suno said that the launch of its new v6 AI music models marked the formal beginning of its relationships with labels like Warner and BMG.

True diligence is following the improbable path. I read the sentence in a detective novel in childhood, when I was 8 or 9 years old, and then the phrase stayed with me forever after.
For a long time I wrote True Diligence in stylized curly letters on the inside page of every notebook, or sometimes on the front cover. I had notebooks for writing down clues, because even at 9 I wanted to work for the Internal Intelligence Service. What child doesn’t secretly wish to be a spy?
We were terrified and fascinated by Service in equal measure. Service was dark cars moving down the block, men and women in forgettable clothing stopping our parents on the street for brief random interrogations. Service was the force that made people disappear—when I was in the first grade, my friend from across the street climbed into the back of a black car with her parents, and their apartment stood empty for a year before other people moved in—but also Service carried a kind of dark glamour, an aura of power that called to us.
We played Ghosts and Agents all the time, my friends and I, but eventually they drifted off into other interests and I still wanted to be a spy, so after high school I applied successfully to the Service Academy in Los Angeles. I was talented and moved through school quickly, and afterward I was posted to Fillmore, a pretty town about 80 kilometers north of LA. My parents came to visit me there in my first year.
“This is lovely, Ibari,” my mother said, when she stepped off the train. The town made a good first impression. The central station was beautiful, one of those Southern California structures with no serious boundary between indoors and out, a tiled platform that turned into a waiting area with benches, then archways opening out to the street.
My parents had been on the train since Ohio, and they looked worn and dazed, blinking in the relentless sunlight. I was only in my mid-twenties at that point, which is to say I hadn’t thought much about the reality of aging parents, and their haziness was a glimpse into a future where I was the adult and they were confused. I didn’t like it.
“Not a cloud in the sky,” my father said.
“Do we need a taxi?” my mother asked. “I wouldn’t mind walking a bit, stretching my legs.”
“My house is close,” I said. “We can easily walk there if you’d like.”
“Downtown residency permit?” my father asked, and whistled softly.
“What can I say,” I said. “I’ve been well-behaved.”
I’ve spent a long time thinking about the nature of life in a surveillance state, which is perhaps obvious given my work, but there are observations I’ve made that I share with no one, and one of them has to do with the way in a place like this, reality splits into two.
This will seem a bit obvious—there’s your actual job, which is Service, and then there’s your cover, which is what you tell everyone you do—but for a long period of my life, at the beginning of my career, there was truth in both versions.
At the Service Academy I’d been trained in espionage and investigation, obviously, in relevant law, in the ins and outs of running down leads, interrogation, documentation, maintaining relationships with confidential informants, etc., but also I’d earned a master’s in urban planning, and this was my cover. As far as my parents and everyone else in my life was concerned, I was an up-and-coming academic with a tenure-track job at the local college. My parents didn’t know I was Service, because no one in my life knew I was Service.
Here was the branching, as I thought of it, the point where one reality split off into another: It was actually true that I was a junior professor in an urban planning department. I’d applied for and earned that position, or so I told myself—if strings were pulled behind the scenes, that was well above my pay grade—and I took that job seriously. With that being the case, was it really just cover? It was a real job, a real life. When I introduced myself as a college instructor in urban planning, it wasn’t a lie. There was an expansiveness about it. It was like getting to live two lives at once.
But in every version of reality I had an absolutely clean record, no subversion or other crimes of any kind, which had qualified me for a permit to live in an attractive neighborhood close to downtown. My parents and I walked out of the train station and up the hill together, and as an exercise in gratitude I tried to see Central Avenue through their eyes: the double row of palm trees, the century-old restored movie theater, the candy-colored awnings above the shops, an overall impression of having been unmoored from time and history sometime around 1965.
“I feel like I’m in a time capsule,” my mother said, and then quickly, “In a good way, I mean. It’s nice here.”
“It is nice,” I said. I really did like it here, for the most part. In Fillmore, as in most backwaters without a significant history of subversion, the State operated with a fairly light touch: identity cards, neighborhood permits, and facial recognition technology, like everywhere, but none of the random interrogations and drone surveillance that one might expect in larger cities.
My father took a nap on my couch while my mother and I went for a walk. We took a circuitous route that led us back through downtown. As we turned back onto Central Avenue, my attention was diverted by a scene playing out farther up the block and across the street. A black van had pulled up in front of the florist’s. The shop had been open an hour earlier, but now a crew had gone to work on it: The sign had been painted over, and two men were carting armloads of flowers into the van. The owners—a couple in their sixties whom I’d been surveilling for some time—were standing nearby, seemingly in shock. A second van pulled up, and the couple were led inside. They didn’t resist.
In a moment, the two vans were gone, and with them all trace of the business and the business’s owners. The shop was locked and blank now, no merchandise, no signs, the erasure complete. I knew, because I’d reported on this couple to my supervising officer, that they’d criticized the State on social media. They might be sent to prison, or to a black site, but I thought it more likely that they’d be sent to a work camp servicing the massive agricultural operations in the valley, a decade or so of picking strawberries or kale in the sun and sleeping in locked dormitories. People were rarely able to return to their previous life after that. I didn’t expect to see them again.
“This weather’s perfect,” my mother said.
Dinner that night was at a metal table I’d purchased for my backyard grove, as I thought of it: two ancient orange trees and a lemon tree that together formed a canopy. This was my favorite place in the world, and the main reason why I’d bought the house.
“Ibari,” my mother said, “I brought something for you from home.”
Home, for them, was Ohio, where they’d moved from New York when I’d left for the academy. I’d never lived there, and hearing the place called home was obscurely irritating. My mother had brought an ancient canvas tote bag to the table—could this possibly be the same one she’d used for grocery shopping in my childhood in New York?—and from it she pulled a battered old notebook, on which TRUE DILIGENCE and associated curlicues took up the entire front cover.
“Good lord,” I said. “Where did you find that?”
“I was cleaning out the storage unit,” she said, “and thought you might like to have it. What does the phrase mean?”
“True diligence?” I was going for lightness. I felt I’d succeeded. “Just a phrase I liked when I was a little kid. I think I must have seen it on TV or read it in a book somewhere.” If asked, I could have cited the book title, the author, and possibly the page number. Why was I lying about it? Because lying was my job. I pushed this thought down.
“I opened it up,” she said, “before I knew what it was. You should’ve been a detective.”
“Why,” I said, “what’s in it?” She was passing it across the table. I opened it, and for a moment didn’t understand what I was looking at. A timetable? No, the times of day when the neighbor at the apartment building across the street entered or left the building, except it was all only between 4 pm and 6 pm, because that was the time when I was sitting at my desk by the window doing homework, between school and dinner. He came and went a lot during that period, which I’d apparently found suspicious. The heading was straightforward: Times when Andy Commidy (sp?) enters or leaves home, with separate columns for enters and leaves. His schedule was remarkably consistent. I’d started the notebook after my friend across the street had disappeared, I remembered now. I was 7. But all these years later, I couldn’t remember my friend’s name.
“Wow,” I said, “I’d forgotten what a weird kid I was.”
“You should’ve been a detective,” she said again. Could she possibly know? It wasn’t possible, I told myself, but on the other hand, how did I know my mother wasn’t Service too? One of the more exhausting aspects of life in a surveillance state is that anyone can be surveilling you at any time, including the person whom you are yourself surveilling.
“I like the academic life,” I said. “It’s peaceful.”
“Anything you did here would seem peaceful, I’d think,” my father said. “Nice little town.”
“Well, Ibari,” my mother said, and raised her wineglass. “It looks like you’ve found a quiet life in a beautiful place.”
“Here’s to that,” my father said, and I smiled and joined them in sipping wine. Why did that comment bother me so much? She’d meant it kindly. Soon enough they returned to Ohio, and I settled back into the rhythms of my life. I was good at my work, both in Service and at the college. My students seemed to like me well enough, and I enjoyed teaching them. My Service work involved surveillance on a handful of local people, adults much older than me, who’d attended the last pro-democracy demonstrations a decade earlier.
It was easy work, observing their activities, listening to their mind-numbingly boring phone calls, meeting regularly with their next-door neighbors, friends, and colleagues. In my cover life, I liked my colleagues at the college. My home was beautiful. The dating pool was small, but I maximized it by dating both women and men. I collected a few local friends and enjoyed their company.
But in the years that followed my parents’ first visit, my mother’s comment—a quiet life in a beautiful place—stayed with me in a way I didn’t understand. It was like a splinter I could ignore for months at a time. Occasionally, in unexpected moments, I was struck by an uneasy sense that I was living the wrong life, or conducting my life in the same way I checked items off my grocery lists, or doing the wrong thing, or in stasis.
Sometime around my 40th birthday, while my friend Nico was visiting, I broke my glasses. I was picking oranges in the backyard when it happened. I’d taken the glasses off for only a moment, to wipe sweat from my face, but managed to drop them. I stepped back, looking at the ground in the dim greenish light under the orange tree, and heard a quiet snap under my shoe. The nose bridge was broken.
“You got a backup pair?” Nico asked, from the lounge chair. She’d been reading a book.
“In my office at the college,” I said.
“Do you have tape?”
“Probably. Keep reading, I’ve got this.” But all I seemed to have in the house, tape-wise, was a reflective silver tape that my cousin Anton had left behind on a recent visit, when he’d come for a few days with his 4-year-old twins, who were forever immersed in complicated art projects. The tape was very narrow but surprisingly strong. I carefully wound it around the broken section, then the right lens popped out, so I added more tape on the right. The glasses felt secure when I put them on, but the overall look was insane. I was staring in the mirror when the doorbell rang.
“Nice repair job, Ibari,” the UPS driver said. He came around often enough that we were on a first-name basis. In those days I did a lot of online shopping.
“Thank you. I just stepped on them.”
“Happens to the best of us,” he said, and raised his device close to my face. “Voice?”
“My voice is my passcode,” I said reflexively, and waited, with the driver, for the signature of my voice and the image of my face to match with my address in the UPS system, so that the driver could leave the small package he held, which I thought was probably my new toothbrush. Instead, his device emitted a sharp warning beep.
“Seems like there’s a problem with the face scan,” the driver said.
“Let’s try that again.” He raised the device.
“My voice is my passcode.” The beep came again.
“Try again without the glasses?”
“My glasses have never been a problem,” I said, but took them off anyway. “You’re sure you can’t just leave the package?”
“Without ID verification?” The driver grinned. “I didn’t know you did stand-up. OK, take three?”
“My voice is my passcode,” I said, with the glasses in my hand, and this time the machine produced a melodic chime.
“There you go,” the driver said. “Enjoy the rest of your day.”
I thanked him, and brought the little package in. I felt very strange. It was as if a curtain had been pulled aside, just for a second, and I’d seen the machinery hidden behind it. I’d never  really thought about facial recognition systems before, because they were everywhere and always had been, my face recorded and uploaded to a central database several times a day since earliest memory. The question was whether the glasses could thwart any facial recognition software, or if it was just a faulty UPS scanner. I returned to the backyard with a feeling of carrying a dangerous secret. I wanted to test my glasses again.
“Nico,” I said, “you want to go for a walk, maybe get some iced tea downtown?”
Nico smiled. “Your poor glasses,” she said. “Yes, iced tea sounds perfect.”
We walked slowly, in the direction of iced tea. It was a hot day, but the solar fans in the business district created a gentle breeze. There was a man walking a block or so ahead of us. One of the former pro-democracy agitators whom I’d been surveilling. I’d studied him so carefully that I’d have known him anywhere.
“When do you need to be back in LA?” I asked.
“I thought I’d take the 4 o’clock train.” It was still only late morning. As we entered the tea shop, a discreet scanner embedded in the door frame flashed white—Face not found—but confirmation didn’t come until I reached the front of the line, ordered an iced tea, and stared directly into the screen to pay with credit.
“I’m sorry,” the barista said, and swiveled the screen so I could read the message: Facial recognition error. “I can’t remember the last time this happened.”
“Oh,” I said, “no problem, let’s do fingerprints.” I pressed my right index finger to the screen, and a moment later a green check mark appeared. Nico was studying the muffins.
“I think these glasses are throwing off the scanners,” I said.
Nico went still for just a second, and shook her head. The movement was barely perceptible. She was still looking at the baked goods.
“The muffins here look good,” she said, as if I’d said nothing.
This was when I understood: My friend was Service. I had no doubt that she was who she said she was, which is to say an associate professor in the physics department at UCLA, but also she was something else. It shouldn’t be disappointing, I told myself. A lot of people were Service. I was Service. The barista could be Service. Anyone around you, at any given moment, could be observing and reporting. But was she reporting on me? We were quiet on the walk back to the house. The iced tea tasted like cardboard.
“I’ve never reported on you,” Nico said, when we were close to my house. She spoke so quietly that I barely heard her, and I knew it wasn’t a coincidence that she’d waited until our backs were to the downtown camera array.
“OK.” I felt vastly relieved. I knew that rationally there was no reason to believe her, but all my life I’ve had a sense of intuition, and I felt very strongly that she was telling the truth. And then, because she was my closest friend and she’d taken the risk first: “I’ve never reported on you either,” I said.
She didn’t stop walking, but I heard a slight intake of breath.
“You know,” she said, again very softly, “I think it doesn’t take that much to become a ghost.”
“You’re probably right.” I appreciated the warning. Ghost was slang for a person who ran afoul of the State. A ghost is undesirable. A ghost lives in the shadows. A ghost is not entitled to a home, or health care, or the protections of the law, or a social security number, bank account, credit, or entry into most spaces, because does a ghost even really entirely exist?

Fire in eastern Congo kills at least 24 students at 2 schools
A fire in Bukavu, eastern Congo, has killed at least 24 students, according to the rebel administration controlling the city
BUKAVU, Congo -- A fire on Thursday in Bukavu, eastern Congo, killed at least 24 students, the rebel administration that controls the city said.
The spokesperson for the M23 rebel group, Lawrence Kanyuka, said 19 girls and five boys were killed, adding that 29 people were being treated at local medical facilities.
The fire started at a house before spreading to two adjoining schools, local neighborhood administrator Moïse Lubala told The Associated Press.
He said several students were trapped inside Furaha secondary school and some suffocated.
A mix of boys and girls of different ages, students at Furaha and at Ujamaa primary school, were brought to the Nyamulagira BDOM health center in their school uniforms, nurse Ciza Jean-Baptiste told the AP.
Medical staff were struggling to keep track of the exact number of injured because there were so many, he said.
“The exit was too narrow, so some students began jumping through windows while others rushed toward the door. As everyone tried to force their way out, students were pushed over and trampled on,” said Lubala.
The cause of the fire is not known, but the neighborhood where the fire started is densely populated and most houses are made out of wood, according to Lubala.
Congo’s government struggles to exert control over the east of the country. M23 rebels, backed by Rwanda, took control of Bukavu in February 2025. More than 100 armed groups are vying for control of eastern Congo’s trillions of dollars in mineral wealth that’s critical for much of the world’s technology.
Health services are under severe strain as the region grapples with the deadliest Ebola outbreak in history that has killed more than 3,300 people, with more than 6,800 confirmed cases recorded.

Italy holds a special place in my heart, which is why I'm always finding excuses to return.
I've visited three times since 2016, including a four-month stay in Florence during college. Thanks to Italy's well-connected transit systems, I've had the chance to visit 21 cities and villages, most often by rail.
Some of the destinations I've been to have blown me away, while others left me wanting more. Here are four Italian cities I'd happily return to — and two I'd leave off my itinerary next time.
Cinque Terre is a beautiful place to hike.
Cinque Terre is a string of five seaside villages on the northwestern coast of Italy.
Although all five villages are accessible by train, hiking between them is a popular activity. I'd recommend starting in the southernmost town, Riomaggiore, and hiking north for stunning views.
Cinque Terre is perfect for anyone looking to relax in a vibrant environment, enjoy traditional Italian culture, or explore five seaside villages in one day.
My trip to Verona felt like something straight out of a fairytale.
I immediately fell in love with how enchanting, quaint, and walkable Verona felt during my first visit in 2016.
Home to Shakespeare's beloved "Romeo and Juliet," visitors commonly visit Juliet's house, calling down to those below from the balcony.
During my time in Verona, I stumbled upon Club di Giulietta, a volunteer group that calls themselves the secretaries of Juliet. They receive thousands of letters addressed to Juliet from around the world, and volunteers sort letters by language before handwriting a response.
I got to spend a few hours reading and writing replies myself, which became the highlight of my trip to Verona.
Overall, the city's walkability, history, and quaint feel make it perfect for a day trip for time-restricted itineraries.
There's so much to do in Florence.
Since living in Florence in 2016, I've been back to visit twice. There's so much to love about the city, which is the capital of the Tuscany region.
For those visiting for the first time, I recommend staying a minimum of four full days to explore the city's museums and local markets. I love visiting the farmers market in Santo Spirito for fresh-baked goodies, local produce, and vintage finds.
I've also enjoyed grabbing gelato and trekking up to Piazzale Michelangelo to watch the sunset. On cooler evenings, St. Mark's Church is a great place to watch affordable live opera.
Outside the city, I suggest horseback riding through the Tuscan hills, attending a pasta making class, and taking a wine tour.
In my opinion, Catania, Sicily, is a must-visit location.
If Sicily is on your itinerary, a trip to Catania is a must. The city is at the foot of Mount Etna, the highest active volcano in Europe.
In fact, the volcano is integral to local tourism, architecture, and wine production. Guides offer hiking tours during dormancy, allowing visitors to walk the crater rim. The volcanic stone is also used to build local churches, plazas, and roadways.
Sicily's food and wine scene is also reason enough to visit this part of Italy. The volcanic ash can help enrich the soil, providing nutrients for vineyards that produce incredible wine.
However, I'd skip Naples and head to Italy's southern coastal gems instead.
Fellow travelers warned me that Naples fell short of their expectations, but I wanted to experience the city for myself. So, I visited twice during a solo trip last year, staying on opposite sides of the city each time.
Although the Neapolitan pizza did not disappoint, navigating the sprawling, hilly city on foot was challenging.
The local metro system was convenient for getting around, but it turned out to be a persistent target for pickpockets. After witnessing a few such instances firsthand, I made the choice to avoid taking the trains at night. However, that meant my taxi fares added up quickly after evenings spent out.
Overall, if I'm going to be in Southern Italy I'd much rather pop over to the Amalfi Coast or other nearby destinations.
In my opinion, one trip to Venice was enough.
There's a lot to love about Venice, from the unique architecture to the outstanding glasswork.
Unfortunately, though, I was underwhelmed by the food and noticed some things like souvenirs, meals, and experiences were more expensive than they were in other Italian cities I'd visited.
Although the architecture is stunning, the narrow, winding streets also made it difficult to navigate the city and added to the feeling of overcrowding.
Additional planning is now needed to visit, as the city requires tourism permits on certain days. Considering the expense, challenges with walkability, and additional planning required, I likely won't return to Venice for another visit.
This story was originally published on May 3, 2025, and most recently updated on September 11, 2026.

Six Nigerians accused of romance scams to be extradited to the US
- Published
South African police are handing over six Nigerians wanted in the US for alleged online romance scams to FBI agents later on Friday.
The group is accused of targeting over 100 women in the US and defrauding them of more than 100m rand ($6m; £5m), the South African authorities said.
Those being extradited were arrested in 2021 and are believed to be members of crime syndicate Black Axe - a Nigerian mafia-style gang tied to human trafficking, internet fraud and murder.
Some of their reported victims included pensioners and businesspeople "who were targeted through sophisticated online relationships used to defraud them of their money", according to South Africa's elite Hawks police unit.
The group will be "transported from a correctional facility in Cape Town" to the airport on Friday morning, where they will be "handed over to officials from the FBI and the United States Secret Service", Hawks spokesperson Colonel Katlego Mogale said in a statement.
They would face wire fraud and money-laundering charges upon their arrival in the US, she added.
- Mass arrests in global crackdown on West African cyber-crime networks 
  - Published25 August
Black Axe is a shadowy criminal network known for its extreme violence and operates across Africa, Europe and North America.
A BBC Eye investigation in 2021 suggested that the syndicate had become one of the most far-reaching and dangerous organised crime groups in the world.
Nigeria is its main recruitment ground and many of its members are university educated and inducted during their schooling.
The group has been on the radar of law enforcement agencies for a number of years.
FBI operations against Black Axe were launched in November 2019 and September 2021, eventually charging more than 35 individuals with multi-million dollar internet fraud.
Since then there have been several other operations across multiple countries targeting Black Axe co-ordinated by the global policing agency Interpol.
Last month, Interpol said during its latest one - which took place between November 2025 and June 2026 - seven sites in South Africa linked to a syndicate involved in romance and investment scams were raided.
It led to the arrests of 39 people, the seizure of money and the blocking of more than 250 bank accounts.

The world is bracing for a “super” El Niño, and its effects are already being felt in India, where the monsoon has brought less rain than average but more intense downpours.
Meteorologists predict that the current El Niño, which is developing over the Pacific, could be one of the strongest in living memory. India is likely to be heavily affected, particularly later in the monsoon, when El Niño’s influence tends to strengthen.
But, as Ligin Joseph of the University of Southampton explains in The Conversation, its effects on India’s monsoon are not straightforward. A previous study in Science found that El Niño tends to bring more extreme summer monsoon rainfall to India.
This year, the southern state of Kerala has felt the brunt of the building super El Niño, with about a fifth less rain than normal. Yet intense downpours in the first week of August triggered flash flooding and landslides, killing 26 people.
The super El Niño is expected to peak after India’s monsoon season, but Indians are already keeping an anxious eye on the skies, wondering where and when the next deluge may come.

Four key takeaways from Republican midterms convention
- Published
The Republican Party's first midterms convention had all the trappings of the traditional presidential election-year gathering: supporters in sparkling costumes, a conveyor belt of candidate speeches, and vendors selling campaign merchandise.
But unlike an ordinary convention, no official party business was conducted in Dallas, with the event instead serving as a rally for Republicans who are seeking to boost turnout and avoid losing control of Congress in November.
President Donald Trump, whose grip over the party remains absolute, delivered a lengthy keynote speech on Wednesday during the opening night of the two-day event. He covered many of the subjects he has returned to time and again this year - with a few surprises thrown in.
Here are the key takeaways from his address.
1. Preaching to the MAGA choir
The vast arena was filled with diehard Trump supporters sporting red MAGA gear from his past presidential campaigns. A decade after his first White House run, Trump is still beloved among his base and he has bent the party to his will in the years since.
The old-style Republican establishment, or what's left of it in the Trump era, was nowhere to be seen. Senator Susan Collins of Maine and other Republicans running in competitive races chose to stay away.
The absence of more moderate Republicans was glaring and offered a reminder of just how much the party has changed.
It also raised questions about the effectiveness of holding an unprecedented midterm convention in the first place.
The core audience, both in the arena and watching on television, appeared to be Trump loyalists, not the moderates and swing voters the Republican Party needs to turn out in large numbers in November.
2. Trump offers $5,000 payout
Trump has long thrown out unconventional ideas at rallies. On Wednesday night, that came in the form of an offer to pay every adult US citizen $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win both chambers of Congress in November.
The only caveat, Trump said, was the money would have to be spent in the US.
He offered no details on how the plan would work, where the money would come from, or how the US government would monitor how it was spent. Democrats quickly labelled it an "empty promise" and others questioned whether such a pledge was even legal.
There are nearly 270 million American adults, which means a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.
Whether the plan was possible or not appeared to be beside the point. The idea drew raucous applause at the convention and Trump seemed to relish the moment.
3. A gamble on affordability
Earlier on Wednesday, as he departed for the convention, Trump acknowledged that Americans may have to wait a while longer to see relief from high fuel prices.
"I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterms," Trump said.
The president reiterated that message in his speech, arguing that short-term economic pain caused by the war in Iran was worth it to prevent Tehran from developing nuclear weapons.
But that may be a difficult message to land with voters who are feeling higher prices.
Polls have consistently indicated in recent months that the cost of living is a top-ranking issue among Americans.
Trump's approval rating, too, has taken a hit as the war in Iran has dragged on. A Financial Times / Focaldata poll released on Sunday indicated that it had hit a new low, with only 33% of registered voters approving of his presidential performance.
Many Republican candidates may well have hoped for a more direct message on addressing the cost of living and quickly ending the war in Iran.
4. It's still Trump's party
Trump's total grip on the party raises some pointed questions about its future. Namely - who will replace him? And more immediately for November's elections, how will it perform when his name isn't on the ballot?
Trump offered a simple solution to the latter question on Wednesday night. After warning that the sitting president tends to lose the midterms, he told the crowd: "I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot."
The remark was an acknowledgement by Trump that he remains the party's best driver of turnout. It also speaks to the challenge Republicans have both in November and in the next presidential election in 2028.
Trump will not be on the ballot again, and though he can continue campaigning for the party, there is not a clear or obvious successor who can rally the base quite like Trump.
In interviews with the BBC, convention goers often looked ahead to the election in two years' time and debated who Trump's successor should be. Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were frequently mentioned as top contenders.
Trump, however, made clear in Dallas that he is still in charge and is not in a hurry to give up the spotlight.

In 2012, Southern California was besotted with an unlikely celebrity: a telegenic mountain lion who had crossed one of the state’s most perilous freeways, seeking a territory to call his own. Widely deemed “LA’s loneliest lion” and “most eligible bachelor,” the chiseled puma in question, named P-22, roamed the bustling but otherwise big cat-less Hollywood Hills, unable to safely return to the home he’d left behind. His search for a mate below the Hollywood Sign rendered him an icon of his city, but also a rueful reminder of the sprawling highways that bifurcated his habitat in the first place, leaving his clan on the other side of I-405 on the verge of local extinction.
An elegant fix for one of America’s deadliest road problems
Highways weren’t built for animals. That’s starting to change.
Beth Pratt, then recently named head of California’s branch of the National Wildlife Federation, remembers strolling through Griffith Park with the wildlife biologist Jeff Sikich in 2012. Pratt knew that P-22 roamed somewhere nearby, and she found herself wondering aloud how she could help. “Well, there’s this little wildlife corridor we need to get built,” Sikich told her.
“I’m like, ‘Sure, how hard can it be?’” she recalled to me with a laugh. “Well, apparently, it’s quite hard.”
Fourteen years later, the project they discussed that day, now known as the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing, is finally scheduled to open in December. When it does, it will be the largest real-life animal crossing in the world, a gorgeous, vegetated overpass offering safe passage to local mountain lions, coyotes, deer, and black bears across the perilous 10-lane Ventura Freeway, where P-22 dodged cars back in 2012.
Though P-22 died before he could take advantage of that crossing himself, he helped engender a movement that, hard as it may have been to pull off in LA, could help revolutionize how animals cross America’s most dangerous roads, preventing some of the hundreds of human deaths, hundreds of millions of animal deaths, and billions in damages caused by wildlife collisions each year.
It is a species of elegant, bipartisan infrastructure that, if you squint, might even make you believe in America’s ability to build again, and to build in a way that still lends a hand — a paw, if you will — to the least empowered among us, a stranded salamander or the loneliest of lions.
As Pratt put it: “What’s more hopeful than rewilding one of the world’s busiest freeways?”
Wildlife crossings used to be rare in the US. Not anymore.
When Pratt first pitched the idea for a wildlife crossing across the 101, such projects were still rare in the US, and rarer still across such a major thoroughfare. As she recalls it, California’s transportation agency initially reacted with bafflement when she put the idea forward, a sign of just how novel the project was at the time. That made the process of getting it built more grueling than it needed to be, and likely more expensive, with a final price tag of over $100 million.
But as LA meandered in its quest to build its unprecedented 210-feet-long Wallis Annenberg — beset, Pratt told me, by its complex engineering mandate, a funding model that relied on philanthropy, and the rising costs associated with construction and extreme weather — the rest of the nation took notice. In the 14 years since P-22 first crossed the 101 and the 405, over 1,000 new wildlife corridors have sprouted up across the country, a trend that culminated with the $350 million Wildlife Crossings Pilot Program, created in 2021 as part of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. Many of these projects were championed by Pete Buttigieg, who was Transportation secretary under the Biden administration, and who told Vox last year that such passages are “not ornamental,” but rather “something that ties into the very core of our mission, which is to secure the safety of the American traveling public.”
America’s burst of new wildlife corridors include a camouflaged overpass for elk crossing Interstate 25 in Colorado; a lush shared land bridge for deer, bobcats, and people passing over a Texan parkway; crossings for alligators passing under I-75 in the Florida everglades; and tiny tunnels under the Atlantic City expressway in New Jersey for migrating toadlets. California’s transportation agency, for its part, now boasts a division explicitly dedicated to building wildlife crossings, though many projects need not be as ambitious as the Wallis Annenberg.
“Sometimes it’s pretty simple,” like a small hole to let hedgehogs through your fencing or a buzz stop for bees and butterflies crossing your lawn, Pratt said. “Sometimes it’s in your own backyard.”
Along the way, a new set of norms have begun settling in at transportation agencies across the country, said Marcel Huijser, a research ecologist at the Western Transportation Institute, who noted that while “road ecology has become more recognized” in the US, the nation still has a very long way to go. Huijser is from the Netherlands, where wildlife crossings have been the norm for decades. The country boasts thousands of them in an area roughly double that of Massachusetts.
“Most other parts of the world have done a better job at taking social and ecological impacts into consideration from the earliest decision processes onwards,” he told me, rather than “making it an afterthought.” And given that highways are already three times more expensive to build and maintain per mile in the US than they are elsewhere, it’s not the cost of conservation alone that has long kept the nation from incorporating such concerns into its road planning.
Instead, as Huijser put it, “the norms, the values, [and] the culture” of the country have, until recently, ensured that planners rarely baked ecological considerations into the way it imagines its roadways. Wildlife advocates have instead been forced to rely, as activists in the US so often must, on a hodgepodge of lawsuits and local lobbying.
The Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing could well be transformative for local wildlife, and help keep Angelenos safer on the road for generations, but its most promising legacy may in fact be how it helped inspire a much broader movement and tranche of funding. The pilot program that P-22 helped inspire is now up for renewal, and seems poised to become permanent by the time that the Wallis Annenberg crossing opens in December.
Few wildlife corridors in the US will benefit from an über famous spokes-cat like P-22, a tireless local advocate like Pratt, or a roster of movie stars and philanthropists willing to pour time and money into building a new kind of bridge. Keeping local and federal governments on board with the projects may also be an uphill battle, given the national tenor. While many wildlife crossings have been embraced on a bipartisan basis, just a few months ago, Pratt received death threats after a smattering of right-wing media outlets assailed the Wallis Annenberg as a “butterfly bridge” to nowhere.
But if the US can successfully channel that cougar’s enduring star power into sustained support for a smart newish-to-us kind of infrastructure, one that’s been consistently shown to make a road much safer — and ultimately, cheaper! — for humans and animals alike, then maybe there’s a fair chance for the rest of us, and maybe this stubborn nation can get better at building things more like it.
“These things should just be part of transportation budgets and embedded in our infrastructure planning,” said Pratt, who is planning her first vacation in seven years once the bridge finally opens in December. “The ultimate goal is you don’t need someone like me.”
