Reform UK has been given a record £36m donation by Ben Delo, a British cryptocurrency billionaire convicted in the US for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls.
The businessman, who has moved back to the UK from Hong Kong, is now the biggest UK political donor by far, dwarfing the £15m contribution to Reform UK from Thailand-based Christopher Harborne.
The huge donation will be a boost for party leader Nigel Farage at a time when he is facing a police investigation into overseas funding for Reform, plus a standards inquiry into a £5m undeclared personal gift from Harborne.
It had been thought Delo could be caught by the overseas cap requiring donors to have been resident in the UK for 12 months before giving more than £100,000 but Reform insisted earlier this month that they were confident Delo would not have to take back any cash.
Delo was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls in his trillion-dollar cryptocurrency business BitMEX, before being pardoned by Donald Trump. He has previously given Reform £8m since the start of the year.
His gifts show the rise of Reform’s mega-donors, which Labour has been considering clamping down on.
Keir Starmer shied away from the idea of a cap on all donations and Andy Burnham also recently backed away from supporting a cap. However, more recently the government said it was looking at ways of dealing with mega-donations to make sure a few figures are not having an excessive influence in politics.
On Friday night, Stella Creasy, the Labour MP pushing for a cap, said: “The government has admitted UK mega-donors are a problem – donations like this show why we must act and the good news is it’s not too late to do something about them.
“We can still stop these people from distorting the next election by confirming what the cap should be on UK donations in the representation of the people bill in the Lords.
“This donation tonight – more for Reform on one day than the entire amount spent by Labour in the general election – shows that cannot come too soon to protect British democracy.”
Many more Labour MPs were also horrified by the prospect of such a huge cash injection for Reform ahead of the next election.
Delo’s donation was revealed in the Telegraph, which was given the information by Reform after the party was approached by the Sunday Times earlier on Friday.
Farage said: “I am honoured and humbled that Ben Delo has shown such confidence in Reform. Ben knows that we are the only party that can turn the country around and reverse Britain’s decline.”
In a Telegraph article in April, Delo explained his motivation for turning to Reform, saying England was his home and that “the biggest obstacle to national recovery is the entrenched self-deception of our elites”.
“Their regime of nonsense now poses such a grave threat to the UK that, for the first time in my life, I’ve become politically active,” he wrote.
He said that as a person on the autism spectrum, he did not like it that “the official culture of government now forces everyone to be chronically dishonest”, citing expression of views on transgender people.
In his Telegraph article, he wrote: “I helped build one of the world’s first major crypto trading platforms, fell foul of US regulators, accepted a plea bargain and a civil fine for a regulatory failing that isn’t even a crime in the UK, but then ended up being pardoned by Donald Trump, the US president, anyway.”
Delo, an Oxford graduate who describes himself as a champion of free speech, supports more than 50 organisations across the political spectrum and public life, as well as non-affiliated groups and individuals, from a political base near Westminster Abbey.
A Guardian investigation into Delo’s political base found he had given support in kind to Rupert Lowe, the anti-migration MP challenging Farage from the right, while also connecting with more mainstream figures including the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, and the former Tory cabinet minister Michael Gove.
Delo’s lawyers previously told the Guardian that he provided space for those with diverse views to express them, and financial support to a broad range of organisations, many of which had conflicting views. This did not mean he endorsed the opinions of each, they said.

Babies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in key regions linked to movement, learning and the regulation of emotion, according to a study.
Researchers said the differences, first detected at the age of one, could lead to cognitive problems when children started school.
More than a third of pregnant women worldwide have anaemia – a condition typically caused by iron deficiency in which the number of red blood cells in the body is lower than normal. Symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath and dizziness. Rates are highest in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia.
Researchers from King’s College London in the UK, and the University of Cape Town in South Africa, followed more than 300 mothers and their babies in Cape Town, scanning the brains of the infants several times between the ages of three months and two years.
On average, the total brain volume of babies born to anaemic mothers was 4% lower than that of babies born to non-anaemic mothers – despite all the anaemic mothers being diagnosed only with a mild version of the condition.
Differences were recorded in three specific regions of the brain: the putamen, caudate nucleus and corpus callosum.
“All three of these brain regions are implicated in key neuropsychological functions,” said Jessica Ringshaw, first author and researcher at King’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) and the University of Cape Town, citing processing speed, emotion regulation and executive function as examples.
The gap between the groups of babies widened over the first two years of life – the corpus callosum, for instance, was about 4% smaller at 12 months in the group whose mothers had been anaemic but 6% by 24 months.
Earlier research in South Africa looking at toddlers and school-age children found comparable differences in brain volume.
“These aren’t children who are catching up, where the brain differences are disappearing over time,” said Ringshaw. “They are still there when the children are six years old and going to school, and when these things might then start translating into more noticeable cognitive difficulties.”
The findings offer a potential explanation for earlier studies showing that children born to mothers with anaemia scored less well on tests of development, she added.
The mothers with and without anaemia were otherwise very similar in terms of factors such as household income and food security, Ringshaw said, making her confident that maternal anaemia caused the differences the team observed.
The results reinforced the importance of tackling anaemia in women of reproductive age, Ringshaw said. “We should be screening for anaemia and iron deficiency, particularly during pregnancy,” she said, recommending the use of oral or even intravenous iron supplementation where appropriate.
The causes of anaemia were complex and could include infectious diseases, she said, with the study finding higher rates of anaemia in women living with HIV, “so having our iron interventions, but also appropriate infection management in conjunction with that [is important]”.
While the World Health Organization lists reducing rates of anaemia as a priority, progress has stagnated over the past two decades.
“Now more than ever, anaemia needs to be placed at the forefront of public health efforts if we are to ensure that children are not only surviving but thriving,” said Ringshaw.
The research, published in the journal Brain Communications, used special new MRI scanners that are cheaper and more portable than the conventional machines used in hospitals.
It compared images taken using the traditional “high-field” MRI machines with those taken by the portable “low-field” options, and found the latter were sensitive enough to detect the same differences in the brains of babies born to anaemic mothers.
Steve Williams, professor of neuroimaging at King’s, said: “This study has proved that our novel technology can measure the impact of malnutrition on the developing brain, at scale, in some of the most challenging environments. This will provide an early, sensitive assessment of planned interventions.”

AI workers with apocalypse fears are facing a troubling, though not unprecedented, career dilemma.
Should they quit their jobs to avoid potentially helping make the doomsday scenario they envision a reality? Or, should they drive change for the better from within?
It's a thorny predicament that came into focus this week when Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI employee, said in an X post that he was resigning from Anthropic because the "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."
Soon after, Evan Hubinger, who leads Anthropic's alignment stress-testing team, essentially backed Coxon, saying he believes there is a greater-than-10% chance AI could kill all humans within the next decade.
Why some workers stay
For AI workers worried that they're contributing to mankind's destruction, deciding whether to quit or stay put is more complicated than it may seem, said Jeremie Harris, CEO and cofounder of Gladstone AI, a Washington, DC-based safety and advisory company focused on national security risks and catastrophic threats from advanced AI. "I don't particularly fault anyone for making either call," he said.
Harris said his job involves regularly talking with staff at Anthropic and other top AI labs, and that in recent months he's heard many express fears similar to those Coxon described. While quitting can be a moral response to building a dangerous technology, he said, Al labs could end up with few or no workers willing to press for change if resignations pile up.
"The people who are left are going to be the ones who are least concerned about safety," Harris said, while "people who care arguably should be the ones in the seat."
In response to Coxon's announcement, Anthropic employee Anna Wang said on X that she works at the company because she thinks she "can do better at reducing risks from the inside." She added that she respects and endorses others "who think that it's better to do so from the outside."
A spokesperson for Anthropic declined to comment after confirming Wang's employment.
Coxon's X post, which also sparked online debate over its impact on Anthropic's image, the company's coming IPO, and the possibility that this is all a strange publicity stunt, echoes concerns of a pending AI calamity previously made by Geoffrey Hinton, the computer scientist widely known as the "Godfather of AI," xAI founder Elon Musk, and others.
The general public is apprehensive about AI, too. Some 52% of Americans are more concerned than excited about the use of the technology in daily life, according to a June study from the Pew Research Center. That's up from 37% who said the same in 2021.
A dilemma with a history
For AI workers who truly believe their employer is creating an existential threat, Alex Wellerstein, a professor at Stevens Institute of Technology, said internal voices of reason have a poor track record of "overcoming preexisting institutional momentum."
"If you stick around, you're participating," he said.
That tension is not new. Technology historian Matthew H. Hersch said the Manhattan Project, a World War II-era program to develop nuclear weapons, is a close parallel.
Ralph Austin Bard, then undersecretary of the US Navy, privately urged officials to warn Japan before using the atomic bomb and resigned weeks before Hiroshima, likely in protest of the decision not to do so, said Hersch, also a professor at Harvard University and a member of the School of Historical Studies at the Institute for Advanced Study.
Other Manhattan Project scientists also unsuccessfully pushed for a demonstration of the bomb before it was used in combat, some of whom were effectively barred from future defense work, he added.
"Whistleblowers can do tremendous good," Hersch told Business Insider, "but are apt to be discredited or harassed into silence, and become unemployable in their industry."

Donald Trump loves rallies. Everyone can see how they energize him, how the crowd’s applause encourages him to ditch the hackneyed prose of his speechwriters and go on wild riffs, how the music and cheering are like water to a parched man. Tonight, at the end of a two-day rally billed as a Republican “midterm convention,” Trump was visibly exhilarated.
But he also protested too much, in the process revealing some political as well as personal fears and insecurities. Right at the outset, Trump made a reference to the arena and how packed it was, apparently stung by images of empty seats during the first night of the festivities. (He blamed those pictures on a dishonest press that was taking pictures of seats left by people going to the bathroom.) He returned to the crowd size issue near the end of the evening, going on at length about the packed seats and boxes. He also made life harder for Republican candidates who might try to get some distance from him by repeatedly stressing that he, Donald Trump, really is on the ballot, even if his name isn’t listed.
A confident president does not hold a faux convention. A man who feels in control of his political future does not promise every American a $5,000 bounty if his party wins the election. A man who thinks he’s winning a war does not boast that America “controls the Strait of Trump” a day after news reports revealed damage to U.S. military assets in an Iranian strike.
And a leader who believes in his voters does not make them recite weird pledges in the middle of a speech.
Trump—apparently in one of his detours away from the teleprompter—was struck by the possibility that his own people wouldn’t vote. He stopped and demanded they follow him in a pledge. “I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States,” he began, as the audience repeated his words, “that loves us so much he can’t even breathe…”
 
 I must pause here and assure you that I am not making any of this up. Trump continued by riffing about promising to “bring friends and family” to vote, even if it involved cheating. By this point, those in the audience had given up and all of them were gamely doing their best to laugh and placate the president. Trump got them back on track with a pledge to vote—and then again detoured, saying that they should vote, even if it’s to vote for Democrats, before adding that no one in the room would do that—a safe assumption at a convention of loyalists.
(The mindlessness of the whole thing was reminiscent of what the comedian Steve Martin captured with a revealing prank he used to pull on his audiences in the late 1970s—the Non-Conformist Oath. They would repeat his vows to be different and unique, without knowing where he was going with the bit. Then Martin would shout: “I promise not to repeat things other people say!” The crowd would start to chant back, of course, and then dissolve into laughter. Trump, too, asked his crowd to repeat his words without knowing what was coming. Unlike Martin’s audiences, the GOP attendees did not seem to get that it’s creepy to uncritically repeat whatever someone else tells you to say.)
Trump ended this fractured pledge by asking the crowd to affirm that they would vote, “so help me God.” The president may have realized that asking people to involve the Almighty in a promise to go to the polls was a bit much, and so he quickly pivoted to joking that if you don’t vote, you go to hell, and as a president who cares, he doesn’t want that for anyone. The prospect of ending up in perdition for not voting isn’t exactly a knee-slapper, but lightening the moment allowed Trump to end the cringe and move on.
This vow was a weird moment in a short speech of weird moments. Trump basically speed-ran the same speech he gave the night before, tumbling through promises of money and his usual (and sometimes factually wifty) boasts about various policies. Finally, he decided that it was time to just hand over the show to Christopher Macchio, the opera singer.
But wait. Did you know that Macchio is better than the great Luciano Pavarotti? You see, the president continued, he knew Pavarotti, Pavarotti was a great friend of his, but Macchio is better than Pavarotti. And Macchio, Trump went on, was too modest to admit it, but…
You get the picture. Trump just couldn’t bring himself to leave the stage. Finally, the president shrugged, almost as if someone off camera had given him the “wrap it up” sign, and said “Vote!” and left.
Trump is likely well aware of the dire situation his party faces. But once again, in front of what he stressed was a packed arena, he could not help but make the election about himself, demanding that Americans vote not based not on their assessment of the Republicans who are actually running, but on their loyalty to him, personally. Democrats could not have asked for a better closer for the evening.

Months after Turning Point USA CEO Charlie Kirk was fatally shot on Sept. 10, 2025, a rumor circulated online that his widow, Erika Kirk, had announced she was pregnant shortly after her husband's death.
The claim about her supposed pregnancy resurfaced (archived) about a year after Kirk's killing, with many people online noting that the baby should have been born by then.
Some social media users speculated it was an example of the "Mandela Effect" — a phenomenon that occurs when people collectively misremember reality.
"Wait wasn't erika kirk supposed to be pregnant or is that some kind of mandela effect?" one TikTok user asked in July 2026. The post (archived), which received more than 4.2 million views as of this writing, was captioned: "It's been well over 9 months."
Dozens of Snopes readers searched searched the site for answers.
While Erika Kirk has repeatedly talked about the two children she had with Charlie Kirk, there's no evidence that she announced she was pregnant again after her husband was assassinated. The rumor has persisted since the shooting took place. We first looked into it in September 2025 and found no evidence that it was true.
In November 2025, during an interview with conservative commentator Megyn Kelly, Erika Kirk said that she and Charlie Kirk had wanted four children.
"I was praying to God that I was pregnant when he got murdered," she said. "I was like, oh goodness, that would be the ultimate blessing out of this catastrophe."
She did not confirm she was pregnant at any point during the interview.
Despite dozens of false claims — often generated using artificial intelligence tools — that Erika Kirk announced she was pregnant after her husband died, Snopes found no evidence in publicly available sources that she made such an announcement.
For further reading, we previously investigated claims that Erika Kirk lost her children in a custody battle and that she had an affair with U.S. Vice President JD Vance.

Major Rishabh Singh Sambyal, who has been dubbed the 'national crush', announced his premature retirement after serving in the Army for 12 years. His retirement has left several disheartened and deepened the intrigue surrounding his career and life. Sambyal, who served as President Droupadi Murmu's Aide-de-Camp (ADC) – a protocol officer who works directly for a high-ranking official – took retirement at the age of 30. He cleared the National Defence Academy (NDA) exam in 2013 and joined the 133rd NDA course in 2014. He secured a Bachelor of Arts degree in International Relations and Affairs in 2017. In the same year, he joined the Indian Military Academy, where he pursued Military Studies and Defence Management. During his service, he led the Jat Regiment's contingent at the 2021 Republic Day Parade and won the prestigious Best Marching Contingent Trophy. The distinguished ex-Army officer served with the elite 4 Para Special Forces, known as the “Daggers”, and even earned the Balidaan Badge, an honour achieved by only a small fraction of volunteers. With roots in military tradition, Major Rishabh Singh Sambyal hails from a Dogra Rajput family of Jammu and Kashmir. The former ADC served in the Indian Army for a total of 12 years, rising from Lieutenant and Captain to Major before taking up the Aide-de-Camp post. He was selected for one of the most prestigious and discreet assignments in the armed forces - President's ADC - in March 2023, according to his LinkedIn profile. An SSB Crack report suggested that he took premature retirement due to personal and family reasons, citing an Instagram Live video. “In everyone’s life there are situations and instances which change your life forever,” he said while revealing that there were no immediate marriage plans. In one of Raj Shamani's podcasts, Sambyal spoke at length about the vigilance required to ensure the President of India's safety. The ex-ADC shared why no one is allowed to touch the feet of the President or shake their hands. "You don't know the intentions of the individual," said Sambyal. He added, "How can you trust the person who is on the other side?" He went on to share that he was even concerned about the glass from which she would have water. "You don't know who has kept it there. You don't know if something is there..." He explained that an area extending up to 1 km around the President is kept sanitised, which means no arms, metal or other dangerous materials are allowed. Sambyal also explained his everyday duties as the person closest to the President. “Everything. I would say presidential requirements, which can be official or unofficial. So we look after everything. Say, for example, the President wishes to speak to the Prime Minister. She will call us, tell us that she wants to speak to the Prime Minister. So we will call up their people, I will speak to the Prime Minister, he is there…then she speaks," he explained. During the conversation, Sambyal also discussed his bond with the President. He shared that meeting President Droupadi Murmu for the first time felt like "my mother was standing in front of me." Ocean Way Festival has been canceled because of beach erosion caused by Hurricane Marie.
The two-day festival was scheduled for Saturday, September 26, and Sunday, September 27, with headliners The Killers and Olivia Dean, along with artists like Jack White, Sublime, Alvvays, Khruangbin, Durand Jones & The Indications, and Hiatus Kaiyote.
“Due to the impacts of Hurricane Marie, the City of Santa Monica has canceled the inaugural Ocean Way Festival,” event organizers said in a statement on Friday, September 11. “Storm surf and runoff has caused significant beach erosion and the festival can no longer be safely held as planned.”
The statement also noted that “plans are already underway to bring the festival to Santa Monica in 2027,” adding, “Refunds are being processed automatically, and no further action is required on your part. Please allow a few business days for the refund to appear in your account. Thank you for your support. See you soon.”

Apple's iPhone Handoff feature will cost you $5 a month on T-Mobile
The ability to use one SIM across two handsets will be available with iOS 27.
Apple is launching a new feature called iPhone Handoff with iOS 27 that will give you a way to use the same eSIM number on two devices. It will initially be available to T-Mobile customers in the US and to Deutsche Telekom users in Germany. Now, T-Mobile has announced that it will cost subscribers an additional $5 a month if they want to be able to access the feature. What a shame there isn't some sort of un-carrier who eliminates these sorts of nickel-and-dime fees from its service.
It's worth noting that the phones can't use the same number at the same time. T-Mobile subscribers will be able to choose which phone is active at any given time, and they will be able to switch devices any time they want. Their calls, voicemail, messages and Find My will automatically move to whatever iPhone they're currently using. Their iCloud data and third-party apps also sync across devices.
Users can set up iPhone Handoff either through Settings on their current device or when they activate a new iPhone. In their newer phone, they have to go to Cellular in Settings and then tap either Set up Cellular or Add eSIM. They then have to select an iPhone > Continue > Transfer. After they follow the onscreen prompts on both devices, they only have to unlock the iPhone they want to use. A message that says "Switched to this iPhone" will appear at the top of their screen to confirm that the device is currently using their number.
To be able to use iPhone Handoff, both devices must be running iOS 27 and share the same Apple ID. Apple is rolling out iOS 27 on September 14.

An Australian teenage girl’s death, suspected to be preceded by consensual “choking” during sex, has renewed calls to ban showing the act in porn.
This latest tragedy, reportedly believed to involve sexual strangulation, comes just months after the UK banned porn showing the practice. But despite all the noise, most people still aren’t aware of just how dangerous the trend is.
Sexual strangulation or “choking” during sex, as it’s referred to colloquially, has become wildly popular—especially among adults aged 18 to 35, despite the risk of severe injury, brain damage, and even death. Some researchers argue that porn is to blame for that normalization, but members of the adult industry say that banning depictions of choking won’t stop this kind of content from flourishing or serve as the kind of sex education and media literacy the public sorely needs.
“With the misinformation that’s out there, especially online, many people do think that maybe at lighter pressures they might be ‘safe,’ and that’s not the case,” says Debby Herbenick, a professor at the Indiana University School of Public Health and one of the leading researchers on sexual strangulation. Herbenick cautions that applying sustained pressure to the front and sides of the throat—via your hands, an object, or otherwise—can lead to blood clots and stroke, tears in the carotid arteries, vision impairment, and cumulative brain injuries.
“It’s these things that we wouldn’t even notice,” she says. “Those tiny, incremental changes in your vision, or your brain, or so on.”
Or, in the most extreme cases, death. Pressing on the front of the throat can lead to airway collapse, Herbenick says. Two weeks ago, a 16-year-old girl in Sydney passed out after authorities believe she was strangled by her equally young partner during sex. She died after being taken to a local hospital in critical condition, and the investigation is ongoing. It’s unknown what her exact injuries were.
The Australian Social Services Minister has since said the government is “very seriously” looking at efforts to ban pornographic depictions of choking in sex, in line with the country’s recently passed age-verification laws that ban social media for children under the age of 16. But critics of these social media bans say they don’t actually work and make it harder for teens to access news and information they need, including sex education around the dangers of choking and strangulation.
The data regarding rates of young people choking and being choked during sex can appear staggering. In Herbenick’s 2021 survey of nearly 5,000 college students in the US, 58 percent of women had been choked during sex and a quarter had been first choked by age 17. Researchers in Australia similarly found rates of around half of people aged 18 to 35 engaging in the practice. Herbenick found that women are usually the ones being choked by men during heterosexual sex and that sexual and gender minorities are also more likely to be choked during sex.
“There are other people who say ‘I asked them to choke me or I said it was OK, but then they really pushed past my limits or it was a lot harder than I expected, or I asked them to stop and they didn’t,’” Herbenick says. She also says that while some young men enjoy the act, others “tell us that they don’t want to be choking their partners, but they think they’re supposed to, or they get asked all the time.”
Most of the self-reported occurrences of sexual strangulation among US college students Herbenick surveyed were described as consensual, but when choking is nonconsensual, it can be even more dangerous. In fact, strangulation is one of the strongest predictors for murder in an abusive relationship.
It’s important to distinguish between the different types of intimate partner strangulation: as a form of abuse, nonconsensual introduction of strangulation into what may have started as a consensual hookup, fully consensual choking, and fictional depictions of choking, like what is usually happening in legal pornography and television. But with the exception of staged or implied choking (like placing a hand over a partner’s neck without actually applying pressure), all of these kinds of strangulation carry major and even deadly health risks for the person on the receiving end.
Clare McGlynn, a law professor at Durham University whose work has contributed to pornography regulation in the UK for 20 years, says the amount of porn involving strangulation has risen over the past few decades and corresponds with an increase in children viewing strangulation content.
“If you ask young people, ‘Where do you get your ideas for sex or sexual activity?’ they say ‘porn.’ And you think, ‘Well, yeah, of course you do,’” McGlynn says. “I think its ubiquity in porn does mean that’s why we see large numbers of young people engaging in this practice consensually, because they think through scripts they’ve seen in mainstream porn that it’s normal, it’s expected.”
The UK’s recent ban on porn showing strangulation or suffocation falls under the country’s Online Safety Act, which requires social media platforms, search engines, and other web services to proactively remove illegal material and employ controversial age-verification measures. According to McGlynn, the strangulation ban was adopted in April but hasn’t been implemented or enforced yet, meaning the government has yet to take action against any companies or individuals.
“The platforms aren’t going to act in and of themselves,” she says. “They’re only going to act if they think the regulator is going to take action against them.”
McGlynn believes that within a few years of the ban on strangulation in porn actually being enforced, a new generation of young people may grow up without seeing choking as a standard part of sex. It’s an optimistic view—one that isn’t shared by everyone.
Cherie DeVille, a well-known pornographic actress, points to the fallout from age-verification laws—requiring proof of age to access adult content—as an example of the futility of banning porn. Consumers can simply use VPNs to get around local laws and turn to the unregulated world of sexually explicit content, often hosted by foreign platforms that don’t comply with any of the laws that major companies are forced to obey.
DeVille, who was a physical therapist prior to entering the adult film industry, describes how talent liaisons assist in the negotiation of what is allowed in specific scenes before filming, including choking, which she says never involves putting actual pressure on the trachea.
Pornhub echoed its consent policy for performers in an email statement to WIRED, writing, “We can be confident that the acts that appear in our content are completely consensual, unlike other platforms that don't have the same consent requirements.” Meanwhile, adult creators on OnlyFans are wary of posting anything involving choking after the service was forced to clamp down on most hardcore content in 2021 to avoid banks freezing payments. (OnlyFans didn’t respond to a request for comment about whether choking and sexual strangulation are technically banned on the platform.)
While Herbenick says that young men are more likely to learn about sexual strangulation from porn, young women are more likely to learn about it from memes, mainstream entertainment, or even erotic fanfiction about One Direction. HBO director Sam Levinson featured it in early episodes of Euphoria and The Idol. It was the opener to a chart-topping Jack Harlow song, where he crooned about choking a woman but not being a “killer.”
“Porn is an appealing boogeyman to say we can stop this by regulating this very specific type of speech, despite the fact that this is ubiquitous throughout culture,” says Mike Stabile, the director of public policy for the Free Speech Coalition, which is the nonprofit trade association for the US adult industry. “The solution is education. The solution is to talk about consent rather than try and find a singular cause that, if you were able to censor it, will solve the problem.”
Herbenick agrees about education. She says one of the biggest cultural changes we need to make is for parents to talk to their kids and teenagers about the dangers of strangulation and the type of messaging they’re consuming about choking during sex—whether it’s in porn or the Billboard Hot 100.

The use of coal to generate electricity on the US grid has been plunging for nearly two decades, and the first Trump administration was unable to affect the trend. So his second administration has attempted more aggressive interventions to prop up coal use. One of its most direct means of doing so is to order coal plants that were scheduled to close to remain open, even if there is no need for them.
The administration’s justification for these orders is a statute that allows the Department of Energy (DOE) to declare an emergency in the case of wartime or a sudden shortfall in generation. A number of parties, including states where coal plants have been slated to close, have challenged this declaration. And on Friday, in the first of these cases to make its way through the courts, the declaration was judged to be contrary to the statute. While this only affects a single coal plant in Michigan, the reasoning of the decision will apply to every coal plant closure that has been blocked by the DOE.
No emergency
The decision was issued by a unanimous three-judge panel from the DC Circuit’s Court of Appeals. It focuses on the J.H. Campbell Generating Plant, which was scheduled to close last year but has been kept open by a total of five emergency declarations by the DOE, each limited to 90 days by the Federal Power Act. At issue was section 202(c) of that Act, which allows the DOE to declare emergencies when the US is at war or when “an emergency exists by reason of a sudden increase in the demand for electric energy, or a shortage of electric energy.”

When it was announced last year that the acclaimed manga “Look Back” by Tatsuki Fujimoto would be getting a live-action adaptation, I was both excited and confused. Excited because the film was being helmed by Hirokazu Koreeda, one of Japan’s best directors, and confused because an anime adaptation had already been released in 2024.
“Look Back,” which hits theaters Sept. 11, is far from the first double-dip in the long history of Japanese visual media. Popular manga titles have often been adapted into both live-action and anime films over the decades. While this can sometimes feel like a money grab, these releases also give audiences the chance to experience multiple takes on the same material.
A semiautobiographical manga by Fujimoto (“Chainsaw Man”), “Look Back” is a coming-of-age tale about two girls who team up to become professional manga artists. The anime film, directed by Kiyotaka Oshiyama, was both a financial and critical success, earning more than ¥2 billion (around $13 million) and bagging a number of awards, including best animated feature at the Japan Academy Awards.

Federal court proceedings brought by the Zionist Federation of Australia (ZFA) against journalist Mary Kostakidis have been discontinued “by consent” with “no order as to costs”.
The former SBS newsreader had been accused by the federation of breaching the Racial Discrimination Act (RDA) by sharing two X posts about a speech by the late Hezbollah secretary general Hassan Nasrallah in January 2024.
Last year, Kostakidis had asked the court to strike the proceedings out, arguing the claim failed to identify which race, ethnicity or nationality was offended by her social media posts about Israel.
The chief executive of the ZFA, Alon Cassuto, had alleged the breach came when Kostakidis shared a video of a speech by Nasrallah on X and added: “The Israeli govt getting some of its own medicine. Israel has started something it can’t finish with this genocide.”
A second post sharing the same video was also part of the claim. The complaint was first raised with the Australian Human Rights Commission but escalated to the federal court.
The court said on Friday that the case had been dismissed with the agreement of both parties.
Kostakidis said in a statement she had spent “two years doing nothing but preparing my defence in a case aimed at silencing me” and the discontinuation was a “win for every Australian who values our democratic right to freedom of political expression”.
“I want to thank my fellow Australians who recognised the significance of what we stand to lose, stood with me and stepped up to assist me to launch my defence,” she said.
“The purpose of journalism is to get to the truth – fearlessly – and to hold power to account. This is a win for press freedom, which has prevailed.
“Watching a people livestream their own genocide while the international community responsible for creating this mess offers the victims sympathy and the perpetrators bombs, diplomatic cover and impunity, has been disgusting.”
In a statement published on Friday, Cassuto said his objectives in bringing the proceedings had been “substantially satisfied” after a public apology by Kostakidis in 2025 for the “hurt, distress and pain” felt by Jews and Israelis in Australia who took her posts “as an edorsement”.
“An important reason I brought this matter was to seek recognition of the harm these posts caused ordinary Jewish Australians,” he said.
“Given everything Ms Kostakidis has chosen to publish since her apology, a further apology compelled by a court would ring hollow.
“The issues that motivated me to bring this proceeding are being examined in the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion. The commissioner’s report will be handed down in December following a national examination of how antisemitism became so normalised in Australia.”
Cassuto added: “Ms Kostakidis can make her own accounting of her conduct. The Australian public can make theirs. I do not intend to spend another year taking Ms Kostakidis’ repugnant commentary from the dark corners of the internet and giving it a federal court platform in her pursuit of martyrdom. My job here is done.”

It was at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona when the mutterings about a new "secret weapon" started.
Dozens of Great Britain athletes had been taking a new product that increased muscle mass and improved athletic performance – a "wonder pill" that didn't fall foul of any doping rules.
They were talking about creatine.
Now found in tubs and bags on many supermarket shelves and tagged in your social feeds, it is the supplement of choice for millions of people and one of the most scientifically researched.
But back then, when it came on the scene at the very top of British elite sport, there were suspicions and stigma around the use of any substance described as 'performance enhancing' – even if it was legal.
From the minute an athlete wakes, to the moment they go to bed, they are thinking about how they can optimise their performance and recovery.
Today, creatine is just one of a long list of supplements taken by elite athletes in this pursuit of marginal gains. Some help with muscle size and strength, while others correct deficiencies in the diet.
"There are various reports in the literature of some studies that say maybe up to 90% of athletes take supplements. I often jokingly say that means 10% are lying," says Prof Graeme Close, professor of human physiology at Liverpool John Moores University.
"The sports teams that I've worked in, I think that's probably closer to 100% of athletes will be taking some form of supplementation."
So, what do supplements actually do and why do athletes take them? And in the world of strict liability, where elite athletes are solely responsible for what they put in their bodies, how do they make sure they stay clean?
While experts like Close advocate for seeking to meet nutritional needs through food in the first instance, it may not always be possible or practical to do this - and that is where supplements come in.
Take, for example, creatine, which is found naturally in meat and fish.
"You would need the best part of a kilogram of raw chicken a day to get the amount of creatine you need," says Close. But it is unsafe to eat raw poultry because of the food poisoning risk from harmful bacteria.
Creatine is a natural compound in the body produced in the kidneys, liver and pancreas. It is a quick source of energy for muscles, which is especially important for short-duration, high intensity activities such as sprinting.
Its big break as a supplement came in the 1990s when two scientists who had been researching it for two decades shared their findings with Steve Jennings, whose Maxim sports nutrition company supplied products to the British Olympic team.
During the 1992 Barcelona Games, investigative reporter Doug Gillon had learned of a 'secret trial' involving British athletes and seen a box of their Ergomax C150 – effervescent creatine tablets. He wrote that if the scientists' claims - that creatine could improve explosive athletic performance by 1-3% - were true, then "sport may never be the same again".
In terms of sport supplements and nutrition, he was right. By the time of the next Olympics in 1996, an estimated 80% of athletes were taking creatine, and since then it has become mainstream, with research suggesting there may be cognitive benefits as well as physical.
According to the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, the creatine breakthrough of the 1990s had "launched a new era in sports nutrition" and "sparked exploration into other supplements".
The global dietary supplements market size was valued at $209.5bn (£154bn) in 2025 and is projected to grow to $431.7bn (£317.4bn) by 2033, according to Grand View Research., external
Close, who oversaw nutrition for last year's British and Irish Lions rugby union tour, sees supplements as the "final piece of the jigsaw" rather than a starting point.
"What we're talking about is small margins of benefit, where actually these athletes who focus on the food, I think what you often find is that they've got the big-ticket items right," he says.
"So they're seeing great performance benefits because their overall diet is immaculate.
"They might be missing out on the one per-centers, but they've really nailed the 99 per-centers. And they often do better than those who chase the one per-centers but have not given enough attention to the 99 per-centers."
Australian cyclist Nicole Frain agrees, adding: "I'm a pretty big believer that they are called sport supplements. They are there to supplement the things you already do right.
"I don't think supplements are the answer to fix my problems.
"You need to be eating a balanced diet, training well, sleeping right, recovering well, hydrating – all of those things – before we add in all of the extras."
Close puts protein powders top of the list of supplements taken by athletes he works with, followed by creatine and vitamin D.
Protein powders maximise muscle repair and contribute to muscle growth, while creatine is a quick source of energy for muscles and important in short-duration, high-intensity activities like sprinting. Vitamin D, meanwhile, is essential for bone health and supports muscle function.
Other popular supplements include carbohydrate gels, which Close says were key in the first sub-two hour marathon run earlier this year by Kenyan long-distance runner Sabastian Sawe.
"As sport nutritionists we were all fascinated at what the fuelling programme was, and it was the sports drinks and gels that played a huge part of that fuelling," Close says.
"There was a calculation done of what it would take to break the two-hour marathon, and that did involve making sure that over 100 grams of supplemental carbohydrate were ingested per hour.
"And the reports coming out of the recent sub-two-hour marathon was that it was 110 grams of carbohydrate per hour that was achieved."
Supplements can improve performance, but there is an uneasy ring to describing them as 'performance enhancing' because of the association with banned substances and anti-doping rule violations.
So what determines whether something is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's (Wada) banned list?
"For Wada to put anything on the list, it's got to hit two out of three criteria: dangerous to health, performance enhancing, and against the spirit of sport," Close explains.
"So just because something enhances performance, if it's not dangerous to health and not against the spirit of sport, Wada will not touch it.
"So creatine is a good example.
"Though something like an anabolic steroid, where it's against the spirit of sport to be injecting yourself for a performance benefit, it's dangerous to health and it's performance enhancing - that hits all three."
But taking a supplement still carries anti-doping risks.
"No guarantee can be given that any particular supplement is free from prohibited substances," UK Anti-Doping advice states, urging athletes to "be vigilant" in using them.
And if you test positive for a prohibited substance, consuming it unintentionally can result in the same four-year ban as if you deliberately took it.
There are supplement-testing programmes which batch test products before they are sold to make sure they do not contain any Wada-prohibited substances.
One of those is Informed Sport, which says as many as one in 10 supplements is contaminated with ingredients and compounds prohibited in sport and points to a study carried out by the Anti-Doping Knowledge Centre that showed product contamination was responsible for 8% of all anti-doping violations between 2005 and 2022.
While Informed Sport is a very well used system among athletes, Wada makes it clear that quality assurance schemes can reduce but do not eliminate the risk of an anti-doping infringement.
If you do accept the risk, you need to be organised to keep track.
In the case of Great Britain rower Heidi Long, it takes a spreadsheet.
"I've recorded the batch number of every product that I've taken and its expiry date because if you take it after the expiry date the Informed Sport [certification] is no longer viable," she says.
Close says he has also done site visits to factories to see where the supplements are made to check the manufacturing processes because "the risk of failing a drugs test is huge".
There are risks to the general population too, he adds, saying: "You can be buying supplements off the internet that are made in somebody's garage and you've got no idea of the manufacturing processes."
He points to studies on creatine products which have found there is no creatine in them and so "you're completely wasting your money" and that in the worst case scenario it may contain substances that are dangerous to your health.
"So it is really important that the message is that while they can play a small role, the safety considerations are the key factor," he says.
There is, however, more than one way for an elite athlete to chase a competitive edge – and some are going back to basics.
For every trending supplement, there is an unprocessed, wholefood alternative – from the anti-inflammatory benefits of turmeric, staving off cramp with pickle juice or consumption of high-nitrate foods like beetroot before competition.
It is what Close calls a "food-first" or "food-only" approach and something he says every athlete should use as a starting point.
The latest to have its moment in the spotlight is an ancient Ethiopian grain called teff.
Used for thousands of years in traditional east African diets, teff is now making its mark globally in performance nutrition.
In comparison to other popular grains like wheat, rice and quinoa, teff has a high mineral content and is rich in calcium, iron and vitamin C. Naturally gluten-free and good for the gut, it is also unique for being a 'complete' protein, meaning it provides all nine essential amino acids required for human nutrition.
These superfood credentials have caught the attention of some of the world's best athletes over the years, from Olympic champion marathon runner Haile Gebrselassie to seven-time Grand Slam singles champion Venus Williams, and it is now becoming a more common sight on UK supermarket shelves.
British boxer Fran Hennessy was introduced to teff by her nutritionist and it is now part of her daily routine.
"I've never looked back," she says. "What I'm putting in my body is good fuel and energy and teff has so much. It energises you so much before a workout and it gives you the fibre you need."
As well as boosting her performances, Hennessy credits teff with being key to recovery.
She says: "Each meal I'm having there's a reason behind and everything that's in it there's a reason behind... I know what I'm putting in my body is fuelling me, recovering me, energising me."
Cost is another consideration when athletes are deciding on supplements.
"The supplement industry is really expensive," says Long. "And we're definitely not made of money. So I think it's really picking and choosing when you want to put that investment in."
She says it makes sense to have more supplements around racing time "when the performance is super critical and very time dependent".
"[But] on a daily basis if I can get the protein intake from my dinner and a glass of milk or yoghurt and breakfast then actually I was going to be eating that food anyway so it's not as expensive."
And then there is taste.
"I would much rather enjoy a coffee in the morning with friends or while I'm working rather than have one of the gels," she says. "Some of the gels ... you'll end up holding your nose when you take it.
"I guess it's just like the enjoyment of what you're taking, you know, it's nicer to eat food than it is to take supplements."

Russian embassy in India's press secretary Petr Sizov has stunned the internet with his fluent Hindi. On the sidelines of BRICS summit, which is being held in Delhi on September 12-13, Sizov expressed optimism about the deliberations.

Carney calls Trump’s latest trade measures ‘relatively modest,’ signals restraint
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney signaled that Canada may hold off on further retaliation against President Donald Trump’s latest trade measures, calling them “relatively modest” compared to earlier U.S. actions
TORONTO -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney signaled Thursday that Canada may hold off on further retaliation against U.S. President Donald Trump’s latest trade measures, calling them “relatively modest” compared to earlier U.S. actions.
The comments came two days after Washington escalated the ongoing trade dispute by banning some Canadian dairy products and motorcycles and most alcoholic beverages after the Canadian retaliatory tariffs took effect. Trump also moved to shut Canadian products out of large, long-term U.S. government contracts.
Carney said his government was still studying the measures and acknowledged they could have significant consequences for individual companies and industries. But he noted that some of the new U.S. tariffs replaced others that Washington had removed.
“We also recognize that, in the context of other things that the U.S. administration has done ... that these are relatively modest measures,” Carney said at a cabinet retreat in Banff, Alberta.
Derek Holt, an economist at the Canadian bank Scotiabank, said this week the latest U.S. measures looked more like an attempt by the Trump administration to “save face” than a major escalation, with the economic impact on Canada relatively limited.
Carney also said he remains in regular contact with Trump and had spoken with him “a couple of times” in recent days about Ukraine, Iran and other global developments, even as the trade dispute between their countries deepens.
“We continue to have to work with the United States. We can compartmentalize across this,” Carney said. He said those conversations dealt with geopolitical, defense and security issues and did not indicate that trade negotiations had resumed.
Carney said his priority was increasingly to strengthen Canada’s economy rather than simply respond to each new move from Trump.
“The biggest impact we can have here is to focus on what we can control: building at home, diversifying abroad and delivering for Canadians,” he said.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford struck a considerably more confrontational tone Thursday, saying he hopes Republicans lose control of both the House and Senate in November’s midterm elections and that voters hold Trump accountable for the trade war.
“Hopefully he’s going to lose the Senate. He’s going to lose Congress. I hope so, and hold him accountable,” Ford said. “But we’ll see how that goes. We aren’t going to interfere in the U.S. election.”
Ford has emerged as one of Trump’s most outspoken Canadian critics, accusing him of trying to strip industry out of Ontario and move it south of the border as the two trade personal insults and threats.
“He’s not reliable at all,” Ford said. “He could make a deal today and then change his mind. And we’ve seen that over and over again.”
Still, Ford said he believes Trump wants an agreement before the midterms and that Canada should return to negotiations as soon as possible.
“I truly believe President Trump wants a deal before the midterms,” Ford said. “I could be wrong, but I think it’s best that we sit down and get a deal.”
Carney also left the door open to renewed negotiations, saying Canada remains ready to return to the table if the talks are conducted professionally and respect Canadian sovereignty.
“We are always ready to sit down” and negotiate, Carney said, adding that he believes “there is a mutually beneficial deal possible that respects our sovereignty and is in the interests of both countries.”
Carney said retaliation remained an option when it served Canadian interests, citing steel as an area where countertariffs had been necessary to protect Canadian companies and workers. But he stopped well short of promising another round of retaliatory measures in response to Trump’s latest action.
Trump abruptly ended trade talks with Canada last year after Ford’s Ontario government aired an anti-tariff television ad in the United States using former President Ronald Reagan’s criticism of tariffs.
Ford said Thursday that Trump had nevertheless strengthened Canada by forcing it to reduce its dependence on the United States.
“The only two good things Donald Trump has ever done for Canada,” Ford said, were that “he woke us up” and “he united the country like I’ve never seen before.”

“I could not breathe. We were brutally dragged up the stairs. I kept saying, ‘Please stop, let me breathe. Tell me where you are taking me.’ But they did not tell us anything.”
This is how journalist Shaheen Khan described the ordeal she and her sister and colleague Nafisa Khan allegedly endured inside Saket police station on September 3, after they were detained while covering the inauguration of Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Delhi attended by Union home minister Amit Shah and Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta.
According to Shaheen, what began as a detention soon turned into an assault. She alleged that their phones were snatched, they were dragged upstairs into a room, slapped, kicked and hit with a baton. She further alleged that the assault intensified after a policewoman saw the name of an incoming caller on her phone and said, “Oh, you are a Muslim. Then I will hit you with four more baton blows and slap you four more times.”
Speaking to Alt News, Shaheen gave a detailed account of what happened at the venue and later at the police station.
The two women journalists work for digital news platform 4PM News Network. The outlet posted a video in which Shaheen appeared visibly distressed and in tears, alleging that she and Nafisa had been assaulted by police officers. The report asked whether asking questions to the chief minister had “become a grave crime” for which journalists could be beaten up, and called for an impartial investigation. It also demanded that all available CCTV footage from the site be preserved.

‘Illegally Detained’
Speaking to Alt News, Shaheen alleged that she and Nafisa had been detained around 11 am and taken to Saket police station. “The SHO threatened us with an FIR and spoke about putting us in the lock-up,” she added.

“We did not know where she was taking us. She dragged us through the area where the SHO’s room is located. She pulled our hair and clothes,” Shaheen alleged.

Shaheen alleged that the assault escalated inside the room.

MLC ‘Delayed’, Police Sought Compromise
Neetu, another colleague of Shaheen and Nafisa, told Alt News that the police did not arrange a medico-legal examination (MLC) after the alleged assault and instead sought a compromise.

Neetu alleged that the MLC was deliberately delayed and took five hours to be conducted. After the medical examination, the journalists returned to Saket police station around 9 pm.
“After that, they made us wait there until around 4 am without registering an FIR. Three SHOs came to the police station and eventually left. We were then told to remove two names from the complaint and that ‘whatever happens will happen’. But the FIR was not registered,” Neetu said.

“Even if we assume that I had committed a crime, under which provision of law and under what procedure were we detained, assaulted, locked inside a room and had our phones snatched? We were literally kidnapped. On what legal basis was all of this done?”

Shaheen claims she was detained for asking questions to the chief minister.

With JD Vance seemingly ready to take the Trump mantle in 2028, Rubio admits he has no plans to run for president
Vice President JD Vance cheered on by audience at GOP midterms convention as Secretary of State Marco Rubio appears to back away from White House challenge
As Vice President JD Vance positioned himself as President Donald Trump’s natural successor at the Republican midterms convention Thursday night, his principal rival, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, ruled himself out of the running.
Vance, 42, delivered a 40-minute address in the American Airlines Center in Dallas that “felt like a presidential nominating convention speech,” according to Reuters, in which he attacked Democrats, paid tribute to Charlie Kirk on the anniversary of his assassination and rebuked a heckler with a Mexican flag.
The VP was met with chants of “48!” by the MAGA crowd, backing him to become the country’s 48th president, and was congratulated by the 47th afterward, who told reporters aboard Air Force One that his deputy had done “very well” and was a “very talented guy.”
Vance has since joined the four previous presidents – Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden – in New York City to observe the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks at Ground Zero, an event the incumbent ducked in order to be at the Pentagon.
By contrast, Rubio, 55, was not present for the two-day event in Dallas. He spent the week touring South America instead, where he gave an interview to Colombia’s RCN where he was asked about his own ambitions for the White House.
“I don’t know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time,” he answered.
“I’m not a candidate for anything right now. And I’m 100 percent focused on my job, and I have to be because I have two jobs.” The secretary was alluding to his secondary role as Trump’s acting national security adviser.
An insider subsequently told NBC News that Rubio “loves being secretary of state and is really enjoying the job” and has no intention of running in 2028 but added: “If you asked him if he’s interested in 2032 or 2036, he would probably say sure.”
As a Florida senator, Rubio did seek the Republican nomination in 2016, a contest in which he sparred nastily with Trump before suspending his campaign after losing his home state.
More recently, he enjoyed a brief bounce in popularity following January’s successful surprise operation to remove Nicolas Maduro from power in Venezuela, only to subsequently fade into the background as the president’s Iran war took center stage.
For a while, it was reported that Trump enjoyed asking conservatives behind the scenes whether they preferred Vance or Rubio as his heir, pitting the two friends against each other, with the latter politely indicating he would not run as a challenger to the VP.
The president has not publicly endorsed either man, nor has Vance definitely said he intends to run – he could yet choose to opt out, given that his wife Usha Vance has just given birth to their fourth child and the likelihood of Democrats profiting from a sharp reaction against Trump, whose approval ratings are currently languishing in the low 30s.
However, in private, the president has reportedly told his party’s donors: “At the end of the day, we need to elect JD.”
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Texas Sen. Ted Cruz are two more names that have recently been put forward, with Trump saying of the former in late August: “I think he’s doing a fantastic job, but it’s very early to talk about that.”
On the opposite side of the aisle, Vance’s predecessor as vice president, Kamala Harris, has been mentioned as a Democratic nominee again, although she has so far refused to commit.
The betting markets meanwhile favor the likes of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who made waves recently by teasing Trump over his relationship with his executive assistant Natalie Harp.
Much will depend on November’s midterms, which the speakers at Trump’s convention attempted to make about immigration, crime and culture war issues, rather than the president’s unpopular war and affordability, two subjects on which voters have routinely expressed their dissatisfaction to pollsters.
Trump himself promised U.S. citizens $5,000 checks as a reward for the GOP hanging onto the House of Representatives and Senate – which some have called a bribe and pointed out would cost $1.3 trillion – and called on attendees to pledge their allegiance to his cause or “go to hell.”

“Obsession’s” origin story is the stuff of legend.
On Sept. 7, 2025, just two days after its rapturously received premiere in the Midnight Madness section of the Toronto International Film Festival, distributor Focus Features offered to acquire its rights for $14-$15 million. The film, about a friend-zoned record store employee named Bear (Michael Johnston) who forces the object of his desire, Nikki (Inde Navarrette), to fall madly — and I do mean madly — in love with him via a mystical toy, was released the following May, where it became a cultural phenomenon, grossing over $500 million worldwide (against a $750,000 budget) and vaulting its 26-year-old writer-director, Curry Barker, and star Inde Navarrette, 25, to the top of the Hollywood A-list. Barker subsequently signed an eight-figure deal with Universal and Blumhouse, who helped shepherd “Obsession,” for his third feature, while Navarrette was cast as Rogue in Marvel’s “X-Men” reboot.
A little over a year after its world premiere, on Friday, Barker and Navarrette returned to TIFF, the place where their lives changed, for a discussion titled “DIALOGUES The ‘Obsession’ Obsession with Curry Barker & Inde Navarrette” at the John Bassett Theatre as part of its inaugural industry-focused hub TIFF: The Market. And to say it was a hot ticket would be an understatement: An hour before showtime, the line for the talk snaked all the way down and around the halls of the Metro Toronto Convention Centre housing the theater.
Popular on Variety
“What a difference a year makes!” declared TIFF Midnight Madness programmer Peter Kuplowsky, who moderated the talk. Barker and Navarrette regaled the packed theater with how wild the past year and change has been.
Barker, who’d risen to prominence acting and directing in YouTube videos, opened up about how he wanted to become “a true storyteller” and thus opted not to act in “Obsession,” unlike most of his other work. Meanwhile, Navarrette dished on how she was drawn to the project because it was the polar opposite of the type of work she’d done before in shows like “13 Reasons Why” and “Superman & Lois.”
“I got sent the script because I wanted to do something completely different than I’d ever done before,” she said. “I had this fire in my belly, and I wanted to show people what I could do.”
Navarrette sent in a self-tape for “Obsession” and was convinced it didn’t go well.
“I thought I bombed it,” she maintained, “but then I was lucky enough that he saw something in me that I didn’t feel like I had shown.”
Chemistry reads with Johnston followed, where she felt more confident in her ability to bring Nikki to life. And the very first day of shooting was the bedroom scene where Nikki freaks out while kissing Bear in bed. Navarrette requested that Barker not tip off Johnston to any of her scene prep so that he’d be genuinely shocked by her (and Nikki’s) decisions.
“I kindly asked Curry if we could not show Michael anything. Even though it doesn’t seem like it, I am quite shy,” she confessed, adding, “Which I think was great because there are so many moments where I scared the shit out of him.”
Barker and Navarrette also discussed some crucial changes that Navarrette made to the character of Nikki, who was originally written “as the girl next door.” According to Navarrette, Barker was “incredibly game for ideas,” including her idea to call Bear “babe” and act “playfully flirty” toward him.
“I wanted the audience to understand why Bear would have the obsession because everything is seen from Bear’s perspective — her laughter, her enticement,” she shared. “I wanted to show what would convince Bear to make that wish.”
At one point during the chat, Kuplowsky brought up the “memeification” of Nikki online, which Navarrette addressed.
“You know, sometimes I feel like it’s not for me, you know what I mean? Because there are so many things growing up that I got to experience of other people,” she offered. “So, I just kind of roll with it. It’s not really for me to analyze one way or the other. It’s kind of for you guys and I love that.”
“It starts to feel like it’s not mine anymore,” Barker said of the life his film has taken online. “It’s not mine anymore.”
Growing up, Navarrette said she was inspired by “Léon: The Professional,” which taught her that young people could act too. She also spoke about how Charlize Theron’s Oscar-winning performance as serial killer Aileen Wuornos in “Monster” made her want to modify her looks for future roles, and, ultimately, how different things are for her since that fateful TIFF premiere.
“Everything changed for me,” she admitted. “I am now in rooms that I could not even imagine. I’m now pitching my own projects and am hopefully able to produce and direct my own stuff. It’s been really, really exciting because I love cinema and I love filmmaking and being a part of Midnight Madness last year lit that fire for me … My whole life has changed, and I just take it day by day.”

IDScan is offering free credit monitoring and ID protection after leaking driver's licenses
The platform was linked to an FBI investigation into a dark web marketplace last week.
IDScan.net, an ID fraud protection platform, has announced it's offering "free credit monitoring and identity protection services" as a make good for customers impacted by a recent data security incident. The company hasn't publicly connected this breach to a report last week that its data was a possible source for a new dark web marketplace selling scans of IDs online. The timing of this announcement certainly raises the possibility, though.
"While the investigation is ongoing, IDScan.net has determined that an unauthorized third party may have accessed and/or copied certain customer information stored within their accounts on the IDScan.net cloud," the company said. "The type of information contained within the affected data may have included full names and driver's license or other government-issued identification numbers."
According to IDScan.net, full access to the information "required payment," but it's still contacting people potentially impacted by the incident and providing free credit monitoring and identity protection services. The company also says it's "cooperating with federal law enforcement on their investigation."
Writing for his blog KrebsonSecurity on September 1, journalist Brian Krebs reported that Nexus, a dark web ID marketplace, was selling scans of over 153 million US and Canadian driver's licenses and millions of other ID documents. Nexus reportedly shuttered ahead of an FBI investigation into the marketplace, but Krebs' report cited IDScan as a possible source for the ID documents it was selling.
Engadget has asked IDScan.net to comment on the report and the possible connection between its security incident and Nexus. We'll update this article if we hear back.

In the past, a ‘healthy plate’ was the single prominent determinant of what constitutes healthy eating. Things, however, are far more complex today, as awareness grows about each meal, micro meals, snacks and what must comprise each such unit.
Even as, on one side, awareness about packaging and labels on packaged foods grows with the new FSSAI (Food Safety and Standards Authority of India) mandates, on the dark side, online/social media continue to influence food fads and generalised opinion gets packaged as expert advice. The flavour of a few seasons now, seems to be protein.
ALSO READ |Paying attention to our packaged food
India is asking the wrong question about protein, the Physicians Association for Nutrition, India (PAN India) said in a White Paper, issued in the context of the National Nutrition Week between September 1 and 7. “Protein has become one of the most talked-about and most misunderstood topics in nutrition. Conversations are dominated by grams, “complete vs incomplete” labels, and high-protein product marketing. These measures are useful, but none of them alone tells you whether someone’s diet is actually healthy or adequate,” the paper says.
The treatise starts by contesting a basic principle: The conventional idea that animal protein is “complete” and plant protein is “incomplete” is oversimplification. Plant foods too contain all the essential amino acids the body needs; the amounts of each just vary by food. Within a varied diet with enough calories, the body gets what it needs across the day; you do not need to combine specific foods at every single meal, the nutritionists argue.
Push for protein
At the heart of the concern is excessive influence wielded on social media that pushes the protein narrative and sits in judgement over those not calibrating their protein per meal or per day. From recommending adding fish and chicken, to protein shakes and even, lately a ‘Profee’ (protein and coffee) the online space has become a hyperactive protein-pushing zone. Algorithms aggressively push recommendations and create fresh anxiety over whether one is getting enough protein or not.
Meenakshi Bajaj, dietician, Tamil Nadu Government Multi Super Speciality Hospital, says: “Unfortunately, social media content is available anytime and everywhere, just a swipe away. As a result, it often appears to have more influence than qualified professionals or evidence-based medicine. It is unfortunate that patients, regardless of age or education, can fall prey to food fads. Content shared by influencers, gym trainers, people with large followings, and unqualified health enthusiasts are being followed without checking the source, credentials, or scientific basis.”
She adds: “Just yesterday, I met a qualified professional undergoing dialysis who had read on social media that people on dialysis require high protein. While that is correct, the post did not explain appropriate protein sources. He was consuming three to four whole eggs daily, along with 17 to 20 almonds and walnuts, which contributed to very high potassium and phosphorus levels that could be life-threatening. Had he consulted a qualified dietitian, she would have explained suitable food sources and cooking methods to control potassium and phosphorus while still meeting his protein needs.”
Another reason why protein has occupied centre stage is the growing use of GLP-1 antagonists, used widely for weight loss. Those on these drugs, are advised to watch muscle loss, a side effect of the process of losing weight. Protein is also said to assist with satiety in managing hunger. During any rapid weight loss process, protein may be burned for energy instead of serving the traditional function of tissue maintenance and repair.
The White Paper —Rethinking Protein in Plant-Based Diets — argues that protein should be understood within the context of a person’s complete diet rather than reduced to grams, amino-acid scores or marketing claims.
As per the Indian Council for Medical Research -National Institute of Nutrition recommendations, a healthy Indian adult must have approximately 0.83 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight daily, making it about 50 grams of protein for a 60-kg adult. This is the generalised norm, however, children in their growth phase, breastfeeding women, sportspersons and older adults might require more protein, the quantity going up to 2 grams per kg per day.
Chennai-based health and fitness coach Priyadarshini Raju says, “I wouldn’t call consuming protein itself a fad, but yes, there is a great deal of hype around protein right now. You don’t need to have protein written on the package of everything that you find in the aisle of a supermarket. However, for our population, a meal is extremely carbohydrate dominant. Just rice, chapati, idlis, dosas.”
For clients, her advise is to add a small amount of protein to each meal, as also fibre. But what kind of protein? “Breakfast can be as simple as besan or oats, or if you’re having dosa, just add a little paneer or tofu to it, if you are a vegetarian. Similarly, for lunch, add the same, or fish or chicken. The meal doesn’t have to be protein dominant but yes, there should be a little protein along with your carbs and fibre; fats, anyway, we get enough of in our traditional diets.”
Plant vs animal proteins
The paper pitches a similar angle: “In a varied diet with adequate calories, people generally do not need to combine specific proteins at every meal. Traditional combinations such as rice and dal, roti and chana, or idli and sambar are useful, but the more important issue is eating sufficient quantities of protein-rich foods,” also challenges the familiar claim that animal proteins are “complete” while plant proteins are “incomplete”.
Almost all plant foods contain all nine essential amino acids; there is a difference of course, and it lies in their relative proportions. It goes on to recommend prioritising pulses, beans, lentils, soy foods, nuts, seeds and whole grains, as they provide protein along with good fibre, unsaturated fats, vitamins, minerals and beneficial plant compounds.
PAN-India also addresses another elephant in the room: Supplements. While arguing that protein supplements are not routinely necessary for healthy adults, they might have a role to play in helping athletes, older people with poor appetite, individuals on GLP-1 medications, or those recovering from illness. Ms. Priyadarshini agrees. “As far as supplements, I might recommend them to people who do are reluctant to bring any protein in their diet, especially vegetarians who have just a carb-loaded diet. Otherwise, I think as long as you’re able to fit in whole foods into your diet, you will be good. That is the best way.” Her vote is for raising awareness of protein consumption and making wholesome food choices.
Dr. Bajaj says: “A diversified, wholesome diet especially one with a high dietary diversity score, age-appropriate portion sizes, and foods that are local, traditional, and seasonal rather than packaged or processed would be considered as an ideal prescription for good health.” She explains that the core principles of nutrition prescription are adequacy, individualisation, and avoiding excess. “Therefore, a therapeutic nutrition plan should be guided by ABCDE: anthropometric measures, biochemical parameters, clinical signs and symptoms, dietary assessment, and exercise type, frequency, and intensity. It must also account for age, gender, medical and surgical history, drug–nutrient interactions, food allergies or intolerances, and economic status,” she adds. Food, ergo, is a complex business, best not left in the hands of social media influence.
“Protein should not be viewed only as a number on a food label. It is an essential macronutrient that supports growth, development, digestion, immunity, healing, and muscle protein synthesis, especially when combined with resistance training,” Dr. Bajaj notes.
