“From the outset, reproduction is a collaborative venture,” writes Anna Louie Sussman, a journalist who has spent years reporting how people all over the world try, and too often fail, to build the families they want. Her work explores how the collaborators of reproduction keep multiplying: doctors, employers, legislators, insurers, and a fertility industry that increasingly promises not just a baby but a better one.
Is it harder to have kids today? Or is it harder to want to?
A new book unpacks why so many people struggle to build the families they want.
In her new book, Inconceivable: The Impossibility of Family in an Age of Uncertainty, Sussman traces the economic, political, and psychological negotiations that stand between people and the children they say they want. Her reporting challenges the assumption that falling birth rates can be fully explained by metrics like income, marriage and education that demographers tend to focus on. She argues the answers are much more personal and resistant to measurement.
I wanted to better understand what Sussman meant by this idea of “impossibility of family” — and how one would even determine that, whether as a prospective parent or as a policymaker. What are the biggest barriers to having kids and how do people tell the difference between what they can’t afford and what they’ve come to believe they need? How much does the media conversation about these issues inform people’s choices?
I spoke with her about what Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s egg freezing reveals about women who aren’t running for president, what countries that subsidize fertility treatment tell us about the demand going unmet here, and why she hesitates to say outright that having children is good. Our conversation has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.
You started working on this book seven years ago. What has most surprised you about how the conversation around fertility and family formation has changed in that time?
There are some people on the left who have always paid attention to family issues, like Elizabeth Warren with her work on bankruptcy and the “two-income trap,” but I do think we’ve been seeing a lot more movement there, with groups like the Congressional Dads Caucus [in 2023], and care infrastructure ideas like those in the Build Back Better Act. There’s also been all this movement around paid leave in the states, 3-K and pre-K, and attempts for more affordable child care.
On the right there’s been the rise of this strange pronatalism and the turn that’s taken with what I’ve wound up calling “kid-maxxing.” Plus this embrace in Silicon Valley and among the super rich with so-called super babies and the really overt embrace of technology to make children on this industrial scale. I also did not expect Roe to be overturned. I would have hoped that would’ve come with a lot more attention on the right to support for mothers and children, but that really hasn’t come to pass in a big way.
I was startled to read that you found some philosophers attempting to reclaim the term “eugenics.” You cite one who wrote a paper called “Defending eugenics,” which sets out to “reclaim the spirit” of eugenicists like Charles Darwin and Francis Galton. You cite another who calls for “liberal eugenics” grounded in the freedom of parents to choose how to enhance their children in accordance with their own values.
One Oxford philosopher even says parents have a duty of “procreative beneficence” and should select embryos or fetuses “most likely to have the best life” based on the genetic information they have.
That was also surprising to me. Like you, I also thought it was a discredited and taboo word. It’s hard to know how widespread those views are. I mean to be clear, eugenics has always been part of our culture in the US. I think people forget that a lot of Nazi policy was inspired by American eugenic policies, and it’s an attitude that has never really gone away. We still see it in a lot of subtler forms that I mention in the book. I mean, even just how people are choosing embryos and terminating pregnancies based on certain genetic conditions.
“Clearly you could have a lot more children being born if these technologies were more accessible.”
This eugenicist rhetoric is gaining steam at a moment when some people are also really hard at work on developing technologies that could enable this sort of thing. While some of these philosophers will definitely make a distinction between parents making some individual choices vs. a state sponsored program, I think it’s the attitude that’s at the root of this, and that’s what we really need to work on criticizing and dismantling.
So the book is arriving just as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has been documenting her egg freezing journey, and talking about how she wants to push to expand insurance coverage and federal support for fertility treatments. What does her experience — and the reaction to it — say about our current moment? Some on the right were so mad, as if she should just throw in the towel or eschew hope and agency at age 36.
What’s so interesting about her experience that I think that people miss is, yes, is it exceptional that she’s contemplating a run for president? Sure. Not many of us are doing that. But on many other levels, she’s doing what a lot of women who can afford to do in their late 30s do when they’re still single. In the book I mention the research of Marcia Inhorn, who interviewed about 150 women who sought to freeze their eggs. And what’s interesting is if you look at their profiles, they were city-dwelling professionals who were on average nearly 37 at the time of freezing.
That is AOC to a tee, and if you asked those study participants why they were doing it, most were not doing so because they felt like they needed to put their families on hold to pursue careers. A full 82 percent cited their lack of a partner as the prime motivation. They wanted to have a family at some point and didn’t want to rule that out.
What do you think we should take from other countries that do subsidize egg freezing?
So the city of Tokyo has subsidized egg freezing and they were totally oversubscribed. So many women took up the city’s offer, and France has also started offering it. More places offer IVF coverage for people who need it because they treat infertility like a disease, which is how the World Health Organization defines it.
What’s interesting is when you look at places where there is more coverage, it also gives you a sense of the scale of need for it. So in Denmark, where you can get something like up to six rounds of treatment publicly funded for your first child and another six rounds for your second child; I believe about one in nine children is born there with assisted reproductive technologies. If you compare that with the US, it’s closer to one in 36. So clearly you could have a lot more children being born if these technologies were more accessible.
In the book you cite historian Sara Matthiesen, who argues that since legal abortion helped transform having a child into more of a personal choice, pregnancy thus became understood as chosen, with parents then sacrificing or forfeiting some of their claim on societal help. I couldn’t tell where you landed on that argument. Do you find it persuasive?
So I find it persuasive in the sense that I feel like conservatives will grab onto any argument to avoid state responsibility towards families and children. The fact that you can terminate a pregnancy is one more reason that can be provided to individualize the responsibility of parenthood.
But I think that we’re also seeing the mirror image of that — where the choice to remain or not remain pregnant has also been taken away in so many places post-Roe. And I don’t think that has resulted in the converse of her argument, which is that when that choice is taken away and you can no longer sever pregnancy and motherhood, then states and society will step up to acknowledge that reality.
In the middle of your book you recall an ex-boyfriend, who was divorced and felt it would be impossible to afford a second kid. You were surprised by this, and later cite a pregnant woman in Venezuela you met while traveling, who was worried about money but excited about parenthood. She told you the Venezuelan proverb that “a baby comes with a loaf of bread under his arm.” The subtext was that they believe things will work out. The subtitle of your book is The Impossibility of Family in Age of Uncertainty. So where do you land? Is it impossible, as your ex said?
I think that’s what people are trying to negotiate with themselves. That’s where things like faith, agency, and disposition come into play. One of the reasons I wanted to write this book was I feel like birth rates and demography are always discussed in terms of these data points that people can measure, like how many people are married and how old are they, and do they have college education or not? Do they earn X, Y, Z income, or not? Do they have a job?
But it’s just all so personal. So the Venezuelan woman was an optimist, whether that’s culturally or dispositionally, and she did believe things would be okay. And I think we all know stories of people who’ve grown up who came from very challenging backgrounds and wound up achieving some sort of fame, fortune, success…so we know that things are always possible. And that’s where questions of what one is prepared to sacrifice come into play, or what expectations do you have of what you want to provide a child.
The thing I really want to highlight is how individual these negotiations are, whether you come down on it being impossible or whether you want to lower your standards and maybe your child doesn’t get in-home violin lessons or if music’s really important to you and you can’t imagine a universe in which your child doesn’t play an instrument.
I cover these issues too and I think about a lot about what our role in the media is. I share your view on reproductive justice, and wanting to help people live the lives they want. But you also wrote about experiencing what you called “money dysmorphia” — when someone is feeling insecure about their financial situation even when they are in fact okay. What role do we have as journalists to help people distinguish between genuine financial impossibility and the fear that they can never be secure enough? And if we don’t do that, how do we not end up in a world where only rich people are encouraged to have kids?
So I try to be optimistic, but I also feel like as a country, there’s no bottom to how far someone can fall in America. As Elizabeth Warren found, having a child is a huge predictor of bankruptcy. I would like to be more positive. And I do believe that there’s so many easy policy fixes, so many ways to make parenting easier. But for people I know who’ve gone through serious financial distress because of things in their life changing, there’s a limit to what I can do or say without giving them all my resources.
Regardless of our job as media, I wish I could say that everything will work out fine. And in some cases it can. Again, people do really great jobs being parents with so much less than I have, which is something I try to keep in mind all the time. But I also would say as a society that we let people fall all the way through the floor and then some. We just don’t have a safety net. So I find it hard to say that everything will work out and you’ll wind up fine.
At the beginning of your book you talk about how having children is an intensely personal decision and you’re not interested in writing about if it’s “good” or “bad” or “worth it.” One of the critiques conservatives make about people like us is that we can be so averse to making any kind of normative statement about having kids that we’ve lost the plot. I’m curious for your thoughts on that. In a book arguing that we need more family-friendly policies, do you think you need to more explicitly say that having kids is a good thing to do?
What I would say is loving relationships are good, and having kids is one of those. I think parenthood is an exceptional one just in the level of responsibility that you’re inviting. Having kids for people who want to have kids is good. But I don’t know, I do hesitate to privilege that relationship above all others because of what doing so means. If you say having kids is good, well, who has kids? That immediately has gendered implications and instantly puts an onus on women.
Though we say public libraries are good and that doesn’t mean we have to make libraries against people’s will. But yeah, I guess I wonder if that position avoids the ways this kind of relationship is different from other loving relationships. While this isn’t what personally motivates me, I think one can definitely make a case that having kids is more of a social good than some other kinds of relationships.
When we say society should be more family-friendly and fund it with tax dollars, it’s not just so everyone can live out the lives they want, but also so we can support our society now and in the future.
Lyman Stone I think gets at this, he says children are good because people are good. Again, I would say if you feel like you might be a good parent and enjoy that relationship, that specific relationship, the whole point of my book is I want that to be more accessible because from what I’ve seen and now in my own experience, it is an amazing relationship. It’s not a relationship like any other one I’ve ever had. But I guess it’s not clear to me what the corollary is of saying having kids is good. It’s definitely good for people who want to have kids, but it’s definitely not good for people who don’t want to have kids.
Though I’m not someone who always wanted to have kids myself. And while I’m strongly against coercing people into having children, I think there are millions of people like me who are like, “I don’t know. I’m not sure. I can’t really picture it.”
There are people on the right who say, “Therefore, just do it because you’ll like it.” And I don’t think that’s appropriate. But it’s also true that for most of human history, people were simply not asked to come down on this question of: “Do I want it or not?” Now today I’m so glad I have a child and the choice to decide, but if you had asked me five years ago I would have said, “I don’t really like little kids. It’s never been my thing.”
So the identity question becomes interesting and confusing to me, and I think it leaves me more uncomfortable with the idea that we should just support whatever anyone’s choice or desire is today when we know that our choices and desires do change, including based on what people absorb in the media.
I think a lot of young people are just really struggling. I see this all the time on Reddit threads or listening to young people talk about their lives who say, “If I can barely take care of myself, how can I take care of someone else?” We don’t have a society that makes any form of caregiving easy, and people are really struggling to find work. We have a society that doesn’t make it easy to care for oneself, for one’s parents, for one’s friends, for one’s partner.
I mean I did have a kid before I felt totally comfortable and I was just really fortunate that it worked out. I do agree with some of the people on the right who say that a lot of the things you think you need to become a parent, you don’t. And we know that really great people grow up all over the world where they have much fewer resources and infrastructure and everything. So I do think kids need a lot less than we often imagine they need. And that is part of thinking about your own expectations and what you want for a child and also, again, what you’re prepared to sacrifice.
I joke that I go to an annual yoga class fairly regularly. I don’t really cook anymore. I had a single mom who was just resourceful, though she was lucky to be in New York City, where there actually are resources to access. If you’re living in Tennessee or Mississippi those types of resources would probably not be available.

Anthropic caught scientists using Claude to further biological weapon research
The company has produced an extensive collection of case studies covering the ways its current AI models have been misused.
Anthropic has flagged and stopped multiple scientists who were using its AI models to create potential biological weapons, according to a new report the company shared on Thursday. "Biological misuse" is just one flavor of troubling AI usage the report documents, but it's of growing importance because newer models like Fable 5 are increasingly good at helping with scientific research.
The company's report includes five case studies of Anthropic's models being used to develop biological weapons, the safety measures that brought the misuse to Anthropic's attention and how it responded. Detecting possible misuse is complicated, as the company stressed to The New York Times, because research into a new vaccine could look a lot like creating a bioweapon. In all cases the company says it erred on the side of being overly cautious because of the possible consequences.
"You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, 'Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,'" Jacob Klein, Anthropic's head of threat intelligence, told The New York Times. "It's an incredibly nuanced situation."
In one case study from May, Anthropic says its "biological safety classifier" flagged a request for Claude to author a grant for gain-of-function research on chikungunya virus. The virus has no licensed treatment and can cause debilitating symptoms for weeks or months, the company says. Gain-of-function research explores methods for genetically altering an organism, and in the case of this specific virus, the grant proposed increasing its transmissibility and ability to evade immune response. The combination sounds dangerous, and Anthropic says the fact that the proposed research was affiliated with a military research institute made it extra questionable.
The company took similar issue with gain-of-function research into bird flu and a separate case of a researcher using Claude to develop an atlas of venom toxin peptides and "a generative pipeline that optimized toxin characteristics." The full report also includes case studies on Anthropic's models being used as a surveillance tool and to create software exploits, propaganda and weapons systems.
According to the company, anyone misusing Claude or Anthropic models had their account banned, and the findings from the investigation are being used to further improve model safeguards and prevent future misuse. Given the tricky nature of biological misuse, Anthropic is also not naming the individuals or institutions its investigation connected to the development of possible biological weapons. "The individuals implicated in these case studies are working scientists," Anthropic says. "We do not assert that they intended harm, and identifying them or their labs could expose them to harm."

Saudi pipeline that bypasses Hormuz shut after attacks
The East-West pipeline has proved to be a critical lifeline for Saudi Arabia’s oil exports, which were disrupted by the war in Iran
Saudi Arabia said it closed its East-West oil pipeline, a key alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz, following multiple attacks on Thursday.
The conduit was shut as a precautionary measure, the Ministry of Energy said on Friday in a post on social media.
The attacks caused several injuries and emergency teams are taking steps to secure the pipeline and assess its safety, the ministry said.
Fighting has intensified across the Middle East in recent days. Yemen-based Houthis said they targeted Saudi’s energy facilities in Abha, Najran and Jazan while the US conducted strikes targeting Iranian oil tankers.
Oil prices were little changed after the ministry’s statement, with Brent futures trading at about US$105 a barrel. Brent surged to almost US$110 on Thursday on speculation about the impact of the latest violence on energy supplies in the region.
The East-West pipeline has proved to be a critical lifeline for Saudi Arabia’s oil exports, which were disrupted by the war in Iran. The 7 million barrel-a-day route quickly reached full capacity after tanker traffic came to a near standstill in the Strait of Hormuz.

The proportion of single Japanese men and women who said they intend to marry one day has fallen below 80% for the first time, a government survey showed Friday.
The result highlighted a declining desire for marriage as more people see few benefits to tying the knot.
“More people believe they will not feel lonely even if they continue living alone, while more people have never interacted with infants, and these trends are also linked to the low desire to marry and have children,” an official at the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research said.
The survey, conducted in June last year, covered unmarried people between the ages of 18 and 54, and married couples in which the wives were under 55. Valid responses were obtained from 6,756 unmarried people and 5,024 couples. The previous survey was conducted in 2021.
Among the 3,459 unmarried people age 18 to 34, 75.1% of men and 77.8% of women said they intend to marry eventually. Both figures fell by more than 6 percentage points from the previous survey, dipping below 80% for the first time since the survey of unmarried people began in 1982.
The proportion of men who said they never intend to marry rose 6.7 points to 24%, while the proportion of women rose 6.9 points to 21.5%, exceeding 20% for the first time.
The proportions of men and women who saw no benefits to marriage rose by about 7 points each to 42.8% and 36%, respectively. Fewer people said they believed marriage would enable them to have children or a family, gain peace of mind or achieve greater financial security.
Of the surveyed married couples, about 20% of those in their first marriage who had been married for less than five years said they met online, doubling from the previous survey and reaching around the same level as those who met through their workplaces or jobs and through introductions by friends or siblings.
The average ideal number of children for married couples was 2.18, a slight decrease from the previous survey. One in 4.4 couples had undergone infertility testing or treatment.

A train derailed between Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northern France, injuring 44 people on Friday (September 11, 2026) evening at around 7:30 p.m. local time, French authorities and the French railway operator said.

The train was carrying 180 passengers and went off the rails near the town of Cleon, French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said in a post on X.
There are 140 firefighters at the scene to help the injured and the passengers, he added.
The local authority, the prefecture of Seine-Maritime, advised the public to avoid the area.
The train service between Rouen and Caen, and Caen and Le Havre was suspended and a replacement bus service will be put in place, SNCF said.

New images show a detailed view of Meta's upcoming mixed reality headset
The device known as Project Phoenix is a new form factor for Meta.
Meta appears to have unintentionally shown off its upcoming mixed reality headset a bit ahead of schedule. Images of the device, which has been known as "Project Phoenix", have surfaced and they provide a fairly detailed look at the lightweight headset.
The images were originally published by UploadVR, which found the files in a HorizonOS app Meta released called "HorizonOS Prescription Lens." The app, which has since been removed, seems to be intended for people who need prescription inserts for the device. But while Meta seems to have released the app as a kind of "placeholder," UploadVR found that it included image files that clearly show the headset from different angles.
The images seem to match what we have heard about the mixed reality device for more than a year. "Phoenix" is a different form factor than other Quest-branded hardware we've seen from Meta. It looks more similar to glasses-like devices like Xreal's Aura headset. And one of the images clearly shows a cable, which lines up with previous rumors that Phoenix will rely on a tethered connection to a separate puck.
One view we can't see in the new images is what the headset looks like from the front, so there are still some details we don't have. But it's likely the front will include some kind of camera setup, much like Xreal's Aura, since the device will reportedly rely on similar hand-tracking controls rather than a dedicated controller. As UploadVR notes, Meta is planning a session at Connect that will cover "a practical guide to controller-free interaction," which would certainly fit with what we've just seen.
Meta didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. But speaking of Connect, it now seems possible we could get our first official glimpse of Phoenix at Meta's annual developer event, which kicks off September 23. The event, which started as a dedicated VR conference, was light on VR and mixed reality news last year since the company's display-enabled smart glasses were the star of the show. We're still expecting to hear a lot about the company's smart glasses this year. But given the timing of the Horizon updates that led to these images, it does seem like Meta could have something big planned for the event.
Whether we'll actually get to see the headset in action, though, is less clear. Previous reports have suggested the device won't be ready until the first half of 2027 after the company pushed back its original timing. But even if Meta isn't planning to sell the headset until next year, it could still make sense for them to tease the device at Connect.

Packard Bell is back, but there's a catch
Thankfully, there's no more beige.
If the name Packard Bell sends you back to beige desktop towers, chunky CRT monitors, floppy disks and the screech of a dial-up modem, Acer has a surprise for you. The PC brand that was seemingly forever attached to American electronics stores in the '90s got a full relaunch at IFA 2026, with lots of orange, purple, green and yellow products that shake off the design language of old.
Don't let the name fool you: the beige is gone. Packard Bell is part of the Acer Group, which is positioning the brand around affordable consumer tech that just works, rather than anything particularly exotic. Valerie Piau, EMEA vice president at Acer Europe SA, said the idea behind its new "Tech it easy" tagline is to keep everyday technology simple and offer it "all at a fair price."
However, there's a major major catch for those in the US who are feeling nostalgic: Acer will only offer its new Packard Bell range to consumers across Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
The new Packard Bell is more than just PCs
The DotBook is a 14.5-inch laptop with a 1,920 x 1,200 IPS display, an Intel Core 3 N355 processor, up to 16GB of DDR4 RAM and up to 512GB of storage. The notebook weighs less than 2.9 pounds and has a battery life of up to seven hours, according to Packard Bell. Prices start at €499 (about $580).
Those specs place the DotBook squarely in everyday computing territory rather than the premium end of the laptop market. Packard Bell itself markets it for browsing, streaming and day-to-day tasks, but even with the familiar badge on the lid, it doesn't necessarily make the DotBook a good deal.
What's more surprising about the return is the extent to which Acer is taking the Packard Bell brand beyond the PC. The first collection includes the DotLoop suitcase turntable, a DotLine 4G feature phone, DotLook audio glasses, headphones, a ring light and other desk accessories. There's even a connected mini-steamer made with Steasy, because apparently a revived '90s PC brand also needs to cater for people's stomachs.
There's at least some established infrastructure behind that mix. Acer says that Packard Bell customers will have access to multilingual support in 28 countries as well as its existing EMEA service-center network. The company's announcement, however, didn't specify warranty terms for individual markets.
There is no US comeback, at least for now
The regional focus seems particularly odd, given how visible Packard Bell once was in the US. Its low-cost home computers were sold at Sears, Walmart, Best Buy, Circuit City, Costco and CompUSA in the early 1990s, putting those bulky beige towers in front of people who weren't necessarily browsing specialist computer stores. For plenty of families, this was what buying a PC looked like.
By 1994, Packard Bell had surpassed IBM to become the third-largest PC manufacturer in the US, with the company saying it held an 11.5 percent market share. The machines weren't exactly objects of desire, but that was hardly the point. You brought it home, cleared a corner of the house and hoped nobody needed the phone while you were online.
This is not the first time that Acer has played the nostalgia card. In 2020, PC stalwart Gateway made a comeback in the US through Walmart with colorful budget laptops and tablets, years after being acquired by Acer. The company made its latest launch possible by acquiring a 75 percent stake in Packard Bell's parent company for $45.8 million way back in 2008.
For now, the revival is primarily focused on the other side of the Atlantic and beyond. Acer says pricing and availability may vary by market and sales channel, with its own announcement giving conflicting timing for the DotBook, mentioning both September and the fourth quarter of 2026. The announcement doesn't state whether this new Packard Bell lineup will eventually reach US stores.

WASHINGTON — The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services this week released guidance for states allowing them to use a “tier system” to determine which Medicaid recipients are too ill to work or volunteer at least 20 hours per week.
The decision, discussed internally with state Medicaid leaders in recent days, was made public via a document earlier this week. It came as a small relief to patient advocacy groups and some medical associations that had criticized “medical frailty” exemptions as confusing and potentially burdensome for patients and medical providers.
The new guidance is “somewhat more encouraging,” said Benjamin Sommers, a primary care provider and professor of medicine at Harvard University, because it allows states to use existing data to automatically exempt people.
“At the same time, it’s still a fairly complicated approach, and there’s just not much time for states to get this right,” he said. Sommers remains worried that very sick people will get caught in red tape and lose their health insurance. Preliminary estimates from the Congressional Budget Office suggest over 7 million people will lose Medicaid coverage in coming years.
Under H.R. 1, passed by Congress last year, states that expanded their Medicaid program must ensure all working-age recipients are meeting the 20-hour-per-week requirement unless they are disabled, caring for young children, or have a serious health condition. However, chronically ill people and their advocates have expressed deep concern over how they’re supposed to prove they are too sick to work.
The guidance this week means that, in addition to compiling lists of diagnostic codes that might indicate “medical frailty,” states can tier diagnoses based on how likely they are to impair someone’s ability to work. People with conditions such as end-stage renal disease, ALS, or end-stage cancer, for example, would be in the highest tier. This designation means their diagnosis is so serious it automatically prevents them from working or conducting daily activities, and no additional paperwork is needed.
Tier 2 conditions may indicate medical frailty but require additional data, such as billing for recent acute care, or pharmacy codes for various medications. “This tier could include individuals with multiple serious chronic conditions in conjunction with high service utilization or repeated inpatient admissions for serious or complex conditions,” the document said.
Tier 3 illnesses would undergo case-by-case review.
Many diagnoses could fall into different tiers depending on the specifics of the patient’s illness, CMS said. For example, someone with vision loss from type 2 diabetes would be classified as tier 1. Another patient with type 2 diabetes, who is on several medications and has possible peripheral neuropathy but no recent hospital admissions, would be tier 3.
States aren’t required to use the tier structure, but given the pressure they are under to establish an eligibility-check system by Jan. 1, more flexibility could be helpful.
“This data-driven approach could reduce the need for beneficiaries and physicians to submit additional documentation,” the American Medical Association said in a national advocacy update. The group has been calling on CMS to clarify whether diagnostic codes alone could show medical frailty for seriously ill patients. (If not, doctors would’ve had to do more documentation, which many say is unrealistic.)
Now, disease groups are lobbying for better placement in the tier structure. Moving up a rung could mean less paperwork for patients, and a lower risk of losing coverage.
#MEAction, a group that represents people with the debilitating condition of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, or ME/CFS — along with co-occurring conditions, such as long Covid and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS — is among those working to climb tiers. The group reached out to dozens of state Medicaid directors, and has met with several, to explain the unique challenges of its community.
People with little-understood conditions, such as ME or long Covid, often struggle for years to get a diagnosis despite experiencing clear and significant declines in their health. That might be OK for the first year of work requirements, during which people can self-attest to their condition, but as of 2028, they will need documentation to keep the frailty exemption.
“We’re looking at two cliffs,” #MEAction Campaigns Director Ben HusuBorger told STAT.
Nebraska, Montana, and Arkansas have begun implementing work requirements early, though they have not released data on how many people have lost coverage so far.
Iowa said it would start implementation on Dec. 1. All other expansion states are set to start Jan. 1.
CMS is still facing a legal challenge from two-dozen states alleging work requirements, and the burden of proving “medical frailty,” are unlawful.

Anthropic said Thursday it has blocked efforts by bad actors to use its artificial intelligence models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance, and research that could have led to biological weapons.
As AI models grow more powerful, elaborate cyberattacks no longer require sophisticated skills and even lone individuals can create threats that would not have been possible even a year ago, Anthropic said. The company said it has added stronger safeguards in its latest models to restrict biological research that could also be used to make weapons.
“The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,” Anthropic said in its third report since March 2025 describing AI misuse. The report includes snippets of the malicious code and AI prompts Anthropic said it found, and urges governments and AI competitors to identify and prevent similar abuse.
“We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services. As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer,” the company said.
The lengthy report by the AI startup, which is planning an initial public offering this fall, was published two days after one of its researchers announced he's resigning over concerns that Anthropic and its competitors are not acting responsibly in AI development. He echoed concerns raised inside and outside of the industry about the technology’s potential to elude human control.
Between December 2025 and August 2026, researchers at Anthropic found misuse by actors ranging from spyware vendors and “politically motivated individuals” to state-sponsored groups spreading propaganda.
Among the findings in the company's report are unnamed actors attempting to use its models for research that could have led to biological weapons. In one instance, Anthropic said its systems blocked a request for Claude’s assistance in authoring a grant application for scientific funding.
“The work discussed in the application involved gain-of-function research (that is, research that genetically alters an organism to create a new or enhanced biological property) on the chikungunya virus. This gain of function research was aimed at the virus’ transmissibility and immune evasion properties,” the report said.
Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne virus that causes debilitating symptoms such as severe pain and fever. The request involved a grant proposal for research seeking to enhance mutations to make the virus progressively more harmful. While such research could “certainly” be used to develop better vaccines and treatments, Anthropic said, “it could also be used to make the pathogen more dangerous.”
None of the cases Anthropic included in its report were found to be using its newer, more powerful Claude Fable or Mythos-class models, with the exception of one illicit distillation case that Anthropic described as “an industrial-scale, covert campaign to extract a model’s capabilities and replicate them in another model without authorization.”
Anthropic said its older models, such as Claude Opus 4 and Claude Sonnet 4.5, from 2025, “were well below the threshold where they could meaningfully assist a sophisticated user in carrying out dangerous biological research.”
“As a result, safeguards on these models were less stringent, directed mostly at preventing access to content that might uplift novices in recreating known bioweapons,” the report said. “But for today’s models — which are capable of assisting in a range of complex scientific research tasks — the evidence is no longer certain, and we cannot make that same assurance.”
Because of this, Anthropic has applied “stronger safeguards that restrict access to a wide range of dual-use biological research queries” in its more recent models, such as Claude Fable 5, the report said.
As companies introduce increasingly powerful AI models, experts have called on governments to regulate the technology, rather than relying on the industry to police itself.
John Thickstun, an assistant professor of computer science at Cornell University, said it is an uncomfortable position for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI to be in when they are expected to determine what is safe vs. unsafe behaviour and make "value judgments at societal scale without any kind of democratic or deliberative oversight.”
Anthropic also found groups that created hundreds of social media accounts that look like they belong to ordinary people and then posted material amplifying the same political view over the course of a week. The company outlined nine such cases it found, originating in Russia, Iran, Turkey and across the Persian Gulf, South Asia, Africa and Europe.
While social media companies can detect influence operations on their platforms once posts are circulating, “we may see it on Claude while the operation is still being built.”
Anthropic released this report after one of its researchers, Jacob Coxon, announced he's resigning amid fears the company and its chief rival OpenAI “are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Coxon's post warned that some of his colleagues now believe AI could threaten human life by the end of the decade.
But Anthropic said it has blocked each of the malicious activities it identified, used the experience to strengthen safeguards and shared information with government authorities and industry partners.
“We hope that the findings in this report will help other developers recognize similar patterns on their own platforms, give governments and civil society a clearer view of how emerging threats take shape, and strengthen collective defenses,” Anthropic said.

Why Houthi military gains in Yemen may further increase gas prices
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates - A tenuous years-long truce in Yemen unraveled further this week as Iran-backed Houthi fighters pushed out Saudi-backed Yemeni forces along a key stretch of Red Sea coastline.
Statements by the Houthis and a rival Yemeni commander, who's cited by The Associated Press, said Friday the Iran-backed group had taken control of the port city of Mokha, just north of the Bab al-Mandeb waterway.
The fighting in Yemen, and the Houthis' targeting of Saudi oil carriers around that waterway, coincided this week with another exchange of fire in the Persian Gulf between the United States and Iran.
As a result, the price of Brent crude—a global metric for oil prices—shot up to nearly $110 a barrel. The London-based research firm Capital Economics says the fighting on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula raises the risk of even further energy price hikes in the coming weeks.
AAA says gasoline prices in the United States are up by 34% from last year at this time, averaging $4.28 a gallon now. Diesel, used for farming and trucks, is up by 61%.
Data from maritime analytics firm Kpler, and cited by multiple news outlets, shows Saudi Arabia exported just 3.2 million barrels a day last month, its lowest level in more than a decade.
While higher oil prices help Gulf Arab producers like Saudi Arabia offset the sharp fall in their energy exports, they still face growing budget deficits, in part due to attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Now, Saudi oil tankers run a gauntlet to bypass the Houthi attacks in the southwestern Bab al-Mandeb shipping corridor, squeezing one of the world's biggest oil producers.
Saudi Arabia is also a key stabilizer of energy prices in OPEC, but with its exports curtailed by the two conflicts and other Gulf Arab producers struggling to get oil and gas out, countries around the world are digging into emergency oil reserves to plug the gap, leading to higher prices.
Saudi Arabia had been re-routing its crude through an east-west pipeline leading to the Red Sea as a fallback measure to keep oil flowing following the closure by Iran of the Strait of Hormuz in response to the U.S.-Israeli war.
The Houthi attacks on shipping have forced Saudi Arabia to use a much longer and costlier route through the Suez Canal to the Mediterranean Sea and around Africa in order to reach buyers in Asia.
The Houthi takeover of the Yemeni port city of Mokha comes just days after the group fired missiles and drones at four regions of southwestern Saudi Arabia. The group says the attacks were in response to dozens of Saudi airstrikes on Yemen, including one that killed civilians at a prison.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said the Houthis struck Saudi oil facilities, sparking fires that halted operations on Tuesday. Saudi Arabia said more than 70 people were wounded in the attacks.
The renewed fighting in Yemen comes 11 years after Saudi Arabia first led a coalition of Arab countries into war in Yemen to roll back a Houthi takeover of the capital, Sanaa, and reinstall Yemen's government to power. More than a decade later, the Houthis still control Sanaa.
The deadly fighting in recent days for control of Mokha and other areas of Yemen's western coast has displaced at least 18,500 people, according to the United Nations' International Organization of Migration.
It says families are fleeing with nothing and arriving at humanitarian sites that already lack emergency food stocks and shelter supplies.

Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured a strategic island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the world’s vital shipping routes.
The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, including the loss of the port city of Mocha on Thursday.
Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.
The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.
Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.
Full Houthi control of shipping in the strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments. Oil prices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.
Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and the Houthis have been allied since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.
British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.
The surge in fighting in the past week had sent more than 46,000 people fleeing, and “overnight, large numbers of people were reportedly seen leaving Mocha with their belongings”, the UN migration agency said on Friday.
The Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.
The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, which is severely damaging the Iranian economy.
The US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025 after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.
On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.
Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, the leader of the National Resistance Forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.
On her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel peace prize winner, Tawakkol Karman, called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial of charges of conspiracy and high treason.
Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.
Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.
There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.

Conservative MP holds independent hearings into COVID-19 vaccine injuries
Government did not sanction MP Dean Allison's four-day probe in Ottawa
Over four days in Ottawa this week, Conservative MP Dean Allison held independent hearings into COVID-19 vaccine injuries.
The Allison Inquiry heard from 50 witnesses drawn from more than 1,400 applicants, according to a news release. Most were Canadians who came to Parliament Hill from across the country to share their personal stories of injury.
According to its terms of reference, the inquiry was intended to listen to Canadians and not "make findings of fact or to reach conclusions."
It did not hear from Health Canada and was unsanctioned by the federal government.
Allison, who represents Niagara West in the House of Commons, said the inquiry "was intended to begin a conversation that should've begun years ago."
"No matter what people think about [COVID-19] or the vaccines or public policy, compassion should never be controversial," Allison said on Friday as the inquiry drew to a close.
Over the four days, the inquiry heard from a range of witnesses including Drue Taylor, a 36-year-old massage therapist who called in virtually from Alberta because she said her doctor decided travelling to Ottawa could take too much of a physical toll.
"I actually haven't been able to fly or travel really at all since becoming injured," Taylor told the inquiry. "Any disruption to my very normal could absolutely put me back into a serious flare where I'm bed-bound for weeks to months."
'Really frustrating'
Taylor said she developed postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), a chronic nervous system condition that causes symptoms such as rapid heartbeat, dizziness, fatigue and nausea when standing up.
After a year and a half of back-and-forth with the government, Taylor said she received an initial payout of $45,000 from the Vaccine Injury Support Program (VISP) . She called her experience with the program "really frustrating," saying she's been in the program's appeal stage for years.
According to Health Canada, VISP received 3,557 claims and paid out over $21 million to claimants between June 2021 and November 2025. Of the 1,433 claims that were assessed by the Medical Review Board, 252 were approved.
To be eligible for the program, people must have experienced "serious or permanent injury" as a result of receiving a vaccine authorized by Health Canada.
Following complaints about its administration, the federal government took it over in 2026. The government had previously contracted a third-party administrator, Oxaro, to administer the program, which was later transitioned to the current Vaccine Impact Assistance Program (VIAP).
"They were supposed to replace my income," Taylor said. "The original payout wouldn't have even replaced my income for that year as a professional massage therapist who owned her own business."
While most witnesses were Canadians sharing their personal injury stories, the inquiry also heard from others like U.S. Senator Ron Johnson.
Johnson used much of his time testifying as a witness on Tuesday to attack Dr. Anthony Fauci, who led the U.S. response to the COVID-19 pandemic. Johnson is part of a U.S. Senate committee that voted to hold Fauci in contempt — and to suggest the COVID-19 virus was manmade.
The origins of COVID-19 are a subject of ongoing debate in the scientific community.
Inquiry was 1st of its kind in Canada
Allison said his independent probe sought to fill a void in Canada where, up to this point, no such inquiry into COVID-19 vaccine injuries has been sanctioned by the federal government.
According to the inquiry's website, "more than 30 democratic countries, including many G7 and Commonwealth nations, have launched major COVID-19 inquiries examining lockdowns, mandates, vaccines and government decision-making."
Some medical experts have called on the federal government to launch a full national inquiry into Canada's pandemic response. No such government-led inquiry has happened.
In 2023, some members of the public conducted their own hearings — known as the National Citizens Inquiry into Canada's Response to COVID-19 — which unfolded across multiple provinces.
- Top medical experts call for national inquiry into Canada's COVID-19 'failures'
- Citizen-led inquiry into Canada's pandemic response makes stop in Winnipeg
- Feds should devise way to reflect on COVID-19 response, says Canada's chief science adviser
Last month, Canada's chief science advisor, Mona Nemer, said in an interview with CBC's The House that the federal government should come up with a way to reflect on its own response to the pandemic to better prepare for future public health challenges.
"I think we have to respect how people feel, and then we need to meet them and hear them and understand where things stand," Nemer said.
Between December 2020 and December 2023, a total of 105 million COVID-19 vaccine doses were given out across Canada.
Health Canada reported that 58,712 adverse event reports were made in that time — representing 0.056 per cent of all shots — and that 11,702 of those were considered serious, or 0.011 per cent of all vaccines given out.

To understand the geopolitical importance of this month’s election breakthrough for Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the small state of Saxony-Anhalt, pay attention to the apparently unrelated commentary from the Kremlin that emerged around it.
On Sunday, Germany’s hard-right populist party won with 44% of the vote, just shy of the majority needed to run the state on its own. Like many of its ideological counterparts across Europe, the AfD is pro-Russia, believing it shares a common enemy with Moscow in Europe’s liberal establishment. These parties are natural allies for Moscow as it tries to secure its best hope for winning the Ukraine war: persuading Europeans to halt the military and financial support that sustains Kyiv’s defense.
The most compelling argument to achieve this goal involves stoke fears among European voters that their governments, far from halting a threat from the east by backing Ukraine, are instead inviting war with a nuclear superpower.

If you want to bring your music everywhere, the humble Bluetooth speaker is your best bet. You’ll lose some audio quality compared to bookshelf speakers, but these days, Bluetooth speakers sound pretty great, and let you blast the tunes wherever you go—the backyard, the beach, and beyond.
Since they first appeared on the audio scene back in 2010, the team at WIRED has reviewed hundreds of Bluetooth speakers at every price range. My top pick for most use cases remains the portable, durable, and affordable JBL Flip 7 ($150), but I’ve got specialized recommendations for nearly every use case and budget. From outdoor parties, beach days and poolside fun, to at-home listening in every room, these are the best speakers for everything you do.
Don’t forget to check out WIRED’s other audio guides, including the Best Soundbars, Best Wireless Earbuds, and Best Computer Speakers.
Updated September 2026: I’ve added the LG xboom Stage 501 and JBL Go 5 to my recommendations, refreshed the Honorable Mentions list, and updated pricing and copy with the most up to date information.
How I Test Bluetooth Speakers
WIRED’s audio experts have spent countless hours listening to, carrying, charging, dropping, and dunking Bluetooth speakers. I’ve been testing audio equipment for more than 20 years and remember the excitement surrounding the launch of the industry-changing Jawbone Jambox way back in 2010. It helped take wireless speakers mainstream and kick-started an entire industry. Since then, I’ve lost count of the number of Bluetooth speakers I’ve tested, but looking around my office today, I count at least 20 cluttering up the place.
Every speaker gets extensive listening with a wide mix of music, podcasts, and recordings of varying quality, including basic Spotify streams and high-resolution lossless audio from Qobuz and Tidal. This guide focuses on portable, battery-powered speakers, so there are inevitable compromises in sound compared to hi-fi speakers, but the difference between the best and worst is still remarkable.
Where possible, I compare similarly priced and sized speakers directly. A $50 speaker does not need to compete with a $500 one, but it does need to outperform the alternatives you might realistically buy instead.
I also test portability, controls, apps, Bluetooth reliability, useful extras, and battery life against manufacturers’ claims. The latter takes increasingly ridiculous amounts of time these days, especially with many speakers breaching the 50 hour mark.
And if a brand says its speaker is built for the beach, backyard, or pool, I test that too. Admittedly, WIRED doesn’t get as many pool days as it would like, but there’s always the bath.
What Should I Look for in a Bluetooth Speaker?
That entirely depends on what you plan to use it for. The best advice we have is to start with how and where you’d like to listen to music and work backwards to a specific model from there. Speakers include tiny keychains, larger boomboxes, and everything in between. We select speakers based largely on how they perform in their specialty, whether that’s audio quality, durability, or some other particular niche.
As far as durability, we look for speakers with solid IP ratings for dust and water resistance and tend to prefer long battery life; batteries with larger capacities tend to still work well even after a few years of degradation.

Small enough to go almost anywhere but big enough to let you properly enjoy your music, the JBL Flip 7 hits a sweet spot that makes it an easy recommendation. It sounds remarkably good for something this compact (and affordable), with plenty of bass and punch, clear vocals, and refined detail. Build quality is excellent too, with IP68 water and dust protection and some drop-proofing (within reason)..
JBL keeps improving the Flip with every iteration. It now has 14 hours of battery life (or 16 with the bass-reducing Playtime Boost mode), and Auracast lets you link newer compatible JBL speakers together for a surround sound experience. The app also has a useful seven-band EQ if you like to tinker with your tones.
As a nice bonus for those who care about bit rates, the Flip 7 can play 24-bit/96kHz lossless audio if you plug it into a source via the USB-C, which is a surprising extra feature at this price point. JBL continues to be the brand to beat in the land of Bluetooth speakers.

I’m happy to admit when I’m wrong, and for a few years, I dismissed Marshall’s mini guitar amp aesthetic as a good looking gimmick. But having spent time with the Kilburn III, I hold my hands up. It’s not "serious" hi-fi, but the design and attention to detail—the tactile, spring-loaded, knurled metal power lever, and illuminated control knobs are a joy—stand apart. It just looks fantastic, and with 50 watts of power and 50 hours of playtime, it plays loud and long. I love being able to charge devices from the speaker’s USB-C port too.
Marshall does not include the charger needed for the fastest recharge, which is a bit annoying, although most laptop users will have one already. There’s no stereo pairing option either, but I find it hard to imagine needing two of these in the size of room it’s designed for.
In his Marshall Kilburn III review, reviewer Simon Cohen was ebullient about the speaker’s performance, and I agree. Paying $250 for a portable Bluetooth speaker is hard to justify if all you need is something loud enough for a picnic blanket, but the Kef Muo feels more like a compact hi-fi component. The seamless aluminum body is beautifully tactile and flawless, although it looks almost identical to the model they first launched in 2015. Maybe I’m just feeling old because I remember that launch like it was yesterday.
While the Muo is getting on a bit aesthetically, its connectivity is bang up to date. The drivers have been rebuilt around a new racetrack-shaped 2.5 x 5-inch mid/bass driver, paired with a 0.74-inch (19mm) tweeter and 40W of Class D amplification. A neat pleated edge to the drivers does brilliant things to the bass too, which is beyond impressive given the size.
Audio quality is seriously impressive here and you may be surprised by how often you reach for it. I heartily recommend plugging in a hi-res streaming (24-bit/48 kHz) source via USB-C and enjoying all the speaker has to offer.
The app is a basic affair, and some might lament the speaker’s lack of Wi-Fi, but with IP67 protection and 24-hour battery life it’s a great buy when fidelity matters.
Best Party Bluetooth Speaker
Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 25 hours |

| Dimensions | 11.73 x 23.38 x 11.56 inches | 
| Weight | 25.79 pounds | 
Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will.i.am, the Stage 501 is a mighty 25.8-pound party starter. Its 2.2-channel setup combines twin 5.25-inch woofers with two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. Together they’re capable of 160 watts on battery or 220 watts plugged in. In simpler terms: It easily filled a huge workshop space with rave-ready bass, and enough volume for a proper party.
What surprised me more than the party capabilities was that it also sounds acceptable at low volume in my office. I was expecting a pint-sized PA system, but dialled back to casual listening volume and it remained composed. Often, speakers designed for loud really struggle with quiet, and just sound muddy, but that wasn’t the case here. Yes, it prefers it when people are dancing, but it manages well when you’re chilling out too.
The xboom app is excellent, with EQ, AI Karaoke, synchronized lighting, and some cheesy but irresistible DJ punch buttons. LG has also included two very sensible smartphone/tablet stands that position your device at the perfect angle for karaoke nights. It comes with two mic inputs, but you will need to buy microphones separately.
Battery life is “up to” 25 hours, and the battery itself is replaceable. It’s big, and not as grown-up sounding as the Soundbox Mix, but it is cheaper and has a surprisingly good LED light show feature that I expected to hate, but didn’t. Party on dudes.
Honorable Mentions
Bang & Olufsen Beosound A1 (Gen 3) for $399: Gorgeously designed, flawlessly finished, and one of the most covetable Bluetooth speakers around. The brushed aluminum puck has barely changed since 2016, which says plenty about the strength of Cecilie Manz’s original design. The latest version adds a richer, more powerful 360-degree sound from its 3.25-inch woofer, 0.6-inch tweeter, and 60 watts of amplification. It is IP67 rated, lasts up to 24 hours, and is appreciably more repairable and upgradable. I love it, but it’s just a little too expensive when the KEF Muo exists and sounds as good as it does.
Soundboks Mix for $799: The 21.4-pound Soundboks Mix is tremendously loud, with a 10-inch woofer, 1.2-inch tweeter, and 40-hour replaceable battery. WIRED writer Parker Hall measured 111 decibels from a meter away, and was surprised at how musical it remained rather than just battering you with volume. IP65 protection, sturdy handles, and rubberized tennis-ball style corners make it particularly well suited to outdoor parties. It’s expensive and heavy compared to the new breed of party speakers from brands like LG and Sony, but it is superb at what it does.
JBL Charge 6 for $150: It’s just too big to be our absolute favorite Bluetooth speaker, but it was a close run thing between two superb JBL options. The great sound and portability of the Flip 7 won out, but the 40 watts from the Charge 6 deliver more bass and scale, while maintaining detail. Battery life stretches to 24 hours, and you also get IP68 protection, Auracast, app EQ, USB-C lossless playback, and reverse charging. Currently on sale too, making it a real bargain at $150.
Bose SoundLink Plus for $269: Sitting neatly between Bose’s little Flex and chunky Max, the Bose SoundLink Plus weighs 3.37 pounds but produces surprisingly substantial sound, with excellent detail, robust bass, and plenty of power without any rawness at volume. IP67 protection is solid, the 20-hour battery is replaceable, and it can also charge your phone over USB-C. There’s multipoint Bluetooth, app EQ, stereo pairing, and aptX Adaptive for Android too. It takes an irritating five hours to recharge, however. Bose could do with a refresh soon, as the competition has caught up with them.
Sonos Roam 2 for $179: The Sonos Roam 2 is a superb little speaker and if the hugely versatile Sonos Play didn’t exist, it would be one of my top picks. It lacks a bit of punch and scale compared to the larger option, but can still be connected over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, so it remains ideal at home, in the garden, or out and about. IP67 protection means beach sand and bathroom splashes aren’t a concern. Battery life is a meager 10 hours, though, and it costs considerably more than similarly sized Bluetooth-only rivals, but if you’re a Sonos fan, you won’t be disappointed.
Ultimate Ears Megaboom 4 for $200: If you don’t mind something a bit large, the 9-inch tall Megaboom 4 is one of the best outdoor speakers you can get, according to former WIRED writer Ryan Waniata. It blasts sound in 360-degrees, with enough bass in every direction to please most listeners. It’s also IP67 dust and waterproof, and it floats, making it especially suited to pool and beach days. Like other Ultimate Ears speakers, you can pair multiple Megaboom 4s together through the app and adjust settings like EQ.
Beats Pill for $150: Remember the Beats Pill? WIRED loved the revived 2024 model when it launched, and it remains an excellent choice if you’re wedded to Apple’s ecosystem. You get one-touch pairing, Find My support, and a friction-free setup Apple does so well. Android gets similarly easy pairing and Find My Device support too. Sound is unmistakably Beats, with crisp treble, impressive clarity, and a whole pile of bass, although there’s still no EQ adjustability (you need to use your streaming service’s settings) to tame some occasional brightness. The 24-hour battery, IP67 protection, reverse USB-C charging, lossless playback over USB-C, and stereo pairing keep it competitive, especially since it’s often on sale.

Washington Spirit sign Luvanga - but is it a record deal?
- Published
Tanzanian striker Clara Luvanga has joined the Washington Spirit from Saudi Arabian club Al-Nassr in a deal believed to be one of the most costly in the history of women's football.
The fee paid by the National Women's Soccer League side has not been officially disclosed.
Some are reporting it to be $2.3m, external (about £1.7m), which would make Luvanga the most expensive female footballer in history.
BBC Sport has not been able to verify this figure, although a well-placed source said they believed it ranked in the top five most expensive signings in the women's game.
The Spirit declined to comment on the fee involved when contacted by BBC Sport.
Luvanga, 21, has signed a contract running to the end of the 2029 NWSL season.
If the reported record figure is correct, it would mean the fee passes the £1.4m that London City Lionesses are said to have paid to Paris St-Germain for Grace Geyoro last year.
However, the Geyoro fee has been disputed, further illustrating how transfer figures in the women's game are often kept private.
With her move, Luvanga becomes the first Tanzanian player in NWSL history.
Luvanga won the Saudi Women's Premier League in all three of her seasons with Al-Nassr, as well as the Saudi Women's Cup, Saudi Women's Super Cup and West Asian Football Federation (WAFF) Women's Clubs Championship.
She also claimed the league's golden boot last season after scoring 24 goals in 14 appearances.
The Washington Spirit are owned by Michele Kang, who also owns London City Lionesses.
London City made a series of high-profile signings during the summer transfer window, including two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas who arrived from Barcelona on a three-year deal.
Luvanga made her senior international debut for Tanzania in 2024. Before joining Al-Nassr in 2023, she played for DUX Logrono in Spain, having developed through the youth system at Tanzanian club Yanga Princess.
When discussing her new club, Luvanga said: "I am very excited to join the Washington Spirit and to take on this new challenge in the NWSL.
"I know I am arriving with the season already under way, but I'm really excited to play in a new league and a new country."
Spirit sporting director James Hocken said: "Clara adds an exciting new dimension to our attack as we head toward the play-offs.
"Despite her young age, she has demonstrated the ability to score goals in different ways and has the profile to be very successful in this league."
Inspired by Ronaldo, dancing her way to the top - analysis
Luvanga's rise from Tanzania to one of the world's most competitive women's football leagues has been remarkably rapid.
She began her career with Yanga Princess in her native country before her big international breakthrough came in August 2023, when she joined Spanish side DUX Logrono. But Spain was only a brief stop on her career journey.
By October of that year, Luvanga headed for Saudi Arabia to join Al-Nassr, a move that would prove transformative for her career.
Over three seasons in the Middle East, she helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Women's Premier League title each time, establishing herself as one of the division's most prolific forwards.
Her time at Al-Nassr also provided an opportunity to meet one of football's biggest stars, Cristiano Ronaldo, who plays for Al-Nassr's men's team. Luvanga has spoken about modelling aspects of her own career on the Portuguese forward.
"The focus and determination that he has, when you look at his life, I wish to live like that," she told BBC Sport Africa in 2025.
There is another side to the Tanzanian forward that goes beyond the goals.
Her former team-mate at Al-Nassr, goalkeeper Sara Khalid Al-Dossary, described Luvanga to BBC Sport Africa as a great player and colleague but also revealed another of her talents: she is a great dancer.
Now Luvanga is taking both her football and her personality to the United States.
Her move to the Washington Spirit makes her the first Tanzanian woman to play in the NWSL, another significant milestone in the internationalisation of Tanzanian women's football.
She will also enter a dressing room containing a sizeable African contingent, with the Washington Spirit's roster now featuring seven African internationals.
For all her success at club level, Luvanga has not enjoyed the same impact in Tanzania colours at senior international level. Her 12 goals for Tanzania have come at youth level — 10 for the U-17 side and two for the U-20 team, while fitness problems have limited her involvement around the past two Women's Africa Cup of Nations campaigns.

Former prime minister Justin Trudeau and his longtime chief of staff, Katie Telford, are swapping the political stage for the entertainment world with the launch of a new media and entertainment production company called Hope & Hard Work.

Obamas also launched production company

Games may be life with all the hard bits removed, but they provide a way to study why people make the choices they make. Traditional games are usually played against a static background: the rewards per outcome are constant. That limits their relevance to behavior because, in real life, the rewards and consequences of strategic choices are ever changing. Now, researchers have used a mathematical model to study a series of games that include evolving strategies and randomly varying returns.
A bit of history
Perhaps the most famous game-theory contest is the prisoner’s dilemma. In the prisoner’s dilemma, a pair of thieves have been captured and are being separately interrogated by the police. If both clam up, they will be punished for a lesser crime. If one prisoner makes a deal (defects) then that prisoner gets to go free and the other gets a heavier sentence. If both make a deal, they both get an in-between punishment.
The person running the game can start it with different rewards for cooperating and defecting to explore how the optimum strategy varies with reward and risk, which the players can figure out by varying the strategies across multiple rounds. Depending on the balance between the reward for staying silent (cooperating) and betrayal, the game stabilizes with everyone betraying everyone. In this simple situation, everyone loses.
Similar dynamics can be found in games of chicken, rock-paper-scissors, and more. The evolution of strategies can lead to stable populations, bistable populations (where the population flips between two stable strategies), or limit cycles, where the population shifts continuously among multiple strategies.
There is also a rich history of changing a game as it is played. Usually, these are within-game variations. For instance, you can set a limit on the amount of reward available, so strategies evolve to take into account increasingly limited resources as the number of rounds goes up. In other words, most of this older work studied situations where the player’s behavior in the current round changed the resources or rewards available for the next round.
