'Canada is everyone, for everyone': Carney meets with Alberta remain campaigners
Prime Minister shook hands with Forever Canadian volunteers on final day of federal cabinet retreat
The head of the Forever Canadian group campaigning for Alberta to remain in the federation said Friday Prime Minister Mark Carney has been a "calm" and "reassuring" presence for Albertans.
Thomas Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier of Alberta, said Carney is showing "there is someone at the helm" by standing up for Canadians in trade negotiations with the White House.
Carney shook hands with volunteers from the Forever Canadian campaign on Friday in Banff, Alta. They were invited to the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity on the final day of the federal cabinet retreat.
The prime minister was cheered by about 50 supporters of the Forever Canadian campaign, almost all holding red and white signs and some wearing the maple leaf.
The prime minister wrote "Canada is everyone and for everyone" with a black marker on the campaign's promotional bright pink recreational vehicle, which it's using to travel around the province.
The crowd then broke out in a rendition of O Canada.
Alberta is set to hold a referendum on Oct. 19 on whether to hold a second vote on leaving Canada.
Carney has called for national unity but has not gone out on the campaign trail to loudly make the case for Albertans to stay in Canada.
The prime minister did not take questions from reporters on Friday. On Thursday, Carney said he sees his role primarily as delivering on his economic agenda for Alberta and Canada to further the cause of co-operative federalism.
He also encouraged Albertans to get out to the polls next month.
"Canada is worth fighting for, and fighting for in this regard means showing up on the 19th or mailing in your ballot or participating in early voting," Carney told reporters on Thursday.
Lukaszuk said he expects there will be "a stage in the campaign" when the prime minister will become "much more personally engaged."
Lukaszuk also said he hopes to see the federal Conservatives get more involved in the campaign.
"The leader of the Official Opposition, Mr. Pierre Poilievre, says that his MPs from Alberta are behind us. You know, I keep looking in the rear-view mirror of this RV. I don't see them," he said.
"But I certainly hope that they get engaged because this is not a partisan issue and this is the time where all hands are on deck."
Federal government acting as a 'strong partner': minister
While the federal cabinet chose to hold their meeting this week in Alberta and to meet with some of the province's mayors, ministers did not spell out any future plans to take part in the remain campaign.
At a closing news conference on Friday, Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski, who represents an Edmonton riding, said it's not the job of the federal government to tell Alberta what to do.
"Our role with respect to this referendum certainly is not to tell Albertans how to do anything. It's not to tell Albertans how to vote. It is to make sure that we are a strong partner with Alberta, that we collaborate in terms of projects and other steps that we're taking to build a unified country together," she said.
Olszewski said the federal government's actions "speak a lot more loudly than if we just stand at a microphone and say some platitudes about Alberta."
But she also said her colleagues are "absolutely" calling for Albertans to vote to remain in Canada.
"We are talking to Albertans about the importance of remaining in Canada," she said. "We're showing Albertans that Canada works, that we're doing our best to ensure that our country works for all regions across the country."
On Thursday, Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas credited Carney and his cabinet for putting in "hard work" in his province and for not taking an off-putting approach to the debate over separation.
"If they had just diminished this to transactions, if they had asked Albertans, 'Well, what's it going to take to keep you?' then I think Albertans are smart. We would have been able to see through that," Farkas told reporters.
"They have been present not just in major events like Stampede but also ... visiting rural communities in Alberta. There's many areas of Alberta that haven't seen a member of Parliament from outside of the province — let alone a Liberal member of Parliament — in many, many decades.
"They're showing up to listen, to learn and to be able to support common cause."

Story so far: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has stepped up action against food companies using “100%” claims on their products, saying such claims can give consumers an impression of absolute purity or completeness that may not match what is actually inside the packet.
The move comes as food regulators are paying closer attention to how products are labelled and advertised. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has also asked food businesses to stop using “100%” claims on food labels, packaging and promotional material.
The key question is: can a company claim “100%” when the product does not actually contain 100% of that ingredient? The CCPA’s orders offer some clues.
What has the CCPA found?
In June 2026, the CCPA imposed a ₹1 lakh penalty each on Mrs. Bectors Food Specialities, which markets English Oven products, and Storia Foods and Beverages for misleading “100%” claims. The companies were also directed to stop using the claims on their packaging, websites and digital platforms.
In the case of Mrs. Bectors, one of its bread products was marketed as “100% Atta Bread” and “100% Whole Wheat Bread”. The company, however, admitted that the bread contained 87% whole wheat flour.
Mrs. Bectors argued that “100% Atta” was meant to convey that wheat flour was the only grain used in the bread. The CCPA did not accept this explanation. It said that “100%” is an exact numerical expression and should not be used loosely or approximately.
The Authority also took into account the use of “Zero Maida” alongside “100% Whole Wheat Bread”. Taken together, these claims could give consumers the impression that the bread was entirely made from whole wheat flour.
What about ‘100% Juice’?
The Storia case involved a similar concern, but with beverages.
Storia marketed one of its products as “100% Tender Coconut Water” and “100% Natural Tender Coconut Water”. However, the ingredient declaration listed water and 9.6% coconut water concentrate, followed by the words “Equivalent to 100% Coconut Water” and “Reconstituted”.
The CCPA found the prominent “100% Tender Coconut Water” claim misleading because an ordinary consumer could understand it to mean that the product was entirely natural tender coconut water.
The CCPA raised a similar concern over Storia’s fruit beverages marketed as “100% Juice”. These products contained water as well as specified quantities of fruit pulp or juice concentrates.
For example, the pomegranate variant contained water, 4% pomegranate juice concentrate and 10% apple juice concentrate. The mango variant contained water, 16% mango pulp and 12.5% apple juice concentrate.
Can the fine print save a claim?
The CCPA’s orders suggest that putting the correct information in the fine print may not be enough if the prominent claim creates a misleading impression.
Consumers typically see the front of a packet before reading its detailed ingredient list. The CCPA has therefore looked at the overall impression created by the packaging and advertising, rather than assuming that a detailed ingredient declaration automatically corrects a prominent claim.
This approach was also seen in the case of McVitie’s Wholewheat Marie biscuits.
The biscuits contained 19.5% whole wheat flour, while refined wheat flour accounted for 52%. The CCPA found that the prominent use of the word “Wholewheat”, along with wheat imagery on the packaging, could lead consumers to believe that the biscuits were predominantly made from whole wheat.
Pladis India, the manufacturer, argued that “Wholewheat” was part of its registered trademark and pointed to a disclaimer on the packaging.
The CCPA, however, said that being a registered trademark does not put a company outside consumer-protection laws. Nor, it held, can a disclaimer necessarily cancel out a prominent representation that may mislead consumers.
What is the FSSAI’s stand on ‘100%’?
The FSSAI too has taken note of a noticeable surge in the use of the term “100%” across food product labels and promotional platforms.
In May 2025, it advised Food Business Operators (FBOs) not to use “100%” on food labels, packaging or promotional material. It said the expression was not defined under the existing food regulations and could create a false impression of absolute purity or superiority.
The FSSAI had earlier taken a more specific position on packaged juice products. In June 2024, it directed food businesses to remove “100% Fruit Juice” claims from labels and advertisements where the juice was made by reconstituting concentrate.
The FSSAI’s action primarily deals with food safety, standards and labelling requirements. The CCPA, on the other hand, looks at whether companies are misleading consumers through their advertisements or product claims.
Under Section 21 of the Consumer Protection Act, the CCPA can order a false or misleading advertisement to be discontinued or modified. It can also impose a penalty of up to ₹10 lakh on a manufacturer, which can rise to ₹50 lakh for every subsequent contravention.
What does this mean for food companies and consumers?
The recent orders show that the ingredient list is not the only thing that matters. The CCPA can also look at how a product is presented on its packaging and in advertisements.
For companies, this means that product names, claims, images and disclaimers may all be considered when assessing whether it could mislead consumers.
For consumers, the front of a packet may not always give the complete picture. The ingredient list can help show what the product actually contains.

Business sentiment among large Japanese companies turned positive in the July-September quarter thanks to stronger semiconductor-related demand and more customers at hotels and restaurants, government data showed Friday.
The business survey index for large companies stood at plus 5.3, compared with minus 0.5 in the previous three months, according to the data released by the Finance Ministry and the Cabinet Office.
The index is calculated by subtracting the percentage of companies reporting deteriorating business conditions over the preceding three months from that of those reporting improved conditions.
The impact of the war in Iran had eased from the April-June quarter, a Finance Ministry official said. Citing the recent rise in crude oil prices, however, the official said, “We’ll continue to closely monitor corporate activities.”
The index for large manufacturers stood at plus 7.6. The production machinery manufacturing sector posted an index reading of plus 23.4 on increased demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
The information and communications equipment manufacturing sector had a reading of plus 19.9, thanks to growing demand tied to artificial intelligence data centers.
The index for large nonmanufacturers was at plus 4.2. The service sector, including hotels and restaurants, posted a reading of plus 7.6, while finance and insurance companies recorded a reading of plus 3.4 as higher lending rates improved earnings.
The index for midsize companies was at plus 0.8, while that for small companies was at minus 10.9.
Companies across all sizes and industries expect to report higher sales and profits for fiscal 2026 from the previous year. Capital investment is projected to increase 11%.

Quick Answer
One UI 9 focuses on control, privacy, and usability with customizable Quick Settings, a redesigned media player, per-app network blocking, unified call history, network speed indicators, PIN-protected shutdown, bypass charging, and dual-camera video recording.
One UI 9 is Samsung’s latest update based on Android 17, which was launched with the Galaxy Z Fold8 and Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra. As for its slab phones, the One UI 9 update is still in beta for the Galaxy S26 series and was recently made available in the US, India, and South Korea for older models like the Galaxy S25 series, Galaxy Z Fold7, Z Flip7, and even the Galaxy S24 series. Samsung has already confirmed that the One UI 9 stable update will soon reach the Galaxy S26 series, but the exact date isn’t confirmed as of yet. One UI 9c isn’t a massive overhaul but is focusing heavily on privacy, aesthetics, and usability. Here are the top new features of One UI 9 that you will get on eligible One UI 9 phones.

One UI 9 Eligible Devices List
Here is the complete list of Samsung devices that are slated to receive the Android 17 One UI 9 update:

| Rugged devices | Galaxy XCover7, Galaxy XCover7 Pro, Galaxy Tab Active5, Galaxy Tab Active5 Pro | 
New One UI 9 features
While we await the One UI 9 Android 17 stable update on our phones, here are the new features that you should know about:
Highly customizable Quick Settings panel
Samsung has tweaked the Quick Settings panel a lot after the One UI 8 update. Now with One UI 9, the company will take things further and introduce a highly customizable Quick Settings panel. While at first glance, you will notice a familiar Samsung identity, the visual tweaks make it more ergonomic and pleasing to the eye. Samsung introduced thicker, more tactile sliders for volume and brightness, making them easier to adjust quickly with your thumb. Additionally, the dark mode toggles and volume settings have also been undocked from these sliders, which gives the interface a much cleaner and less cramped look.
However, you will notice that with One UI 9, you will be able to resize the brightness and volume sliders to a compact 2×1 grid size. This is fantastic for those who want to get more quick setting toggles on a single page. You also get dedicated new toggles for accessibility features such as “Select to speak,” which reads aloud what is displayed on your screen.
Redesigned media player
The media player Quick Settings tile has also been refreshed. Noticeably, the album and podcast get new circular toggles for play/pause, rewind, and skip. The visualizer waveform on playback now dynamically extracts hues and colors from your currently playing album art. This gives your lockscreen a visual overhaul and a rich look.
Network restriction controls
Let us face it. We have been in this situation so many times where we download an offline game, a calculator app, or even a flashlight tool, and are suddenly bombarded with full-screen ads. These ads not only waste a lot of time, but sometimes they are so intrusive that you cannot close them, or they force you to purchase the pro version. One UI 9 fixes this and introduces a feature that power users have been begging for.
Network Restriction Controls is the new setting that is buried within the main Settings app; you now have a master kill-switch to block specific applications from connecting to the internet entirely. This is a massive win for privacy and data management. If an app does not strictly need an external internet connection to function, you can cut its Wi-Fi and mobile data access with a single turn of a toggle. This will stop ad-filled apps from quietly phoning home with your personal data in the background.
A unified phone app
Calling is no longer limited to standard cellular calls. You now make calls on WhatsApp, Google Meet, or message family members on Viber. But the problem with all this is that all of your call logs are scattered across various apps. WhatsApp calls will be available in its app, Google Meet’s call history is available in its app, and so on. You have to switch between apps just to view the call history.
One UI 9 fixes this issue and introduces a unified phone app. It fixes the headache by merging all of your calling applications into one centralized feed inside the Samsung Phone app. Now, when you open your dialer, your WhatsApp calls, Google Meet calls, and standard carrier calls all live in one neatly organized timeline.
Status bar enhancements
If you are someone who loves keeping a close eye on the device’s performance, then One UI 9 brings a highly requested feature: a native network speed indicator in the status bar. While this has been a staple on many Chinese smartphone brands, Samsung models will finally get a built-in way to see real-time download and upload speeds. It is an incredibly useful diagnostic tool to quickly see if your Wi-Fi is acting up or if you are getting the correct speed with it or not.
Note that you still need to make use of the Good Lock “Quickstar” module to enable it. But it is well worth the two minutes if you want to keep an eye on your internet speed. Plus, Samsung has also adjusted the size of the status bar pill area, basically the area that shows background activities like active calls or screen recordings. The pill is noticeably larger now, which allows it to display more content.
Everyday usability and multitasking tweaks
When it comes to multitasking, Samsung has always been the king. The One UI 9 update brings a few quality-of-life improvements that only help get things done much easier.
- Browser Windows in Recents menu: After using Google Chrome for years, I ditched it for Samsung Internet Browser as my default. One UI 9 brings a massive usability bump, as you can now configure individual browser tabs to show up as separate cards in your phone’s Recent Apps menu. This way, you don’t have to open the Samsung Internet Browser app just to close these tabs. You can do that from the Recent Apps menu.
- Mandatory PIN for shutdown: Smartphone theft is a real concern. Just the other day during a stroll around Hyde Park, my phone was almost snatched by a thief. While my phone was not stolen, thieves, when they get their hands on a phone they usually turn it off to stop tracking immediately. One UI 9 adds a crucial security layer, and you now you need to enter your PIN, password, or biometric data before the phone lets you restart or power off your phone.
- Clearer Routines: For those who use Samsung Routines to automate their device, they will be happy to know that Samsung has finally added plain-English explanation text for all the presets. You no longer have to guess what a specific routine means.
- Floating Bars return: Throughout various first-party apps, Samsung has brought back floating action bars. This gives you a cleaner gesture area at the bottom of your screen, good for those who customize their home screen.
- Bypass Charging: Mobile gamers are getting a new Bypass Charging feature. With this, the phone will route the power directly to the processor rather than charging the battery. This will reduce heat and protect your battery in the long-term.
- Dual Vertical Video: Samsung’s Camera app is packed with features, but One UI 9 adds some more elements to it, especially tailored for social media creators. You can now record vertical video using both the front and back camera simultaneously. The phone will record the footage in a 1:1 square aspect ratio.
Final thoughts
One UI 9, based on Android 17, may not be the biggest visual overhaul update that you might be expecting, but that was already done with the One UI 8 update. Now, with the latest update, Samsung is aiming to give users more control. It is a mature, polished, and thoughtful update that makes every Galaxy device a little bit more intuitive. More details will come about the update after the stable update is pushed.

The father of a Japanese victim of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the United States reflects on his loss 25 years later.
About 3,000 people were killed in the attacks.
“My sorrow and anger will persist until I die,” said Kazusada Sumiyama, 89.
His first son, Yoichi Sugiyama, was killed in the attacks at age 34.
“I don’t know how to live with this feeling,” he said.
Sugiyama worked at the New York branch of then Fuji Bank, now Mizuho Bank, in the South Tower of the World Trade Center complex that collapsed. His death was confirmed in April 2002.
He studied English intensively from his school days, hoping to go abroad. In 2000, he was assigned to the New York branch, a posting he had long hoped for.
While Sumiyama was proud of his son as he worked “at the center of global finance,” he was also uneasy following a series of terror attacks that occurred before the Sept. 11 incident.
Sumiyama learned of the Sept. 11 attacks on television that day and flew to New York four days later. However, Sugiyama’s safety was unknown.
The father visited hospitals for information and put up posters to find his son.
“It was painful work,” he recalled. “I was full of anxiety.”
Sumiyama continued to convey the brutality of terrorism and the feelings of bereaved families, holding exhibitions of photographs taken in New York.
“I want people to know that there were Japanese victims,” he said.
He spent about eight years independently translating a report by the National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States and published a Japanese version in 2021.
Recently, however, he said he often feels his physical strength declining. He ended the photo exhibition project this year.
Still, he remains eager to share his experience.
“It’s getting hard to walk, but I can talk,” he said. “If I have an opportunity, I want to continue to talk about my experience.”

Paramount’s lawyers filed a legal response to the states’ antitrust lawsuit against the Warner Bros. Discovery merger on Friday, sketching out arguments and defenses it may use at a trial next March.
Among other defenses, Paramount’s lawyers said they may claim that the coalition of 12 states lacks the authority to regulate the merger, “which is vested in the U.S. Department of Justice.”
Paramount also noted that Cinema United, the trade group for theater chains, has called for a settlement.
“Day by day, the weak case against this Merger gets even weaker,” the company argued, adding that it also plans to challenge the states’ market definitions. “Plaintiffs’ case amounts to a series of attempted shortcuts and assumptions that collapse under scrutiny.”
Popular on Variety
California led the state coalition in suing to block the merger in July, arguing that the deal will create unlawful concentration in the basic cable market and in the wide-release and blockbuster theatrical markets. The DOJ had earlier approved the merger, issuing a memo laying out its reasoning for why the deal should be allowed to go forward.
States typically work with the DOJ in antitrust cases, but under the Trump administration California and several others have often charted their own course.
Paramount has repeatedly argued that the deal will be pro-competitive, and will result in more movies and TV shows.
In its answer to the complaint, the company denied the states’ allegations — a requisite formality to establish a legal controversy. The company also added a few pages of argument, alleging that the states’ case ignores the broader context of an industry in rapid transition to streaming.
“The way audiences consume content is changing rapidly. Streaming services now have greater viewership than movie theaters and cable television,” Paramount argues. “Plaintiffs’ case depends on ignoring this reality. It involves a series of gerrymandered markets based on cherry-picked data from the past. The alleged markets are not the product of sound economic analysis or current market realities. They have been invented for one purpose and one purpose only: to trigger a presumption — any presumption, no matter how weak — in the hopes the Court will look no further.”
The Writers Guild of America has filed its own lawsuit arguing that the merger will reduce the marketplace for writers’ work. That case is set to be heard alongside the states’ challenge at trial on March 2, 2027.
Paramount has agreed not to close the deal until a ruling is issued after the trial — though it is asking the court to require the plaintiffs to post a $1.88 billion bond as the price of continuing the litigation. A judge is set to hear arguments on that request on Sept. 24.
Meanwhile, a court will hold a two-day settlement conference in the antitrust case with the parties in late October. That’s a standard part of civil procedure and does not indicate whether a deal is in the offing.

Xi Jinping heads to India for BRICS summit overshadowed by war
Conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, along with global trade turbulence and energy security, are expected to dominate the two-day meeting of the 11-nation bloc.
NEW DELHI: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in New Delhi on Saturday (Sep 12) for a BRICS summit alongside leaders from India, Russia and Iran, as wars, trade and energy test the divided grouping.
The conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, along with global trade turbulence and energy security, are expected to dominate the two-day meeting of the 11-nation bloc.
But Xi's visit will also be closely watched as his first to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
His arrival comes six years after a deadly 2020 military clash along their disputed Tibetan border, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
Beijing said Friday it was "ready to work with India ... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences".
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500km high-altitude border along Tibet.
"SUBSTANTIAL HARVEST"
Xi is due to hold face-to-face talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi later on Saturday, according to New Delhi's foreign ministry.
"They are looking for 'early and substantial harvest' when it comes to the border issue," said Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne.
"You cannot have a buildup of your forces on the border ... but at the same time say 'we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships.'"
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
Modi on Friday embraced Russian President Vladimir Putin before talks. Putin, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow's war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, also in New Delhi on Friday, said that pressure on Iran "has reached a critical and dangerous stage" following the "military aggression by the United States and Israel".
Modi and Pezeshkian also held talks.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
"BIG CONSTRAINT"
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
As well as Iran, BRICS includes Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates - countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.
UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi are also to attend.
Brazil is represented by Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, with President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva campaigning for a fourth term in October elections.
BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
"The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit," said Harsh V Pant of India's Observer Research Foundation.
"What was seen until last year as an achievement - the expansion of BRICS - today looks like a big constraint on BRICS," Pant said.

On April 12, 1955, America threw a vaccine party.
That morning, Thomas Francis Jr. — who had overseen trials of polio vaccines developed by Jonas Salk — held a press conference to announce the results.
Only it wasn’t a press conference. It was an event.
Reporters packed the room. Tens of thousands of physicians gathered in movie theaters to hear the broadcast. Millions of Americans huddled around their radios.
The verdict: The vaccine worked. A disease that had devastated families for decades had finally met its match.
A documentary describes the reaction: “Factory whistles blew, school children cheered, parents wept.” Newspapers ran headlines like “POLIO IS CONQUERED” across their front pages. Store owners wrote “Thank you, Dr. Salk” messages on their windows. Salk took the stage at the press conference to a prolonged standing ovation, on his way to becoming a living legend.
Fast forward 71 years, to 2026.
On Sept. 2, major medical societies released an independent research evaluation covering flu, Covid-19, and RSV shots. There was another press conference, and more good news: These vaccines are still safe and continue to provide strong protection against death and severe illness.
But this was no event.
Experts talked about “informed decisions” and “shared commitment” and “restoring trust.” The American Medical Association launched a new website with JAMA articles and PDF charts, but no real people or stories. The tone was somber, the mood dour.
So much for a party.
As a communications consultant, I have spent years supporting vaccine advocates. Every conversation right now feels bleak. Measles has come roaring back. Vaccination rates keep dropping. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is a wreck. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the ringleader of the country’s vaccine critics, is somehow still in charge of the Department of Health and Human Services.
For the pro-vaccine side, this is all excruciating. We spend our days debunking and fact-checking. We debate repeatedly whether to confront wellness influencers or engage them. We search endlessly for just the right analogy or metaphor to reach the hesitant parent.
We take vaccines really, really seriously. As we should. It’s a matter of life and death.
Somewhere along the way, though, we forgot how to celebrate. We are sorely lacking in optimism and excitement. There’s no sense of togetherness or belonging. We’ve gotten wound up so tightly that there’s no joy in what we’re doing.
We need to remember how to have fun again.
Consider how Children’s Health Defense, the organization Kennedy previously led, rallies people to its cause. This group is deceitful and dangerous. But it knows how to build a movement.
They fight for “health freedom.” Their volunteers are “defenders” who join an “army of truth.” They hold banners and make street signs. They host book clubs and movie screenings. They sell merch. They encourage people to “grab a couple friends” on the first Saturday of every month and go around debating opponents.
Right now, no pro-vaccine equivalent comes close to matching that energy. Which is a crying shame, because that’s exactly what’s worked for us in the past.
Francis’ press conference in 1955 was the culmination of a movement that had been building for years. More than 1.8 million children participated in Salk’s vaccine trials. They were known as “polio pioneers.” Each received a keepsake card, which many kept for decades. Moms and dads across the country rallied Americans to contribute research donations. Millions did so.
The campaign paid off. Less than a decade after that national vaccine party, cases of polio in the U.S. dropped by 97%.
We experienced a similar surge in vaccine enthusiasm during the pandemic. I received my first Covid vaccine in the parking lot of a Six Flags amusement park; everyone honked their horns after getting a shot. On social media, people posted vaccine selfies and wore “I got vaccinated” stickers. States got creative with all sorts of financial incentives, from million-dollar prizes to college scholarships. Major League Baseball offered free tickets to games.
Once again, the campaign paid off. Covid vaccines saved millions of lives.
Of course, this time, the enthusiasm didn’t last. The ensuing backlash to Covid vaccines seems to have convinced the pro-vaccine side to become more cautious, more restrained, and more clinical in our approach.
Problem is, we’ve learned the wrong lesson.
To increase vaccination rates, we need to match our seriousness of purpose with a renewed spirit of possibility. We need to give people who support vaccination — and those who aren’t sure — something to get excited about and a team they feel good about joining.
That should start with how we talk about vaccines. One thing I never see in any vaccination messaging guide is an exclamation point. Vaccines are incredible! They do amazing things! Let’s try getting people fired up for a change!
It should also include incentive programs for vaccinations. Evidence from the pandemic was mixed, but these programs showed more than enough potential to warrant additional exploration.
But the biggest opportunity lies in building our team. Think of everything we could do with just one vaccination clinic. Much as election officials recruit volunteer poll workers, health departments could recruit volunteers to staff information tables. Cities could match volunteers with older residents who need rides. Civic groups could “adopt” a clinic and bring food and swag. Schools could provide service learning hours to students who lend a hand.
Our side will always stand up for science, data, and facts. But some of the best vaccine pushes in history were marked by factory whistles blaring, car horns honking, and people cheering for a cause bigger than themselves.
It’s gotten far too quiet on the pro-vaccine side. Let’s start making some noise again.
Adam Zimmerman is a public health communications consultant.

Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd gen) review: Upgraded in all the right places
Ultra-level features and a few design tweaks highlight the updates.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
When I think about Bose headphones, the iconic QuietComfort line immediately comes to mind. No, not the more recent Ultra version with all of today's bells and whistles. I'm talking about the business-traveler-chic models that popularized active noise cancellation (ANC). They were never going to win any design contests, but you could rely on them to give you some relief on a flight while also offering decent audio quality.
The company rebranded these to the QuietComfort Headphones a few years back, and now Bose returns with the second-generation version. This time, there are some modest design changes, although the understated look is still intact. What's more, the second-gen QC Headphones borrow features from the pricier QuietComfort Ultra Headphones which enhance both audio and ANC overall.
What's new on the second-generation QuietComfort Headphones?
While this new version undoubtedly fits the aesthetic of the regular QuietComfort line, Bose made two notable design changes. First, there's an updated headband that slides smoothly to adjust. Next, the company refined the shape of the earcups while installing improved ear pads for better cushioning. In a third change, a decidedly less exciting one, Bose relocated the power/Bluetooth pairing switch from the outside of the right ear cup to the bottom edge of the left ear cup. This doesn't really impact the experience, but it does give the headphones a cleaner look on both sides.
In terms of features, Bose brought Immersive Audio to the regular QuietComfort Headphones for the first time. This is the company's take on spatial audio that doesn't rely on specially created content. Instead, the tool upscales any movies, shows or music as needed for enhanced listening. Before now, Immersive Audio was exclusive to the Ultra line of QuietComfort Headphones. Plus, Bose's Cinema Mode, which enhances dialogue without constraining the wide soundstage of Immersive Audio, is on the second-gen QC Headphones too.
The company's CustomTune feature is also a new addition, a tool that calibrates audio and noise cancellation to the acoustic properties of your ears. It's like room calibration for a soundbar, but for your headphones. And if you're into lossless audio, you can listen with a cable over USB-C at up to 24-bit/48kHz. What's more, the headphones can be charged while you're using them with a cable. If you'll recall, the previous QuietComfort Headphones still had a 3.5mm port for wired use. Bose ditched that on this new version as the only wired connectivity is over USB-C — for both charging and listening. For in-flight entertainment systems, there's a USB-C to 3.5mm cable in the box, or you could opt for a $30 accessory like the AirFly for wireless use.
The company also improved ANC performance on this new model with the addition of ActiveSense. This feature automatically applies noise cancellation when the headphones detect sudden spikes of noise if you're using Aware (transparency) mode. Bose says ActiveSense now responds more naturally to those brief periods of disruption before returning to ambient sound mode. The company also explains that the ANC system on the second-gen QC Headphones can better compensate for changes in the ear cup seal due to glasses. And last but not least, you can disable ANC entirely in the Bose app this time around.
What's good about these headphones?
I'll get to audio and ANC performance in a minute, but I must first applaud Bose for refining the QC Headphones without raising the price. This second-gen version costs $359, same as the previous installment did when it debuted. At a time where almost everything is more expensive, I'd expect any headphone company to raise prices on new models by at least $50, but that didn't happen here. Plus, this price tag gives Bose fans a compelling alternative to the $449 second-gen QuietComfort Ultra headphones that costs significantly less.
ANC has long been the trademark feature of the QuietComfort lineup, and that doesn't change here. These headphones continue Bose's strong track record for effective noise cancellation with this model does well against constant noise sources (like fans) in addition to respectably lowering the volume on human voices (on TV and IRL). The second-gen QC Headphones don't completely silence a chatty neighbor, but they consistently reduce the distraction.
While I concede the second-gen QuietComfort Ultra Headphones are Bose's best option in terms of pure sound quality, this regular model is no slouch. The tuning is balanced, providing adequate low-end thump when a song demands it — like Nine Inch Noize's "Vessel." Even without Immersive Audio active, these QuietComfort Headphones provide plenty of fine detail in the texture and grit of the synthesizers on that track. Switch over to Basement's WIRED and you get the same level of clarity and nuance in the band's alt-grunge songs, particularly in the guitars. And it's no surprise that more mellow genres sound great here. Billy Strings' "Bluewater Breakdown" is embedded with all of the string-instrument subtleties that a lot of headphones don't offer.
When I first took the new QC Headphones out of the case, I was immediately struck by how lightweight they are. Compared to the current Ultra headphones, this model is about 34 grams lighter, which makes a huge difference in comfort. I could tell the difference as soon as I put them on, and the disparity only increased the longer I wore both sets. Plus, the soft ear pads are both pillowy and sturdy enough that you can't feel the edges of the ear cups. Lastly, the clamping pressure of the headband is adequate for respectable ANC performance without becoming a burden on my large head.
What's not so good about the new QuietComfort Headphones?
If you didn't like the design of the regular QuietComfort Headphones line before now, I highly doubt Bose did enough to change your mind. These are still the less-polished option compared to the pricier, shinier QC Ultra Headphones. I can appreciate fans of this model prefer it that way, and the company offers a dark pink and two green color variants if you need a splash of personality.
My only real complaint with the new QC Headphones is that battery life remains the same as the previous model. You get 24 hours of ANC use on a charge, which should be enough for multiple days, but the QC Ultra Headphones last 30 hours. I would've liked to see at least a modest bump in longevity here to go along with the feature additions and other improvements.
Wrap-up
After all these years, the QuietComfort line still lives up to its name. The second-generation QuietComfort Headphones are an all-around upgrade over the 2023 version, a compelling option that costs less than the QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (second-gen). I would've loved to see the upgrades extend to longer battery life, but if that's my only gripe, the company did well. And if a few more hours of use would've come with a higher price, I can be happy with what's here.
The regular QuietComfort Headphones remain a perfectly suitable, highly comfortable option that's adept at noise cancellation and provides above average sound quality. That all combines to bolster Bose's decades-long run of consistent performance, a source of reliability that isn't likely to disappoint customers anytime soon.

One woman survived 9/11. Another helped out in Gander. Now they’re as close as sisters
New Yorker and Newfoundlander met over a piece of dried fish in Gander
Jeanette Gutierrez grew up with one sister, but now has two.
Her sister, Gail, saved her life when Gutierrez was working across from the World Trade Center during the Sept. 11 attacks, 25 years ago.
But the New Yorker says she met her friend-turned-sister in Gander, N.L., a decade ago. She was attending a 9/11 commemoration in the small Canadian town, where dozens of flights were diverted in the hours after the attacks. With thousands stranded, Newfoundlanders stepped up to offer shelter.
Gutierrez wanted to meet the people behind that kindness, she told The Current.
“I decided to come here on a tour of gratitude to basically thank the people of Newfoundland for doing such a wonderful thing,” she said.
But once in Gander, she found herself staring down the stinky eye of a tiny fish, as she was being screeched-in.
“I don't eat seafood anyway. Not cooked and certainly not a stinky, little skinny fish. But I had to do it — I wanted so badly to be an honorary Newfoundlander,” she said.
Her salvation came in the form of a local woman, Kelly Sceviour, who spied her discomfort.
“She's a New Yorker so you could tell by her face what was happening … the look on her face was like, I am not [eating this!],” said Sceviour, the town’s special events co-ordinator.
Sceviour motioned to Gutierrez, indicating she should take a small bite and hand over the rest, which she promptly disposed of.
When the ceremony was over, Gutierrez approached Sceviour at the bar.
“[She] said, ‘I owe you a beer,’” Sceviour recalled. “And I was like, ‘Well, I don't drink beer, but I'll take a vodka!’”
“That's when we became friends.”
That friendship has blossomed into both women feeling as close as sisters, which Gutierrez says has helped her navigate the memories of 9/11. While she feels a kinship and comfort with other survivors, she says she finds it hard to be in New York on the anniversary, often travelling to Gander instead.
“I still get to honour and mourn and cry … everything that I do in New York. But I do it — for me — in a better place. In a place that I can also smile and laugh and be with this sister.”
My big sister saved my life
On the morning of the attacks, Gutierrez was working at Three World Financial Center, when she heard the first plane hit the North Tower at 8:46 a.m.
She called her sister Gail, who also worked downtown. Like many people, Gail initially thought there had been an accident. But when the second plane hit, Gail called back, urging Gutierrez to leave — she hesitated.
“Eventually she convinced me to leave by saying she would come to me and we would leave together,” Gutierrez said.
Gutierrez says if Gail hadn’t persuaded her to leave when she did, she might have been caught in the towers’ collapse.
“My big sister Gail saved my life that day.”
In Gander, Sceviour was working for the municipal government when she heard something had happened. She was sent home, but told she might be needed later.
Sceviour went to her mother’s house, which was right on the flight path for Gander International Airport.
“I watched as plane after plane descended. And I thought, 'Oh dear, what are we going to do with all these people?'”
Sceviour was called back into work at midnight, where she spent the night taking phone calls from people looking for loved ones on redirected flights. Working off a passenger list, she was able to reassure them that their family members were OK.
“To hear that relief in their voice … it felt really good to be able to help,” she said.
An unbreakable bond
Dozens of planes were redirected to airports in Newfoundland and Labrador that day. Gander took in nearly 7,000 stranded passengers, hosting them for several days as the community stepped up with food, accommodation and whatever assistance they could provide.
“We're born and raised in Newfoundland to be those kind and helpful and compassionate people,” she said.
Canada’s relationship with the U.S. has grown tense in recent years, as U.S. President Donald Trump launched a trade war and repeatedly threatened to use economic force to make Canada the 51st state.
But Gutierrez said politics can’t break her bond with Sceviour, and nothing can ever erase what the people of Newfoundland and Labrador did 25 years ago.
“Nobody sitting anywhere in any office can change who Canadians are,” Gutierrez said.
“It might change some relationships. It will never change ours.”

Rules Designed to Create Chaos
The Trump administration is hoping to put so many restrictions on mail-in balloting that people simply won’t be able to vote that way at all.
Donald Trump hates mail-in voting. He has described it as “dangerous,” “corrupt,” “horrible,” and “a fraud.” Last year, in a Truth Social post festooned with capital letters and exclamation points, he announced that he would be signing an executive order to do away with mail-in ballots entirely. That order never materialized, possibly because the president has absolutely no legal authority to carry out such a ban. The federal government plays only a small role in administering elections, and the Constitution locates those authorities with Congress, not the president.
But now, with some ballots already heading to voters as the midterms draw near, the Trump administration is waging another fight against voting by mail, this time through its control over the U.S. Postal Service. Trump’s plan wouldn’t outright prohibit mail-in voting but would throw so many wrenches into the machinery that it could grind to a halt. Federal courts at both the district and appellate levels have blocked the rule, and now the Supreme Court is in the process of weighing whether to allow this effort to move forward before the midterms; it could make a decision as soon as later today. If the justices let USPS take these steps in the coming weeks, the risk, the election-law expert Rick Hasen told me, is “mass disenfranchisement.”
Historically, the Postal Service has simply mailed every ballot provided by state and local election officials. But in a March executive order, Trump directed USPS to develop a new plan that would erect a series of hoops for election workers to jump through before a ballot can be sent to an expectant voter. If the rule goes into effect, USPS will require state and local jurisdictions to obtain federal sign-off on the design of the envelope and then mark each ballot envelope with barcodes. States must also upload a full list of every voter receiving a mail ballot to a so-called federal ballot mail portal. Only then, once USPS cross-checks the barcodes with the voter list in the portal, will the ballot be delivered.
In the abstract, this might sound inoffensive. But the process is so hopelessly tangled that it seems almost designed to fail. Take the portal, which is still not online. On September 3—a week ago—the Postal Service stated in a court filing that the website would be ready “by sometime next week.” Even if the portal were functional, it might not operate fairly. A whistleblower recently filed a disclosure warning that the Postal Service is planning to use the system with a “zero percent failure rate.” USPS will scan ballots in large batches, the whistleblower says, and if a single ballot fails to match the uploaded list of voters, none of the ballots in the batch will be mailed.
Election rules take a long time to change, and states begin preparing the polls long before Election Day. When Trump announced the order, in March, experts did not immediately think that the midterms would be affected. “I had assumed that this was going to be put on hold” until after November, Hasen said. But USPS quickly began putting together the detailed plans requested by the White House, even though the order itself faced multiple legal challenges and was racking up court judgments against it. (Another section of the executive order directed the Department of Homeland Security to produce a mechanism by which states can review “citizenship lists” of potential voters. DHS has yet to provide these lists, and the nonprofit Electronic Privacy Information Center recently sued to block the agency from compiling and distributing them.)
The Supreme Court ruled on August 24 that the executive order’s challengers had gone to court too soon, before USPS’s plans were far enough along. Now the Postal Service claims that its work is ready—mostly—to be rolled out, if the justices will let it.
The court dockets are crammed with statements by election experts and state and local officials explaining all of the different problems created by the rule. In their breadth and variety, these declarations are a reminder of just how big the United States is, and how many people must work together across multiple states and levels of government to pull off a successful election season. Hawaii has spent more than $79,000 printing ballot envelopes, the state’s chief election officer wrote in one filing; he worried that if officials need to order new envelopes, they may not arrive from the continental U.S. in time for the election. Rhode Island’s deputy secretary of state explained that the state’s laws regulating ballot-envelope design effectively prohibit officials from affixing the two barcodes required by USPS. In Wisconsin, some rural jurisdictions may not have the ability to print the required barcodes, the chair of the Wisconsin Elections Commission said. The elections director in Oregon, which conducts all of the state’s elections completely by mail, worried that the state’s “aging” computer systems are not equipped to efficiently upload 3 million voters’ personal information into the USPS portal. “If the system fails,” she wrote, “Oregon may be unable to mail ballots to voters at all.”
Election officials who have long relied on the Postal Service are now thinking through alternatives. Cisco Aguilar, Nevada’s secretary of state, told me that he has reached out to private mail carriers about delivering ballots in a pinch. “We got a quote from UPS of about eight bucks per ballot, which is about three dollars more than we pay the Postal Service,” he said. “With 2.1 million ballots in Nevada, that’s a pretty significant expense.” Nevada sends mail-in ballots to voters by default, and mail-in voting is popular: 60 percent of Nevadans voted by mail in the state’s primary elections, Aguilar said. Now his office is figuring out how to communicate clearly with voters who may be alarmed or confused if USPS refuses to mail Nevada’s ballots. “Do we just start to message, Hey, just skip the mail ballot altogether and show up in person?”
Experts are hoping that the Supreme Court takes these concerns seriously. Because of the emergency status of the litigation, the justices can consider not just the legality of the federal government’s actions but also the “equities”—that is, the potential harms suffered by each side depending on how the Court rules. There are strong legal arguments that the administration has no authority to put such a program in place. (Perhaps tellingly, the federal government has been reduced to arguing that the Post Office can impose requirements for mailing ballots in the same way that it can put safeguards in place for mailing cremated human remains.) On the equities, though, the matter seems particularly stark. If the Supreme Court allows the policy to go into effect, the outcome could be catastrophic. But if the policy remains blocked, what is the harm to the federal government? The administration’s briefs make little attempt to answer this question other than vague insinuations about voter fraud.
Then again, a victory at the Court wouldn’t appear to gain much for the administration, either. If the goal is partisan sabotage, there is little reason to think that the USPS plan would help Republicans. “If this actually happens, the burden is going to fall hardest on the most vulnerable of our voters—the elderly, the disabled, rural voters, voters on reservations, voters in the military,” Hasen said. Older voters and rural Americans have tended to be reliable GOP constituencies, and in a season when the Republican Party is struggling to build up voter enthusiasm, there is a real risk that inconvenienced voters who never receive a ballot will simply stay home. Democrats furious with Trump, meanwhile, may be more motivated to find a way to the polls.
Still, the widespread confusion that the USPS rule would inevitably create may have its own appeal to the White House. A group of election officials, including several Republican secretaries of state, warned in an amicus brief before the Supreme Court that “a chaotic election erodes confidence in the result.” For a president long obsessed with undermining Americans’ trust in elections, perhaps that’s victory enough.

The Best Mushroom Coffee
Featured in this article
The world has been addicted to caffeine for centuries, and in the year 2026, the scientific argument over whether coffee is good or bad for you remains unsettled. One might believe the lack of consensus is a Mainstream Media™ psyop to keep people scrambling for marketable solutions to a problem that’s completely made up, but the cottage industry of coffee alternatives that’s proliferated during this endless tug of war is an interesting outcome regardless of which side you’re on. This is where mushroom coffee makes its inevitable entrance.
Some quick googling revealed the known players in the game, all of which offer their own riff on a common base formula of dried mushrooms–usually a combo of lion’s mane, chaga, and cordyceps—boosted with buzzy add-ons like probiotics and nootropics. I spent a week with each, including our top pick, Atlas Coffee Club’s Latte Superblend ($26), swapping out my morning coffee for each brand's recommended dose of powder and hot water. After day five I allowed myself to experiment with sweeteners and milks, which you’ll need with almost all of these to get through the entire cup without gagging.
Some hit like a mild cup of coffee, some were actual coffee, and others were uncanny concoctions no normal person would ever crave unless they were fully indoctrinated in the heady lifestyle this unique alt-beverage industry revolves around. I laughed, I cried, I got the runs, and I crashed on my couch in the early afternoon more times than I could count, all for science, and all so you don’t have to try this on your own.
Be sure to check out our other coffee and caffeinated coverage, including the Best Coffee Subscriptions, Best Coffee Makers, Best Energy Drinks, and Best Electric Kettles.
Updated September 2026: We've added new mushroom coffees from Wunderground, Bullet Proof, and Vahdam; moved some previous picks to honorable mentions; and ensured up-to-date links and prices.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Others Tested
Lifeboost Mindflow for $45: The flavor of this instant powder is snappy and astringent at first, then it mellows into a warm middle ground after a few sips and a short cooling period. By the middle of the cup I forgot I was drinking something other than coffee, and the mild acidity on the finish–likely a product of the CognatiQ Coffee Fruit Extract that’s lauded on the back of Mindflow’s mylar pouch–tastes similar to a nice cup of Ethiopian or Rwandan coffee if you close your eyes and pretend for just a moment. Regarding its potency, if mushroom supplements were attendees at a state college keg party, Lifeboost would be the unremarkable guy pacing himself in the back while everyone else is getting blitzed like the world is ending. It’s unassuming yet self-assured, patiently waiting for all other entrants to crap out so it can make its move. I copped a mild buzz just a few sips in, and I felt alert and wide-eyed for a good two hours after the silty final sips of the cup were consumed. Electrolytes are uncommon in this space, which means this is a rare entry in the mushroom supplement world that purports to be a good pick if hydration is a trivial concern.
Four Sigmatic Organic Coffee for $20: Four Sigmatic’s Focus blend is labeled as a dark roast, but it’s missing the cigarette-butts-and-bowling-alley aftertaste that looms on the finish of similar blends. Despite my preference for lighter beans, this hit like a hug from an old friend after weeks of sipping murky silt. The caffeine buzz normalized after two days of using Think in lieu of more standard shroom-based coffee replacements, so I added a three-quarter-teaspoon hit of the powdered Focus blend to my daily cup to see what would happen. Within 10 minutes I felt an overwhelming urge to sort my finances spreadsheet in preparation for tax season, then I set up a new template in Loopy Pro to accommodate a friend who planned to join my basement jam session that evening. He bailed, but I was jacked on Genius Adaptogens so I played all the instruments myself into the wee hours of the night.
Terrasoul Superfoods Sun Alchemy Cognitive Coffee for $15: Sun Alchemy plays directly to the interests of busy professionals who only recently stopped using the #riseandgrind tag on their LinkedIn posts, with a greatest hits collection of buzzy adjuncts punctuating the top of its ingredient list. Fans of the bulletproof coffee craze will love the addition of MCT oil and organic coconut milk powder, while mushroomheads of all stripes will find the blend of mushrooms in the sachet to be standard and proper. The package recommends a frothing wand for stirring, but I tried whipping this up in a Wawa with hot water and a stir stick to see if it might be a good fit for a haggard road warrior like me. A fair amount of sediment remained in the bottom of the cup in both scenarios, rendering the last sip or two basically undrinkable. Until that point, this is a totally fine drink, with prominent notes of medium-roast pre-ground grocery store coffee, a light tickle of coconut on the finish, and a sharp, mildly bitter nose a newbie might dislike but a lifelong coffee addict will find endearing.
Everyday Dose Premium Adaptogenic Mushroom Coffee for $40: One month of this fantastical dust promises better sleep and boosted mood. Two months promises a healthy gut, and three months promises glowing skin and boosted immunity. It’s easy to acquire three months of Everyday Dose because its subscription-only model is damn near impossible to cancel. It’s difficult to drink this daily for even a week, though, but best of luck if a guy with an alpha jawline and yacht full o’ thots in Croatia told you otherwise! Unlike MUD/WTR (below), which seems to be the closest analog as far as aesthetics and cheekiness go, Everyday Dose boasts a wee bit of caffeine, which is appealing for coffee addicts like yours truly. I first mixed 1 tablespoon of the powder with 8 ounces of hot water and drank it straight up, which yielded an unappetizing liquid that tasted like a mix of Chex Mix and bong water. Some frothed oat milk and a squirt of simple syrup turned out to be the most drinkable form, but I’d be lying if I said I enjoyed any of it.
Om Master Blend Organic Mushroom Powder for $20: The bulk of Om’s catalog is billed as “dietary supplements,” so its Master Blend is not exactly the kind of thing you’ll want to drink on its own. I tried this for science, of course, and it wasn’t terrible! There’s a vegetal flavor on the sip that tastes like potato water, and the finish has an astringent tingle that’s akin to the tiniest dose of Sichuan peppercorns steeped in hot water. Om really shines when it’s added to a cup of coffee brewed with beans from the Global South. One teaspoon of this sand-colored dust added a savory pop that smoothed out the brightness of my favorite Colombian Supremo beans from Costco, and the requisite jitters that usually kicked in after three cups of the brew felt mellower than usual with Om mixed in. The silty residue at the bottom of the cup is best avoided, but it won’t harsh your vibe too much on the whole.
North Spore Functional-5 Mushroom Coffee for $18: Most mushroom-infused ground coffee blends are filed under the “Medium Roast” category, which is typically a safe catch-all that grocery store brands and discount purveyors describe their preground product as to avoid pissing off discerning light-roast aficionados such as yours truly. Nine times out of 10 they hit like a dark roast, with an ashy taste and a healthy dose of the oil that seeps out of the beans during the elongated roasting process, shimmering and swirling around the top of your cup like a puddle in a parking lot. This coffee from North Spore, which makes our favorite mushroom-growing monotub and spray-and-grow mushroom kit, lacks all of those off notes while still retaining a sturdy, earthy flavor that’s far enough removed from the citric and buttery notes I love most about classic high-end light roasts to stand up as its own unique thing. There’s a hint of mushroom flavor on the swallow if you really look for it, but you could easily swap this in for someone's morning cup of Folgers or Illy medium roast and they’d be none the wiser.
Ryze Superfoods Mushroom Coffee for $75: One could consider two different approaches to how purveyors of mushroom coffee dial in the flavor profile of their product: They can go all in with a bombastic brew filled with spices and overtones, or they can play it safe and concoct the base of a beverage that tastes more like memories of other drinks than a beverage with an identity of its own. The underwhelming flavor of Ryze falls in the latter camp. In fairness, there are plenty of folks who have no interest in savoring their morning beverage and instead need to put the liquid inside them as fast as possible so they can “adult” that day. Twenty-one-year-old Pete thought people who claimed to enjoy espresso were insane, yet here I am, two decades later wishing I could sip bitter bean water instead of this sour cup of forgettable swill that curdled the whole milk I tried to cut it with. A week with Ryze did little to boost my mood, focus, or energy. It mostly made me cranky and sad.
Cuppa Medium Roast Mushroom Coffee for $30: Like the friendly foreigner who calls his daily cup of tea or coffee his “cuppa,” this newcomer is polite, congenial, and inoffensive. The first sip brought to mind a really good cup of coffee at a nameless diner, with a light body and very mellow acidic notes on the swallow. The small dose of ruddy powder pulled from the bag with the included plastic scoop dissolved thoroughly with a few stirs, and the pristine lack of sediment in the cup was exactly as advertised. The boost of energy is also unassuming and easy to relegate to the background, which could be a welcome respite from the blast of caffeine many coffee addicts think they need right when they wake up every morning. After a week with Cuppa I started to enjoy easing into my daily brain vibrations rather than white-knuckling it off the rip at 7 am on the dot every morning.
Not Recommended
MUD/WTR Original Blend for $60: The packaging of MUD/WTR isn’t quite as unhinged as a bottle of Dr. Bronner's, but it’s definitely in the same realm. The spicy dust inside the can is a maximalist circus of weirdness as well, with herbaceous stalwarts like turmeric and masala chai holding it down alongside the usual shroom suspects. It took me a few days to realize that properly emulsifying this ruddy power per the suggested instructions—1 tablespoon with ¾ cup of water, battered thoroughly with the included handheld immersion blender—is an impossible task, so I started experimenting with supplemental ingredients in hopes that some blend of milk, fat, and sugar would minimize the gritty aftertaste that overwhelms the palate. I landed on 1 tablespoon of simple syrup and 4 ounces of whole milk frothed in my trusty Subminimal NanoFoamer Pro. The final result hits somewhere between a chai latte and the kind of hot cocoa you’d order at a coffee shop with boring ’90s music, mean baristas, and a dirty bin full of stale vegan + gluten-free snacks next to the register. I didn’t hate it, but the bottom quarter of the cup is an undrinkable gunky mess. And don’t get me started on the chunky brown lacing that clings to the edge of the cup. The physical and mental effects of MUD/WTR felt more like a facsimile of a boost than a visceral kick in the pants, but a placebo high is better than nothing, right? Combine that with the amount of adjunct ingredients required to make this drinkable and I ended up with a beverage I would only drink every now and then as a treat on a chilly day rather than a daily sipper I can rely on for increased focus, energy, virility, and the million other things this product promises within the wall of text that adorns its packaging.

The Sapiens Health Foundation has welcomed the Tamil Nadu Government’s announcement of a salt reduction campaign in the Assembly on Tuesday.
Reducing salt intake could help lower the burden of hypertension, stroke, heart attacks and kidney disease. In a press release, the foundation cited the UK’s salt-reduction campaign, initiated in 2005 by Graham MacGregor of the World Action on Salt, Sugar and Health (WASSH), which resulted in a reported 30% reduction in salt in bread.
The Foundation’s salt-reduction campaign began in 2010 with a walkathon at Marina Beach, followed by similar events in Tiruchi and Puducherry and awareness programmes in colleges. In 2014, its founder-chairman Rajan Ravichandran received the Notable Achievement Award from the World Hypertension League for the campaign.
The Foundation has written to more than 300 food manufacturers seeking reductions in salt content and cited reductions in salt in noodles by Nestlé and Hindustan Lever as examples of industry response. It also organised international conferences on salt and health with IIT-Madras and IIT-Bombay in 2017.
The Foundation has conducted salt and health workshops for more than 500 physicians in Chennai, Mumbai, Delhi and Vijayawada. It also welcomed the growing focus on front-of-pack food labelling and said the State’s decision to take forward the campaign will be an important step towards improving population health.

Ujjain (Madhya Pradesh): The municipal corporation has put on hold the proposed relocation of the Khade Hanuman Temple to widen the Kanthal Chauraha-Chhatri Chowk road and postponed a proposed inspection by an IIT team.
The halt is also expected to impact the removal of other religious structures for road-widening projects.
The corporation was preparing to remove four major religious structures, but officials now fear that their removal could also face resistance.
The Khade Hanuman Temple relocation issue has remained in the spotlight for the past eight days.
Temple priest Mahesh Bairagi had reportedly given his consent to shifting the temple but has now clarified that it was conditional. In a letter made public, he said shifting shops on the temple premises would affect his family's livelihood.
According to sources, the municipal corporation had agreed to almost all of the priest's conditions, but the issue of compensation for the shops led to a deadlock.
Corporation officials were reportedly unable to provide a written assurance in this regard. Opposition to the relocation intensified after removal of the temple dome began last Thursday.
Bairagi said he had agreed to the relocation subject to eight conditions. According to him, the corporation has fulfilled only one condition, providing documents related to the temple's ownership, while the remaining seven have not been met.
Offerings rise with footfall
Khade Hanuman Temple has gained popularity across the country and abroad through social media. Around 25% of people coming to Ujjain to visit Mahakaleshwar and Kaal Bhairav are reportedly also visiting Khade Hanuman Temple.
E-rickshaw and auto-rickshaw drivers have added the temple to their regular Ujjain sightseeing routes. The increase in devotees has also resulted in a sharp rise in offerings at the temple.
MLA Malviya backs retaining temple
The proposed relocation has also taken a political turn, with BJP MLA Chintamani Malviya visiting the temple on Friday and advocating for retaining it at its existing location.
Malviya said public sentiment was in favour of keeping Baba at the present site and that the road had already been widened sufficiently. Referring to the 'shahi sawari' held last Monday, he said around 8 lakh devotees had attended without major problems related to traffic or arrangements.
He said the matter was in the knowledge of Chief Minister Mohan Yadav and expressed hope that a decision would be taken in accordance with public sentiment.
Hindu outfits demand temple's preservation
The Anterrastreey Hindu Parishad and Rashtriya Bajrang Dal, along with devotees, have demanded that the temple be preserved at its existing location.
The government and administration had planned to remove the temple with the consent of all concerned and re-establish it in the Tanki Chowk area.
Workers of the organisations took out a rally to the temple premises, where they recited the Hanuman Chalisa.
They subsequently submitted a memorandum addressed to the Prime Minister and Chief Minister, demanding that Khade Hanuman Temple be retained at its present location.
Hindu Helpline Mahanagar president Kuldeep Sharma said Khade Hanuman Temple on Gopal Mandir Road is more than 1,000 years old and an important centre of faith for the Sanatan community.
The organisation alleged that a portion of the temple's 'shikhara' and wall had been demolished in the name of development works and road widening for Simhastha 2028.

25 years after 9/11, the GOP has never been more anti-Muslim
The GOP wants America to fear Muslims.
Hi readers — today marks 25 years since 9/11. In New York City, Washington, and Pennsylvania, survivors, families, and politicians are gathering to grieve and commemorate the attacks.
Today, we wanted to focus on one small part of the story in New York City, where former Mayor Rudy Giuliani singled out Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who is Muslim, with an Islamophobic screed about Mamdani’s participation in memorial ceremonies.
Giuliani’s rant, to be clear, is not really news in its own right; 25 years on, he’s less “America’s mayor” than he is the twice-disbarred, disgraced former lawyer of President Donald Trump. (And Mamdani did attend the event, even shaking hands with Giuliani.)
But Giuliani’s remarks are, unfortunately, emblematic of a disturbing trend in Republican politics, where open, aggressive Islamophobia is on the rise — 25 years after a particularly ugly brand of it emerged in response to 9/11. One major difference between then and now? In 2001, many politicians tried to tamp it down rather than inflame it.
As Nathan Lean, an assistant teaching professor at North Carolina State University and author of the book The Islamophobia Industry, explained to my colleague Christian Paz last month: “Islamophobia has passed the dinner table test. You can say things about Muslims with basic impunity today. And it’s institutionalized in the way that prejudice that targets other marginalized communities is not.”
The GOP is running on Islamophobia in 2026
The 2026 midterm elections have provided a particularly clear showcase for the right’s Islamophobic turn.
On Thursday, at the second and final night of the GOP’s unusual midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) told attendees that “communism” and “Islamism” were allying against Republicans. “They share the same enemies,” he said. “They hate Christians. They hate Jews. They hate capitalism. They hate the Constitution, and they hate America.”
At another point in Cruz’s speech, attendees screamed “he should be shot” as Cruz name-checked Mamdani, Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (who is Muslim, and who Cruz said “says he has an obligation to Sharia Law”), and Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.
As Christian reports, Michigan and especially Texas have both been on the front lines of rising Islamophobia.
Michigan has a large Muslim population in cities like Dearborn and Hamtramck, and El-Sayed has drawn particular vitriol; Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) wrote last month that “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a Trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic.”
And in Texas, as the New York Times reported at length last month, Islamophobia has become a matter of policy as well as rhetoric from Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and other politicians in the state.
El-Sayed, in Michigan, has described the attacks as an attempt to distract voters from other issues. “They’re going to point at me, they’re going to point at my name, like, ‘Wow, he’s different,’” he said last month. “My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”
Without much else to run on, though, Republicans seem to have decided they’re all-in on Islamophobia.
