DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin uses his 9/11 speech to rail against sanctuary cities
The Trump administration has consistently criticized sanctuary cities for limiting cooperation between local police and federal immigration agents
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sharply criticized sanctuary cities on Friday in a speech reflecting on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terror attacks.
Mullin accused these jurisdictions, which limit cooperation between local police and federal immigration agencies, of creating the conditions for the next terror attack.
“It’s tough to sometimes fight — and I’m not trying to get political here, but I will — sanctuary cities that they don’t want us to go into,” Mullin told a crowd at Resilience Plaza at DHS headquarters in Washington, D.C.
“They can say it’s for humanitarian purposes, but the truth is, when you become a sanctuary city and you’re not supporting law enforcement, when you're not allowing law enforcement to do their job, it’s a safe haven that incubates terrorist activity,” Mullin added.
Sanctuary cities do not stop federal agents from operating in their boundaries but typically prohibit local police and jails from being deputized into carrying out federal immigration work, such as making arrests or holding migrant detainees solely on immigration-related accusations.
Backers of sanctuary cities often argue that jointly conducting immigration operations with federal agencies undermines immigrant communities’ trust in local police and strains budgetary resources.
Even in sanctuary cities, federal agencies have the legal authority to pursue arrests and detain suspected criminals. DHS also has numerous local cooperation agreements with police departments and sheriff’s offices, including in sanctuary states.
The Trump administration has consistently criticized sanctuary cities and has threatened to cut their federal funding.
Elsewhere in his speech, Mullin wondered why the reputation of DHS had become so politicized, given its mission of protecting all Americans.
“Why should the Department of Homeland Security be controversial?” he told the crowd. “We’re taking care of your backyard. Why did it become political? Because some people want to score political points?”
Indeed, under the Trump administration, support for DHS has eroded.
About half of Americans support abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a DHS agency, a July poll from The Economist and YouGov found.
Between 2023 and 2025, Americans ceased viewing DHS as generally favorable, the Pew Research Center found.
DHS under Trump has pursued a variety of boundary-pushing tactics compared to predecessors, including using masked agents, sending heavily armed officers to conduct warrantless raids and ramping up arrests at sensitive locations such as schools and medical facilities.
In January, DHS agents fatally shot two American protesters in a matter of weeks in Minneapolis, prompting mass demonstrations.
In the face of these criticisms, former heads of the agency have called for a “reset” at DHS refocusing on the mission of stopping security threats.
“When I stepped into the job of secretary in 2013, the department was still, I think, viewed primarily as security,” Obama administration DHS secretary Jeh Johnson recently told NBC News. “Now I fear in many communities DHS has become a pariah, radioactive, the department of mass deportations, heartless, locking up kids, and that is one of the reasons why I think we need a reset.”
In a statement to The Independent, DHS defended its record under Trump and its overall mission.
“Counterterrorism and immigration enforcement go hand in hand,” a spokesperson said. “Child exploitation, trafficking, terrorism, scams, and smuggling all have a nexus to illegal immigration.”
“Despite multiple Democrat shutdowns of DHS, the Department is more than equipped to keep Americans safe in an ever-changing threat landscape. DHS has been recruiting, reforming, and modernizing at a record pace—including in areas of counterterrorism,” the spokesperson added.

India calls for local currency trade among BRICS to enhance economic resilience
External Affairs Minister Jaishankar emphasized self-reliance amid global economic challenges.
India on Friday urged Brics nations to create a predictable business environment, build resilient supply chains and link their payment systems to allow trade in local currencies, as Russia proposed a Brics grain exchange to strengthen food security across the bloc.
Delivering the keynote address at the Brics Business Forum, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said India’s chairship was focused on resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability. “We meet at a time when [the] global political and economic order is under churn. Volatility, uncertainty, and complexity have become defining features of the world around us. We are witnessing the economic consequences of geopolitical conflicts, of pandemics, and of climate-related disruptions,” he said.
Jaishankar called for “greater self-reliance” within Brics to strengthen economic security. “The objective is to strengthen our ability to absorb shocks while remaining connected and competitive,” he said, listing genuine market practices, dependable logistics, a predictable business environment, diversified commercial relationships and transparent trade and investment as priorities. Energy systems capable of coping with disruption, and transition pathways suited to different national circumstances, were also needed, he added, citing digital public infrastructure (DPI), artificial intelligence, fintech and advanced manufacturing as areas of major opportunity.

I don’t know about you, but whenever I go to see my primary care doctor, my mental health isn’t usually at the top of my list of things to talk about. But it should be. In fact, experts say that all of us could benefit from more candid conversations with our doctors about our mental health.
How — and why — to tell your doctor you’re feeling depressed
Your doctor can be your mental health ally. Here’s how to talk about it.
(This story discusses mental health issues and suicide. If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. You are not alone. You can call the national 988 hotline for support.)
For years, the United States has been trying to figure out “parity” for mental health care — to have it treated and paid for like any other medical need, not something that is carved out and separate. A big part of that has been pushing primary care doctors and OB/GYNs to do more screenings, to make your mental state a part of your well-being that you discuss with your doctor the same as your blood pressure or any physical ailment.
But that is easier said than done. A lot of people may not even realize that their depression or anxiety or stress is something they should talk about with their primary care doctor. Others might fear being judged, and for good reason — national policymakers warn there continues to be a stigma toward mental health conditions among doctors.
About one in three Americans say they have never been asked about their mental health by a doctor, which is unsettling considering that the nation has been going through a collective mental health crisis for several years. Men are significantly less likely to be asked about their mental health than women — perhaps a reflection of a culture that expects men to “tough it out” when it comes to their feelings. But those attitudes come with a price: Men are diagnosed with depression at half the rate as women, but die by suicide much more frequently.
Much of the burden for starting these conversations should fall on your doctor to be more curious and accommodating during annual exams. But you don’t have to wait to be asked to bring it up. Regularly talking to your provider about your mental health is the best way to get ahead of any problems and get treated if you need to be. In honor of Suicide Prevention Month, I reached out to a handful of doctors who have studied why it’s sometimes so hard for patients and doctors to talk about depression, anxiety, and stress — and learned some novel strategies for how you can take charge, push through any stigma, and start having more honest talks with your doctor about your state of mind. Here’s what you should know.
Know the relevant symptoms before you talk to your doctor
One of the tricky things about depression or any serious mental health problem is that it isn’t always easy to identify when you’re the one experiencing it. “Patients need to recognize their distress…as potentially emanating from depression,” Dr. Richard Kravitz, a general medicine professor at UC Davis who has studied depression screening in primary care, told me.
There is a checklist of sorts that you can go through on your own to understand whether you’re just having a tough couple of days or there’s something more serious at work, said Dr. Maria Garcia, an internal medicine physician at UC San Francisco. You might be feeling down or unmotivated or have a lack of energy, or be more agitated, angry, or irritable than usual. Sometimes there are less obvious signs, like trouble with money or problems at work.
Symptoms of depression
Here are some of the possible signs of depression, according to the Mayo Clinic. If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. You can call the national 988 hotline for support.
- Feeling sad or hopeless or like you are a burden to others
- Feeling more irritable and angry than usual, losing your temper more easily
- Losing interest in most or all normal day-to-day activities and hobbies
- Sleep problems, whether you are sleeping too little or too much
- Feeling less energetic than usual
- Changes in appetite — whether you are eating less and losing weight or eating more and gaining weight
- Concentration and memory problems
- Unexplained physical symptoms
“If you’re not getting enjoyment from your normal hobbies or talking to the people that you would normally really enjoy talking to, if you find yourself isolating from people that you normally really enjoy spending time with, I think those are certainly triggers,” she said. Consider the duration of your symptoms, too: “If it’s every day for a couple of weeks, that definitely isn’t normal.”
And oftentimes, depression symptoms can mirror symptoms of other ailments or problems, like a lack of sleep, low appetite, or physical aches and pains. This is one reason why it is so important to talk with your doctor about it, Garcia said. Is that fatigue a result of depression — or is it a problem with your thyroid? Your primary care physician is best positioned to help you figure that out. One of the benefits of a long-term relationship with a physician is that they may be able to help you recognize symptoms of depression even if they aren’t obvious to you.
It’s hard to be that self-aware; I’m certainly not all the time. But the more you pay attention to your mood and how it’s affecting your life, the more you can tell your doctor about what’s really going on. You don’t have to know all the fancy clinical terms, said Paul Duberstein, a clinical psychologist and professor of health behavior, society, and policy at the Rutgers School of Public Health. “The language that people are most comfortable using are words like stress or frustrated or impatient or something like that,” Duberstein told me. “Those are the kinds of things we really do want to incentivize and encourage people to talk to their doctors about.”
How to bring up your mental health with your doctor
Okay, you feel like something might be off and you have a doctor’s appointment coming up. What do you do?
You might not have to do anything. These days, you are likely to be given a depression screening by your physician’s office before you ever arrive (usually as part of your pre-visit paperwork). Garcia said it’s important to be honest and to be thorough when answering those questions, as that will tell your doctor that your mental health should be a focus for your upcoming visit.
Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems. How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American healthcare policy. Sign up here.
But if you aren’t proactively screened for depression and you have some of the symptoms described above or you just have a hunch that something might be wrong, try to alert your doctor in advance that your mental health is something you want to talk about. If that’s not possible, tell your doctor early on in the appointment that your mental state is something you want to discuss. Garcia said that, rightly or wrongly, doctors can sometimes be reluctant to dive deep into a discussion about mental health late into a visit; they only have so much time with individual patients, and they might balk at trying to squeeze in a mental health discussion at the end. The conversation is more likely to be productive if you proactively start it before your physician is sidetracked with your blood sugar.
During this conversation, you can ask for a depression screening outright. Doctors have become adept at recognizing code words; if you say your mood has been off, they may pick up the signal that you may be experiencing mental health struggles. But there is a good argument for being very direct about how you’re feeling, Kravitz said.
“My advice…is just simply to say to the doctor, ‘I’ve been feeling down’ or ‘I’ve been feeling irritable’ or ‘I’ve been losing sleep’ or ‘Something’s wrong and I don’t know what it is. Do you think it might be depression?’ Just ask,” Kravitz said. If you aren’t sure if it’s a mental or physical issue, tell them that. Activate your doctor’s curiosity, Kravitz told me. Get them invested in figuring out what’s going on with you.
Once the conversation starts, your doctor is likely to ask how long you have been experiencing symptoms and how they are affecting your day-to-day function. When that happens, you should be as thorough and truthful as possible.
“Is it affecting your ability to take care of your family? Is it affecting your ability to go to work, get up in the morning, cook dinner, get out of the house, go grocery shopping?” Garcia said. “Those things are really helpful because then we can tailor the treatments for the amount of functional impairment.”
Talk to your doctor about your sleep, too, Duberstein said. Not only is it an important indicator of your physical health, but it will also tell your doctor something about your mental well-being. And it doesn’t require any special emotional vocabulary: You probably know if you’re sleeping well or not.
“If you think about major depression as a collection of, say, nine symptoms and you ask, ‘Well, what symptoms appear first? Is it the depressed mood? Or the difficulty concentrating?’ The first thing that appears typically is sleep,” Duberstein told me. “Disrupted sleep is something that I think people do feel comfortable talking with their doctor about.”
How to talk to your doctor about a treatment plan
If you have a productive conversation with your doctor and they recognize symptoms of depression, they’ll want to establish a treatment plan. This has historically been another barrier to honest conversations between doctors and patients about mental health: Patients don’t want to be prescribed antidepressants or referred to therapy, so they don’t bring it up.
But ignoring your symptoms is, of course, not the solution. Instead, use your appointment as an opportunity to ask all of your questions to make sure that you are fully comfortable with the doctor’s proposed treatment plan and can get on the road to better mental health.
Many Americans have doubts about antidepressants, which have been egged on by high-profile figures like US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. If you’re hesitant to take meds, you should tell your provider about the things that you’ve heard that give you pause, the negative experiences people have shared, or whatever major questions or concerns you have. They can help you understand the very real trade-offs that come with taking an antidepressant, Kravitz said. Your doctor can also debunk some of the misconceptions that make people hesitant to take these drugs even when they are struggling.
“The duration of therapy sometimes surprises people. But no, it doesn’t mean that you’ll have to be on it forever. No, most people don’t have serious withdrawal symptoms. Those can usually be managed by careful tapering if necessary and so on,” Kravitz said. He said you can ask your doctor outright: “What can I expect to happen over time? How long will I need to be on this?”
If you’d rather not go on medication immediately, that’s totally valid. Your doctor may instead be able to help you find a therapist with a referral, Duberstein said. Therapists have historically been hard to find in the US — but one positive outcome of the pandemic was the proliferation of online mental health services.
“I think it’s important for the public to know that one of the major barriers to getting into psychotherapy or even seeing a therapist — like getting into your car, driving, finding a bus, finding a subway, whatever — that those barriers are gone,” he told me. “Because you could see a therapist online now in all 50 states.”
The goal is that you leave your doctor’s office feeling heard and feeling on-board with the approach, even if you still have some trepidation (which is very common). And if you don’t feel comfortable talking to your doctor about these issues, that may be a sign you need to find a new provider whom you feel you can trust with those sensitive discussions, Duberstein said.
The point is, your doctor should be your ally in pursuing whatever treatment you need for whatever ails for your mental health. Nobody has to go through it alone.

It is unclear whether TMZ's photos of Matthews with an enlarged chin and jawline and bulging muscles are authentic, meaning not generated or edited using artificial intelligence software. However, Matthews later told the outlet his look in the pictures was a result of prosthetics for an ad campaign, not plastic surgery.
In early September 2026, alleged photos circulated online purportedly showing former NFL linebacker Clay Matthews after extensive plastic surgery.
One X user who shared the images, which showed Matthews with an enlarged chin and jawline, bulging arm and leg muscles and loading bags into a car, wrote (archived): "TRENDING: Packers legend Clay Matthews was spotted out grabbing groceries, looking VERY different after getting some work done. An absolutely shocking transformation."
(X)
The pictures, originally published by celebrity magazine TMZ, also circulated on Facebook, Instagram and Reddit, where social media users discussed whether they were real.
It is unclear whether TMZ's images of Matthews are authentic, meaning not generated or edited using artificial intelligence software. Pangram, a highly regarded artificial intelligence detector, determined that several images from TMZ's gallery were "fully AI." Such tools are fallible though and should not be entirely relied upon for answers to media's authenticity.
Regardless, TMZ's images do not show Matthews after plastic surgery. Therefore, we rate this claim false.
The outlet reported on Sept. 9, 2026 (archived), that Matthews had prosthetics fitted for an ad campaign for a sports betting platform that created the look seen in TMZ's pictures. That sports betting platform sponsored that TMZ article. It was not possible to independently confirm whether the outlet's images of Matthews were staged as part of the platform's advertising campaign. Snopes contacted TMZ to ask about the authenticity of its images and await a reply.
The TMZ article features a video of Matthews saying it took four hours to fit the prosthetics, which another video (archived) posted to the former Green Bay Packers linebacker's Facebook page shows also included his calves. The sports betting platform Matthews advertised for when he wore the prosthetics also posted a video on X (archived) that shows them being fitted to the former NFL star's face.
Given that Matthews did wear the prosthetics in question, it is likely that TMZ's images of him are authentic.
The prosthetics' cartoonishly enlarged jawline and muscles played on the "looksmaxxing" trend that the Merriam-Webster dictionary defines as "efforts, sometimes extreme, young men take to look more attractive."
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated a number of other rumors about the NFL.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, the first foreign dignitary to arrive in New Delhi for the BRICS Summit, held a bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday (September 11, 2026) and reviewed the full spectrum of bilateral ties. Mr. Modi reemphasized that “India stood ready to assist in peace efforts.”
“During today’s meeting we talked about: closer trade ties, including implementation of the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030. Cooperation in areas like infrastructure, energy, technology, defence, culture, and more,” said Prime Minister Modi in his remarks.
BRICS Summit 2026 updates on September 11
Sources said the two sides discussed steps to increase the bilateral trade target to $100 billion by 2030 and projects on civil nuclear cooperation. Mr. Modi reiterated his call to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict that has continued for more than four-and-a-half years.
“The two leaders reviewed progress in bilateral cooperation in political, economic, defence, energy, space, skill mobility, and people-to-people domains,” said the External Affairs Ministry after the meeting. The two leaders exchanged views on the conflict in West Asia and the spillover effects of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in the Black Sea region, affecting Indian seafarers. Several Indian sailors were killed in attacks by Russian and Ukrainian forces on foreign-flagged vessels.
“Prime Minister once again reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy was the way forward in resolving conflicts and India stood ready to assist in peace efforts,” the Ministry said in a press note. President Putin invited Prime Minister Modi for the 24th India-Russia Annual Summit, which India accepted. The dates of the summit will be decided as per “mutual convenience” following diplomatic consultations.
The talks featured ways to expand industrial cooperation with Russia, collaboration in railway and tunneling, developing a steel value chain, and more business-to-business opportunities. Russia has been increasing employment opportunities for Indian blue-collar professionals and cooperation in the mobility of skilled manpower.
Against the backdrop of the conflict in West Asia and supply chain disruptions, measures to ensure the flow of energy and fertilizers through strategic joint ventures were discussed, as was cooperation in critical minerals.
Prime Minister Modi gifted President Putin a Russian translation of Thirukkural,the classical Tamil poem collection authored by poet and philosopher Thiruvalluvar. Mr. Modi was accompanied by External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, National Security Adviser Ajit Doval, Principal Secretary Shaktikanta Das, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, and other senior officials in the meeting. The two leaders last met on the sidelines of the SCO summit in the Kyrgyz Republic’s capital, Bishkek, on August 31. Mr. Modi had called for an end to the Ukraine war then.
In a news release, the Kremlin said President Putin is expected to visit the INNOPROM exhibition organised jointly by the Indian and Russian Ministries of Commerce. He is scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with leaders of other countries during his stay in New Delhi. “The main agreements reached are expected to be reflected in the summit’s final document,” the Kremlin said.

Queiroz returns as Ghana head coach
- Published
Carlos Queiroz has been reappointed as head coach of Ghana's men's national team.
The 73-year-old, who had two spells as assistant manager at Manchester United under Sir Alex Ferguson, took charge of the Black Stars in April and led the side to the last 32 at this year's Fifa World Cup, where they were beaten 1-0 by Colombia.
Queiroz appeared to announce his own departure on social media shortly after that defeat, but the Ghana Football Association (GFA) has decided to re-engage him for another spell in charge following internal discussions.
The GFA has not announced the length of his new deal but said he will prepare the team for "a successful new phase on the international stage".
"The GFA believes Queiroz's extensive international experience, technical expertise and knowledge of the Black Stars position him strongly to lead the team into this next chapter," a statement added.
Queiroz has previously led Iran, Portugal and Egypt at major tournaments and has had stints in charge of South Africa, Colombia and Qatar.
Further details on his mandate will be announced by the GFA in due course.
Queiroz said the chance to continue in the role gave him "immense pride and honour".
"Serving Ghana is far more than coaching a football team," he added in a post on Instagram.
"It is a privilege, a responsibility and a mission to honour one of Africa's greatest football nations and its incredible and passionate football people.
"Our ambition is clear: improve every day, unite the nation, make Ghana stronger and fight for every victory with passion, humility and pride. The mission continues."
Queiroz will begin his second spell in charge of the West Africans with qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, which begin later this month.
The Black Stars are yet to announce the dates and venues for their first two fixtures in Group C, where they have been drawn alongside Ivory Coast, The Gambia and Somalia.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

How shofars became the spiritual soundtrack of Rosh Hashanah
(RNS and NPR) It can be the small, curved horn of a ram or the dramatic spiral of an African antelope. The sound it creates is unmistakable.
Creating that sound is not difficult, but it does take some practice, said Rabbi Alicia Jo Rabins, a musician based in Portland, Oregon.
You take a deep breath and purse your lips, like you are playing a brass instrument.
Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish new year, begins at sunset Friday. Across the world, Jews will spend the two-day holiday in prayer, reflection and celebration. And for many, a highlight will be hearing the shofar: an animal's horn blown like a trumpet.
How did this primal instrument become a holiday's spiritual soundtrack?
" The most basic answer is that it makes noise, right? It calls people to attention," said Daniel Picus, an associate professor at Western Washington University in Bellingham who researches religious practices and rituals. "All of the instances in which a shofar is used in the Hebrew Bible, that is what it's doing."
Shofar blasts marked the revelation of the Torah at Mt. Sinai and the start of the Jubilee year, Picus said. Priests blew shofars when they circled the walls of Jericho to bring down the walls. The shofar marks moments of heightened experience and emotion — and Rosh Hashanah.
"In the Hebrew Bible, Rosh Hashanah is the day of trumpeting and the day of remembrance," Picus said. "The association of the shofar with Rosh Hashanah is right there in the Biblical text."
Centuries later, the Mishnah, the earliest rabbinic codification of law, drilled down into greater detail in the tractate Rosh Hashanah, laying out exactly how a shofar should be prepared (hollowed out), repaired (it depends), blown (a complex series of blasts at several times during the service, thanks to debate over linguistic interpretation), and whether or not it can be blown when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat (no, although some modern synagogues have changed course).
And within the Talmud and for centuries thereafter, people have debated the meaning of the shofar.
Rabbi Micha'el Rosenberg, who teaches at the Hadar Institute, a center for Jewish learning based in New York City, pointed to several sources that compare the sound of the shofar to the cry of a mother in pain — the mother of the slain biblical military commander Sisera, and the cries of a woman in labor.
Rosenberg said you can hear that in the sound — especially the broken staccato blasts, known as "teruah."
"You can really imagine someone so caught up that they can't get the full sound out even, that they're gasping with their cries," he said.
Another interpretation comes from Maimonides, the medieval Jewish rabbi and scholar known as the Rambam, who wrote "The Laws of Repentance." He describes the blast of the shofar as a sort of spiritual wake-up call to become your best self.
"In Jewish law, we have this expression of daled amos, my four cubits: I focus on the 6 feet around me, as it were," he said. "It's easy to do that — and there's value in doing that sometimes. But the shofar, per the Rambam, wakes us up and says, 'No, there's more beyond what I can immediately see around me.'"
Rosenberg also pointed to Hasidic theories that the blowing of the shofar reenacts the breathing of life into the world. But he said one of the most powerful things about the shofar is that it doesn't say anything at all. "It transcends my words, it transcends my rational thoughts, and it really is just a feeling that I can hope to hold onto," he said.
Rabins, the Portland rabbi and musician, said the shofar can call across time to speak to those wordless places inside us. "It really brings you into the moment, and you also feel connected to your ancestors, who have been hearing this sound and making this sound for thousands of years," she said.
It's a sound, Rabin said, that can wake you up to all the joy and sadness of life, whether it be a birthday horn or a mother's cry. And it makes you pay attention — both to this moment, and to the year to come.

Billionaire and member of the famed Koch family Bill Koch tried to offload his massive compound in Aspen for nine figures, but ended up selling it at auction for nearly $100 million below the listing price.
The founder of Oxbow Carbon bought the ski-town property in 2007 for $26.5 million and later added 31 acres.
The compound hit the market in 2015 with an asking price of $100 million. Koch eventually dropped the price to $80 million the following year. In 2020, he sold the additional 31 acres he added for $14.5 million, but held on to the lodge and the rest of the 52-acre property.
In 2025, Koch relisted the property at $125 million, but it didn't sell. In 2026, Koch went the auction route — a tactic sometimes employed for notable properties. The property finally sold in July, but for a fraction of its original listing price.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the winning bid was $33.5 million — a 73% decrease from its peak listing price. Koch's lofty $125 million price would have been the most expensive sale in Colorado history, beating Palatir Alex Karp's recent $120 million ranch purchase in nearby Snowmass, Colorado.
Koch, who has a net worth of $2 billion, according to Forbes, sold his stake in Koch Industries to his brothers for $470 million in 1983. That left him with plenty of money to make renovations to his Colorado ranch.
The recently sold main lodge spans 16,600 square feet and is accompanied by seven cabins — one of which is a home gym. The property also includes hot tubs, hiking trails, and an altitude-acclimation room.

Jaishankar flags global uncertainty at BRICS forum: 'Political and economic order under churn'
Speaking at the BRICS Business Forum, Jaishankar said geopolitical conflicts, pandemics and climate-related disruptions were having economic consequences.
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Friday flagged growing uncertainty in the global political and economic order, saying volatility and complexity had become defining features of the world.
Speaking at the BRICS Business Forum, Jaishankar said geopolitical conflicts, pandemics and climate-related disruptions were having economic consequences, while rapid digitisation and technological advances were creating new opportunities for growth, productivity and development.
Follow BRICS Summit LIVE updates here.
"We meet at a time when global political and economic order is under churn. Volatility, uncertainty, and complexity have become defining features of the world around us. We are witnessing the economic consequences of geopolitical conflicts, of pandemics, and of climate-related disruptions," he said.
He also said rapid digitisation and technological advances are opening up new possibilities for growth, productivity and development. “The result is an economic landscape where both risks and opportunities are becoming more widely distributed and where the ability to anticipate, adapt and respond is acquiring greater importance,” he added.
Deep Dive
BRICS Summit on Sept 12-13
New Delhi is all set to host the BRICS Summit on September 12 and 13, with several world leaders and senior delegations arriving in the national capital from late Thursday evening through early Friday morning.
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in New Delhi on Friday, marking the beginning of a three-day visit to India to participate in the BRICS Summit and meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi to discuss expanding bilateral trade, investment and energy cooperation.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Indonesian counterpart Prabowo Subianto, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali and Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung are among the top leaders attending the summit.

As the curtains fell on Jammu and Kashmir’s first International Film Festival in Srinagar, officials from various states who attended the four-day event returned with more than memories of films and red-carpet ceremonies. The festival gave them an opportunity to experience Kashmir beyond its conventional tourist image, they say.
Officials from the Departments of Information, Culture and Tourism said the festival allowed them to interact with local people, explore different parts of the Valley and gain a closer understanding of its culture, lifestyle and people.
Sudhakar T, Director, Information and Publicity, Government of Puducherry, described his participation in the inaugural International Film Festival of Jammu and Kashmir as a “truly memorable experience”, both personally and professionally.
“From the ceremonial opening at INOX Srinagar to the grand opening ceremony at SKICC, the festival was executed with remarkable precision,” he said, referring to the lamp lighting, felicitation of the jury and personalities of Indian cinema, musical performances and the address by the chief guest.
“It was heartening to see a festival of this scale being hosted for the very first time in the Valley, bringing together filmmakers, artists and industry voices from across the world,” Sudhakar said.
For him, however, the experience went beyond the festival venues and the glamour surrounding the event.
“What struck me most, beyond the glamour of the red carpet, was the opportunity the festival gave to explore Kashmir itself — both the urban rhythm of Srinagar and the quieter, rural stretches beyond it,” he said.
He said interacting with local people and understanding their daily lives, warmth and connection with the land added “an entirely different dimension” to his experience.
The festival’s focus on Jammu and Kashmir’s cinematic heritage also helped visitors understand the region beyond its tourist attractions, he said. Sections such as “Cinematic Echoes”, celebrating the stories and legacy of J&K cinema, and the “J&K Library”, documenting local filmmakers and talent, provided a window into the region’s creative landscape.
The festival was also spread across different venues, including SKICC, INOX Srinagar, Gulmarg and Wave Mall in Jammu. The floating cinema concept, which took films to Kashmir’s iconic waterscapes, further connected the event with the region’s landscape and culture.
A tourism official from Himachal Pradesh, whose department had set up a stall at the festival, said the event provided an opportunity to showcase the state while interacting with filmmakers, visitors and officials from different parts of the country.
Alka, an official from Punjab’s Department of Information, also described the experience as “great”, saying the festival provided an opportunity to learn about Kashmir and interact with people from different parts of the country.
Officials said the festival had successfully brought together cinema, culture and tourism while creating opportunities for people from different parts of India to engage with Kashmir beyond the usual tourist experience.
For Sudhakar, the festival’s strongest impression was the sense of place it created.
“The cinema was world cinema, but the spirit was unmistakably Kashmiri — its people, its culture and its landscape formed as much a part of this festival as the films themselves,” he said.

Properly handle differences, be friends: China ahead of PM Modi-Xi talks at BRICS
China's Ambassador to India Xu Feihong said Beijing and New Delhi are arranging a Xi-Modi meeting, urging both sides to "properly handle differences", strengthen communication and cooperation, and be "friends enjoying good-neighbourliness" ahead of the BRICS summit.
China's Ambassador to India Xu Feihong said Beijing and New Delhi are arranging a bilateral meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, stressing that the two countries should "properly handle differences" and be "friends enjoying good-neighbourliness".
In a post on X, Xu said China would work with India to follow the strategic guidance of the two leaders, view bilateral relations from a strategic and long-term perspective, step up communication, enhance cooperation and properly handle differences.
"China will work with India to act on the strategic guidance of the two leaders, handle the bilateral relations from a strategic height and long-term perspective, step up communication, enhance cooperation, properly handle differences, and be friends enjoying good-neighborliness and partners helping each other succeed," Xu said.
THIRD STRAIGHT YEAR OF XI-MODI MEETING
Xu said the proposed meeting would mark the third consecutive year in which Xi and Modi meet, following their meetings in Kazan and Tianjin.
Xi is scheduled to arrive in New Delhi on Saturday to attend the 18th BRICS Summit and hold bilateral talks with Modi on the sidelines. The visit will be Xi's first trip to India in nearly seven years.
CHINA STRESSES COMMUNICATION, COOPERATION
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning also said Beijing was ready to work with India to act on the strategic guidance of the two leaders and handle bilateral relations from a strategic and long-term perspective.
Mao said the two countries should step up communication, enhance cooperation and properly handle their differences. She described China and India as "friends enjoying good neighbourliness and partners helping each other succeed".
The proposed talks come against the backdrop of efforts by India and China to maintain high-level engagement despite differences over bilateral issues.
BRICS SUMMIT AMID GLOBAL CONFLICTS
Mao also said China was ready to work with BRICS countries to settle disputes through dialogue and negotiation and contribute to peace and stability amid the Iran-US conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war.
She said BRICS had emerged as a key platform for emerging markets and developing countries and had become "a real force standing at the forefront of the Global South".
India, as the current chair of BRICS, is hosting the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12 and 13.
Xi last visited India in 2019 for an informal summit with Modi in Mamallapuram near Chennai. He had earlier travelled to Goa for the BRICS summit in 2016 and made his first visit to India in September 2014.

When Sidhartha Bandha’s 63-year-old father suffered a stroke, the hospital did what it was supposed to do: it saved his life. But when he came back home, another struggle began.
His father could no longer do things on his own. The doctors told the family that rehabilitation and physiotherapy were important for his recovery. But the physiotherapy service available to them was far away. For a family dependent on daily earnings, travelling repeatedly for treatment meant spending money on transport, losing working days and managing the difficulty of moving a person who could barely move independently.
The family eventually had to give up on regular rehabilitation. Over time, Sidhartha’s father developed contractures, a condition in which muscles and joints become stiff and shortened when a person remains immobile for a long period. Sitting, standing, changing position and doing everyday activities can become a struggle.
Sidhartha remembers a different life for his father, a life where he worked in the fields and helped with household chores. His father was alive now, his life saved. But what kind of a life was it?
Where should healthcare end?
If a person survives a stroke but cannot regain the ability to move, work, participate in family life or live with some independence because rehabilitation was out of reach, is it fair to say that the job of healthcare was completed?
There is no doubt that acute medical care saves lives. But saving a life is only the first part of recovery. Rehabilitation helps a person live the life that has been saved in the way they want to.
In India, while a lot of attention has been rightfully given to improving emergency and critical care, far less has been given to what happens to patients after they leave a hospital. Physiotherapy and rehabilitation are crucial components of recovering after a number of conditions, including damage to the nervous system, heart disease and orthopaedic injuries. The question before the country today, however, is: how many people can physiotherapists actually reach?
What India needs
Global organisation World Physiotherapy’s profile of the Indian Association of Physiotherapists estimates 52,000 practising physiotherapists in India, equivalent to only 0.36 physiotherapists per 10,000 people, whereas, for instance, several countries in Europe have over 10 per 10,000 people.
The number tells only part of the story. The more important question is where these physiotherapists are and how many people each one can realistically reach. Are they available close to the homes of people living in rural areas? Can a person from a low-income family receive regular treatment that can last from days to months without spending a large part of the family’s income on travel and treatment?
The problem, therefore, is two-fold: there are not enough physiotherapists, and those that are available are not able able to reach the people who need them.
And the need is enormous.
Physiotherapy is not limited to treating back pain or helping an injured athlete. It can make a meaningful difference to people recovering from stroke, heart disease, injury, surgery and many other conditions. It can help a person stand again, walk again, use an affected limb, improve balance, become physically active and return to everyday life.
With India’s growing burden of non-communicable diseases, including heart disease and stroke, the need for physiotherapy is increasing. Someone with heart disease may need help becoming physically active safely. An older person may need help maintaining strength and balance. A person recovering from an injury or surgery may need rehabilitation to return to work. For all of them, physiotherapy can be the bridge between being medically stable and becoming an active, functioning member of the family and community. But that bridge is often missing.
Strategies that can help
There are a number of measures that can help, ranging from policy change to simple steps hospitals can take.
A model that has worked is community-based learning. This model gives physiotherapy students opportunities to work in rural and underserved communities and understand the barriers people face in accessing rehabilitation. Students are encouraged to see these communities not just as places for academic postings, but as places where physiotherapists can build meaningful careers and take rehabilitation closer to people’s homes. It deserves wider attention across physiotherapy education and healthcare policy.
Another measure is to teach families how to safely continue simple rehabilitation at home. A physiotherapist does not have to be physically present for every exercise. Families can be shown how to help with safe movement, positioning, walking and everyday activities, while the physiotherapist checks progress and changes the programme when needed.
Technology can help too. Tele-rehabilitation cannot replace hands-on treatment when a person needs physical examination or direct treatment. But it can allow a physiotherapist to follow up, demonstrate exercises, answer questions and keep in touch with patients who find regular travel difficult.
India also needs to think about where physiotherapists work. If most opportunities are concentrated in large cities and private clinics, many people who need rehabilitation will continue to be left behind. Students should have meaningful opportunities to work in villages, smaller towns, primary healthcare centres and underserved communities -- not as an afterthought, but as an important part of the profession.
It is high time we treated physiotherapy as an important component of lifesaving care, not as an optional service tacked on after the treatment. No one should be left unable to move simply because rehabilitation was too far away or too expensive.
(Dr. Shakeeb Ahmed Khan is a physiotherapist & disability and development professional khan.shakeebahmed@gmail.com; Dr. Christianez Ratna Kiruba is an internal medicine physician and a freelance health journalist based in Guwahati, Assam. christianezdennis@gmail.com)

At least 44 people injured after train derails in northern France
Police say train came off tracks between Rouen and Caen after striking unidentified object
At least 44 people were injured, one critically, after a passenger train derailed in Normandy, northern France, on Friday evening.
The incident occurred at around 7.30pm local time along the line running between Rouen and Caen, according to French authorities and the national railway operator.
The critically injured passengers were evacuated to hospital by helicopter, head of the local authority, the prefect, Jean-Benoit Albertini, told reporters. A French police spokesperson stated that the train came off the tracks after striking an unidentified object.
The service was carrying 180 passengers when it left the rails near the town of Cleon, French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said in a post on X. He added that 140 firefighters were deployed to the scene to assist the injured and remaining travellers.
Rail company SNCF confirmed an investigation was underway to determine the cause of the accident.
Meanwhile, the prefecture of Seine-Maritime advised the public to avoid the area.
Train services between Rouen and Caen, as well as Caen and Le Havre, were suspended, with replacement buses put in place.

Benn defies concerns to make weight for Garcia bout
- Published
Conor Benn and Ryan Garcia both comfortably made the welterweight limit for their WBC title fight despite concerns at how they would fare on the scales.
Briton Benn, 29, weighed in at 10st 6lb (66kg) for Saturday's bout - half a pound heavier than the champion.
The official weigh-in took place behind closed doors at the UFC Apex on Friday, in front of about 50 members of the media, before a ceremonial event later in the day which will be open to the public.
Garcia has won 25 of his 28 professional contests, including 20 knockout victories, with two defeats and one no-contest. Benn has 25 wins - 14 by knockout - and one loss, and is fighting for his first world title.
American Garcia, 28, won the WBC belt with a dominant points victory over Mario Barrios in February and is making his first defence against Benn.
- Eggs, insults & a champion with a fake beard - Garcia and Benn face off 
  - Published18 hours ago
- Why Nigel Benn can't walk away from Conor 
  - Published22 hours ago
- Benn does not deserve world title shot - Garcia 
  - Published1 day ago
How did they look?
Much of the build-up this week has centred on how Benn would cope with returning to the 10st 7lb welterweight limit for the first time in more than four years.
His two fights against Chris Eubank Jr were both at middleweight, with Benn weighing 11st 2lb (71kg) for the first and 11st 5lb (72kg) for the rematch. For his win over Regis Prograis in April, Benn weighed 10st 10lb (69kg).
He has already said he will vacate the title and move back up in weight if he beats Garcia.
Benn had looked increasingly gaunt and drawn during fight week and told BBC Sport the cut had taken him to the "pits of hell".
But Benn smiled as his weight was announced and looked in good shape, surprising several observers who had expected the effects of the cut to be far more visible.
A handful of undercard fighters weighed in after Benn while Garcia was still nowhere to be seen, prompting questions about whether the Californian was having difficulties making the limit.
Garcia has had problems on the scales before. He weighed more than three pounds over the light-welterweight limit before his fight against Devin Haney in 2024.
There was no such drama this time. Garcia sprinted towards the scales about 10 minutes after Benn and also looked at ease as he comfortably made weight.
Why does the weight matter?
The weight is particularly significant because of the contrasting styles.
Benn relies heavily on aggression, explosiveness and sustained pressure, while Garcia is a fast and dangerous counter-puncher who is comfortable catching opponents as they come forward.
Any draining effects of the cut could therefore leave Benn more vulnerable to Garcia's speed and powerful left hook, while also raising questions over whether the Briton can maintain his usual intensity over 12 rounds.
With no rehydration clause in place, Benn said he could weigh as much as 12st 7lb (80kg) by the time he steps into the ring on Saturday.
He is still an underdog against Garcia - a fighter with greater amateur pedigree and a more accomplished professional resume - but Benn's size and physical pressure could become one of his biggest advantages.

UEFA urged a U.S. court on Thursday to reject an attempt by FIFA’s American subsidiaries to intervene in its bid to obtain evidence for a potential Swiss criminal case against FIFA President Gianni Infantino over his abandoned World Cup commercial-rights plan.
In a filing in Manhattan federal court, European football’s governing body said FIFA (Americas) Inc and FWC2026 US Inc were improperly trying to act as stand-ins for FIFA and Infantino, neither of whom has sought to join the case.
UEFA said its request under a U.S. discovery law seeks documents and testimony from Thrive Capital Management and its founder Joshua Kushner, who it says may hold information about the proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise transaction.
The plan, which Infantino withdrew on August 1 after a backlash from football bodies and other critics, envisaged selling a permanent stake in commercial and operational rights connected to the World Cup and other FIFA events to private investors.
UEFA CONSIDERING CRIMINAL COMPLAINT AGAINST INFANTINO
UEFA has said it is considering filing a criminal complaint in Switzerland alleging criminal mismanagement by Infantino and potentially other FIFA officials. Infantino and FIFA have not been charged with wrongdoing.
FIFA accused UEFA last week of running a “smear campaign” and characterized the discovery applications as a fishing expedition intended to damage FIFA and its leadership.
FIFA did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and Infantino has denied doing anything wrong.
In Thursday’s response, UEFA said the subsidiaries had no direct legal interest in the New York proceeding because they were not targets of the contemplated Swiss case and were not recipients of the proposed subpoenas.
RELATED | Will FIFA World Cup 2030 final be played in Morocco? Governing body responds
It said the confidentiality concerns cited by the U.S. subsidiaries belonged, if to anyone, to their Swiss parent, FIFA. UEFA also argued that Thrive and Kushner already have lawyers who can challenge any subpoenas after they are served.
Thrive did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Thrive founder Kushner is the brother of Jared Kushner, son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump.
UEFA said granting the subsidiaries a role before the court rules would depart from the usual process for requests under Section 1782, which are commonly granted initially without opposition and then tested through motions to quash.
The European body argued that the subsidiaries’ intervention would create unnecessary delay by adding another round of merits briefing before UEFA could seek the records.
The court has not yet ruled on either UEFA’s discovery application or the intervention motion.

Fears that modern electronic devices may harm children are nothing new. Gadgets with screens of any size have long been allegedly melting, rotting, and/or corrupting the brains of youths for decades. However, a medical case report published this week offers a new and alarming way our digital doodads may cause physical harm.
In BMJ Case Reports, two UK doctors, Mara Znagoveanu and Edward Artley, report the case of a boy who came to an emergency department with alarming marks on his abdomen. The marks were described as being in a patch about 15 centimeters (six inches) wide, made of flat, reddish-brown “interlacing lines forming irregular circles and a lace-like morphology.” A picture of the marks is here.
Mysterious marks
The boy, whom they described only as being in “mid-childhood,” was not in any pain, and the rash was not warm to the touch or tender. He and his parents said they couldn’t think of any recent injuries or trauma that might explain the marks. He was otherwise healthy, hadn’t recently been ill, and had no systemic symptoms, such as fever or fatigue. Everything about the boy’s health, growth, and medical history looked normal.
Nurses in the emergency department initially described it as “spontaneous bruising.” A physical exam yielded no insights; there were no other skin abnormalities, abdominal tenderness, or signs of organ trouble. They did a chest X-ray, searching for an explanation. It revealed a small patch of whiteness over his left lung, indicating cells or fluid, such as pus or blood.
As the doctors were taking blood for further testing, the boy told them that he did have one injury: About a week prior, around when the marks appeared, he was play-fighting with his siblings and got pushed into a chair. He said he didn’t mention it before because he didn’t want his siblings to get in trouble.
The new information pointed the doctors to the idea of an underlying traumatic injury. They did a computed tomography (CT) scan, looking for internal abdominal injuries. But they found none, besides the small blip in his lungs that the X-ray showed—which could have just been incidental from a minor infection.

In DUSU election, Satya Niketan building collapse, turns common cause for rivals
More than half of the students enrolled are estimated to require hostel accommodation. But the available official pool is only a measly 7,224 hostel beds.
The ramifications of the building collapse in South Delhi’s Satya Niketan that killed five students, will be a common thread running through rival campaigns for the Delhi University Students’ Union (DUSU) elections scheduled for September 18, representatives of students’ organisations said on Friday.
The organisations will demand steps to address the varsity’s chronic shortage of accommodation for students, as well as concerns over the safety of students and affordability of hostel rooms, these representatives said on a day they announced their candidates for the DUSU elections. The Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), National Students’ Union of India (NSUI), and the left alliance of All India Students’ Association (AISA) and Students’ Federation of India (SFI) will contest four DUSU posts in the election.
More than half of the university’s 251,474 students enrolled in conventional programmes are estimated to require hostel accommodation.
But the available official pool is only a measly 7,224 hostel beds. Students take refuge in hubs like Satya Niketan that have emerged due to this perennial problem, where relatively affordable options are limited to cramped, unsanitary rooms, often in rickety buildings that violate the rules.
The ABVP, which is aligned with the Bharatiya Janata Party that rules Delhi, said it would extend a campaign it had launched after the building collapse on September 6 to the DUSU polls.
It had sought the resignation of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi’s commissioner over the incident.
“The Satya Niketan incident has also brought the urgent need for safe PGs and student accommodation into focus. Through the ‘Aakhir Kab Tak?’ campaign and ‘No more Satya Niketan.in’ website, we are continuing to raise this issue. Our campaign will remain focused on genuine student concerns and finding practical solutions to them,” ABVP Delhi secretary Sarthak Sharma said.
Sharma told HT the ABVP’s manifesto will focus on how DU needs more hostel rooms. “We will raise this demand, apart from rent control of PGs and hostels, as well as audit of students’ accommodation by the MCD. We continue to demand the MCD commissioner’s resignation,” he added.
Rival NSUI, aligned with the opposition Congress, said their manifesto will “present a comprehensive vision for Delhi University – from affordable accommodation and better infrastructure to student safety, and academic opportunities.”
In a statement, NSUI’s national president Vinod Jhakar said, “The Satya Niketan tragedy has once again raised serious questions about student safety and institutional accountability. NSUI will continue to fight for justice and ensure that the voices of affected students and families are not ignored.”
NSUI national media incharge, Ravi Pandey, said his party will put pressure on the government and university to ensure compensation to the families of the victims of Satya Niketan, and adequate hostels for students.

“Our demands since the Satya Niketan incident have been clear– ₹1 crore compensation to the families of the victims by the government, and on-campus accommodation for the majority of students who come to DU from other states. These demands will be strongly reflected in our manifesto,” said Pandey.
AISA-SFI said they would carry forward the momentum built during the month-long Cockroach Janata Party protest at Jantar Mantar, while also taking up students’ concerns over the lack of adequate on-campus accommodation.
“This year’s DUSU elections are taking place against an unusual backdrop, marked by a series of major student-led movements and developments. These include the Cockroach Janta Party movement, which led to the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, as well as the Satya Niketan tragedy, which claimed the lives of seven students. Our key manifesto points include the rollback of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, improved campus infrastructure, and safer campuses for women. However, we are placing greater emphasis on ensuring accessible hostel accommodation for all students, conducting structural safety audits in student hubs such as Kamla Nagar and Malkaganj, and introducing a rent-control law for these areas,” said DU AISA secretary Anjali.
ABVP fielded Yash Dabas for President, Ishu Maurya for Vice-President, Riya Chhawadi for Secretary, and Lakshya Raj Singh for Joint Secretary.
NSUI’s candidates for the four central panel posts are Vijay Shankar Meena for President, Vir Chatrath for Vice-President, Namrata Choudhary for Secretary, and Gopal Choudhary for Joint Secretary.
AISA-SFI has announced a joint panel for the DUSU elections, fielding Ananya Raturi (AISA) for President, Akshat Shikhar (AISA) for Vice-President, Stanzin Deskyong (SFI) for Secretary, and B. Parijaat (SFI) for Joint Secretary.
As campaigning is set to intensify, DU Proctor Manoj Kumar Singh said the university would step up its oversight of election activities.
“So far, the campaign has largely remained free of any major violations. But with a week left before polling, stricter scrutiny will begin to ensure that the campaign remains clean and safe,” he said.

Can Trump really pay $5,000 to every American adult?
- Published
US President Donald Trump has offered every adult American $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win November's midterm elections, but it is unclear how such a plan would be funded and whether it is legal.
His remarks prompted raucous applause from supporters at a party convention on Wednesday night, but Democrats labelled it an "empty promise".
Trump also told the Republican conference that the money would have to be spent in the US, but it is unclear how that would be monitored.
The US president has given no details on how it would be funded, though Vice-President JD Vance suggested it might be paid for by tariff revenue and that such cheques would not go to wealthy Americans.
Is Trump's offer legal?
Under US federal law, it is illegal to give payments that are intended to influence the way a person is voting.
However, some experts have said the offer made by Trump in Texas on Wednesday could be seen as a pledge to cut taxes, which is legal.
Dr Joan Mahoney, lecturer in law at the University of Southampton, told the BBC she thought the offer would be legal as it would be similar to a campaign promise - though she said politicians "don't usually do it quite this explicitly".
"On the one hand it sounds a bit like a bribe, vote for the Republicans and you'll get money, which would be decidedly illegal," she said.
"But on the other hand it would go to everyone, regardless of how they voted so it isn't in that sense a bribe.
"I think it would be legal. It's the same kind of campaign pledge as saying 'if my party wins we'll reduce taxes'. Every party does that all the time... and that's obviously perfectly legal."
However, Laurel Rapp, director of the US and North America programme at Chatham House, told the BBC that Trump's offer seemed to be "a very different, very transactional agreement" from the kind of promise usually made by candidates in an election period.
How much would it cost?
Aside from the question of legality, some have also asked whether Trump's offer would be feasible financially in the context of increasing US debt, partially as a result of the war in Iran.
There are nearly 270 million American adults, meaning a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.
Trump gave no details on how such cheques would be funded.
Congress authorises spending in the US, but the president did not say whether he planned to ask for legislative approval for any payments.
And legal experts said it was unlikely he could approve such a vast sum via a presidential executive order.
Erica York, a senior economist at the Washington DC-based Tax Foundation, told the BBC she would be "extremely surprised" if Congress approved any proposal.
"This would be one of the worst ways to use $1.3 trillion," she said.
"We're on a very unsustainable track, with deficits only projected to grow and grow," York added.
Could tariff revenue fund it?
Speaking to Fox News after Trump's speech, Vice-President Vance indicated that the payments could be funded by money raised by the president from tariffs.
However, such revenue to date falls far short of the money that would be needed to account for Trump's $5,000 cheques offer.
According to the Bipartisan Policy Center, the US has brought in around $475bn in tariff and excise tax revenue since the beginning of 2025.
But more than $100bn has been refunded after the Supreme Court struck down many tariffs earlier this year.
When asked how the payouts could work, the White House said in a statement to the BBC: "The doomers and naysayers have consistently doubted President Trump."
"With the continued support of the American people, President Trump will keep delivering real results," added spokesman Davis Ingle.

Why has Trump made the offer?
One former Republican strategist and pollster said Trump's latest offer should be firmly seen in the context of an election that is now less than two months away.
"It is an extraordinary promise, and I'm not sure where that money is going to come from - but it is campaign season," Robert Moran told the BBC.
Chatham House's Rapp said Trump was thinking short term to try to keep hold of Congress as he enters the final two years of his term in office.
"Money is something that he is now resorting to because the polling is not looking good for Republicans and the polling is not looking good for him," she continued.
Has anything similar happened before?
Trump has previously proposed $2,000 cheques to be funded by tariff revenues, but those payouts have not materialised.
Former President Joe Biden was accused of buying votes when he promised $2,000 Covid stimulus cheques for Americans if two Democratic candidates in Georgia would win election to the US Senate in January 2021.
A similar issue of legality came to the fore ahead of the 2024 presidential election, during which billionaire Trump supporter Elon Musk offered cash incentives to registered voters in seven swing states who signed a certain petition.
