Fintech company stocks — Paytm, Pine Labs, Mobikwik and AvenuesAI — rallied today amid reports suggesting that the merchant discount rate (MDR) fees on UPI transactions could soon be notified. Pine Labs’ stock surged the most, jumping 16.9% to close the day at ₹202.35 on the BSE. Mobikwik climbed just over 8% to close at ₹209.80, while AvenuesAI jumped 6.1% to ₹16.31. Meanwhile, shares of Paytm ended today’s trading session 3.9% higher at ₹1,806.25. The stock jumped as much as 5.2% during intraday trade to touch a fresh all-time high of ₹1,829.50. The rally came after reports earlier in the day suggested that MDR fees on UPI payments are likely to be set at around 40 basis points (bps), or 0.4%, of the transaction value. This comes around a month after the Centre amended the Payment and Settlement Systems Act (PSSA), 2007, to remove a blanket prohibition barring banks and system providers from charging fees on UPI payments. MDR is likely to be charged on P2M transactions only and exclude P2P transactions, with a turnover-based threshold to ensure that only merchants with an annual turnover of around ₹1 Cr-₹1.5 Cr or more. There may be differential fees for businesses across sectors, as was earlier reported. Third-party application providers (TPAPs) – UPI apps – would receive roughly 30% of the MDR, or 12 bps of the transaction value, as per an Economic Times report earlier today. The proposal would unlock a revenue stream of around ₹5,000-10,000 Cr for payments platforms like the four aforementioned companies, brokerage Jefferies had said earlier in a research note. It must be noted that the brokerage firm had estimated a slightly lower MDR of 15-30 bps on transactions above ₹2,000 in its calculations. “Assuming 25% CAGR in value of P2M over FY26-28, we estimate the revenue pool could be about ₹5,000-10,000 Cr in FY28 (estimated),” said Jefferies. As a result, Paytm’s FY28 EBITDA and profit could grow around 15-35% while Pine Labs’ FY28 EBIT and profit could jump 9-23% in this scenario, per the brokerage’s estimates. Another brokerage, Bernstein, had previously projected that Paytm could add ₹1,320 Cr to its EBITDA in the case of 35 bps MDR on a subset of UPI transactions. “We estimate MDR will apply to~50% of transaction value and that Paytm can realise ~3-4bps of incremental net payments margin, translating into ₹2,200 Cr of incremental EBITDA by FY30 (estimated),” it noted. However, Jefferies had raised a question around slippage between the notified MDR rate and the earned take-rate in the event that competition to onboard merchants intensified among payments platforms.

One rural hospital offers hope amid nationwide rural maternity ward closures
When Nikki Johnson heard Mayo Clinic Health System was closing its labor and delivery unit at her local clinic in Fairmont, Minnesota, she was shocked. It was 2024, and she was 33 weeks pregnant. Instead of giving birth in her small rural town, she was suddenly faced with having to drive to Mayo's Mankato clinic about an hour away when she went into labor.
"I asked the doctor, so what happens if I go into labor and it goes pretty fast and I have to pull over on the side of the road on the way to Mankato?" Johnson recalled. "I was like, that would be terrifying. Giving birth is scary to begin with."
Johnson's experience isn't unique. Labor and delivery units have been closing across the state and the nation in recent years. The latest data from the University of Minnesota Rural Health Research Center shows that in 2010, 56% of U.S. counties had at least one hospital with obstetrics services. 14 years later, that dropped by 9% — almost 300 counties had lost hospital-based obstetrics services and rural areas had been hardest hit.
Labor and delivery units require 24/7 staffing since births can happen at any time. That makes it expensive. Rural hospitals see more low-income patients on Medicaid, which offers lower reimbursement, and they see fewer births, so labor and delivery units rarely pay for themselves. They tend to have fewer resources for simulation training and telemedicine support.
Katy Kozhimannil, co-director of the Rural Health Research Center, said when rural units close, it can make giving birth more dangerous.
"Certainly in rural areas, for every hospital that closes its obstetric unit or closes entirely, the nearest place to give birth gets further and further away, and that distance is associated with poor outcomes for moms and for babies," Kozhimannil explained.
She said many pregnant people are forced to give birth in under-resourced rural emergency rooms, in ambulances, or even on the side of the road, leading to more instances of pre-term birth and infant mortality.
Bucking the trend
However, there's one rural hospital birthing center that is thriving, and its success could offer a template for others. Minnesota's United Hospital District runs a small critical access hospital and three clinics in rural counties. Johnson gave birth to her daughter Sylvie at the hospital. It's located in Blue Earth, Minnesota. 3,000 people live in the town and the hospital is the only one in the county.
"We're the last one here," said United Hospital District CEO Richard Ash. "If we're not doing OB, there's a big desert here, and there's a lot of people that are going to either have to move or take the risk."
Ash said during much of his time leading the hospital, about 50 babies a year were born at the facility in Blue Earth. However, since 2020 there's been an increase every year and in 2025, they delivered 178 babies. He said the hospital's on track to follow suit this year.
Ash says has United Health District implemented a few different tactics to remain open. It joined Headwaters, a clinically integrated network of rural hospitals in Minnesota. That gave the hospital more negotiating power in purchasing supplies and allowed them to lower other costs. The hospital is also able to offset financial losses in labor and delivery by providing other services, like outpatient surgery, that bring in more money.
UHD's Chief Medical Officer Aaron Johnson said cross training is also crucial to balancing the hospital's budget.
"The biggest thing, I think, that allows us to keep our head above water, is that people can do multiple things," Johnson said. "If our labor and delivery staff were just L&D nurses it wouldn't work. There's no way it would work."
Building close relationships with patients is key
Maija Whitefeather Manning and her husband chose to give birth to both their sons in Blue Earth instead of other larger hospital system affiliates nearby because of the rave reviews she heard from her colleagues.
"I mean, we live in a world of technology, right?" Whitefeather Manning said. "And you can look at reviews, and you can read all these things. But also, when you live in a small community, what people say is true and has a lot of weight."
Both Whitefeather Manning and Johnson said they feel heard and understood at the Blue Earth hospital. They also recalled little homey touches that stood out: seasonally-inspired baby hats crocheted by church volunteers in town; the gift basket the hospital sent them home with; and a special multi-course meal for the new parents during their last night at the hospital.
"They gave us a little menu, it was like, steak or chicken breast and dessert and a bottle of sparkling grape juice," Johnson said jokingly that was not the sort of thing she'd come to expect with hospital care. "Like they are not setting up a little romantic meal for you and your husband."
Kozhimannil, co-director of the Rural Health Research Center said the hospital's strategy is a textbook example of what some rural hospitals are doing in order to succeed. And staying open and building capacity to serve more patients is crucial to improving the delivery of health care in rural areas.
For many of those who work at United Hospital District, the commitment to keeping the labor and delivery unit open feels personal.
"I mean for us, these are our neighbors," chief medical officer Aaron Johnson said. "These are our family members. These are the people that we go to church with, go to school with, go to football games with. We want to provide the best care for them."

On food labelling and misleading claims, weight loss drugs, climate change, rabies, cancer care, and more
(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Ramya Kannan writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
This past week, as with the previous week, the nation continues to be concerned with food labelling. With the Supreme Court bringing up the packaged food labelling issue up again, a couple of weeks ago, it has been surely and firmly dragged into the public platform. There has been a great deal of interest in the Food Safety and Standards Association of India’s recommendations on front-of-pack labels, and debate about the merits of the case.
What are these standards that FSSAI promises to hold the packaged food in India up to? We took a long,hard look.
For an idea of what the whole FSSAI submission on labelling was, initially, check out this conversation between Zubeda Hamid and I; we also indicate trends worldwide, in Sunday’s Health Wrap video. While appreciable that some standards have come to play in this entirely unregulated sector, there are questions about the caveats in the proposed recommendations. FSSAI has proposed that the warning initially apply to products high in two or more of the three “nutrients of concern” — added sugar, added saturated fat and salt — as well as specified highly sweetened beverages. Activists find the “two or more” classification problematic.
For a more detailed explanation on what the Red hexagon on your snack pack means, read what Bindu Shajan Perappadan wrote. FSSAI has proposed a two-phase rollout. In the first phase, products high in at least two of the three nutrients would carry the red hexagon, along with specified highly sweetened beverages. In the second phase, the warning would extend to products high in any one of the three nutrients. However, FSSAI has not specified a firm timeline for moving to the second phase. The FSSAI proposal refers to added sugar and added saturated fat, rather than total sugar and total fat. The plan is to exempt single-ingredient foods and products inherently rich in these nutrients, including ghee, edible oil, jaggery and honey.
Meanwhile, Soibam Rocky Singh explains why the Central Consumer Protection Authority is cracking down on ‘100%’ claims on food products. Such claims can give consumers an impression of absolute purity or completeness that may not match what is actually inside the packet. The FSSAI has also asked food businesses to stop using “100%” claims on food labels, packaging and promotional material.
Here, Prabalika M. Borah examines the hype behind Proffee: protien+coffee, and here are the highlights of an ICMR-NIN study which shows that Vitamin D3 outperforms D2 in supporting muscles and heart.
Close on the nutrition topic is weight loss drugs. A recent study showed that GLP-1 weight loss drugs are effective even at low starter doses, with lower side effects. Yet another study in the United States showed that more children under 12 in U.S. are being prescribed weight-loss drugs. Prescriptions for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs among children under 12 in the U.S. have risen more than 300-fold since 2019.
Here is a supervised experiment of a fitness coaching putting himself through a GLP 1 course, recording minute observations through the course. Arvind Ashok writes: ‘I’m a fitness coach. I tried a GLP-1 drug for three weeks’, issuing a statutory warning to readers not to attempt the same at home without a prescription.

Mumbai man used ChatGPT to fake PMO ID ‘to boost social standing’, police tell court
Police told the court that multiple forged English-language documents linked to the PMO were recovered during a search of Parikh's residence.
AI tool ChatGPT was allegedly used to create fake PMO credentials and official documents by a 24-year-old man arrested after claiming to be a Prime Minister's Office official during a confrontation with security guards at a luxury mall in Mumbai on Monday.
The police submitted while opposing bail for Rohan Parikh and his associate Dilip Kunde, 49, at the end of their custodial remand, PTI reported.
Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate D S Khedekar of the Esplanade Court rejected the police's plea for further custody and sent both accused to 14 days in judicial custody.
The duo subsequently moved a bail application, arguing that their further detention was unwarranted and served no purpose.
Also Read: Man claiming to be PMO official, ‘bodyguard’ with gun arrested in Mumbai
Fake PMO documents
Police told the court that multiple forged English-language documents linked to the PMO were recovered during a search of Parikh's residence. Police said the documents were created using ChatGPT.
"Parikh has confessed to fabricating the fake PMO ID and related official documents using ChatGPT since 2025 to elevate his social standing and boost his self-esteem within his family and social circles," the police said in their remand application.
The police also said data extracted from Parikh's phone showed a search history related to drafting PMO correspondence. They sought further custody to investigate whether he had used the forged PMO identity card or documents at any other locations.
Police also highlighted the role of Kunde, a former Army personnel, from whom a revolver was allegedly recovered. Investigators said Kunde admitted that the weapon, which he claimed was for personal use, was being used commercially while he worked as a professional bodyguard for Parikh.
Advocate Satish Maneshinde, appearing for both accused, argued that they had already confessed to preparing the documents themselves and that no third party was involved.
Maneshinde told the court that police had already seized the accused's mobile phones, laptop and various other documents, leaving nothing further to be recovered. "Nothing further remains to be seized from the accused," he argued.
After hearing both sides, the court held that the grounds cited in the remand report did not justify extending police custody and sent Parikh and Kunde to judicial custody.
What happened at Mumbai mall
The incident took place on September 7 at Jio World Plaza in Mumbai's Bandra-Kurla Complex (BKC), a day before Prime Minister Narendra Modi was scheduled to attend an event at the adjacent Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre for the Global Fintech Fest 2026.
Parikh was arrested after he was found carrying a fake PMO card. Kunde, who was accompanying him, was allegedly carrying a firearm, leading to an argument between the two men and mall security staff.
During the confrontation, Parikh allegedly claimed that he was a PMO official.
Police later clarified that the incident had no connection with the prime minister's scheduled event the following day.

The Supreme Court on Thursday (September 10, 2026) refused to entertain a PIL raising concerns over the government-run nationwide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign for adolescent girls to prevent cervical cancer.
A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana said whenever there is a case of incorrect vaccination, ordinary rules of compensation will apply.
"Would you like to withdraw? Do you want us to comment something?" the Bench observed.
"Don't ask us to make harsh observations. If petitioner members are doctors, it's a very very serious issue. It's a question of health of millions of our daughters. And you want to derail this," it said.
The top court orally said that the PIL was filed with an ulterior motive and lacked bonafide.
The lawyer appearing for the petitioner said that he was only pressing on adverse events and compensation, nothing on HPV.
"I am not at all anti-vaccine. My first contention is the way it is being implemented. Second, there is no adverse event mechanism. Whenever there is an adverse event, it must be monitored. There should also be a compensation scheme," the lawyer said.
When the apex court refused to entertain the plea, the counsel withdrew the plea and the matter was dismissed as withdrawn.
The top court was hearing a plea filed by the Universal Health Organisation challenging the manner in which the government-backed HPV vaccination programme is being implemented.
The plea alleged that it violates constitutional guarantees of informed consent, bodily autonomy, transparency and accountability.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the nationwide HPV vaccination campaign for 14-year-old girls from Ajmer in Rajasthan on February 28.
A single-dose Gardasil 4 vaccine, a quadrivalent HPV vaccine, is being used under the campaign. The injection provides protection against HPV types 16 and 18, which are responsible for cervical cancer, as well as types 6 and 11.

Quick Answer
Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, could give the stagnant foldable market a much-needed push. It may not reinvent the category, but Apple’s reach, software focus, and mainstream appeal could make foldables far more popular.
September is here and so are the new iPhones. This year at Apple’s Surprise and Shine event, the Cupertino tech giant came with a number of changes, not just in terms of devices but in terms of management too. There was a new CEO – it was John Ternus’ first event as CEO – as well as new Apple Watches, AirPods and, of course, new iPhones too.
The Duo dominates the new iPhones
Even though Apple showcases a number of products during its September event, it is mainly the iPhones that the world waits for. And even in iPhones, it is usually the Pro and Pro Max iPhones that make the headlines (barring the odd occasion when the Air popped up). The plain iPhones are usually pushed to the sidelines and launched as the more “economical”, “affordable” iPhones whose price tags and generally minor upgrades in specs and design are the only things that get them any attention.
For the longest time, we have been feeling for the plain iPhones because they are quite capable and bring in big sales numbers (especially in markets like India, where they are bestsellers) and yet do not get the hype they deserve. Well, this time around, the iPhone Pro and the Pro Max got the taste of this bitter medicine. The two smartphones had to fold (pun intended) and give up all their headline space for the more expensive, exclusive, and most different iPhone since the inception of the original iPhone: the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone.
With the iPhone Duo, Apple has finally marked its official entry in the world of foldables. It comes with a starting price of Rs. 299,900 in India ($1,999 in the US), which has naturally inspired a tsunami of reinvented kidney jokes and all sorts of comparisons about all that you can buy for that price. It has also got many competing brands scoffing at Apple’s very late attempt at foldables, calling the Duo a “copy”. While some of the criticism and cynicism around the Duo is valid, we think a foldable phone from Apple is just what the foldable market needed to make foldables mainstream. Not because the Duo is an out-of-the-tech-world, never-seen-before, and extraordinary folding smartphone (hey, we haven’t reviewed it yet), but for much simpler reasons.
Ghost of foldables past: A story mainly of Samsung
Samsung is considered by many to be the modern foldable phone pioneer. It was the trailblazer that was responsible for actually bringing in foldable phones that not only landed on the tech moon but also managed to stick around for seven2 years – Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold arrived in 2019, followed by the Galaxy Z Flip in 2020. The brand did not really have a working blueprint that they could have used back then to have perfected their foldables and technology around it, but it enjoyed an early mover’s advantage in the segment and managed to create a very strong reputation for itself. They built a strong rapport with the consumers that none of the other brands could develop, even after launching just as good, just as powerful foldable smartphones.
Following Samsung’s start, many leading tech brands have been surfing the foldable wave for a while now. The OG flip phone master, Motorola; the Android originator Google; the flagship killer OnePlus; the Chinese Apple, Xiaomi; Vivo, Oppo, and others have created foldables with their own touches and twists. Huawei has gone one step further and has launched a tri-fold – a smartphone that folds twice. But even after all this effort, none of them could really be a standout foldable smartphone brand. Only Samsung did.
But in spite of Samsung’s consistency and the efforts of other brands, foldable smartphones have not become mainstream. They have never really made impressive numbers or become popular/common devices. Yes, most of them come with premium price tags, but even those that are relatively affordable – mostly flips or budget foldables (yes, there are some) – have not gained the kind of traction that had been expected. The foldable revolution that many had predicted seemed to have stalled, and apart from a few devices (mainly from Samsung), growth was largely limited.
Apple and the tech snowball effect… could it come to foldables?
Now Apple has stepped into the foldable ring, and while there are many contenders in it already, we think the Cupertino tech giant might get the buzz around foldables going. It has been quite a trend setter in the tech world, and is identified with premium innovation. Features, functions, and devices that existed long before Apple “reinvented” them suddenly became popular once they started shipping with an Apple logo and Apple’s own unique take on them. They not only became mainstream but also often became a common sight on products from other brands as well. Touchscreen phones, apps and app stores, music stores, portrait mode, notches (Dynamic Island), are just some of the products that Apple did not invent, but made a part of
everyday technology.
Of course, every time this happens, the Internet is flooded with techies pointing out how the particular feature or product has been around for years and how Apple is not really innovating or, rather, thinking differently (Apple’s very tagline). Despite all the chatter and gossip around this topic, somehow the feature picks up momentum, and soon enough the world gets interested in knowing how it works and then owning a device that lets them use it. This initiates a snowball effect of sorts, which leads to that feature or device becoming extremely popular.
We will keep it simple: quite often, it basically takes an Apple device or feature to grab mainstream attention. It happened with GUI, MP3 players, ultra-portable notebooks, touchscreen phones, tablets, TWS, smartwatches, and we think it could happen with foldables too. The Duo has the potential to put the seemingly jammed foldable wheels in motion.
It is important to remember that it is not like whatever Apple does just becomes a hit automatically. The brand has a loyal following, but it has released many features, devices, and functions that did not strike a chord with consumers and have faded away. The Apple Vision Pro, HomePod, iPhone Mini and iPhone Plus, the Touch Bar on the Mac…Apple’s failure list is quite long. It may be one of the most successful tech brands in history, but Apple is no tech Midas – there is no real guarantee that the iPhone Duo would be an absolute hit. The stakes are quite high for the Duo, especially given its price tag (which is even higher in India).
It has got the hype, but what would make the Duo click?
Unlike Samsung, Apple has not had to reinvent the foldable wheel. It has had time to read, research, develop, try, and make mistakes, and fix them all, even while observing the efforts of other tech brands. And while the Duo’s design and specs, and indeed, many of its features, are nothing we have not seen before, these are not areas where Apple differentiates itself from the regular crowd. The iPhone Duo needs to bring Apple’s attention to detail when it comes to user experience, and software tuned exactly to suit the needs and capabilities of the device it supports.
We have not yet had the pleasure (or pain) to experience the device but so far, from the looks and the videos on the Internet, we can tell you there are a few things we love about the iPhone Duo – the TouchID on the side (yes, we actually love it), the vertical tool bar for easy access, the matte display layer which makes the crease largely invisible, and yes, of course, the animation that blurs out the side/front screen when the phone is being opened or folded. But it’s not all pink skies and red roses. We are not very convinced by the asymmetrical shape of the device, the insanely high price tag, and, well, even the name. Duo? Really, Apple? We are also really curious about how Apple has worked on apps for the cover display as well as the inner ones.
But these are early days. The iPhone Duo is more than a month away, and we are sure Apple will fine-tune it even further before releasing it. In the meantime, we expect the kidney jokes to continue and even gather momentum, but on the flip side, curiosity will also grow, as we are sure more will be revealed about the device and its features and functions.
The iPhone Duo has generated more buzz about the foldables in a few months than other players in the field got in years, but it is all going to boil down to how well and how differently it works from other foldables. Given the interest levels around it, it might just prove to be the elixir that foldables need.

UK lawmakers reject bill to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales
The bill had proposed allowing adults with fewer than six months to live to apply for an assisted death, subject to approval
UK lawmakers on Friday voted down legislation to allow terminally ill adults in England and Wales to choose to end their lives.
The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill was opposed by 286 members of parliament, while 270 voted for it.
The vote brings an end to a two-year debate in parliament about assisted dying.
On two previous occasions in 2024 and 2025, the elected House of Commons had backed the bill, but it did not become law because it was effectively filibustered by unelected lawmakers in the revising House of Lords chamber.
The bill had proposed allowing adults in England and Wales, with fewer than six months to live, to apply for an assisted death subject to the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.
The government took a neutral stance, saying it was a matter of conscience.
The new UK leader, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, did not vote because he said he did not want to “unduly influence the debate”.

Iranian media: Houthis take control of Strait of Mandeb after seizing Mayyun Island
Yemen’s Houthis control the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait after seizing Mayyun Island, also known as Perim Island, Iran’s Tasnim News Agency reported.
Located at the centre of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, Mayyun Island is a key monitoring point overlooking the vital maritime passage.
Two Yemeni sources also told Reuters that Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces had withdrawn from Perim Island.
The development came after Houthis seized the western coastal city of Mocha, forcing the government forces to retreat toward the south and the city of Dhubab.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree was also reported as saying that navigation in the Red Sea was safe except for Saudi ships, suggesting the group now has control over the Strait of Mandeb.
Known as the "Gate of Tears" in Arabic, because of its history of shipwrecks, the strait sits at the southern tip of the Red Sea, connecting it with the Gulf of Aden in the Indian Ocean.
About 100 kilometres long and just 30 kilometres wide at its narrowest point, it separates Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula from Djibouti and Eritrea on the Horn of Africa.
With the Red Sea linking maritime trade between Europe and Asia, the strait is usually one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
Oil tankers and cargo ships use it to reach the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal, shortening journeys between Asia and Europe and North America by thousands of kilometres (miles).
In 2024, as the Houthis attacked Red Sea shipping during the Gaza war, Suez Canal traffic fell sharply and has yet to recover, according to IMF PortWatch data analysed by AFP.
Total transits dropped from 26,895 vessels in 2023, or 73.7 per day, to 14,498 in 2024 and 14,070 in 2025, AFP reported.

The bodies of passengers killed in a ferry fire off the Philippines arrived at a port near the resort town of Coron, Palawan, on Saturday morning, as the country’s coast guard warned the death toll of 35 would grow.
Tents were being set up to receive 30 bodies brought from the M/V June Aster, which ran aground near the tourist hotspot after a fire erupted on Wednesday evening and tore through the vessel “in seconds”.
Coast guard spokesperson Noemie Cayabyab told a Saturday press conference the remains would be turned over to police forensic investigators for “proper disposition and identification” before allowing local authorities to inform family members.
“Currently, we are focused on the retrieval, and after that we will proceed with the investigation,” she said, confirming the bodies had been found in the ship’s economy accommodation area.
Police investigators were seen arriving at the port shortly after the press conference ended.
Asked how many bodies remained aboard the ship, she said authorities would provide an update later in the day.
Cayabyab told AFP on Friday evening that the first transfer had been capped at 30 bodies because of the capacity of the patrol vessel transporting them and that additional cadavers remained on the ferry.
Five others had been confirmed dead in the immediate wake of the fire.
Photos released by the coast guard showed rows of body bags being placed into a small ship alongside men in hazmat suits. Thirty passengers and 13 crew have so far been rescued, while 54 people remain unaccounted for.
On Friday, Cayabyab had told a radio station the fire had begun in the cargo hold, then tore through the ship within seconds.
“From the time that they heard the loud explosion, the appearance of smoke, and then fire. It spread very quickly,” she said of survivors’ accounts.
“Everything happened in seconds,” she said, adding that those who made it off the ship had not even had time to put on lifejackets.
Myra Cabilan said she had flown to Coron to find her missing brother, 40-year-old Rammel Gonzaga, who had taken the ferry from Manila on a business trip with his brother-in-law.
“His wife had just given birth a month ago. He was so happy he was given a daughter,” Cabilan said, fighting back tears.
“At dawn, I still believed he survived. But he’s still missing. I have lost hope.”
Hundreds of people desperate for news about the incident have taken to leaving comments on the Facebook page of a local mayor, searching for relatives, friends and even a dog.
The ferry’s manifest listed 134 crew and passengers, but two had not boarded, according to the coast guard. The ferry was also carrying goods, an electric vehicle, a pickup truck, and motorcycles.
The archipelago nation of 116 million has a long history of disasters involving the inter-island ferries that ply its seas.
Many rely on cheap and poorly regulated boats and ships for transport between the country’s more than 7,000 islands, despite regular accidents.
On Thursday, the company that owns the M/V June Aster, Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc, said it was fully cooperating with the investigation.

Amid war and sanctions, many Iranians are losing their jobs and struggling to get by
ISTANBUL — Rasoul had a plan for the worst-case scenario. A 42-year-old engineer in Tehran with a steady job at a tech company, he often reassured his wife about their financial security. If times ever got truly tough, he would tell her, he could always drive for Snapp—Iran's local ride-sharing equivalent to Uber.
Then the war hit, and the worst-case scenario arrived.
Since the United States and Israel attacked Iran over six months ago, ordinary Iranians have borne the brunt of a collapsing economy. Inflation has skyrocketed, driving up the costs of gas, food, and rent. Livelihoods across the country are unraveling, forcing many to borrow just to survive and put major life milestones on hold.
While the official unemployment rate in Iran sits at 9%, independent analysts say the true figure is significantly higher. The desperation for work is palpable: Jobvision, a prominent Iranian job-seeking portal, reported a 50% spike in resume submissions in late April alone.
Even state-sanctioned labor leaders acknowledge the depth of the crisis. In May, Alireza Mahjoob, head of Iran's Workers House—the country's primary labor organization—admitted on state television that joblessness was far worse than anticipated.
"We don't know how much it will afflict our already fragile working class, leaving us all helpless and powerless," Mahjoob said.
Disrupted Networks and Shut Down Transit
For Rasoul, the decline was swift. In January, during a brutal government crackdown on protests, Iranian authorities severely restricted internet access to cut off communication with the outside world.
Because his company depended on worldwide networks that were cut off by the regime, the disruptions severely damaged his company's delivery services.
"The company's situation got really bad," Rasoul said. "They were losing customers one by one."
By mid-February, he was laid off, triggering a period of severe depression. Like all Iranians interviewed for this report, he spoke on the condition that his full name be withheld out of fear of government retribution.
Desperate to pay his bills, Rasoul reluctantly turned to his backup plan and began driving for Snapp at night.
"I remember being extremely anxious—accepting a ride, waiting, having the passenger get in, and so on," he recalled.
The strategy failed. The U.S. and Israel launched a war against Iran at the end of February, and ever-tighter US sanctions and a naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz led to rising fuel prices, and costly vehicle repairs quickly ate into his meager earnings. Ongoing U.S. airstrikes made navigating the streets at night far too dangerous. Eventually, he had to rely on extended family to stay afloat. Personal plans, including starting a family, have been completely shelved.
"I thought that after marriage I could keep working and traveling, going places together," Rasoul said. "But since we got married, nothing."
Other industries have faced complete collapse due to supply chain blockades and regional instability. Kayvan, a 42-year-old materials engineer from Tehran, helped a Chinese firm establish a business supplying raw materials to Iran's vital oil sector.
When fighting escalated, the maritime trade came to a halt.
"The environment became so unsafe," Kayvan said. "Transit routes and shipping routes were shut down, the Strait of Hormuz was closed, sea transport became impossible."
With clients unable to place orders, the business collapsed.
"It was like those American movies where people dump their belongings into a box and clear out their desk," Kayvan said about the day he had to leave his job.
"Passengers on a Train"
To survive the job loss, Kayvan's family relied entirely on his wife's income and rapidly dwindling personal savings—a cushion eroding fast against extreme economic headwinds.
"Terrifying inflation, unprecedented price hikes... we've genuinely never experienced days like these before," Kayvan said, adding that the conflict simply needs to stop. "We're all just falling apart."
For some, temporary relief has come, though it offers little peace of mind. In July, Rasoul managed to secure a new role as a sales manager. Yet with the conflict continuing and the broader economy in freefall, stability feels like an illusion.
"We're like passengers on a train," Rasoul said. "We don't know if the bridge ahead is broken or intact."

Brilliant Lowry surges clear as McIlroy struggles
- Published
Shane Lowry carded a course-record 62 to take control of the Irish Open as putting woes prevented defending champion Rory McIlroy from making a second-round charge at Doonbeg.
Irishman Lowry, who won his national title as an amateur in 2009, made six birdies in the space of seven holes on his front nine to surge clear in more favourable conditions after Thursday's heavy wind and rain.
Three more birdies - and a bogey on 13 - followed as the 39-year-old established a three-shot lead over China's Li Haotong and Denmark's Jacob Skov Olesen at Trump International Golf Links in County Clare on the west coast of the Republic of Ireland.
"It was real fun out there. I got off to a nice start and then I just kept going," said Lowry, who is playing his first tournament since failing to make the final two PGA Tour play-off events.
"I felt great out there. Just kept my foot on the gas and tried to keep hitting good shots and keep holing putts and it was a nice day."
With all parts of his game operating efficiently, Lowry started with two pars before reeling off a hat-trick of birdies from the third.
After a par on the sixth, the 2019 Open champion drained a 24-foot putt for a birdie two on the next and closed out his front nine with two more birdies to turn in six-under 30.
Lowry, who has not won an individual title in four years, scrambled for a par five at 10 when he hacked out of long rough before holing a 10-footer.
Birdies at 11 and 12 ignited hopes of a 59 at the par-70 venue before a sloppy bogey on 13 when he three-putted from 18 feet.
But the world number 53, who attracted large galleries around the spectacular links course, rolled in a 19-footer for birdie at 15 to return to -11 before finishing with three pars.
"I thought about it," Lowry, who has not returned a top-20 finish since February, said when asked if a sub-60 round entered his mind.
"Yeah, I did think about it until I three-putted 13. No, I did have a little laugh. Out in 30 and the back nine is only 34, so, yeah, you do kind of think about it a little bit."
He added: "I know I made a little mistake on 13, but I think I did a good job after that of playing the rest of the round really well and giving myself a couple of chances on the way in."
While Lowry prospered in more benign conditions, his good friend and Ryder Cup team-mate McIlroy failed to climb the leaderboard as he finished the day nine shots back.
Six-time major winner McIlroy, who is chasing a third Irish Open triumph, was even par for his round before a stunning fairway metal from 267 yards to two feet set up an eagle three at the eighth.
That moment of brilliance failed to ignite McIlroy's challenge, however, as he bogeyed the 11th and missed a series of birdie putts before sinking a 40-footer to pick up a shot at the 17th.
Northern Ireland's McIlroy looked set for a birdie-birdie finish after firing his approach at the final hole to four feet, but he took three putts to drop a shot and card a second consecutive 69.
"I just didn't have it on the greens. I really struggled to read them," said McIlroy.
He added: "It's been a tough one on the greens the last two days. But tee to green I've actually been pretty happy with how everything else is. I just need to try to hole a few more over the weekend."
MacIntyre and McKibbin well placed
With the late groups still to complete their rounds, Li and Olesen established themselves as Lowry's closest challengers.
Li, who finished tied fourth in last year's Open Championship at Royal Portrush, carded seven birdies, an eagle and two bogeys to shoot 63, while Olesen mixed seven birdies with a single bogey in a 64.
Northern Ireland's Tom McKibbin shaved a shot off his opening 68 to reach five under, a group which includes Scotland's Ewen Ferguson (66) and 2024 winner Rasmus Hojgaard (63).
Playing with McIlroy, Scotland's Robert MacIntyre bounced back from an opening 72 with a fine 65 to sit eight shots back alongside two-time winner Jon Rahm, who recorded four birdies in a 67.
Race to Dubai leader and 2018 Masters winner Patrick Reed is one shot better off on four under, but five-time major champion Brooks Koepka needed a birdie on 18 to shoot 66 and sneak inside the projected cut line on one over.

Iliman Ndiaye's journey to Manchester City has been something of a scenic route after he completed a move to Etihad Stadium from Everton in a deal worth up to £65m.
The deadline day move for the Senegal winger, 26, is worth £60m plus a further £5m in add-ons - a little over six years since he made his professional debut playing in the seventh tier of English football.
"I've worked my whole life for an opportunity like this," said Ndiaye, who has signed a five-year contract with the club.
"City are one of the best clubs in the world and I've seen them win everything as I've grown up. To be able to write my own chapter in a story that special is the chance of a lifetime and I'm determined to grab it with both hands."
Ndiaye had held talks with Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal earlier in the summer while Tottenham had agreed terms with Everton on Friday night for Ndiaye, when it looked as though Richarlison would move the other way in a separate transfer.
However, sources indicated Richarlison failed to agree personal terms with his former club and as a result, Spurs were unable to proceed with the Ndiaye transfer.
The move comes on the same day City agreed to pay a joint-British transfer record fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez.
The Argentian international is set to become City's eighth summer arrival with Enzo Maresca's side having also signed Elliot Anderson, Geronimo Rulli, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Allan Elias, Jeremy Monga and Pierce Charles.
Ndiaye's journey from non-league football to City
As a 19-year-old living in London, Ndiaye was in the youth ranks of Boreham Wood and playing Sunday league football when he was invited for a one-week trial with Sheffield United.
Two trial games were enough for the then-Premier League club to sign the talented teenager, although it would be another 18 months until he made an appearance for the Blades.
Instead, he spent the second half of the 2019-20 campaign on loan at Hyde United in the Northern Premier Division, six levels below the top division.
He made six appearances in his very first taste of professional football, often risking missing the last train back to Sheffield to stay out on the training pitch.
"It's not always been easy in my career," said Ndiaye.
"But I always had the belief that I could play for a team challenging for the biggest prizes and now I'm here."
After returning to Bramall Lane, Ndiaye made his Premier League debut in March 2021 against Leicester City but it would be another three-and-a-half years until he became established at the highest level following the Blades' relegation.
Two seasons in the Championship culminated in Ndiaye spearheading their return to the top flight in 2023 with 14 goals in 43 starts but he was then sold to Marseille that summer.
Ndiaye struggled during a season in France before joining Everton for an initial £16m fee in July 2024.
A firm fan favourite on Merseyside, "Skiliman" scored 15 goals and provided four assists in 67 Premier League games for the Toffees before his City move.
Is £65m a fair price for Ndiaye?
In a summer of highly-inflated transfer fees, value has become increasingly hard to determine.
On one hand, the Senegal international is a player of superlative skill, evasive, quick and wonderfully entertaining with the ball at his feet.
Ndiaye was responsible for 73 of Everton's 250 completed dribbles last season, the highest share of any Premier League player.
Everton fans may also point to recent moves in the Premier League involving City, such as the sale of Savio to Tottenham for an initial £75m, as further evidence that the club should have demanded more for Ndiaye.
On the other hand, Everton are effectively quadrupling the initial £16m they paid Marseille to sign Ndiaye two years ago for a player whose underlying numbers, at this stage at least, are not truly elite.
In the Premier League last season, Ndiaye only ranked joint third at Everton alone for goal contributions (nine), with Beto (10) and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall (12) providing more.
It is reasonable to assume that those numbers for Ndiaye will improve in a more attacking team at City but his general creativity is also middling as things stand.
He created 36 chances in total in the Premier League last season, ranking him only fourth at Everton. Toffees midfielder James Garner created 26 more. Jack Grealish, whose season ended in January because of injury, created eight more.
Grealish has effectively replaced Ndiaye at Everton following his loan move from Enzo Maresca's side.
Casting the net a little wider, 45 Premier League players have recorded more goal contributions than Ndiaye's 19 since he made his Everton debut two years ago.
As a 26-year-old set to be surrounded by better players, it would be no surprise should his numbers flourish at the Etihad.
But even in today's money, £65m for Ndiaye's current output may not be as questionable a deal as it sounds.

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.
Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.
Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.
The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.
Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”
The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”
Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.
Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.
Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

In Summary
- Apple’s new CEO John Ternus is expected to take centrestage on 9 September in Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event. This will be
- Ternus’ first appearance in an Apple event since he took over from Tim Cook.
- Apple is expected to launch new iPhones at the event, including the much-talked-about iPhone Ultra, its first foldable phone.
- As the event draws near, we write an open letter to Apple’s new CEO, requesting something that was once very much Apple – being different.
Dear John,
You will shortly be making your first public appearance as CEO at a major Apple event. Over the years, the iPhone launch pretty much sets out the tech agenda for the rest of the year. For the iPhone is not just a tech launch but a trend setter of sorts – it influences which colors, shapes, features, and functions matter in the industry in the coming days. About a decade ago, we would have laughed at the notion of a notch in any device. Until last year, orange was associated more with juice than tech. You get the idea.
Indeed, very few names have influenced our lives in the way in which Apple has over the past few decades. The brand made computers and touchscreen smartphones that were effortlessly easy to use, put thousands of songs in our pockets, created notebooks that could be carried in stationery envelopes, showed us that Bluetooth earbuds could exist without wires, added a third screen to many of our lives in the form of a tablet, got us looking at our watches for more than just the time, made us realize that there was “an app for that…”, and much more. It was seldom the first to come out with a particular product, but it often put a different spin on products, making them easier to use. It was the brand that thrived on its legendary motto, ‘Think Different’. Other brands could match Apple’s features and spec sheet, perhaps, but never the ‘feel’ or ‘vibe’ of an Apple product.
In recent times, however, this Apple feel or vibe has been getting increasingly diminished. Some would say that perhaps an “inspired” (read “copycat”) competition is closing the gap on the market leader. Perhaps. But then, it is not as if competition and “copy and paste” mode did not exist in the past. Remember how Steve Jobs went ballistic at Google for Android, claiming that it had been copied from Apple? “I’m going to destroy Android, because it’s a stolen product. I’m willing to go thermonuclear war on this,” Jobs raged when speaking of the topic, in Walter Isaacson’s biography. But even then, Apple’s products continued to be strikingly different. The competition could offer a similar appearance (camera units, straight sides, similar colors), but beneath that familiar surface, it was clear that they were just knockoffs.
That is no longer the case. Somewhere in its pursuit of market share over the past decade, Apple started losing its mystique, going from Hogwarts to Harvard. The brand’s sales volumes and capital value have shot up exponentially, but all this has come at a creative cost. Apple now seems more a part of the crowd rather than apart from it. Don’t get me wrong. Apple’s products are still very good, but while their pricing is more premium than ever, the products themselves are not as different as they used to be. In fact, in many cases, they do not even seem to be too different from their own predecessors.
The brand that championed “Think DIfferent” has been increasingly thinking similarly of late. From being among the first to popularise graphical UIs, capacitive touchscreens, app screens and face unlock systems, it has graduated to being last in line in the foldables and AI race. It might end up winning both of those contests even now, such is its market domination, but that would be a victory of volumes rather than delivered value, similar to how IBM ended up bossing the PC market in the early eighties even though it was a latecomer. IBM’s motto was incidentally “Think,” and is believed to have inspired Apple’s “Think Different.” Oh, the irony.
There has always been a large section of people who believed that most people who bought Apple products did so just to “show off the logo,” as products from other brands were just as good. For a while, this was a very unfair accusation, as in spite of their premium price tags (even more so in India, because of customs duties, we are told), Apple’s products seemed to be in a totally different league. Today, Apple still has the high ground in privacy and security and its face unlock remains unmatched, but in many other regards (yes, even in apps and interface), the brand seems content to swim in the mainstream, rather than walloping the competition from within its famous “walled garden.”
We are coming to the stage when a lot of people are actually buying Apple products for the logo on them rather than what they do. At one level, it tells us that the Apple brand has such equity that people are willing to invest large amounts in a product because it has an apple engraved on it. At another, it tells us that the products are now being defined by the brand rather than the other way around – a foldable phone is special because it comes from Apple, rather than Apple being special because it made a foldable phone.
Today, Apple is arguably the world’s greatest tech brand, but it has more money than mojo. For other brands, that would be just perfect. But since when was Apple just another brand? Mind you, money is a wonderful thing. After all, it enables one to do things and invest in ideas that don’t have a short-term payback. We did not say that; Steve Jobs did. Well, Apple has the money. Perhaps it is time for it to do things. Differently.
All this is easier said than done, of course. My colleague Akriti Rana recently wrote eloquently of how you now hold not just the reins of arguably the most high-profile tech company in the world, but also bear the burden of two massive, yet contrasting legacies. How you decide to honor them is your choice. You could choose to sail in a sea of successful sameness. Or maybe just spend more time in that walled garden.
Still, as someone whose first ever story in tech was about an Apple product (the iBook in 1999) and who confidently predicted that the first iPhone would fail (and was delighted to be proved wrong) in 2007, I have a request.
I am not asking for slimmer portfolios. Or lower price tags. I am asking for something much more basic – the experience of going to an event without having any idea of what will happen.
Of seeing a product without having seen it being leaked more often than a local municipal pipeline.
Of feeling a sense of wonder while using a product, because there is nothing else quite like it.
Of looking at the Apple logo and thinking of wizardry rather than wealth.
The universe is waiting, John Ternus. Go put a ding in it.
Regards,
Nimish Dubey

Ahead of the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, people shared a rumor claiming U.S. President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York said he wouldn't be allowed to speak at the museum's remembrance ceremony, adding that his administration was "looking into shutting them down permanently."
For example, on Sept. 1, a Facebook user shared (archived) an image showing the alleged Truth Social post:
(Irmawati via Facebook)
The purported Trump post read as follows:
"The National September 11 Memorial and Museum commission decided I'm not allowed to speak at the remembrance. Imagine that? A native new Yorker. The greatest president in history. We're looking into shutting them down permanently, remove the memorial and building a statue of me as tall as the World Trade Center. Not to brag or anything, but I single handedly saved 500 thousand people in those burning buildings. I ran 110 floors at least 50 times within 30 minutes pulling people out of tight spaces. I almost died." DJT
According to a reverse image search of the supposed Trump post screenshot, users primarily shared the image on Facebook. It also appeared on the 9GAG meme website.
Snopes readers emailed us to investigate the alleged screenshot's legitimacy, asking, for example, "I believe the fact that he won't attend is true, but is this X post for real?"
To investigate the rumor, we first checked Trump's Truth Social page and found no such post. We then searched on DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo for reports about the supposed post possibly being shared then deleted. If Trump had falsely posted he saved 500,000 people and mentioned plans of building a massive statue after removing the memorial and museum, journalists with reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or The New York Times, would have widely reported on it, and our search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence. We found no such articles.
While some Facebook commenters questioned whether the post was real, many others recognized the image as fabricated humor, specifically calling it "satire."
In sum, the purported Trump Truth Social post screenshot's fake nature and extremely outlandish, false claims, suggested the image originated as satire. We will update this article if we locate the origin of the image.
Trump reportedly not going to NY ceremony
The story spread in the days before the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people. Ahead of that anniversary, Trump and the White House disputed a New York Times report alleging he decided against attending the New York remembrance because he couldn't speak at the event. The reporting cited three anonymous sources "with knowledge of the events." We did not locate evidence that might conclusively confirm or debunk that claim.
A spokesperson for the 9/11 Memorial & Museum previously told Snopes that the organization has historically "intentionally worked to keep the commemoration free of politics because remembering those we lost on 9/11 should never be a partisan issue," and that politicians are not to deliver remarks and must "remain in a designated area."
In an authentic post on Aug. 28, Trump posted (archived) an attack on Times journalist Maggie Haberman, one of several reporters who worked on the Times' story, calling her "Maggot Hagerman" and writing, "I would love not to speak, because I'm speaking all the time, and this is a day to remember the victims, and their beautiful family members."
Trump's post also said he plans to attend the remembrance at the Pentagon.
Via email, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Snopes of Trump's plans:
As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001. On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans.
The White House also said Vice President JD Vance plans to travel to New York, as well as that all three 9/11 sites, including Shanksville, Pennsylvania, will be represented with administration officials in attendance.
For further reading, we previously reported about the claim Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wore nothing but underwear during a visit to the 9/11 memorial.
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work.

Houthis claim major advance in Yemen and tighten grip on Red Sea shipping lane
- Published
Yemen's Houthis have claimed a major advance on the western Red Sea coast, consolidating their grip on the key international shipping route.
The Iran-backed group seized Perim Island at the mouth of the waterway in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a source from Yemen's internationally-recognised government told the BBC.
It comes a day after the Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed pro-government forces, according to military sources. A Yemeni military official told the AFP news agency the Houthis now control the entire coastline.
The Houthis earlier said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated their threat to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis during their rapid advance, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News - the BBC's media partner in North America.
Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.
A senior Trump administration official later told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."
On Friday, Yemeni pro-government forces withdrew from Perim (also known as Mayyun).
Witnesses and news agencies reported that Houthi forces moved on to the island.
The Houthis later issued a statement, saying that their military operation to expel Saudi-backed forces had been a "success" and that "maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels".
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the "large-scale" military operation was launched on 3 September due to Saudi Arabia's "blatant aggression" against "our dear people".
Sarea also said the Houthis had expelled "Saudi enemy" forces from six districts in the Taiz and Hodeidah regions, claiming that hundreds of troops had been killed, wounded or captured.
The Houthi statement, however, did not mention Perim Island.
Saudi Arabia has not publicly commented on the latest developments.
Perim Island sits at the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which has become increasingly important following the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz - another crucial waterway - in the conflict between the US and Iran.
Saudi Arabia has been relying on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait for shipping oil to customers in Asia.
The escalation of the conflict between the Houthis, Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia has contributed to a surge in oil prices.
Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed and thousands displaced since the Houthis launched an offensive in the south-west a week ago.
A Saudi-led coalition has also carried out air strikes on Houthi-controlled areas in western Yemen in support of the pro-government forces, and the Houthis have launched missiles and drones at cities and oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia.
Since fighting escalated, at least 46,000 people have been displaced in Yemen, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
On Friday, the IOM said the number was "alarmingly rising by the hour".
Amy Pope, IOM director general, said: "Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left."
The Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government in 2015, triggering Saudi military intervention in the civil war.
The group currently control much of Yemen, including the capital Sanaa. A truce that had largely held for more than four years effectively collapsed in July.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy said on Friday (September 11, 2026) that it had shut down a major cross-country oil pipeline after it was attacked the day before. The statement did not specify who carried out the attacks and called the shutdown "a precautionary measure."
Built in the 1980s, the East-West pipeline has played a key role in Saudi Arabia's ability to continue exporting oil following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz during Iran's war with the U.S. and Israel.
The shutdown comes as Houthi rebels in Yemen have seized coastal territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, threatening Saudi oil exports through a key shipping lanes.
The Houthis’ biggest territorial gains in years, along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, could boost Iran’s strategy of driving up world oil and gas prices to pressure the United States.

Tobacco use is linked to infertility in women as well as poorer sperm quality and sexual function in men, according to the latest World Health Organisation (WHO) report, which further warned that second-hand smoke may also affect fertility. Women who quit smoking may have a 25% lower infertility risk than continuing smokers, it said.
The report highlighted evidence that tobacco use is associated with potentially lower chances of success for some fertility treatments. It said that evidence on newer products, including e-cigarettes, waterpipes, and smokeless tobacco, is still emerging, stating that while evidence is strongest for cigarette smoking, other tobacco and nicotine products may also pose risks to fertility and require further research.
Globally, one in six people of reproductive age will experience infertility at some point in their lifetime. Infertility is defined as the failure to achieve pregnancy after 12 months or more of regular unprotected sex.
40% rise in risk
The publication cites decades of evidence showing that smoking can harm women’s reproductive health. A systematic review of studies conducted between 2000 and 2026 found that women who currently smoke tobacco have a 40% higher risk of infertility compared to those who do not smoke.
The publication also notes that women who smoked tobacco in the past but are not currently smoking may have a 25% lower risk of infertility compared with women who continue to smoke, suggesting that quitting tobacco can make a meaningful difference.
The WHO stressed that infertility is not only a women’s health issue. "A recent review of 44 studies involving more than 60,000 men found that smoking was associated with reproductive dysfunction, including semen abnormalities and sexual dysfunction. The evidence indicated that men who smoke were more likely to have erectile dysfunction, ejaculation problems, and related issues such as absence of sperm in semen, poor sperm motility and abnormal sperm shape," it said.
Impact on treatments
For people using fertility treatment, tobacco smoking may reduce the chance of success. The publication cites earlier research from 21 studies, showing that cigarette smoking was linked to fewer live births and fewer pregnancies following assisted reproduction, such as in vitro fertilisation, with findings suggesting that the chances of successful outcomes may be roughly halved by cigarette smoking.
The WHO has recommended that healthcare providers inform individuals and couples planning a pregnancy about the reproductive risks of tobacco use and offer evidence-based support to help them quit. It also recommended that brief advice on quitting be consistently provided to all tobacco users in all healthcare settings.
